<a id="1-java-foundations-and-program-structure"></a>
## 1. Java Foundations and Program Structure

This chapter establishes the ground every later chapter stands on: what the
Java platform actually is, how source text becomes a running process, and the
core syntax for data, expressions, control flow, and the two aggregate types
you will touch daily — arrays and strings. None of this is object-oriented
design yet, but writing good classes is impossible without fluency here, and
most "mysterious" Java bugs trace back to a misunderstanding on one of these
pages.

<a id="11-the-java-platform"></a>
### 1.1 The Java Platform

Java is not just a language; it is a language plus a virtual machine plus a
standard library, and knowing which of the three you are talking about removes
most of the confusion beginners have about how Java runs.

#### History and Design Goals of Java

In 1991 a team at Sun Microsystems led by James Gosling started the Green
Project, aimed at software for consumer devices such as set-top boxes. The
constraint was brutal: the code had to run on a zoo of chips from different
manufacturers, and a crash in a living room appliance could not be patched
easily. C and C++ were the obvious tools, but both compile to one specific
processor, and both let a stray pointer corrupt memory silently.

The team's answer was to stop compiling to a real processor and start compiling
to an *imaginary* one, then write a small program for each real device that
pretends to be that imaginary processor. The language was first called Oak,
renamed Java, and released in 1995 just as the web created enormous demand for
code that could be shipped to unknown machines.

The original whitepaper listed a set of goals ("simple, object-oriented,
distributed, robust, secure, architecture-neutral, portable, high-performance,
multithreaded, dynamic"). Each one is a concrete decision, not marketing:

| Design goal          | Concrete mechanism in Java                              |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Simplicity           | No manual memory management, no pointer arithmetic, no multiple class inheritance, no operator overloading |
| Robustness           | Mandatory type checking, array bounds checks, null checks, exceptions |
| Security             | Bytecode verification, classloader isolation, no direct memory access |
| Architecture-neutral | Compile to bytecode for a virtual machine, not to native code |
| Portability          | Fixed sizes for primitive types, defined arithmetic semantics |
| High performance     | Just-In-Time compilation of hot code to native instructions |
| Multithreaded        | Threads, locks, and a memory model built into the language |

```text
1991  Green Project starts (Gosling, Sheridan, Naughton) -- language "Oak"
1995  Java 1.0 announced; applets make it famous on the early web
1998  Java 2 (J2SE/J2EE/J2ME split); collections framework arrives
2004  Java 5: generics, annotations, enums, enhanced for -- a huge language jump
2006  Java open-sourced as OpenJDK
2010  Oracle acquires Sun
2014  Java 8: lambdas and streams -- functional programming goes mainstream
2017  Java 9: modules; six-month release cadence begins
2018+ LTS releases: 11 (2018), 17 (2021), 21 (2023), 25 (2025)
```

Two consequences of this history still shape daily work. First, Java is
obsessive about *backward compatibility*: code compiled in 2005 generally still
runs today, which is why some awkward APIs were never removed. Second, since
2017 a new feature release ships every six months, with a Long-Term Support
(LTS) release roughly every two years; most companies target an LTS version
such as 17, 21, or 25 rather than the newest release.

> Key Takeaways
> - Java was designed for heterogeneous consumer hardware, which is why it
>   targets a virtual machine instead of a real CPU.
> - Safety features (no pointer arithmetic, bounds checks, garbage collection)
>   are deliberate trades of raw control for fewer catastrophic bugs.
> - Backward compatibility is a core value, so old code keeps running and old
>   APIs linger.
> - Since Java 9, releases ship every six months; production systems normally
>   sit on an LTS version.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For each of the seven design goals in the table, name one bug class it
>    prevents that a C program would be vulnerable to.
> 2. Find which Java version introduced `var`, records, and text blocks, then
>    decide the minimum version a project using all three must target.
> 3. Interview: Why did Java choose a virtual machine instead of compiling
>    directly to native code, and what does that cost at runtime? (Hint: think
>    about what has to happen the first time a method is executed.)

#### JDK, JRE, and JVM Distinctions

Beginners routinely install the wrong thing or misread an error message because
these three acronyms get used interchangeably. They are nested, and the
distinction is about *who needs what*.

- The **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine) is the engine that executes bytecode. It
  is a specification, and there are several implementations (HotSpot, OpenJ9,
  GraalVM). It knows nothing about `.java` files.
- The **JRE** (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the standard class
  library (`java.lang`, `java.util`, `java.io`, ...). This is the minimum to
  *run* an application.
- The **JDK** (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus development tools:
  `javac` the compiler, `javadoc`, `jar`, `jshell`, `jdb`, `javap`, and more.
  This is the minimum to *build* an application.

The car analogy is worth the cliché: the JVM is the engine, the JRE is the
complete drivable car, and the JDK is the car plus the workshop and tools you
need to build another one.

```text
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|  JDK  (develop + run)                                         |
|                                                               |
|   javac   javadoc   jar   jshell   javap   jdb   jlink ...    |
|                                                               |
|   +-------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |  JRE  (run only)                                      |   |
|   |                                                       |   |
|   |   Standard library: java.lang, java.util, java.io,    |   |
|   |                     java.net, java.time, ...          |   |
|   |                                                       |   |
|   |   +-----------------------------------------------+   |   |
|   |   |  JVM                                          |   |   |
|   |   |   class loader | bytecode verifier            |   |   |
|   |   |   interpreter  | JIT compiler | GC            |   |   |
|   |   +-----------------------------------------------+   |   |
|   +-------------------------------------------------------+   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
```

```bash
java -version     # reports the runtime version; present in both JRE and JDK
javac -version    # reports the compiler version; JDK only
jshell            # interactive REPL for experimenting; JDK only (Java 9+)

# The classic symptom of installing only a runtime:
$ javac Hello.java
javac: command not found
```

One modern wrinkle: since Java 11, Oracle and most vendors no longer ship a
standalone JRE. You install a JDK, and if you need a slimmed-down runtime for
deployment you build one yourself with `jlink`, which bundles only the modules
your application uses. In containerised deployments this is how images get
small.

| Component | Contains                      | Who needs it                 |
| --------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| JVM       | Execution engine only         | Nobody installs it alone     |
| JRE       | JVM + standard library        | End users running an app     |
| JDK       | JRE + compiler and tools      | Every developer              |

> Key Takeaways
> - JVM executes bytecode, JRE adds the standard library, JDK adds the tools.
> - `javac` lives in the JDK only; "command not found" almost always means a
>   runtime-only installation or a broken `PATH`.
> - The JVM is a specification with several competing implementations.
> - Standalone JREs are obsolete; use `jlink` to produce a minimal runtime.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run `java -version` and `javac -version` on your machine and confirm they
>    report the same version. If they differ, explain what that implies.
> 2. List which of these are JDK-only tools: `java`, `javac`, `jar`, `javap`,
>    `jshell`.
> 3. Interview: A colleague says "we only need the JRE on the production
>    server." Is that still good advice in a modern Java version? (Hint:
>    consider what vendors ship today and what `jlink` was created for.)

#### Bytecode and Platform Independence

A C compiler produces instructions for one processor family; move the binary to
a different architecture and it is meaningless. Java breaks that coupling by
compiling to *bytecode*: a compact instruction set for a machine that does not
physically exist. The only thing that must be ported to a new platform is the
JVM itself, and that work is done once by the JVM vendor rather than by every
application developer.

Bytecode lives in `.class` files. Each instruction is one byte of opcode plus
optional operands, and the machine model is a *stack machine*: operands are
pushed onto an operand stack and instructions consume them, rather than being
addressed in named registers.

```java
public class Add {
    public static int sum(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}
```

```text
$ javac Add.java
$ javap -c Add.class

public static int sum(int, int);
  Code:
     0: iload_0        // push local variable 0 (parameter a) onto the stack
     1: iload_1        // push local variable 1 (parameter b) onto the stack
     2: iadd           // pop two ints, add them, push the result
     3: ireturn        // pop the int result and return it
```

Note the `i` prefix on every opcode: bytecode is typed, and the verifier
rejects a class that tries to, for example, add two references. This is a
large part of why the JVM can run untrusted code safely.

```text
                       ONE compilation                MANY runtimes
   Hello.java  ---javac--->  Hello.class  ------+---> JVM on Linux/x64
   (source)                  (bytecode)         +---> JVM on macOS/ARM
                                                +---> JVM on Windows/x64
                                                +---> JVM on Linux/ARM (a Pi)
```

The slogan is "write once, run anywhere". The honest version, coined by
skeptics early on, is "write once, test everywhere": bytecode is portable, but
file path separators, default character encodings, locale-dependent formatting,
and thread scheduling can still differ between platforms. Portability of the
*instructions* is guaranteed; portability of *behaviour* still requires care.

> Key Takeaways
> - Bytecode targets an abstract stack machine, so one compilation runs on
>   every platform that has a JVM.
> - `.class` files are typed and verified before execution, which underpins
>   Java's security model.
> - `javap -c` disassembles bytecode and is the definitive way to answer "what
>   does this code actually compile to".
> - Portability covers instructions, not environment-dependent behaviour such
>   as encodings, paths, and locales.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compile a class with a `for` loop and run `javap -c` on it. Identify the
>    comparison and the backward jump that implement the loop.
> 2. Write two small methods, one adding `int` values and one adding `double`
>    values, and compare the opcodes.
> 3. Interview: If bytecode is portable, why do JDK downloads still list an
>    operating system and CPU architecture? (Hint: what exactly is being
>    downloaded?)

#### Compilation and Execution Workflow

Understanding the pipeline from text to execution explains most build errors
and a good deal of Java's performance behaviour.

The compiler `javac` performs syntax analysis, type checking, and a handful of
desugarings (enhanced `for` becomes an iterator loop, string concatenation
becomes builder or `invokedynamic` calls, generics are erased). It emits one
`.class` file per class, including nested and anonymous ones. Crucially,
`javac` does almost no optimisation; it leaves that to the runtime, which knows
things a static compiler cannot, such as which branches are actually taken.

At runtime, `java` starts the JVM, which:

1. **Loads** the requested class through a classloader, searching the
   classpath or module path.
2. **Links** it: verifies the bytecode is well-formed and type-safe, prepares
   static fields with default values, and resolves symbolic references.
3. **Initialises** it: runs static initialisers, on first active use.
4. **Executes** it, starting interpreted, while a profiler counts method
   invocations and loop iterations.
5. **Compiles hot code** with the JIT compiler into native instructions, and
   may recompile at a higher optimisation tier or *deoptimise* if a speculative
   assumption turns out to be wrong.

```text
  Hello.java
      |
      | javac        syntax check, type check, desugar
      v
  Hello.class  (bytecode + constant pool + metadata)
      |
      | java Hello   JVM starts
      v
  +-------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  class loader  ->  verifier  ->  prepare  ->  initialise     |
  |         |                                                    |
  |         v                                                    |
  |   interpreter  --- method gets "hot" ---> JIT (C1 then C2)   |
  |         |                                        |           |
  |         +----------- deoptimise if needed <------+           |
  |                                                              |
  |   garbage collector reclaims unreachable objects throughout  |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

```bash
javac Hello.java          # produces Hello.class in the current directory
java Hello                # note: the CLASS name, not the file name

javac -d out src/Hello.java   # write class files into out/
java -cp out Hello            # run with out/ on the classpath

java Hello.java           # Java 11+: compile in memory and run, single file
```

This is why a Java program is often slower for its first second and then
speeds up: the JIT has not yet compiled the hot paths. It is also why
microbenchmarks written naively are worthless, a point revisited when
performance is discussed in later chapters.

> Key Takeaways
> - `javac` type-checks and desugars but barely optimises; the JIT does the
>   real optimisation at runtime with profile data.
> - Class loading proceeds through load, verify, prepare, resolve, initialise,
>   and initialisation is lazy.
> - `java` takes a class name, not a file name, unless you use single-file
>   source mode.
> - Performance warms up over time, which makes naive benchmarks misleading.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compile a class into a separate `out` directory and run it using only
>    `-cp`. Then delete the `.class` file and observe the error.
> 2. Write a class whose `static` block prints a message, and demonstrate that
>    the message appears only when the class is first used.
> 3. Interview: A method runs 10x faster on its ten-thousandth call than on its
>    first. Explain why. (Hint: consider what the JVM is doing while it counts
>    invocations.)

#### Setting Up a Development Environment

A working setup needs three decisions: which JDK distribution, which version,
and which editor. All three are reversible, so do not overthink them.

**Distribution.** OpenJDK is the reference implementation, and several vendors
ship builds of it: Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Microsoft
Build of OpenJDK, and Oracle's own. For learning and for most production work
these are functionally interchangeable; Temurin is a safe default because it is
vendor-neutral and free for commercial use.

**Version.** Choose an LTS release unless you have a specific reason not to.
Java 17, 21, and 25 are all reasonable in 2026; this guide assumes 17 or later
and flags anything newer.

**Verification.** After installation, three checks:

```bash
java -version      # expect: openjdk version "21.0.x" or similar
javac -version     # expect: javac 21.0.x -- must match the runtime
echo $JAVA_HOME    # should point at the JDK root, not the bin directory
```

`JAVA_HOME` matters because build tools (Maven, Gradle) and IDEs read it to
find the JDK. On Unix-like systems it is set in a shell profile:

```bash
# ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc -- adjust the path to your installation
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/temurin-21-jdk
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"   # put the JDK's tools ahead of any others
```

If you juggle projects on different versions, a version manager such as SDKMAN!
(`sdk install java 21.0.2-tem`, `sdk use java 17.0.10-tem`) is far less painful
than editing paths by hand.

**Editor.** IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition, Eclipse, and VS Code with the Java
extension pack all work. An IDE is not cheating: it gives you real-time type
errors, refactoring, and a debugger, which accelerate learning considerably.
That said, compile and run from the command line at least a few times, because
an IDE hides exactly the pipeline described in the previous topic.

A conventional project layout, which build tools assume by default:

```text
my-project/
├── src/
│   └── main/
│       ├── java/          # production sources, mirroring package names
│       │   └── com/example/app/Main.java
│       └── resources/     # config files, bundled into the artifact
├── test/  or  src/test/java/   # test sources
├── out/   or  target/  or  build/   # compiled output (never committed)
└── pom.xml  or  build.gradle       # build definition
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Any OpenJDK build will do; Temurin is a good vendor-neutral default.
> - Prefer an LTS version (17, 21, or 25) for anything you intend to keep.
> - `JAVA_HOME` must point at the JDK root, and build tools depend on it.
> - Use an IDE for productivity, but compile from the command line at least
>   once so the toolchain is not a black box.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Install a JDK, then verify that `java`, `javac`, and `JAVA_HOME` all agree
>    on the same installation.
> 2. Create the directory layout above by hand, put a class in package
>    `com.example.app`, and compile it with `javac -d out` from the project
>    root.
> 3. Install a second JDK version and switch between them, confirming with
>    `java -version` each time.

#### Anatomy of a Minimal Java Program

Java's "hello world" is famously verbose, and every token in it exists for a
reason worth knowing early.

```java
package com.example.intro;          // 1. optional: namespace for this class

import java.time.LocalDate;         // 2. optional: shorten a type's name

/**                                  
 * The classic first program, with one extra line so it does something.
 */
public class Greeter {              // 3. class name must match Greeter.java

    public static void main(String[] args) {   // 4. the entry point
        String name = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "world";
        System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
        System.out.println("Today is " + LocalDate.now());
    }
}
```

Taking the numbered pieces in order:

1. **`package`** declares the namespace. If present it must be the first
   statement, and the directory structure must mirror it:
   `com/example/intro/Greeter.java`. Omitting it puts the class in the
   *default package*, which is fine for scratch work and discouraged in real
   projects because such classes cannot be imported from a named package.
2. **`import`** does not "include" code the way C's `#include` does. It only
   lets you write `LocalDate` instead of `java.time.LocalDate`. Everything in
   `java.lang` (including `String` and `System`) is imported implicitly.
3. **`public class Greeter`** declares the type. A source file may hold only
   one `public` top-level class, and its name must match the file name exactly,
   case included. This rule is what lets the compiler find a class by name.
4. **`public static void main(String[] args)`** is the entry point, recognised
   by exact signature. `public` so the launcher can call it, `static` so no
   instance is needed before the program starts, `void` because there is no
   return value (exit codes come from `System.exit`), and a `String[]`
   parameter for command-line arguments.

```text
Greeter.java
│
├── package declaration        at most one, first
├── import declarations        zero or more, next
└── type declarations          class / interface / enum / record
     │
     └── class Greeter
          ├── fields           state
          ├── constructors     initialisation
          └── methods          behaviour  ── main() is just a method
                                             with a special signature
```

```bash
$ javac -d out com/example/intro/Greeter.java
$ java -cp out com.example.intro.Greeter Ada
Hello, Ada!
Today is 2026-09-25
```

Note the fully qualified class name on the `java` command: once a class is in a
package, that package is part of its identity.

> Key Takeaways
> - Order within a file is fixed: `package`, then `import`, then type
>   declarations.
> - One public top-level class per file, named exactly like the file.
> - `import` is a naming convenience, not textual inclusion; `java.lang` is
>   imported automatically.
> - `main` is recognised by its exact signature, and a packaged class is run by
>   its fully qualified name.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Move `Greeter` into package `com.example.intro`, then compile and run it
>    from the project root using only `javac -d` and `java -cp`.
> 2. Rename the class without renaming the file and read the compiler error
>    carefully. Then do the reverse.
> 3. Interview: Why must `main` be `static`? (Hint: what would the JVM have to
>    do first if it were an instance method?)

<a id="12-syntax-fundamentals"></a>
### 1.2 Syntax Fundamentals

Before types and control flow come the mechanical rules of the language: what
you may name things, how to document them, where a name is visible, and how a
program talks to the outside world.

#### Identifiers, Keywords, and Naming Conventions

An *identifier* is any name you choose: classes, methods, variables, packages,
labels. The compiler enforces a small set of rules, and the community enforces
a much larger set of conventions. The compiler rules prevent code from
compiling; the conventions prevent code from being unreadable, which in a
long-lived codebase matters just as much.

**Compiler rules.** An identifier must start with a letter, `$`, or `_`, and
may then contain letters, digits, `$`, or `_`. It cannot be a keyword, and it
cannot be `true`, `false`, or `null` (these are literals, not keywords). Java
is case-sensitive and Unicode-aware, so `café` and `наименование` are legal.
By convention `$` is reserved for generated code, and a lone `_` has been
illegal as an identifier since Java 9.

```java
int count;          // fine
int _count;         // legal, but unconventional in Java
int $count;         // legal, reserved by convention for generated code
int 2ndPlace;       // ERROR: cannot start with a digit
int class;          // ERROR: reserved keyword
int my-count;       // ERROR: hyphen is the minus operator
int _;              // ERROR since Java 9: '_' alone is reserved
```

**Keywords.** Roughly fifty words are reserved. You do not need to memorise
the list; the IDE colours them and the compiler complains. Worth knowing is
that some are reserved but unused (`goto`, `const`), and that several recent
additions (`var`, `record`, `sealed`, `permits`, `yield`) are *contextual*
keywords: they are only special in certain positions, so existing code that
used them as variable names still compiles.

**Conventions.** These are near-universal in the Java ecosystem:

| Element            | Convention              | Example                       |
| ------------------ | ----------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Package            | all lowercase, dotted   | `com.example.billing`         |
| Class / interface  | UpperCamelCase, noun    | `InvoiceParser`, `Comparable` |
| Method             | lowerCamelCase, verb    | `calculateTotal()`            |
| Variable / field   | lowerCamelCase, noun    | `unitPrice`                   |
| Constant           | UPPER_SNAKE_CASE        | `MAX_RETRIES`                 |
| Type parameter     | single capital letter   | `T`, `E`, `K`, `V`            |
| Boolean accessor   | `is` / `has` prefix     | `isEmpty()`, `hasNext()`      |

```java
// Conventional and self-documenting
public class OrderProcessor {
    private static final int MAX_RETRY_COUNT = 3;
    private double totalAmount;
    public boolean isComplete() { ... }
}

// Legal, but every reader will resent it
public class order_processor {
    private static final int maxretrycount = 3;
    private double TotalAmount;
    public boolean complete_check() { ... }
}
```

Name length should scale with scope. A loop counter living for three lines can
be `i`; a field read across a 300-line class should say exactly what it holds.

> Key Takeaways
> - Identifiers may contain letters, digits, `$`, and `_`, but cannot start
>   with a digit or be a keyword.
> - `true`, `false`, and `null` are literals, not keywords, and are still
>   unusable as names.
> - Contextual keywords such as `var` and `record` are only reserved in
>   specific positions.
> - Conventions are not optional in practice: UpperCamelCase types,
>   lowerCamelCase members, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Classify each as legal or illegal and say why: `_value`, `2fast`,
>    `Value$`, `null`, `récord`, `my var`, `_`.
> 2. Rewrite this declaration set to follow conventions:
>    `class bank_account { int Balance; static final int maxwithdraw = 500;
>    void GetBalance() {} }`.
> 3. Interview: Why can `var` be used as a variable name even though it was
>    added to the language in Java 10? (Hint: think about what breaking that
>    rule would do to existing code.)

#### Comments and Javadoc Syntax

Java has three comment forms, and the third is a documentation language rather
than a comment in the usual sense.

```java
// Line comment: everything to the end of the line.

/*
   Block comment: spans lines. These do NOT nest, so a /* inside
   another block comment is a syntax error waiting to happen.
 */

/**
 * Javadoc comment: consumed by the javadoc tool to produce HTML API docs.
 * Attaches to the declaration immediately following it.
 */
```

The distinction that matters: line and block comments are stripped by the
compiler and exist only for readers of the source. Javadoc comments are
*extracted* into published documentation and are also displayed by IDEs on
hover, so they are read by people who never open your source file.

A well-formed Javadoc comment starts with a summary sentence, then optional
detail, then block tags:

```java
/**
 * Transfers funds between two accounts.
 *
 * <p>The transfer is atomic: either both balances change or neither does.
 * Both accounts must be open and denominated in the same currency.
 *
 * @param from   the account to debit; must not be {@code null}
 * @param to     the account to credit; must not be {@code null}
 * @param amount the positive amount to move, in minor units
 * @return the resulting transaction record
 * @throws InsufficientFundsException if {@code from} lacks the balance
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException   if {@code amount} is not positive
 * @see Account#getBalance()
 * @since 2.1
 */
public Transaction transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) { ... }
```

Common tags:

| Tag           | Purpose                                              |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `@param`      | One per parameter, in declaration order              |
| `@return`     | What the method yields; omit for `void`              |
| `@throws`     | Each exception and the condition that triggers it    |
| `@deprecated` | Why it is obsolete and what replaces it              |
| `@see`        | Cross-reference to a related element                 |
| `@since`      | Version in which the element appeared                |
| `{@code x}`   | Inline literal, escapes HTML and angle brackets      |
| `{@link T#m}` | Inline hyperlink to another element                  |

```bash
javadoc -d docs -private com/example/billing/*.java   # generate HTML docs
```

The first sentence is special: it becomes the summary in the method index, so
write it as a complete, standalone statement ending in a period.

A note on style. Comments that restate the code (`i++; // increment i`) are
noise that rots as soon as the code changes. Comments that explain *why*
(`// vendor API rejects batches over 500, see ticket OPS-4412`) are the ones
worth writing, because that reasoning appears nowhere else.

> Key Takeaways
> - Line and block comments are for source readers; Javadoc is extracted into
>   published API documentation.
> - Block comments do not nest.
> - The first Javadoc sentence is the summary and should stand alone.
> - Document *why*, not *what*; the code already states what.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a complete Javadoc comment for a method
>    `int indexOf(int[] array, int target)` that returns `-1` when absent.
> 2. Run `javadoc` on a small class and open the generated HTML. Find where
>    your summary sentence and `@param` text appear.
> 3. Take a method you have written and delete every comment that merely
>    restates the code. Note how many remain.

#### Statements, Blocks, and Scope

A *statement* is a single instruction terminated by a semicolon. A *block* is
a sequence of statements wrapped in braces, and it acts as one statement
wherever a statement is expected. That equivalence is why `if`, `for`, and
`while` can take either a single statement or a whole block.

*Scope* is the region of source in which a name is visible. In Java, scope is
lexical and follows the braces: a local variable is visible from its
declaration to the closing brace of the enclosing block, and not before.

```java
public class ScopeDemo {

    private int field = 1;          // class scope: visible to all methods

    public void demo(int parameter) {   // parameter scope: the whole method

        int local = 2;              // visible from here to the method's end

        {                           // a bare block is legal and creates scope
            int inner = 3;
            System.out.println(field + parameter + local + inner);  // all OK
        }
        // System.out.println(inner);   // ERROR: inner is out of scope

        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {   // i is scoped to the for statement
            int perIteration = i * 2;   // a fresh variable each iteration
        }
        // System.out.println(i);       // ERROR: i is out of scope

        if (parameter > 0) {
            int conditional = 4;
        }
        // System.out.println(conditional);  // ERROR: out of scope
    }
}
```

```text
class body ......................................  field
  │
  └── method body ..............................  parameter, local
        │
        ├── nested block ........................  inner
        ├── for statement .......................  i, perIteration
        └── if block ............................  conditional

Visibility flows INWARD only: an inner block sees outer names,
never the reverse.
```

Two rules trip people up:

**No shadowing of locals.** Unlike C, Java forbids declaring a local variable
with the same name as another local still in scope. You *can* shadow a field,
which is why constructors conventionally write `this.name = name`.

```java
int total = 0;
{
    // int total = 5;    // ERROR: total is already defined in this method
}

class Point {
    private int x;
    Point(int x) {       // parameter x SHADOWS field x -- this is allowed
        this.x = x;      // 'this.' disambiguates: field = parameter
    }
}
```

**Definite assignment.** A local variable has no default value. The compiler
proves that every read is preceded by a write on every possible path, and
rejects the code otherwise.

```java
int value;
if (someCondition) {
    value = 1;
}
System.out.println(value);   // ERROR: variable value might not be initialized
```

Keeping scopes tight is a real design technique, not pedantry: a variable
declared in the smallest block that needs it cannot be accidentally reused,
cannot hold a stale value, and tells the reader its lifetime at a glance.

> Key Takeaways
> - A block is a statement, which is why control structures accept either.
> - Local scope runs from declaration to the enclosing closing brace.
> - Locals cannot shadow other locals, but parameters may shadow fields, hence
>   `this.x = x`.
> - Locals have no default value; the compiler enforces definite assignment.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method with a nested block, then try to use the inner variable
>    outside it. Read the exact compiler error.
> 2. Write code that fails definite-assignment analysis, then fix it two ways:
>    by adding an `else`, and by initialising at declaration.
> 3. Interview: Why does Java allow a parameter to shadow a field but not a
>    local to shadow a local? (Hint: which of the two has an unambiguous way to
>    refer to the hidden name?)

#### The main Method Signature

The JVM needs one specific entry point, and it identifies it by an exact
signature rather than by a name alone. Get one token wrong and you get a
runtime error, not a compile error, because the class compiles perfectly well;
it simply cannot be launched.

```java
public static void main(String[] args) { }
```

| Token          | Why it must be there                                          |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `public`       | The launcher calls it from outside the class and its package  |
| `static`       | No instance exists yet; the JVM cannot construct one first    |
| `void`         | The process exit code comes from `System.exit`, not a return  |
| `main`         | The name the launcher looks for                               |
| `String[] args`| Command-line arguments; the parameter type is part of the match |

Permitted variations:

```java
public static void main(String... args) { }   // varargs compiles to String[]
static public void main(String[] args) { }    // modifier order is free
public static void main(String[] arguments) { }  // parameter name is free
public static final void main(String[] args) { } // extra modifiers allowed
```

Rejected variations and their symptoms:

```java
public void main(String[] args) { }        // not static
public static void main(String args) { }   // wrong parameter type
public static int main(String[] args) { }  // wrong return type
public static void Main(String[] args) { } // wrong name (Java is case-sensitive)
```

```text
$ java Broken
Error: Main method not found in class Broken, please define the main method as:
   public static void main(String[] args)
or a JavaFX application class must extend javafx.application.Application
```

A class may contain *other* methods named `main` with different signatures;
they are ordinary overloaded methods and the launcher ignores them. Likewise,
every class in a program may have a `main`, which is a common trick for giving
each class a small self-test; the launcher runs whichever class you name.

```java
public class Calculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {      // the entry point
        System.out.println(main(2, 3));           // calls the overload below
    }
    public static int main(int a, int b) {        // just a method named main
        return a + b;
    }
}
```

Since Java 21, preview features have explored simplified entry points for
beginners (instance `main` methods without `String[]`), but the classic
signature remains the one to know and the only one guaranteed everywhere.

> Key Takeaways
> - `main` is matched by exact signature: `public static void` with a
>   `String[]` parameter.
> - A wrong signature fails at launch time, not compile time.
> - Modifier order, parameter name, and varargs form are all flexible.
> - Multiple classes may each define `main`; the launcher runs the one named on
>   the command line.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Deliberately break `main` in four different ways and record the exact
>    error message each produces.
> 2. Write a class with both `main(String[])` and an overloaded
>    `main(int, int)`, and confirm which the launcher uses.
> 3. Interview: Can `main` be overloaded? Can it be `private`? Answer both and
>    explain the consequence. (Hint: compiling and launching are separate
>    events.)

#### Command-Line Arguments

`args` is an ordinary `String[]` holding the tokens typed after the class name.
Two details surprise newcomers: the array never contains the program name (as
`argv[0]` does in C), and it is never `null` — when no arguments are supplied
it is an empty array of length zero.

```java
public class ArgsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Count: " + args.length);
        for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) {
            System.out.println("  [" + i + "] = " + args[i]);
        }
    }
}
```

```text
$ java ArgsDemo alpha beta 42
Count: 3
  [0] = alpha
  [1] = beta
  [2] = 42

$ java ArgsDemo
Count: 0            <- empty array, NOT null

$ java ArgsDemo "two words" 'single quoted'
Count: 2            <- the SHELL groups quoted tokens, not Java
```

Everything arrives as text, so numeric arguments must be parsed explicitly, and
that parsing is the first place a real program meets bad input:

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    if (args.length < 1) {                      // always validate first
        System.err.println("Usage: java Squarer <number>");
        System.exit(1);                         // non-zero = failure
    }
    try {
        int n = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);      // String -> int, may throw
        System.out.println(n + " squared is " + n * n);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        System.err.println("Not an integer: " + args[0]);
        System.exit(2);
    }
}
```

Note `System.err` for diagnostics and `System.exit` with a non-zero code for
failure: these are the conventions other programs and shell scripts rely on
when they invoke yours.

Arguments passed to the JVM itself are distinct from arguments passed to your
program, and position decides which is which:

```text
java -Xmx512m -Denv=prod   MyApp   --verbose input.txt
     \___________________/  \___/  \__________________/
       JVM options and        |       your args array
       system properties   main class
```

For anything beyond two or three parameters, hand-rolled parsing becomes a
liability; real projects use a library such as picocli or Apache Commons CLI.

> Key Takeaways
> - `args` excludes the program name and is empty rather than `null` when no
>   arguments are given.
> - Argument splitting and quote handling are done by the shell, before Java
>   sees anything.
> - All arguments are strings; convert with `Integer.parseInt` and handle
>   `NumberFormatException`.
> - JVM options precede the class name; program arguments follow it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program that sums every argument as an integer and reports a clear
>    error naming the first token that is not numeric.
> 2. Demonstrate the difference between `java -Dkey=value App` and
>    `java App -Dkey=value` by printing both `System.getProperty("key")` and
>    `args`.
> 3. Write a program that accepts an optional `--upper` flag anywhere in the
>    arguments and applies it to the remaining words.

#### Console Input and Output Basics

`System.out`, `System.err`, and `System.in` are the three standard streams,
available without any import because `System` lives in `java.lang`.

**Output.** `println` appends a line separator, `print` does not, and `printf`
formats:

```java
System.out.print("no newline");
System.out.println("with newline");
System.out.printf("%s is %d years old and %.2f m tall%n", "Ada", 36, 1.7);
// %s string, %d integer, %f float, %.2f two decimals, %n platform newline
// %-10s left-aligns in 10 columns, %08.3f zero-pads to width 8
```

`System.err` writes to the error stream, which is unbuffered and separately
redirectable. Use it for diagnostics so that `program > output.txt` captures
results without swallowing error messages.

**Input.** `Scanner` is the usual starting point:

```java
import java.util.Scanner;

public class InputDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in)) {  // auto-closed
            System.out.print("Name: ");
            String name = scanner.nextLine();

            System.out.print("Age: ");
            int age = scanner.nextInt();      // reads the number, NOT the newline
            scanner.nextLine();               // consume the leftover newline

            System.out.print("City: ");
            String city = scanner.nextLine(); // now reads correctly

            System.out.printf("%s, %d, from %s%n", name, age, city);
        }
    }
}
```

The commented line is the single most common `Scanner` bug. `nextInt()` stops
at the end of the number and leaves the newline in the buffer, so the following
`nextLine()` returns an empty string unless you consume it.

| Method         | Reads                        | Leaves newline in buffer |
| -------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `nextLine()`   | Rest of the line             | No                       |
| `next()`       | One whitespace-delimited word| Yes                      |
| `nextInt()`    | One integer                  | Yes                      |
| `nextDouble()` | One floating-point number    | Yes                      |
| `hasNextInt()` | Nothing; tests the next token| n/a                      |

A robust read loop tests before it reads rather than catching exceptions:

```java
System.out.print("Enter an integer: ");
while (!scanner.hasNextInt()) {          // look before you leap
    System.out.print("Not an integer, try again: ");
    scanner.next();                      // discard the offending token
}
int value = scanner.nextInt();
```

For performance-sensitive input, `BufferedReader` is considerably faster than
`Scanner` because it does no tokenising or regex work; `Console` (from
`System.console()`) additionally supports reading passwords without echo, but
returns `null` when the process is not attached to a terminal, such as inside
an IDE.

> Key Takeaways
> - `System.out`, `System.err`, and `System.in` need no import.
> - `printf` uses `%n` for the platform line separator; `\n` is always a
>   line feed.
> - Mixing `nextInt()` and `nextLine()` requires consuming the leftover
>   newline.
> - Prefer `hasNextInt()` over catching exceptions; prefer `BufferedReader`
>   when input volume is large.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program that reads a name and an age and prints them, and make the
>    `nextInt`/`nextLine` bug appear, then fix it.
> 2. Write a menu loop that keeps prompting until the user enters a valid
>    integer between 1 and 5.
> 3. Use `printf` to print a three-column table of products, prices, and
>    quantities with the prices right-aligned to two decimal places.

<a id="13-primitive-types-and-variables"></a>
### 1.3 Primitive Types and Variables

Java is statically typed: every variable has a type fixed at compile time, and
the compiler rejects operations that type does not permit. This subchapter
covers the eight built-in types that are not objects, and the rules for
declaring, initialising, and converting them.

#### The Eight Primitive Types

Most values in Java are objects, accessed through references. Eight types are
the exception: they hold their value directly, have no methods, and cannot be
`null`. They exist for performance — an `int` is a machine word, not a
heap-allocated object with a header.

A defining Java decision is that these sizes are *fixed by the specification*,
not by the platform. In C, `int` might be 16, 32, or 64 bits; in Java it is
always exactly 32 bits with two's-complement semantics. That guarantee is a
precondition of portability.

| Type      | Size    | Range                                   | Default  | Literal example |
| --------- | ------- | --------------------------------------- | -------- | --------------- |
| `byte`    | 8 bit   | -128 to 127                             | `0`      | `(byte) 100`    |
| `short`   | 16 bit  | -32,768 to 32,767                       | `0`      | `(short) 1000`  |
| `int`     | 32 bit  | about -2.1e9 to 2.1e9                   | `0`      | `42`            |
| `long`    | 64 bit  | about -9.2e18 to 9.2e18                 | `0L`     | `42L`           |
| `float`   | 32 bit  | about 7 decimal digits of precision     | `0.0f`   | `3.14f`         |
| `double`  | 64 bit  | about 15 decimal digits of precision    | `0.0d`   | `3.14`          |
| `char`    | 16 bit  | 0 to 65,535 (unsigned, a UTF-16 unit)   | `'\u0000'`| `'A'`          |
| `boolean` | unspec. | `true` or `false`                       | `false`  | `true`          |

```java
byte    fileFlags   = 0b0010_1101;   // binary literal, underscores for reading
short   portOffset  = 8080;
int     population  = 1_400_000_000; // underscores are ignored by the compiler
long    nanoseconds = 9_000_000_000L; // L required: too big for int
float   ratio       = 0.75f;          // f required: 0.75 alone is a double
double  distance    = 1.496e11;       // scientific notation
char    grade       = 'A';            // single quotes; "A" is a String
boolean isActive    = true;           // no implicit int-to-boolean in Java
```

Four properties deserve emphasis.

**`char` is unsigned and 16 bits.** It stores one UTF-16 code unit, so
characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (many emoji, some CJK
extensions) need two `char` values. `char` participates in arithmetic:
`'A' + 1` is the `int` 66.

**`boolean` has no defined size** and no conversion to or from numbers. `if
(x = 5)` — the classic C bug — simply does not compile in Java unless `x` is a
`boolean`.

**Floating-point types are binary**, so values like `0.1` are not exactly
representable:

```java
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);        // 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3); // false
// For money, use long minor units (cents) or BigDecimal -- never double.
```

**Every primitive has a wrapper class** (`Integer`, `Double`, `Character`, ...)
for the times an object is required, such as inside collections. Conversion is
automatic in both directions ("autoboxing"), which is convenient and
occasionally expensive.

```java
int primitive = 42;
Integer boxed  = primitive;   // autoboxing:   int -> Integer
int unboxed    = boxed;       // unboxing:  Integer -> int
Integer maybe  = null;
int broken     = maybe;       // compiles, throws NullPointerException at runtime
```

```text
   PRIMITIVE                          REFERENCE (wrapper)
   int x = 42;                        Integer y = 42;

   stack                              stack            heap
   +--------+                         +--------+      +-------------+
   |  x  42 |  value lives here       |  y  ---+----> | Integer: 42 |
   +--------+                         +--------+      +-------------+
   no object, no null possible        may be null, has identity
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Eight primitives hold values directly, have no methods, and cannot be
>   `null`.
> - Sizes are fixed by the specification, which is what makes arithmetic
>   portable.
> - `char` is an unsigned 16-bit UTF-16 code unit and behaves numerically.
> - `boolean` does not convert to or from numbers.
> - Binary floating point cannot represent `0.1` exactly; use `BigDecimal` or
>   integer minor units for money.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` and explain the result in terms of
>    two's-complement wraparound.
> 2. Write a loop that prints the `char` and `int` value of every character
>    from `'a'` to `'z'`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` in Java, and what would you use for
>    a currency field? (Hint: think about representing one tenth in base two.)

#### Variable Declaration and Initialization

A declaration binds a name to a type; an initialisation gives it a first value.
Java distinguishes sharply between three kinds of variable, and the rules on
default values differ between them — a distinction that causes real confusion.

```java
public class VariableKinds {

    static int classVariable;      // static field: defaults to 0
    int instanceVariable;          // instance field: defaults to 0

    void method(int parameter) {   // parameter: always assigned by the caller
        int localVariable;         // local: NO default, must be assigned
        // System.out.println(localVariable);  // ERROR: might not be initialized
        localVariable = 5;         // now definitely assigned
        System.out.println(localVariable);
    }
}
```

**Fields are zero-initialised**: numeric types to `0`, `boolean` to `false`,
`char` to `'\u0000'`, and references to `null`. This is guaranteed by the JVM,
which wipes the memory for a new object before any code sees it.

**Locals are not.** The compiler performs *definite assignment analysis* and
refuses to compile a read that is not preceded by a write on every path. This
is deliberate: a silent default hides bugs, whereas an error at compile time
does not.

Declaration forms:

```java
int a;                       // declare only
int b = 10;                  // declare and initialise
int c = 1, d = 2, e = 3;     // multiple in one statement (legal, often unclear)
int f = 0, g = f + 1;        // later ones may use earlier ones
final int h = 100;           // cannot be reassigned after initialisation

int[] values = {1, 2, 3};    // array initialiser shorthand
```

Assignment is an *expression*, not merely a statement, so it produces a value.
That enables chaining and the read-and-test idiom:

```java
int x, y, z;
x = y = z = 0;               // assignment associates right to left

int line;
while ((line = reader.read()) != -1) {   // assign, then compare the result
    process(line);
}
```

Prefer declaring a variable at the point of first use rather than at the top of
a method. It shortens the variable's live range, makes the initialiser visible
next to the declaration, and often lets you mark it `final`.

```java
// Less good: declared far from use, briefly meaningless
String result;
// ... twenty lines ...
result = compute();

// Better: declaration and meaning arrive together
// ... twenty lines ...
String result = compute();
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Fields (static and instance) are zero-initialised automatically; locals are
>   not.
> - Definite assignment is enforced at compile time for locals.
> - Assignment is an expression whose value is the assigned value, enabling
>   `while ((x = next()) != -1)`.
> - Declare variables at first use to keep scope and lifetime minimal.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with an uninitialised `int` field and an uninitialised `int`
>    local, print the field, and try to print the local. Explain the difference
>    in outcome.
> 2. Predict the output of `int i = 0; i = i++ + ++i;` then verify it and work
>    through the evaluation order.
> 3. Rewrite a method that declares all its variables at the top so each is
>    declared at first use, marking as many `final` as possible.

#### Literals and Numeric Representations

A *literal* is a value written directly in source code. Java's rules about
literal types are the source of several confusing compile errors.

**The two default types.** An integer literal is an `int` unless suffixed with
`L`. A floating-point literal is a `double` unless suffixed with `f`. Both
defaults cause errors when they are wrong:

```java
long big = 3_000_000_000;      // ERROR: the literal is an int and overflows
long ok  = 3_000_000_000L;     // correct

float f1 = 3.14;               // ERROR: double cannot narrow to float silently
float f2 = 3.14f;              // correct

long millis = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;        // fine, fits in int
long micros = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000; // OVERFLOWS as int, then widens
long fixed  = 24L * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000; // one L makes the whole expression long
```

The last pair is a classic production bug: the multiplication happens in `int`
arithmetic and wraps around *before* the widening to `long` takes place.

**Radix prefixes.** The same number can be written in four bases:

```java
int decimal     = 255;
int hexadecimal = 0xFF;        // 0x or 0X
int octal       = 0377;        // leading zero -- a trap, see below
int binary      = 0b1111_1111; // 0b or 0B, since Java 7
// All four are the same value: 255
```

The leading-zero octal form is a hazard worth remembering: `int month = 08;`
fails to compile because `8` is not an octal digit, and `int code = 0123;` is
83, not 123.

**Underscores** may appear between digits, purely for legibility, and are
ignored by the compiler. They cannot start or end a literal or sit next to the
decimal point or a suffix.

```java
long cardNumber = 1234_5678_9012_3456L;   // legal and readable
double pi       = 3.141_592_653_589_793;
int bad1        = _100;      // ERROR: that is an identifier
int bad2        = 100_;      // ERROR: trailing underscore
double bad3     = 1._5;      // ERROR: adjacent to the decimal point
```

**Character and escape literals.** A `char` literal is a single character in
single quotes, or an escape sequence:

```java
char newline = '\n';    char tab    = '\t';
char quote   = '\'';    char slash  = '\\';
char unicode = 'é';   // é, by code point
char asInt   = 65;         // 'A' -- an int literal in char range is allowed
```

| Escape | Meaning         | Escape   | Meaning                 |
| ------ | --------------- | -------- | ----------------------- |
| `\n`   | Line feed       | `\'`     | Single quote            |
| `\t`   | Tab             | `\"`     | Double quote            |
| `\r`   | Carriage return | `\\`     | Backslash               |
| `\b`   | Backspace       | `\uXXXX` | Unicode by code point   |
| `\f`   | Form feed       | `\0`     | Null character          |

Unicode escapes are processed extremely early, before the source is tokenised,
so `\u000A` inside a line comment actually terminates the comment and can
produce baffling errors. It is a curiosity, but it explains one of Java's
stranger puzzle questions.

> Key Takeaways
> - Integer literals default to `int`, floating-point literals to `double`;
>   suffix with `L` and `f` when you need otherwise.
> - Arithmetic on `int` literals overflows before any widening assignment, so
>   promote early with `L`.
> - A leading `0` means octal; `0x` is hex and `0b` is binary.
> - Underscores improve readability and must sit strictly between digits.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Explain why `long ms = 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 365;` gives a wrong result,
>    and fix it with a single character change.
> 2. Write the value 1,000,000 as a decimal, hexadecimal, and binary literal,
>    each with underscores, and verify all three are equal.
> 3. Interview: What does `System.out.println(0123 + 1);` print, and why?
>    (Hint: look hard at the leading zero.)

#### Type Casting and Promotion

Converting between numeric types happens constantly, sometimes silently and
sometimes only when you demand it. The rule is simple: Java converts
automatically when no information can be lost, and requires an explicit cast
when it can.

**Widening (implicit).** Moving to a type with a larger range is safe and
automatic:

```text
byte -> short -> int -> long -> float -> double
                  ^
        char -----+
```

```java
int    i = 100;
long   l = i;        // widening, automatic
double d = l;        // widening, automatic
```

The two rightmost steps are safe in range but not in *precision*: `long` has 64
bits of integer precision while `float` has about 24 bits of mantissa, so large
values lose exactness:

```java
long  big     = 123_456_789_123L;
float asFloat = big;             // legal, but no longer exact
System.out.println((long) asFloat);  // 123456790528 -- silently different
```

**Narrowing (explicit).** Moving to a smaller type requires a cast, and the
cast is an assertion by you that the value fits. If it does not, the extra
high-order bits are simply discarded:

```java
int  large = 300;
byte small = (byte) large;   // 300 is 0b1_0010_1100; keeping 8 bits gives 44
System.out.println(small);   // 44 -- no warning, no exception

double pi = 3.99;
int    truncated = (int) pi; // 3 -- casting to an integer TRUNCATES toward zero
int    rounded   = (int) Math.round(pi);  // 4 -- round explicitly if you mean to
```

**Binary numeric promotion.** In any arithmetic expression, operands are first
promoted to a common type by these rules, applied in order: if either operand
is `double`, both become `double`; else if either is `float`, both become
`float`; else if either is `long`, both become `long`; otherwise both become
`int`. That last clause is the surprising one — `byte`, `short`, and `char`
are *always* promoted to `int` before arithmetic:

```java
byte a = 10, b = 20;
// byte sum = a + b;        // ERROR: a + b is an int, cannot narrow implicitly
byte sum = (byte) (a + b);  // explicit cast required
int  fine = a + b;          // or just accept the int

char c1 = 'A';
int  code = c1 + 1;         // 66
// char c2 = c1 + 1;        // ERROR: int cannot narrow to char implicitly
char c2 = (char) (c1 + 1);  // 'B'
```

Compound assignment operators contain a *hidden* cast, which is why this
compiles when the equivalent explicit form does not:

```java
byte counter = 10;
counter += 5;        // legal: expands to counter = (byte) (counter + 5)
// counter = counter + 5;   // ERROR: right side is int

byte overflow = 120;
overflow += 10;      // compiles, silently yields -126
```

**Integer division truncates**, which is a constant source of off-by-one and
zero results:

```java
int  half      = 7 / 2;            // 3, not 3.5
double wrong   = 7 / 2;            // 3.0 -- division happened in int first
double right   = 7 / 2.0;          // 3.5
double alsoOk  = (double) 7 / 2;   // 3.5
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Widening is implicit, narrowing requires an explicit cast that may silently
>   truncate.
> - `byte`, `short`, and `char` are promoted to `int` before any arithmetic.
> - Casting a floating-point value to an integer truncates toward zero; use
>   `Math.round` to round.
> - Compound assignment hides a narrowing cast, so it can overflow silently.
> - Integer division discards the remainder; promote one operand to get a
>   fractional result.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Predict then verify: `byte b = (byte) 130;`, `(int) -3.7`,
>    `(char) 97`, `5 / 2 * 2.0`.
> 2. Explain why `short s = 1; s += 1;` compiles but `short s = 1; s = s + 1;`
>    does not.
> 3. Write a method computing a percentage from two `int` counts that returns
>    the correct fractional `double`, and explain each cast you needed.

#### Constants with final

`final` means "assigned exactly once". Applied to a variable, it prevents
reassignment; it does not make the referenced object immutable, and conflating
those two ideas is the single most common misunderstanding of the keyword.

```java
final int maxAttempts = 3;
// maxAttempts = 4;              // ERROR: cannot assign a value to final variable

final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ada");                // FINE: the list object is mutable
// names = new ArrayList<>();    // ERROR: the reference cannot be repointed
```

```text
final reference, mutable object

  names ==FINAL==> +----------------------+
  (cannot be       |  ArrayList           |
   repointed)      |  ["Ada"]  <- can     |
                   |            still     |
                   |            change    |
                   +----------------------+
```

**Blank finals.** A `final` variable need not be initialised at its
declaration; it must simply be definitely assigned exactly once before use.
For fields, that means in every constructor or in an initialiser block.

```java
public class Circle {
    private final double radius;   // blank final field

    public Circle(double radius) {
        this.radius = radius;      // assigned exactly once, in the constructor
    }
}

final int limit;
if (isProduction) {
    limit = 1000;
} else {
    limit = 10;                    // every path assigns it exactly once: legal
}
```

**Constants.** The idiomatic named constant is `static final`, named in
UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. `static` because one copy suffices for the whole class, and
`final` because it must not change.

```java
public class Physics {
    public static final double SPEED_OF_LIGHT = 299_792_458.0;
    public static final int    MAX_RETRIES    = 3;

    // A mutable "constant" is a bug waiting to happen:
    public static final List<String> BAD  = new ArrayList<>();        // mutable!
    public static final List<String> GOOD = List.of("a", "b");        // immutable
}
```

A `static final` field of primitive or `String` type initialised with a
constant expression becomes a *compile-time constant*: the compiler inlines its
value at every use site. That has a real consequence — if a library changes
such a constant, dependent code must be recompiled, not merely relinked.

**Other uses of `final`** appear in later chapters: a `final` method cannot be
overridden, and a `final` class cannot be extended. A related rule matters for
lambdas: a local variable captured by a lambda or anonymous class must be
`final` or *effectively final*, meaning never reassigned after initialisation.

```java
int counter = 0;
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(counter);  // OK: effectively final
// counter++;    // adding this line breaks the lambda above
```

Marking locals and parameters `final` by default is a defensible style: it
documents intent and lets the compiler catch accidental reassignment. Many
teams skip it on locals as visual noise but apply it rigorously to fields.

> Key Takeaways
> - `final` prevents reassignment of the variable, not mutation of the object
>   it points to.
> - A blank final must be definitely assigned exactly once before use.
> - The constant idiom is `static final` in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, and the value
>   should itself be immutable.
> - Compile-time constants are inlined at use sites, so changing one requires
>   recompiling dependents.
> - Lambdas may only capture `final` or effectively final locals.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with a `final` array field, then demonstrate that you can
>    change its elements but not reassign the field.
> 2. Create a blank final field assigned differently in two constructors, and
>    then try to assign it twice in one constructor.
> 3. Interview: Is `final` the same as immutable? Give a concrete counterexample.
>    (Hint: consider a `final` field holding a `StringBuilder`.)

#### Local Variable Type Inference with var

Java 10 introduced `var`, which lets the compiler infer a local variable's type
from its initialiser. This is *not* dynamic typing: the variable still has one
fixed static type, decided at compile time and unchangeable afterwards. The
only thing that changed is that you no longer have to type it out.

```java
var message = "hello";            // inferred as String
var count   = 10;                 // inferred as int
var list    = new ArrayList<String>();  // inferred as ArrayList<String>

// message = 42;                  // ERROR: still a String, statically typed
```

The motivation is readability in cases where the type is long, obvious, or
both:

```java
// Before: the type is stated twice, and the line wraps
Map<String, List<CustomerOrder>> ordersByRegion = new HashMap<String, List<CustomerOrder>>();

// After: the information content is identical
var ordersByRegion = new HashMap<String, List<CustomerOrder>>();

// Especially clear in loops over a typed collection
for (var entry : ordersByRegion.entrySet()) {
    process(entry.getKey(), entry.getValue());
}
```

**Where `var` is not allowed.** Inference needs an initialiser and a local
context, so these all fail:

```java
var x;                       // ERROR: no initialiser, nothing to infer from
var y = null;                // ERROR: null has no useful type
var z = { 1, 2, 3 };         // ERROR: array initialiser needs a target type
// class Foo { var field = 1; }        // ERROR: fields cannot use var
// void m(var parameter) { }           // ERROR: parameters cannot use var
// var method() { return 1; }          // ERROR: return types cannot use var
```

`var` is restricted to local variables, indexes of enhanced `for` loops,
classic `for` loop variables, and resources in `try`-with-resources.

**When it helps and when it hurts.** The guideline used by the JDK team
themselves: `var` is appropriate when the reader can see the type immediately
from the right-hand side, and inappropriate when it hides information they
need.

| Use `var`                                    | Avoid `var`                              |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `var users = new ArrayList<User>();`         | `var result = service.process(input);`   |
| `var entry : map.entrySet()`                 | `var x = 0;` (int? long? double?)        |
| `var reader = new BufferedReader(...)`       | `var data = parse(raw);`                 |
| Long generic types repeated on both sides    | When the method name conveys no type     |

Two subtle behaviours worth knowing. Inference is on the *static* type of the
initialiser, so `var n = 0;` gives `int`, not `long` or `double`. And for
diamond initialisers, `var list = new ArrayList<>();` infers
`ArrayList<Object>`, which is almost never what you wanted:

```java
var oops = new ArrayList<>();      // ArrayList<Object> -- probably a mistake
oops.add("text");
// String s = oops.get(0);         // ERROR: element type is Object
var fine = new ArrayList<String>();  // be explicit on the right-hand side
```

`var` is also a contextual keyword rather than a reserved word, so legacy code
containing `int var = 5;` still compiles.

> Key Takeaways
> - `var` is compile-time inference, not dynamic typing; the type is fixed and
>   checked as usual.
> - It is limited to locals, loop variables, and try-with-resources; never
>   fields, parameters, or return types.
> - It requires an initialiser that is not `null` and not a bare array
>   initialiser.
> - Use it when the right-hand side makes the type obvious, and avoid it when
>   it hides a type the reader needs.
> - `var list = new ArrayList<>();` infers `ArrayList<Object>`; state the type
>   argument explicitly.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite five verbose declarations using `var`, then judge which two became
>    harder to read and revert them.
> 2. Try each illegal use listed above and record the compiler message.
> 3. Interview: Does `var` make Java dynamically typed? Justify the answer with
>    a code example that fails to compile. (Hint: try reassigning a different
>    type.)

<a id="14-operators-and-expressions"></a>
### 1.4 Operators and Expressions

Operators combine values into expressions, and every expression in Java has a
type and produces a value. The rules here are mostly familiar from C-family
languages, with a few Java-specific corrections that remove entire bug classes.

#### Arithmetic and Compound Assignment Operators

The five arithmetic operators are `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and `%`. Their subtleties
all come from the fact that they operate on fixed-width types.

```java
int a = 17, b = 5;
System.out.println(a + b);   // 22
System.out.println(a - b);   // 12
System.out.println(a * b);   // 85
System.out.println(a / b);   // 3   <- integer division truncates
System.out.println(a % b);   // 2   <- remainder
```

**Division and remainder with negatives.** Java truncates toward zero, so the
remainder takes the sign of the *dividend*. This differs from mathematical
modulo and bites when implementing circular indexing:

```java
System.out.println( 7 /  2);   //  3
System.out.println(-7 /  2);   // -3   (not -4; truncation, not floor)
System.out.println( 7 %  3);   //  1
System.out.println(-7 %  3);   // -1   (not 2)

// Safe "always positive" modulo:
int index = ((-7 % 3) + 3) % 3;          // 2
int alsoOk = Math.floorMod(-7, 3);       // 2 -- clearer, since Java 8
```

**Division by zero behaves differently for integers and floating point.**
Integer division by zero throws; floating point produces special values defined
by IEEE 754:

```java
// System.out.println(1 / 0);     // throws ArithmeticException: / by zero
System.out.println(1.0 / 0.0);    // Infinity
System.out.println(-1.0 / 0.0);   // -Infinity
System.out.println(0.0 / 0.0);    // NaN
System.out.println(Double.NaN == Double.NaN);      // false -- NaN is unequal to itself
System.out.println(Double.isNaN(0.0 / 0.0));       // true -- test this way
```

**Overflow is silent.** Integer arithmetic wraps around in two's complement
without any error:

```java
int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;      // 2_147_483_647
System.out.println(max + 1);      // -2147483648, silently wrapped

// When silent wraparound is unacceptable, ask for an exception:
System.out.println(Math.addExact(max, 1));   // throws ArithmeticException
```

**`+` is overloaded for strings.** If either operand is a `String`, `+` means
concatenation, and the other operand is converted to its string form. Because
`+` is left-associative, evaluation order changes the result:

```java
System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3");     // "33"  -- 1+2 first, then concatenation
System.out.println("1" + 2 + 3);     // "123" -- concatenation all the way
System.out.println('a' + 1);         // 98    -- char arithmetic, no String here
System.out.println("" + 'a' + 1);    // "a1"
```

**Increment and decrement.** `++` and `--` exist in prefix and postfix form.
Prefix updates then yields the new value; postfix yields the old value then
updates:

```java
int i = 5;
System.out.println(i++);   // prints 5, i becomes 6
System.out.println(++i);   // i becomes 7, prints 7

int j = 5;
int k = j++ + ++j;         // (5) + (7) = 12, j ends at 7
```

Expressions that modify the same variable twice are legal but unreadable; write
them out as separate statements in real code.

**Compound assignment.** `x += y` is equivalent to `x = (T) (x + y)` where `T`
is the type of `x` — note the implicit cast, discussed earlier, which makes
these compile where the expanded form would not.

| Operator | Equivalent to    | Operator | Equivalent to    |
| -------- | ---------------- | -------- | ---------------- |
| `x += y` | `x = (T)(x + y)` | `x /= y` | `x = (T)(x / y)` |
| `x -= y` | `x = (T)(x - y)` | `x %= y` | `x = (T)(x % y)` |
| `x *= y` | `x = (T)(x * y)` | `x <<= y`| `x = (T)(x << y)`|

> Key Takeaways
> - Integer division truncates toward zero, and `%` takes the sign of the
>   dividend; use `Math.floorMod` for a non-negative result.
> - Integer division by zero throws; floating-point division by zero yields
>   `Infinity` or `NaN`.
> - `NaN` is not equal to itself; test with `Double.isNaN`.
> - Integer overflow wraps silently; `Math.addExact` and friends throw instead.
> - `+` concatenates when either operand is a `String`, and left associativity
>   decides the outcome of mixed expressions.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method `boolean isEven(int n)` that works correctly for negative
>    inputs, and explain why `n % 2 == 1` fails.
> 2. Predict then verify: `"Result: " + 1 + 2`, `1 + 2 + " is the result"`,
>    `'A' + 'B'`, `"" + 'A' + 'B'`.
> 3. Interview: How would you detect that an `int` addition overflowed, without
>    using `Math.addExact`? (Hint: compare the signs of the operands and the
>    result.)

#### Relational and Equality Operators

Relational operators compare magnitudes and always produce a `boolean`. There
is no implicit conversion from number to truth value, so the C bug of writing
`=` instead of `==` inside a condition is a compile error in Java.

```java
int a = 5, b = 10;
System.out.println(a <  b);    // true
System.out.println(a <= b);    // true
System.out.println(a >  b);    // false
System.out.println(a >= b);    // false
System.out.println(a == b);    // false
System.out.println(a != b);    // true

// if (a = b) { }   // ERROR: int cannot be converted to boolean
```

The critical Java-specific rule concerns `==` on reference types. For
primitives, `==` compares values. For references, `==` compares *identities*:
whether both variables point at the same object. Content comparison is the job
of `equals`.

```java
String s1 = new String("hello");
String s2 = new String("hello");
System.out.println(s1 == s2);        // false -- two distinct objects
System.out.println(s1.equals(s2));   // true  -- same characters

String s3 = "hello";
String s4 = "hello";
System.out.println(s3 == s4);        // true -- both refer to the pooled literal
```

```text
  s1 ---> +-------------+        s3 ---+
          | String      |              |     +-------------+
          | "hello"     |              +---> | "hello"     |  (string pool)
          +-------------+              |     +-------------+
  s2 ---> +-------------+        s4 ---+
          | String      |
          | "hello"     |     s1 == s2 is false (different boxes)
          +-------------+     s3 == s4 is true  (same box)
```

That the pooled case happens to work is exactly what makes `==` on strings so
dangerous: code that tests fine with literals fails the moment a string arrives
from user input or a file.

The same trap exists for wrapper types, made worse by a caching optimisation.
The JVM caches `Integer` objects for values from -128 to 127, so small numbers
compare equal by identity and large ones do not:

```java
Integer x = 127, y = 127;
System.out.println(x == y);       // true  -- both from the cache

Integer p = 128, q = 128;
System.out.println(p == q);       // false -- outside the cache range
System.out.println(p.equals(q));  // true  -- always use equals
```

Comparison also has a floating-point caveat: never test computed `double`
values for exact equality, because representation error accumulates.

```java
double sum = 0.1 + 0.2;
System.out.println(sum == 0.3);                    // false
System.out.println(Math.abs(sum - 0.3) < 1e-9);    // true -- compare within a tolerance
```

Finally, `==` on references of unrelated types is a compile error, which
catches some mistakes early:

```java
String text = "5";
Integer number = 5;
// System.out.println(text == number);  // ERROR: incomparable types
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Relational operators yield `boolean`, and numbers never convert to
>   booleans, so `if (x = 5)` will not compile.
> - `==` compares values for primitives and identities for references.
> - Use `equals` for content comparison; string literals share a pooled
>   instance, which makes `==` deceptively work.
> - Wrapper caching makes `Integer` `==` true for -128..127 and false beyond.
> - Compare floating-point values with a tolerance, not `==`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program demonstrating all four string comparison cases: pooled
>    literals, `new String`, `intern()`, and `equals`.
> 2. Show the `Integer` cache boundary by comparing 127 and 128 with `==`.
> 3. Interview: Two `String` variables print the same text but `==` is false.
>    Explain how that happens and how you would compare them. (Hint: where did
>    each string come from?)

#### Logical and Short-Circuit Operators

Java offers two families of boolean operators. `&&` and `||` are
*short-circuiting*: they evaluate the right operand only when the result is
still undetermined. `&` and `|` always evaluate both operands.

```java
boolean t = true, f = false;

System.out.println(t && f);   // false -- AND
System.out.println(t || f);   // true  -- OR
System.out.println(!t);       // false -- NOT
System.out.println(t ^ f);    // true  -- XOR: exactly one is true
```

| a     | b     | `a && b` | `a \|\| b` | `a ^ b` | `!a`  |
| ----- | ----- | -------- | ---------- | ------- | ----- |
| true  | true  | true     | true       | false   | false |
| true  | false | false    | true       | true    | false |
| false | true  | false    | true       | true    | true  |
| false | false | false    | false      | false   | true  |

Short-circuiting is not merely an optimisation; it is a correctness tool. The
guard idiom below is ubiquitous, and it only works because `&&` stops early:

```java
String name = null;

if (name != null && name.length() > 3) {   // safe: length() never runs on null
    System.out.println(name);
}

if (name != null & name.length() > 3) {    // NullPointerException: & evaluates both
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

The same pattern with `||` short-circuits on the first `true`:

```java
if (list == null || list.isEmpty()) {      // safe
    return "nothing to do";
}
```

```text
   a && b                          a || b

   evaluate a                      evaluate a
       |                               |
   a == false? --yes--> false      a == true? --yes--> true
       |                               |
       no                              no
       |                               |
   evaluate b, result is b         evaluate b, result is b
```

The non-short-circuiting forms have two legitimate uses. First, when the right
operand has a side effect you always want:

```java
// Both validators run, so the user sees every error, not just the first
boolean valid = validateName(form) & validateEmail(form);
```

Second, `&`, `|`, and `^` double as bitwise operators on integer types, covered
next. On booleans they are logical; on integers they are bitwise.

Java has no `^^` operator, because XOR cannot short-circuit: both operands are
always needed to know the answer.

De Morgan's laws are worth internalising for simplifying conditions:

```java
!(a && b)  is equivalent to  !a || !b
!(a || b)  is equivalent to  !a && !b

// Applied: this
if (!(age >= 18 && hasLicence)) { deny(); }
// reads better as
if (age < 18 || !hasLicence) { deny(); }
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `&&` and `||` short-circuit; `&` and `|` always evaluate both operands.
> - Null-guard idioms depend on short-circuiting for correctness, not speed.
> - `&`, `|`, `^` are logical on booleans and bitwise on integers.
> - There is no `^^`, because exclusive-or can never be decided from one
>   operand.
> - De Morgan's laws let you push negations inward and simplify conditions.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method with a side effect that prints, then use it on both sides
>    of `&&` and `&` to observe which calls happen.
> 2. Rewrite `!(x > 0 && y > 0)` and `!(a == b || c == d)` using De Morgan's
>    laws.
> 3. Write a safe check that a string is non-null, non-empty, and starts with a
>    digit, in a single condition.

#### Bitwise and Shift Operators

Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integer types. They matter for
flags packed into one value, low-level protocols, hashing, and performance-
sensitive code — and they appear regularly in interviews.

| Operator | Name                   | Effect                                      |
| -------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `&`      | AND                    | 1 only where both bits are 1                |
| `\|`     | OR                     | 1 where either bit is 1                     |
