**Abstraction** — exposing what something does while hiding how it does it. A
caller of `list.add(x)` does not know or care whether an array is being resized
underneath. Encapsulation is the mechanism; abstraction is the resulting
simplification for the caller.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();   // the interface is the abstraction
names.add("Ada");                         // the resizing algorithm is hidden
```

**Inheritance** — defining a new class in terms of an existing one, reusing its
fields and methods. Covered in chapter 3.

```java
class Animal {
    void breathe() { System.out.println("breathing"); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {          // Dog gains breathe() automatically
    void bark() { System.out.println("woof"); }
}
```

**Polymorphism** — one reference type serving many concrete types, with the
actual method chosen at runtime. Also chapter 3.

```java
Animal pet = new Dog();     // a Dog referred to through an Animal variable
pet.breathe();              // works; the runtime picks Dog's version if overridden
```

```text
   ENCAPSULATION            ABSTRACTION
   +--------------+         "add an element"     <- what the caller sees
   | private data |                 |
   |   guarded by |                 v
   | public methods|        [ resize array, shift, insert ]  <- hidden how
   +--------------+

   INHERITANCE              POLYMORPHISM
        Animal                  Animal ref ---> could be Dog, Cat, or Bird
        /    \                             |
      Dog    Cat                  call speak(); the object decides which runs
```

| Pillar        | Question it answers                     | Primary Java mechanism        |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Encapsulation | Who is allowed to change this?          | `private` fields, accessors   |
| Abstraction   | What do I need to know to use this?     | Interfaces, abstract classes  |
| Inheritance   | What can I reuse from an existing type? | `extends`                     |
| Polymorphism  | Which implementation runs?              | Overriding, dynamic dispatch  |

The pillars are frequently recited without being understood, so it is worth
stating what each actually buys you. Encapsulation limits the blast radius of a
bug. Abstraction limits how much a caller must learn. Inheritance limits
duplication. Polymorphism limits the number of places that must change when a
new case appears. All four are about *limiting* something, which is why they
matter most in large systems and can feel like bureaucracy in small ones.

A common exam distinction: encapsulation and abstraction are related but not
identical. Encapsulation is about *access* (keeping data private); abstraction
is about *complexity* (keeping details irrelevant). A class can be encapsulated
but a poor abstraction if its public methods expose implementation concepts.

> Key Takeaways
> - The four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and
>   polymorphism.
> - Encapsulation restricts access; abstraction hides complexity; they are
>   related but distinct.
> - Inheritance reuses an existing type; polymorphism selects behaviour at
>   runtime.
> - Each pillar exists to limit something: blast radius, required knowledge,
>   duplication, or change sites.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a `BankAccount` class, name one concrete way each of the four pillars
>    could apply.
> 2. Give an example of a class that is well encapsulated but is nevertheless a
>    leaky abstraction.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation?
>    (Hint: one is about permission, the other about relevance.)

#### Identifying Classes from Requirements

Knowing the syntax does not tell you *which* classes to write. A practical
starting technique, useful in interviews and in real design sessions, is noun
and verb analysis: nouns in the requirements suggest candidate classes and
fields, verbs suggest methods.

Take a requirement statement:

> A library lends books to members. Each book has a title, an author, and an
> ISBN. A member can borrow up to five books at a time. A loan records which
> member borrowed which book and when it is due. Overdue loans incur a fine of
> 20 cents per day.

Extracting the nouns and classifying them:

| Noun     | Candidate  | Decision                                            |
| -------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Library  | Class      | Yes — it coordinates lending                        |
| Book     | Class      | Yes — has its own identity and attributes           |
| Member   | Class      | Yes — has identity and a borrowing limit            |
| Loan     | Class      | Yes — connects member and book, has its own data    |
| Title    | Field      | No — an attribute of `Book`, a `String`             |
| Author   | Field?     | Maybe — a class if authors need their own data      |
| ISBN     | Field      | Attribute of `Book`, though a value type is arguable |
| Fine     | Computed   | Not a class — derived from a `Loan` and a date      |
| Due date | Field      | Attribute of `Loan`, a `LocalDate`                  |

Verbs map to behaviour, and the important question is *which class owns each
verb*:

| Verb            | Belongs to | Reasoning                              |
| --------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------- |
| lends / borrows | `Library`  | It knows about both members and books  |
| is overdue      | `Loan`     | It owns the due date                   |
| calculates fine | `Loan`     | Derived from its own data              |
| has capacity    | `Member`   | The five-book limit is a member rule   |

```java
public class Book {
    private final String isbn;        // identity: an ISBN identifies a book
    private final String title;
    private final String author;
    private boolean available = true;
    // constructor, accessors
}

public class Member {
    private final String memberId;
    private final String name;
    private final List<Loan> activeLoans = new ArrayList<>();

    public boolean canBorrow() {                  // the rule lives with the data
        return activeLoans.size() < MAX_LOANS;
    }
    private static final int MAX_LOANS = 5;
}

public class Loan {
    private final Book book;
    private final Member member;
    private final LocalDate dueDate;

    public boolean isOverdue(LocalDate today) {
        return today.isAfter(dueDate);            // Loan owns its own due date
    }

    public long fineInCents(LocalDate today) {
        if (!isOverdue(today)) return 0;
        long daysLate = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(dueDate, today);
        return daysLate * FINE_PER_DAY_CENTS;     // money in minor units, not double
    }
    private static final long FINE_PER_DAY_CENTS = 20;
}

public class Library {
    private final Map<String, Book> catalogue = new HashMap<>();

    public Loan lend(Member member, String isbn, LocalDate today) {
        if (!member.canBorrow()) {                // delegate the rule to Member
            throw new IllegalStateException("Borrowing limit reached");
        }
        Book book = catalogue.get(isbn);
        // ... availability checks, create and return the Loan
    }
}
```

Four heuristics make this analysis more reliable than mechanical noun-hunting:

1. **A class should have one reason to change.** If a class would change both
   when tax rules change and when the database changes, it is probably two
   classes.
2. **Behaviour belongs with the data it uses.** A method that reads only
   `Loan`'s fields belongs on `Loan`, not on a `LoanService`. Pulling data out
   of an object to compute something elsewhere is the "anemic domain model"
   smell.
3. **Not every noun is a class.** Attributes, computed values, and transient
   concepts are not. Creating a class per noun produces bloat.
4. **Watch for missing nouns.** `Loan` does not appear as a highlighted noun in
   some phrasings, yet it is essential. Relationships with their own data
   almost always deserve a class.

> Key Takeaways
> - Nouns suggest classes and fields; verbs suggest methods, and the key
>   question is which class owns each verb.
> - Put behaviour on the class that owns the data it needs.
> - Not every noun becomes a class; attributes and derived values do not.
> - Relationships that carry their own data, such as a loan, usually deserve
>   their own class.
> - A class with two unrelated reasons to change should be split.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Perform noun and verb analysis on: "A cinema shows films in screens.
>    Customers book seats for a showing. A booking can be cancelled up to one
>    hour before the start."
> 2. Take the library example and decide whether `Author` should be a class,
>    justifying the answer from the requirements.
> 3. Interview: You are given a `Loan` class and a `LoanService` that computes
>    fines by reading the loan's getters. What is the design problem, and how
>    would you fix it? (Hint: which object owns the due date?)

<a id="22-defining-classes"></a>
### 2.2 Defining Classes

With the motivation established, this section covers the mechanics: how to
declare a class, what its members look like, and what actually happens in memory
when you create an instance.

#### Class Declaration Syntax

A class declaration names a type and lists its members. The full form has more
parts than a beginner needs, so it helps to see the skeleton first and then the
options.

```java
public class Rectangle {          // modifier, keyword, name
    // fields, constructors, methods, nested types go here
}
```

The general shape, with optional parts in brackets:

```text
[modifiers] class ClassName [extends Superclass] [implements Interface, ...] {
    [fields]
    [constructors]
    [methods]
    [nested types]
    [initializer blocks]
}
```

A complete example using most of the available slots:

```java
package com.example.geometry;      // must be first, at most one

import java.util.Objects;          // imports come next

public class Rectangle {           // 'public' -> visible everywhere

    private static int instanceCount;     // static field: one per class
    private final double width;           // instance field, immutable
    private final double height;

    public Rectangle(double width, double height) {    // constructor
        if (width <= 0 || height <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Dimensions must be positive");
        }
        this.width = width;
        this.height = height;
        instanceCount++;
    }

    public double area() {                 // instance method
        return width * height;
    }

    public static int getInstanceCount() { // static method
        return instanceCount;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {             // overriding an inherited method
        return "Rectangle(" + width + " x " + height + ")";
    }

    private static class Corner { }        // nested type
}
```

**Class modifiers** that may appear on a top-level class:

| Modifier   | Effect                                                       |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `public`   | Visible from any package; requires a matching file name       |
| (none)     | Package-private: visible only within its own package          |
| `final`    | Cannot be extended                                            |
| `abstract` | Cannot be instantiated; may contain abstract methods          |
| `sealed`   | Only the listed classes may extend it (Java 17+)              |
| `strictfp` | Legacy floating-point rule; obsolete since Java 17            |

`private` and `protected` are not permitted on a top-level class, because there
would be no scope in which they meant anything. They are legal on *nested*
classes.

**File rules**, which trip up beginners more than the modifiers do:

```java
// File: Rectangle.java
public class Rectangle { }      // OK: public class matches the file name
class Helper { }                // OK: package-private classes may share the file
// public class Other { }       // ERROR: a second public class in one file
```

A source file may contain at most one `public` top-level class, and its name
must match the file name exactly including case. Other top-level classes in the
same file must be package-private. In practice, one class per file is the
convention regardless.

**Member ordering** is not enforced by the compiler but is strongly
conventional, and reviewers will expect it:

```text
1. static fields        (constants first)
2. instance fields
3. constructors
4. static factory methods
5. instance methods      (public before private, or grouped by purpose)
6. nested types
```

Unlike C or C++, Java has no separate declaration and definition: there are no
header files, and a member may be used before it is declared in the file,
because the compiler reads the whole class before resolving references.

```java
public class Order {
    public double total() {
        return computeSubtotal() + tax;    // both declared BELOW; this is fine
    }
    private double tax = 5.0;
    private double computeSubtotal() { return 100.0; }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A class declaration is `[modifiers] class Name [extends] [implements] { members }`.
> - At most one `public` top-level class per file, named exactly like the file.
> - `private` and `protected` are illegal on top-level classes but legal on
>   nested ones.
> - Member order is conventional, not enforced; follow the standard ordering
>   for readability.
> - Java has no headers and no forward declarations; members may be used before
>   they appear.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a `Temperature` class in package `com.example.weather` with a
>    private field, a constructor, and one method, and compile it from the
>    command line.
> 2. Put two classes in one file, one public and one package-private, then add
>    a second public class and read the error.
> 3. Reorder a class's members to follow the conventional ordering and note
>    whether readability improved.

#### Instance Fields and Default Values

Instance fields hold the state that makes each object distinct. Every object
created from a class receives its own complete set of them, allocated on the
heap when the object is constructed.

```java
public class Employee {
    private String name;        // reference field -> defaults to null
    private int age;            // numeric field   -> defaults to 0
    private double salary;      //                 -> defaults to 0.0
    private boolean active;     //                 -> defaults to false
    private char grade;         //                 -> defaults to '\u0000'
    private int[] scores;       // array reference -> defaults to null
}
```

Unlike local variables, fields are **automatically initialised** to a defined
default before any constructor runs. The JVM guarantees this by zeroing the
memory it allocates for the object, which means a field is never garbage.

| Field type              | Default value |
| ----------------------- | ------------- |
| `byte`, `short`, `int`  | `0`           |
| `long`                  | `0L`          |
| `float`                 | `0.0f`        |
| `double`                | `0.0d`        |
| `char`                  | `'\u0000'`    |
| `boolean`               | `false`       |
| Any reference type      | `null`        |

```java
Employee e = new Employee();
System.out.println(e.getAge());      // 0    -- not an error, not garbage
System.out.println(e.getName());     // null -- the field exists, points nowhere
// System.out.println(e.getName().length());   // NullPointerException
```

The `null` default is where most beginner bugs originate. A reference field is
initialised to "points at nothing", so any method call on it fails until it is
assigned. Three common remedies:

```java
public class Employee {
    private String name = "Unknown";                 // 1. field initialiser
    private List<String> skills = new ArrayList<>(); // 2. never-null collection

    public Employee(String name) {                   // 3. require it at construction
        this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name must not be null");
    }
}
```

Initialising collection fields at declaration is a particularly valuable habit:
a method that returns an empty list is far easier for callers than one that
returns `null`.

**Field initialisers run in declaration order**, before the constructor body,
and may call methods or reference earlier fields:

```java
public class Config {
    private int base = 10;
    private int doubled = base * 2;      // 20 -- 'base' is already assigned
    // private int broken = later + 1;   // ERROR: illegal forward reference
    private int later = 5;
}
```

**Fields versus local variables**, a comparison worth memorising:

| Aspect            | Instance field                  | Local variable                 |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Declared in       | Class body                      | Method, constructor, or block  |
| Default value     | Yes, zero-equivalent            | None; must be assigned         |
| Lifetime          | As long as the object lives     | Until the block exits          |
| Memory location   | Heap, inside the object         | Stack frame                    |
| Access modifiers  | Allowed                         | Not allowed                    |
| Scope             | The whole class                 | The enclosing block            |

A final note on design: the number of instance fields is a rough measure of a
class's complexity. A class with fifteen fields is usually several classes that
have not been separated yet, because most methods will touch only a subset of
them.

> Key Takeaways
> - Every object gets its own copy of each instance field.
> - Fields are zero-initialised automatically; locals are not.
> - Reference fields default to `null`, which is the origin of most beginner
>   `NullPointerException`s.
> - Initialise collection fields at declaration so they are never `null`.
> - Field initialisers run in declaration order and cannot reference fields
>   declared later.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with one field of each primitive type plus a `String`, and
>    print all of them immediately after construction.
> 2. Cause a `NullPointerException` by calling a method on an uninitialised
>    reference field, then fix it three different ways.
> 3. Interview: Why do fields have defaults while local variables do not?
>    (Hint: think about what the JVM does with memory when allocating an
>    object, versus what a stack frame contains.)

#### Instance Methods and Return Types

An instance method is behaviour that operates on a particular object's state.
It is declared inside the class body and called on a reference.

```java
[modifiers] returnType methodName([parameters]) [throws ExceptionType] {
    // body
}
```

```java
public class Circle {
    private double radius;

    public double area() {                      // no parameters, returns double
        return Math.PI * radius * radius;
    }

    public void scale(double factor) {          // parameter, returns nothing
        if (factor <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Factor must be positive");
        }
        radius *= factor;                       // mutates this object's state
    }

    public boolean isLargerThan(Circle other) { // takes another object
        return this.area() > other.area();      // may read other's private fields
    }

    public Circle enlarged(double factor) {     // returns a NEW object
        Circle copy = new Circle();
        copy.radius = this.radius * factor;     // same class: private access allowed
        return copy;
    }
}
```

That last pair illustrates an important design choice. `scale` *mutates* the
receiver and returns nothing; `enlarged` leaves the receiver untouched and
returns a new object. The second style composes better and is safer in
concurrent code, which is why the standard library moved toward it (`String`,
`LocalDate`, and the stream API are all built this way).

**Return types.** Every method declares exactly one return type, or `void`.

```java
public void log(String message) {       // void: no value produced
    System.out.println(message);
    return;                             // optional: exits early
}

public int size() {
    return items.length;                // MUST return an int on every path
}

public String describe(boolean verbose) {
    if (verbose) {
        return "a long description";
    }
    return "short";                     // compiler requires a return on all paths
    // omitting this line gives: "missing return statement"
}
```

The compiler proves that a non-void method returns on every reachable path.
Throwing counts as an exit, so this compiles:

```java
public int parse(String input) {
    if (input == null) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("null input");   // a valid exit
    }
    return Integer.parseInt(input);
}
```

**Returning objects returns references**, not copies, which has consequences
explored in the defensive-copying topic later:

```java
public List<String> getSkills() {
    return skills;         // the CALLER can now modify this object's internal list
}
```

**Method chaining** is enabled by returning `this`, a style used widely in
builders:

```java
public class Query {
    private final StringBuilder sql = new StringBuilder();

    public Query select(String cols) { sql.append("SELECT ").append(cols); return this; }
    public Query from(String table)  { sql.append(" FROM ").append(table);  return this; }
    public Query where(String cond)  { sql.append(" WHERE ").append(cond);  return this; }
    public String build()            { return sql.toString(); }
}

String sql = new Query().select("id, name").from("users").where("active").build();
```

| Return style        | Example                    | Characteristic                  |
| ------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `void` mutator      | `list.add(x)`              | Changes state, returns nothing  |
| Value query         | `list.size()`              | Reads state, changes nothing    |
| New-object producer | `str.toUpperCase()`        | Leaves receiver unchanged       |
| Fluent builder      | `query.select(...)`        | Returns `this` for chaining     |

A widely used guideline, "command-query separation", says a method should
either change state or return a value, not both. It is a guideline rather than
a law — `Map.put` deliberately violates it by returning the previous value —
but methods that quietly mutate while appearing to be queries are a real source
of confusion.

> Key Takeaways
> - Instance methods operate on one object's state and are called on a
>   reference.
> - A non-void method must return a value on every reachable path; throwing
>   counts as an exit.
> - Returning an object returns a reference, so callers can mutate what they
>   receive.
> - Mutating methods and new-object-producing methods are different designs;
>   prefer the latter for value-like types.
> - Returning `this` enables fluent chaining.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Money` class with an `add` method that returns a new `Money`
>    rather than mutating, and explain one benefit.
> 2. Write a method with an `if`/`else` where both branches return, then delete
>    one return and read the compiler error.
> 3. Build a small fluent `PizzaBuilder` with three chained methods and a
>    terminal `build()`.

#### Creating Objects with new

The `new` operator is the standard way to bring an object into existence. A
single expression triggers four distinct steps, and knowing them explains
several behaviours that otherwise look arbitrary.

```java
Employee e = new Employee("Ada", 36);
```

```text
  Employee e = new Employee("Ada", 36);
  |________|   |__|  |_________________|
      |          |            |
      |          |            +-- constructor invocation with arguments
      |          +--------------- allocate memory on the heap, zero it
      +-------------------------- a reference variable on the stack
```

The four steps, in order:

1. **Class loading.** If `Employee` has not been used before, the JVM loads,
   verifies, and initialises the class, running its static initialisers. This
   happens once, on first use.
2. **Allocation.** Memory for all instance fields is reserved on the heap and
   zeroed, giving every field its default value.
3. **Initialisation.** Field initialisers and instance initialiser blocks run in
   declaration order, then the constructor body executes.
4. **Reference assignment.** The address of the finished object is stored in the
   variable.

```java
public class Demo {
    static { System.out.println("1. class initialised (once)"); }
    private int x = printAndReturn("2. field initialiser");
    { System.out.println("3. instance initialiser block"); }
    public Demo() { System.out.println("4. constructor body"); }

    private int printAndReturn(String s) { System.out.println(s); return 0; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("--- first object ---");
        new Demo();
        System.out.println("--- second object ---");
        new Demo();          // note: step 1 does NOT repeat
    }
}
```

```text
--- first object ---
1. class initialised (once)
2. field initialiser
3. instance initialiser block
4. constructor body
--- second object ---
2. field initialiser
3. instance initialiser block
4. constructor body
```

**Every `new` creates a distinct object**, even with identical arguments:

```java
Employee a = new Employee("Ada", 36);
Employee b = new Employee("Ada", 36);
System.out.println(a == b);        // false -- two separate heap objects
System.out.println(a.equals(b));   // false unless equals() is overridden
```

**Objects can be created without a named variable**, which is common when the
object is used immediately or passed directly:

```java
System.out.println(new Employee("Ada", 36).getName());   // used and discarded
list.add(new Employee("Grace", 45));                     // passed straight in
process(new int[]{1, 2, 3});                             // array creation
```

**Alternatives to `new`** exist and are often preferable:

| Mechanism             | Example                              | Why                                  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| Static factory method | `List.of("a")`, `Integer.valueOf(1)` | Can cache, can return a subtype      |
| Builder               | `new Builder().a().b().build()`      | Readable with many parameters        |
| Cloning               | `array.clone()`                      | Copies an existing object            |
| Deserialization       | Reading an object stream             | Reconstructs without a constructor   |
| Reflection            | `clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()` | Frameworks, when the type is dynamic |

Static factory methods deserve a mention here because they are so common in the
modern standard library. `Integer.valueOf(5)` may return a cached object rather
than a new one, and `List.of(...)` returns an immutable implementation whose
class you never name. Both are impossible with a bare constructor.

Finally, note that Java has no `delete`. An object becomes eligible for garbage
collection when it is no longer reachable from any live reference, which is
covered in chapter 10.

```java
Employee e = new Employee("Ada", 36);
e = null;        // the object is now unreachable and may be collected later
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `new` loads the class if needed, allocates and zeroes memory, runs
>   initialisers and the constructor, then yields a reference.
> - Static initialisation happens once per class; instance initialisation
>   happens per object.
> - Every `new` produces a distinct object, so `==` on two equal-looking
>   objects is `false`.
> - Static factories and builders are frequently better than a direct
>   constructor.
> - There is no `delete`; unreachable objects are collected automatically.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with a static block, a field initialiser, an instance block,
>    and a constructor, then create two instances and predict the output before
>    running it.
> 2. Create two objects with identical constructor arguments and show that `==`
>    is false.
> 3. Interview: Name two things a static factory method can do that a
>    constructor cannot. (Hint: think about the return value and about caching.)

#### Object References versus Values

Java variables hold one of two things: a primitive *value*, or a *reference* to
an object. Almost every confusing assignment or mutation bug traces back to not
distinguishing the two.

```java
int a = 10;
int b = a;         // COPIES the value 10
b = 20;
System.out.println(a);   // 10 -- unaffected

Point p = new Point(1, 2);
Point q = p;             // COPIES the reference, not the object
q.x = 99;
System.out.println(p.x); // 99 -- both variables point at the SAME object
```

```text
   PRIMITIVES: independent values        REFERENCES: shared object

   a: +----+     b: +----+               p: +-----+      +--------------+
      | 10 |        | 20 |                  |  •--+----->| Point        |
      +----+        +----+               q: +-----+  /   | x = 99       |
                                            |  •--+-+    | y = 2        |
   two separate storage locations           +-----+      +--------------+
                                            two references, ONE object
```

This distinction determines what `==` means, as seen in chapter 1: for
primitives it compares values, for references it compares which object is being
pointed at.

```java
Point p1 = new Point(1, 2);
Point p2 = new Point(1, 2);
Point p3 = p1;

System.out.println(p1 == p2);   // false -- different objects
System.out.println(p1 == p3);   // true  -- same object
```

**Aliasing** is the term for two references pointing at one object, and it is
neither good nor bad in itself — it is how objects are shared efficiently. It
becomes a hazard when one holder mutates an object another holder assumed was
stable:

```java
List<String> original = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
List<String> alias = original;      // NOT a copy
alias.add("c");
System.out.println(original);       // [a, b, c] -- surprising if you expected a copy

List<String> copy = new ArrayList<>(original);   // an actual copy
copy.add("d");
System.out.println(original);       // [a, b, c] -- unaffected
```

**Copying comes in two depths**, a distinction that matters constantly:

```java
class Person {
    String name;
    List<String> hobbies;
}

// SHALLOW copy: new Person object, but the SAME hobbies list
Person shallow = new Person();
shallow.name = original.name;
shallow.hobbies = original.hobbies;        // shared!

// DEEP copy: new Person AND a new hobbies list
Person deep = new Person();
deep.name = original.name;                 // String is immutable, safe to share
deep.hobbies = new ArrayList<>(original.hobbies);
```

```text
   SHALLOW COPY                          DEEP COPY

   original --> [Person]                 original --> [Person]
                 hobbies --+                           hobbies --> [List A]
                           |
   shallow  --> [Person]   |             deep     --> [Person]
                 hobbies --+                           hobbies --> [List B]
                     one shared list                     two independent lists
```

Immutable objects sidestep the whole problem. Because a `String` or a
`LocalDate` cannot change, sharing a reference to one is always safe, and a
"copy" is unnecessary. This is a major reason immutability is favoured in
modern Java.

| Concept     | Primitive                | Reference                        |
| ----------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| Variable holds | The value             | An address                       |
| Assignment copies | The value          | The address, not the object      |
| `==` compares | Values                 | Identity                         |
| Can be `null` | No                     | Yes                              |
| Stored in   | Stack (as a local)       | Object on the heap               |

> Key Takeaways
> - Primitive variables hold values; object variables hold references.
> - Assigning a reference copies the address, so both variables see the same
>   object.
> - Two references to one object are *aliases*; mutation through either is
>   visible to both.
> - A shallow copy shares nested objects; a deep copy duplicates them.
> - Immutable objects make aliasing harmless, which is why they are preferred.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method that takes a `StringBuilder`, appends to it, and
>    demonstrate that the caller sees the change.
> 2. Create a class with a `List` field, make a shallow copy, mutate the list,
>    and show both objects change. Then fix it with a deep copy.
> 3. Interview: After `List<String> b = a;` and `b.add("x")`, what does `a`
>    contain, and why? (Hint: how many list objects exist?)

#### The null Reference and NullPointerException

`null` is a special reference meaning "points at no object". It is the default
for every uninitialised reference field, the conventional "absent" return value
in older APIs, and the cause of by far the most common runtime exception in
Java.

Its inventor, Tony Hoare, called it his "billion-dollar mistake", because the
type system permits `null` wherever an object is expected, so the compiler
cannot warn you.

```java
String text = null;
System.out.println(text);            // "null" -- printing is safe
System.out.println(text + "!");      // "null!" -- concatenation is safe
System.out.println(text == null);    // true -- comparison is safe
System.out.println(text.length());   // NullPointerException -- any CALL fails
```

The rule is simple: you may assign, compare, and print a `null` reference, but
you may not dereference it — that is, access any field or call any method on
it.

**Where nulls come from:**

```java
private String name;                     // 1. uninitialised field
map.get("missing");                      // 2. lookup miss returns null
System.getenv("NOT_SET");                // 3. absent environment or config
list.get(0);                             // 4. element that was itself null
someMethod();                            // 5. a method that returns null on failure
```

**Reading the exception.** Since Java 14, helpful messages pinpoint exactly
which part of an expression was null, which removes most of the guesswork:

```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException:
  Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of
  "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null
        at com.example.Demo.main(Demo.java:12)
```

Before this, a chained expression such as `a.getB().getC().getD()` produced a
line number and nothing else.

**Defences, roughly in order of preference:**

```java
// 1. Do not produce nulls. Return an empty collection instead.
public List<String> getTags() {
    return tags == null ? List.of() : tags;
}

// 2. Reject nulls at the boundary, failing fast with a clear message.
public void setName(String name) {
    this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name must not be null");
}

// 3. Use Optional for a genuinely absent RESULT (not for fields or parameters).
public Optional<Customer> findById(String id) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(database.get(id));
}
customer.map(Customer::getName).orElse("unknown");

// 4. Null-safe library helpers.
Objects.equals(a, b);                    // handles either side being null
Objects.toString(value, "default");
Objects.requireNonNullElse(value, "fallback");

// 5. Guard with short-circuit evaluation where a null is legitimately possible.
if (name != null && name.startsWith("A")) { ... }
```

| Approach                      | Use when                                  |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Empty collection / default    | The absence has an obvious neutral value  |
| `Objects.requireNonNull`      | Null indicates a programming error        |
| `Optional` return type        | Absence is an expected, normal outcome    |
| Null check with `&&`          | Null is legitimate and locally handled    |
| `@Nullable` annotations       | Documenting intent for static analysers   |

Two closing cautions. First, autoboxing hides dereferences: `int x = map.get(k)`
throws if the key is missing, because unboxing calls `intValue()` on `null`.
Second, `Optional` is designed as a *return type*; using it for fields or
parameters is widely considered misuse, since it adds an allocation and a layer
of indirection without removing the underlying question.

> Key Takeaways
> - `null` means "no object"; assigning, comparing, and printing it are safe,
>   dereferencing it is not.
> - Helpful `NullPointerException` messages since Java 14 name the exact
>   expression that was null.
> - Prefer designs that never produce null: empty collections, defaults, and
>   `Optional` returns.
> - `Objects.requireNonNull` fails fast at the boundary with a clear message.
> - Autoboxing an absent map value throws, because unboxing dereferences.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write code producing a `NullPointerException` from a map lookup, then fix
>    it with `getOrDefault`.
> 2. Rewrite a method that returns `null` for "not found" so that it returns an
>    `Optional`, and update a caller.
> 3. Interview: Why is returning an empty list usually better than returning
>    `null`? (Hint: consider what every caller has to write otherwise.)

<a id="23-constructors-and-initialization"></a>
### 2.3 Constructors and Initialization

A constructor's job is to leave a new object in a valid state. This section
covers the forms constructors take, how they delegate to each other, and the
exact order in which everything runs.

#### Default and Parameterized Constructors

A constructor is a special member invoked by `new`. It has the same name as the
class, declares no return type at all (not even `void`), and runs after field
initialisers to complete the object's setup.

```java
public class Book {
    private String title;
    private String author;
    private int year;

    public Book(String title, String author, int year) {   // parameterized
        this.title = title;         // 'this.' distinguishes field from parameter
        this.author = author;
        this.year = year;
    }
}

Book b = new Book("Dune", "Herbert", 1965);
```

**The default constructor.** If a class declares no constructor at all, the
compiler inserts a no-argument constructor that does nothing beyond calling the
superclass constructor. It has the same access level as the class.

```java
public class Point {
    int x, y;
    // compiler generates:  public Point() { super(); }
}

Point p = new Point();      // works: uses the generated default
```

The moment you declare any constructor, the default is no longer generated:

```java
public class Point {
    int x, y;
    public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
}

// Point p = new Point();       // ERROR: no no-arg constructor exists
Point p = new Point(3, 4);      // the only available form
```

This is a frequent source of confusion when adding a parameterized constructor
to an existing class breaks code elsewhere that called `new Point()`. If both
forms are needed, declare both.

**Constructors are not methods.** The differences are worth listing because the
similarity is superficial:

| Aspect          | Constructor                      | Method                        |
| --------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Name            | Must match the class exactly     | Any valid identifier          |
| Return type     | None declared, not even `void`   | Required                      |
| Invocation      | Only via `new`, `this()`, `super()` | Called on a reference or class |
| Inheritance     | Not inherited                    | Inherited                     |
| Overriding      | Cannot be overridden             | Can be                        |
| `static`        | Never                            | Allowed                       |
| Implicit version| Generated if none declared       | Never generated               |

A classic trap exploits exactly that first row:

```java
public class Trap {
    private int value;

    public void Trap(int value) {     // NOT a constructor -- it has a return type
        this.value = value;           // it is a method that happens to be named Trap
    }
}

Trap t = new Trap();       // compiles! uses the generated default constructor
                           // value stays 0; the "constructor" was never called
```

Adding a return type silently turns a constructor into an ordinary method. The
compiler cannot warn you because the result is perfectly legal code.

**Access modifiers on constructors** control who may instantiate the class:

```java
public class Service {
    public Service() { }           // anyone may construct
}

public class Helper {
    private Helper() { }           // nobody may construct: utility class idiom
    public static void help() { }
}

public class Session {
    Session() { }                  // package-private: only this package
    public static Session create() { return new Session(); }   // controlled creation
}
```

A `private` constructor is the standard way to prevent instantiation of a
utility class, and the standard way to force creation through a static factory
method when you want to control caching or return a subtype.

> Key Takeaways
> - A constructor shares the class name and declares no return type.
> - The compiler generates a no-argument constructor only when none is
>   declared.
> - Declaring any constructor removes the generated default, which can break
>   existing callers.
> - Writing a return type turns a would-be constructor into a silent ordinary
>   method.
> - A `private` constructor blocks instantiation and enables factory-only
>   creation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with only a parameterized constructor, try to call
>    `new ClassName()`, and read the error.
> 2. Add a return type to a constructor and demonstrate that the object's
>    fields remain at their defaults.
> 3. Write a utility class with a private constructor and one static method,
>    and explain why the private constructor is there.

#### Constructor Overloading

Overloading a constructor means providing several versions with different
parameter lists, so callers can supply only what they have. The compiler selects
one at compile time based on the argument types and count.

```java
public class Pizza {
    private String size;
    private String crust;
    private List<String> toppings;

    public Pizza(String size, String crust, List<String> toppings) {
        this.size = size;
        this.crust = crust;
        this.toppings = new ArrayList<>(toppings);
    }

    public Pizza(String size, String crust) {          // no toppings
        this(size, crust, List.of());                  // delegate, see next topic
    }

    public Pizza(String size) {                        // size only
        this(size, "classic");
    }

    public Pizza() {                                   // all defaults
        this("medium");
    }
}
```

```java
new Pizza();                                        // medium, classic, no toppings
new Pizza("large");                                 // large, classic, no toppings
new Pizza("large", "thin");                         // large, thin, no toppings
new Pizza("large", "thin", List.of("olives"));      // fully specified
```

Overloads must differ in their **parameter list** — the number, types, or order
of parameters. They cannot differ only by parameter *names*, because names are
not part of the signature:

```java
public Rectangle(double width, double height) { }
// public Rectangle(double height, double width) { }   // ERROR: same signature
```

This restriction causes a genuine design problem when a class has several
constructors taking the same types with different meanings:

```java
public class Temperature {
    // public Temperature(double celsius) { }
    // public Temperature(double fahrenheit) { }    // ERROR: identical signature

    private Temperature(double celsius) { this.celsius = celsius; }

    public static Temperature ofCelsius(double c)    { return new Temperature(c); }
    public static Temperature ofFahrenheit(double f) {
        return new Temperature((f - 32) * 5 / 9);
    }
}
```

Static factory methods solve it cleanly because they can have distinct,
descriptive names. This is one of their main advantages over constructors.

**Ambiguity** arises when more than one overload matches equally well, and the
compiler refuses to guess:

```java
public class Ambiguous {
    public Ambiguous(int a, long b) { }
    public Ambiguous(long a, int b) { }
}
// new Ambiguous(1, 1);    // ERROR: reference to Ambiguous is ambiguous
                           // 1,1 could widen either way
```

**Too many overloads is a design smell.** A constructor with five parameters of
the same type is unreadable at the call site, and the overload chain multiplies
the problem:

```java
// What do these arguments mean? The reader must consult the declaration.
new Account("Ada", "Lovelace", true, false, true, 3, 0);

// The builder pattern makes each value self-describing:
Account a = new Account.Builder("Ada", "Lovelace")
        .active(true)
        .overdraftAllowed(false)
        .maxCards(3)
        .build();
```

The rule of thumb used by many teams: up to three or four parameters, use
overloaded constructors; beyond that, use a builder.

> Key Takeaways
> - Overloaded constructors differ in the number, type, or order of parameters.
> - Parameter names are not part of the signature, so two constructors cannot
>   differ by name alone.
> - Static factory methods work around signature clashes and document intent.
> - Equally-matching overloads produce a compile-time ambiguity error.
> - Beyond three or four parameters, prefer a builder to a long constructor.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Rectangle` class with constructors for width and height, for a
>    square, and for a unit square.
> 2. Try to declare two constructors that differ only in parameter names and
>    read the error.
> 3. Interview: A class needs to be constructible from either a radius or a
>    diameter, both `double`. How would you design it? (Hint: constructors are
>    not your only option.)

#### Constructor Chaining with this()

Duplicating initialisation logic across overloaded constructors is a
maintenance hazard: a rule added to one and forgotten in another creates objects
that are valid only some of the time. `this(...)` lets one constructor delegate
to another, so the real work lives in exactly one place.

```java
public class Employee {
    private final String name;
    private final String department;
    private final double salary;

    // The "primary" constructor: all validation and assignment happens here
    public Employee(String name, String department, double salary) {
        if (name == null || name.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name is required");
        }
        if (salary < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Salary cannot be negative");
        }
        this.name = name;
        this.department = department;
        this.salary = salary;
    }

    public Employee(String name, String department) {
        this(name, department, 30_000);      // delegate; validation is inherited
    }

    public Employee(String name) {
        this(name, "Unassigned");            // chains to the two-arg version,
    }                                        // which chains to the primary
}
```

```text
   new Employee("Ada")
        |
        +--> Employee(String)
                |  this("Ada", "Unassigned")
                v
             Employee(String, String)
                |  this("Ada", "Unassigned", 30000)
                v
             Employee(String, String, double)   <- all the real work, once
```

**The rules for `this(...)`:**

1. It must be the **first statement** in the constructor. Nothing may precede
   it, not even a field assignment or a log line.
2. Only one of `this(...)` or `super(...)` may appear, never both, since each
   must be first.
3. The chain must terminate; recursive delegation is a compile error.

```java
public class Example {
    private int value;

    public Example() {
        // System.out.println("before");   // ERROR: must be first statement
        this(0);
        System.out.println("after");       // fine: statements may FOLLOW
    }

    public Example(int value) { this.value = value; }
}

public class Cycle {
    public Cycle()        { this(1); }     // ERROR: recursive constructor
    public Cycle(int x)   { this(); }      //        invocation
}
```

**Why delegation beats duplication** is easiest to see by adding a requirement.
Suppose employees now need a non-null department. With chaining, the check goes
in the primary constructor and every other form gets it automatically. Without
chaining, you must find and update every constructor, and any one you miss
becomes a latent bug.

```java
// WITHOUT chaining -- validation duplicated and already drifting
public Employee(String name, String department, double salary) {
    if (name == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    ...
}
public Employee(String name, String department) {
    if (name == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException();   // copy 2
    this.name = name;
    this.department = department;
    this.salary = 30_000;          // forgot the salary check that exists above
}
```

A useful convention is to designate one constructor as primary — usually the
one with the most parameters — and have every other constructor eventually reach
it. Some teams mark the others with a comment saying so.

Note the interaction with `final` fields: a `final` field must be assigned
exactly once. Delegation satisfies this correctly, because only the terminal
constructor performs the assignment.

> Key Takeaways
> - `this(...)` delegates to another constructor of the same class.
> - It must be the first statement, and cannot coexist with `super(...)`.
> - Recursive delegation chains are a compile error.
> - Designate one primary constructor holding all validation, and chain the
>   rest to it.
> - Delegation keeps `final` field assignment to exactly one place.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Refactor a class with three constructors that duplicate validation so that
>    all delegate to one primary constructor.
> 2. Try placing a statement before `this(...)` and read the compiler message.
> 3. Write two constructors that delegate to each other and observe the
>    recursive-invocation error.

#### Instance Initializer Blocks

An instance initializer is a bare block in the class body, outside any method or
constructor. Its contents are copied by the compiler into the start of every
constructor, after any `super()` call and after field initialisers in source
order.

```java
public class Widget {
    private List<String> parts;

    {                                  // instance initializer block
        parts = new ArrayList<>();     // runs before EVERY constructor body
        parts.add("frame");
    }

    public Widget()             { parts.add("default"); }
    public Widget(String extra) { parts.add(extra); }
}

new Widget().getParts();          // [frame, default]
new Widget("wheel").getParts();   // [frame, wheel]
```

Their purpose is to hold initialisation common to all constructors that cannot
be expressed as a single field initialiser — typically because it needs several
statements or a try-catch.

```java
public class Config {
    private final Properties properties;

    {                                      // multi-statement setup, shared
        properties = new Properties();
        properties.setProperty("mode", "default");
        properties.setProperty("retries", "3");
    }

    public Config() { }
    public Config(String mode) { properties.setProperty("mode", mode); }
}
```

**Rules and ordering.** Multiple blocks are permitted and run in source order,
interleaved with field initialisers:

```java
public class Order {
    private int a = print("1. field a");
    { print("2. first block"); }
    private int b = print("3. field b");
    { print("4. second block"); }

    public Order() { print("5. constructor body"); }

    private static int print(String s) { System.out.println(s); return 0; }
}
// Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -- strictly source order, constructor body last
```

**When to use them, and when not to.** In practice, instance initializer blocks
are rare in application code, because constructor chaining usually expresses the
same thing more clearly and more visibly.

| Situation                                  | Better choice              |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------- |
| One-expression field setup                 | Field initialiser          |
| Logic shared by several constructors       | Constructor chaining       |
| Multi-statement setup shared by all constructors, no parameters needed | Instance initializer |
| Initialisation depending on parameters     | Constructor body           |

Their main legitimate appearance in modern code is inside anonymous classes,
which cannot declare constructors at all — they have no name to give one:

```java
Map<String, Integer> ages = new HashMap<>() {{   // double-brace initialisation
    put("Ada", 36);          // inner braces are an instance initializer
    put("Alan", 41);         // of an anonymous subclass of HashMap
}};
```

This "double-brace" idiom is clever and generally discouraged: it creates an
extra anonymous subclass for every use, holds a hidden reference to the
enclosing instance (a memory-leak risk), and breaks `equals` against ordinary
maps. `Map.of(...)` or an explicit builder is better.

> Key Takeaways
> - An instance initializer is a bare block copied into the start of every
>   constructor.
> - Field initialisers and instance blocks run in source order, before the
>   constructor body.
> - They suit multi-statement setup common to all constructors, but constructor
>   chaining is usually clearer.
> - Anonymous classes cannot declare constructors, so initializer blocks are
>   their only option.
> - Avoid the double-brace idiom: it creates a subclass and can leak the
>   enclosing instance.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with two field initialisers and two instance blocks
>    interleaved, and predict the output order before running it.
> 2. Convert a class that uses an instance initializer into one that uses
>    constructor chaining, and judge which is clearer.
> 3. Interview: Why can an anonymous class not have a constructor, and what is
>    used instead? (Hint: what would you name it?)

#### Initialization Order of a Class

Putting the previous topics together yields a single sequence that explains
every "why is this field still zero?" question. The order is fixed by the Java
Language Specification and never varies.

**Static initialisation, once per class, on first active use:**

1. Static fields are given default values (zero, false, null).
2. Static field initialisers and static blocks run in source order.

**Instance initialisation, on every `new`:**

3. Instance fields are given default values.
4. The superclass constructor runs to completion (implicitly or via `super()`).
5. Instance field initialisers and instance blocks run in source order.
6. The constructor body runs.

```java
class Parent {
    static { System.out.println("1. Parent static block"); }
    { System.out.println("4. Parent instance block"); }
    Parent() { System.out.println("5. Parent constructor"); }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static { System.out.println("2. Child static block"); }
    private int field = print("6. Child field initialiser");
    { System.out.println("7. Child instance block"); }

    Child() {
        super();                                  // implicit if omitted
        System.out.println("8. Child constructor");
    }

    private static int print(String s) { System.out.println(s); return 0; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("3. --- creating first Child ---");
        new Child();
        System.out.println("--- creating second Child ---");
        new Child();
    }
}
```

```text
1. Parent static block          <- static, once, superclass first
2. Child static block           <- static, once
3. --- creating first Child ---
4. Parent instance block        <- superclass instance init runs first
5. Parent constructor
6. Child field initialiser
7. Child instance block
8. Child constructor
--- creating second Child ---
4. Parent instance block        <- steps 4-8 repeat; 1-2 do not
5. Parent constructor
6. Child field initialiser
7. Child instance block
8. Child constructor
```

**The consequence that bites hardest** is step 4 preceding step 5: the
superclass constructor completes *before* the subclass's fields are initialised.
If a superclass constructor calls an overridable method, the subclass version
runs against uninitialised fields:

```java
class Base {
    Base() {
        init();                      // DANGER: calls the overridden version
    }
    void init() { }
}

class Derived extends Base {
    private String value = "assigned";

    @Override
    void init() {
        System.out.println(value);   // prints null! The field initialiser
    }                                // has not run yet (step 5 comes later)
}

new Derived();     // prints: null
```

The rule that follows: **never call an overridable method from a constructor.**
Make such methods `private`, `static`, or `final`.

```text
   TIME ---->

   [class loading]      [new Child()]              [new Child()]
   static init          instance init              instance init
   (once)               Parent ctor, Child ctor    Parent ctor, Child ctor
```

A second consequence concerns `final` fields: because step 5 runs after step 4,
a `final` field is definitely assigned only once the subclass constructor has
finished, which is why the object should not be published to other threads
before that point.

> Key Takeaways
> - Static initialisation happens once per class, superclass first, on first
>   use.
> - Instance initialisation runs the superclass constructor before the
>   subclass's field initialisers.
> - Field initialisers and instance blocks run in source order, then the
>   constructor body.
> - Calling an overridable method from a constructor exposes uninitialised
>   subclass fields.
> - Make constructor-called methods `private`, `static`, or `final`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Reproduce the numbered example and verify the output order matches your
>    prediction.
> 2. Write a superclass constructor that calls an overridden method and observe
>    the `null` field, then fix it by making the method `final`.
> 3. Interview: A field with an initialiser prints as `null` inside a method
>    called from the superclass constructor. Explain why. (Hint: order the six
>    steps.)

#### Defensive Copying in Constructors

A constructor that stores a caller-supplied mutable object keeps a reference to
something the caller still holds. The caller can then change the object's state
from outside, bypassing every validation the class performs. Defensive copying
closes that hole.

```java
public class Period {
    private final Date start;
    private final Date end;

    public Period(Date start, Date end) {
        if (start.after(end)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("start must precede end");
        }
        this.start = start;      // BROKEN: stores the caller's object
        this.end = end;
    }

    public Date getStart() { return start; }   // BROKEN: hands it back out
}
```

```java
Date start = new Date();
Date end = new Date();
Period p = new Period(start, end);    // validated: start precedes end

end.setYear(70);                      // the caller mutates it afterwards
// p now represents a period that ends before it starts, despite the check
```

```text
   WITHOUT defensive copy                WITH defensive copy

   caller's date --+                     caller's date --> [Date A]
                   |
                   v                     Period.start   --> [Date B]  (a copy)
   Period.start ---> [Date]
                                         mutating A cannot affect B
   mutating it changes the Period
```

The fix has two halves, and both are required:

```java
public final class Period {                // final: no subclass can subvert it
    private final Date start;
    private final Date end;

    public Period(Date start, Date end) {
        this.start = new Date(start.getTime());   // 1. COPY FIRST
        this.end   = new Date(end.getTime());

        if (this.start.after(this.end)) {         // 2. VALIDATE THE COPIES
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("start must precede end");
        }
    }

    public Date getStart() { return new Date(start.getTime()); }  // 3. copy on the way out
    public Date getEnd()   { return new Date(end.getTime()); }
}
```

Note the ordering in step 1 and 2. Copying *before* validating is essential:
validating the original and then copying leaves a window in which another thread
could change the object between the check and the copy. This is a
time-of-check-to-time-of-use race, and it is a real security issue, not a
theoretical one.

**Collections need the same treatment**, and this is by far the more common
case in practice:

```java
public class Team {
    private final List<String> members;

    public Team(List<String> members) {
        this.members = new ArrayList<>(members);       // copy the caller's list
        // or: List.copyOf(members) for an immutable copy (Java 10+)
    }

    public List<String> getMembers() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(members);  // read-only view out
        // or: List.copyOf(members) for a snapshot
    }
}
```

**When copying is unnecessary.** Immutable objects cannot be changed, so sharing
them is always safe. This is a substantial practical argument for immutability:

```java
public class Meeting {
    private final LocalDateTime start;   // immutable: no copy needed
    private final String title;          // immutable: no copy needed
    private final List<String> attendees;

    public Meeting(LocalDateTime start, String title, List<String> attendees) {
        this.start = start;                          // safe to share
        this.title = title;                          // safe to share
        this.attendees = List.copyOf(attendees);     // mutable input: copy
    }
}
```

| Parameter type                         | Defensive copy needed? |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `String`, `Integer`, other wrappers     | No, immutable          |
| `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `Instant` | No, immutable          |
| `Date`, `Calendar`                      | Yes, mutable legacy    |
| Arrays                                  | Yes, always mutable    |
| `List`, `Set`, `Map` implementations    | Yes, unless already immutable |
| `List.of(...)` results                  | No, already immutable  |
| Any of your own mutable classes         | Yes                    |

Note that `Collections.unmodifiableList` returns a *view*, not a copy: the
returned list rejects modification, but it still reflects later changes to the
backing list. `List.copyOf` takes an independent snapshot. Which you want
depends on whether callers should see subsequent changes.

Defensive copying costs an allocation. For hot paths with large collections,
teams sometimes document the sharing contract instead and skip the copy. That is
a deliberate trade-off, and the key word is *documented*.

> Key Takeaways
> - Storing a caller's mutable object lets the caller change your object's
>   state afterwards.
> - Copy first, then validate the copy, to close the time-of-check-to-time-of-use
>   window.
> - Copy on the way out as well, or return an unmodifiable view.
> - Immutable parameter types need no copying, which is a strong argument for
>   using them.
> - `unmodifiableList` is a live view; `List.copyOf` is an independent
>   snapshot.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class storing a `Date` without copying, then break its invariant
>    from the calling code.
> 2. Fix it with defensive copies on both the constructor and the getter, and
>    verify the attack no longer works.
> 3. Interview: Why must you validate the copy rather than the original?
>    (Hint: imagine a second thread running between the two statements.)

<a id="24-methods-in-depth"></a>
### 2.4 Methods in Depth

Methods were introduced as behaviour attached to objects. This section examines
how arguments are actually passed, how the compiler chooses between overloads,
and what happens on the call stack.

#### Parameter Passing Semantics in Java

Java is **always pass-by-value**. This single sentence is correct, frequently
disputed, and the source of endless confusion — because for object parameters,
the *value being copied is a reference*.

```java
public static void modify(int number) {
    number = 99;                    // modifies the LOCAL copy only
}

int x = 5;
modify(x);
System.out.println(x);              // 5 -- unchanged
```

That case is uncontroversial. The interesting case is an object:

```java
public static void rename(StringBuilder sb) {
    sb.append(" modified");         // follows the reference, changes the OBJECT
}

StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder("original");
rename(text);
System.out.println(text);           // "original modified" -- the object changed
```

People conclude from this that objects are passed by reference. They are not,
and the following experiment proves it:

```java
public static void replace(StringBuilder sb) {
    sb = new StringBuilder("replaced");   // reassigns the LOCAL copy of the reference
    sb.append("!");                       // affects only the new object
}

StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder("original");
replace(text);
System.out.println(text);           // "original" -- caller's variable UNCHANGED
```

If Java were pass-by-reference, the caller's variable would now point at the new
object. It does not, because the method received a *copy* of the reference.

```text
   BEFORE THE CALL                     INSIDE replace()

   text: +-----+                       text: +-----+
         |  •--+---> [ "original" ]          |  •--+---> [ "original" ]
         +-----+                             +-----+
                                       sb:   +-----+
                                             |  •--+---> [ "replaced!" ]
                                             +-----+
                                       sb was a COPY; reassigning it
                                       cannot repoint 'text'
```

The precise rule, worth memorising in this form:

| What is passed         | What the method can do                       |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| A primitive            | Change its own copy; caller sees nothing      |
| A reference            | Mutate the pointed-to object; caller sees it  |
| A reference            | Reassign its own copy; caller sees nothing    |

So a method can change an object's *contents* but never the caller's *variable*.

**Practical consequences.** First, there is no way to write a `swap` method for
two caller variables:

```java
public static void swap(int a, int b) {        // does nothing useful
    int temp = a; a = b; b = temp;
}
public static void swap(Integer a, Integer b) { // also does nothing:
    // Integer is immutable, so there is no mutation available either
}

// The only options: return a result, use an array or holder object, or swap inline.
public static void swap(int[] pair) {
    int temp = pair[0]; pair[0] = pair[1]; pair[1] = temp;   // mutates the array
}
```

Second, passing a mutable object is an invitation for the method to change it,
which is why immutable parameter types make code easier to reason about:

```java
public void process(List<String> items) {
    items.clear();                 // legal, and the caller's list is now empty
}
```

If a method should not modify what it receives, either document that or take an
immutable type. Defensive copying, covered earlier, is the other half of the
same concern.

Third, `final` on a parameter prevents reassignment inside the method but does
nothing about mutation:

```java
public void handle(final List<String> items) {
    // items = new ArrayList<>();   // ERROR: cannot reassign
    items.add("still mutable");     // perfectly legal
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Java is always pass-by-value; for objects, the value copied is the
>   reference.
> - A method can mutate the object a reference points to, and the caller sees
>   that.
> - A method cannot repoint the caller's variable, which is what
>   pass-by-reference would allow.
> - No `swap` method for two caller variables is possible.
> - `final` on a parameter blocks reassignment, not mutation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write methods that attempt to reassign and to mutate an array parameter,
>    and show which one the caller observes.
> 2. Explain why a method taking a `String` can never change the caller's
>    string, using two reasons.
> 3. Interview: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Defend your answer
>    with a code example. (Hint: try reassigning the parameter inside the
>    method.)

#### Method Overloading and Resolution Rules

Overloading gives several methods the same name with different parameter lists.
It exists so that conceptually identical operations read identically regardless
of argument type — `println` accepts a dozen types and you never think about it.

```java
public class Printer {
    public void print(int value)     { System.out.println("int: " + value); }
    public void print(double value)  { System.out.println("double: " + value); }
    public void print(String value)  { System.out.println("String: " + value); }
    public void print(int a, int b)  { System.out.println("two ints"); }
}
```

**The signature** consists of the method name plus the ordered list of parameter
types. Return type and thrown exceptions are *not* part of it:

```java
public int    compute(int x) { return x; }
// public double compute(int x) { return x; }   // ERROR: same signature
```

**Resolution is a compile-time decision** based on the static types of the
arguments. The compiler works through three phases, stopping at the first that
finds a match:

1. **Exact match or widening**, without boxing or varargs.
2. **Boxing or unboxing** allowed.
3. **Varargs** considered.

```java
public class Resolution {
    static void f(long x)      { System.out.println("long"); }
    static void f(Integer x)   { System.out.println("Integer"); }
    static void f(Object x)    { System.out.println("Object"); }
    static void f(int... x)    { System.out.println("varargs"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        f(5);       // "long" -- phase 1: widening int->long wins
    }               // Integer would need boxing (phase 2), varargs is phase 3
}
```

Remove the `long` overload and the answer becomes `Integer`; remove that too and
it becomes `Object`; remove that and only varargs remains. This ordering
explains most "why did it call that one?" surprises.

**Most specific wins** when several overloads match in the same phase:

```java
static void g(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); }
static void g(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }

g("text");        // "String" -- String is more specific than Object
g(null);          // "String" -- null matches both; the most specific is chosen
```

That `g(null)` case becomes an error if two equally specific unrelated types are
available, since neither is more specific:

```java
static void h(String s)  { }
static void h(Integer i) { }
// h(null);      // ERROR: reference to h is ambiguous
// h((String) null);   // resolved by casting
```

**Overloading with autoboxing** produces the classic interview puzzle:

```java
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
list.remove(1);                       // removes at INDEX 1 -> removes 20
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(20));     // removes the OBJECT 20
```

`List` declares both `remove(int index)` and `remove(Object o)`. The literal `1`
matches the primitive overload exactly in phase 1, so index removal wins.

**Overloading versus overriding**, a distinction examined fully in chapter 3:

| Aspect          | Overloading                  | Overriding                        |
| --------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Where           | Same class (or inherited)    | Subclass                          |
| Signature       | Must differ                  | Must be identical                 |
| Return type     | May differ freely            | Same or covariant                 |
| Resolved        | At compile time, static type | At runtime, actual object type    |
| Also called     | Static polymorphism          | Dynamic polymorphism              |

The guidance from the JDK designers is to overload conservatively. Because
resolution uses static types and can surprise, avoid overloads with the same
number of parameters where the types are related or where one is a primitive and
another a wrapper. Distinct names are often clearer than an overload.

> Key Takeaways
> - A signature is the name plus ordered parameter types; return type is
>   excluded.
> - Resolution happens at compile time using static types, in three phases:
>   widening, then boxing, then varargs.
> - When several candidates match, the most specific wins; ties are ambiguity
>   errors.
> - `list.remove(1)` removes by index, `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))` by
>   value.
> - Overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write four overloads taking `int`, `long`, `Integer`, and `Object`, call
>    each with an `int` literal, and explain which runs.
> 2. Demonstrate the `List.remove` ambiguity and both ways of resolving it.
> 3. Interview: Can two methods differ only by return type? Why or why not?
>    (Hint: consider how the compiler would resolve a call whose result is
>    discarded.)

#### Varargs Methods

Varargs, introduced in Java 5, let a method accept any number of arguments of a
given type. Before it, callers had to build an array by hand for every call.

```java
public static int sum(int... numbers) {     // three dots
    int total = 0;
    for (int n : numbers) {                 // 'numbers' IS an int[]
        total += n;
    }
    return total;
}

sum();                    // 0  -- empty array, NOT null
sum(1);                   // 1
sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);       // 15
sum(new int[]{1, 2, 3});  // 6 -- an array may be passed directly
```

The compiler turns the call site into an array creation: `sum(1, 2, 3)` becomes
`sum(new int[]{1, 2, 3})`. Inside the method, the parameter is an ordinary
array with a `length` field.

**The rules:**

1. Only one varargs parameter per method.
2. It must be the **last** parameter.
3. The array is never `null`; with no arguments it has length zero.

```java
public static void log(String level, String... messages) { }   // valid
// public static void bad(String... parts, String suffix) { }  // ERROR: not last
// public static void bad(int... a, double... b) { }           // ERROR: two varargs
```

A typical use combining a required parameter with optional ones:

```java
public static void log(String level, String... details) {
    System.out.print("[" + level + "]");
    for (String d : details) {
        System.out.print(" " + d);
    }
    System.out.println();
}

log("INFO");                                  // [INFO]
log("ERROR", "file not found", "retrying");   // [ERROR] file not found retrying
```

**Ambiguity with overloads.** Because varargs is the last resolution phase, a
fixed-arity overload always wins when it matches:

```java
static void f(int a, int b)   { System.out.println("two ints"); }
static void f(int... values)  { System.out.println("varargs"); }

f(1, 2);      // "two ints" -- the fixed version wins
f(1, 2, 3);   // "varargs"  -- nothing else matches
f();          // "varargs"
```

Two varargs overloads that could both match are a compile error, so keep them
distinct.

**The generics pitfall.** A varargs parameter of a generic type produces an
"unchecked generic array creation" warning, because arrays and generics do not
mix cleanly (the reasons are covered in chapter 6):

```java
@SafeVarargs        // asserts the method does not misuse the array
public static <T> List<T> listOf(T... elements) {
    return Arrays.asList(elements);
}
```

`@SafeVarargs` suppresses the warning and is permitted only on methods that
cannot be overridden — `static`, `final`, or `private` — because a subclass
could otherwise violate the promise.

**A performance note.** Every varargs call allocates an array. In a tight loop
this is measurable, which is why the standard library sometimes provides fixed
overloads alongside the varargs form:

```java
// The JDK does exactly this for List.of:
static <E> List<E> of(E e1);
static <E> List<E> of(E e1, E e2);
// ... up to ten fixed-arity overloads ...
static <E> List<E> of(E... elements);     // fallback for more
```

Avoid `Object...` parameters where a specific type would do, since they accept
literally anything and defer every type error to runtime.

> Key Takeaways
> - A varargs parameter is an array at runtime, never `null`, empty when no
>   arguments are given.
> - Only one varargs parameter, and it must come last.
> - Fixed-arity overloads win over varargs during resolution.
> - Generic varargs need `@SafeVarargs`, which is allowed only on non-overridable
>   methods.
> - Each varargs call allocates an array, which is why the JDK adds fixed
>   overloads for common sizes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `max` method accepting any number of ints and handling the
>    zero-argument case explicitly.
> 2. Write overloaded methods with a fixed two-argument version and a varargs
>    version, and determine which is called for two, three, and zero arguments.
> 3. Write a varargs method and call it by passing an existing array directly.

#### Recursion and Call Stack Behavior

A recursive method calls itself with a smaller version of the problem, until it
reaches a case simple enough to answer directly. It suits problems that are
naturally self-similar: trees, nested structures, and divide-and-conquer
algorithms.

Every correct recursion has two parts:

1. A **base case** that returns without recursing.
2. A **recursive case** that moves measurably closer to the base case.

```java
public static long factorial(int n) {
    if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("n must be non-negative");
    if (n <= 1) return 1;                 // BASE CASE
    return n * factorial(n - 1);          // RECURSIVE CASE: n-1 approaches 1
}
```

**The call stack.** Each invocation gets a *stack frame* holding its parameters,
locals, and return address. Frames are pushed on entry and popped on return:

```text
   factorial(4)

   push  factorial(4)  ->  needs factorial(3)
   push  factorial(3)  ->  needs factorial(2)
```
