> - Avoid `util` and `common` packages; name by what the contents share.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Derive the correct package name for an organisation owning
>    `data-labs.co.uk` building a project called "atlas".
> 2. Restructure a small layered project into feature packages and note which
>    classes could become package-private.
> 3. Interview: Why does the convention reverse the domain name? (Hint: what
>    problem does global uniqueness solve?)

#### Introduction to the Java Module System

Packages solve namespacing but not encapsulation *between* JARs. Any public
class in any JAR on the classpath is callable by anything else, which means a
library cannot have public internal code without exposing it. The Java Platform
Module System, added in Java 9, addresses this.

**The two problems it solves:**

1. **No strong encapsulation across JARs.** A class must be public to be used by
   another package in the same library, and public means public to the whole
   world.
2. **No reliable dependency declaration.** The classpath is a flat list;
   missing or duplicated JARs are discovered at runtime, often late.

**A module** is a named collection of packages with an explicit declaration,
placed in a file called `module-info.java` at the source root:

```java
module com.example.billing {

    requires java.sql;                        // dependencies, checked at startup
    requires transitive com.example.core;     // consumers also get com.example.core

    exports com.example.billing.api;          // visible to everyone
    exports com.example.billing.spi
            to com.example.plugins;           // visible to named modules only

    // com.example.billing.internal is NOT exported: inaccessible outside,
    // even though its classes are public

    provides InvoiceFormatter                 // service registration
            with com.example.billing.internal.PdfFormatter;

    uses PaymentGateway;                      // service consumption
}
```

```text
   CLASSPATH                          MODULE PATH

   +---------------------------+      +--------------------------------+
   |  everything.jar           |      |  module com.example.billing    |
   |   all public classes      |      |   exports ...api               |
   |   reachable by anything   |      |   hides   ...internal          |
   +---------------------------+      +--------------------------------+
                                                    | requires
   dependencies discovered at        +--------------------------------+
   runtime, when something fails     |  module com.example.core       |
                                     +--------------------------------+
                                      dependencies verified at startup
```

| Directive              | Effect                                              |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `requires`             | This module depends on another                      |
| `requires transitive`  | Dependents automatically read that module too       |
| `requires static`      | Needed at compile time, optional at runtime         |
| `exports`              | Makes a package readable by other modules           |
| `exports ... to`       | Qualified export to named modules only              |
| `opens`                | Permits deep reflection, for frameworks             |
| `provides ... with`    | Registers a service implementation                  |
| `uses`                 | Declares consumption of a service                   |

```bash
javac -d out --module-source-path src $(find src -name "*.java")
java --module-path out --module com.example.billing/com.example.billing.Main
```

**The practical situation in 2026.** The JDK itself is fully modularised, which
is what makes `jlink` able to produce a runtime containing only the modules your
application uses — the basis of small container images. Adoption in application
code has been much more limited, and most projects still build on the classpath,
where they run in the *unnamed module* with the old rules intact.

The `opens` directive exists because frameworks such as Hibernate and Jackson
use reflection to access private members. Strong encapsulation blocks that by
default, which caused significant friction during the migration from Java 8.

For a class in this chapter's scope, the essential points are: modules add a
layer above packages, they make internal packages genuinely internal, and they
declare dependencies explicitly. Whether to modularise an application is a
project-level decision, and using the classpath remains entirely legitimate.

> Key Takeaways
> - Modules add strong encapsulation between JARs, which packages alone cannot
>   provide.
> - `module-info.java` declares `requires` dependencies and `exports` packages.
> - A public class in a non-exported package is inaccessible from other
>   modules.
> - Dependencies are verified at startup rather than discovered on failure.
> - The JDK is modular, enabling `jlink`; most application code still runs on
>   the classpath in the unnamed module.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `module-info.java` for a module exporting one API package and
>    hiding an internal one, then compile and run it.
> 2. Try to use a class from the non-exported package from another module and
>    read the error.
> 3. Interview: Why is `public` insufficient for encapsulation across JARs, and
>    what does a module add? (Hint: who can see a public class on the
>    classpath?)


<a id="3-inheritance-and-polymorphism"></a>
## 3. Inheritance and Polymorphism

Chapter 2 built single classes that protect their own state. This chapter
connects classes to each other: how one type can be defined in terms of another,
how a subclass can replace inherited behaviour, and how a single reference can
drive many different implementations chosen at runtime. Polymorphism in
particular is what lets you add a new case to a program without editing the code
that uses it, which is the central mechanism behind most Java frameworks and
design patterns.

<a id="31-class-inheritance"></a>
### 3.1 Class Inheritance

Inheritance establishes an "is-a" relationship between two classes, letting the
subclass reuse and extend what the superclass already defines.

#### The extends Keyword

Two classes frequently share most of their data and behaviour while differing in
a few details. Copying the shared parts into both means every future fix must be
applied twice, and eventually is not. Inheritance lets you write the shared part
once and describe only the difference.

```java
public class Vehicle {
    protected String make;
    protected String model;
    protected int wheels;

    public void start() { System.out.println(make + " starting"); }
    public void stop()  { System.out.println(make + " stopping"); }
}

public class Motorcycle extends Vehicle {     // Motorcycle IS-A Vehicle
    private boolean hasSidecar;

    public void wheelie() {                   // behaviour unique to Motorcycle
        System.out.println("Performing a wheelie");
    }
}
```

```java
Motorcycle m = new Motorcycle();
m.make = "Ducati";       // inherited field
m.start();               // inherited method: "Ducati starting"
m.wheelie();             // its own method
```

The subclass gains every accessible member of the superclass without restating
any of it. The vocabulary varies by source and all of it means the same thing:

| Term          | Synonyms                          |
| ------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Superclass    | Parent class, base class          |
| Subclass      | Child class, derived class, extension |
| Inheritance   | Generalisation, specialisation    |

**Java supports single inheritance only.** A class may extend exactly one
superclass, though it may implement many interfaces:

```java
public class Car extends Vehicle { }                       // fine
// public class Hybrid extends Car, Engine { }             // ERROR: only one
public class Hybrid extends Car implements Electric, Fuel { }   // fine
```

The restriction avoids the "diamond problem", where a class inherits two
conflicting implementations of the same method through different parents. C++
permits multiple inheritance and needs complex rules to resolve it; Java chose
to make state inheritance single and allow multiple *type* inheritance through
interfaces, which is covered in chapter 4.

**Every class ultimately extends `Object`.** A class with no `extends` clause
implicitly extends `Object`, so the hierarchy is a single tree with `Object` at
its root:

```text
                    Object
                   /   |   \
             Vehicle  String  Number
             /     \             |   \
          Car    Motorcycle   Integer  Double
          /
    SportsCar

   Every class has exactly one parent; Object has none.
```

```java
public class Vehicle { }
// is exactly equivalent to:
public class Vehicle extends Object { }
```

**What is and is not inherited:**

| Member                   | Inherited?                                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `public` members         | Yes                                              |
| `protected` members      | Yes                                              |
| Package-private members  | Only if the subclass is in the same package      |
| `private` members        | No — they exist in the object but are inaccessible |
| Constructors             | No — but the subclass must invoke one            |
| Static members           | Accessible, but hidden rather than overridden    |
| Instance initialiser blocks | Not inherited; each class runs its own        |

The `private` row is subtle and worth stating precisely: a private field of the
superclass *is present in memory* in every subclass instance, but the subclass
has no name for it. It can only be reached through inherited accessor methods.

```java
public class Account {
    private double balance;                          // exists in every subclass
    public double getBalance() { return balance; }   // the only way in
}

public class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    public void addInterest(double rate) {
        // balance *= (1 + rate);         // ERROR: balance has private access
        double current = getBalance();    // reachable only through the accessor
    }
}
```

**`final` prevents extension.** A class marked `final` cannot be subclassed,
which is how `String`, `Integer`, and `LocalDate` guarantee their behaviour
cannot be subverted:

```java
public final class Password { }
// public class Weak extends Password { }   // ERROR: cannot inherit from final
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `extends` creates an is-a relationship and gives the subclass the
>   superclass's accessible members.
> - Java allows single class inheritance, avoiding the diamond problem; multiple
>   interfaces are permitted.
> - Every class implicitly extends `Object`, so the hierarchy is one tree.
> - Private members are present in subclass instances but inaccessible except
>   through inherited methods.
> - Constructors are never inherited, and `final` classes cannot be extended.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a `Shape` class with a `name` field and a `describe()` method, then
>    extend it with `Square` adding a `side` field.
> 2. Add a private field to a superclass and try to use it directly from a
>    subclass; then expose it correctly.
> 3. Interview: Why does Java forbid extending two classes but allow
>    implementing two interfaces? (Hint: what does each one contribute — state,
>    behaviour, or just a type?)

#### Superclass and Subclass Relationships

Inheritance is not merely code reuse; it declares that instances of the subclass
*are* instances of the superclass. That claim has consequences the compiler
enforces and that your design must honour.

**Substitutability.** Anywhere a `Vehicle` is expected, a `Motorcycle` is
acceptable. This is what makes polymorphism possible:

```java
Vehicle v = new Motorcycle();       // upcasting: always safe, always implicit

public void service(Vehicle vehicle) { ... }
service(new Motorcycle());          // a Motorcycle IS a Vehicle
service(new Car());
```

The relationship is one-directional. Every `Motorcycle` is a `Vehicle`, but not
every `Vehicle` is a `Motorcycle`:

```java
// Motorcycle m = new Vehicle();    // ERROR: a Vehicle is not necessarily a Motorcycle
```

**The `instanceof` operator** tests the relationship at runtime and returns true
for the class and every ancestor:

```java
Motorcycle m = new Motorcycle();

System.out.println(m instanceof Motorcycle);   // true
System.out.println(m instanceof Vehicle);      // true -- it is also a Vehicle
System.out.println(m instanceof Object);       // true -- everything is an Object

Vehicle v = null;
System.out.println(v instanceof Vehicle);      // false -- null is never an instance
```

**Designing a hierarchy** means asking whether the is-a claim is genuinely true
in every context the superclass is used. The classic counterexample:

```java
// Mathematically a square IS a rectangle. In code, it breaks.
public class Rectangle {
    protected int width, height;
    public void setWidth(int w)  { width = w; }
    public void setHeight(int h) { height = h; }
    public int area() { return width * height; }
}

public class Square extends Rectangle {
    @Override public void setWidth(int w)  { width = w; height = w; }
    @Override public void setHeight(int h) { width = h; height = h; }
}

// Code written against Rectangle now misbehaves:
Rectangle r = new Square();
r.setWidth(5);
r.setHeight(4);
System.out.println(r.area());     // 16, not 20 -- the caller's assumption broke
```

The fault is not in `Square`; it is in claiming that a mutable square is
substitutable for a mutable rectangle. This is a violation of the Liskov
Substitution Principle, covered in chapter 9. The practical lesson: an is-a
relationship in the real world does not automatically hold for *objects with
behaviour*.

**Levels of hierarchy.** Java permits arbitrarily deep chains, and each level
accumulates the members of all its ancestors:

```java
class Animal   { void breathe() { } }
class Mammal   extends Animal { void nurse()   { } }
class Dog      extends Mammal { void bark()    { } }
class Puppy    extends Dog    { void whimper() { } }

Puppy p = new Puppy();
p.breathe(); p.nurse(); p.bark(); p.whimper();   // all four available
```

```text
   Animal      breathe()
      |
   Mammal      breathe(), nurse()
      |
    Dog        breathe(), nurse(), bark()
      |
   Puppy       breathe(), nurse(), bark(), whimper()

   Members accumulate downward; a change at the top affects everything below.
```

That last line is the real cost of deep hierarchies. A change to `Animal`
potentially affects every descendant, and understanding `Puppy` requires reading
four classes. Most style guides suggest keeping hierarchies shallow — two or
three levels — and preferring composition, the subject of section 3.6, when a
hierarchy starts growing deeper.

> Key Takeaways
> - Inheritance asserts substitutability: a subclass instance is usable wherever
>   the superclass is expected.
> - Upcasting is implicit and safe; the reverse is not, because the claim is
>   one-directional.
> - `instanceof` is true for the class and all its ancestors, and false for
>   `null`.
> - A real-world is-a relationship does not guarantee behavioural
>   substitutability, as the square-rectangle case shows.
> - Deep hierarchies concentrate risk at the top; keep them shallow.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a three-level hierarchy and verify with `instanceof` that the most
>    derived instance matches all three types.
> 2. Implement the `Square extends Rectangle` example and write a method that
>    behaves incorrectly when given a square.
> 3. Interview: Give an example where an is-a relationship is true in the real
>    world but a bad inheritance choice in code. (Hint: think about what the
>    superclass lets callers do.)

#### Inherited Members and Access Rules

Which members a subclass can actually use depends on the access modifier and,
for package-private members, on whether the two classes share a package. This
topic turns the access table from chapter 2 into concrete inheritance rules.

```java
package com.example.base;

public class Base {
    private   String secret    = "private";
    /*default*/ String internal = "package";
    protected String shared    = "protected";
    public    String open      = "public";

    private   void hidden()    { }
    protected void helper()    { }
    public    void api()       { }
}
```

**A subclass in the same package** sees everything except the private members:

```java
package com.example.base;

public class SamePackageChild extends Base {
    void test() {
        // secret;             // ERROR: private
        System.out.println(internal);   // OK: same package
        System.out.println(shared);     // OK
        System.out.println(open);       // OK
    }
}
```

**A subclass in a different package** loses the package-private members too:

```java
package com.example.other;
import com.example.base.Base;

public class OtherPackageChild extends Base {
    void test() {
        // secret;                      // ERROR: private
        // internal;                    // ERROR: different package
        System.out.println(shared);     // OK: protected, via inheritance
        System.out.println(open);       // OK
    }
}
```

| Member access   | Subclass, same package | Subclass, different package | Non-subclass, other package |
| --------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `private`       | No                     | No                          | No                          |
| package-private | Yes                    | No                          | No                          |
| `protected`     | Yes                    | Yes                         | No                          |
| `public`        | Yes                    | Yes                         | Yes                         |

**The protected subtlety**, introduced in chapter 2 and worth repeating here
because it only bites in inheritance code: from a different package, a subclass
may access a protected member through `this` or through a reference of its own
type, but not through a reference of the superclass type.

```java
package com.example.other;

public class Child extends Base {
    void test(Base anyBase, Child anotherChild) {
        System.out.println(this.shared);          // OK
        System.out.println(anotherChild.shared);  // OK: same subclass type
        // System.out.println(anyBase.shared);    // ERROR: not through Base
    }
}
```

The rule exists so a subclass cannot use `protected` as a backdoor into
unrelated sibling objects. `Motorcycle` should not be able to read
`Car`'s protected fields just because both extend `Vehicle`.

**Private members still occupy memory.** A subclass instance contains every
field declared anywhere in its ancestry; the subclass simply has no name for the
private ones:

```text
   new Dog() memory layout

   +--------------------------------+
   |  Object header                 |
   |  Animal.age      (private)     |  <- present, unreachable by name from Dog
   |  Animal.name     (protected)   |  <- present and accessible
   |  Dog.breed       (private)     |
   +--------------------------------+
```

**Accessors bridge the gap**, which is the recommended design anyway:

```java
public class Animal {
    private int age;                              // hidden representation
    protected int getAge() { return age; }        // controlled access for subclasses
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    public String describe() {
        return "Dog aged " + getAge();            // uses the accessor
    }
}
```

Preferring protected *methods* over protected *fields* keeps the superclass free
to change how the value is stored, exactly as public getters do for outside
callers. A protected field is a commitment to every present and future subclass.

> Key Takeaways
> - Private members are never accessible to subclasses, though they exist in
>   every instance.
> - Package-private members are inherited usefully only within the same package.
> - `protected` grants access through `this` or the subclass's own type, not
>   through a superclass reference.
> - Prefer protected accessor methods to protected fields, to keep the
>   representation changeable.
> - The access level of a member is part of the contract with every future
>   subclass.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build the four-member `Base` class and test every access combination from
>    both a same-package and a different-package subclass.
> 2. Try to access a protected field through a superclass-typed reference from
>    another package and read the error.
> 3. Convert a protected field into a protected getter and explain what
>    flexibility you gained.

#### The super Keyword for Fields and Methods

`super` refers to the superclass portion of the current object. It is needed
whenever a subclass member hides or overrides an inherited one and you still
want the original.

**Calling an overridden method.** This is by far the most common use, and it
enables the "extend, do not replace" pattern:

```java
public class Logger {
    public void log(String message) {
        System.out.println("[LOG] " + message);
    }
}

public class TimestampLogger extends Logger {
    @Override
    public void log(String message) {
        System.out.print(LocalTime.now() + " ");
        super.log(message);              // delegate to the inherited behaviour
    }
}

new TimestampLogger().log("started");    // 14:32:01.123 [LOG] started
```

Without `super.`, writing `log(message)` inside the override would call the
override itself, producing infinite recursion and a `StackOverflowError`:

```java
@Override
public void log(String message) {
    log(message);          // INFINITE RECURSION: calls itself, not the parent
}
```

**Accessing a hidden field.** When a subclass declares a field with the same
name as an inherited one, the subclass field *hides* the superclass field. Both
exist, and `super` selects the parent's:

```java
public class Parent {
    protected String name = "parent";
}

public class Child extends Parent {
    protected String name = "child";       // HIDES Parent.name, does not replace it

    public void print() {
        System.out.println(name);          // "child"  -- nearest declaration
        System.out.println(this.name);     // "child"
        System.out.println(super.name);    // "parent" -- the hidden one
        System.out.println(((Parent) this).name);   // "parent" -- same thing
    }
}
```

```text
   One Child object, TWO name fields

   +----------------------------+
   |  Parent.name = "parent"    |  <- super.name
   |  Child.name  = "child"     |  <- this.name
   +----------------------------+
```

Field hiding is legal and almost always a mistake: it produces two fields that
readers assume are one. Rename one of them.

**`super` works one level up only.** There is no `super.super` to reach a
grandparent:

```java
class A { void greet() { System.out.println("A"); } }
class B extends A { @Override void greet() { System.out.println("B"); } }
class C extends B {
    @Override void greet() {
        super.greet();            // calls B.greet()
        // super.super.greet();   // ERROR: no such syntax
    }
}
```

This is deliberate. Skipping a level would let `C` bypass whatever invariant `B`
established in its override, breaking `B`'s contract.

**Where `super` is unnecessary.** If the subclass does not hide or override
anything, inherited members are reachable by their plain names, and writing
`super.` adds noise:

```java
public class Dog extends Animal {
    public void describe() {
        breathe();           // inherited and not overridden: 'super.' is redundant
        super.breathe();     // same effect, but implies an override exists
    }
}
```

Using `super.` gratuitously misleads readers into looking for an override that
is not there.

**Static context.** `super` is an instance reference and does not exist in
static methods, for the same reason `this` does not.

> Key Takeaways
> - `super.method()` invokes the superclass version, which is how an override
>   extends rather than replaces behaviour.
> - Omitting `super.` inside an override calls the override again and recurses
>   infinitely.
> - `super.field` reaches a hidden superclass field; both fields exist in the
>   object.
> - Field hiding is legal and almost always a naming mistake.
> - There is no `super.super`, and `super` is unavailable in static context.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an override that prints something and then delegates with
>    `super.method()`.
> 2. Deliberately omit `super.` in an override and observe the
>    `StackOverflowError`.
> 3. Create a subclass that hides a superclass field, then print both values
>    from one method.

#### Constructor Invocation with super()

Constructors are not inherited, yet every object contains its superclass's
fields, and those fields must be initialised. Java guarantees this by requiring
every constructor to invoke a superclass constructor before doing anything else.

```java
public class Person {
    private final String name;

    public Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        System.out.println("Person constructor");
    }
}

public class Employee extends Person {
    private final String employeeId;

    public Employee(String name, String employeeId) {
        super(name);                      // MUST be the first statement
        this.employeeId = employeeId;
        System.out.println("Employee constructor");
    }
}

new Employee("Ada", "E-1");
// Person constructor
// Employee constructor
```

**The implicit `super()`.** If a constructor does not begin with `this(...)` or
`super(...)`, the compiler inserts a no-argument `super()`:

```java
public class Child extends Parent {
    public Child() {
        // super();      <- inserted automatically by the compiler
        System.out.println("Child");
    }
}
```

This is the source of a very common compile error. If the superclass has no
no-argument constructor, the implicit call has nothing to target:

```java
public class Parent {
    public Parent(String name) { }        // only a parameterized constructor
}

public class Child extends Parent {
    public Child() {
        // ERROR: constructor Parent in class Parent cannot be applied to
        //        given types; required: String, found: no arguments
    }
}

// Fix 1: call the existing constructor explicitly
public class Child extends Parent {
    public Child() { super("default"); }
}

// Fix 2: give the parent a no-argument constructor
```

**The rules:**

1. `super(...)` must be the **first statement** in a constructor.
2. A constructor may contain `super(...)` or `this(...)`, never both.
3. If neither is written, `super()` is inserted.
4. The chain always terminates at `Object`'s constructor.

```text
   new Employee("Ada", "E-1")

   Employee(String, String)
       |  super(name)
       v
   Person(String)
       |  implicit super()
       v
   Object()
       |
       +--> returns, then Person's body runs, then Employee's body runs

   Construction goes UP the chain, then bodies execute DOWNWARD.
```

**Combining with `this(...)`.** A constructor that delegates within its own
class does not call `super` itself; the constructor it delegates to does:

```java
public class Employee extends Person {
    public Employee(String name) {
        this(name, "UNASSIGNED");         // delegates within Employee
    }

    public Employee(String name, String employeeId) {
        super(name);                      // this one reaches the superclass
        this.employeeId = employeeId;
    }
}
```

**Why "first statement" is required.** Until the superclass constructor
completes, the superclass fields hold default values. Allowing code before
`super(...)` would let a subclass observe or use a half-initialised parent:

```java
public class Child extends Parent {
    public Child() {
        // System.out.println(getParentName());   // would read null
        super("name");
    }
}
```

This is the same principle behind the initialisation order from chapter 2, and
the reason calling an overridable method from a constructor is dangerous.

Java 22 relaxed this slightly with statements permitted before `super(...)` as a
preview feature, provided they do not reference the instance. The classic rule
remains what you will encounter in existing code and interviews.

> Key Takeaways
> - Constructors are not inherited, but every constructor must invoke one from
>   its superclass.
> - An implicit `super()` is inserted when neither `super(...)` nor `this(...)`
>   is written.
> - A superclass without a no-argument constructor forces every subclass
>   constructor to call `super(...)` explicitly.
> - `super(...)` must come first and cannot coexist with `this(...)`.
> - Construction walks up to `Object`, then constructor bodies execute from the
>   top down.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a superclass with only a parameterized constructor, then write a
>    subclass constructor and fix the resulting error.
> 2. Add print statements to a three-level hierarchy's constructors and verify
>    the execution order.
> 3. Interview: Why must `super(...)` be the first statement? (Hint: what state
>    are the superclass fields in before it runs?)

#### Single Inheritance and the Class Hierarchy

Java's decision to permit only one superclass shapes how hierarchies are
designed and why interfaces exist in the form they do.

**The diamond problem** is what single inheritance avoids. If a class could
inherit from two classes that both define the same method, which implementation
wins?

```text
           Device
          /      \
    Printer      Scanner        both override  powerOn()
          \      /
        MultiFunction           which powerOn() does it inherit?
```

Languages allowing multiple inheritance need explicit rules for this
(C++ uses virtual inheritance and scope resolution). Java sidesteps it: a class
has exactly one implementation parent, so there is never ambiguity about
inherited *state* or inherited *implementation*.

```java
// public class MultiFunction extends Printer, Scanner { }   // ERROR
```

**Interfaces provide multiple type inheritance.** A class can be many types
while having one implementation ancestry:

```java
public interface Printable { void print(Document d); }
public interface Scannable { Document scan(); }

public class MultiFunction extends Device implements Printable, Scannable {
    @Override public void print(Document d) { ... }
    @Override public Document scan()        { ... }
}

MultiFunction mf = new MultiFunction();
Device d    = mf;     // it is a Device
Printable p = mf;     // and a Printable
Scannable s = mf;     // and a Scannable
```

Default methods, added in Java 8, reintroduced a limited form of the problem,
and Java resolves it by requiring the class to override when two interfaces
supply conflicting defaults. Chapter 4 covers the exact rules.

**The single-rooted hierarchy.** Because every class descends from `Object`,
some useful guarantees follow:

```java
Object[] anything = { "text", 42, new Dog(), null };   // any object fits
for (Object o : anything) {
    System.out.println(o);        // toString() is guaranteed to exist
}
```

Every object has `toString`, `equals`, `hashCode`, and `getClass`, which is what
makes generic containers and frameworks possible at all. The cost is that these
methods exist even where they make little sense.

**Designing a hierarchy well.** Three practical guidelines:

**1. Keep it shallow.** Each level adds coupling and reading effort. Two or
three levels is typical; more suggests composition is the better tool.

**2. Put only genuinely common behaviour in the superclass.** A method that
half the subclasses override to do nothing does not belong there:

```java
// Poor: not every Bird flies
public class Bird {
    public void fly() { System.out.println("Flying"); }
}
public class Penguin extends Bird {
    @Override public void fly() {
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException();   // a red flag
    }
}

// Better: separate the capability from the classification
public class Bird { }
public interface Flying { void fly(); }
public class Sparrow extends Bird implements Flying { public void fly() { ... } }
public class Penguin extends Bird { }         // simply does not implement Flying
```

Throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` from an override is a reliable signal
that the hierarchy is wrong.

**3. Design for inheritance or forbid it.** A class intended for subclassing
must document which methods are overridable and how they interact. A class not
intended for it should be `final`:

```java
public final class Password { }               // explicitly closed
public abstract class Shape { }               // explicitly open, and incomplete
```

| Approach                 | Type inheritance | Implementation inheritance | State inheritance |
| ------------------------ | ---------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `extends` a class        | Single           | Yes                        | Yes               |
| `implements` interfaces  | Multiple         | Default methods only       | No (constants only) |
| Composition (chapter 3.6)| None             | By delegation              | By containment    |

> Key Takeaways
> - Single inheritance eliminates ambiguity about inherited state and
>   implementation.
> - Interfaces give multiple type inheritance without that ambiguity.
> - Every class descends from `Object`, which guarantees a small universal API.
> - An override that throws `UnsupportedOperationException` signals a broken
>   hierarchy.
> - Classes should be explicitly designed for extension or marked `final`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model a `MultiFunction` device using one superclass and two interfaces,
>    and assign it to three different reference types.
> 2. Find the design flaw in a `Bird` hierarchy where `Penguin` overrides
>    `fly()` to throw, then fix it.
> 3. Interview: What is the diamond problem, and how does Java avoid it while
>    still allowing multiple interfaces? (Hint: what does an interface
>    historically not contain?)

<a id="32-method-overriding"></a>
### 3.2 Method Overriding

Inheritance alone only reuses behaviour. Overriding lets a subclass replace an
inherited method with its own version, which is the mechanism that makes
polymorphism useful.

#### Overriding Rules and Signature Matching

To override a method, the subclass must declare a method the JVM recognises as
the *same method*. Get any part of it wrong and you have written a new,
unrelated method instead, which compiles silently and does nothing.

```java
public class Animal {
    public String speak() { return "Some sound"; }
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Woof"; }       // overrides Animal.speak()
}

Animal a = new Dog();
System.out.println(a.speak());    // "Woof" -- the subclass version runs
```

**The requirements:**

| Element            | Rule                                                       |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Method name        | Identical                                                  |
| Parameter list     | Identical in type, order, and count                        |
| Return type        | Identical, or a subtype (covariant)                        |
| Access modifier    | Same or more permissive; never narrower                    |
| Checked exceptions | Same, narrower, fewer, or none; never broader              |
| `static`           | Cannot override; declaring it again hides instead          |
| `final`            | Cannot be overridden at all                                |
| `private`          | Not inherited, so not overridable                          |

**The parameter-list trap** is the one that catches everyone:

```java
public class Animal {
    public void feed(String food) { }
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    public void feed(int amount) { }        // NOT an override -- it is an overload
    public void Feed(String food) { }       // NOT an override -- different name
    public void feed(Object food) { }       // NOT an override -- different parameter type
}

Animal a = new Dog();
a.feed("bone");        // calls Animal.feed -- the Dog versions are irrelevant here
```

None of those three declarations produces a compile error. They are all valid
new methods, and the inherited one remains in place. This is precisely why
`@Override` exists, covered in a moment.

**Access may widen, never narrow.** A subclass cannot make an inherited method
less accessible, because that would break substitutability — code holding a
superclass reference is entitled to call the method:

```java
public class Animal {
    public void speak() { }
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    // private void speak() { }        // ERROR: attempting to assign weaker
    // protected void speak() { }      //        access privileges
    public void speak() { }            // OK: same level
}
```

```text
   Widening is allowed:   private -> package -> protected -> public
   Narrowing is not:      public  -> protected  is a compile error
```

**Exceptions may narrow, never broaden.** The same reasoning applies: a caller
holding a superclass reference wrote a `catch` block based on the superclass
declaration.

```java
public class Reader {
    public void read() throws IOException { }
}

public class FileReader extends Reader {
    @Override public void read() throws FileNotFoundException { }   // OK: subtype
}

public class StrictReader extends Reader {
    @Override public void read() { }                                // OK: none at all
}

public class BadReader extends Reader {
    // @Override public void read() throws Exception { }     // ERROR: broader
}
```

Unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException` and its subclasses) are exempt from
this rule entirely — an override may throw any of them without declaring
anything.

**Instance methods only.** Constructors, static methods, private methods, and
final methods cannot be overridden. Each for a different reason: constructors
are not inherited, static methods have no dispatch target, private methods are
invisible, and `final` explicitly forbids it.

> Key Takeaways
> - An override must match the name and parameter list exactly; anything else
>   creates a new method.
> - Access may widen but never narrow, and checked exceptions may narrow but
>   never broaden.
> - Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted in overrides.
> - `static`, `private`, `final`, and constructors cannot be overridden.
> - A failed override compiles silently, which is why `@Override` matters.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an intended override with a slightly different parameter type and
>    demonstrate that the superclass version still runs.
> 2. Try narrowing the access modifier of an override and read the error.
> 3. Interview: Why can an override not throw a broader checked exception?
>    (Hint: think about what a caller holding a superclass reference already
>    wrote.)

#### Covariant Return Types

Before Java 5, an override had to declare exactly the same return type as the
method it overrode. That forced callers to cast constantly. Covariant returns
relaxed the rule: an override may return a *subtype* of the original return
type.

```java
public class Animal {
    public Animal reproduce() { return new Animal(); }
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public Dog reproduce() { return new Dog(); }    // Dog is a subtype of Animal
}
```

```java
Dog parent = new Dog();
Dog puppy = parent.reproduce();      // no cast needed

Animal a = parent;
Animal offspring = a.reproduce();    // still type-safe through the supertype
```

Without covariance, the second line would need `(Dog) parent.reproduce()`, which
is both noisy and unchecked.

**Why it is safe.** Substitutability is preserved: anyone expecting an `Animal`
back receives a `Dog`, which *is* an `Animal`. The promise is strengthened, not
weakened. The reverse would be unsafe and is rejected:

```java
public class Dog extends Animal {
    // @Override public Object reproduce() { }   // ERROR: Object is not a subtype
}                                                //        of Animal
```

```text
   Superclass:  Animal reproduce()       promises "at least an Animal"
   Override:    Dog    reproduce()       delivers "a Dog"  -> stronger, allowed
   Override:    Object reproduce()       delivers "maybe not an Animal" -> rejected
```

**The classic application is `clone`**, and more generally any method returning
"one of me":

```java
public class Shape implements Cloneable {
    @Override
    public Shape clone() {                        // Object.clone() returns Object
        try {
            return (Shape) super.clone();         // covariant: narrows to Shape
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) {
            throw new AssertionError(e);
        }
    }
}

public class Circle extends Shape {
    @Override
    public Circle clone() { return (Circle) super.clone(); }   // narrows further
}

Circle c = new Circle().clone();       // no cast at the call site
```

**Builders use it heavily**, though the generic version is more common in
practice:

```java
public class Builder {
    public Builder name(String n) { ...; return this; }
}

public class AdvancedBuilder extends Builder {
    @Override
    public AdvancedBuilder name(String n) { super.name(n); return this; }

    public AdvancedBuilder extra(String e) { ...; return this; }
}

new AdvancedBuilder().name("x").extra("y");    // chaining survives the override
```

**Restrictions:**

| Situation                          | Allowed?                            |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Subtype of the original return     | Yes                                 |
| Supertype of the original return   | No                                  |
| Unrelated type                     | No                                  |
| Primitive to wrapper, or reverse   | No — covariance applies to references only |
| `void` changed to anything         | No                                  |

```java
public class Base { public long count() { return 0; } }
public class Derived extends Base {
    // @Override public int count() { return 0; }   // ERROR: int is not a subtype
}                                                   //        of long
```

Numeric widening is not subtyping, so `int` cannot covariantly override `long`
even though an `int` value fits in a `long`.

> Key Takeaways
> - An override may return a subtype of the declared return type.
> - This is safe because it strengthens the promise made to callers.
> - It removes casts at call sites, most visibly for `clone` and fluent
>   builders.
> - Covariance applies to reference types only; primitive widening does not
>   qualify.
> - Returning a supertype or an unrelated type is rejected.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a hierarchy where each class overrides a `copy()` method returning
>    its own type, and verify no casts are needed.
> 2. Try to override a method returning `Integer` with one returning `Object`
>    and explain the error.
> 3. Interview: Why is a covariant return type safe while a covariant parameter
>    type would not be? (Hint: consider who supplies each one.)

#### The @Override Annotation

`@Override` tells the compiler that the annotated method is intended to override
an inherited one. If it does not, compilation fails. It costs nothing and
prevents an entire class of silent bugs.

```java
public class Animal {
    public String speak() { return "..."; }
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Woof"; }     // verified at compile time
}
```

**The bug it catches.** Without the annotation, a typo or signature mismatch
produces a new method and no warning:

```java
public class Dog extends Animal {
    public String Speak() { return "Woof"; }     // capital S -- silently useless
}

Animal a = new Dog();
System.out.println(a.speak());     // "..." -- the Animal version, not what you wrote
```

Add the annotation and the compiler refuses:

```java
public class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String Speak() { return "Woof"; }
    // ERROR: method does not override or implement a method from a supertype
}
```

**The most costly instance of this bug** is a mistyped `equals`:

```java
public class Point {
    private int x, y;

    // Intended as an override of Object.equals -- it is not
    public boolean equals(Point other) {          // parameter should be Object
        return this.x == other.x && this.y == other.y;
    }
}

Set<Point> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(new Point(1, 2));
System.out.println(set.contains(new Point(1, 2)));   // false!
```

`HashSet` calls `equals(Object)`, which is still `Object`'s identity-based
version. The overload is never invoked by the collection. With `@Override`, this
fails to compile immediately.

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {        // correct signature, verified
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Point p)) return false;
    return x == p.x && y == p.y;
}
```

**It also works for interface methods**, since Java 6:

```java
public class Task implements Runnable {
    @Override
    public void run() { }            // verified against the interface
}
```

This catches the case where an interface method is renamed and implementations
silently stop implementing it.

**A second benefit is documentation.** A reader sees immediately that a method
participates in polymorphism and that a superclass version exists, which is
information they would otherwise have to go looking for.

**Where it does not apply:**

```java
public class Example {
    // @Override
    public void brandNewMethod() { }        // ERROR: nothing to override

    // @Override
    public static void staticMethod() { }   // ERROR: hiding is not overriding
}
```

That second case is useful in itself: it prevents the mistaken belief that a
static method is being overridden.

Every modern style guide and IDE treats a missing `@Override` as a warning. Turn
that warning on; there is no reason to omit the annotation.

> Key Takeaways
> - `@Override` makes the compiler verify that a method really overrides
>   something.
> - It catches typos and signature mismatches that would otherwise compile
>   silently.
> - The mistyped `equals(Point)` bug is the canonical example, and breaks
>   collections.
> - It works for interface implementations too, catching renamed interface
>   methods.
> - It documents participation in polymorphism for readers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with `equals(Point)` instead of `equals(Object)` and show
>    that a `HashSet` fails to find an equal element.
> 2. Add `@Override` to that method and observe the compile error.
> 3. Interview: What does `@Override` actually do at runtime? (Hint: check its
>    retention policy.)

#### Access Modifier Widening Constraints

The rule that an override may widen but never narrow access follows directly
from substitutability, and is worth examining on its own because it also governs
how a hierarchy's public surface evolves.

```java
public class Service {
    protected void process() { }
}

public class PublicService extends Service {
    @Override
    public void process() { }        // widening protected -> public: allowed
}

public class BrokenService extends Service {
    // @Override
    // private void process() { }    // ERROR: attempting to assign weaker
}                                    //        access privileges; was protected
```

**Why narrowing must be forbidden.** Consider what would happen if it were
allowed:

```java
Service s = new BrokenService();     // legal: BrokenService IS-A Service
s.process();                         // the compiler permits this: Service.process
                                     // is protected and we are in a subclass...
                                     // but the object's method is private!
```

The compiler checks access against the *static* type, while dispatch uses the
*runtime* type. If narrowing were permitted, a call the compiler approved would
hit a method the caller was not allowed to invoke. Forbidding narrowing keeps
the two views consistent.

```text
   Declared:  Service.process()      protected
                  |
                  | a caller with a Service reference may call it
                  v
   Runtime:   BrokenService.process()  private  <- would be unreachable

   The compiler's promise and the runtime's behaviour must not diverge.
```

**The permitted direction:**

```text
   private  ->  package-private  ->  protected  ->  public

   An override may move RIGHT along this line, or stay put. Never left.
```

| Superclass method | Legal override modifiers                |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `public`          | `public` only                           |
| `protected`       | `protected`, `public`                   |
| package-private   | package-private, `protected`, `public`  |
| `private`         | Not inherited; any modifier, but it is a new method |

That last row is worth expanding. A private method is invisible to the subclass,
so declaring the same signature creates an unrelated method rather than an
override:

```java
public class Parent {
    private void secret() { System.out.println("Parent"); }
    public void run() { secret(); }              // binds to Parent.secret at compile time
}

public class Child extends Parent {
    private void secret() { System.out.println("Child"); }   // unrelated method
}

new Child().run();      // "Parent" -- NOT polymorphic, because private methods
                        // are resolved statically
```

This is a known interview question, and the reasoning is that private methods
are implicitly final: since no subclass can see them, the compiler binds the
call directly with no virtual dispatch.

**Practical implications for design.** Because access can only widen,
overridable methods should start at the narrowest level that makes sense. A
`protected` hook can later be widened to `public` if needed, while a `public`
one can never be pulled back.

```java
public abstract class Template {
    public final void execute() {         // the public, fixed algorithm
        validate();
        performStep();                    // the extension point
        cleanup();
    }

    protected abstract void performStep();   // protected: for subclasses only

    private void validate() { }              // private: not an extension point
    private void cleanup()  { }
}
```

This is the template method pattern, revisited in chapter 9. Note how the access
modifiers document exactly which methods a subclass may participate in.

> Key Takeaways
> - An override may widen access or keep it the same, never narrow it.
> - Narrowing would let the compiler approve a call the runtime object forbids.
> - Private methods are not inherited, so a same-named subclass method is
>   unrelated and non-polymorphic.
> - Private methods are effectively final and bound at compile time.
> - Start extension points at the narrowest workable access level, since
>   widening later is always possible.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Attempt every narrowing combination in the table and record which produce
>    errors.
> 2. Reproduce the private-method example and explain why the parent version
>    runs.
> 3. Interview: Are private methods polymorphic in Java? Justify the answer.
>    (Hint: can a subclass even see one?)

#### Preventing Overriding with final

`final` on a method forbids subclasses from overriding it. On a class, it
forbids extension entirely. Both are tools for protecting behaviour you cannot
allow a subclass to change.

```java
public class Account {
    private double balance;

    public final double getBalance() {        // cannot be overridden
        return balance;
    }

    public final void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        balance += amount;                    // the rule is now unbreakable
    }
}

public class Savings extends Account {
    // @Override public double getBalance() { return 1_000_000; }   // ERROR
}
```

Without `final`, a subclass could override `getBalance()` to lie, and every
piece of code holding an `Account` reference would be deceived.

**Where `final` methods matter most:**

| Reason                    | Example                                        |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Security-critical logic   | Authentication, permission checks               |
| Invariant enforcement     | Methods that maintain a class's guarantees      |
| Template method skeletons | The fixed algorithm, with overridable hooks     |
| Constructor-called methods| Prevents the uninitialised-field hazard         |

That last row connects to the initialisation-order problem from chapter 2:

```java
public class Base {
    public Base() {
        init();                 // safe ONLY because init is final
    }
    protected final void init() { ... }   // no subclass can intercept this
}
```

**`final` classes** close the type entirely:

```java
public final class Password {
    private final char[] value;
    public boolean matches(char[] attempt) { ... }
}
// public class FakePassword extends Password { }   // ERROR
```

The JDK uses this for `String`, `Integer`, `LocalDate`, and the other value
types. If `String` were extensible, a malicious subclass could override
`equals` or `hashCode` and subvert every security check that compares strings.

**The performance argument is largely obsolete.** `final` once helped the JIT
inline methods. Modern JVMs perform class-hierarchy analysis and inline
non-final methods when only one implementation is loaded, deoptimising if a
second appears. Use `final` for design reasons, not for speed.

**The design argument is the real one**, and is stated forcefully in *Effective
Java*: design and document a class for inheritance, or else prohibit it. An
un-final class that was never considered as a superclass will eventually be
subclassed by someone, and its internal method calls become an accidental,
undocumented API.

```java
// Fragile: addAll calls add internally, which a subclass may override
public class CountingList<E> extends ArrayList<E> {
    private int addCount;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) { addCount++; return super.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);      // super.addAll internally calls add()
    }                                // -> addCount is incremented TWICE per element
}
```

This is the self-use problem: the superclass's internal calls are part of its
behaviour, and subclasses that override those methods change it unpredictably.
Composition, the subject of section 3.6, avoids the issue entirely.

| Modifier target | Effect                                    |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `final` class   | Cannot be extended                        |
| `final` method  | Cannot be overridden                      |
| `final` field   | Cannot be reassigned (chapter 1)          |
| `final` parameter or local | Cannot be reassigned           |

> Key Takeaways
> - `final` on a method prevents overriding; on a class it prevents extension.
> - Use it for security-critical logic, invariant enforcement, and methods
>   called from constructors.
> - The JDK's value types are final so their behaviour cannot be subverted.
> - The performance justification is obsolete; the design justification is not.
> - Either design and document a class for inheritance, or make it `final`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class whose `getBalance()` is final and try to override it.
> 2. Reproduce the `CountingList` double-counting bug and explain why it
>    happens.
> 3. Interview: Why is `String` declared final? (Hint: think about what
>    `equals` is used for in security checks.)

#### Overriding versus Overloading versus Hiding

Three mechanisms let two methods share a name. They behave completely
differently, and distinguishing them is a standard interview topic because the
consequences are easy to get wrong.

**Overriding** replaces an inherited instance method. The version that runs is
decided at runtime by the object's actual class.

```java
class Parent { void show() { System.out.println("Parent.show"); } }
class Child extends Parent {
    @Override void show() { System.out.println("Child.show"); }
}

Parent p = new Child();
p.show();        // "Child.show" -- runtime type decides
```

**Overloading** declares a different method with the same name but a different
parameter list. The version that runs is decided at compile time by the static
types of the arguments.

```java
class Printer {
    void print(int x)    { System.out.println("int"); }
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }
    void print(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); }
}

Printer p = new Printer();
Object value = "text";     // static type Object, runtime type String
p.print(value);            // "Object" -- compile-time decision, not runtime
```

That example is the crux of the distinction: overloading never looks at the
runtime type.

**Hiding** occurs with static methods and with fields. The version used is
decided at compile time by the reference type.

```java
class Parent {
    static void greet() { System.out.println("Parent.greet"); }
    String name = "parent";
}
class Child extends Parent {
    static void greet() { System.out.println("Child.greet"); }   // HIDES
    String name = "child";                                       // HIDES
}

Parent p = new Child();
p.greet();                 // "Parent.greet" -- static type decides
System.out.println(p.name);// "parent"       -- static type decides

Child c = new Child();
c.greet();                 // "Child.greet"
System.out.println(c.name);// "child"
```

```text
   Parent p = new Child();

   p.show()   -> Child.show    OVERRIDING: runtime type
   p.greet()  -> Parent.greet  HIDING:     static type
   p.name     -> "parent"      HIDING:     static type
   p.print(o) -> chosen by the compiler from the declared argument type
```

| Aspect             | Overriding             | Overloading            | Hiding                 |
| ------------------ | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Applies to         | Instance methods       | Any methods            | Static methods, fields |
| Location           | Subclass               | Same or subclass       | Subclass               |
| Signature          | Must match             | Must differ            | Must match             |
| Resolved at        | Runtime                | Compile time           | Compile time           |
| Based on           | Object's actual class  | Argument static types  | Reference's static type |
| Also called        | Dynamic polymorphism   | Static polymorphism    | Shadowing              |
| `@Override` valid  | Yes                    | No                     | No                     |

**A combined example** that appears in interviews in various forms:

```java
class A {
    static  String s() { return "A.static"; }
            String i() { return "A.instance"; }
    String field = "A.field";
}

class B extends A {
    static  String s() { return "B.static"; }
    @Override String i() { return "B.instance"; }
    String field = "B.field";
}

A ref = new B();
System.out.println(ref.s());      // "A.static"    -- hidden, static type
System.out.println(ref.i());      // "B.instance"  -- overridden, runtime type
System.out.println(ref.field);    // "A.field"     -- hidden, static type
```

Only the instance method is polymorphic. Everything else follows the declared
type of `ref`.

**Practical guidance.** Never hide a static method or a field deliberately: the
result is code whose behaviour depends on the declared type of a variable, which
no reader expects. If you need polymorphic behaviour, use instance methods. If
two methods do genuinely different things, give them different names rather than
overloading.

> Key Takeaways
> - Overriding is resolved at runtime by the object's class; overloading and
>   hiding are resolved at compile time.
> - Overloading selects on the static types of the arguments, never the runtime
>   types.
> - Static methods and fields are hidden, not overridden, and follow the
>   reference's declared type.
> - Only instance methods participate in polymorphism.
> - Avoid hiding entirely; it makes behaviour depend on a variable's declared
>   type.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build the combined `A`/`B` example and predict all three outputs before
>    running it.
> 2. Write an overloaded method taking `Object` and `String`, call it with an
>    `Object`-typed variable holding a string, and explain the result.
> 3. Interview: `Parent p = new Child();` — which of an overridden method, a
>    hidden static method, and a hidden field use the child's version? (Hint:
>    only one is dispatched dynamically.)

<a id="33-polymorphism"></a>
### 3.3 Polymorphism

Polymorphism, from the Greek for "many forms", lets one reference type stand for
many concrete types, with the actual behaviour selected at runtime. It is the
mechanism that makes object-oriented code extensible.

#### Subtype Polymorphism and Upcasting

A reference of a supertype may point at an object of any subtype. This is
*upcasting*, and it is implicit, always safe, and the foundation of everything
else in this section.

```java
public class Animal { public void speak() { System.out.println("..."); } }
public class Dog extends Animal { @Override public void speak() { System.out.println("Woof"); } }
public class Cat extends Animal { @Override public void speak() { System.out.println("Meow"); } }
```

```java
Animal a1 = new Dog();       // upcast: implicit, no syntax required
Animal a2 = new Cat();
Animal a3 = (Animal) new Dog();   // explicit cast: legal but redundant

a1.speak();      // "Woof"
a2.speak();      // "Meow"
```

```text
   The reference type determines WHAT YOU MAY CALL.
   The object type determines WHICH CODE RUNS.

   Animal a = new Dog();
   |_____|    |_______|
      |            |
      |            +--> Dog.speak() executes
      +-----------------> only Animal's members are visible
```

**The visibility restriction** is the price of the abstraction:

```java
public class Dog extends Animal {
    public void fetch() { System.out.println("Fetching"); }
}

Animal a = new Dog();
a.speak();        // OK: declared in Animal
// a.fetch();     // ERROR: Animal has no fetch(), even though the object is a Dog
```

The compiler only knows the declared type. To reach `fetch`, you must downcast,
which is the next topic.

**Why this is useful** becomes obvious when writing code that handles many
types:

```java
// Without polymorphism: every new type requires editing this method
public void makeSound(Object animal) {
    if (animal instanceof Dog) { ((Dog) animal).bark(); }
    else if (animal instanceof Cat) { ((Cat) animal).meow(); }
    else if (animal instanceof Bird) { ((Bird) animal).chirp(); }
    // ... and so on forever
}

// With polymorphism: this method never changes again
public void makeSound(Animal animal) {
    animal.speak();
}
```

Adding a `Horse` class requires writing `Horse` and nothing else. The calling
code is closed to modification but open to extension, which is the Open-Closed
Principle from chapter 9.

**Polymorphic collections** are the most common practical use:

```java
List<Animal> zoo = List.of(new Dog(), new Cat(), new Dog());

for (Animal animal : zoo) {
    animal.speak();        // each one behaves according to its actual class
}
// Woof
// Meow
// Woof
```

```java
// Method parameters and return types work the same way
public void feedAll(List<? extends Animal> animals) { ... }
public Animal createRandom() { return Math.random() < 0.5 ? new Dog() : new Cat(); }
```

**Four kinds of polymorphism** appear in Java, and it helps to know the
vocabulary:

| Kind          | Java mechanism                       | Resolved   |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------- |
| Subtype       | Overriding through a supertype reference | Runtime |
| Parametric    | Generics (`List<T>`)                 | Compile time |
| Ad hoc        | Method overloading                   | Compile time |
| Coercion      | Implicit type conversion (`int` to `long`) | Compile time |

When the word "polymorphism" is used unqualified in Java discussions, it almost
always means the first one.

> Key Takeaways
> - Upcasting a subclass reference to a supertype is implicit and always safe.
> - The reference type controls which members are visible; the object's class
>   controls which override runs.
> - Polymorphic code is extended by adding classes, not by editing existing
>   methods.
> - Collections of a supertype hold any mixture of subtypes.
> - Java has four kinds of polymorphism; only subtype polymorphism is resolved
>   at runtime.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build an `Animal` hierarchy with three subclasses, put them in one list,
>    and call the same method on each.
> 2. Try to call a subclass-only method through a superclass reference and read
>    the error.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between the reference type and the
>    object type, and what does each control? (Hint: one is checked by the
>    compiler, the other by the JVM.)

#### Dynamic Method Dispatch

Dynamic dispatch is the runtime mechanism that makes overriding work: the JVM
selects the method implementation based on the object's actual class, not the
reference's declared type.

```java
Animal a = new Dog();
a.speak();       // the JVM looks at the OBJECT, finds Dog.speak, runs it
```

**How it works.** Each loaded class has a *method table* (conceptually a vtable)
mapping method signatures to implementations. A subclass's table starts as a
copy of its superclass's, with overridden entries replaced:

```text
   Animal method table            Dog method table (inherits, then overrides)
   +---------------------+        +---------------------+
   | speak  -> Animal.speak|      | speak  -> Dog.speak   |  <- replaced
   | eat    -> Animal.eat  |      | eat    -> Animal.eat  |  <- inherited
   | toString -> Object... |      | toString -> Object... |
   +---------------------+        | fetch  -> Dog.fetch   |  <- added
                                  +---------------------+

   Every object header points at its class, so the JVM can find the right table.

   a.speak()  ->  read a's class (Dog)  ->  look up "speak"  ->  Dog.speak
```

The bytecode instruction is `invokevirtual`, which performs exactly this lookup.
Compare it with the others:

| Instruction       | Used for                          | Dispatch   |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------- | ---------- |
| `invokevirtual`   | Normal instance methods           | Dynamic    |
| `invokeinterface` | Methods called through an interface | Dynamic  |
| `invokestatic`    | Static methods                    | Static     |
| `invokespecial`   | Constructors, `private`, `super.` calls | Static |
| `invokedynamic`   | Lambdas, string concatenation     | Bootstrapped |

`invokespecial` explains why private methods and `super.` calls are not
polymorphic: they are bound at compile time.

**Only instance methods are dispatched dynamically.** Fields and static methods
are not, which is the hiding behaviour from the previous section:

```java
class Parent {
    String label = "parent";
    static  void stat() { System.out.println("Parent.stat"); }
    void inst()         { System.out.println("Parent.inst"); }
}
class Child extends Parent {
    String label = "child";
    static  void stat() { System.out.println("Child.stat"); }
    @Override void inst() { System.out.println("Child.inst"); }
}

Parent p = new Child();
p.inst();                       // "Child.inst"   <- dynamic
p.stat();                       // "Parent.stat"  <- static
System.out.println(p.label);    // "parent"       <- static
```

**A practical consequence: dispatch inside the superclass.** When a superclass
method calls another overridable method, the call is also dispatched
dynamically, which means the subclass's version runs:

```java
public class Report {
    public void generate() {
        System.out.println(header());       // dispatched dynamically
        System.out.println("body");
    }
    protected String header() { return "=== Report ==="; }
}

public class SalesReport extends Report {
    @Override protected String header() { return "=== Sales ==="; }
}

new SalesReport().generate();
// === Sales ===          <- the subclass version, called from the superclass
// body
```

This is the engine of the template method pattern, and also the reason calling
an overridable method from a constructor is hazardous, as established in chapter
2.

**Performance.** Dynamic dispatch is not free in principle, but modern JVMs
optimise it aggressively. When only one implementation of a method is loaded,
the JIT compiles a direct call ("monomorphic inline cache") and deoptimises if a
second class appears. Call sites seeing two types stay fast; sites seeing many
("megamorphic") fall back to a table lookup. In practice this is rarely a
bottleneck, and designing around it prematurely is a mistake.

> Key Takeaways
> - The JVM selects an override by looking at the object's class, using its
>   method table.
> - `invokevirtual` and `invokeinterface` dispatch dynamically; `invokestatic`
>   and `invokespecial` do not.
> - Fields, static methods, private methods, and `super.` calls are bound at
>   compile time.
> - A superclass method calling an overridable method reaches the subclass
>   version.
> - The JIT optimises call sites with few implementations to direct calls.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a superclass method that calls an overridable helper, then override
>    the helper and observe which runs.
> 2. Use `javap -c` on a class to find `invokevirtual` and `invokestatic`
>    instructions.
> 3. Interview: A superclass constructor calls an overridden method. What does
>    the subclass see, and why? (Hint: combine dynamic dispatch with
>    initialisation order.)

#### Static versus Dynamic Binding

*Binding* is the association of a method call with a specific implementation.
Java does some of this at compile time and some at runtime, and knowing which
applies where explains nearly every polymorphism puzzle.

**Static binding** (also early binding) happens at compile time, using the
declared types. It applies to:

- `static` methods
- `private` methods
- `final` methods
- Constructors
- Field access
- Overload selection

**Dynamic binding** (also late binding) happens at runtime, using the object's
actual class. It applies to:

- Non-final, non-private, non-static instance methods

```java
class Base {
    static  void s()  { System.out.println("Base.s");  }
    private void p()  { System.out.println("Base.p");  }
    final   void f()  { System.out.println("Base.f");  }
            void v()  { System.out.println("Base.v");  }
    void callAll() { s(); p(); f(); v(); }
}

class Derived extends Base {
    static void s()  { System.out.println("Derived.s"); }
    private void p() { System.out.println("Derived.p"); }
    @Override void v() { System.out.println("Derived.v"); }
}

Base b = new Derived();
b.callAll();
// Base.s        static  -> statically bound
// Base.p        private -> statically bound
// Base.f        final   -> statically bound
// Derived.v     virtual -> dynamically bound
```

| Bound statically        | Bound dynamically        |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `static` methods        | Instance methods         |
| `private` methods       |                          |
| `final` methods         |                          |
| Constructors            |                          |
| Fields                  |                          |
| Which overload is chosen| Which override runs      |

**The overload-versus-override interaction** is the subtlest case, because both
happen to one call. The compiler picks the *signature* statically; the JVM picks
the *implementation* dynamically:

```java
class Parent {
    void handle(Object o) { System.out.println("Parent.handle(Object)"); }
    void handle(String s) { System.out.println("Parent.handle(String)"); }
}
class Child extends Parent {
    @Override void handle(Object o) { System.out.println("Child.handle(Object)"); }
}

Parent p = new Child();
Object value = "text";

p.handle(value);       // "Child.handle(Object)"
```

Two decisions happened. The compiler saw `value` declared as `Object` and chose
`handle(Object)`. The JVM then saw the object was a `Child` and ran the
override. Change `Object value` to `String value` and the output becomes
`Parent.handle(String)`, because a different signature was selected and `Child`
does not override it.

```text
   p.handle(value)

   COMPILE TIME              RUNTIME
   which signature?          which implementation of that signature?
   -> handle(Object)         -> Child.handle(Object)
      (from value's
       declared type)           (from the object's actual class)
```

**A second classic puzzle**, mixing fields and methods:

```java
class A {
    int x = 1;
    int getX() { return x; }
}
class B extends A {
    int x = 2;
    @Override int getX() { return x; }    // 'x' here means B.x
}

A a = new B();
System.out.println(a.x);        // 1 -- field access: static binding
System.out.println(a.getX());   // 2 -- method call: dynamic binding
```

The same conceptual value gives two different answers depending on how it is
reached. This is precisely why field hiding should be avoided.

**Practical guidance.** Rely on dynamic binding for behaviour that varies by
type, and never design around static binding of fields or static methods —
readers will not expect it. If you want a value to be polymorphic, expose it
through a method, not a field.

> Key Takeaways
> - Static binding uses declared types at compile time; dynamic binding uses
>   the object's class at runtime.
> - Fields, static, private, and final methods are bound statically; ordinary
>   instance methods are bound dynamically.
> - Overload selection is static even when the chosen method is then dispatched
>   dynamically.
> - Accessing a hidden field and calling an overridden getter can return
>   different values for the same concept.
> - Expose polymorphic values through methods, never through fields.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Reproduce the `A`/`B` field-versus-getter example and explain both
>    outputs.
> 2. Write the overload-plus-override case and change the variable's declared
>    type to see the output change.
> 3. Interview: Which of these are polymorphic: fields, static methods,
>    private methods, final methods, instance methods? (Hint: which ones can a
>    subclass actually replace?)

#### Downcasting and the instanceof Operator

Upcasting loses access to subtype-specific members. *Downcasting* converts a
supertype reference back to a subtype so those members become visible again. It
is checked at runtime and fails loudly when the object is not of the expected
type.

```java
Animal animal = new Dog();       // upcast: implicit and safe

// animal.fetch();               // ERROR: Animal has no fetch()

Dog dog = (Dog) animal;          // downcast: explicit, checked at runtime
dog.fetch();                     // now visible
```

```text
   UPCAST (widening)                DOWNCAST (narrowing)

   Dog  ------>  Animal             Animal  ------>  Dog
   implicit, always safe            explicit, may throw ClassCastException

   Every Dog IS an Animal           Not every Animal IS a Dog
```

**The failure mode:**

```java
Animal animal = new Cat();
Dog dog = (Dog) animal;      // ClassCastException: class Cat cannot be cast to Dog
```

This compiles, because `Cat` and `Dog` are both `Animal` subtypes and the
compiler cannot rule it out. It fails at runtime.

The compiler does reject impossible casts between unrelated types:

```java
String s = "text";
// Integer i = (Integer) s;      // ERROR: incompatible types, no relationship
```

**`instanceof` guards the cast:**

```java
public void handle(Animal animal) {
    if (animal instanceof Dog) {        // test before casting
        Dog dog = (Dog) animal;
        dog.fetch();
    }
}
```

`instanceof` returns `false` for `null`, so a null check is unnecessary:

```java
Animal animal = null;
if (animal instanceof Dog) { }     // false, no exception
```

**Pattern matching** (Java 16) merges the test and the cast, eliminating the
repetition. It is covered fully in the next topic.

```java
if (animal instanceof Dog dog) {    // test, cast, and bind in one step
    dog.fetch();
}
```

**When downcasting signals a design problem.** A chain of `instanceof` tests
usually means polymorphism was available and was not used:

```java
// Code smell: the method must change every time a subtype is added
public double area(Shape shape) {
    if (shape instanceof Circle) {
        return Math.PI * Math.pow(((Circle) shape).getRadius(), 2);
    } else if (shape instanceof Square) {
        return Math.pow(((Square) shape).getSide(), 2);
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown shape");
}

// Better: let each shape answer for itself
public abstract class Shape {
    public abstract double area();
}
public double area(Shape shape) { return shape.area(); }
```

**When downcasting is legitimate:**

| Situation                                    | Why it is acceptable                     |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Implementing `equals(Object)`                | The signature is fixed by `Object`        |
| Reading from a pre-generics or raw collection| No type information available             |
| Deserialization and reflection               | Types are only known at runtime           |
| A sealed hierarchy with exhaustive handling  | The set of subtypes is closed and known   |
| Framework code dispatching on runtime type   | The framework cannot modify user classes  |

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {          // signature imposed by Object
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Point)) return false;
    Point other = (Point) o;               // a necessary downcast
    return x == other.x && y == other.y;
}
```

**`getClass()` versus `instanceof`.** They answer different questions:

```java
Animal a = new Dog();
System.out.println(a instanceof Animal);          // true  -- "is a kind of"
System.out.println(a.getClass() == Animal.class); // false -- "is exactly"
System.out.println(a.getClass() == Dog.class);    // true
```

`instanceof` includes subtypes; `getClass()` comparison is exact. The choice
matters when implementing `equals` across a hierarchy, a subtlety revisited in
section 3.5.

> Key Takeaways
> - Downcasting is explicit and checked at runtime, throwing
>   `ClassCastException` on mismatch.
> - `instanceof` returns `false` for `null`, so no separate null check is
>   needed.
