The maxim is "favour", not "never use". Inheritance within a deliberately
designed hierarchy is fine; inheritance across a library boundary, of a concrete
class you do not control, is where the trouble is.

> Key Takeaways
> - Inheritance couples a subclass to its superclass's implementation, including
>   undocumented self-use.
> - The `CountingSet` double-count bug is the canonical demonstration.
> - Composition with delegation avoids self-use, works with any implementation,
>   and narrows the exposed API.
> - The cost is forwarding boilerplate, mitigated by a reusable forwarding
>   class or IDE generation.
> - Inheritance remains correct for hierarchies explicitly designed and
>   documented for extension.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build the `CountingSet` bug by extending `HashSet`, confirm the double
>    count, then fix it with composition.
> 2. Write a `LoggingList` wrapper that logs every mutation and delegates the
>    rest.
> 3. Interview: Why does extending `HashSet` and overriding `add` produce a
>    wrong count from `addAll`? (Hint: what does `addAll` call internally?)

#### Delegation Patterns

Delegation is the mechanism that makes composition useful: an object forwards a
request to a component instead of implementing it itself. It is the runtime
counterpart to inheritance's compile-time reuse.

```java
public class Printer {
    private final PrintEngine engine;                // the delegate

    public Printer(PrintEngine engine) { this.engine = engine; }

    public void print(Document d) {
        engine.render(d);                            // delegate the work
    }
}
```

**Delegation plus an interface gives runtime substitution**, which inheritance
cannot do:

```java
public interface SortStrategy { void sort(int[] data); }

public class QuickSort  implements SortStrategy { public void sort(int[] d) { ... } }
public class MergeSort  implements SortStrategy { public void sort(int[] d) { ... } }

public class Sorter {
    private SortStrategy strategy;

    public Sorter(SortStrategy strategy) { this.strategy = strategy; }
    public void setStrategy(SortStrategy s) { this.strategy = s; }   // swap at runtime

    public void sort(int[] data) { strategy.sort(data); }
}

Sorter sorter = new Sorter(new QuickSort());
sorter.sort(smallArray);
sorter.setStrategy(new MergeSort());       // impossible with inheritance
sorter.sort(hugeArray);
```

A subclass is fixed at construction; a delegate can change at any time.

**Common delegation-based patterns**, each covered in chapter 9:

```java
// STRATEGY: the delegate is an interchangeable algorithm  (above)

// DECORATOR: the delegate is the same type, and the wrapper adds behaviour
public class BufferedReader extends Reader {
    private final Reader in;                  // wraps another Reader
    public int read() { ... in.read() ... }   // adds buffering
}
new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));   // JDK's own I/O design

// ADAPTER: the delegate has a different interface, translated by the wrapper
public class LegacyLoggerAdapter implements Logger {
    private final OldLogger old;
    @Override public void info(String msg) { old.writeLine("INFO: " + msg); }
}

// PROXY: the delegate is the real object, and the wrapper controls access
public class CachingRepository implements Repository {
    private final Repository real;
    private final Map<String, Entity> cache = new HashMap<>();
    @Override public Entity find(String id) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(id, real::find);      // delegate on a miss
    }
}
```

```text
   DELEGATION SHAPES

   Strategy    Context --> [ interchangeable algorithm ]
   Decorator   Wrapper --> [ same interface, adds behaviour ]
   Adapter     Adapter --> [ different interface, translates ]
   Proxy       Proxy   --> [ same interface, controls access ]

   All four are one object holding another and forwarding calls.
```

**Dependency injection** is delegation applied systematically: a class declares
what it needs and receives it rather than constructing it.

```java
// Hard-wired: impossible to test without a real database
public class OrderService {
    private final Repository repo = new PostgresRepository();
}

// Injected: the collaborator is chosen by the caller
public class OrderService {
    private final Repository repo;
    public OrderService(Repository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
}

new OrderService(new PostgresRepository());     // production
new OrderService(new InMemoryRepository());     // tests
```

This is the basis of Spring and every other dependency-injection framework, and
it is covered in chapter 13.

**Delegation in Java 8 and later** is often expressed with a functional
interface rather than a class, which removes the boilerplate entirely:

```java
public class Sorter {
    private final Consumer<int[]> strategy;
    public Sorter(Consumer<int[]> strategy) { this.strategy = strategy; }
    public void sort(int[] data) { strategy.accept(data); }
}

new Sorter(Arrays::sort);                       // a method reference as the delegate
new Sorter(d -> customSort(d, comparator));     // or a lambda
```

**The one genuine drawback** is indirection: following a delegated call means
finding which implementation was injected, which a reader cannot determine from
the source alone. Naming the field well and keeping the delegation shallow
mitigates it.

> Key Takeaways
> - Delegation forwards a request to a held component, and is the runtime
>   counterpart of inheritance.
> - Combined with an interface, it permits swapping behaviour at runtime.
> - Strategy, decorator, adapter, and proxy are all delegation with different
>   intents.
> - Dependency injection is delegation applied to a class's collaborators.
> - Functional interfaces let a delegate be a lambda or method reference
>   instead of a class.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a `Sorter` that accepts a strategy and swap it at runtime.
> 2. Write a decorator that wraps a `List` and logs every `add` call.
> 3. Interview: What can delegation do that inheritance cannot? (Hint: think
>    about when the relationship is fixed.)

#### Fragile Base Class Problem

The fragile base class problem is the general name for the failure mode seen in
`CountingSet`: a change to a superclass that is correct in isolation breaks a
subclass that was also correct in isolation.

**Cause 1: self-use changes.** The superclass alters which of its own methods it
calls internally:

```java
// Library version 1
public class Collection {
    public void addAll(List<String> items) {
        for (String s : items) add(s);          // addAll USES add
    }
    public void add(String s) { ... }
}

// A subclass written against version 1
public class LoggingCollection extends Collection {
    @Override public void add(String s) {
        log("adding " + s);
        super.add(s);
    }
    // addAll is inherited, and logs each element because addAll calls add
}

// Library version 2: an internal optimisation, documented as a bug fix
public class Collection {
    public void addAll(List<String> items) {
        bulkInsert(items);                      // no longer calls add()
    }
}
// LoggingCollection now silently logs nothing for addAll. Nothing failed
// to compile, and no test of the library caught it.
```

**Cause 2: a new superclass method collides.** A method added to the superclass
accidentally matches a subclass method's signature:

```java
// Subclass, written today
public class MyList extends AbstractList<String> {
    public boolean addIfAbsent(String s) { ... }    // our own helper
}

// A later JDK version adds AbstractList.addIfAbsent with different semantics
// -> our method silently becomes an override, and may now violate the
//    superclass's documented contract, or fail to compile if the return
//    type differs.
```

**Cause 3: a new superclass field shadows one in the subclass**, or an added
constructor changes which one is selected.

```text
   THE FRAGILE BASE CLASS PROBLEM

   Base v1                Subclass                 Result
   +----------+          +------------+
   | addAll   |--calls-->| add (over- |            works correctly
   | add      |          |  ridden)   |
   +----------+          +------------+

   Base v2                same Subclass            Result
   +----------+          +------------+
   | addAll   |--calls-->| bulkInsert |            subclass behaviour
   | add      |          | (not over- |            silently changed
   | bulkInsert|         |  ridden)   |
   +----------+          +------------+
```

**Mitigations, from strongest to weakest:**

**1. Use composition.** The delegate's internal calls are its own business, so
none of these failure modes reach the wrapper.

**2. Make the class `final`.** If nobody can extend it, its internals stay
internal:

```java
public final class ImmutableList<E> { ... }
```

**3. Design for inheritance explicitly.** Document self-use, and mark extension
points clearly. The JDK does this in places:

```java
/**
 * ...
 * @implSpec This implementation calls {@code add(e)} once for each element,
 *           in the order returned by the collection's iterator. Overriding
 *           {@code add} therefore affects this method.
 */
public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { ... }
```

The `@implSpec` tag exists precisely to turn undocumented self-use into a
documented contract.

**4. Make self-used methods `final` or `private`.** If the superclass calls a
method that subclasses cannot override, the coupling disappears:

```java
public class Collection {
    public void addAll(List<String> items) {
        for (String s : items) addInternal(s);     // private: not an override point
    }
    public void add(String s) { addInternal(s); }
    private void addInternal(String s) { ... }
}
```

**5. Provide a skeletal implementation** that subclasses extend, keeping the
concrete classes final, as `AbstractList` and `ArrayList` do.

**The practical rule** stated in *Effective Java*: design and document for
inheritance or else prohibit it. A concrete class that is neither is a
liability, because its behaviour becomes accidentally load-bearing for
subclasses you never anticipated.

| Situation                                          | Recommended approach       |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Reusing a class you do not control                  | Composition                |
| Reusing a class across a library boundary           | Composition                |
| A hierarchy you own, designed for extension         | Inheritance, documented    |
| A value type                                        | `final`, no inheritance    |
| A framework extension point                         | Abstract class or interface |

> Key Takeaways
> - A superclass change that is correct in isolation can break subclasses that
>   are also correct in isolation.
> - The causes are changed self-use, newly added colliding methods, and
>   shadowed fields.
> - Composition eliminates the problem entirely, because delegate internals stay
>   internal.
> - If inheritance is intended, document self-use with `@implSpec` and make
>   non-extension points `private` or `final`.
> - Design and document a class for inheritance, or make it `final`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a base class whose `addAll` calls `add`, subclass it, then change
>    the base to stop calling `add` and observe the silent behaviour change.
> 2. Make the self-used method private and show that the fragility disappears.
> 3. Interview: What does `@implSpec` document, and why does it exist? (Hint:
>    what does a subclass author need to know that the signature does not
>    say?)

#### Sealed Classes and Permitted Subtypes

Java historically offered only two extremes: a class was either open to
extension by anyone, or `final` and closed to everyone. Sealed classes, standard
since Java 17, add a middle option — extensible by a *known, fixed* set of
subclasses.

```java
public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle { }

public final class Circle extends Shape { }
public final class Square extends Shape { }
public non-sealed class Triangle extends Shape { }   // reopens the hierarchy
```

Any other class attempting to extend `Shape` fails to compile:

```java
// public final class Hexagon extends Shape { }
// ERROR: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Shape
```

**Every permitted subclass must choose one of three modifiers:**

| Modifier     | Meaning                                              |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `final`      | No further extension                                 |
| `sealed`     | Extensible by its own permitted list                 |
| `non-sealed` | Open to anyone again, ending the seal on that branch |

```java
public sealed interface Vehicle permits Car, Truck { }

public sealed class Car implements Vehicle permits Sedan, Hatchback { }   // nested seal
public final class Sedan extends Car { }
public final class Hatchback extends Car { }

public non-sealed class Truck implements Vehicle { }    // anyone may extend Truck
```

**The `permits` clause may be omitted** when all subclasses are in the same
source file, which is the most common form for small hierarchies:

```java
public sealed interface Result {            // no permits clause needed
    record Success(String value) implements Result { }
    record Failure(String error) implements Result { }
}
```

**The two motivations:**

**1. Modelling a closed set of alternatives.** Some concepts genuinely have a
fixed number of cases. A payment is card, transfer, or cash; a result is success
or failure. Sealing states that in the type system.

**2. Exhaustive pattern matching.** Because the compiler knows every subtype, a
`switch` over a sealed type needs no `default`:

```java
public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square { }
public record Circle(double radius) implements Shape { }
public record Square(double side)   implements Shape { }

static double area(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
        case Square s -> s.side() * s.side();
        // no default: the compiler verifies all cases are covered
    };
}
```

Adding a `Triangle` to the `permits` clause causes every such switch to fail
compilation until it is handled. That is the key benefit: the compiler finds
every place that must change, instead of a `default` branch silently
mishandling the new case at runtime.

```text
   WITHOUT SEALING                      WITH SEALING

   switch (shape) {                     switch (shape) {
     case Circle c -> ...                 case Circle c -> ...
     case Square s -> ...                 case Square s -> ...
     default -> throw ...  <- new type   }  <- new permitted type
   }                          silently                 breaks the build
                              hits here                at every switch
```

**Requirements:**

- Permitted subclasses must be in the same module, or the same package if the
  code is not modularised.
- Each permitted subclass must directly extend the sealed class.
- Each must be declared `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.

**Sealed types plus records** produce something close to algebraic data types
from functional languages, which is why the two features arrived together:

```java
public sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { }
public record Num(int value)          implements Expr { }
public record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }
public record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }

static int eval(Expr e) {
    return switch (e) {
        case Num n -> n.value();
        case Add(Expr l, Expr r) -> eval(l) + eval(r);    // record pattern
        case Mul(Expr l, Expr r) -> eval(l) * eval(r);
    };
}
```

Ten lines give a complete, exhaustively-checked expression evaluator.

| Class kind   | Who may extend                    | Use for                       |
| ------------ | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| open (default)| Anyone                           | Framework extension points    |
| `final`      | Nobody                            | Value types, security-critical |
| `sealed`     | A fixed, declared list            | Closed sets of alternatives   |
| `abstract`   | Anyone, and must be extended      | Partial implementations       |

> Key Takeaways
> - `sealed` permits extension by a declared, fixed list of subclasses.
> - Each permitted subclass must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
> - The `permits` clause is optional when subclasses share the source file.
> - Sealing enables exhaustive `switch` with no `default`, so a new subtype
>   breaks the build rather than failing at runtime.
> - Sealed interfaces plus records model closed sets of alternatives
>   concisely.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define a sealed `PaymentMethod` with three permitted records and write an
>    exhaustive switch over it.
> 2. Add a fourth permitted type and observe which code stops compiling.
> 3. Interview: What does `non-sealed` mean, and why would you use it? (Hint:
>    what if one branch of the hierarchy should stay open?)


<a id="4-interfaces-and-abstraction-contracts"></a>
## 4. Interfaces and Abstraction Contracts

Chapter 3 used inheritance to share implementation down a single family tree.
This chapter introduces the other half of Java's abstraction toolkit: the
interface, which describes *what* a type can do without committing to *how* or
to any particular ancestry. Interfaces are how unrelated classes acquire a
common capability, how libraries stay swappable, and how lambdas, collections,
and nearly every framework API are wired together; the chapter closes with
enums, records, and nested types, the specialised class forms that most often
appear alongside interface-driven designs.

<a id="41-interface-fundamentals"></a>
### 4.1 Interface Fundamentals

An interface is a named set of abilities that any class can promise to provide,
regardless of what it already extends.

#### Declaring and Implementing Interfaces

Inheritance couples a subclass to one specific parent. That is fine when the
types genuinely form a family, but most real requirements cut across families.
A `Robot`, a `Dog`, and a `Car` share no sensible superclass, yet all three can
*move*. You want a way to say "these types support this operation" without
inventing an artificial common ancestor.

An interface does exactly that. Think of it as a job description rather than a
family tree: it lists the tasks a candidate must be able to perform and says
nothing about who they are or where they came from.

```java
public interface Movable {
    void move(int distance);        // implicitly public and abstract
    void stop();                    // no body: the interface states WHAT, not HOW
}
```

Two rules of interface declarations save a lot of confusion:

- Every method is implicitly `public abstract` unless it is `default`,
  `static`, or `private` (covered in 4.2). Writing `public abstract` is legal
  but redundant, and most codebases omit it.
- An interface cannot be instantiated, because none of its abstract methods
  have bodies.

A class signs the contract with `implements` and must supply a body for every
abstract method it inherits:

```java
public class Robot implements Movable {
    private int position;

    @Override                                    // compiler-checked: catches typos
    public void move(int distance) {
        position += distance;
        System.out.println("Robot rolled to " + position);
    }

    @Override
    public void stop() {
        System.out.println("Robot powered down");
    }
}

public class Dog implements Movable {            // unrelated to Robot entirely
    @Override
    public void move(int distance) {
        System.out.println("Dog ran " + distance + " metres");
    }

    @Override
    public void stop() {
        System.out.println("Dog sat down");
    }
}
```

The implementing method must be `public`. This surprises people: the interface
method is implicitly public, and chapter 3 established that an override may
never reduce visibility, so anything less than `public` fails to compile.

```java
public class Broken implements Movable {
    @Override
    void move(int distance) { }      // ERROR: attempting to assign weaker
                                     // access privileges; was public
    ...
}
```

If a class cannot implement every method, it must be declared `abstract` and
leave the remainder to its own subclasses:

```java
public abstract class PartialMover implements Movable {
    @Override
    public void stop() { System.out.println("Halted"); }
    // move(int) is left abstract; a concrete subclass must supply it
}
```

```text
        <<interface>>
          Movable
     +move(int): void
     +stop(): void
            ^
            | implements  (dashed in UML)
   +--------+--------+
   |        |        |
 Robot     Dog      Car          no shared superclass required
```

> Key Takeaways
> - An interface declares capability without implementation, letting unrelated
>   classes share a type.
> - Interface methods are implicitly `public abstract`; implementations must
>   declare them `public`.
> - A class uses `implements` and must define every abstract method, or be
>   declared `abstract` itself.
> - Interfaces cannot be instantiated directly.
> - `@Override` on implementing methods is optional but catches signature
>   mistakes at compile time.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Drawable` interface with a `draw()` method and implement it in
>    `Circle` and `TextLabel`.
> 2. Try implementing an interface method with default (package-private)
>    visibility and read the compiler error carefully.
> 3. Interview: Why can an interface not be instantiated, and what exactly does
>    `new Runnable() { ... }` create then? (Hint: something is being declared
>    between those braces.)

#### Interfaces as Behavioral Contracts

A signature is only half of what an interface promises. `int compare(T a, T b)`
tells the compiler the shape of the call, but not that the result must be
negative, zero, or positive consistently, or that `compare(a, b)` and
`compare(b, a)` must disagree in sign. Those rules live in the documentation
and are every bit as binding: code that calls the method relies on them, and an
implementation that breaks them produces corrupt behaviour far from the bug.

This is the difference between the **syntactic contract** (enforced by the
compiler) and the **semantic contract** (enforced only by discipline and
tests).

```java
/**
 * A rule for accepting or rejecting an order.
 *
 * Implementations MUST be side-effect free and MUST return the same
 * answer for the same order. Callers may invoke check() repeatedly,
 * in any order, and from multiple threads.
 */
public interface OrderRule {
    boolean check(Order order);
}
```

```java
// Honours the contract: pure, repeatable, thread-safe.
public class MinimumTotalRule implements OrderRule {
    private final double minimum;

    public MinimumTotalRule(double minimum) { this.minimum = minimum; }

    @Override
    public boolean check(Order order) { return order.total() >= minimum; }
}

// Compiles perfectly; violates the contract.
public class OncePerOrderRule implements OrderRule {
    private boolean used = false;

    @Override
    public boolean check(Order order) {
        if (used) return false;      // second call gives a different answer
        used = true;                 // hidden mutable state
        return true;
    }
}
```

Both classes satisfy the compiler. Only the first is usable by a framework that
caches, retries, or parallelises rule evaluation. When you write an interface,
document the obligations; when you implement one, read them.

Contracts commonly specify:

| Obligation        | Typical wording                                        |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Null handling     | "throws `NullPointerException` if `order` is null"     |
| Return range      | "returns a value in [0, 1]"                            |
| Idempotence       | "repeated calls have no additional effect"             |
| Exceptions        | "throws `IllegalStateException` if not yet opened"     |
| Threading         | "implementations must be safe for concurrent use"      |
| Ordering relation | "must be transitive and consistent with `equals`"      |

> Key Takeaways
> - An interface carries a syntactic contract the compiler checks and a
>   semantic contract only documentation and tests can enforce.
> - Document preconditions, postconditions, null behaviour, exceptions, and
>   threading expectations on the interface, not on each implementation.
> - Code that compiles can still violate the contract, usually by hiding
>   mutable state or returning inconsistent results.
> - Callers are entitled to rely on the documented contract; that reliance is
>   what makes implementations interchangeable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write Javadoc for a `Validator` interface stating null handling and
>    idempotence, then implement it twice.
> 2. Deliberately write an implementation that breaks the stated contract and
>    describe a caller that would misbehave as a result.
> 3. Interview: `Comparable` requires consistency with `equals`. What goes
>    wrong in a `TreeSet` if an implementation ignores that? (Hint: think about
>    which method the set actually uses to detect duplicates.)

#### Implementing Multiple Interfaces

Java permits only one superclass because inheriting two sets of *fields and
implementations* creates ambiguity. Inheriting two sets of *requirements* does
not: if two interfaces each demand a method, the class writes one method that
satisfies both. So a class may implement any number of interfaces.

This is how Java gets the useful part of multiple inheritance without the
diamond problem. A type can be a `Vehicle` by ancestry while separately being
`Serializable`, `Comparable`, and `Rentable` by capability.

```java
public interface Swimmer { void swim(); }
public interface Flyer   { void fly(); }
public interface Diver   { void dive(); }

public class Duck extends Bird implements Swimmer, Flyer, Diver {
    @Override public void swim() { System.out.println("Paddling"); }
    @Override public void fly()  { System.out.println("Flapping"); }
    @Override public void dive() { System.out.println("Ducking under"); }
}
```

The order matters syntactically: `extends` comes before `implements`, and there
may be only one `extends` clause for a class.

```java
// public class Duck implements Swimmer extends Bird { }   // ERROR: wrong order
```

When two interfaces declare a method with the same signature, one
implementation satisfies both:

```java
public interface Walker { void move(); }
public interface Roller { void move(); }

public class Skateboarder implements Walker, Roller {
    @Override
    public void move() { System.out.println("Pushing off"); }  // satisfies both
}
```

If the signatures match but the return types are incompatible, the class is
simply impossible to write and the compiler rejects it:

```java
public interface A { int  value(); }
public interface B { long value(); }
// public class C implements A, B { }   // ERROR: unrelated return types
```

Each implemented interface is an independent view of the object:

```java
Duck duck = new Duck();
Swimmer s = duck;        // seen as a swimmer
Flyer   f = duck;        // seen as a flyer
s.swim();
f.fly();
// s.fly();              // ERROR: the Swimmer view has no fly()
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A class may implement unlimited interfaces but extend only one class.
> - `extends` must precede `implements` in the declaration.
> - Identical abstract signatures from different interfaces are satisfied by a
>   single method.
> - Same-name methods with incompatible return types make the class
>   uncompilable.
> - Each interface gives a narrower view of the same object, exposing only its
>   own members.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define `Printable` and `Scannable` and write one `MultiFunctionDevice`
>    implementing both.
> 2. Create two interfaces declaring `String id()` and `int id()` and try to
>    implement both in one class; explain the error.
> 3. Interview: Java bans multiple class inheritance but allows multiple
>    interface inheritance. What changed in Java 8 that made this slightly less
>    clear-cut? (Hint: interfaces gained something they never had before.)

#### Interface Constants

Every field declared in an interface is implicitly `public static final`. There
is no such thing as an instance field in an interface, because an interface has
no instances and no state of its own.

```java
public interface Physics {
    double GRAVITY = 9.81;          // implicitly public static final
    int MAX_RETRIES = 3;            // must be initialised at declaration
    // int counter;                 // ERROR: = expected (no value given)
}
```

Because the modifiers are implicit, the constant is accessible through the
interface name, and, more confusingly, through any implementing class:

```java
System.out.println(Physics.GRAVITY);        // preferred: names the source

public class Rocket implements Physics {
    public double weight(double mass) {
        return mass * GRAVITY;              // inherited, usable unqualified
    }
}
System.out.println(Rocket.GRAVITY);         // legal, but obscures the origin
```

That last line illustrates the **constant interface antipattern**: implementing
an interface purely to import its constants. It pollutes the class's public API
with fields that are an implementation detail, and it commits the type to an
interface it has no behavioural relationship with. Prefer a final class of
static members, or an enum:

```java
public final class PhysicsConstants {
    public static final double GRAVITY = 9.81;

    private PhysicsConstants() { }          // prevent instantiation
}

// At the call site, if you want unqualified names:
import static com.example.PhysicsConstants.GRAVITY;
```

| Placement                   | When it is appropriate                          |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Constant in an interface    | Value is part of the contract itself, e.g. a sentinel returned by the interface's methods |
| `public final` utility class | General shared constants unrelated to a contract |
| `enum`                      | A fixed set of related named values              |
| `private static final` field | Constant used only inside one class             |

> Key Takeaways
> - Interface fields are always `public static final`, and must be assigned at
>   declaration.
> - Interfaces cannot hold instance state.
> - Constants are inherited by implementing classes and can be referenced
>   unqualified, which hides where they came from.
> - Implementing an interface only to gain its constants is an antipattern; use
>   a utility class with static import, or an enum.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Declare an interface with two constants and read one through the interface
>    name and through an implementing class.
> 2. Attempt to declare a non-final or uninitialised field in an interface and
>    note the errors.
> 3. Rewrite a constant interface as a final utility class with a private
>    constructor, and use `import static` at the call site.

#### Interface Inheritance with extends

Interfaces form their own hierarchy, separate from the class hierarchy. One
interface `extends` another to say "everything that contract requires, plus
more". Unlike classes, an interface may extend several interfaces at once,
because it only accumulates requirements and never conflicting state.

```java
public interface Readable  { String read(); }
public interface Writable  { void write(String data); }

public interface ReadWrite extends Readable, Writable {   // multiple extends
    default void copyFrom(ReadWrite other) {              // adds its own member
        write(other.read());
    }
}
```

A class implementing `ReadWrite` must supply `read()`, `write(String)`, and may
inherit `copyFrom`:

```java
public class MemoryBuffer implements ReadWrite {
    private String contents = "";

    @Override public String read() { return contents; }
    @Override public void write(String data) { this.contents = data; }
}
```

The subtype relationship works exactly as you would expect:

```java
MemoryBuffer buffer = new MemoryBuffer();
Readable  r = buffer;                    // ReadWrite IS-A Readable
Writable  w = buffer;
System.out.println(buffer instanceof Readable);    // true
```

```text
   Readable        Writable         interfaces may have many parents
        \             /
         \           /
          ReadWrite                 extends both
              ^
              : implements
         MemoryBuffer               a class implements the leaf
```

Note the deliberate asymmetry in vocabulary, which is a common exam question:

| Relationship            | Keyword      | How many allowed |
| ----------------------- | ------------ | ---------------- |
| Class to class          | `extends`    | Exactly one      |
| Class to interface      | `implements` | Any number       |
| Interface to interface  | `extends`    | Any number       |
| Interface to class      | not possible | -                |

> Key Takeaways
> - An interface extends other interfaces with `extends`, never `implements`.
> - Interface inheritance is multiple: one interface may extend many.
> - A sub-interface inherits all abstract and default methods and may add more.
> - Implementing a sub-interface obliges the class to satisfy the entire
>   inherited set.
> - Every ancestor interface is a valid supertype for assignment and
>   `instanceof`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build `Identifiable`, `Timestamped`, and `AuditRecord extends
>    Identifiable, Timestamped`; implement the last in one class.
> 2. Try writing `interface X implements Y` and explain the compiler error.
> 3. Interview: `List` extends `Collection` extends `Iterable`. What does a
>    method taking `Iterable<String>` gain over one taking `List<String>`?
>    (Hint: think about which callers you exclude.)

#### Interfaces as Reference Types

The real payoff of interfaces appears at the *declaration site*. Declaring a
variable, parameter, field, or return type as the interface rather than the
concrete class means the code depends only on the capability, so the
implementation behind it can change without touching a single caller. This is
**programming to an interface**.

```java
// Tightly coupled: this method can only ever accept an ArrayList.
public void printAll(ArrayList<String> items) { ... }

// Flexible: accepts ArrayList, LinkedList, Arrays.asList(...), and any
// future List implementation, including test doubles.
public void printAll(List<String> items) { ... }
```

The same principle applies to local variables and fields:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();        // swap the right side freely
names = new LinkedList<>(names);               // no other line needs to change

Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
```

Polymorphic dispatch works through interface references exactly as it does
through class references: the method that runs is decided by the object, not
the reference:

```java
List<Movable> fleet = List.of(new Robot(), new Dog(), new Car());

for (Movable m : fleet) {
    m.move(10);      // Robot.move, Dog.move, or Car.move, chosen at runtime
}
```

An interface reference exposes only the interface's members. To reach
implementation-specific behaviour you must downcast, guarded by `instanceof`:

```java
Movable m = new Robot();
// m.recharge();                     // ERROR: not part of Movable

if (m instanceof Robot robot) {      // pattern matching, Java 16+
    robot.recharge();                // safe: the compiler knows the type here
}
```

Needing that cast often is a design smell: it suggests the interface is missing
a method, or the parameter type is too abstract for what the code actually
does.

Interfaces also make testing straightforward, because a hand-written or mocked
implementation slots in wherever the real one does:

```java
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;      // an interface

    public OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) {   // injected, not created
        this.gateway = gateway;
    }
}

// In production:
new OrderService(new StripeGateway());
// In a unit test:
new OrderService(order -> true);           // a trivial stub implementation
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Declare variables, parameters, and return types with the most general
>   interface that supports what the code needs.
> - The reference type decides which members are visible; the object decides
>   which implementation runs.
> - Programming to interfaces lets implementations be swapped, including for
>   test doubles, without changing callers.
> - Frequent downcasting from an interface signals a design problem.
> - Interface-typed constructor parameters are the basis of dependency
>   injection, revisited in chapter 13.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a method that takes `ArrayList<Order>` to take `List<Order>` and
>    call it with `List.of(...)`.
> 2. Store several implementations of one interface in a `List` and loop over
>    them, observing dynamic dispatch.
> 3. Interview: What does "programming to an interface, not an implementation"
>    buy you in practice? (Hint: name two things that become possible that were
>    not before, one about change and one about testing.)

<a id="42-modern-interface-features"></a>
### 4.2 Modern Interface Features

Java 8 and later relaxed the rule that interfaces hold no code, so that
libraries could grow without breaking the classes that already implement them.

#### Default Methods and Backward Compatibility

Before Java 8, adding a method to a published interface was a breaking change:
every existing implementation stopped compiling overnight. That froze the
standard library. `Collection` could not gain `stream()` without invalidating
every custom collection ever written.

A **default method** solves this by shipping an implementation inside the
interface. Existing classes inherit it silently and keep compiling; classes
that want different behaviour override it.

```java
public interface Logger {
    void log(String message);                      // still abstract

    default void logError(String message) {        // new, with a body
        log("ERROR: " + message);                  // may call abstract methods
    }

    default void logAll(List<String> messages) {
        for (String m : messages) log(m);
    }
}
```

```java
public class ConsoleLogger implements Logger {
    @Override
    public void log(String message) { System.out.println(message); }
    // logError and logAll come for free
}

ConsoleLogger logger = new ConsoleLogger();
logger.logError("disk full");        // prints "ERROR: disk full"
```

Any implementation may override a default to specialise it:

```java
public class TimestampLogger implements Logger {
    @Override public void log(String message) { System.out.println(message); }

    @Override
    public void logError(String message) {             // replaces the default
        log("[" + java.time.Instant.now() + "] ERROR: " + message);
    }
}
```

Inside an overriding method you can still reach the inherited default with the
`InterfaceName.super` syntax:

```java
public class CountingLogger implements Logger {
    private int errors = 0;

    @Override public void log(String message) { System.out.println(message); }

    @Override
    public void logError(String message) {
        errors++;
        Logger.super.logError(message);    // delegate to the interface default
    }
}
```

Two limits keep defaults honest. A default method has no access to instance
fields, because interfaces have none, so it can only work through other
interface methods. And a default cannot override a method of `Object`:

```java
public interface Bad {
    // default String toString() { return "nope"; }   // ERROR: not allowed
}
```

Real examples from the standard library are worth recognising:
`Collection.stream()`, `Collection.removeIf(...)`, `List.sort(...)`,
`Iterable.forEach(...)`, `Comparator.reversed()`, `Map.getOrDefault(...)`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `default` methods carry an implementation inside an interface so new
>   methods can be added without breaking existing implementors.
> - They may call the interface's abstract methods but cannot touch instance
>   fields, because interfaces have no state.
> - Any implementing class may override a default; `Interface.super.method()`
>   calls the inherited version.
> - Defaults cannot override `equals`, `hashCode`, or `toString`.
> - Defaults are for evolution and convenience, not a replacement for abstract
>   classes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `default String describe()` to an existing interface and confirm old
>    implementations still compile.
> 2. Override that default in one class and call the inherited version with
>    `Interface.super`.
> 3. Interview: Do default methods give Java multiple inheritance? (Hint:
>    distinguish inheritance of behaviour from inheritance of state.)

#### Static Interface Methods

Helper methods related to an interface used to live in a separate companion
class: `Collections` for `Collection`, `Arrays` for arrays, `Paths` for `Path`.
That split forced readers to know two names for one concept. Since Java 8 an
interface can hold its own `static` methods, keeping the factory and utility
code next to the contract it serves.

```java
public interface Shape {
    double area();

    static Shape circle(double radius) {          // factory method
        return () -> Math.PI * radius * radius;   // a lambda IS a Shape here
    }

    static Shape rectangle(double w, double h) {
        return () -> w * h;
    }

    static Shape largest(Shape a, Shape b) {      // utility method
        return a.area() >= b.area() ? a : b;
    }
}
```

```java
Shape c = Shape.circle(2);            // called on the interface name only
Shape r = Shape.rectangle(3, 4);
System.out.println(Shape.largest(c, r).area());
```

The critical difference from default methods: **static interface methods are
not inherited.** They are not visible through an implementing class or an
instance reference.

```java
public class Square implements Shape {
    private final double side;
    public Square(double side) { this.side = side; }
    @Override public double area() { return side * side; }
}

// Square.circle(2);          // ERROR: not inherited
// new Square(2).circle(2);   // ERROR: static method on an instance
Shape.circle(2);              // the only legal form
```

| Member kind | Has a body | Inherited | Called on             |
| ----------- | ---------- | --------- | --------------------- |
| `abstract`  | No         | Yes       | An instance           |
| `default`   | Yes        | Yes       | An instance           |
| `static`    | Yes        | No        | The interface name    |
| `private`   | Yes        | No        | Inside the interface  |

Standard library examples: `List.of(...)`, `Map.entry(...)`,
`Comparator.comparing(...)`, `Function.identity()`, `Predicate.not(...)`.

> Key Takeaways
> - Interfaces may declare `static` methods with bodies, typically factories or
>   utilities for the type.
> - Static interface methods are not inherited and must be qualified with the
>   interface name.
> - They remove the need for separate companion utility classes.
> - They cannot be overridden, so their behaviour is fixed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a static `of(...)` factory to an interface you wrote and use it to
>    create instances.
> 2. Try calling that static method through an implementing class and explain
>    the error.
> 3. Compare `Collections.sort(list)` with `list.sort(null)` and say which
>    method kind each one is.

#### Private Interface Methods

Once interfaces could hold code, they could hold *duplicated* code. Two default
methods that share logic had nowhere to put it: a second default would expose
an implementation detail as public API, and a static method could not touch the
instance. Java 9 added `private` interface methods for exactly this.

```java
public interface Report {
    List<String> rows();

    default String asCsv() {
        return format(",");            // shared logic, hidden from callers
    }

    default String asTsv() {
        return format("\t");
    }

    private String format(String separator) {      // instance private helper
        return String.join(separator, rows());     // may call abstract methods
    }

    static Report empty() {
        return withRows(List.of());
    }

    private static Report withRows(List<String> rows) {   // static private
        return () -> rows;
    }
}
```

The rules are short:

- A `private` method must have a body and cannot be `abstract`.
- A private instance method may be called from `default` and other private
  instance methods, and can invoke abstract methods.
- A `private static` method may be called from `static`, `default`, and private
  methods.
- Neither form is inherited, overridable, or visible outside the interface.

```java
public class SalesReport implements Report {
    @Override public List<String> rows() { return List.of("a", "b"); }
    // format(...) is invisible here; only asCsv() and asTsv() are inherited
}
// new SalesReport().format(",");     // ERROR: format has private access
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `private` interface methods hold logic shared between default or static
>   methods without exposing it.
> - They must have a body; `private abstract` is a contradiction and illegal.
> - Private instance methods serve `default` methods; `private static` methods
>   serve `static` ones.
> - They are never inherited and never part of the published contract.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an interface with two default methods that duplicate logic, then
>    extract the shared part into a private method.
> 2. Try calling the private method from an implementing class and note the
>    error.
> 3. Explain when a helper should be `private` versus `private static` in an
>    interface.

#### Resolving Conflicting Default Methods

Multiple interface inheritance was safe while interfaces carried no code. Once
defaults arrived, a class could inherit two competing bodies for the same
signature, which is the diamond problem in a new form. Java does not guess: it
refuses to compile and makes you choose.

```java
public interface Alarm  { default void trigger() { System.out.println("Beep"); } }
public interface Siren  { default void trigger() { System.out.println("Wail"); } }

// public class Device implements Alarm, Siren { }
// ERROR: class Device inherits unrelated defaults for trigger() from
//        types Alarm and Siren
```

The class must override and may delegate explicitly:

```java
public class Device implements Alarm, Siren {
    @Override
    public void trigger() {
        Alarm.super.trigger();      // pick one
        Siren.super.trigger();      // or both, in your chosen order
        System.out.println("Flashing lights");   // or something else entirely
    }
}
```

When there is no genuine ambiguity, Java applies two resolution rules in order:

**1. Classes win over interfaces.** A method inherited from a superclass beats
any default with the same signature.

```java
public class BaseDevice {
    public void trigger() { System.out.println("Class wins"); }
}

public class Siren2 extends BaseDevice implements Alarm { }

new Siren2().trigger();      // "Class wins": no error, no ambiguity
```

**2. The most specific interface wins.** If one interface extends the other,
its default overrides the inherited one.

```java
public interface LoudAlarm extends Alarm {
    @Override default void trigger() { System.out.println("BEEEEP"); }
}

public class Klaxon implements Alarm, LoudAlarm { }   // fine

new Klaxon().trigger();      // "BEEEEP": LoudAlarm is more specific
```

```text
  Conflict?  ->  Is one inherited from a CLASS?  -> yes: the class method wins
                       | no
                 Is one interface a SUBTYPE of the other? -> yes: subtype wins
                       | no
                 COMPILE ERROR: the class must override and choose
```

Note that an abstract redeclaration cancels a default, forcing implementors to
decide:

```java
public interface StrictAlarm extends Alarm {
    @Override void trigger();       // reinstated as abstract: no default now
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Inheriting unrelated defaults with the same signature is a compile error,
>   not a silent choice.
> - The fix is to override the method, optionally delegating with
>   `Interface.super.method()`.
> - A superclass method always beats an interface default.
> - The most specific interface wins when one extends the other.
> - Redeclaring a method as abstract in a sub-interface removes the inherited
>   default.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create two interfaces with identical default methods and a class
>    implementing both; resolve the error two different ways.
> 2. Demonstrate the class-wins rule by adding a superclass with the same
>    method.
> 3. Interview: Why does Java report an error here instead of choosing the
>    first interface listed? (Hint: what would happen to your program if
>    someone reordered the `implements` clause?)

#### Marker Interfaces

Some information is about a type as a whole rather than about any method it
has: "instances of this class may be serialised", "this class supports
cloning". A **marker interface** carries that fact and nothing else, with an
empty body. Implementing it is a statement about the class, checkable at
runtime with `instanceof`.

```java
public interface Auditable { }        // no members at all

public class Invoice implements Auditable { }
public class TempFile { }             // deliberately not auditable
```

```java
public void process(Object record) {
    if (record instanceof Auditable) {      // the marker is the whole test
        writeAuditTrail(record);
    }
}
```

The standard library uses several: `Serializable`, `Cloneable`,
`RandomAccess`, and `Remote`. Each changes how other code, often inside the
JVM or the library itself, treats the object. `Collections.binarySearch`, for
instance, chooses a different algorithm for a `List` that implements
`RandomAccess`.

Markers have a real advantage over annotations: they create a **type**, so the
compiler can enforce them in a signature.

```java
public void archive(Auditable record) { ... }    // compile-time guarantee
archive(new Invoice());                          // fine
// archive(new TempFile());                      // ERROR: caught at compile time
```

| Aspect                  | Marker interface       | Annotation (`@Retention(RUNTIME)`) |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Creates a type          | Yes                    | No                                 |
| Compile-time checking   | Yes, via parameters    | No, only reflection at runtime     |
| Carries extra data      | No                     | Yes, through elements              |
| Applies to              | Classes and interfaces | Classes, methods, fields, params   |
| Inherited by subclasses | Always                 | Only with `@Inherited`             |

Modern Java usually prefers annotations when the marker needs parameters or
must apply to methods, and marker interfaces when the mark should be enforced
by the compiler. Annotations are covered in chapter 10.

> Key Takeaways
> - A marker interface has no members and exists to tag a type with metadata.
> - Tests are written with `instanceof` or enforced through parameter types.
> - `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, and `RandomAccess` are the canonical examples.
> - Markers give compile-time safety; annotations give flexibility and data.
> - Do not add a marker where a real method would express the capability
>   better.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define a `Cacheable` marker and a method that only caches objects
>    implementing it.
> 2. Rewrite the same idea as a runtime annotation and compare how the check
>    looks.
> 3. Interview: `Cloneable` is often called a broken marker. Why? (Hint: which
>    class declares `clone()`, and what visibility does it have?)

#### Functional Interfaces and @FunctionalInterface

An interface with exactly one abstract method describes a single operation, so
an instance of it is effectively just a function. Java 8 made that observation
into a language feature: wherever such an interface is expected, you can supply
a lambda expression or a method reference instead of writing a class.

Such an interface is called a **functional interface**, and its single abstract
method is the SAM (single abstract method).

```java
@FunctionalInterface                    // optional, but compiler-enforced
public interface Transformer {
    String apply(String input);         // exactly one abstract method
}
```

```java
Transformer upper   = s -> s.toUpperCase();      // lambda
Transformer trimmed = String::trim;              // method reference
Transformer verbose = new Transformer() {        // anonymous class, pre-Java 8
    @Override public String apply(String input) { return "<" + input + ">"; }
};

System.out.println(upper.apply("hello"));        // HELLO
```

The annotation does not make an interface functional; the single abstract
method does. What `@FunctionalInterface` adds is a compile-time guard against
accidentally breaking that property later:

```java
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Broken {
    String apply(String input);
    // int count();          // ERROR: Broken is not a functional interface
                             //        (multiple non-overriding abstract methods)
}
```

Three kinds of member do *not* count against the single-abstract-method rule:

```java
@FunctionalInterface
public interface StillFunctional {
    String apply(String input);                       // the one SAM

    default String twice(String s) {                  // defaults don't count
        return apply(apply(s));
    }

    static StillFunctional identity() {               // statics don't count
        return s -> s;
    }

    boolean equals(Object other);                     // public Object methods
                                                      // don't count either
}
```

That last rule explains why `Comparator` is a functional interface despite
declaring both `compare` and `equals`: `equals` is already public in `Object`,
so it is not counted.

The standard library ships a full set of ready-made functional interfaces in
`java.util.function`, covered in chapter 8:

| Interface        | Abstract method     | Typical use                |
| ---------------- | ------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `Runnable`       | `void run()`        | A task with no input/output |
| `Supplier<T>`    | `T get()`           | Produces a value           |
| `Consumer<T>`    | `void accept(T)`    | Uses a value               |
| `Function<T,R>`  | `R apply(T)`        | Transforms a value         |
| `Predicate<T>`   | `boolean test(T)`   | Tests a condition          |
| `Comparator<T>`  | `int compare(T,T)`  | Defines an ordering        |

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("bob", "ann", "cy"));
names.removeIf(n -> n.length() < 3);             // Predicate<String>
names.forEach(System.out::println);              // Consumer<String>
names.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length));// Comparator<String>
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A functional interface has exactly one abstract method and can be
>   implemented by a lambda or method reference.
> - `@FunctionalInterface` is optional documentation that makes the compiler
>   enforce the single-method rule.
> - `default`, `static`, `private`, and public `Object` methods do not break
>   functionality.
> - `java.util.function` provides standard functional interfaces; prefer them
>   over inventing your own.
> - Lambdas are the syntax; functional interfaces are the type system that
>   makes them work.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `@FunctionalInterface` called `Validator` with
>    `boolean validate(String)` and implement it with a lambda.
> 2. Add a second abstract method and observe the compiler error, then convert
>    that method into a `default` and watch it compile again.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Comparator` still a functional interface even though it
>    declares two abstract methods? (Hint: look up where `equals` is originally
>    declared.)

<a id="43-abstract-classes-versus-interfaces"></a>
### 4.3 Abstract Classes versus Interfaces

Both express abstraction, and since Java 8 they overlap more than they used to,
so choosing between them is a design decision rather than a technical one.

#### Capability Comparison

Chapter 3 introduced abstract classes; this chapter introduced interfaces.
Because interfaces gained method bodies in Java 8 and private methods in Java
9, the practical gap between them has narrowed to two things: **state** and
**how many you can have**. Everything else is detail.

```java
public abstract class AbstractAccount {
    protected double balance;                  // state: only a class can do this
    private final String id;                   // private instance field

    protected AbstractAccount(String id) { this.id = id; }   // constructor

    public abstract double interestRate();     // abstract method
    public double interestEarned() { return balance * interestRate(); }
    protected void audit() { }                 // protected: interfaces cannot
}

public interface Account {
    double interestRate();                     // abstract
    double MIN_BALANCE = 0.0;                  // public static final only
    default double interestEarned(double balance) {
        return balance * interestRate();       // must receive state as a param
    }
}
```

| Feature                      | Abstract class            | Interface                     |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Instance fields (state)      | Yes                       | No                            |
| Constants                    | Any modifier              | `public static final` only    |
| Constructors                 | Yes, for subclass use     | No                            |
| Abstract methods             | Yes                       | Yes                           |
| Concrete methods             | Yes                       | Yes, as `default`/`static`    |
| `private` methods            | Yes                       | Yes, since Java 9             |
| `protected` members          | Yes                       | No                            |
| `static` methods             | Yes, inherited            | Yes, not inherited            |
| `final` methods              | Yes                       | No                            |
| Can be instantiated          | No                        | No                            |
| How many per class           | Exactly one (`extends`)   | Unlimited (`implements`)      |
| Can override `Object` methods | Yes                      | No                            |
| Initialisation blocks        | Yes                       | No                            |
| Default member access        | Package-private           | `public`                      |

Two rows deserve emphasis because they are the source of most exam questions.
An interface cannot declare `protected` or `final` methods, and it cannot
provide `toString`, `equals`, or `hashCode`. An abstract class can do all of
that, but a class can only have one of them.

> Key Takeaways
> - Interfaces cannot hold instance state, constructors, or `protected` and
>   `final` methods.
> - Abstract classes can do everything an interface can except be implemented
>   more than once per class.
> - Interface members are public by default; class members are package-private
>   by default.
> - Neither can be instantiated directly.
> - Default methods narrowed the gap but did not close it: state remains the
>   dividing line.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same small contract twice, once as an abstract class and once as
>    an interface, and list what each version can express that the other
>    cannot.
> 2. Try declaring a `protected default` method in an interface and read the
>    error.
> 3. Attempt to give an interface a constructor and explain why the language
>    forbids it.

#### State versus Behavior Contracts

The cleanest way to decide is to ask what you are actually sharing. If
subtypes must share *data* and the invariants that protect it, that is a class.
If they must share only an *ability*, that is an interface.

An abstract class can own fields and therefore enforce invariants in a
constructor. Every subclass inherits a valid, initialised state:

```java
public abstract class Employee {
    private final String name;          // shared state, guarded
    private double salary;

    protected Employee(String name, double salary) {
        if (salary < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative salary");
        this.name = name;               // the invariant holds for EVERY subclass
        this.salary = salary;
    }

    public final String name() { return name; }     // final: cannot be subverted
    public abstract double bonus();                 // subclasses differ here
}
```

An interface has no such power. A default method can only reach state through
abstract accessors that the implementing class supplies:

```java
public interface Taxable {
    double taxableIncome();                         // the class provides state

    default double taxDue(double rate) {            // behaviour only
        return taxableIncome() * rate;
    }
}
```

Trying to keep state in an interface fails immediately:

```java
public interface Counter {
    // private int count = 0;     // ERROR: fields are public static final,
                                  //        and shared by ALL implementors
    int count();                  // the honest alternative
}
```

The consequence is important: a field in an interface is one value shared
across the whole program, not per object. If you write `int count = 0;` in an
interface, you have created a constant that no instance can change.

| You need to share                       | Use              |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| Fields and the invariants protecting them | Abstract class |
| A constructor that validates on creation  | Abstract class |
| A capability unrelated types can adopt    | Interface      |
| A method signature and nothing more       | Interface       |
| Behaviour derived entirely from other methods | Interface with defaults |

The two combine well. A common arrangement is a public interface for the
contract plus an abstract class that holds the shared state for those
implementations that want it, which is the skeletal implementation pattern
covered at the end of this subchapter.

> Key Takeaways
> - Abstract classes exist to share state plus the invariants that protect it.
> - Interfaces exist to share capability across unrelated types.
> - Interface fields are constants shared program-wide, never per-instance
>   state.
> - Interface default methods can only reach state through abstract accessors.
> - A constructor that must validate arguments requires a class.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Design `Vehicle` as an abstract class with a validated `wheels` field and
>    `Rentable` as an interface, then combine them in `RentalCar`.
> 2. Declare `int total = 0;` inside an interface and try to modify it from two
>    instances; explain what happens.
> 3. Convert an abstract class that has no fields into an interface and note
>    what you had to change.

#### Multiple Inheritance of Type

Java separates three things that other languages bundle together: inheritance
of type (being usable as a `T`), of implementation (getting method bodies), and
of state (getting fields). Java allows multiple inheritance of the first two,
and single inheritance of the third.

| Kind                         | Multiple allowed? | Mechanism           |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------- |
| Type (subtyping)             | Yes               | `implements`        |
| Implementation (method bodies) | Yes, since Java 8 | `default` methods |
| State (fields)               | No                | `extends` only      |

Restricting state is what keeps the diamond problem tractable. If a class could
inherit the same field through two paths, the JVM would have to decide whether
there is one copy or two, which is the C++ virtual-inheritance rabbit hole.
Method bodies have no such problem: conflicts are rare, detectable at compile
time, and resolved by the rules in 4.2.

```java
public interface Serializer   { default String serialize()  { return "{}"; } }
public interface Validator    { default boolean isValid()   { return true; } }
public interface Auditable    { default String auditLine()  { return "ok"; } }

public class Order extends BaseEntity                   // one state parent
        implements Serializer, Validator, Auditable {   // many capabilities
}
```

`Order` now has four usable types, and any of them can be the declared type of
a variable:

```java
Order order = new Order();
BaseEntity e = order;
Serializer s = order;
Validator  v = order;
Auditable  a = order;
```

```text
  BaseEntity      Serializer  Validator  Auditable
      |  state        \          |         /   behaviour + type
      |                \         |        /
      +--------------- Order ---+--------+
                     one class, four supertypes
```

This is the structural reason interface-based designs scale: adding a
capability to a type never disturbs its existing hierarchy, so capabilities can
be introduced by different teams, in different modules, at different times.

> Key Takeaways
> - Java allows multiple inheritance of type and, since Java 8, of
>   implementation, but never of state.
> - Banning inherited state is what keeps the diamond problem manageable.
> - A class has one superclass but as many supertypes as it implements
>   interfaces.
> - Any supertype may be used as the declared type of a reference.
> - Capabilities can be added to a class without altering its class hierarchy.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Give one class three interfaces and assign the same object to four
>    differently typed references.
> 2. Draw the type graph for `ArrayList`, listing every supertype you can find
>    in the Javadoc.
> 3. Interview: Java inherits implementation from multiple interfaces but state
>    from only one class. Why is state the dangerous one? (Hint: ask how many
>    copies of a duplicated field an object should contain.)

#### Choosing the Right Abstraction

With the mechanics settled, the decision comes down to a few questions asked in
order. Work down the list and stop at the first clear answer.

1. **Will unrelated classes need this?** If the types share no natural parent,
   it must be an interface. A class hierarchy cannot span `File`, `Socket`, and
   `Connection`, but `AutoCloseable` can.
2. **Is there shared mutable state or a constructor invariant?** If yes, an
   abstract class, because interfaces cannot hold fields.
3. **Will implementors need to also extend something else?** If yes, an
   interface, because they have only one `extends` to spend.
4. **Is this a capability or an identity?** Capabilities ("can be compared",
   "can be closed") are interfaces. Identity ("is an employee") is usually a
   class.
5. **Do you expect to add methods later?** Interfaces with defaults evolve
   well; abstract classes evolve well too, but they cost the implementor their
   single inheritance slot.

A useful naming heuristic follows from question 4: interfaces are often
adjectives or `-able` words (`Comparable`, `Runnable`, `Closeable`,
`Serializable`), while abstract classes are nouns (`AbstractList`,
`InputStream`, `Employee`).

```java
// Capability shared by unrelated types -> interface
public interface Exportable {
    byte[] export();
}

// Identity with shared, validated state -> abstract class
public abstract class Document {
    private final String title;
    protected Document(String title) {
        this.title = Objects.requireNonNull(title);
    }
    public String title() { return title; }
    public abstract int pageCount();
}

// Both together
public class Invoice extends Document implements Exportable {
    public Invoice(String title) { super(title); }
    @Override public int pageCount() { return 1; }
    @Override public byte[] export() { return title().getBytes(); }
}
```

The modern default in library design is to **start with an interface**. It
costs the implementor nothing, keeps every future option open, and can always
be paired with an abstract helper class later. Reach for an abstract class only
when shared state or a validated constructor makes it necessary.

> Key Takeaways
> - Use an interface when unrelated types need the capability or when
>   implementors need their `extends` slot.
> - Use an abstract class when subtypes must share fields or a validating
>   constructor.
> - Capability abstractions tend to be `-able` interfaces; identity
>   abstractions tend to be noun classes.
> - A type can and often should do both: extend a class and implement several
>   interfaces.
> - Default to an interface, and add an abstract class only when state demands
>   it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For each of `Comparable`, `InputStream`, `Runnable`, and `AbstractMap`,
>    say why the library chose interface or abstract class.
> 2. Model a plugin system and justify your choice of abstraction in two
>    sentences.
> 3. Interview: You are designing a public library API. Would you publish an
>    interface or an abstract class, and what does each choice commit you to?
>    (Hint: think about what you can add in version 2 without breaking
>    callers.)

#### Skeletal Implementation Pattern

Interfaces give flexibility; abstract classes give code reuse. The skeletal
implementation pattern, popularised by *Effective Java*, takes both: publish
the interface as the type, and ship an abstract class beside it that implements
the tedious parts in terms of a few primitive operations.

The Java Collections Framework is built this way. `List` is the interface,
`AbstractList` is the skeleton, and `ArrayList` is a concrete class that
extends the skeleton. A custom list can either extend `AbstractList` and write
two methods, or implement `List` directly and write twenty-five.

```java
public interface Cache<K, V> {
    V get(K key);
    void put(K key, V value);
    boolean contains(K key);
    void clear();
    int size();
    boolean isEmpty();
    V getOrDefault(K key, V fallback);
}
```

```java
// The skeleton: implements everything derivable from the primitives.
public abstract class AbstractCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {

    // Primitive operations: subclasses must supply these.
    @Override public abstract V get(K key);
    @Override public abstract void put(K key, V value);
    @Override public abstract int size();

    // Derived operations: written once, in terms of the primitives.
    @Override
    public boolean contains(K key) { return get(key) != null; }

    @Override
    public boolean isEmpty() { return size() == 0; }

    @Override
    public V getOrDefault(K key, V fallback) {
        V found = get(key);
        return found != null ? found : fallback;
    }
}
```

```java
// A concrete cache now needs only the three primitives plus clear().
public class MapCache<K, V> extends AbstractCache<K, V> {
    private final Map<K, V> store = new HashMap<>();

    @Override public V get(K key)            { return store.get(key); }
    @Override public void put(K key, V v)    { store.put(key, v); }
    @Override public int size()              { return store.size(); }
    @Override public void clear()            { store.clear(); }
}
```

Crucially, the skeleton is optional. A class that already extends something
else can implement `Cache` directly, and can still reuse the skeleton through
composition by forwarding to a private inner subclass. That escape hatch is
what makes the pattern safe to offer.

```text
        <<interface>> Cache          the published type; what callers use
                 ^
                 : implements
        AbstractCache (abstract)     optional reuse; the derived methods
                 ^
                 | extends
           MapCache                  the primitives only
```

Naming conventions to recognise in the wild: `AbstractList`, `AbstractSet`,
`AbstractMap`, and `AbstractQueue` in `java.util`; the same idea appears as
`*Adapter` classes such as `MouseAdapter` and `WindowAdapter` in older UI
libraries.

> Key Takeaways
> - Publish the interface as the type and offer an abstract skeleton for reuse.
> - The skeleton implements every method that can be derived from a small set
>   of primitive operations.
> - Implementors choose the skeleton for convenience or the interface directly
>   for freedom.
> - `AbstractList`, `AbstractSet`, and `AbstractMap` are the standard library's
>   examples.
> - Default methods can absorb some of this role, but only for logic that needs
>   no state.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Stack<T>` interface with six methods and an `AbstractStack` that
>    implements four of them from two primitives.
> 2. Extend your skeleton with an array-backed concrete class, then write a
>    second implementation that implements the interface directly.
> 3. Interview: When would you move a skeleton's derived methods into the
>    interface as `default` methods instead? (Hint: what does the skeleton have
>    access to that a default method does not?)

<a id="44-core-java-interfaces"></a>
### 4.4 Core Java Interfaces

A handful of standard interfaces appear everywhere in Java; implementing them
correctly plugs your own classes into language features and library machinery.

#### Comparable and Natural Ordering

Sorting requires knowing which of two objects comes first. For `int` the
answer is built in, but for an `Employee` only the class itself knows. Rather
than teach every sorting algorithm about every type, Java inverts the
responsibility: a class declares its own **natural ordering** by implementing
`Comparable`, and all sorting machinery then works with it.

```java
public interface Comparable<T> {
    int compareTo(T other);
}
```

The return value is a sign, not a magnitude:

| `a.compareTo(b)` returns | Meaning                     |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------- |
| Negative                 | `a` comes before `b`        |
| Zero                     | `a` and `b` rank equally    |
| Positive                 | `a` comes after `b`         |

```java
public class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    private final String name;
    private final int salary;

    public Employee(String name, int salary) {
        this.name = name;
        this.salary = salary;
    }

    public String name() { return name; }           // used by 4.4's comparators
    public int salary()   { return salary; }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.salary, other.salary);  // ascending salary
        // NOT this.salary - other.salary: that overflows for large values
    }

    @Override public String toString() { return name + "(" + salary + ")"; }
}
```

```java
List<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
        new Employee("Ada", 90_000),
        new Employee("Bo", 70_000),
        new Employee("Cy", 110_000)));

Collections.sort(staff);            // uses compareTo
staff.sort(null);                   // same thing: null means natural ordering
System.out.println(staff);          // [Bo(70000), Ada(90000), Cy(110000)]

TreeSet<Employee> ranked = new TreeSet<>(staff);   // sorted set needs ordering
```

The overflow warning above is not theoretical. `this.salary - other.salary`
wraps around for values near `Integer.MIN_VALUE` or `MAX_VALUE` and silently
returns the wrong sign. Always use `Integer.compare`, `Double.compare`, or
delegate to an existing `compareTo`.

The contract has four obligations:

- **Sign reversal**: `a.compareTo(b)` and `b.compareTo(a)` must have opposite
  signs.
- **Transitivity**: if `a > b` and `b > c`, then `a > c`.
- **Consistency**: if `a.compareTo(b) == 0`, then `a.compareTo(c)` and
  `b.compareTo(c)` must agree.
- **Consistency with `equals`** (strongly recommended, not required):
  `a.compareTo(b) == 0` should imply `a.equals(b)`.

That last point has a visible consequence. Sorted collections use `compareTo`,
not `equals`, to detect duplicates:

```java
// compareTo compares salary only, so two different people "tie"
Set<Employee> set = new TreeSet<>();
set.add(new Employee("Ada", 90_000));
set.add(new Employee("Zoe", 90_000));
System.out.println(set.size());      // 1: Zoe was treated as a duplicate

Set<Employee> hashed = new HashSet<>();   // uses equals/hashCode instead
// ... would contain 2
```

For multi-field ordering, compare in priority order and return at the first
difference:

```java
@Override
public int compareTo(Employee other) {
    int bySalary = Integer.compare(this.salary, other.salary);
    if (bySalary != 0) return bySalary;          // primary key decided it
    return this.name.compareTo(other.name);      // tie-break on name
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Comparable` defines a single natural ordering inside the class itself.
> - `compareTo` returns a negative, zero, or positive number, never a
>   meaningful magnitude.
> - Use `Integer.compare` and friends; subtraction overflows.
> - The ordering must be antisymmetric, transitive, and consistent, and should
>   agree with `equals`.
> - Sorted collections such as `TreeSet` and `TreeMap` use `compareTo` for
>   duplicate detection, not `equals`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Make a `Book` class comparable by title and sort a list of them.
> 2. Extend `compareTo` to sort by year first and title second, then verify
>    with a list containing ties.
> 3. Interview: Why can subtracting two ints be a bug inside `compareTo`?
>    (Hint: try it with `Integer.MIN_VALUE` and a positive number.)

#### Comparator and Custom Ordering

`Comparable` gives a type one ordering, fixed at compile time inside the class.
That is not enough when you need several orderings, when the ordering depends
on context, or when the class is not yours to modify. `Comparator` moves the
comparison *outside* the class, so any number of orderings can coexist.

```java
public interface Comparator<T> {
    int compare(T first, T second);     // the SAM; same sign convention
}
```

Because it is a functional interface, a comparator is usually a lambda or, more
readably, built from the static factory methods:

```java
Comparator<Employee> bySalary = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.salary(), b.salary());
Comparator<Employee> byName   = Comparator.comparing(Employee::name);
Comparator<Employee> byLength = Comparator.comparingInt(e -> e.name().length());
```

The combinators are where `Comparator` earns its place. They chain into
readable, multi-key orderings:

```java
Comparator<Employee> ordering =
        Comparator.comparing(Employee::department)      // primary key
                  .thenComparing(Employee::salary,      // tie-break
                                 Comparator.reverseOrder())
                  .thenComparing(Employee::name);       // final tie-break

staff.sort(ordering);
```
