| `LinkedHashMap` | -               | O(1)     | O(1)           | O(1)     |
| `TreeMap`       | -               | O(log n) | O(log n)       | O(log n) |
| `PriorityQueue` | -               | O(n)     | O(log n)       | O(log n) at head |

Three cautions about reading that table:

- The O(1) hash figures assume a decent `hashCode`. A type whose `hashCode`
  returns a constant is still correct but pushes every entry into one bucket,
  degrading lookups to O(log n) after treeification.
- Constant factors are real. For fewer than about a hundred elements, a linear
  scan of an `ArrayList` frequently beats a `HashSet`, because there is no
  hashing and the data sits in cache.
- "Search" for a `List` means `contains`. If membership testing is a hot path
  in your code, that is a signal you wanted a `Set`.

The one classic swap worth knowing: replacing `List.contains` inside a loop
with a `HashSet` turns an O(n*m) algorithm into O(n+m).

```java
// SLOW: contains is O(n), called m times
List<String> blocked = loadBlockedUsers();
for (String user : allUsers) {
    if (blocked.contains(user)) { ... }
}

// FAST: build the set once, then every lookup is O(1)
Set<String> blocked = new HashSet<>(loadBlockedUsers());
for (String user : allUsers) {
    if (blocked.contains(user)) { ... }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Choose the interface from the data's shape, then the implementation from
>   the ordering guarantee you need.
> - Hash implementations are O(1), tree implementations O(log n), and trees buy
>   you sorting and range queries.
> - `ArrayList`, `HashSet`, and `HashMap` are the correct defaults.
> - O(1) hashing assumes a well-distributed `hashCode`.
> - For small collections, constant factors often beat asymptotic complexity.
> - Repeated `List.contains` is the signal to switch to a `Set`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Given "track unique visitor IDs and report them alphabetically", name the
>    implementation and justify it.
> 2. Rewrite a nested loop that uses `List.contains` to use a `HashSet`, and
>    measure both on 100,000 elements.
> 3. Choose implementations for: an undo history, a browser's open tabs, a
>    phone book, and a print spooler.
> 4. Interview: When might an `ArrayList` outperform a `HashSet` for
>    membership tests? (Hint: how large does n have to be before hashing pays
>    for itself?)

#### Immutable and Unmodifiable Collections

A collection that can be modified by anyone holding a reference is a shared
mutable variable. Handing one out from a getter lets callers rewrite your
object's internals behind its back. Unmodifiable collections close that hole.

The problem in three lines:

```java
public class Team {
    private final List<String> members = new ArrayList<>();

    public List<String> getMembers() { return members; }   // LEAK
}

team.getMembers().clear();     // any caller can wipe the team's state
```

`final` does not help. It stops the *field* being reassigned; it says nothing
about the object the field points at.

Since Java 9 the factory methods produce genuinely immutable collections:

```java
List<String> list = List.of("a", "b", "c");
Set<String> set = Set.of("x", "y");
Map<String, Integer> map = Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2);

// More than ten map entries, or clearer formatting:
Map<String, Integer> big = Map.ofEntries(
    Map.entry("a", 1),
    Map.entry("b", 2)
);

list.add("d");    // UnsupportedOperationException at runtime
```

These factories have three behaviours that surprise people:

- They reject `null` elements, keys, and values with a
  `NullPointerException`.
- `Set.of` and `Map.of` throw `IllegalArgumentException` on duplicate elements
  or keys, rather than silently collapsing them.
- Their iteration order is unspecified *and deliberately randomised between
  JVM runs*, so code must not depend on it.

The older `Collections.unmodifiableList` family behaves differently in an
important way. It returns a read-only **view** of a collection, not a copy. The
view forbids modification, but the underlying collection can still change, and
those changes are visible through the view.

```java
List<String> backing = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(backing);

view.add("c");             // UnsupportedOperationException, as expected
backing.add("c");          // but this succeeds...
System.out.println(view);  // [a, b, c] -- the view changed underneath
```

Java 10 added `List.copyOf`, `Set.copyOf`, and `Map.copyOf`, which take a
snapshot and are the correct tool for a defensive getter:

```java
public class Team {
    private final List<String> members = new ArrayList<>();

    public List<String> getMembers() {
        return List.copyOf(members);   // immutable snapshot, safe to hand out
    }
}
```

| Approach                      | Modifiable | Reflects source changes | Rejects null |
| ----------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------- | ------------ |
| `new ArrayList<>(source)`     | Yes        | No, it is a copy        | No           |
| `Collections.unmodifiableList`| No         | Yes, it is a view       | No           |
| `List.of(...)`                | No         | Not applicable          | Yes          |
| `List.copyOf(source)`         | No         | No, it is a snapshot    | Yes          |

One last limit to be honest about. Immutability here is **shallow**: the
collection cannot be restructured, but the objects inside it can still be
mutated if they are mutable themselves.

```java
List<StringBuilder> l = List.of(new StringBuilder("a"));
// l.add(...)         -> throws
l.get(0).append("b");  // allowed: the ELEMENT is still mutable
```

Deep immutability requires immutable element types, which is one of the
arguments for records and for `String`.

> Key Takeaways
> - A `final` field still exposes a mutable object; defensive copying is what
>   protects state.
> - `List.of`, `Set.of`, and `Map.of` create truly immutable collections.
> - Those factories reject nulls, reject duplicate keys, and randomise
>   iteration order between runs.
> - `Collections.unmodifiableList` returns a view, so the backing collection
>   can still change beneath it.
> - `List.copyOf` takes an immutable snapshot and is the right tool for a
>   getter.
> - Collection immutability is shallow; mutable elements remain mutable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with a `List` field and demonstrate an external caller
>    mutating it through the getter, then fix it with `List.copyOf`.
> 2. Show that an unmodifiable view reflects later changes to its backing list.
> 3. Call `Set.of("a", "a")` and `List.of("a", null)` and record which
>    exceptions each throws.
> 4. Interview: Is `List.of(new ArrayList<>())` immutable? (Hint: distinguish
>    the structure of the outer list from the state of its elements.)

<a id="73-working-with-collections"></a>
### 7.3 Working with Collections

This subchapter covers the operations you perform *on* collections: ordering
them, searching them, converting them, and meeting the contracts they rely on.

#### Sorting with Comparable and Comparator

Sorting requires a definition of "smaller". Java offers two places to put that
definition, and the choice between them is about ownership: does the *type*
have one obvious order, or does the *caller* need a different order each time?

**`Comparable<T>`** defines a type's single **natural ordering**. The type
implements it, and the rule travels with every instance. `String` orders
lexicographically, `Integer` numerically, `LocalDate` chronologically.

```java
public class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    private final String name;
    private final int salary;

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        // Contract: negative if this < other, zero if equal, positive if >
        return Integer.compare(this.salary, other.salary);
        // NOT this.salary - other.salary: that overflows for extreme values
    }
}

List<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>(...);
Collections.sort(staff);      // uses compareTo
staff.sort(null);             // same thing: null means natural ordering
```

The subtraction warning is worth taking seriously. `Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1`
wraps around to a positive number, and the resulting comparator is inconsistent
in a way that can make `TreeMap` lose entries. Always use `Integer.compare`,
`Double.compare`, and friends.

**`Comparator<T>`** defines an ordering *outside* the type. It is the tool when
you do not own the class, when there is no single sensible order, or when you
need several orderings.

```java
// Pre-Java 8, as an anonymous class
Comparator<Employee> byName = new Comparator<Employee>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(Employee a, Employee b) {
        return a.getName().compareTo(b.getName());
    }
};

// Java 8 onwards, with a key extractor
Comparator<Employee> byName2 = Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName);
```

The factory methods compose, which is where comparators become genuinely
pleasant to use:

```java
Comparator<Employee> ordering =
        Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)        // primary key
                  .thenComparing(Employee::getSalary,
                                 Comparator.reverseOrder())  // tie-break, desc
                  .thenComparing(Employee::getName);         // final tie-break

staff.sort(ordering);
```

| Factory / method                     | Purpose                             |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| `Comparator.comparing(fn)`           | Order by an extracted key           |
| `comparingInt` / `Long` / `Double`   | Same, avoiding boxing               |
| `thenComparing(fn)`                  | Tie-breaker                         |
| `reversed()`                         | Invert the whole comparator         |
| `Comparator.reverseOrder()`          | Reverse natural ordering            |
| `nullsFirst(cmp)` / `nullsLast(cmp)` | Position nulls instead of throwing  |

Note the difference between `.reversed()` at the end of a chain, which inverts
everything before it, and passing `Comparator.reverseOrder()` to a single
`thenComparing`, which inverts only that one key. Mixing them up is a common
source of "the secondary sort is backwards" bugs.

```text
  comparing(dept).thenComparing(salary).reversed()
      -> reverses BOTH keys

  comparing(dept).thenComparing(salary, reverseOrder())
      -> dept ascending, salary descending
```

Side by side:

| Aspect          | `Comparable`              | `Comparator`                  |
| --------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Package         | `java.lang`               | `java.util`                   |
| Method          | `compareTo(T other)`      | `compare(T a, T b)`           |
| Where it lives  | Inside the class          | Outside, as a separate object |
| How many        | One per type              | As many as you like           |
| Modifies class  | Yes                       | No                            |

Both must obey the same contract, and violating it causes real failures:

- `compare(a, b)` and `compare(b, a)` must have opposite signs.
- The ordering must be transitive.
- It should be **consistent with `equals`**: `compare(a, b) == 0` should
  coincide with `a.equals(b)`. If it does not, `TreeSet` and `TreeMap` behave
  in ways that contradict the `Set` and `Map` contracts, because they decide
  equality by comparison.

Java's `sort` is stable for object arrays and lists, using TimSort: elements
that compare equal keep their relative order. That is what makes successive
sorts compose, so sorting by name and then by department yields departments in
order with names still sorted inside each one.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Comparable` gives a type one natural ordering via `compareTo`.
> - `Comparator` supplies external orderings, and you can define many.
> - Use `Integer.compare` rather than subtraction to avoid overflow.
> - `Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...)` composes multi-key
>   orderings.
> - `.reversed()` inverts the whole chain; a per-key reversal goes inside
>   `thenComparing`.
> - Orderings should be consistent with `equals`, or `TreeSet` and `TreeMap`
>   misbehave.
> - `sort` is stable, so equal elements keep their prior relative order.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Make a `Book` class `Comparable` by title, then sort a list of books.
> 2. Sort the same list by year descending, then by title ascending, with a
>    composed comparator.
> 3. Sort a list containing nulls using `Comparator.nullsFirst`.
> 4. Interview: What breaks if `compareTo` is inconsistent with `equals`?
>    (Hint: add two such objects to a `TreeSet` and count the elements.)

#### Searching and Bulk Operations

Beyond adding and removing one element at a time, collections support searching
and whole-collection operations. Knowing them avoids writing loops that the
library already provides.

**Linear search** is what `contains`, `indexOf`, and `lastIndexOf` do. They
compare with `equals`, walk from one end, and cost O(n):

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Grace", "Alan", "Grace");

names.contains("Alan");        // true
names.indexOf("Grace");        // 1: first occurrence
names.lastIndexOf("Grace");    // 3: last occurrence
names.indexOf("Nobody");       // -1: absent, never an exception
```

**Binary search** is O(log n) but carries a precondition that the library
cannot check for you: the list must already be sorted by the same ordering you
search with. Searching an unsorted list compiles, runs, and returns nonsense.

```java
List<Integer> sorted = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30, 40, 50));

int found = Collections.binarySearch(sorted, 30);    // 2: the index
int missing = Collections.binarySearch(sorted, 35);  // negative

// A negative result encodes where the value WOULD go: -(insertionPoint) - 1
int insertionPoint = -missing - 1;      // 3
sorted.add(insertionPoint, 35);         // keeps the list sorted
```

That negative-return convention is a frequent interview question. The result is
never a plain `-1`, because index 0 needs its own distinct "not found" value.

**Bulk operations** apply set-style logic to whole collections. Each returns a
boolean saying whether the receiver changed:

```java
List<String> a = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
List<String> b = List.of("y", "z", "w");

a.addAll(b);       // union-ish: [x, y, z, y, z, w] -- duplicates kept in a List
a.retainAll(b);    // intersection: keep only elements also in b
a.removeAll(b);    // difference: remove every element found in b
a.containsAll(b);  // subset test
```

With sets these correspond exactly to the mathematical operations:

```text
  A = {1, 2, 3}      B = {3, 4, 5}

  A.addAll(B)     -> {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}    union
  A.retainAll(B)  -> {3}                intersection
  A.removeAll(B)  -> {1, 2}             difference
```

```java
Set<Integer> a = new HashSet<>(Set.of(1, 2, 3));
Set<Integer> b = Set.of(3, 4, 5);

Set<Integer> union = new HashSet<>(a);
union.addAll(b);                        // {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

Set<Integer> intersection = new HashSet<>(a);
intersection.retainAll(b);              // {3}
```

Note that each of these mutates the receiver, which is why the examples copy
first. There is a genuine performance trap here too: `removeAll` and
`retainAll` call `contains` on the argument for each element, so passing a
`List` makes the whole operation O(n*m). Pass a `Set` and it is O(n).

```java
// SLOW when blocked is a List: O(n*m)
users.removeAll(blocked);

// FAST: O(n)
users.removeAll(new HashSet<>(blocked));
```

Two more bulk methods worth knowing, both added in Java 8:

```java
list.removeIf(s -> s.isBlank());        // conditional removal, in place
list.replaceAll(String::toUpperCase);   // transform every element, in place
map.replaceAll((k, v) -> v * 2);        // the map equivalent
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `contains` and `indexOf` are linear searches using `equals`, returning -1
>   when absent.
> - `binarySearch` is O(log n) but requires a list already sorted by the same
>   ordering.
> - A negative `binarySearch` result encodes the insertion point as
>   `-(point) - 1`.
> - `addAll`, `retainAll`, `removeAll`, and `containsAll` give union,
>   intersection, difference, and subset.
> - These methods mutate the receiver, so copy first if you need the original.
> - Pass a `Set` to `removeAll` and `retainAll` to avoid O(n*m) behaviour.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the union, intersection, and difference of two `Set<Integer>`
>    values without mutating either input.
> 2. Use `Collections.binarySearch` on a missing value and insert it at the
>    decoded insertion point.
> 3. Demonstrate `binarySearch` returning a wrong answer on an unsorted list.
> 4. Interview: Why does `binarySearch` return `-(insertionPoint) - 1` rather
>    than just `-insertionPoint`? (Hint: what would a value that belongs at
>    index 0 return?)

#### The Collections Utility Class

`java.util.Collections` is a class of `static` helpers that operate on
collections. It cannot be instantiated; it exists purely because Java had no
interface default methods when the framework was designed. Knowing what is in
it saves writing algorithms that already exist.

The most used members, grouped by purpose:

```java
List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6));

// --- Ordering ---
Collections.sort(nums);                      // natural ordering, in place
Collections.sort(nums, Comparator.reverseOrder());
Collections.reverse(nums);                   // flip the current order
Collections.shuffle(nums);                   // random permutation
Collections.shuffle(nums, new Random(42));   // reproducible shuffle
Collections.swap(nums, 0, 3);                // exchange two positions
Collections.rotate(nums, 2);                 // shift right, wrapping around

// --- Extremes and counting ---
int min = Collections.min(nums);
int max = Collections.max(nums, Comparator.naturalOrder());
int ones = Collections.frequency(nums, 1);   // how many times 1 appears

// --- Whole-collection edits ---
Collections.fill(nums, 0);                   // replace every element
List<String> blanks = Collections.nCopies(3, "-");   // immutable [-, -, -]

// --- Tests ---
boolean apart = Collections.disjoint(listA, listB);  // no elements in common
```

A second group produces wrapper collections. All of them return views backed by
the original, not copies:

| Factory                           | Returns                             |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `unmodifiableList/Set/Map`        | Read-only view                      |
| `synchronizedList/Set/Map`        | View with every method synchronised |
| `checkedList(list, Class)`        | View that rejects wrong-typed inserts at runtime |
| `emptyList()`, `emptySet()`       | Shared immutable empty instances    |
| `singletonList(e)`, `singleton(e)`| Immutable one-element collection    |

`synchronizedList` has a sharp edge worth stating explicitly. Each individual
method is synchronised, but *iteration* is not, so you must lock manually
around any loop:

```java
List<String> sync = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());

synchronized (sync) {               // required: iteration is not atomic
    for (String s : sync) {
        process(s);
    }
}
```

This is one reason the `java.util.concurrent` collections are preferred for new
concurrent code: `ConcurrentHashMap` and `CopyOnWriteArrayList` need no such
external locking.

`checkedList` is a debugging aid. When legacy code passes a raw `List` around,
an `Integer` can end up inside a `List<String>` and the `ClassCastException`
surfaces far from the culprit. A checked view fails at the insertion instead:

```java
List<String> safe = Collections.checkedList(new ArrayList<>(), String.class);
List raw = safe;
raw.add(42);      // ClassCastException HERE, at the bad insert
```

Since Java 9, `List.of` and friends have replaced most uses of `emptyList` and
`singletonList`, and `sort`/`removeIf`/`replaceAll` exist directly on `List`.
Prefer the instance methods where they exist:

```java
Collections.sort(list);   // older style
list.sort(null);          // modern equivalent
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Collections` is a static utility class of algorithms over collections.
> - It provides `sort`, `reverse`, `shuffle`, `swap`, `rotate`, `min`, `max`,
>   `frequency`, and `disjoint`.
> - Its wrapper factories return views over the original, never copies.
> - `synchronizedList` synchronises individual methods but not iteration, which
>   you must lock yourself.
> - `checkedList` catches raw-type pollution at the point of the bad insert.
> - Prefer modern instance methods such as `list.sort` over the older static
>   equivalents.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Shuffle a list with a seeded `Random` twice and confirm both orders match.
> 2. Use `Collections.frequency` to find the most common element in a list.
> 3. Wrap a list with `checkedList`, assign it to a raw variable, and trigger
>    the `ClassCastException`.
> 4. Interview: Why is iterating a `synchronizedList` not thread-safe even
>    though every method is synchronised? (Hint: how many method calls does one
>    loop make, and what can happen between them?)

#### Hashing Requirements for Keys and Set Elements

Hash-based collections are fast because they compute where an element belongs
instead of searching for it. That only works if your objects answer two
questions consistently, and getting it wrong produces bugs that look like the
collection is broken.

The two questions are `hashCode()`, "which bucket?", and `equals()`, "is this
the same element?". A lookup does both: hash to find the bucket, then compare
with `equals` inside it.

```text
  set.contains(x)
        |
        1. h = x.hashCode()  -> bucket index
        |
        2. for each entry in that bucket: entry.equals(x) ?
        |
        +-- found -> true        +-- bucket empty or no match -> false
```

The failure follows directly. If two equal objects produce different hash
codes, they land in different buckets and step 2 never runs:

```java
public class Point {
    private final int x, y;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {          // equals overridden...
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Point p)) return false;
        return x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }
    // ...but hashCode is NOT: inherited identity hash
}

Set<Point> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(new Point(1, 2));
System.out.println(set.contains(new Point(1, 2)));   // false!
set.add(new Point(1, 2));
System.out.println(set.size());                      // 2: "duplicates"
```

Hence the **contract**, which the compiler cannot enforce:

1. If `a.equals(b)`, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()`. Mandatory.
2. Unequal objects *may* share a hash code. That is a collision, handled
   correctly, just slower.
3. `hashCode` must be stable for as long as the object is in a hash
   collection.

A correct implementation, using the JDK helpers rather than hand-rolled
arithmetic:

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Point p)) return false;
    return x == p.x && y == p.y;
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(x, y);   // same fields as equals, in the same spirit
}
```

The golden rule: **use exactly the same fields in both methods**. If `equals`
compares `x` and `y`, `hashCode` must be computed from `x` and `y`.

Rule 3 is the subtler trap. Mutating a field used by `hashCode` after insertion
strands the object in the wrong bucket, where it cannot be found even by its
own reference:

```java
Set<MutablePoint> set = new HashSet<>();
MutablePoint p = new MutablePoint(1, 2);
set.add(p);                           // filed under hash of (1, 2)

p.setX(99);                           // hash is now that of (99, 2)
System.out.println(set.contains(p));  // false: looks in the wrong bucket
System.out.println(set.size());       // 1: still there, but unreachable
```

The lesson is to use immutable types as keys and set elements. `String`,
`Integer`, `LocalDate`, enums, and records are all safe. Records are especially
convenient, because the compiler generates `equals` and `hashCode` from all
components automatically:

```java
public record Point(int x, int y) { }   // equals and hashCode: done correctly
```

A final note on distribution. Returning a constant is *legal*, since it
satisfies the contract, but it puts every element in one bucket:

```java
@Override
public int hashCode() { return 42; }   // correct, but every lookup degrades
```

The collection still works. It just stops being a hash table.

> Key Takeaways
> - Hash lookups use `hashCode` to pick a bucket and `equals` to match inside
>   it.
> - Equal objects must have equal hash codes; overriding one without the other
>   breaks lookups.
> - Unequal objects sharing a hash code is a legal collision, only a
>   performance cost.
> - Use the same fields in `equals` and `hashCode`, and build the latter with
>   `Objects.hash`.
> - Mutating a hash-relevant field after insertion makes the element
>   unreachable.
> - Prefer immutable keys; records generate both methods correctly for free.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class overriding `equals` but not `hashCode`, add two equal
>    instances to a `HashSet`, and print the size.
> 2. Add the correct `hashCode` and confirm the size becomes 1.
> 3. Insert a mutable object into a `HashSet`, change a key field, and show
>    `contains` returning false for that very object.
> 4. Interview: Is a `hashCode` that always returns 42 correct? (Hint:
>    separate the contract's correctness requirement from the performance
>    consequence.)

#### Converting Between Arrays and Collections

Arrays and collections solve the same problem in different eras of the
language, and real code crosses between them constantly: a varargs parameter
arrives as an array, a library returns one, a `List` must be handed to an
older API. The conversions are short but contain two genuine traps.

**Array to `List`.** `Arrays.asList` is the obvious call and the more dangerous
one. It returns a *fixed-size view backed by the array*, not an independent
list:

```java
String[] array = {"a", "b", "c"};
List<String> view = Arrays.asList(array);

view.set(0, "z");                  // allowed: writes THROUGH to the array
System.out.println(array[0]);      // "z": the array changed

view.add("d");                     // UnsupportedOperationException: fixed size
view.remove(0);                    // UnsupportedOperationException
```

For a real, growable list, wrap it:

```java
List<String> real = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(array));  // an independent copy
List<String> immutable = List.of(array);                    // immutable copy
```

The second trap involves primitives. Generics cannot hold `int`, so an `int[]`
is treated as a *single object*, giving a one-element list:

```java
int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};
List<int[]> wrong = Arrays.asList(nums);      // size 1: the array itself
System.out.println(wrong.size());             // 1

Integer[] boxed = {1, 2, 3};
List<Integer> right = Arrays.asList(boxed);   // size 3
System.out.println(right.size());             // 3

// The clean way for primitives, using streams from chapter 8
List<Integer> fromPrimitives = Arrays.stream(nums).boxed().toList();
```

**`List` to array.** The modern form passes a zero-length array, which tells
the list the element type while letting it allocate the right size:

```java
List<String> list = List.of("a", "b", "c");

String[] arr = list.toArray(new String[0]);   // preferred
Object[] objects = list.toArray();            // loses the element type
String[] arr2 = list.toArray(String[]::new);  // Java 11 generator form
```

Passing `new String[0]` rather than `new String[list.size()]` is the
recommended idiom: on modern JVMs the empty array is faster, because the
allocation is intrinsified and the sized version gets zero-filled before being
overwritten.

The whole set of conversions in one table:

| From      | To            | Call                                          |
| --------- | ------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `T[]`     | fixed `List`  | `Arrays.asList(arr)`                          |
| `T[]`     | mutable `List`| `new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(arr))`         |
| `T[]`     | immutable `List` | `List.of(arr)`                             |
| `T[]`     | `Set`         | `new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(arr))` or `Set.of(arr)` |
| `int[]`   | `List<Integer>` | `Arrays.stream(arr).boxed().toList()`       |
| `List<T>` | `T[]`         | `list.toArray(new T[0])`                      |
| `List<Integer>` | `int[]` | `list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray()` |
| `Collection` | `List`     | `new ArrayList<>(collection)`                 |

A few related array utilities that come up alongside these conversions:

```java
int[] a = {3, 1, 2};

Arrays.sort(a);                      // in-place sort
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));          // [1, 2, 3]: readable output
System.out.println(Arrays.equals(a, new int[]{1, 2, 3}));   // true, by content

int[][] grid = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};
System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(grid));   // [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

int[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(a, 5);    // [1, 2, 3, 0, 0]: padded with zeros
int[] slice = Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 1, 3);       // [2, 3]
```

`Arrays.toString` is worth remembering on its own: printing an array directly
gives you something like `[I@1b6d3586`, because arrays do not override
`toString`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Arrays.asList` returns a fixed-size view that writes through to the
>   original array.
> - Wrap it in `new ArrayList<>(...)` for an independent, growable list.
> - `Arrays.asList(int[])` yields a one-element `List<int[]>`; box with
>   `Arrays.stream(...).boxed()` instead.
> - Convert to an array with `toArray(new String[0])`, which is both typed and
>   fast.
> - `list.toArray()` without an argument returns `Object[]` and loses the
>   element type.
> - Use `Arrays.toString` and `Arrays.deepToString` to print arrays readably.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create an array, wrap it with `Arrays.asList`, modify element 0 through
>    the list, and print the array.
> 2. Call `Arrays.asList` on an `int[]` and on an `Integer[]`, and print both
>    sizes.
> 3. Round-trip a `List<String>` to a `String[]` and back, confirming equality.
> 4. Interview: Why does `Arrays.asList` support `set` but not `add`? (Hint:
>    what resource is the returned list actually backed by, and can it grow?)

<a id="8-functional-programming-in-an-object-oriented-language"></a>
## 8. Functional Programming in an Object-Oriented Language

Java 8 added a second way of expressing computation: instead of saying *how* to
loop, you say *what* should happen to each element and let the library run the
loop. This chapter covers lambdas and the functional interfaces they implement,
method references, the Stream API that chains them into pipelines, and
`Optional` as a disciplined answer to `null`. None of it replaces objects;
these are tools layered on top of the type system from chapters 4 and 6, and
they work because a lambda is just a compact way to supply one method.

<a id="81-lambda-expressions"></a>
### 8.1 Lambda Expressions

This subchapter covers the syntax of lambdas, how the compiler decides what
type they have, and the scoping rules that make them behave unlike the
anonymous classes they replace.

#### Lambda Syntax and Target Typing

Before Java 8, passing behaviour to a method meant wrapping it in an object.
Sorting a list by name required a whole class definition just to carry one
comparison:

```java
Collections.sort(people, new Comparator<Person>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(Person a, Person b) {
        return a.getName().compareTo(b.getName());   // the only line that matters
    }
});
```

Five of those six lines are ceremony. The compiler already knows the interface,
the method name, and the parameter types, because `sort` declared them. A
**lambda expression** removes everything the compiler can work out for itself:

```java
people.sort((a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName()));
```

The syntax has three parts: a parameter list, the arrow `->`, and a body.

```text
   (String a, String b)  ->  a.length() - b.length()
   |__________________|      |____________________|
        parameters                   body
```

Each part has shorthands:

```java
// Zero parameters: empty parentheses are required
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("running");

// One parameter: parentheses optional, types inferred
Consumer<String> c1 = (String s) -> System.out.println(s);
Consumer<String> c2 = (s) -> System.out.println(s);
Consumer<String> c3 = s -> System.out.println(s);        // most idiomatic

// Expression body: the value is returned implicitly, no return, no semicolon
Comparator<String> byLength = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length();

// Block body: braces require explicit return and semicolons
Comparator<String> verbose = (a, b) -> {
    int diff = a.length() - b.length();
    return diff != 0 ? diff : a.compareTo(b);
};
```

Types are all-or-nothing: write them for every parameter or for none.
`(String a, b) -> ...` does not compile. The `var` form, `(var a, var b) ->`,
is allowed since Java 11 and is mainly useful when you need to attach an
annotation to a parameter.

The deeper question is what *type* a lambda has. The answer is that it has no
type of its own. A lambda is only legal where the compiler can see a
**target type**: a **functional interface**, meaning an interface with exactly
one abstract method.

```java
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hi");
// The compiler reasons: Runnable has one abstract method, run().
// It takes no arguments and returns void. This lambda matches. Accept it.
```

The same lambda text can mean different things depending on the target:

```java
interface Validator { boolean check(String s); }
interface Length    { int measure(String s); }

Validator v = s -> s.isEmpty();      // becomes a Validator
Predicate<String> p = s -> s.isEmpty();   // the SAME text, a different type

// var bad = s -> s.isEmpty();       // ERROR: no target type to infer from
```

That last line is the practical consequence. A lambda cannot stand alone; it
needs a variable declaration, a parameter, a return type, or a cast to give it
meaning.

Where a target type is available, lambdas appear in four places:

```java
Predicate<String> assigned = s -> s.isBlank();        // assignment
list.removeIf(s -> s.isBlank());                      // method argument
Supplier<String> returned = makeSupplier();           // return value
Object o = (Runnable) () -> System.out.println("x");  // cast
```

`@FunctionalInterface` is an optional annotation that makes the compiler verify
the single-abstract-method rule. It changes nothing at runtime but turns a
later accidental second method into a compile error rather than a puzzle:

```java
@FunctionalInterface
interface Transformer {
    String apply(String input);      // exactly one abstract method
    default Transformer twice() {    // default methods do not count
        return s -> apply(apply(s));
    }
    // String other(String s);       // would break the annotation's check
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A lambda is a compact expression supplying the body of a single method.
> - The syntax is parameters, `->`, then an expression body or a braced block.
> - An expression body returns its value implicitly; a block body needs
>   explicit `return`.
> - Parameter types are written for all parameters or for none.
> - A lambda has no standalone type; it requires a functional interface as its
>   target type.
> - A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, and `default` and
>   `static` methods do not count.
> - `@FunctionalInterface` asks the compiler to enforce that rule.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write lambdas for `Runnable`, `Comparator<String>`, and a custom
>    `interface Greeter { String greet(String name); }`.
> 2. Convert a three-line block-bodied lambda into an expression-bodied one.
> 3. Try `var f = x -> x + 1;` and explain the compiler error in terms of
>    target typing.
> 4. Interview: Why can a lambda not be assigned to `Object`? (Hint: what does
>    the compiler need in order to know which method the body implements?)

#### Lambdas versus Anonymous Classes

Lambdas look like shorthand for anonymous inner classes, and for everyday use
they are. Underneath they differ in what the compiler generates, what `this`
means, and what they are allowed to do. The differences explain several
otherwise baffling behaviours.

Start with what they have in common, since both can supply an implementation
inline:

```java
// Anonymous class
Runnable a = new Runnable() {
    @Override public void run() { System.out.println("anon"); }
};

// Lambda: same effect, one line
Runnable b = () -> System.out.println("lambda");
```

The first real difference is **what each can implement**. An anonymous class
can implement an interface with any number of methods, or extend a class. A
lambda is restricted to functional interfaces:

```java
// Two abstract methods: only an anonymous class can do this
MouseListener ml = new MouseListener() {
    @Override public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e)  { }
    @Override public void mouseReleased(MouseEvent e) { }
    // ...
};
// MouseListener ml2 = e -> { };    // ERROR: not a functional interface
```

The second is **state**. An anonymous class is a class, so it can hold fields
and a constructor-like initialiser. A lambda is a single expression with no
place to put fields:

```java
Supplier<Integer> counter = new Supplier<>() {
    private int count = 0;               // a lambda cannot do this
    @Override public Integer get() { return ++count; }
};
```

The third is **`this`**, covered in detail two topics further on. In an
anonymous class `this` refers to the anonymous instance; in a lambda it refers
to the enclosing object.

The fourth is **compilation strategy**, which is where the performance
difference comes from. An anonymous class produces a separate class file,
`Outer$1.class`, loaded and instantiated like any other class. A lambda
produces no class file. The compiler emits a private method holding the body
plus an `invokedynamic` instruction, and the JVM builds an implementation at
first execution.

```text
  ANONYMOUS CLASS                    LAMBDA

  javac -> Outer$1.class             javac -> private static method
              |                                + invokedynamic call site
  new Outer$1() on every use                    |
              |                        first execution: JVM links it once
    a fresh object each time                    |
                                       stateless lambdas are CACHED and reused
```

That caching is observable. A lambda that captures nothing can return the same
instance on every evaluation, whereas `new` always produces a fresh object:

```java
Supplier<Runnable> anon = () -> new Runnable() {
    @Override public void run() { }
};
System.out.println(anon.get() == anon.get());   // false: always new

Supplier<Runnable> lam = () -> () -> { };
System.out.println(lam.get() == lam.get());     // often true: cached instance
```

Never rely on lambda identity for that reason. Using a lambda as a map key, or
comparing two with `==`, is undefined behaviour in practice. This also bites
when removing a listener: the lambda you pass to `removeListener` is a
different object from the one you passed to `addListener`, so the removal
silently fails. Keep a reference to the original if you need to remove it.

| Aspect               | Anonymous class          | Lambda                   |
| -------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------ |
| Target               | Any interface or class   | Functional interface only |
| Can hold fields      | Yes                      | No                       |
| `this` refers to     | The anonymous instance   | The enclosing instance   |
| Shadowing locals     | Allowed                  | Compile error            |
| Generated artifact   | A `.class` file          | `invokedynamic`, no class file |
| Instance identity    | Always new               | May be cached and reused |
| Class loading cost   | Per class, at load time  | Deferred to first use    |

Use a lambda by default. Reach for an anonymous class when you need state,
multiple methods, a class rather than an interface, or a reference to the
instance itself.

> Key Takeaways
> - Lambdas implement functional interfaces only; anonymous classes have no
>   such limit.
> - Anonymous classes can hold fields and state; lambdas cannot.
> - An anonymous class generates a `.class` file; a lambda uses
>   `invokedynamic` and generates none.
> - Stateless lambdas may be cached, so two evaluations can yield the same
>   instance.
> - Never depend on lambda identity, and keep a reference if you need to
>   unregister a listener.
> - Prefer lambdas; use anonymous classes when you need state or multiple
>   methods.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same `Comparator` as an anonymous class and as a lambda, and
>    compare the line counts.
> 2. Compile a class containing both, list the generated `.class` files, and
>    explain what you see.
> 3. Register a lambda as a listener, then try to remove it by passing an
>    identical lambda, and observe the result.
> 4. Interview: When must you use an anonymous class instead of a lambda?
>    (Hint: think about instance fields and about interfaces with two abstract
>    methods.)

#### Variable Capture Rules

A lambda often needs data from around it. Java allows that, but only under a
restriction that surprises newcomers: captured local variables must be
**final or effectively final**. Understanding why removes the frustration and
explains a family of compile errors.

The reason is lifetime. A local variable lives on the stack frame of the method
that declared it, and that frame disappears when the method returns. A lambda
can outlive its method, so it cannot point at the frame. Instead the compiler
**copies** the value into the lambda at creation time.

```text
  makeGreeter() runs                  after it returns

  +---------------------+             +---------------------+
  | stack frame         |             |   (frame is gone)   |
  |   greeting = "Hi"   |             +---------------------+
  +---------------------+
            | copied at creation
            v
  +---------------------+             +---------------------+
  | lambda object       |             | lambda object       |
  |   greeting = "Hi"   |  ---------> |   greeting = "Hi"   |
  +---------------------+             +---------------------+
                                       still valid: it owns a copy
```

Once the lambda holds a copy, letting the original change would be incoherent:
the two would disagree, and nobody could say which one the lambda should see.
Java forbids the question rather than picking a confusing answer.

**Effectively final** means the variable is never reassigned after
initialisation, whether or not you wrote the keyword `final`:

```java
String greeting = "Hello";                    // never reassigned
Runnable ok = () -> System.out.println(greeting);   // effectively final: fine

String name = "Ada";
name = "Grace";                               // reassigned...
// Runnable bad = () -> System.out.println(name);
// ERROR: local variables referenced from a lambda must be final or
//        effectively final
```

Note that the error appears even if the reassignment happens *after* the
lambda. The rule is about the whole method body, not about ordering.

The classic loop cases follow directly:

```java
// WORKS: each iteration of a for-each gets a FRESH variable
for (String s : List.of("a", "b")) {
    runnables.add(() -> System.out.println(s));
}

// FAILS: one variable i, mutated by the loop, so not effectively final
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    // runnables.add(() -> System.out.println(i));   // ERROR
}

// FIX: copy into a fresh local per iteration
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    int captured = i;                       // a new variable each time
    runnables.add(() -> System.out.println(captured));
}
```

The restriction applies only to **local variables**. Fields are reached through
a reference to the object, not copied, so they may be reassigned freely:

```java
public class Counter {
    private int count = 0;                   // an instance FIELD

    public Runnable increment() {
        return () -> count++;                // legal: captures `this`, not a copy
    }
}
```

That distinction is worth stating precisely: a lambda that touches an instance
field captures `this`, which keeps the whole enclosing object alive. In a
long-lived lambda stored in a listener list, that can hold far more memory than
you expect.

Finally, "effectively final" constrains the *reference*, not the object it
points to. A captured mutable object can still be mutated:

```java
List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();        // reference never reassigned
Runnable r = () -> log.add("event");         // legal: we mutate, not reassign
r.run();
System.out.println(log);                     // [event]

// log = new ArrayList<>();                  // this WOULD break the capture
```

That is the standard escape hatch when a lambda must accumulate something: use
a one-element array, an `AtomicInteger`, or a collection rather than a plain
local. Do so sparingly, since needing it usually means a `reduce` or a
`Collector` would express the intent better.

```java
int[] total = {0};                           // the array reference is final
List.of(1, 2, 3).forEach(n -> total[0] += n);
System.out.println(total[0]);                // 6
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Captured local variables must be final or effectively final.
> - The reason is that locals are copied into the lambda, because the stack
>   frame may be gone.
> - Effectively final means never reassigned anywhere in the method.
> - A classic `for` loop variable is not effectively final; copy it into a
>   fresh local.
> - Instance and static fields are not restricted, because they are reached
>   through a reference.
> - Capturing a field captures `this`, which can keep the enclosing object
>   alive.
> - The restriction applies to the reference, not to the referenced object's
>   contents.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method returning a `Supplier<String>` that captures a local
>    variable, and call it after the method returns.
> 2. Reproduce the "must be final or effectively final" error with a `for` loop
>    counter, then fix it.
> 3. Accumulate a sum inside a `forEach` using an `AtomicInteger`, then rewrite
>    it without one.
> 4. Interview: Why are captured locals restricted when fields are not? (Hint:
>    compare how long a stack frame lives with how long a heap object lives.)

#### Scope and this Semantics in Lambdas

An anonymous class introduces a new scope; a lambda does not. This single
difference explains how `this` resolves, why you cannot shadow a local inside a
lambda, and a well-known bug class in code migrated from anonymous classes.

A lambda is **lexically scoped**: it sees the enclosing method's scope as if
its body had been written inline. There is no new "instance" for names to
resolve against.

```java
public class Widget {
    private String name = "widget";

    public void anonymousVersion() {
        Runnable r = new Runnable() {
            private String name = "anon";     // a NEW scope, own field
            @Override public void run() {
                System.out.println(this.name);        // "anon"
                System.out.println(Widget.this.name); // "widget"
            }
        };
        r.run();
    }

    public void lambdaVersion() {
        Runnable r = () -> {
            System.out.println(this.name);    // "widget": `this` is the Widget
        };
        r.run();
    }
}
```

```text
  ANONYMOUS CLASS                   LAMBDA

  Widget instance                   Widget instance
       |                                 ^
       | encloses                        | this
       v                                 |
  Runnable$1 instance  <- this      lambda body (no new scope)
       |
       | Widget.this reaches out
       v
  Widget instance
```

Inside a lambda, `this`, `super`, and unqualified field names all refer to the
enclosing instance. That is almost always what you want, and it removes the
need for the `Outer.this` qualifier.

The bug this prevents, and the one it introduces, are two sides of the same
coin. With anonymous classes, a method named the same in both scopes silently
resolved to the inner one:

```java
public class Task {
    public void run() { System.out.println("Task.run"); }

    public void schedule() {
        Runnable anon = new Runnable() {
            @Override public void run() {
                // this.run() would be infinite recursion on the ANON object
                Task.this.run();          // qualification required
            }
        };
        Runnable lam = () -> run();       // unambiguous: Task.run
    }
}
```

Conversely, a lambda registered as a callback keeps a strong reference to the
enclosing object whenever it touches an instance member. If the callback lives
in a static registry, the enclosing object cannot be collected:

```java
public class Screen {
    private byte[] pixels = new byte[10_000_000];

    public void register() {
        // Captures `this`, so the whole Screen (and its 10 MB) stays alive
        EventBus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println(pixels.length));

        // Captures only the int, so Screen can be collected
        int size = pixels.length;
        EventBus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println(size));
    }
}
```

The second scope consequence is **shadowing**. Because a lambda adds no scope,
its parameters and locals collide with the enclosing method's:

```java
public void process() {
    String value = "outer";

    // Consumer<String> c = value -> System.out.println(value);
    // ERROR: variable value is already defined in method process()

    Consumer<String> ok = v -> System.out.println(v + value);  // different name
}
```

An anonymous class would have allowed the shadow, silently hiding the outer
variable. The lambda's compile error is the better outcome, and the fix is to
pick a distinct parameter name.

| Behaviour               | Anonymous class          | Lambda                  |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| Introduces a scope      | Yes                      | No                      |
| `this`                  | The anonymous instance   | The enclosing instance  |
| Reaching the outer `this` | `Outer.this`           | Plain `this`            |
| Shadowing an outer local| Allowed                  | Compile error           |
| Unqualified method call | Resolves to the inner one| Resolves to the enclosing one |

> Key Takeaways
> - A lambda body shares the enclosing method's scope and creates none of its
>   own.
> - `this` inside a lambda is the enclosing instance, not the lambda.
> - Anonymous classes need `Outer.this` to reach the enclosing object; lambdas
>   do not.
> - A lambda parameter cannot shadow an enclosing local, and the compiler says
>   so.
> - Touching an instance member captures `this` and keeps the whole object
>   reachable.
> - Capture a local copy instead when a long-lived lambda only needs one field.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print `this.getClass().getName()` from inside an anonymous `Runnable` and
>    from inside a lambda, and compare.
> 2. Try to name a lambda parameter the same as an enclosing local and read the
>    error.
> 3. Write a class whose lambda captures `this`, then rewrite it to capture
>    only the field value it needs.
> 4. Interview: How can a lambda passed to a long-lived registry cause a memory
>    leak? (Hint: what does the lambda hold onto when its body mentions an
>    instance field?)

<a id="82-built-in-functional-interfaces"></a>
### 8.2 Built-In Functional Interfaces

This subchapter covers the `java.util.function` package: the handful of generic
interfaces that almost every lambda in the standard library targets.

#### Function and BiFunction

If every library defined its own functional interface, the ecosystem would
fracture: your `Transformer` and my `Converter` would describe the same shape
but be incompatible types. The `java.util.function` package solves this with a
small set of general-purpose interfaces that everything targets, so a lambda
written for one API composes with another.

`Function<T, R>` is the most general of them: take one value, return another,
possibly of a different type. Its single abstract method is `apply`.

```java
Function<String, Integer> length = s -> s.length();   // String in, Integer out
System.out.println(length.apply("hello"));            // 5

Function<Integer, Integer> square = n -> n * n;
System.out.println(square.apply(4));                  // 16
```

```text
   Function<T, R>

      T  ------>  [ apply ]  ------>  R
   input                              output
```

The type parameters read in order: the first is the input, the last is the
result. That convention holds across the whole package.

`Function` carries three non-abstract methods, which is what makes it more than
a naming convention:

```java
Function<String, Integer> parse = Integer::parseInt;
Function<Integer, Integer> doubler = n -> n * 2;

// andThen: run this first, then the argument
Function<String, Integer> parseThenDouble = parse.andThen(doubler);
System.out.println(parseThenDouble.apply("21"));      // 42

// compose: run the argument first, then this. The order is REVERSED
Function<String, Integer> same = doubler.compose(parse);
System.out.println(same.apply("21"));                 // 42

// identity: returns its input unchanged
Function<String, String> id = Function.identity();
```

The distinction between `andThen` and `compose` is a reliable exam question:
`f.andThen(g)` is `g(f(x))`, while `f.compose(g)` is `f(g(x))`. Read `andThen`
left to right and `compose` right to left.

```text
  f.andThen(g):   x --> [ f ] --> [ g ] --> result
  f.compose(g):   x --> [ g ] --> [ f ] --> result
```

`Function.identity()` looks useless until you meet `Collectors.toMap`, where
one of the two arguments is often "the element itself":

```java
Map<String, String> byItself = Stream.of("a", "bb")
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), String::toUpperCase));
```

`BiFunction<T, U, R>` is the two-argument version. Java stops at two: there is
no `TriFunction`, and if you need three inputs you either define your own
interface or pass an object that groups them.

```java
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;
System.out.println(add.apply(3, 4));                  // 7

// Different types are fine, including a different result type
BiFunction<String, Integer, String> repeat = (s, n) -> s.repeat(n);
System.out.println(repeat.apply("ab", 3));            // "ababab"
```

`BiFunction` has `andThen` but no `compose`, because composing *into* two
arguments is not well defined:

```java
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> sum = (a, b) -> a + b;
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, String> describe =
        sum.andThen(total -> "total=" + total);       // takes the single result
System.out.println(describe.apply(2, 3));             // "total=5"
```

These interfaces turn up throughout the library, which is the real reason to
learn them:

| Method                       | Functional parameter          |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `Stream.map`                 | `Function<T, R>`              |
| `Map.computeIfAbsent`        | `Function<K, V>`              |
| `Map.merge`, `Map.compute`   | `BiFunction`                  |
| `Optional.map`               | `Function<T, R>`              |
| `Collectors.toMap`           | `Function` for key and value  |

> Key Takeaways
> - `java.util.function` supplies shared interfaces so lambdas are portable
>   between APIs.
> - `Function<T, R>` takes one argument and returns a result via `apply`.
> - The last type parameter is always the return type.
> - `f.andThen(g)` runs `f` first; `f.compose(g)` runs `g` first.
> - `Function.identity()` returns its input and is common in `Collectors.toMap`.
> - `BiFunction<T, U, R>` takes two arguments and has `andThen` but no
>   `compose`.
> - There is no three-argument version; group the inputs into an object
>   instead.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Function<String, String>` that trims and uppercases, using
>    `andThen`.
> 2. Build the same behaviour with `compose` and confirm the argument order
>    differs.
> 3. Use a `BiFunction<Double, Double, Double>` to compute a discounted price,
>    then chain `andThen` to format it as a string.
> 4. Interview: Why does `BiFunction` have `andThen` but not `compose`? (Hint:
>    how many values would the composed function have to produce?)

#### Predicate and BiPredicate

A `Function<T, Boolean>` would technically express a test, but it would box
every result into a `Boolean` object and read poorly. `Predicate<T>` is the
dedicated interface for "does this value satisfy a condition?", returning a
primitive `boolean` from its `test` method.

```java
Predicate<String> isEmpty = s -> s.isEmpty();
Predicate<Integer> isEven = n -> n % 2 == 0;

System.out.println(isEmpty.test(""));      // true
System.out.println(isEven.test(7));        // false
```

Its value comes from the combinators, which let you build complex conditions
from simple named pieces instead of one unreadable boolean expression:

```java
Predicate<String> notBlank = s -> !s.isBlank();
Predicate<String> shortEnough = s -> s.length() <= 20;
Predicate<String> noDigits = s -> s.chars().noneMatch(Character::isDigit);

// Combine with and / or / negate
Predicate<String> validName = notBlank.and(shortEnough).and(noDigits);

System.out.println(validName.test("Ada Lovelace"));   // true
System.out.println(validName.test("Ada2"));           // false
```

| Method                   | Meaning                                   |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `test(t)`                | The abstract method; returns `boolean`    |
| `and(other)`             | Both must hold; short-circuits            |
| `or(other)`              | Either may hold; short-circuits           |
| `negate()`               | Logical NOT                               |
| `Predicate.not(p)`       | Static NOT, useful on method references   |
| `Predicate.isEqual(o)`   | Tests with `Objects.equals`               |

`and` and `or` short-circuit exactly like `&&` and `||`, so an expensive test
placed second may never run. Order your predicates cheapest-first.

`Predicate.not`, added in Java 11, exists because you cannot call `.negate()`
directly on a method reference:

```java
// list.removeIf(String::isBlank.negate());     // does not compile
list.removeIf(Predicate.not(String::isBlank));  // works
```

`BiPredicate<T, U>` tests two values together:

```java
BiPredicate<String, Integer> lengthIs = (s, n) -> s.length() == n;
System.out.println(lengthIs.test("hello", 5));        // true

BiPredicate<Order, Customer> canShip =
        (order, customer) -> order.total() <= customer.creditLimit();
```

Predicates appear wherever the library filters or tests:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ada", "", "Grace", " "));

names.removeIf(String::isBlank);              // Collection.removeIf
List<String> longNames = names.stream()
        .filter(s -> s.length() > 3)          // Stream.filter
        .toList();
Optional<String> maybe = Optional.of("Ada").filter(s -> s.length() > 2);
```

One design note. Naming a predicate and reusing it beats inlining the same
condition in five places, and it makes the intent testable on its own:

```java
// Harder to read, impossible to unit test in isolation
orders.stream().filter(o -> o.total() > 100 && !o.cancelled() && o.paid());

// Named, reusable, testable
Predicate<Order> isBillable = Order::isPaid;
Predicate<Order> isLarge = o -> o.total() > 100;
orders.stream().filter(isBillable.and(isLarge));
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Predicate<T>` tests a value and returns a primitive `boolean` from `test`.
> - It exists rather than `Function<T, Boolean>` to avoid boxing and to read
>   better.
> - `and`, `or`, and `negate` build compound conditions from named pieces.
> - `and` and `or` short-circuit, so put cheap tests first.
> - `Predicate.not(...)` negates a method reference, which `.negate()` cannot.
> - `BiPredicate<T, U>` tests two values at once.
> - Naming predicates makes filters readable and independently testable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a `Predicate<Integer>` for "positive and even" by combining two
>    simple predicates.
> 2. Filter a list of strings with `Predicate.not(String::isBlank)`.
> 3. Write a `BiPredicate<String, String>` that tests whether one string is an
>    anagram of another.
> 4. Interview: Why does `Predicate` exist when `Function<T, Boolean>` would
>    compile? (Hint: what happens to a primitive `boolean` when it is used as a
>    type argument?)

#### Consumer and Supplier

`Function` and `Predicate` both take input and produce output.
The remaining two shapes cover the cases where one side is missing: a
`Consumer` takes a value and returns nothing, and a `Supplier` takes nothing
and returns a value.

```text
   Consumer<T>:   T ---> [ accept ] --->  (nothing)
   Supplier<T>:     (nothing) ---> [ get ] ---> T
```

A **`Consumer<T>`** exists for side effects: printing, logging, saving,
mutating. Because it returns nothing, a consumer that has no side effect does
nothing at all.

```java
Consumer<String> print = s -> System.out.println(s);
print.accept("hello");

// andThen chains consumers: both run, in order, on the SAME input
Consumer<String> log = s -> logger.info(s);
Consumer<String> both = print.andThen(log);
both.accept("event");        // printed, then logged
```

Note that `Consumer.andThen` differs from `Function.andThen`: it does not feed
one result into the next, because there is no result. It simply runs both on
the original argument.

`BiConsumer<T, U>` takes two arguments, and is the shape used by
`Map.forEach`:

```java
Map<String, Integer> ages = Map.of("Ada", 36, "Grace", 45);
BiConsumer<String, Integer> show = (name, age) ->
        System.out.println(name + " is " + age);
ages.forEach(show);
```

A **`Supplier<T>`** produces a value on demand. Its purpose is **deferral**:
the value is not computed until, and unless, `get()` is called.

```java
Supplier<String> lazy = () -> expensiveComputation();
// Nothing has run yet.
String value = lazy.get();      // now it runs
```

That deferral is the whole point, and it shows up in three recurring places:

```java
// 1. Avoid building a message that is usually discarded
logger.debug(() -> "state: " + expensiveToString());

// 2. Provide a fallback only when it is actually needed
String name = optional.orElseGet(() -> lookupDefaultName());   // not orElse

// 3. Construct an exception lazily, including its stack trace
Order order = repo.find(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
```

The `orElse` versus `orElseGet` distinction returns in 8.5, and it is the
clearest illustration of why suppliers exist: `orElse(expensive())` evaluates
its argument every time, even when the value is present.

Suppliers also power factories and lazy caches:

```java
public class Lazy<T> {
    private final Supplier<T> factory;
    private T value;                       // computed at most once

    public Lazy(Supplier<T> factory) { this.factory = factory; }

    public T get() {
        if (value == null) {
            value = factory.get();         // deferred until first access
        }
        return value;
    }
}
```

The four core shapes, side by side:

| Interface       | Method     | Takes | Returns | Typical use          |
| --------------- | ---------- | ----- | ------- | -------------------- |
| `Function<T,R>` | `apply`    | 1     | Yes     | Transform            |
| `Predicate<T>`  | `test`     | 1     | boolean | Filter               |
| `Consumer<T>`   | `accept`   | 1     | No      | Side effect          |
| `Supplier<T>`   | `get`      | 0     | Yes     | Deferred production  |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Consumer<T>` accepts a value and returns nothing, so it exists purely for
>   side effects.
> - `Consumer.andThen` runs both consumers on the same input rather than
>   chaining results.
> - `BiConsumer<T, U>` is the shape of `Map.forEach`.
> - `Supplier<T>` takes nothing and produces a value only when `get` is called.
> - Suppliers exist for deferral: lazy logging, lazy defaults, lazy exceptions.
> - `orElseGet` takes a supplier and skips the work when the value is present;
>   `orElse` does not.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Chain two `Consumer<String>` instances with `andThen` and confirm both
>    run.
> 2. Write a method that logs only when a level is enabled, taking a
>    `Supplier<String>` instead of a `String`.
> 3. Implement a `Lazy<T>` class and prove the factory runs exactly once.
> 4. Interview: When does passing a `Supplier` measurably beat passing the
>    value? (Hint: consider a default that requires a database call but is
>    rarely needed.)

#### UnaryOperator and BinaryOperator

Some transformations return the same type they consume: uppercasing a string,
negating a number, merging two totals. Writing `Function<String, String>`
repeats the type and hides the intent. The operator interfaces are named
shorthands for exactly that case.

`UnaryOperator<T>` **extends** `Function<T, T>`, adding no new abstract method.
`BinaryOperator<T>` extends `BiFunction<T, T, T>` the same way.

```java
// These two declarations are interchangeable in behaviour
Function<String, String> f = s -> s.toUpperCase();
UnaryOperator<String> u = s -> s.toUpperCase();      // clearer intent

BinaryOperator<Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;       // Integer, Integer -> Integer
System.out.println(add.apply(2, 3));                 // 5
```

```text
   UnaryOperator<T>     T ---> [ apply ] ---> T        (same type in and out)

   BinaryOperator<T>    T ---+
                             |--> [ apply ] ---> T
                        T ---+
```

Because they are subtypes, an `UnaryOperator<String>` can be passed anywhere a
`Function<String, String>` is expected. The reverse is not true, which is the
one practical gotcha:

```java
Function<String, String> fn = s -> s.trim();
// UnaryOperator<String> op = fn;            // ERROR: Function is the supertype
UnaryOperator<String> op = fn::apply;        // wrap it if you really need to
```

`UnaryOperator` is the shape used by in-place transformation:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("ada", "grace"));
names.replaceAll(String::toUpperCase);       // replaceAll takes a UnaryOperator
System.out.println(names);                   // [ADA, GRACE]

Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2)                // the generator is a UnaryOperator
      .limit(5)
      .forEach(System.out::println);         // 1 2 4 8 16
```

`BinaryOperator` is the shape of reduction and of map merging, which is where
you will meet it most:

```java
// Reduction: fold a stream down to one value
int total = Stream.of(1, 2, 3).reduce(0, Integer::sum);          // BinaryOperator

// Map merge conflicts: decide what to keep when two keys collide
Map<String, Integer> merged = Stream.of("a", "bb", "a")
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(s -> s, String::length,
                                  (existing, replacement) -> existing));
```

`BinaryOperator` also provides two static factories that build an operator out
of a comparator, which is a neat way to express "keep the larger of the two":

```java
BinaryOperator<String> longest =
        BinaryOperator.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));
System.out.println(longest.apply("hi", "hello"));   // "hello"

BinaryOperator<Integer> smaller = BinaryOperator.minBy(Comparator.naturalOrder());
```

| Interface            | Extends              | Shape        | Common use           |
| -------------------- | -------------------- | ------------ | -------------------- |
| `UnaryOperator<T>`   | `Function<T, T>`     | T -> T       | `List.replaceAll`, `Stream.iterate` |
| `BinaryOperator<T>`  | `BiFunction<T,T,T>`  | (T, T) -> T  | `Stream.reduce`, merge functions |

An important constraint for reduction: a `BinaryOperator` used with `reduce`
must be **associative**, meaning `(a op b) op c` equals `a op (b op c)`.
Addition and `max` qualify; subtraction does not. Non-associative operators
give correct results sequentially and wrong ones in parallel, which is a
genuinely hard bug to find.

> Key Takeaways
> - `UnaryOperator<T>` extends `Function<T, T>`; `BinaryOperator<T>` extends
>   `BiFunction<T, T, T>`.
> - They add no methods and exist to state intent and shorten declarations.
> - An operator can be used where a function is expected, but not the reverse.
> - `List.replaceAll` and `Stream.iterate` take `UnaryOperator`.
> - `Stream.reduce` and `Collectors.toMap` merge functions take
>   `BinaryOperator`.
> - `BinaryOperator.maxBy` and `minBy` build operators from a comparator.
> - Reduction operators must be associative or parallel results will be wrong.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Use `List.replaceAll` with a `UnaryOperator<String>` that strips
>    whitespace.
> 2. Reduce a list of integers to their product with a `BinaryOperator`.
> 3. Use `BinaryOperator.maxBy` to find the longest string in a list via
>    `reduce`.
> 4. Interview: Why must a `reduce` operator be associative? (Hint: imagine
>    splitting the input across four threads and combining the partial
>    results.)

#### Primitive Specializations

Generics cannot hold primitives, so `Function<Integer, Integer>` really means
"object in, object out". Every call boxes an `int` into an `Integer` and
unboxes it again. For a loop over ten million elements that overhead dominates.
The primitive specializations exist to remove it.

The cost, made concrete:

```java
// Boxed: each apply allocates an Integer for the argument and the result
Function<Integer, Integer> boxed = n -> n * 2;

// Primitive: no allocation at all
IntUnaryOperator unboxed = n -> n * 2;
```

```text
   BOXED PATH                          PRIMITIVE PATH

   int 5
     | box -> new Integer(5)           int 5
     v                                   |
   apply(Integer) -> Integer             v
     |                                 applyAsInt(int) -> int
     | unbox -> int                      |
     v                                   v
   int 10                              int 10

   two allocations per call            zero allocations
```

The naming follows two rules. A prefix names the **input** type, and a suffix
of `ToX` names the **output** type.

| Interface               | Signature            | Note                     |
| ----------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `IntPredicate`          | `int -> boolean`     | Input is `int`           |
| `IntFunction<R>`        | `int -> R`           | Primitive in, object out |
| `ToIntFunction<T>`      | `T -> int`           | Object in, primitive out |
| `IntToDoubleFunction`   | `int -> double`      | Both primitive           |
| `IntUnaryOperator`      | `int -> int`         |                          |
| `IntBinaryOperator`     | `(int, int) -> int`  |                          |
| `IntConsumer`           | `int -> void`        |                          |
| `IntSupplier`           | `() -> int`          |                          |

The same family exists for `Long` and `Double`. Only those three primitives are
covered, plus `BooleanSupplier`, because `int`, `long`, and `double` can
represent the others without loss.

Their abstract methods are named after the return type, which trips people up
when implementing them by hand:

```java
IntPredicate isEven = n -> n % 2 == 0;
System.out.println(isEven.test(4));               // test

ToIntFunction<String> len = String::length;
System.out.println(len.applyAsInt("hello"));      // applyAsInt, not apply

IntUnaryOperator twice = n -> n * 2;
System.out.println(twice.applyAsInt(21));         // applyAsInt

IntSupplier roll = () -> 6;
System.out.println(roll.getAsInt());              // getAsInt, not get
```

In practice you meet them through the primitive streams, where they are the
natural parameter types:

```java
int total = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100)
        .filter(n -> n % 3 == 0)      // IntPredicate
        .map(n -> n * n)              // IntUnaryOperator
        .sum();                       // no boxing anywhere in this pipeline

// mapToInt takes a ToIntFunction and leaves the object world behind
int chars = Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
        .mapToInt(String::length)
        .sum();
```

A word on when this matters. For a collection of a few hundred elements, the
difference is unmeasurable, and clarity should win. The specializations earn
their awkward names in hot loops over large data, and in APIs where you want to
guarantee no allocation. The compiler will not warn you either way, so the
usual advice applies: write the clear version, measure, and specialise the part
that shows up in the profile.

> Key Takeaways
> - Generic functional interfaces box primitives on every call, costing
>   allocations.
> - Primitive specializations take and return primitives directly.
> - A prefix such as `Int` names the input; a `ToInt` suffix names the output.
> - Only `int`, `long`, and `double` have families, since they cover the rest.
> - Their methods are named for the return type: `applyAsInt`, `getAsInt`,
>   `test`.
> - `mapToInt` and the primitive streams are where you meet them in practice.
> - Reach for them in hot loops over large data, not everywhere.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a `Function<Integer, Integer>` that triples a number as an
>    `IntUnaryOperator`.
> 2. Sum the lengths of a list of strings using `mapToInt` and no boxing.
> 3. Time summing one million integers with `Stream<Integer>` against
>    `IntStream`.
> 4. Interview: Why is there no `CharFunction` or `ShortPredicate`? (Hint:
>    which primitive can hold every `char` and `short` value without loss?)

#### Composing Functions and Predicates

The default methods introduced across the previous topics share one purpose:
building complex behaviour from small named pieces at runtime. Gathering them
in one place makes the pattern visible, and the pattern is what distinguishes
functional code from lambdas sprinkled through a loop.

The complete set of combinators:

| Interface   | Combinators                                |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `Function`  | `andThen`, `compose`, `identity`           |
| `Predicate` | `and`, `or`, `negate`, `not`, `isEqual`    |
| `Consumer`  | `andThen`                                  |
| `Comparator`| `thenComparing`, `reversed`, `comparing`   |
| `BinaryOperator` | `minBy`, `maxBy`                      |

Composition gives you a pipeline assembled from parts that are individually
testable:

```java
Function<String, String> trim = String::trim;
Function<String, String> lower = String::toLowerCase;
Function<String, String> collapse = s -> s.replaceAll("\\s+", " ");

// Build the whole normalisation from three named steps
Function<String, String> normalise = trim.andThen(lower).andThen(collapse);

System.out.println(normalise.apply("  Hello   WORLD "));   // "hello world"
```

The real gain appears when the pipeline is **assembled at runtime** from data,
which a hand-written `if` chain cannot do:

```java
// Build a filter from whatever criteria the user supplied
Predicate<Product> filter = p -> true;                    // start permissive

if (params.containsKey("minPrice")) {
    double min = Double.parseDouble(params.get("minPrice"));
    filter = filter.and(p -> p.price() >= min);           // narrow it
}
if (params.containsKey("category")) {
    String category = params.get("category");
    filter = filter.and(p -> p.category().equals(category));
}
if (params.containsKey("inStock")) {
    filter = filter.and(Product::inStock);
}

List<Product> results = products.stream().filter(filter).toList();
```

Note the `p -> true` starting point. It is the **identity element** for `and`,
the same role `0` plays for addition, and it lets the loop treat every criterion
uniformly. For an `or` chain the identity is `p -> false`.

Reducing a collection of predicates makes that explicit:

```java
List<Predicate<String>> rules = List.of(
        s -> s.length() >= 8,
        s -> s.chars().anyMatch(Character::isDigit),
        s -> s.chars().anyMatch(Character::isUpperCase));

// All rules must hold
Predicate<String> allRules = rules.stream()
        .reduce(s -> true, Predicate::and);

System.out.println(allRules.test("Passw0rdX"));   // true
```

Higher-order functions take the idea one step further: a method that *returns*
a function, parameterised by ordinary values.

```java
// A factory for predicates, not a predicate
public static Predicate<String> longerThan(int n) {
    return s -> s.length() > n;      // captures n
}

public static <T> Function<T, T> twice(UnaryOperator<T> op) {
    return t -> op.apply(op.apply(t));
}

System.out.println(twice((String s) -> s + "!").apply("hi"));   // "hi!!"
```

Two cautions. Composition chains are readable up to about four steps; beyond
that, name the intermediate results. And a composed function is only as
debuggable as its parts, since a stack trace through `andThen` shows lambda
frames with synthetic names. Naming each step as a local variable, rather than
inlining all of them, makes both problems manageable.

```java
// Hard to read and to debug
Function<String, Integer> f = ((Function<String, String>) String::trim)
        .andThen(String::toLowerCase).andThen(s -> s.replace(" ", ""))
        .andThen(String::length);

// Same behaviour, each step nameable in a stack trace and testable alone
Function<String, String> clean = trim.andThen(lower).andThen(collapse);
Function<String, Integer> f2 = clean.andThen(String::length);
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Combinators build complex behaviour from small, independently testable
>   pieces.
> - `andThen` and `compose` chain functions; `and`, `or`, and `negate` chain
>   predicates.
> - Composition can be assembled at runtime from data, which an `if` chain
>   cannot.
> - `p -> true` is the identity for `and`, and `p -> false` for `or`.
> - `reduce(s -> true, Predicate::and)` folds a collection of rules into one.
> - Higher-order methods return functions parameterised by ordinary arguments.
> - Keep chains short and name the steps, since stack traces through lambdas
>   are opaque.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compose three `UnaryOperator<String>` steps into one normalisation
>    function.
> 2. Write `Predicate<Integer> inRange(int lo, int hi)` returning a predicate
>    built from two smaller ones.
> 3. Build a search filter that combines an arbitrary list of predicates with
>    `reduce`.
> 4. Interview: Why is `p -> true` the right starting value when combining
>    predicates with `and`? (Hint: what is the equivalent starting value when
>    summing numbers?)

<a id="83-method-and-constructor-references"></a>
### 8.3 Method and Constructor References

This subchapter covers the `::` shorthand: what each of its four forms means,
and when it reads better than the equivalent lambda.

#### Static Method References
