Many lambdas do nothing but forward their arguments to an existing method:

```java
Function<String, Integer> parse = s -> Integer.parseInt(s);
```

The parameter `s` is named, passed along, and never used for anything else. A
**method reference** removes that ceremony by naming the method directly:

```java
Function<String, Integer> parse = Integer::parseInt;
```

The syntax is `ClassName::staticMethodName`, with no parentheses and no
arguments. You are naming the method, not calling it. The compiler matches the
method's signature against the functional interface's abstract method and wires
the arguments across positionally.

```text
   Function<String, Integer>      abstract method: Integer apply(String)

   Integer::parseInt              actual method:   static int parseInt(String)

              String -----------> String     (argument passes through)
              Integer <---------- int        (autoboxed result)
```

Common static references:

```java
Function<String, Integer> toInt = Integer::parseInt;
BinaryOperator<Integer> max = Integer::max;             // (a, b) -> Integer.max(a, b)
Function<Object, String> str = String::valueOf;
Predicate<String> blank = String::isBlank;              // see the next topics
DoubleUnaryOperator sqrt = Math::sqrt;

// Your own static methods work identically
public static boolean isValid(String s) { return s != null && !s.isBlank(); }
Predicate<String> valid = MyUtils::isValid;
```

Arity must match, and this is the main source of "incompatible types" errors:

```java
// Math.max takes two arguments, so it needs a two-argument interface
BinaryOperator<Integer> ok = Math::max;
// Function<Integer, Integer> bad = Math::max;    // ERROR: wrong arity
```

An overloaded method is resolved by the target type, which is why the same
reference text can mean different methods in different contexts:

```java
// Math.abs is overloaded for int, long, float, double
IntUnaryOperator absInt = Math::abs;          // picks abs(int)
DoubleUnaryOperator absDouble = Math::abs;    // picks abs(double)
```

Where no unique overload matches, the compiler reports ambiguity and you fall
back to an explicit lambda with typed parameters.

A genuinely useful case is converting a static utility into a reusable
function object:

```java
List<String> raw = List.of("1", "2", "3");
List<Integer> numbers = raw.stream()
        .map(Integer::parseInt)     // clearer than s -> Integer.parseInt(s)
        .toList();
```

One limitation worth naming early: a method reference cannot do anything extra.
The moment you need to adjust an argument, add a null check, or call two
methods, you need a lambda.

```java
// A reference cannot express this: the argument is transformed first
Function<String, Integer> f = s -> Integer.parseInt(s.trim());
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A method reference is shorthand for a lambda that only forwards its
>   arguments.
> - The static form is `ClassName::staticMethod`, with no parentheses.
> - The compiler matches parameters positionally against the functional
>   interface.
> - Argument counts must match exactly, so `Math::max` needs a two-argument
>   interface.
> - Overloads are resolved from the target type.
> - Any extra logic, even a `trim()`, forces you back to a lambda.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)` and `d -> Math.sqrt(d)` with method
>    references.
> 2. Write a static `isPalindrome(String)` and use it as a `Predicate` via a
>    reference.
> 3. Try assigning `Math::max` to `Function<Integer, Integer>` and read the
>    error.
> 4. Interview: How does the compiler pick between overloads of `Math.abs` in a
>    method reference? (Hint: what information does the target functional
>    interface supply?)

#### Instance Method References on a Specific Object

The second form references a method on **one particular object** that already
exists. The syntax is `objectReference::methodName`, and the object is captured
when the reference is created, exactly as a lambda captures a variable.

```java
String prefix = "Hello, ";

// Lambda: calls concat on the captured `prefix`
Function<String, String> greetLambda = s -> prefix.concat(s);

// Method reference on that specific object
Function<String, String> greet = prefix::concat;

System.out.println(greet.apply("Ada"));      // "Hello, Ada"
```

The receiver is fixed; the functional interface's argument becomes the method's
argument.

```text
   prefix::concat                     prefix is BOUND at creation

   apply("Ada")  ---->  prefix.concat("Ada")
                          ^        ^
                          |        |
                   captured object  the interface's argument
```

The most common example in all of Java is printing:

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Grace");

names.forEach(System.out::println);
// System.out is a specific PrintStream object;
// println is an instance method on it
```

That line is worth dissecting, because it is often typed without being
understood. `System.out` is a static *field* holding a `PrintStream` instance,
and `::println` references an instance method on that instance. It is a bound
reference, not a static one.

Other everyday uses:

```java
Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyClass.class);
Consumer<String> log = logger::info;             // bound to this logger

List<String> collected = new ArrayList<>();
Consumer<String> collect = collected::add;       // bound to this list

String target = "hello world";
Predicate<String> contained = target::contains;  // target.contains(arg)
```

References to methods on `this` and `super` are the same form, used inside a
class:

```java
public class OrderService {
    private boolean isValid(Order o) { return o.total() > 0; }

    public List<Order> filterValid(List<Order> orders) {
        return orders.stream()
                .filter(this::isValid)      // instance method on this object
                .toList();
    }
}
```

One subtlety matters for correctness. The receiver is evaluated **once**, when
the reference is created, not on each call. If the variable is later reassigned,
the reference keeps pointing at the original object:

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("first");
Supplier<String> get = sb::toString;       // sb evaluated NOW

sb = new StringBuilder("second");          // rebinding the variable
System.out.println(get.get());             // "first": still the original object
```

Mutating the captured object is a different matter, and is visible:

```java
StringBuilder sb2 = new StringBuilder("a");
Supplier<String> g = sb2::toString;
sb2.append("b");
System.out.println(g.get());               // "ab": same object, new contents
```

This form also explains a common `NullPointerException`. Creating the reference
dereferences the receiver immediately, so a null receiver throws at the
*declaration*, not at the first call:

```java
String s = null;
// Supplier<Integer> len = s::length;      // NPE right here, before any call
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The bound form is `object::instanceMethod`, referencing a method on one
>   existing object.
> - The interface's arguments become the method's arguments; the receiver is
>   fixed.
> - `System.out::println` is this form, since `System.out` is a specific
>   object.
> - `this::method` and `super::method` are the same form inside a class.
> - The receiver is evaluated once, at creation, so later reassignment has no
>   effect.
> - Mutations to the captured object are still visible through the reference.
> - A null receiver throws immediately when the reference is created.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace `s -> System.out.println(s)` with a bound method reference in a
>    `forEach`.
> 2. Create a `Consumer<String>` bound to a specific list's `add` method and
>    fill the list.
> 3. Demonstrate that reassigning the receiver variable does not change an
>    existing reference.
> 4. Interview: Why does `s::length` throw when `s` is null, even before the
>    function is called? (Hint: what must the runtime capture at the moment the
>    reference is built?)

#### References to Arbitrary Instance Methods

The third form is the one that genuinely confuses people, because it looks
identical to a static reference but behaves differently. `String::toUpperCase`
names an *instance* method using a *class* name.

```java
Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase;
System.out.println(upper.apply("hello"));    // "HELLO"
```

`toUpperCase` is not static, so which string does it run on? The answer: the
**first argument becomes the receiver**. The lambda it replaces is:

```java
Function<String, String> upper = s -> s.toUpperCase();
```

```text
   BOUND (previous topic)          UNBOUND (this topic)

   prefix::concat                  String::toUpperCase

   arg -> prefix.concat(arg)       arg -> arg.toUpperCase()
            ^                              ^
       fixed receiver                 the ARGUMENT is the receiver
```

The shift generalises. With an unbound reference, argument one is the receiver
and the remaining arguments are passed to the method:

```java
// One interface argument, zero method arguments
Function<String, Integer> len = String::length;          // s -> s.length()

// Two interface arguments: first is the receiver, second is the parameter
BiFunction<String, String, Boolean> startsWith = String::startsWith;
System.out.println(startsWith.apply("hello", "he"));     // true
// equivalent to: (a, b) -> a.startsWith(b)

// A comparator built this way
Comparator<String> cmp = String::compareTo;              // (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b)
```

Because both forms use `ClassName::method`, the only way to tell a static from
an unbound reference is to know whether the method is static. The compiler
knows; a reader has to check. It is also why a class with both a static and an
instance method of the same name cannot be referenced this way at all: the
reference is ambiguous and rejected.

This form is what makes stream pipelines read so cleanly, since the element is
almost always the receiver:

```java
List<String> names = List.of("ada", "grace", "alan");

List<String> result = names.stream()
        .filter(s -> !s.isEmpty())
        .map(String::toUpperCase)              // each element is the receiver
        .sorted(String::compareTo)
        .toList();

// Comparator.comparing takes an unbound reference as its key extractor
people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName));
```

`Person::getName` deserves a note. It is an unbound reference producing a
`Function<Person, String>`, and that is exactly the key extractor
`Comparator.comparing` wants. Every getter reference you write in a comparator
or a collector is this form.

The three `ClassName::method` cases, disambiguated:

| Reference               | Method kind        | Equivalent lambda          |
| ----------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| `Integer::parseInt`     | static             | `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)` |
| `String::toUpperCase`   | instance, unbound  | `s -> s.toUpperCase()`     |
| `prefix::concat`        | instance, bound    | `s -> prefix.concat(s)`    |

A final caution: an unbound reference invokes the method on the argument, so a
null element throws inside the pipeline.

```java
Stream.of("a", null, "c")
      .map(String::toUpperCase);     // NPE when it reaches the null element
```

Filter nulls out first, or use a lambda with a guard.

> Key Takeaways
> - The unbound form is `ClassName::instanceMethod`, where the first argument
>   becomes the receiver.
> - `String::toUpperCase` means `s -> s.toUpperCase()`, not a static call.
> - Remaining arguments map to the method's parameters in order.
> - Static and unbound references look identical, so you must know the method.
> - A class with a static and an instance overload of one name cannot be
>   referenced.
> - Getter references such as `Person::getName` are unbound and power
>   comparators and collectors.
> - A null element throws, because the reference dereferences the argument.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite `s -> s.trim()` and `s -> s.length()` as unbound method
>    references.
> 2. Sort a list of objects with `Comparator.comparing` and a getter reference.
> 3. Express `(a, b) -> a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)` as an unbound reference and
>    identify the interface type.
> 4. Interview: How does the compiler distinguish `Integer::parseInt` from
>    `String::length`? (Hint: both are `ClassName::method`, so what does it
>    look up first?)

#### Constructor References

The fourth form references a constructor with `ClassName::new`. It follows the
same rule as the others: the functional interface's arguments become the
constructor's arguments, and the new object is the result.

```java
Supplier<ArrayList<String>> maker = ArrayList::new;   // () -> new ArrayList<>()
List<String> list = maker.get();

Function<String, StringBuilder> sb = StringBuilder::new;   // s -> new StringBuilder(s)
System.out.println(sb.apply("hi").reverse());              // "ih"
```

The interface arity selects which constructor is used, which means the same
`ClassName::new` text can refer to different constructors:

```java
public record Person(String name, int age) { }

Supplier<ArrayList<Person>> empty = ArrayList::new;             // no-arg
IntFunction<ArrayList<Person>> sized = ArrayList::new;          // (int capacity)
BiFunction<String, Integer, Person> make = Person::new;         // (String, int)

Person p = make.apply("Ada", 36);
```

```text
   Person::new  with target BiFunction<String, Integer, Person>

     ("Ada", 36) ---> new Person("Ada", 36) ---> Person
       |    |
       +----+--- matched positionally to the constructor parameters
```

The most frequent use is as a **factory** handed to a library that needs to
create objects without knowing the type:

```java
List<String> raw = List.of("Ada", "Grace");

// Build objects from data
List<Person> people = raw.stream()
        .map(name -> new Person(name, 0))
        .toList();

// Supply the collection type to a collector
Set<String> set = raw.stream().collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));

// Supply the array type to toArray
String[] array = raw.stream().toArray(String[]::new);
```

`String[]::new` is the **array constructor reference**, and it is worth
learning separately. It is an `IntFunction<String[]>`: given a length, it
allocates an array of that size. That is precisely what `toArray` needs, since
it knows the count but not the element type.

```java
IntFunction<String[]> arrayMaker = String[]::new;
String[] five = arrayMaker.apply(5);      // new String[5]
```

Constructor references also give clean dependency wiring, where the caller
decides which implementation to build:

```java
public class Repository<T> {
    private final Supplier<List<T>> listFactory;

    // The caller chooses ArrayList::new, LinkedList::new, CopyOnWriteArrayList::new
    public Repository(Supplier<List<T>> listFactory) {
        this.listFactory = listFactory;
    }

    public List<T> newBatch() { return listFactory.get(); }
}

Repository<Order> repo = new Repository<>(ArrayList::new);
```

Two limits. You cannot reference the constructor of an abstract class or an
interface, since there is nothing to instantiate. And for a generic class the
type argument comes from the target type, though you may state it explicitly
when inference needs help:

```java
// Supplier<List<String>> s = ArrayList::new;          // inferred
Supplier<List<String>> s = ArrayList<String>::new;     // explicit, also legal
```

| Reference           | Target interface            | Creates                |
| ------------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `ArrayList::new`    | `Supplier<ArrayList<T>>`    | `new ArrayList<>()`    |
| `ArrayList::new`    | `IntFunction<ArrayList<T>>` | `new ArrayList<>(n)`   |
| `Person::new`       | `BiFunction<String,Integer,Person>` | `new Person(s, i)` |
| `String[]::new`     | `IntFunction<String[]>`     | `new String[n]`        |

> Key Takeaways
> - `ClassName::new` references a constructor, with arguments matched
>   positionally.
> - The target interface's arity decides which overloaded constructor is used.
> - `TreeSet::new` and similar are how collectors are told which collection to
>   build.
> - `String[]::new` is an `IntFunction` that allocates an array of the given
>   length.
> - Passing a `Supplier` of constructors lets callers choose the
>   implementation.
> - Abstract classes and interfaces have no constructor reference.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Use `Person::new` with a `BiFunction` to build objects from two lists of
>    values.
> 2. Collect a stream into a `TreeSet` using `Collectors.toCollection` and a
>    constructor reference.
> 3. Convert a stream to a typed array with `toArray(String[]::new)` and
>    explain why `toArray()` alone is insufficient.
> 4. Interview: Why can the same text `ArrayList::new` mean two different
>    constructors? (Hint: what does the compiler examine besides the reference
>    itself?)

#### When to Prefer a Reference Over a Lambda

Method references are shorter, but shorter is not automatically better. The
right criterion is whether the reference makes the *intent* clearer, and there
are cases where a lambda genuinely wins.

**Prefer a reference** when the lambda only forwards its arguments unchanged.
The parameter name adds nothing:

```java
.map(s -> s.toUpperCase())      ->  .map(String::toUpperCase)
.filter(s -> s.isBlank())       ->  .filter(String::isBlank)
.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s)) -> .forEach(System.out::println)
.map(p -> p.getName())          ->  .map(Person::getName)
```

**Prefer a lambda** when any of the following is true.

The body does more than a single call:

```java
.map(s -> s.trim().toUpperCase())        // two calls: no reference exists
.map(s -> Integer.parseInt(s.trim()))    // the argument is transformed first
```

The argument order does not line up:

```java
// Wanted: check whether a fixed target contains each element
Predicate<String> p = s -> "haystack".contains(s);
// "haystack"::contains works here, but the general reordering case does not:
BiFunction<String, String, Boolean> flipped = (a, b) -> b.startsWith(a);
// no reference can express the swap
```

A null guard or any conditional is involved:

```java
.map(s -> s == null ? "" : s.trim())
```

The parameter name carries meaning a reader needs:

```java
// The reference is shorter, but the lambda documents the domain
.sorted((older, newer) -> older.date().compareTo(newer.date()))
```

The type is ambiguous or inference struggles. An explicit lambda lets you write
the types:

```java
// Sometimes needed when the compiler cannot infer
.map((String s) -> s.length())
```

Summarised:

| Situation                        | Use          |
| -------------------------------- | ------------ |
| Pure forwarding of arguments     | Reference    |
| Getter in a comparator/collector | Reference    |
| Printing or logging an element   | Reference    |
| Multiple chained calls           | Lambda       |
| Argument transformed first       | Lambda       |
| Conditional or null handling     | Lambda       |
| Reordered or dropped arguments   | Lambda       |
| Parameter name aids readability  | Lambda       |

Two practical notes to finish. First, references genuinely help when a getter
is used as a key, because `Person::getName` states the intent better than
`p -> p.getName()`. Second, be careful when converting a lambda to a reference
on a type you do not control: `String::valueOf` and `Object::toString` behave
differently on null, and swapping one for the other has changed behaviour in
real code.

```java
Stream.of("a", null).map(String::valueOf);   // "a", "null": no exception
Stream.of("a", null).map(Object::toString);  // NPE on the null element
```

Finally, both forms compile to the same `invokedynamic` machinery, so the
choice is about readability, not speed. Modern IDEs will offer the conversion
in both directions; accept it when it removes a redundant parameter and decline
it when it hides a meaningful name.

> Key Takeaways
> - Use a reference when the lambda only forwards its arguments unchanged.
> - Use a lambda when there are multiple calls, transformed arguments, or a
>   conditional.
> - A meaningful parameter name can be worth more than the shorter form.
> - Reordered or dropped arguments cannot be expressed as a reference.
> - `String::valueOf` and `Object::toString` differ on null, so convert
>   carefully.
> - Both compile to the same mechanism, so the decision is purely about
>   clarity.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take five lambdas from existing code and convert only those that are pure
>    forwarding.
> 2. Find a lambda that cannot become a reference and explain which rule blocks
>    it.
> 3. Compare `map(String::valueOf)` and `map(Object::toString)` on a stream
>    containing a null.
> 4. Interview: Is a method reference faster than the equivalent lambda?
>    (Hint: what bytecode instruction does each one compile to?)

<a id="84-the-stream-api"></a>
### 8.4 The Stream API

This subchapter covers streams: how to create them, the operations that
transform them, how laziness makes long pipelines cheap, and where parallelism
helps or hurts.

#### Stream Creation Sources

A `Stream<T>` is a sequence of elements supporting a pipeline of operations. It
is not a data structure. It stores nothing, and it is consumed once. Thinking
of it as "a collection with nicer methods" leads directly to the mistakes at
the end of this topic.

The better mental model is a conveyor belt. Elements travel along it, stations
transform or discard them, and at the end something collects what survives. The
belt itself holds nothing once the run is over.

```text
  source          intermediate ops              terminal op
  ------          ----------------              -----------
  [a, b, c]  -->  filter --> map --> sorted  -->  collect --> result
```

Every pipeline starts with a **source**. The most common is a collection:

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Grace", "Alan");

Stream<String> s1 = names.stream();            // any Collection
Stream<String> s2 = names.parallelStream();    // the parallel variant
```

From explicit values or an array:

```java
Stream<String> s3 = Stream.of("a", "b", "c");
Stream<String> s4 = Arrays.stream(new String[]{"a", "b"});
Stream<String> s5 = Arrays.stream(array, 1, 3);      // a sub-range

IntStream s6 = Arrays.stream(new int[]{1, 2, 3});    // primitive array
```

Ranges of numbers, which replace most counting `for` loops:

```java
IntStream.range(0, 5);          // 0, 1, 2, 3, 4   (upper bound excluded)
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5);    // 1, 2, 3, 4, 5   (upper bound included)
```

**Infinite** streams, which must be bounded by `limit` or a predicate:

```java
// iterate: apply a function repeatedly to the previous value
Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2).limit(5).forEach(System.out::println);  // 1 2 4 8 16

// The three-argument form has a built-in stop condition (Java 9+)
Stream.iterate(1, n -> n < 100, n -> n * 2).forEach(System.out::println);

// generate: call a supplier over and over, with no relation between elements
Stream.generate(Math::random).limit(3).forEach(System.out::println);
Stream.generate(() -> "x").limit(3).toList();      // [x, x, x]
```

Forgetting `limit` on an infinite stream is a hang, not an exception. The
program simply never reaches the terminal operation.

Other useful sources:

```java
// A file, line by line. It holds an OS handle, so close it
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("data.txt"))) {
    lines.filter(l -> !l.isBlank()).forEach(System.out::println);
}

Stream<String> words = Pattern.compile(",").splitAsStream("a,b,c");
IntStream chars = "hello".chars();               // an IntStream of code points
Stream<String> empty = Stream.empty();
Stream<String> maybe = Optional.of("a").stream();          // 0 or 1 elements
Stream<String> nullable = Stream.ofNullable(maybeNull);    // 0 or 1 elements

// Map entries
Map<String, Integer> ages = Map.of("Ada", 36);
ages.entrySet().stream().map(Map.Entry::getKey);
```

| Source                       | Produces                       |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `collection.stream()`        | Sequential stream of elements  |
| `Stream.of(...)`             | Stream of explicit values      |
| `Arrays.stream(arr)`         | Stream over an array           |
| `IntStream.range(a, b)`      | Primitive int range            |
| `Stream.iterate(seed, f)`    | Infinite, each from the last   |
| `Stream.generate(supplier)`  | Infinite, independent elements |
| `Files.lines(path)`          | Lines of a file; must be closed |
| `"abc".chars()`              | `IntStream` of characters      |

Now the two rules that the conveyor-belt model explains.

**A stream may be consumed once.** After a terminal operation the stream is
closed, and reusing it throws:

```java
Stream<String> s = names.stream();
s.forEach(System.out::println);
// s.count();      // IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated
                   // upon or closed
```

The fix is to create a new stream from the source each time, or to keep a
`Supplier<Stream<T>>`:

```java
Supplier<Stream<String>> factory = names::stream;
factory.get().forEach(System.out::println);
System.out.println(factory.get().count());     // a fresh stream
```

**A stream does not modify its source.** Operations produce new streams and a
final result; the original collection is untouched.

```java
List<String> original = new ArrayList<>(List.of("b", "a"));
List<String> sorted = original.stream().sorted().toList();
System.out.println(original);      // [b, a]: unchanged
System.out.println(sorted);        // [a, b]
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A stream is a pipeline over elements, not a data structure, and stores
>   nothing.
> - Every pipeline is a source, zero or more intermediate operations, and one
>   terminal operation.
> - Sources include collections, arrays, explicit values, ranges, files, and
>   generators.
> - `Stream.iterate` and `Stream.generate` are infinite and need `limit` or a
>   stop predicate.
> - A stream can be consumed only once; reuse throws `IllegalStateException`.
> - Keep a `Supplier<Stream<T>>` when you need the same pipeline twice.
> - Streams never modify their source collection.
> - Close file-backed streams with try-with-resources.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create streams from a list, an array, and `Stream.of`, and print each
>    one's count.
> 2. Generate the first ten powers of three with `Stream.iterate` and `limit`.
> 3. Trigger `IllegalStateException` by consuming a stream twice, then fix it
>    with a supplier.
> 4. Interview: Why can a stream not be reused? (Hint: what state would a
>    pipeline need to keep in order to restart, and where would that state
>    live?)

#### Intermediate Operations: filter, map, sorted

Intermediate operations transform one stream into another. They are the
stations on the conveyor belt. Each returns a new `Stream`, which is what makes
chaining possible, and none of them does any work until a terminal operation
runs.

**`filter(Predicate<T>)`** keeps elements matching a condition and discards the
rest. The stream gets shorter; the element type is unchanged.

```java
List<Integer> evens = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
        .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
        .toList();                       // [2, 4, 6]
```

**`map(Function<T, R>)`** transforms each element. The length is unchanged; the
type may change.

```java
List<Integer> lengths = Stream.of("ada", "grace")
        .map(String::length)             // Stream<String> -> Stream<Integer>
        .toList();                       // [3, 5]
```

```text
   filter: same type, fewer elements     map: same count, possibly new type

   [1, 2, 3, 4]                          ["ada", "grace"]
        |  filter(even)                       |  map(length)
        v                                     v
   [2, 4]                                [3, 5]
```

**`sorted()`** orders elements by natural ordering, or by a comparator. It is a
**stateful** operation: it must buffer the entire stream before it can emit the
first element.

```java
List<String> names = Stream.of("grace", "ada", "alan")
        .sorted()                                       // natural ordering
        .toList();                                      // [ada, alan, grace]

List<Person> byAge = people.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age).reversed())
        .toList();
```

The other intermediate operations, all used the same way:

| Operation              | Effect                                          |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `filter(p)`            | Keep matching elements                          |
| `map(f)`               | Transform each element                          |
| `distinct()`           | Remove duplicates, using `equals`/`hashCode`    |
| `sorted()`, `sorted(c)`| Order the elements; buffers everything          |
| `limit(n)`             | Keep at most the first `n`                      |
| `skip(n)`              | Discard the first `n`                           |
| `peek(c)`              | Run an action on each element and pass it along |
| `takeWhile(p)`         | Keep elements until the first failure (Java 9)  |
| `dropWhile(p)`         | Discard elements until the first failure        |
| `mapMulti(...)`        | Emit zero or more elements per input (Java 16)  |

`takeWhile` and `dropWhile` differ from `filter` in an important way: they stop
at the first element that fails, rather than testing every element.

```java
List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3, 10, 4, 5);

nums.stream().takeWhile(n -> n < 5).toList();   // [1, 2, 3]: stops at 10
nums.stream().dropWhile(n -> n < 5).toList();   // [10, 4, 5]
nums.stream().filter(n -> n < 5).toList();      // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]: tests all
```

`peek` is intended for debugging. It lets you observe elements mid-pipeline
without changing them:

```java
List<String> out = Stream.of("a", "b")
        .peek(s -> System.out.println("before: " + s))
        .map(String::toUpperCase)
        .peek(s -> System.out.println("after: " + s))
        .toList();
```

Do not use `peek` for side effects in production code. Because the pipeline is
lazy, a `peek` before an operation that never runs will not execute, and some
optimisations can skip it entirely.

Order matters for performance. Filtering before mapping means fewer elements
get transformed:

```java
// Maps all 1000, then discards most: wasteful
list.stream().map(this::expensiveTransform).filter(x -> x.isValid());

// Discards first, transforms only survivors
list.stream().filter(this::isValid).map(this::expensiveTransform);
```

The same reasoning applies to `sorted`: filter first so there is less to sort,
and place `limit` after `sorted` only when you genuinely need the top N, since
`sorted` cannot short-circuit.

> Key Takeaways
> - Intermediate operations return a new stream and run nothing until a
>   terminal operation.
> - `filter` shortens the stream; `map` transforms elements and can change the
>   type.
> - `sorted` is stateful and buffers every element before emitting any.
> - `distinct` relies on `equals` and `hashCode`.
> - `takeWhile` and `dropWhile` stop at the first failure; `filter` tests
>   everything.
> - `peek` is a debugging tool and unreliable for side effects because of
>   laziness.
> - Put `filter` before `map` and before `sorted` to reduce the work done.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. From a list of words, keep those longer than four characters, uppercase
>    them, and sort them.
> 2. Show a case where `takeWhile` and `filter` give different results on the
>    same input.
> 3. Use `skip` and `limit` together to extract page three of ten-item pages.
> 4. Interview: Why is `sorted` called a stateful operation? (Hint: how many
>    elements must it see before it can emit the first one?)

#### flatMap and Nested Structures

`map` transforms one element into one element. When each element expands into
*several*, `map` gives you a stream of streams, which is almost never what you
want. `flatMap` is the operation that transforms and then flattens in one step.

The problem, concretely:

```java
List<List<String>> nested = List.of(
        List.of("a", "b"),
        List.of("c", "d"));

// map gives a Stream<Stream<String>>: awkward and hard to consume
Stream<Stream<String>> wrong = nested.stream().map(List::stream);

// flatMap concatenates the inner streams into one flat stream
List<String> flat = nested.stream()
        .flatMap(List::stream)
        .toList();                       // [a, b, c, d]
```

```text
   map(List::stream)                  flatMap(List::stream)

   [ [a,b], [c,d] ]                   [ [a,b], [c,d] ]
          |                                  |
          v                                  v
   [ <a,b>, <c,d> ]                   [ a, b, c, d ]
   a stream of streams                one flat stream
```

The mental model: the function you pass returns a *stream* for each element,
and `flatMap` splices all those streams together end to end. An element that
maps to an empty stream simply disappears, which makes `flatMap` a filter as
well as an expander.

The classic case is splitting text:

```java
List<String> sentences = List.of("hello world", "good morning");

List<String> words = sentences.stream()
        .flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" ")))    // one sentence -> many words
        .toList();                                    // [hello, world, good, morning]

// Unique words across all sentences
Set<String> unique = sentences.stream()
        .flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" ")))
        .collect(Collectors.toSet());
```

Navigating object graphs is the other everyday use. When each object owns a
collection and you want all the inner elements:

```java
record Order(String id, List<Item> items) { }
record Item(String name, double price) { }

List<Order> orders = loadOrders();

// Every item across every order
List<Item> allItems = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.items().stream())
        .toList();

double revenue = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.items().stream())
        .mapToDouble(Item::price)
        .sum();
```

`flatMap` also removes empty `Optional` values cleanly, which is the idiomatic
way to turn a stream of optionals into a stream of present values:

```java
List<Optional<String>> maybes = List.of(
        Optional.of("a"), Optional.empty(), Optional.of("c"));

List<String> present = maybes.stream()
        .flatMap(Optional::stream)      // empty contributes nothing
        .toList();                      // [a, c]
```

Flattening more than one level requires more than one `flatMap`:

```java
List<List<List<String>>> deep = ...;
List<String> flattened = deep.stream()
        .flatMap(List::stream)          // depth 3 -> depth 2
        .flatMap(List::stream)          // depth 2 -> depth 1
        .toList();
```

Two related tools. `mapMulti`, added in Java 16, expresses the same idea by
pushing elements into a consumer instead of building intermediate streams,
which avoids allocation when most elements expand to zero or one result. And
the primitive variants `flatMapToInt`, `flatMapToLong`, and `flatMapToDouble`
flatten into a primitive stream directly.

```java
// Cartesian product: pair every letter with every number
List<String> pairs = Stream.of("a", "b")
        .flatMap(letter -> Stream.of(1, 2)
                .map(number -> letter + number))
        .toList();                       // [a1, a2, b1, b2]
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `map` produces one output per input; `flatMap` produces zero or more.
> - The mapping function must return a `Stream`, and `flatMap` concatenates
>   them.
> - Mapping to an empty stream removes the element, so `flatMap` can also
>   filter.
> - It is the standard way to split text and to walk nested object graphs.
> - `flatMap(Optional::stream)` drops empty optionals in one step.
> - Each `flatMap` removes exactly one level of nesting.
> - `mapMulti` avoids allocating intermediate streams when expansion is small.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Flatten a `List<List<Integer>>` into a single sorted list of distinct
>    values.
> 2. Count the distinct words across a list of sentences.
> 3. From a list of orders each holding items, find the most expensive item
>    overall.
> 4. Interview: What is the difference between `map` and `flatMap` in terms of
>    element counts? (Hint: compare the output size of each when every input
>    maps to a three-element list.)

#### Terminal Operations and Reduction

A terminal operation ends the pipeline. It triggers execution, produces a
result that is not a stream, and closes the stream. Until one runs, nothing
happens at all.

They fall into four groups.

**Collecting into a container:**

```java
List<String> list = stream.toList();                          // immutable, Java 16+
List<String> mutable = stream.collect(Collectors.toList());   // usually ArrayList
Set<String> set = stream.collect(Collectors.toSet());
Map<String, Integer> map = stream.collect(
        Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), String::length));
String[] array = stream.toArray(String[]::new);
```

**Searching and matching**, all of which short-circuit:

```java
Optional<String> first = stream.findFirst();      // first in encounter order
Optional<String> any = stream.findAny();          // any element, cheaper in parallel

boolean allOk = stream.allMatch(s -> !s.isBlank());
boolean someOk = stream.anyMatch(s -> s.startsWith("A"));
boolean noneOk = stream.noneMatch(String::isBlank);
```

A logical quirk worth knowing: on an empty stream `allMatch` returns `true` and
`anyMatch` returns `false`. That is "vacuous truth", and it is the standard
mathematical convention, not a bug.

**Aggregating:**

```java
long n = stream.count();
Optional<String> longest = stream.max(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));
Optional<String> shortest = stream.min(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));
```

**Iterating:**

```java
stream.forEach(System.out::println);          // no order guarantee in parallel
stream.forEachOrdered(System.out::println);   // encounter order, even in parallel
```

The most general terminal operation is **`reduce`**, which folds the stream
down to a single value by repeatedly combining elements. It has three forms.

```java
// 1. Identity plus accumulator: always returns a value
int sum = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).reduce(0, Integer::sum);        // 10

// 2. Accumulator only: returns Optional, since an empty stream has no result
Optional<Integer> product = Stream.of(1, 2, 3).reduce((a, b) -> a * b);  // 6

// 3. Identity, accumulator, and combiner: for parallel with a different result type
int totalLength = Stream.of("ab", "cde")
        .reduce(0,                          // identity
                (acc, s) -> acc + s.length(),   // accumulate into the result type
                Integer::sum);                  // combine partial results
```

```text
   reduce(0, Integer::sum) over [1, 2, 3, 4]

   0 + 1 = 1
       1 + 2 = 3
           3 + 3 = 6
               6 + 4 = 10
```

Three rules govern a correct reduction, and breaking them produces wrong
answers only under parallelism, which makes them hard to catch:

- The **identity** must satisfy `f(identity, x) == x`. Zero for addition, one
  for multiplication, the empty string for concatenation.
- The accumulator must be **associative**, so grouping does not matter.
- The accumulator must be **stateless** and must not mutate anything outside
  itself.

The classic misuse is string concatenation, which is associative but allocates
a new string at every step:

```java
// O(n^2): each concatenation copies the accumulated string
String bad = words.stream().reduce("", (a, b) -> a + b);

// O(n): the collector uses a StringBuilder internally
String good = words.stream().collect(Collectors.joining());
```

The distinction between `reduce` and `collect` is worth stating plainly.
`reduce` combines **immutable** values into a new value at each step. `collect`
performs a **mutable** reduction, accumulating into a container. Use `reduce`
for numbers and other immutable results, and `collect` whenever the result is a
collection or a string.

| Operation      | Returns              | Short-circuits |
| -------------- | -------------------- | -------------- |
| `toList`       | `List<T>`            | No             |
| `collect`      | Whatever the collector builds | No    |
| `reduce`       | `T` or `Optional<T>` | No             |
| `count`        | `long`               | No             |
| `min` / `max`  | `Optional<T>`        | No             |
| `findFirst` / `findAny` | `Optional<T>` | Yes        |
| `anyMatch` / `allMatch` / `noneMatch` | `boolean` | Yes |
| `forEach`      | `void`               | No             |

> Key Takeaways
> - A terminal operation produces a non-stream result and triggers the whole
>   pipeline.
> - `toList` returns an immutable list; `Collectors.toList` usually returns a
>   mutable one.
> - `findFirst`, `findAny`, and the match operations short-circuit.
> - On an empty stream `allMatch` is `true` and `anyMatch` is `false`.
> - `reduce` folds elements into one value using an identity and an
>   associative accumulator.
> - The two-argument `reduce` returns `Optional` because an empty stream has no
>   result.
> - Use `reduce` for immutable values and `collect` for containers and strings.
> - Reducing with string concatenation is quadratic; use `Collectors.joining`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the sum, maximum, and count of a list of integers using three
>    terminal operations.
> 2. Concatenate strings with `reduce` and with `Collectors.joining`, and time
>    both on 100,000 elements.
> 3. Use `reduce` with an identity to find the longest string in a list.
> 4. Interview: Why does the one-argument `reduce` return an `Optional` while
>    the two-argument form does not? (Hint: what should each return for an
>    empty stream?)

#### Lazy Evaluation and Short-Circuiting

The single most important thing to understand about streams is that
intermediate operations do nothing when you call them. They build a plan. The
plan executes only when a terminal operation arrives, and then all the
operations run together, element by element.

This code prints nothing:

```java
Stream.of("a", "b", "c")
      .filter(s -> { System.out.println("filter " + s); return true; })
      .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s; });
// No terminal operation, so no output at all
```

Add `.toList()` and the output reveals the execution model:

```text
  filter a
  map a          <- element "a" goes through the WHOLE pipeline
  filter b
  map b          <- then element "b"
  filter c
  map c
```

Elements are processed **vertically**, one at a time down the whole chain, not
horizontally with each stage completing before the next begins. This is called
fusion, and it has two consequences that matter in practice.

The first is that a long chain does not mean many passes over the data. Five
intermediate operations still make one pass, with no intermediate collections
allocated.

The second is **short-circuiting**: operations that can finish early stop the
whole pipeline, so elements past that point are never even looked at.

```java
Optional<String> found = Stream.of("apple", "banana", "cherry", "date")
        .filter(s -> { System.out.println("checking " + s); return s.length() > 5; })
        .findFirst();

// Output:
//   checking apple
//   checking banana      <- matches, so the pipeline STOPS here
// "cherry" and "date" are never examined
```

The short-circuiting operations:

| Operation                    | Stops as soon as                     |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `findFirst()`, `findAny()`   | One element is produced              |
| `anyMatch(p)`                | One element matches                  |
| `allMatch(p)`                | One element fails                    |
| `noneMatch(p)`               | One element matches                  |
| `limit(n)`                   | `n` elements have passed             |
| `takeWhile(p)`               | One element fails the predicate      |

Short-circuiting is what makes infinite streams usable at all:

```java
// Terminates: limit stops the source after 5 elements
List<Integer> powers = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2).limit(5).toList();

// Terminates: findFirst stops at the first match
Optional<Integer> firstBig = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2)
        .filter(n -> n > 1000)
        .findFirst();                   // 1024

// HANGS: count() must consume everything
// long forever = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n + 1).count();
```

Laziness also explains why operation order changes the amount of work done,
even though the result is identical:

```java
// limit AFTER filter: filters until 2 matches are found, then stops
Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).limit(2).toList();  // [2, 4]

// limit BEFORE filter: takes 2 elements, then filters those
Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).limit(2).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).toList();  // [2]
```

Two operations break the flow because they cannot emit anything until they have
seen everything. `sorted` and `distinct` are **stateful barriers**:

```java
// sorted must buffer all elements, so the elements after it wait
stream.filter(...).sorted().map(...).toList();
//              ^ everything upstream completes before map sees anything
```

Placing an expensive `sorted` before a `limit` is therefore costly, because the
sort cannot short-circuit. If you only need the top three, a bounded
`PriorityQueue` or `Collectors` with a limit does less work.

A final practical consequence: because `peek` runs only when elements actually
flow, a `peek` in a pipeline that short-circuits will print less than you
expect, and a `peek` in a pipeline with no terminal operation prints nothing.
That is the main reason `peek` is unreliable for anything but debugging.

> Key Takeaways
> - Intermediate operations build a plan; nothing runs until a terminal
>   operation.
> - Elements flow one at a time through the entire chain, so a long pipeline is
>   still one pass.
> - No intermediate collections are allocated between stages.
> - Short-circuiting operations stop the pipeline early and skip remaining
>   elements.
> - Infinite streams are only usable because of `limit`, `findFirst`, and the
>   match operations.
> - `sorted` and `distinct` are stateful barriers that must consume everything
>   first.
> - Operation order changes how much work is performed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `println` to a `filter` and a `map`, run with and without a terminal
>    operation, and compare.
> 2. Show that `findFirst` stops the pipeline by printing every element the
>    filter examines.
> 3. Compare the element counts examined by `filter().limit(2)` versus
>    `limit(2).filter()`.
> 4. Interview: Why does `Stream.iterate(1, n -> n + 1).filter(n -> n > 10)
>    .findFirst()` terminate while `.count()` does not? (Hint: which of the two
>    can stop before the source is exhausted?)

#### Collectors and Grouping

`Collectors` is the class that turns a stream back into a data structure. It
holds far more than `toList`, and the grouping collectors in particular replace
loops that would otherwise take ten lines and a `computeIfAbsent`.

The basic collectors:

```java
List<String> list = stream.collect(Collectors.toList());
Set<String> set = stream.collect(Collectors.toSet());
TreeSet<String> tree = stream.collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));

String joined = Stream.of("a", "b", "c").collect(Collectors.joining());       // "abc"
String csv = Stream.of("a", "b").collect(Collectors.joining(", "));           // "a, b"
String wrapped = Stream.of("a", "b")
        .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));                         // "[a, b]"
```

`Collectors.toMap` needs a key function and a value function, and it throws on
duplicate keys unless you supply a merge function:

```java
Map<String, Integer> lengths = Stream.of("ada", "grace")
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), String::length));

// Duplicate keys throw IllegalStateException without a third argument
Map<Integer, String> byLength = Stream.of("ab", "cd", "efg")
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(String::length, Function.identity(),
                                  (first, second) -> first));   // keep the first
```

**`groupingBy`** is the most valuable collector. It partitions elements into a
`Map` keyed by whatever the classifier returns.

```java
record Employee(String name, String dept, double salary) { }

Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));
```

```text
   [ Ada/Eng, Bob/Sales, Cy/Eng ]
              |
              |  groupingBy(Employee::dept)
              v
   { "Eng"   -> [Ada, Cy],
     "Sales" -> [Bob] }
```

The second argument is a **downstream collector**, applied to each group. This
is what makes `groupingBy` compose into real aggregations:

```java
// Count per department
Map<String, Long> countByDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept, Collectors.counting()));

// Average salary per department
Map<String, Double> avgByDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept,
                 Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary)));

// Just the names, not whole objects
Map<String, List<String>> namesByDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept,
                 Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.toList())));

// Highest earner per department
Map<String, Optional<Employee>> topByDept = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept,
                 Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::salary))));
```

The third argument chooses the map implementation, which matters when you need
sorted keys:

```java
TreeMap<String, List<Employee>> sorted = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept, TreeMap::new,
                                       Collectors.toList()));
```

Grouping nests, which handles multi-level reports in one expression:

```java
Map<String, Map<Boolean, List<Employee>>> byDeptThenSenior = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept,
                 Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e.salary() > 100_000)));
```

**`partitioningBy`** is the special case of grouping by a predicate. It always
returns a map with exactly the keys `true` and `false`, even when one side is
empty, which `groupingBy` would omit.

```java
Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> split = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4)
        .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0));
// {false=[1, 3], true=[2, 4]}
```

The statistical and utility collectors:

| Collector                       | Produces                         |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `counting()`                    | `Long` count                     |
| `summingInt/Long/Double(f)`     | Total                            |
| `averagingInt/Long/Double(f)`   | `Double` average                 |
| `summarizingInt(f)`             | Count, sum, min, max, average    |
| `minBy(c)` / `maxBy(c)`         | `Optional<T>`                    |
| `mapping(f, downstream)`        | Transform before collecting      |
| `filtering(p, downstream)`      | Filter within a group (Java 9)   |
| `flatMapping(f, downstream)`    | Flatten within a group (Java 9)  |
| `collectingAndThen(c, finisher)`| Post-process the result          |
| `teeing(c1, c2, merger)`        | Two collectors at once (Java 12) |

`collectingAndThen` is how you make a collected result immutable:

```java
List<String> immutable = stream.collect(
        Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), List::copyOf));
```

A note on `toList()` versus `Collectors.toList()`. The stream method added in
Java 16 returns an **unmodifiable** list and is the better default. The
collector's contract does not guarantee mutability or immutability, though it
returns an `ArrayList` in practice. Use `Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new)`
when you specifically need a mutable result.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Collectors` converts a stream into lists, sets, maps, and strings.
> - `Collectors.toMap` throws on duplicate keys unless given a merge function.
> - `groupingBy` builds a `Map` from a classifier function.
> - A downstream collector aggregates within each group, and groupings nest.
> - A third argument selects the map implementation, such as `TreeMap::new`.
> - `partitioningBy` always yields both `true` and `false` keys.
> - `collectingAndThen` post-processes the result, commonly to make it
>   immutable.
> - `stream.toList()` returns an unmodifiable list and is the modern default.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Group a list of words by their first letter.
> 2. Compute the average salary per department with `groupingBy` and
>    `averagingDouble`.
> 3. Partition numbers into primes and non-primes with `partitioningBy`.
> 4. Build a `Map<String, List<String>>` of employee names by department using
>    `mapping`.
> 5. Interview: What is the difference between `groupingBy(p)` and
>    `partitioningBy(p)` when no element matches? (Hint: how many keys does
>    each resulting map contain?)

#### Primitive Streams and Statistics

`Stream<Integer>` boxes every element. For numeric work that is both slower and
clumsier, since `Stream` has no `sum` method. The three primitive streams,
`IntStream`, `LongStream`, and `DoubleStream`, fix both problems.

```java
// Boxed: an Integer object per element, and no sum() available
int sum1 = Stream.of(1, 2, 3).mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();

// Primitive throughout: no allocation
int sum2 = IntStream.of(1, 2, 3).sum();
```

Creating them:

```java
IntStream.of(1, 2, 3);
IntStream.range(0, 5);              // 0..4
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5);        // 1..5
Arrays.stream(new int[]{1, 2, 3});
"hello".chars();                    // IntStream of char values
new Random().ints(5, 1, 7);         // 5 random ints in [1, 7)
```

Converting between the object and primitive worlds is explicit in both
directions:

```java
// Object stream -> primitive stream
IntStream lengths = Stream.of("ab", "cde").mapToInt(String::length);
DoubleStream prices = orders.stream().mapToDouble(Order::total);

// Primitive stream -> object stream
Stream<Integer> boxed = IntStream.range(0, 3).boxed();
Stream<String> names = IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> "item" + i);

// Between primitive streams
LongStream longs = IntStream.of(1, 2).asLongStream();
DoubleStream doubles = IntStream.of(1, 2).asDoubleStream();
```

`boxed()` is needed whenever you want to collect into a collection, since
`Collectors` works on object streams:

```java
List<Integer> list = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).boxed().toList();
```

The extra numeric operations are the main attraction:

```java
IntStream nums = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10);

int sum = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).sum();                 // 55
OptionalInt max = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).max();         // 10
OptionalDouble avg = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).average();  // 5.5
long count = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).count();            // 10
```

Note the return types. `max` returns `OptionalInt`, not `Optional<Integer>`,
and `average` returns `OptionalDouble` regardless of the stream type. These are
primitive-specialised optionals with `getAsInt` and `getAsDouble` accessors.

**`summaryStatistics()`** computes count, sum, min, max, and average in a
single pass, which beats running five separate pipelines:

```java
IntSummaryStatistics stats = IntStream.of(3, 1, 4, 1, 5).summaryStatistics();

System.out.println(stats.getCount());     // 5
System.out.println(stats.getSum());       // 14
System.out.println(stats.getMin());       // 1
System.out.println(stats.getMax());       // 5
System.out.println(stats.getAverage());   // 2.8
```

The collector equivalent works on object streams, which is how you get
statistics over a field:

```java
DoubleSummaryStatistics salaryStats = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.summarizingDouble(Employee::salary));
```

Three cautions.

`IntStream.sum()` returns an `int` and **overflows silently** on large data.
Use `asLongStream().sum()` or `mapToLong` when totals may be large:

```java
int overflow = IntStream.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1).sum();          // negative
long safe = IntStream.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1).asLongStream().sum();
```

`"hello".chars()` yields `int` code points, so printing them directly gives
numbers rather than letters:

```java
"abc".chars().forEach(System.out::println);                    // 97 98 99
"abc".chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c).forEach(System.out::println);  // a b c
```

And `average()` returns an empty `OptionalDouble` for an empty stream, which is
correct rather than zero. Handle it with `orElse`.

| Feature                | `Stream<Integer>` | `IntStream`        |
| ---------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ |
| Boxing                 | Yes               | No                 |
| `sum`, `average`, `max`| Not available     | Built in           |
| `summaryStatistics`    | Via a collector   | Built in           |
| Collecting             | Direct            | Needs `boxed()`    |
| Optional type          | `Optional<Integer>` | `OptionalInt`    |

> Key Takeaways
> - Primitive streams avoid boxing and add numeric operations that `Stream`
>   lacks.
> - `mapToInt`, `mapToDouble`, and `mapToLong` enter the primitive world.
> - `boxed()` and `mapToObj` return to the object world, which collecting
>   requires.
> - `max` and `average` return `OptionalInt` and `OptionalDouble`, not
>   `Optional<T>`.
> - `summaryStatistics()` gives count, sum, min, max, and average in one pass.
> - `IntStream.sum()` overflows silently; widen to `long` for large totals.
> - `String.chars()` produces code points, so cast to `char` before printing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Sum the squares of 1 through 100 with `IntStream` and no boxing.
> 2. Compute count, min, max, and average of a list of prices with
>    `summarizingDouble`.
> 3. Count vowels in a string using `chars()` and a filter.
> 4. Interview: Why does `IntStream.average()` return `OptionalDouble` rather
>    than `double`? (Hint: what is the average of an empty stream?)

#### Parallel Streams and Their Caveats

Adding `.parallel()` splits a stream across multiple threads. It is a one-word
change, which is exactly why it is dangerous: the syntax hides a large increase
in complexity and frequently makes code slower rather than faster.

```java
long count = hugeList.parallelStream()
        .filter(this::isExpensive)
        .count();

// Equivalent
long same = hugeList.stream().parallel().filter(this::isExpensive).count();
```

How it works: the stream's source is recursively split, each chunk is processed
by a thread in the common `ForkJoinPool`, and the partial results are combined.

```text
             [ 1 .. 1000 ]
                   |  split
        +----------+----------+
   [1..500]                [501..1000]
        |  split                |  split
   +----+----+            +-----+-----+
 [1..250] [251..500]  [501..750] [751..1000]
      |        |           |          |
    process  process    process    process     (separate threads)
      |        |           |          |
      +--------+-----------+----------+
                   combine
```

The pool has `availableProcessors() - 1` threads by default and is **shared by
the entire JVM**. One slow parallel stream can therefore starve every other
one, and blocking inside a parallel stream, on a network call for instance, is
particularly harmful because it occupies a pool thread doing nothing.

Parallelism pays off when all of the following hold:

- The data set is **large**, typically tens of thousands of elements or more.
- The per-element work is **substantial**, not a field access.
- The source **splits cheaply**: arrays, `ArrayList`, and `IntStream.range` are
  ideal; `LinkedList` and most `Stream.iterate` sources are not.
- The operations are **stateless and independent**.
- The terminal operation combines cheaply: `sum` and `count` are fine,
  `Collectors.toMap` much less so.

The costs it always pays are splitting, thread coordination, and merging. For
small collections those dominate, and a parallel stream is reliably slower than
a plain loop.

The correctness hazards are more serious than the performance ones.

**Shared mutable state** breaks silently. This is the single most common
parallel stream bug:

```java
List<Integer> results = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, 10_000).parallel()
         .forEach(results::add);      // ArrayList is not thread-safe
// Lost updates, wrong size, or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

// Correct: let the framework handle collection
List<Integer> safe = IntStream.range(0, 10_000).parallel().boxed().toList();
```

**Non-associative operations** give different answers depending on how the data
was split:

```java
// Subtraction is not associative: results vary run to run
int odd = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).parallel().reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b);
```

**Order-dependent operations** cost more in parallel. `findFirst` must
establish which match is genuinely first, while `findAny` may return whatever
appears soonest; `forEachOrdered` re-imposes ordering and discards much of the
benefit.

```java
list.parallelStream().forEach(System.out::println);         // arbitrary order
list.parallelStream().forEachOrdered(System.out::println);  // ordered, slower
```

Stateful lambdas are unsafe even when they look harmless:

```java
int[] counter = {0};
list.parallelStream().forEach(x -> counter[0]++);   // lost updates, wrong total
```

If you must run parallel work on a pool you control, submit the pipeline to
your own `ForkJoinPool`:

```java
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
long result = pool.submit(() -> hugeList.parallelStream().filter(...).count())
                  .get();
pool.shutdown();
```

| Use parallel when                  | Avoid parallel when                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Tens of thousands of elements      | Small collections                    |
| CPU-heavy per-element work         | Trivial per-element work             |
| `ArrayList`, arrays, `IntStream`   | `LinkedList`, `iterate`, I/O sources |
| Stateless, independent operations  | Shared mutable state                 |
| Associative reduction              | Non-associative operations           |
| Order does not matter              | Encounter order is required          |
| No blocking calls                  | Network or database calls inside     |

The honest summary: write the sequential version first, and only add
`.parallel()` if a profiler shows the pipeline is a bottleneck and measurement
proves the parallel version is actually faster on realistic data.

> Key Takeaways
> - `.parallel()` splits work across the shared `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`.
> - The pool is JVM-wide, so one slow pipeline affects every other one.
> - Parallelism needs large data, heavy per-element work, and a cheaply
>   splittable source.
> - Splitting, coordinating, and merging are fixed costs that small streams
>   never recover.
> - Shared mutable state produces lost updates and corrupted results.
> - Reduction operations must be associative or parallel answers will differ.
> - `findAny` and `forEach` are cheaper than `findFirst` and `forEachOrdered`.
> - Never block inside a parallel stream, and always measure before adopting
>   one.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Sum 1 to 10,000,000 sequentially and in parallel, and compare the timings.
> 2. Do the same for a 100-element list and explain why parallel loses.
> 3. Demonstrate corruption by adding to an `ArrayList` inside a parallel
>    `forEach`.
> 4. Show that `reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b)` gives inconsistent parallel
>    results.
> 5. Interview: Why is a parallel stream over a `LinkedList` usually slower
>    than over an `ArrayList`? (Hint: to split a range in half, what must each
>    structure do first?)

<a id="85-optional-and-null-safety"></a>
### 8.5 Optional and Null Safety

This subchapter covers `Optional`: how to create one, how to transform it
without unwrapping, and the usage rules that separate it from a null check in
disguise.

#### Creating Optional Values

`null` has a well-known problem: it carries no information. A method returning
`String` might return `null`, and nothing in the signature says so. The caller
either writes a defensive check everywhere or eventually meets a
`NullPointerException` far from the cause.

```java
// Does this ever return null? The signature does not say.
public User findUser(String id) { ... }

User user = findUser("123");
System.out.println(user.getName());     // NPE, if it did
```

`Optional<T>` is a container holding either one value or nothing, and it makes
the possibility of absence **part of the type**:

```java
public Optional<User> findUser(String id) { ... }
// The caller cannot ignore this: the value must be unwrapped deliberately
```

```text
   Optional<User>

   present:  [ User(...) ]        isPresent() -> true
   empty:    [           ]        isEmpty()   -> true
```

Think of it as a single-element box. It is either occupied or not, and you must
open it to get at the contents.

There are three factory methods, and choosing the wrong one is a common error.

```java
// 1. of: the value must NOT be null, or it throws immediately
Optional<String> a = Optional.of("hello");
// Optional<String> bad = Optional.of(null);     // NullPointerException

// 2. ofNullable: accepts null, producing an empty Optional
Optional<String> b = Optional.ofNullable(maybeNull);

// 3. empty: an explicitly absent value
Optional<String> c = Optional.empty();
```

The rule is simple. Use `of` when you know the value is present, because the
immediate exception documents a broken assumption. Use `ofNullable` when
wrapping something that might legitimately be null, typically a value from a
legacy API or a map lookup:

```java
public Optional<User> findUser(String id) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(database.get(id));   // get may return null
}
```

Checking the contents:

```java
Optional<String> opt = Optional.of("hello");

opt.isPresent();      // true
opt.isEmpty();        // true if absent (Java 11)
opt.get();            // "hello", but throws NoSuchElementException if empty
```

`get()` is the method to avoid. Calling it without first proving presence
simply moves the `NullPointerException` to a `NoSuchElementException`, gaining
nothing. Java 10 added `orElseThrow()` with no arguments as a clearer
equivalent, and modern code uses that or, better, the transformation methods in
the next two topics.

```java
// The anti-pattern: this is a null check wearing a costume
if (opt.isPresent()) {
    System.out.println(opt.get().toUpperCase());
}

// The idiomatic form
opt.map(String::toUpperCase).ifPresent(System.out::println);
```

Two conditional methods cover the common branches:

```java
opt.ifPresent(v -> System.out.println(v));                  // do X if present

opt.ifPresentOrElse(                                        // Java 9
        v -> System.out.println("found " + v),
        () -> System.out.println("nothing found"));
```

An important limit to state early: `Optional` is **not `Serializable`** and is
designed as a return type, not a universal null replacement. The guidelines
topic covers where it belongs and where it does not.

Finally, note that there are primitive variants, `OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`,
and `OptionalDouble`, returned by the primitive streams. They avoid boxing but
lack `map` and `flatMap`, so they are less useful for chaining.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Optional<T>` makes possible absence visible in the type signature.
> - `Optional.of` throws on null; `ofNullable` converts null to empty;
>   `empty` is explicit absence.
> - Wrap legacy or lookup results with `ofNullable`, not `of`.
> - `get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` and should be avoided.
> - An `isPresent` and `get` pair is just a null check in disguise.
> - `ifPresent` and `ifPresentOrElse` express the two branches directly.
> - `Optional` is not serialisable and is intended as a return type.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `Optional<String> findById(int id)` over a map, using `ofNullable`.
> 2. Show that `Optional.of(null)` throws while `Optional.ofNullable(null)`
>    does not.
> 3. Replace an `isPresent`/`get` block with `ifPresentOrElse`.
> 4. Interview: Does `Optional` eliminate `NullPointerException`? (Hint: what
>    happens if a method returns a null `Optional` reference?)

#### map, flatMap, and filter on Optional

The real value of `Optional` is not the presence check. It is that you can
transform the contained value without ever unwrapping it, and absence
propagates through the chain automatically. This is the same idea as a stream,
applied to a container of at most one element.

**`map`** applies a function if a value is present, and does nothing if it is
not:

```java
Optional<String> name = Optional.of("ada");

Optional<String> upper = name.map(String::toUpperCase);   // Optional[ADA]
Optional<Integer> length = name.map(String::length);      // Optional[3]

Optional<String> none = Optional.<String>empty();
Optional<Integer> stillNone = none.map(String::length);   // Optional.empty
// The function was never called. No null check was needed.
```

```text
   present:  [ "ada" ] --map(toUpperCase)--> [ "ADA" ]

   empty:    [       ] --map(toUpperCase)--> [       ]   (function skipped)
```

That skipping behaviour is what removes the nested `if` blocks. Compare:

```java
// Imperative: three levels of null checking
public String getCityImperative(User user) {
    if (user != null) {
        Address address = user.getAddress();
        if (address != null) {
            City city = address.getCity();
            if (city != null) {
                return city.getName().toUpperCase();
            }
        }
    }
    return "UNKNOWN";
}

// With Optional: one chain, absence handled once at the end
public String getCity(User user) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(user)
            .map(User::getAddress)        // skipped if user is absent
            .map(Address::getCity)        // skipped if address is null
            .map(City::getName)
            .map(String::toUpperCase)
            .orElse("UNKNOWN");
}
```

Note a convenience: if `getAddress()` returns a plain `Address` that may be
null, `map` still works, because it wraps the result with `ofNullable`
internally. A null result becomes an empty `Optional` rather than an
`Optional` containing null.

**`flatMap`** is for the case where the function *itself* returns an
`Optional`. Using `map` there produces a doubly wrapped value:

```java
public Optional<Address> getAddress() { ... }   // already returns Optional

// map gives a nested Optional: almost never useful
Optional<Optional<Address>> nested = optUser.map(User::getAddress);

// flatMap unwraps one level
Optional<Address> address = optUser.flatMap(User::getAddress);
```

The rule mirrors the stream version: use `map` when the function returns a
plain value, `flatMap` when it returns an `Optional`.

```java
// A chain over an API that returns Optional at every step
String city = findUser(id)
        .flatMap(User::getAddress)      // Optional<Address>
        .flatMap(Address::getCity)      // Optional<City>
        .map(City::getName)             // plain String, so map
        .orElse("UNKNOWN");
```

**`filter`** keeps the value only if it matches a predicate, and turns it into
an empty `Optional` otherwise:

```java
Optional<User> adult = findUser(id).filter(u -> u.age() >= 18);

// Combines naturally with the rest of the chain
String result = findUser(id)
        .filter(User::isActive)
        .map(User::getName)
        .orElse("no active user");
```

**`or`**, added in Java 9, supplies a fallback `Optional` rather than a
fallback value, which lets you try sources in order:

```java
Optional<User> user = findInCache(id)
        .or(() -> findInDatabase(id))       // only runs if the cache missed
        .or(() -> findInBackup(id));
```

**`stream`**, also from Java 9, bridges into the Stream API and is the clean
way to drop empties from a collection of optionals:

```java
List<String> names = userIds.stream()
        .map(this::findUser)            // Stream<Optional<User>>
        .flatMap(Optional::stream)      // Stream<User>, empties removed
        .map(User::getName)
        .toList();
```

| Method        | Function returns | Result            |
| ------------- | ---------------- | ----------------- |
| `map(f)`      | A plain value    | `Optional<R>`     |
| `flatMap(f)`  | An `Optional<R>` | `Optional<R>`     |
| `filter(p)`   | A boolean        | Same or empty     |
| `or(supplier)`| An `Optional<T>` | This, or the fallback |
| `stream()`    | -                | A 0 or 1 element stream |

> Key Takeaways
> - `map` transforms the contained value and skips the function when empty.
> - Absence propagates automatically, replacing nested null checks with a
>   chain.
> - `map` wraps its result with `ofNullable`, so a null result becomes empty.
> - Use `flatMap` when the function already returns an `Optional`, to avoid
>   nesting.
> - `filter` empties the `Optional` when the predicate fails.
> - `or` supplies an alternative `Optional`, evaluated lazily.
> - `Optional.stream()` flattens a stream of optionals into present values
>   only.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Chain `map` calls to get an uppercased city name from a possibly null
>    user.
> 2. Write two methods returning `Optional` and chain them with `flatMap`.
> 3. Use `filter` to return a user only when active, defaulting otherwise.
> 4. Convert a `List<Optional<String>>` into a `List<String>` of present
>    values.
> 5. Interview: When does `map` produce `Optional<Optional<T>>`? (Hint: what is
>    the return type of the function you passed in?)

#### orElse, orElseGet, and orElseThrow

Eventually a chain must produce a real value. The unwrapping methods differ in
what they do when the `Optional` is empty, and the difference between two of
them is a genuine performance trap.

**`orElse(T other)`** returns the value, or the given default:

```java
String name = findUser(id).map(User::getName).orElse("guest");
```

**`orElseGet(Supplier<T>)`** returns the value, or calls the supplier:

```java
String name = findUser(id).map(User::getName).orElseGet(() -> lookupDefault());
```

These look interchangeable, and for a constant they are. The difference is
**when the default is evaluated**. `orElse` takes a value, so the expression
producing it runs *before* the call, whether or not it is needed. `orElseGet`
takes a supplier, so the work happens only on the empty path.

```java
public String expensiveDefault() {
    System.out.println("computing default");
    return "default";
}

Optional<String> present = Optional.of("value");

present.orElse(expensiveDefault());
// prints "computing default", then returns "value"
// The work was done and thrown away.

present.orElseGet(this::expensiveDefault);
// prints nothing, returns "value"
```

```text
   orElse(expensive())            orElseGet(() -> expensive())

   1. evaluate expensive()        1. is the value present?
   2. is the value present?            yes -> return it, supplier never runs
        yes -> return it,               no -> run the supplier
        discarding the default
```

The rule: use `orElse` for constants and cheap literals, and `orElseGet`
whenever the default involves a method call, an allocation, or any side effect.
The trap is worse than wasted work when the default has side effects, such as
inserting a row or incrementing a counter, since those happen even on the
happy path.

**`orElseThrow(Supplier<X>)`** throws a chosen exception when empty. This is
the standard way to convert "not found" into a domain error at a service
boundary:

```java
User user = findUser(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException("No user with id " + id));
```

The supplier matters here for the same reason: constructing an exception fills
in a stack trace, which is not free, so it should happen only when the
exception is actually thrown.

The no-argument `orElseThrow()`, added in Java 10, throws
`NoSuchElementException` and is the intended replacement for `get()`:

```java
String value = opt.orElseThrow();     // clearer than opt.get()
```

The complete set:

| Method                 | When empty                         | Evaluates default |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `orElse(v)`            | Returns `v`                        | Always            |
| `orElseGet(supplier)`  | Calls the supplier                 | Only when empty   |
| `orElseThrow()`        | Throws `NoSuchElementException`    | -                 |
| `orElseThrow(supplier)`| Throws the supplied exception      | Only when empty   |
| `get()`                | Throws `NoSuchElementException`    | -                 |
| `ifPresent(consumer)`  | Does nothing                       | -                 |
| `ifPresentOrElse(c, r)`| Runs the empty-case runnable       | -                 |

A practical pattern, combining several of them:

```java
public Order loadOrder(String id) {
    return repository.findById(id)
            .filter(Order::isVisible)                     // hide soft-deleted
            .map(this::enrich)                            // add computed fields
            .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFound(id));     // fail with context
}

public String displayName(String userId) {
    return findUser(userId)
            .map(User::getNickname)
            .filter(n -> !n.isBlank())
            .orElseGet(() -> buildDefaultName(userId));    // only if needed
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `orElse` takes a value that is always evaluated, even when one is present.
> - `orElseGet` takes a supplier that runs only on the empty path.
> - Use `orElse` for constants and `orElseGet` for anything computed.
> - A default with side effects in `orElse` executes even on the happy path.
> - `orElseThrow(supplier)` converts absence into a meaningful domain
>   exception.
> - The no-argument `orElseThrow()` is the modern replacement for `get()`.
> - Exception suppliers also defer the cost of building a stack trace.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print a message from inside a default method and show that `orElse` runs
>    it while `orElseGet` does not.
> 2. Rewrite a method that returns null on failure to return `Optional` and
>    throw via `orElseThrow`.
> 3. Chain `filter`, `map`, and `orElseGet` to produce a display name with a
>    computed fallback.
> 4. Interview: Both `orElse` and `orElseGet` return the same value here, so
>    why prefer one? (Hint: what happens to the argument expression before the
>    method is even entered?)

#### Optional Usage Guidelines and Misuse

`Optional` was introduced for one specific purpose, and its designers said so
explicitly: to be the **return type** of methods that may have no result. Using
it everywhere produces code that is more verbose than the null checks it
replaced.

**The intended use** is a return type signalling possible absence:

```java
public Optional<User> findByEmail(String email) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(repository.lookup(email));
}
```

Everything below is a documented misuse.

**Do not use `Optional` for fields.** It adds an object per field, it is not
