```java
CompletionService<String> cs = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool);
tasks.forEach(cs::submit);

for (int i = 0; i < tasks.size(); i++) {
    Future<String> done = cs.take();    // blocks for the next COMPLETED task
    System.out.println(done.get());     // process in completion order
}
```

**`Future` has a real weakness: you cannot say what to do next without
blocking.** Reading a result means calling `get()` and waiting.
`CompletableFuture` (Java 8) fixes that by letting you attach continuations, so
the pipeline is described up front and runs as results arrive.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Composition {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

        CompletableFuture<String> pipeline =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUserId(), pool)
                // thenApply: transform the value with a plain function
                .thenApply(id -> "user-" + id)
                // thenCompose: chain a call that ITSELF returns a future (flatMap)
                .thenCompose(name -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                        () -> loadProfile(name), pool))
                // exceptionally: supply a fallback if anything above failed
                .exceptionally(ex -> "anonymous");

        System.out.println(pipeline.get());

        // Combine two independent futures once both complete
        CompletableFuture<Integer> a = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 20, pool);
        CompletableFuture<Integer> b = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 22, pool);
        System.out.println(a.thenCombine(b, Integer::sum).get());     // 42

        // Wait for a whole group
        CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join();

        pool.shutdown();
    }

    static String fetchUserId() { return "7"; }
    static String loadProfile(String n) { return "profile of " + n; }
}
```

| Method              | Purpose                                                    |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `supplyAsync`       | Start an asynchronous computation that returns a value       |
| `runAsync`          | Start one that returns nothing                               |
| `thenApply`         | Transform the result with a function                         |
| `thenCompose`       | Chain another future-returning call, avoiding nesting         |
| `thenCombine`       | Merge two independent futures                                |
| `allOf` / `anyOf`   | Wait for all, or for the first                                |
| `exceptionally`     | Provide a fallback value on failure                           |
| `handle`            | Handle success and failure in one function                     |

Always pass an explicit executor to the `*Async` methods. The default is the
common `ForkJoinPool`, which is shared process-wide and sized for CPU-bound
work, so blocking in it can starve unrelated code including parallel streams.

| Aspect                | `Future`             | `CompletableFuture`         |
| --------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Get the result        | Blocking `get()` only | Blocking or via callbacks    |
| Chain operations      | No                   | Yes, `thenApply` and friends |
| Combine several       | Manually             | `thenCombine`, `allOf`       |
| Error handling        | Catch at `get()`      | `exceptionally`, `handle`    |
| Complete manually     | No                   | Yes, `complete(value)`        |

On Java 21, **structured concurrency** is available as a preview feature and is
worth knowing about. `StructuredTaskScope` ties a group of subtasks to a lexical
scope, so they are all cancelled and joined together, which removes the
leaked-task and forgotten-cancellation failure modes. Being a preview, it needs
`--enable-preview` and may change.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Runnable` returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions; `Callable`
>   does both.
> - `submit` returns immediately with a `Future` standing in for the eventual
>   result.
> - `get()` blocks, so prefer the timed overload in production.
> - A task's exception surfaces from `get()` wrapped in `ExecutionException`;
>   unwrap with `getCause()`.
> - `cancel(true)` interrupts a running task, and interruption is still
>   cooperative.
> - `invokeAll` waits for every task, so one slow task delays all results.
> - `CompletionService` delivers results in completion order instead.
> - `CompletableFuture` lets you compose non-blocking pipelines with
>   `thenApply`, `thenCompose`, and `thenCombine`.
> - Always pass an explicit executor to `*Async`, or you share the common
>   `ForkJoinPool`.
> - Structured concurrency in Java 21 is a preview that scopes and cancels
>   subtasks as a unit.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert a `Runnable` that prints a computed value into a `Callable` that
>    returns it, and retrieve it through a `Future`.
> 2. Submit a task that throws, then write the `try`/`catch` that prints the
>    original exception message rather than the wrapper's.
> 3. Submit three tasks sleeping 3 s, 1 s, and 2 s. Print results with
>    `invokeAll` and then with a `CompletionService`, and compare the orders.
> 4. Build a `CompletableFuture` pipeline that fetches an id, loads a profile,
>    and falls back to a default on failure, using an explicit executor
>    throughout.
> 5. Interview: What is the difference between `thenApply` and `thenCompose`,
>    and what goes wrong if you use the first where the second belongs? (Hint:
>    what is the type of the result when the function itself returns a future?)

#### Concurrent Collections Overview

The obvious way to make a collection thread-safe is to wrap it so every method
takes a lock, and Java has done that since 1.0:

```java
List<String> list = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
Map<String, String> map = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
```

This is rarely good enough, for two reasons.

**One lock for the whole collection serializes everything.** Sixteen threads
reading a map take turns, so the collection becomes the serial fraction in
Amdahl's law.

**Compound operations are still not atomic**, and neither is iteration.

```java
// Each call is atomic; the PAIR is not. Two threads can both pass the check.
if (!syncMap.containsKey(key)) {
    syncMap.put(key, value);
}

// Iteration is a long compound operation. Without external locking this throws
// ConcurrentModificationException if another thread modifies the list.
for (String s : syncList) { }

// Correct but coarse: the whole loop is one critical section
synchronized (syncList) {
    for (String s : syncList) { }
}
```

`java.util.concurrent` replaces the single lock with data structures designed
for concurrency from the start.

**`ConcurrentHashMap`** is the workhorse. Instead of one lock it locks
individual hash bins, and read operations usually take no lock at all, so
throughput scales with cores.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Counts {
    private final ConcurrentMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void record(String key) {
        // Each of these is a SINGLE atomic operation, unlike check-then-act
        counts.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);
    }

    public void ensure(String key) {
        counts.putIfAbsent(key, 0);                       // atomic
        counts.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> expensive(k));   // atomic, computed once
        counts.compute(key, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);
    }

    private int expensive(String k) { return k.length(); }
}
```

Two behaviours to internalize. Its iterators are **weakly consistent**: they
never throw `ConcurrentModificationException`, they reflect the state at some
point during traversal, and they may or may not show concurrent updates. And
`size()` is an **estimate**, because computing an exact total would require
locking everything. Two restrictions: `null` keys and values are forbidden,
because `get` returning `null` would be ambiguous, and the function passed to
`computeIfAbsent` must not modify the same map, which can deadlock.

**`CopyOnWriteArrayList`** takes the opposite approach: every mutation copies
the entire backing array. Reads are completely lock-free and iterators are
immutable snapshots.

```java
// Ideal for a listener list: thousands of iterations, a handful of mutations
private final List<Listener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

public void fire(Event e) {
    for (Listener l : listeners) {   // snapshot: safe, no lock, never throws
        l.onEvent(e);                // safe even if a listener removes itself
    }
}
```

Use it only when reads vastly outnumber writes. A thousand-element list written
frequently copies a thousand references per write.

**`BlockingQueue`** is the coordination primitive that replaces most
`wait`/`notify` code. It blocks a consumer when empty and a producer when full,
which makes the producer-consumer pattern almost trivial and gives you
backpressure for free.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ProducerConsumer {
    private static final String POISON = "STOP";     // a sentinel to end cleanly

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);   // bounded

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
                    queue.put("item-" + i);   // BLOCKS while the queue is full
                }
                queue.put(POISON);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });

        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                while (true) {
                    String item = queue.take();      // BLOCKS while empty
                    if (POISON.equals(item)) break;  // shutdown signal
                    process(item);
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });

        producer.start(); consumer.start();
        producer.join();  consumer.join();
    }

    private static void process(String s) { }
}
```

The queue methods come in four flavours for the same operation, and picking the
wrong one is a common bug:

| Operation | Throws            | Returns special value | Blocks   | Times out              |
| --------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | -------- | ---------------------- |
| Insert    | `add(e)`          | `offer(e)`            | `put(e)` | `offer(e, time, unit)` |
| Remove    | `remove()`        | `poll()`              | `take()` | `poll(time, unit)`     |
| Examine   | `element()`       | `peek()`              | n/a      | n/a                    |

Use `put` and `take` for producer-consumer, because they provide the
backpressure. Using `add` on a full bounded queue throws instead of waiting.

The full landscape:

| Collection                | Replaces                 | Characteristics                           |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `ConcurrentHashMap`       | `HashMap`                | Bin-level locking, lock-free reads, atomic compute methods |
| `ConcurrentSkipListMap`   | `TreeMap`                | Sorted, concurrent, `O(log n)`              |
| `CopyOnWriteArrayList`    | `ArrayList`              | Snapshot iteration, expensive writes       |
| `CopyOnWriteArraySet`     | `HashSet`                | Same trade-offs                            |
| `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`   | `LinkedList` as a queue   | Unbounded, non-blocking, lock-free          |
| `ArrayBlockingQueue`      | Hand-written buffer       | Bounded, blocking, one lock                 |
| `LinkedBlockingQueue`     | Hand-written buffer       | Optionally bounded, separate head and tail locks |
| `SynchronousQueue`        | Direct handoff           | Zero capacity; each put waits for a take    |
| `PriorityBlockingQueue`   | `PriorityQueue`          | Unbounded, ordered, blocking                 |
| `DelayQueue`              | Scheduling by hand       | Elements become available at a set time      |

Finally, the iteration semantics, which differ from the standard collections:

| Behaviour            | Standard collections           | Concurrent collections                  |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Concurrent modification | `ConcurrentModificationException` (fail-fast) | Tolerated (weakly consistent) |
| What the iterator sees | The live collection           | A snapshot, or an approximation          |
| `size()`             | Exact                          | Possibly an estimate                     |
| Needs external locking | Yes, for iteration           | No                                       |

The guidance is simple: **default to the concurrent collections and never use
`Collections.synchronizedX` for new code.** They are faster, they need no
external locking for iteration, and their compound methods eliminate the
check-then-act races that wrappers invite.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Collections.synchronizedX` uses one lock for the whole collection, which
>   serializes all access.
> - Wrapper collections still leave compound operations and iteration unsafe
>   without external locking.
> - `ConcurrentHashMap` locks individual bins and reads mostly without locking.
> - Use its atomic compound methods such as `merge`, `putIfAbsent`, and
>   `computeIfAbsent` instead of check-then-act.
> - `ConcurrentHashMap` forbids `null` keys and values, and its `size()` is an
>   estimate.
> - Concurrent iterators are weakly consistent and never throw
>   `ConcurrentModificationException`.
> - `CopyOnWriteArrayList` gives lock-free snapshot reads at the cost of copying
>   on every write, which suits listener lists.
> - `BlockingQueue` replaces `wait`/`notify` for producer-consumer and supplies
>   backpressure.
> - Queue operations come in throwing, special-value, blocking, and timed forms;
>   use `put` and `take` for backpressure.
> - Prefer concurrent collections over synchronized wrappers in all new code.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace a `Collections.synchronizedMap` with a `ConcurrentHashMap` and
>    rewrite one check-then-act block as a single atomic call.
> 2. Iterate a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` while another thread adds to it, then try
>    the same with an `ArrayList` and compare what happens.
> 3. Implement producer-consumer with an `ArrayBlockingQueue` of capacity 5, two
>    producers, and three consumers, terminating cleanly with a sentinel.
> 4. Benchmark `ConcurrentHashMap` against `Collections.synchronizedMap` with
>    eight threads at 90% reads, and report the ratio.
> 5. Interview: Why does `ConcurrentHashMap` reject `null` values, and why is
>    its `size()` only approximate? (Hint: what would a `null` return from
>    `get()` mean, and what would an exact count require locking?)

<a id="13-input-output-and-serialization"></a>
## 13. Input, Output, and Serialization

Every chapter so far kept its data inside one running process, where objects are
reachable by reference and vanish when the JVM exits. Real programs read
configuration from disk, stream gigabytes they cannot hold in memory, and turn
live object graphs into bytes that survive a restart or cross a network. This
chapter covers the stream abstractions that move bytes and characters, the
NIO.2 file API that replaced the flawed `java.io.File`, and the built-in
serialisation mechanism together with the substantial reasons to distrust it.

<a id="131-streams-and-file-access"></a>
### 13.1 Streams and File Access

This subchapter covers the four stream families that every Java I/O operation is
built from, and the modern API for naming, inspecting, and manipulating the
files themselves.

#### Streams, Readers, and Writers

A program's own heap is fast, structured, and gone the moment the process ends.
Everything else — a file, the keyboard, a socket, another process, a
compression codec — lives outside it. Those sources differ in every physical
respect, yet they share one property: data arrives or departs as an *ordered
sequence*, a piece at a time, in one direction. Java names that shared property
a **stream**, and builds all of its I/O on it.

An array and a stream are opposites in a useful way. An array is a warehouse
shelf: everything is present at once and you can reach for item 500 directly. A
stream is a conveyor belt: items pass you one at a time, you cannot skip ahead
cheaply, and once an item has gone by it is gone. That restriction is what
allows the same four interfaces to describe a 2 KB file and an endless network
socket.

One naming collision must be cleared up immediately, because it confuses
everyone.

| Name                     | Package             | What it is                              |
| ------------------------ | ------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `InputStream` / `OutputStream` | `java.io`     | A byte pipe to an external resource     |
| `Stream<T>`              | `java.util.stream`  | A pipeline of in-memory values (Chapter 8) |

They are unrelated types with unrelated purposes. The rest of this topic means
the `java.io` kind.

**Why there are two families, not one.** A byte stream moves raw 8-bit values,
which is exactly right for a JPEG, a ZIP archive, or a protocol frame, where
every byte is significant and no interpretation is wanted. Text is different: a
character is not a byte. Turning `'è'` into bytes requires a **charset**, and
different charsets produce different byte counts for the same character.

```text
   FILE ON DISK  (UTF-8 bytes)          IN MEMORY  (Java chars, UTF-16)
   48 65 6C 6C 6F          decode
   C3 A8                   ------->     'H' 'e' 'l' 'l' 'o' 'è'
   21                      charset
                                         6 chars from 8 bytes
   ^^^^^                                 (C3 A8 is ONE character)
```

Reading that file with a byte stream and casting each byte to `char` produces
mojibake, and splitting the byte array in the middle of a multi-byte sequence
corrupts a character. Reader and Writer exist so that the decoding happens in
one correct place.

That gives four abstract root classes, one per combination of direction and
unit.

|          | Bytes (binary data)  | Characters (text)  |
| -------- | -------------------- | ------------------ |
| **Input**  | `InputStream`      | `Reader`           |
| **Output** | `OutputStream`     | `Writer`           |

Their core contracts are deliberately tiny, because every concrete subclass must
implement them over a different physical medium.

| Method                        | Declared on           | Returns                                  |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `int read()`                  | `InputStream`         | Next byte as 0..255, or `-1` at end      |
| `int read(byte[] b, int off, int len)` | `InputStream` | Count actually read, or `-1` at end      |
| `int read(char[] c)`          | `Reader`              | Count of characters, or `-1` at end      |
| `void write(int b)`           | `OutputStream`        | Writes the low 8 bits                    |
| `void flush()`                | Output side           | Pushes buffered data onward              |
| `void close()`                | All four              | Flushes, then releases the OS handle     |

Two details in that table cause real bugs. `read()` returns an `int`, not a
`byte`, precisely so that `-1` can mean end-of-stream without colliding with the
legitimate byte value `0xFF`. And the bulk `read` returns *how many* elements it
filled, which is often fewer than the array length even when the stream is not
finished, because it returns as soon as some data is available.

**The decorator pattern is the organising idea.** Rather than offering a
`BufferedEncryptedFileReader`, Java gives you thin wrappers that each add one
capability and delegate the rest, exactly the structural pattern from Chapter
9.4. You compose the stack you need.

```text
   new BufferedReader( new InputStreamReader( new FileInputStream(f), UTF_8 ) )
        |                      |                       |
        |                      |                       +-- SOURCE: raw bytes off disk
        |                      +-- BRIDGE: bytes -> chars using a charset
        +-- BUFFER: batches syscalls, and adds readLine()

   Each layer IS-A Reader, so callers never care how deep the stack goes.
```

`InputStreamReader` and `OutputStreamWriter` are the only bridges between the
two families, and they are where a charset belongs.

**Why buffering is not optional.** An unbuffered `read()` can mean one system
call per byte. Copying a one-megabyte file that way issues over a million
transitions into the kernel. An 8 KB buffer turns the same work into 128 of
them.

```text
   Unbuffered: app -> kernel -> disk, once per byte      1,048,576 crossings
   Buffered:   app -> buffer (in-process) ... refill     128 crossings
               |
               +-- roughly three orders of magnitude fewer boundary crossings
```

Here is the canonical binary copy. Note the handling of the returned count.

```java
try (InputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream("source.bin"));
     OutputStream out = new BufferedOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("dest.bin"))) {

    byte[] buffer = new byte[8192];          // one page-sized chunk
    int n;
    while ((n = in.read(buffer)) != -1) {    // -1 means end; 0 is possible and legal
        out.write(buffer, 0, n);             // write exactly n bytes, never buffer.length
    }
}                                            // close() flushes, then releases handles
```

Writing `out.write(buffer)` instead of `out.write(buffer, 0, n)` is a classic
corruption bug: the final partial chunk pads the output with stale bytes from
the previous iteration.

Text input follows the same shape, with the charset stated explicitly.

```java
try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(
         new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream("data.csv"),
                               StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {

    String line;
    while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {   // null ends; "" is a blank line
        process(line);
    }
}
```

`readLine()` strips the terminator and accepts `\n`, `\r`, or `\r\n`
interchangeably, so it silently normalises line endings and cannot tell you
which convention the file used.

On the output side, `PrintWriter` is the convenient choice and the one with a
trap.

```java
try (PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(
         new BufferedWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(
             new FileOutputStream("report.txt"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)))) {

    out.printf("total=%d%n", 42);     // %n is the platform line separator
    if (out.checkError()) {           // PrintWriter SWALLOWS IOException
        throw new IOException("write failed");
    }
}
```

`PrintWriter` and `PrintStream` never throw `IOException` from their write
methods; they set an internal error flag instead. `System.out` behaves the same
way, which is why a failed console write is silent.

**Charset defaults have changed, so state the charset anyway.** `FileReader` and
`FileWriter` had no charset parameter at all until Java 11, and before Java 18
the default charset came from the operating system locale, so the same program
produced different bytes on a developer laptop and a server. Java 18 fixed the
default to UTF-8. Code that must run correctly on older releases, or that must
read a file in a stated encoding, passes `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly
every time.

**Unflushed data is lost data.** Buffered output sits in memory until the buffer
fills, `flush()` is called, or `close()` runs. A program that exits without
closing leaves the tail of its output unwritten. Try-with-resources, covered in
Chapter 5.3, is the mechanism that makes this reliable; nothing in this topic
should be written without it.

The standard streams are ordinary members of these families.

| Field            | Type           | Notes                                    |
| ---------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `System.in`      | `InputStream`  | Raw bytes; wrap in a Reader for text     |
| `System.out`     | `PrintStream`  | Buffered, flushed on newline by default  |
| `System.err`     | `PrintStream`  | Unbuffered, so errors are not lost       |
| `System.console()` | `Console`    | `null` when not attached to a terminal; offers `readPassword()` |

Beyond the basics, the decorator catalogue covers most needs.

| Decorator                       | Adds                                              |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `BufferedInputStream` / `BufferedReader` | Batched syscalls, `readLine()`           |
| `DataInputStream` / `DataOutputStream`   | Portable big-endian primitives and UTF-8 strings |
| `ObjectInputStream` / `ObjectOutputStream` | Whole object graphs (see 13.2)         |
| `GZIPInputStream` / `GZIPOutputStream`   | Transparent compression                  |
| `ByteArrayInputStream` / `StringReader`  | An in-memory source, ideal for tests     |
| `PushbackInputStream`           | `unread()`, for hand-written parsers              |
| `SequenceInputStream`           | Concatenates several streams into one             |

Finally, modern JDKs offer shortcuts that remove the loop entirely when the data
is small enough to hold in memory.

```java
String text  = Files.readString(Path.of("small.txt"));     // whole file, UTF-8
byte[] bytes = in.readAllBytes();                          // Java 9+
in.transferTo(out);                                        // Java 9+, the whole copy
```

Use them for configuration and fixtures. Use the explicit loop when the input
might be larger than the heap.

> Key Takeaways
> - A `java.io` stream is a one-directional, sequential pipe to something
>   outside the heap, and is unrelated to `java.util.stream.Stream`.
> - Byte streams (`InputStream`, `OutputStream`) carry raw data; character
>   streams (`Reader`, `Writer`) carry decoded text.
> - Text is not bytes: converting between them requires a charset, and
>   `InputStreamReader` and `OutputStreamWriter` are the bridges.
> - `read()` returns an `int` so that `-1` can signal end-of-stream
>   unambiguously.
> - Bulk `read` returns the count actually filled, so always write back exactly
>   that many elements.
> - Streams are composed with the decorator pattern, one capability per wrapper.
> - Buffering replaces one syscall per byte with one per block, and is a
>   thousandfold difference in practice.
> - `PrintWriter` and `PrintStream` never throw on write; they set an error flag
>   you must check.
> - Always pass the charset explicitly, because the default was
>   platform-dependent before Java 18.
> - Buffered output is lost unless the stream is flushed or closed, so use
>   try-with-resources.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a file copier that reads with `FileInputStream` one byte at a time,
>    then a second that uses an 8 KB buffer, and time both on a 50 MB file.
> 2. Write the string `"café"` to a file as UTF-8, read it back as
>    ISO-8859-1, and print what you get. Explain the result byte by byte.
> 3. Build a stack that writes GZIP-compressed UTF-8 text, then read it back
>    with the mirror-image stack, using try-with-resources on both sides.
> 4. Take a program that prints to `System.out` inside a loop and make it write
>    to a `BufferedWriter` instead, then deliberately omit the close and observe
>    what reaches the file.
> 5. Interview: Why does Java provide both `InputStream` and `Reader` rather
>    than one hierarchy with a charset parameter? (Hint: what is the correct
>    charset for a JPEG, and what happens if a buffer boundary falls inside a
>    multi-byte sequence?)

#### File Handling with the NIO.2 API

Streams move the *contents* of a file. Something else must name files, create
and delete them, list a directory, and ask how large or how old a file is.
Java's original answer was `java.io.File`, and it was weak enough that Java 7
replaced it wholesale with the `java.nio.file` package, universally called
**NIO.2**.

The complaints against `java.io.File` are worth knowing, because they explain
every design decision in its replacement.

| Problem with `java.io.File`              | Consequence                                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `delete()` returns `boolean`             | You learn it failed, never *why*: missing, locked, or denied |
| `listFiles()` returns `null` on error    | A `NullPointerException` far from the cause  |
| No copy method at all                    | Everyone hand-rolled a stream loop           |
| `renameTo()` is platform-dependent       | Works in testing, fails across filesystems   |
| No symbolic-link awareness               | Traversals follow links into infinite loops  |
| One syscall per attribute query          | Slow, and open to time-of-check races        |
| No access to POSIX permissions or owners | Fell back to shelling out                    |

NIO.2 fixes these by splitting one overloaded class into two collaborators with
a clean division of labour.

- **`Path`** is a *name*. It is pure syntax, like an address written on an
  envelope: it can be manipulated, joined, and compared without any file
  existing anywhere.
- **`Files`** is a toolbox of static methods that *act* on the filesystem,
  throwing a specific `IOException` subtype when something goes wrong.

```text
   Path  ------------- names ------------->  a location
    |                                            |
    | (pure text manipulation, no disk access)   |
    v                                            v
   Files ----------- operates on -----------> the actual file
         (readString, copy, delete, walk, ... each throws on failure)
```

A third piece, `FileSystems`, makes the whole API pluggable: the same `Path` and
`Files` code can address entries inside a ZIP archive, because a ZIP is exposed
as a filesystem provider.

**Working with `Path`.** Every method here is string surgery; none of it touches
the disk.

```java
Path base = Path.of("/srv/app");
Path cfg  = base.resolve("conf/app.properties");   // /srv/app/conf/app.properties
Path rel  = base.relativize(cfg);                  // conf/app.properties
Path sib  = cfg.resolveSibling("app.bak");         // /srv/app/conf/app.bak

Path messy = Path.of("/srv/app/../app/./logs");
Path clean = messy.normalize();                    // /srv/app/logs  (text only)

cfg.getFileName();      // app.properties
cfg.getParent();        // /srv/app/conf
cfg.getNameCount();     // 3
cfg.isAbsolute();       // true
```

Two subtleties matter. `resolve` on an absolute argument discards the base
entirely, so `base.resolve("/etc/passwd")` is `/etc/passwd`. And `normalize` is
purely textual: if `app` is a symbolic link, removing `../` can change which
file you mean. `Files.toRealPath` resolves links properly, but it touches the
disk and fails if the file does not exist.

`Path.equals` is likewise syntactic. Two different paths can name one file
through a link or a case-insensitive filesystem, and only `Files.isSameFile`
answers that question honestly.

That syntactic nature gives the standard defence against **path traversal**,
where user input like `../../etc/passwd` escapes an intended directory.

```java
Path root = Path.of("/var/www").toAbsolutePath().normalize();
Path target = root.resolve(userSuppliedName).normalize();   // normalize AFTER resolve
if (!target.startsWith(root)) {                             // syntactic containment check
    throw new SecurityException("path escapes the served root");
}
```

**Working with `Files`.** The static methods group into five jobs.

| Job        | Methods                                                             |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Read       | `readString`, `readAllLines`, `readAllBytes`, `lines`, `newBufferedReader`, `newInputStream` |
| Write      | `writeString`, `write`, `newBufferedWriter`, `newOutputStream`       |
| Create     | `createFile`, `createDirectory`, `createDirectories`, `createTempFile`, `createSymbolicLink` |
| Manipulate | `copy`, `move`, `delete`, `deleteIfExists`                           |
| Inspect    | `exists`, `size`, `isDirectory`, `isReadable`, `readAttributes`, `probeContentType` |
| Traverse   | `list`, `walk`, `find`, `newDirectoryStream`, `walkFileTree`         |

Whole-file reads and writes collapse a stream loop into one line, at the cost of
holding the content in memory.

```java
String text = Files.readString(cfg, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(cfg, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

Files.writeString(out, text, StandardCharsets.UTF_8,
                  StandardOpenOption.CREATE,             // make it if absent
                  StandardOpenOption.TRUNCATE_EXISTING); // otherwise empty it first

// For a file larger than the heap, stream it lazily instead:
try (Stream<String> lazy = Files.lines(cfg, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {   // IS a resource
    long errors = lazy.filter(l -> l.contains("ERROR")).count();
}
```

The try-with-resources on `Files.lines` is mandatory, not stylistic: unlike most
streams, the ones returned by `lines`, `list`, `walk`, and `find` hold an open
file handle, as Chapter 5.3 explained.

Copy, move, and delete take option flags that state intent precisely.

| Option                | Effect                                                   |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `REPLACE_EXISTING`    | Overwrite the target instead of throwing `FileAlreadyExistsException` |
| `COPY_ATTRIBUTES`     | Carry timestamps and permissions across                  |
| `ATOMIC_MOVE`         | The move either fully happens or does not; same filesystem only |
| `NOFOLLOW_LINKS`      | Act on the symbolic link itself, not its target          |

`ATOMIC_MOVE` enables the single most useful pattern in file handling: never let
a reader see a half-written file.

```java
Path target = Path.of("/srv/app/conf/app.properties");
Path tmp = Files.createTempFile(target.getParent(), "app", ".tmp");  // same filesystem

Files.writeString(tmp, newContent, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
Files.move(tmp, target,                                   // the swap is instantaneous
           StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING,
           StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE);
```

**Traversing directories.** Four methods differ in depth and in what they hand
back.

```text
   /srv/app
   |-- conf
   |   |-- app.properties
   |   `-- log4j2.xml
   |-- logs
   |   `-- app.log
   `-- lib
       `-- core.jar

   Files.newDirectoryStream(dir, "*.jar") -> (nothing here; one level, glob filter)
   Files.list(dir)                        -> conf, logs, lib          (one level)
   Files.walk(dir)                        -> every path, depth-first  (recursive)
   Files.find(dir, 5, (p, a) -> a.size() > 1024)  -> walk plus an attribute test
   Files.walkFileTree(dir, visitor)       -> callbacks, including error handling
```

```java
// Every .java file under src, sorted, with the handle released afterwards
try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(Path.of("src"))) {
    paths.filter(Files::isRegularFile)
         .filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".java"))
         .sorted()
         .forEach(System.out::println);
}
```

`walk` does not follow symbolic links unless you pass `FOLLOW_LINKS`, which is
the sane default: following them invites cycles. Deleting a tree needs
`walkFileTree` or a reverse-sorted `walk`, because a directory cannot be removed
until it is empty.

**Reading metadata.** Asking one question at a time costs one syscall each and
opens a window in which the file changes between questions.

```java
// Three separate trips to the filesystem, and three chances to race
long size = Files.size(p);
FileTime when = Files.getLastModifiedTime(p);
boolean dir = Files.isDirectory(p);

// One trip, one consistent snapshot
BasicFileAttributes a = Files.readAttributes(p, BasicFileAttributes.class);
a.size(); a.lastModifiedTime(); a.isDirectory(); a.creationTime();
```

`Files.exists` deserves suspicion. It is three-valued in disguise: `exists` and
`notExists` can *both* return `false` when the answer is unknown, for instance
when a parent directory denies traversal. Worse, anything you do after checking
is a race. Prefer attempting the operation and catching `NoSuchFileException` or
`FileAlreadyExistsException`.

Finally, the mapping from old code to new.

| `java.io.File`            | NIO.2 equivalent                               |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `new File(s)`             | `Path.of(s)`                                   |
| `f.exists()`              | `Files.exists(p)`, or just attempt the operation |
| `f.delete()`              | `Files.delete(p)` (throws) or `deleteIfExists` |
| `f.renameTo(g)`           | `Files.move(p, q, REPLACE_EXISTING)`           |
| `f.listFiles()`           | `Files.list(p)` or `newDirectoryStream(p)`     |
| `f.length()`              | `Files.size(p)`                                |
| `f.mkdirs()`              | `Files.createDirectories(p)`                   |
| (no equivalent)           | `Files.copy`, `ATOMIC_MOVE`, `walk`, `WatchService`, POSIX permissions |

Interoperation is easy in both directions with `file.toPath()` and
`path.toFile()`, so legacy APIs are never a reason to avoid NIO.2.

For reacting to changes rather than polling, `WatchService` registers a
directory with the operating system's notification mechanism.

```java
try (WatchService watcher = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService()) {
    Path.of("/srv/app/conf").register(watcher,
            StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE,
            StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_MODIFY);

    WatchKey key = watcher.take();            // blocks until something happens
    for (WatchEvent<?> event : key.pollEvents()) {
        System.out.println(event.kind() + " on " + event.context());
    }
    key.reset();                              // REQUIRED, or no further events arrive
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - NIO.2 splits naming (`Path`) from acting (`Files`), which `java.io.File`
>   confused.
> - `Path` operations are pure text and never touch the disk, so a `Path` can
>   name a file that does not exist.
> - `Files` methods throw specific `IOException` subtypes instead of returning
>   an unexplained `boolean`.
> - `resolve` against an absolute path discards the base, and `normalize` is
>   textual, so symbolic links can defeat it.
> - Guard against path traversal by resolving, normalising, then checking
>   `startsWith` the intended root.
> - Streams from `list`, `walk`, `find`, and `lines` hold file handles and need
>   try-with-resources.
> - Write-to-temp then `ATOMIC_MOVE` is the standard way to publish a file
>   without exposing a partial state.
> - `readAttributes` gets a consistent metadata snapshot in one syscall.
> - `Files.exists` can be false when the truth is unknown, and any check is a
>   race; prefer attempting the operation.
> - `toPath()` and `toFile()` bridge to legacy APIs, so there is no reason to
>   keep writing `java.io.File`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print the absolute, normalised, and real paths of `./../<your project>` and
>    explain any differences between the last two.
> 2. Write a method that counts the lines of every `.java` file under a
>    directory, using `Files.walk` and `Files.lines`, with both handles closed.
> 3. Implement a safe file server helper that maps a user-supplied name to a
>    path under `/var/www` and rejects any input that escapes it. Test it with
>    `../../etc/passwd` and with an absolute path.
> 4. Implement `saveConfig` so that a reader never observes a partial file, and
>    explain why the temporary file must live in the target's own directory.
> 5. Write a recursive delete using `walkFileTree`, then explain why the naive
>    `Files.walk(...).forEach(Files::delete)` version fails.
> 6. Interview: Why did `java.nio.file` replace `java.io.File` rather than
>    extending it? (Hint: what does `delete()` returning `false` tell the
>    caller, and what would a subclass have to do about that?)

<a id="132-object-serialization"></a>
### 13.2 Object Serialization

This subchapter restates the `Serializable` marker from Chapter 4.4 and then
goes beneath it, covering how the object graph becomes bytes, how to control
and version that format, and why most projects should choose something else
entirely.

#### The Serializable Marker and a File Round Trip

Chapter 4.4 introduced `Serializable` alongside the other core Java interfaces.
This topic restates the essentials so the rest of the subchapter stands on its
own, and builds the round-trip helper that the later examples use.

The problem is easy to state. An object's fields hold references, and a
reference is an address that means something only inside one running JVM. To
store an object on disk or send it to another machine, that structure has to
become a flat sequence of bytes and then be rebuilt at the other end. Java
automates the whole job for any class that declares itself willing.

Declaring willingness is all `Serializable` does:

```java
public interface Serializable { }    // no methods, no constants, nothing
```

This is a **marker interface**, the idiom covered in Chapter 4.4 alongside
`Cloneable` and `RandomAccess`. You are not supplying an implementation; you
are granting permission. The JVM supplies the reading and writing machinery
itself, reflectively, by walking your fields.

```java
public class Session implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;   // version stamp, see below

    private String user;
    private int requestCount;
    private transient String authToken;         // deliberately NOT written
    private static String appName = "demo";     // static: belongs to the class
}
```

Four rules account for almost everything the mechanism does.

| Element             | Written to the stream?                          |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Instance field      | Yes, if its type is also serialisable            |
| `transient` field   | No; restored as `null`, `0`, or `false`          |
| `static` field      | No; it belongs to the class, not to any instance |
| Referenced object   | Yes, recursively, the entire reachable graph     |

The two streams that drive it are decorators in exactly the sense of 13.1: they
add object semantics on top of any byte stream, so the destination can be a
file, a socket, or an array in memory.

```java
Path file = Path.of("session.bin");
Session session = new Session();

// WRITE: flatten the object and everything it can reach
try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(
         new BufferedOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(file)))) {
    out.writeObject(session);
}

// READ: rebuild it
try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(
         new BufferedInputStream(Files.newInputStream(file)))) {
    Session restored = (Session) in.readObject();   // the stream is untyped
}
```

Two details in that example matter later. `readObject` returns `Object`, so the
cast is yours to write, and the security topic explains why it comes far too
late to protect you. And it declares `ClassNotFoundException`, because the
stream names its classes as text that the reader must be able to load.

Pointing the same pair at a byte array instead of a file gives the helper used
by the examples in the rest of this subchapter.

```java
static <T extends Serializable> T roundTrip(T original)
        throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {

    ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
    try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(bytes)) {
        out.writeObject(original);                  // flatten into memory
    }
    try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(
             new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes.toByteArray()))) {
        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        T copy = (T) in.readObject();               // rebuild a detached graph
        return copy;
    }
}
```

When something goes wrong, the exception tells you which half of the process
failed.

| Exception                   | Raised at  | Usual cause                                      |
| --------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `NotSerializableException`  | Write time | Some reachable object's class is not `Serializable` |
| `InvalidClassException`     | Read time  | `serialVersionUID` mismatch, or no valid constructor |
| `ClassNotFoundException`    | Read time  | The class named in the stream is not on the classpath |
| `StreamCorruptedException`  | Read time  | The bytes are not a valid object stream           |
| `OptionalDataException`     | Read time  | Primitive data found where an object was expected |

`NotSerializableException` is the one beginners meet first, and its message
names the offending class rather than the object you asked to write, because
the failure is usually several references deep in the graph.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Serializable` is a marker interface with no members; implementing it grants
>   permission rather than supplying behaviour.
> - The JVM provides the read and write machinery reflectively by walking the
>   declared fields.
> - Instance fields are written, `transient` and `static` fields are not, and
>   referenced objects are written recursively.
> - `ObjectOutputStream` and `ObjectInputStream` are decorators, so the same
>   code serialises to a file, a socket, or a byte array.
> - `readObject` returns `Object` and declares `ClassNotFoundException`, because
>   the stream carries class names as text.
> - `NotSerializableException` fires at write time and names the deep class that
>   caused it, not the object you passed in.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a small class, serialise an instance to a file, read it back in a
>    second program run, and print every field.
> 2. Add a field of a non-serialisable type, observe the exception and its
>    message, then fix it two ways: with `transient`, and by making that type
>    serialisable.
> 3. Implement the generic `roundTrip` helper above and use it to deep-copy an
>    object holding a nested list. Prove the copy is independent by mutating it.
> 4. Interview: `Serializable` declares no methods, so what does implementing it
>    actually change? (Hint: who writes the code that reads your private fields,
>    and what is it checking before it runs?)

#### Object Serialization Mechanics

An object in memory is a node in a graph. Its fields point at other objects,
those point at more, and the whole structure is held together by addresses that
mean nothing once the process exits. **Serialisation** is the act of flattening
that graph into a linear byte sequence; **deserialisation** rebuilds an
equivalent graph elsewhere. Java ships a mechanism that does this automatically
for any class marked `Serializable`.

The crucial thing to understand before the syntax is that this mechanism gives
your class a **second public API that you never wrote**. The byte format is
derived from your private field names and types, it is visible to anyone holding
the bytes, and it constrains how you may refactor the class forever after.

**The graph problem, and how handles solve it.** Naively writing each referenced
object recursively fails on two structures: a cycle loops forever, and a shared
object is written twice, so reading it back produces two distinct copies where
the original had one.

Java's format solves both with a **handle table**. The first time an object is
written it receives a sequential handle and its contents follow. Every later
appearance of the same object writes only a back-reference to that handle.

```text
   IN MEMORY                                 IN THE STREAM
                                             +----------------------------+
   order ------> customer <----+             | #1 Order    (fields...)    |
     |                         |             | #2 Customer "Ada"          |
     +--> items[0] ------------+             | #3 Item   owner -> ref #2  |
     |                         |             | #4 Item   owner -> ref #2  |
     +--> items[1] ------------+             +----------------------------+

   one Customer, referenced three times      written ONCE, referenced twice more
```

The consequence is that **sharing and cycles survive the round trip**, while the
result is a deep copy disconnected from the originals.

```java
Customer ada = new Customer("Ada");
Order original = new Order(ada, List.of(new Item(ada), new Item(ada)));

Order copy = roundTrip(original);            // the helper from the topic above

copy.items().get(0).owner() == copy.items().get(1).owner();  // true: sharing preserved
copy.customer() == ada;                                      // false: it is a deep copy
```

That property makes serialisation a convenient deep-clone tool, and also
explains a common memory surprise: writing one small object can drag its entire
reachable graph into the stream, including a collection you did not think was
part of it.

**The wire format, briefly.** Every stream begins with a magic number and a
version, followed by typed records.

```text
   AC ED 00 05   73   72   00 07  53 65 73 73 69 6F 6E  ...
   ^^^^^ ^^^^^   ^^   ^^   ^^^^^  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   magic  ver     |    |   length  "Session" (the class NAME, as text)
                  |    +-- TC_CLASSDESC: a class description follows
                  +-- TC_OBJECT: an object follows
```

A class descriptor carries the class name, its `serialVersionUID`, flags, and
the name and type of every non-transient, non-static field. Field values are
then written superclass-first. Two facts follow directly from this layout: the
stream names classes as *strings*, which the receiver will resolve and load, and
your private field names are written in plain text.

**What actually happens on read.** The sequence is unusual enough to be worth
memorising, because several surprising behaviours fall out of it.

```text
   1. Read the class descriptor; resolve the name to a Class
                                   -> ClassNotFoundException if absent
   2. Compare serialVersionUID with the local class
                                   -> InvalidClassException on mismatch
   3. Allocate the instance WITHOUT running any of its constructors
   4. Run the no-arg constructor of the nearest NON-serialisable superclass
   5. Fill fields class by class, calling each private readObject hook
   6. If readResolve exists, call it and use whatever it returns
```

Step 3 is the origin of the constructor-bypass problem from Chapter 4.4: field
validation written in a constructor simply never runs. Step 4 is a rule people
trip over: if the first non-serialisable superclass lacks an accessible no-arg
constructor, the class cannot be deserialised at all, and you get
`InvalidClassException: no valid constructor`.

**The hook methods.** Serialisation is customised through five specially named
members that the mechanism finds reflectively.

| Member             | Signature                                          | Purpose                                     |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `writeObject`      | `private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream)`      | Control what is written                     |
| `readObject`       | `private void readObject(ObjectInputStream)`        | Control what is read, and validate          |
| `readObjectNoData` | `private void readObjectNoData()`                   | Initialise when the stream lacks this class |
| `writeReplace`     | `Object writeReplace()`                             | Substitute a stand-in object before writing |
| `readResolve`      | `Object readResolve()`                              | Substitute a different object after reading |

`writeObject` and `readObject` are `private` on purpose. They are not overrides
and are never inherited; the mechanism invokes the one declared on each class in
the hierarchy separately, so making them `protected` or `public` would only
invite accidental overriding.

The idiomatic pair calls the default machinery first, then adds whatever the
default machinery could not handle.

```java
private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream out) throws IOException {
    out.defaultWriteObject();              // all non-transient, non-static fields
    out.writeInt(entries.size());          // then the transient state, by hand
    for (Entry e : entries) {
        out.writeObject(e.key());
        out.writeObject(e.value());
    }
}

private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in)
        throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
    in.defaultReadObject();                // restore the ordinary fields
    int n = in.readInt();                  // read back in EXACTLY the same order
    entries = new ArrayList<>(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        entries.add(new Entry(in.readObject(), in.readObject()));
    }
    if (n < 0) throw new InvalidObjectException("negative size");   // validate here
}
```

This is exactly how `HashMap` serialises itself. Its bucket array is
`transient`, because writing a hash table's internal layout would be both
wasteful and wrong: hash codes can differ between JVMs, so the table is
rebuilt by re-inserting the entries on read.

**`writeReplace` and `readResolve` substitute objects.** The most famous use is
protecting a singleton, which plain serialisation otherwise breaks by
manufacturing a second instance.

```java
public class Registry implements Serializable {
    public static final Registry INSTANCE = new Registry();
    private Registry() { }

    private Object readResolve() {
        return INSTANCE;      // discard the freshly built copy, return the real one
    }
}
```

Enums need no such care: they are serialised by name alone and resolved back
through `valueOf`, which is one of the reasons Chapter 4.5 recommends an enum
for singletons.

**`Externalizable` hands you the whole job.** It replaces the automatic
mechanism rather than adjusting it.

| Aspect                  | `Serializable`                       | `Externalizable`                        |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Fields written          | Automatically, by reflection         | Only what you write                     |
| Superclass state        | Handled for you                      | Your responsibility                     |
| Constructor on read     | Bypassed                             | Public no-arg constructor IS called      |
| Control and speed       | Limited, slower                      | Total, usually faster                   |
| Risk                    | Forgetting `transient`               | Forgetting a field, silently losing data |

```java
public class Point implements Externalizable {
    private int x, y;

    public Point() { }                              // REQUIRED, public, no-arg

    @Override public void writeExternal(ObjectOutput out) throws IOException {
        out.writeInt(x);
        out.writeInt(y);
    }

    @Override public void readExternal(ObjectInput in) throws IOException {
        x = in.readInt();                           // same order, or garbage results
        y = in.readInt();
    }
}
```

**Records change the picture for the better.** A record's serialised form is
defined by its state components, and deserialisation goes *through the canonical
constructor* rather than bypassing it. Validation in a compact constructor
therefore runs on every read, and the stream cannot forge an invalid instance.

```java
public record Money(String currency, long cents) implements Serializable {
    public Money {                                  // compact constructor
        if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative");
    }
}
// Deserialising a stream that claims cents = -1 throws. A normal class would not.
```

This is the mechanism serialisation should always have had, and it is the
direction the platform is moving.

> Key Takeaways
> - Serialisation flattens the whole reachable object graph, not just the one
>   object you named.
> - A handle table gives each object a number, so cycles terminate and shared
>   references stay shared after the round trip.
> - The result is a deep copy: identity inside the graph is preserved, identity
>   with the originals is not.
> - The stream names classes as text and writes private field names, making the
>   format a de facto public API of your class.
> - Reading allocates the object without running its constructors, then runs the
>   no-arg constructor of the nearest non-serialisable superclass.
> - `writeObject` and `readObject` are private, are not inherited, and must read
>   back in exactly the order they wrote.
> - `readResolve` substitutes an object after reading and is how a singleton
>   survives; enums get this for free.
> - `Externalizable` gives total control including superclass state, calls a
>   public no-arg constructor, and loses data silently if you forget a field.
> - Records deserialise through their canonical constructor, so their invariants
>   actually hold.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Serialise an object whose two fields point at the same `List`, read it
>    back, and prove with `==` that the sharing survived.
> 2. Create a class with a cyclic reference (`a.peer = b; b.peer = a;`),
>    serialise it, and explain why the write terminates.
> 3. Write a class with a `transient` collection and restore it in
>    `readObject`, then verify the round trip. Compare your approach with the
>    JDK source of `HashMap.writeObject`.
> 4. Make a singleton that breaks under serialisation, prove it with `==`, then
>    fix it with `readResolve`.
> 5. Convert a small serialisable class into a record with validation, and show
>    that a hand-edited stream of an invalid value is now rejected.
> 6. Interview: A serialisable class extends a non-serialisable one. What must
>    that superclass provide, and what happens to its fields? (Hint: walk
>    through steps 3 and 4 of the read sequence.)

#### transient Fields and serialVersionUID

Two keywords control the two dimensions in which a serialised class goes wrong:
`transient` decides *what* crosses the boundary in space, and
`serialVersionUID` decides what is compatible across time. Both are easy to
ignore and expensive to get wrong.

**`transient` marks a field as not part of the object's persistent state.** Four
distinct situations call for it.

| Reason                     | Example field                          | What happens without `transient`         |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| The value is *derived*     | A cached hash, a computed total        | Wasted bytes, and stale data on read      |
| The type cannot be written | `Socket`, `Thread`, `Connection`, a lambda | `NotSerializableException` at write time |
| The value is a *secret*    | A password, a session token, a key     | The secret is written in the clear        |
| The value is *huge*        | A memoisation table, a loaded image     | A tiny object drags megabytes with it     |

A transient field is not merely skipped on write; on read it is left at the
JVM's default value, `null` for references and zero or `false` for primitives.
Nothing warns you. If an invariant depended on that field being non-null, the
object comes back broken.

```java
public class SearchIndex implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    private final List<String> documents;        // the real state, written
    private transient Map<String, List<Integer>> index;   // derived, not written
    private transient volatile int hash;          // cached, recomputed lazily

    private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in)
            throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        in.defaultReadObject();                   // documents is restored, index is null
        this.index = buildIndex(documents);       // rebuild what was deliberately skipped
    }
}
```

`static` fields are excluded too, for a different reason: they belong to the
class, not to any instance, so there is no instance state to write. A common
beginner bug is expecting a `static` counter to travel with an object.

One combination is a genuine trap: **`transient final`**. A final field cannot
be reassigned inside `readObject`, so there is no legal way to restore it.
Escape routes are reflection (ugly), dropping `final`, or the serialisation
proxy pattern covered in the next topic.

**`serialVersionUID` is the compatibility stamp.** Every serialisable class has
one. If you do not declare it, the JVM computes it at runtime as a hash over the
class name, its modifiers, its implemented interfaces, and the signatures of its
fields, constructors, and *methods*.

That last inclusion is what makes the implicit value unusable. Adding a private
helper method changes the hash. So does changing a field from `private` to
`package-private`, or compiling with a different compiler that orders members
differently. Any of those makes yesterday's files unreadable.

```java
private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
```

The declaration must be exactly `static final long`; `private` is not required
but is strongly recommended, because a non-private one is inherited by
subclasses, which then wrongly share their parent's identity. Once declared, the
value changes only when *you* decide the format has broken compatibility.

A mismatch produces an unmistakable message.

```text
java.io.InvalidClassException: com.example.Session; local class incompatible:
    stream classdesc serialVersionUID = -4938261571854927892,
    local class serialVersionUID = 1
```

The JDK ships `serialver` for inspecting the computed value of a compiled class:

```bash
serialver -classpath build/classes com.example.Session
```

**Keeping the UID fixed is a promise, and you must know which changes you can
keep it through.** The rule of thumb is that changes which only add or remove
optional state are compatible; changes to the *shape* of existing state are not.

| Change to the class                      | Compatible? | Effect on data written by the old version |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Add a field                              | Yes         | New field reads as `null` / `0` / `false`  |
| Remove a field                           | Yes         | The old value in the stream is discarded   |
| Add or remove a method or constructor    | Yes         | None                                       |
| Change a field from `transient` to normal | Yes        | Old streams have no value; reads as default |
| Change a field from normal to `transient` | Yes        | Value is present but ignored on read       |
| Change a field's type                    | **No**      | `InvalidClassException`                    |
| Rename a field                            | **No**      | Treated as remove plus add; the value is lost silently |
| Change a field from instance to `static`  | **No**      | The field stops being written               |
| Change the position of a class in the hierarchy | **No** | Field values attach to the wrong class      |
| Change `class` to `enum`, `interface`, or a record | **No** | Fundamentally different serialised form |
| Remove `implements Serializable`          | **No**      | Nothing can be read                        |

Two compatible changes still deserve care. A field added in version 2 arrives as
`null` when reading version 1 data, so any code assuming it is populated needs a
fallback, which is what `readObject` validation is for. And a renamed field is
the worst case in the table, because nothing throws: the old value is dropped
and the new field silently holds a default.

```java
// Version 2 of the class: 'region' did not exist in version 1
private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in)
        throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
    in.defaultReadObject();
    if (region == null) {
        region = "UNKNOWN";        // migrate old streams to a usable default
    }
}
```

The honest conclusion is that keeping the UID unchanged says the stream can
still be *read*, not that the resulting object is *meaningful*. Long-lived data
needs an explicit version field and migration code, at which point a format
designed for versioning, covered next, is the better tool.

> Key Takeaways
> - `transient` excludes a field from the serialised form and is required for
>   derived, unserialisable, secret, and oversized state.
> - A transient field comes back as `null`, `0`, or `false` with no warning, so
>   rebuild it in `readObject` if an invariant depends on it.
> - `static` fields are never serialised, because they belong to the class.
> - `transient final` cannot be restored in `readObject`, which is a reason to
>   use a serialisation proxy.
> - An undeclared `serialVersionUID` is computed from the class structure and
>   changes when you add a mere private method.
> - Declare `private static final long serialVersionUID`, and change it only
>   when you intend to break old data.
> - Adding and removing fields is compatible; changing a type, renaming a field,
>   or moving a class in the hierarchy is not.
> - Renaming a field fails silently: the old value is discarded and the new
>   field holds a default.
> - A matching UID guarantees readability, never meaningfulness, so versioned
>   data needs explicit migration.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Serialise an object with a `transient` field holding a non-null value, read
>    it back, and print the field. Then restore it correctly in `readObject`.
> 2. Write a class without a `serialVersionUID`, serialise an instance to a
>    file, add an unused private method, recompile, and read the file back.
>    Record the exact exception message.
> 3. Repeat exercise 2 with an explicitly declared UID and explain the
>    difference in one sentence.
> 4. Take a serialised version-1 file, add a field to the class, and write the
>    `readObject` migration that gives the new field a sensible default.
> 5. Rename a field between versions while keeping the UID fixed, then explain
>    what the deserialised object contains and why nothing threw.
> 6. Interview: Why does the implicitly computed `serialVersionUID` include
>    method signatures when methods are not serialised? (Hint: what question was
>    the designers' hash originally trying to answer about two class versions?)

#### Serialization Risks and Alternatives

Java serialisation is not merely old-fashioned. It is the source of an entire
class of remote code execution vulnerabilities, it welds your private fields to
your compatibility story, and the platform's own architects describe it as a
mistake to be undone. Understanding why leads directly to what to use instead.

**Risk 1: deserialising untrusted bytes can execute arbitrary code.** This is
the important one, and the reason it surprises people is a matter of *ordering*.

```text
   attacker-controlled bytes arrive
        |
        v
   readObject()
        |-- reads class NAMES from the stream
        |-- loads those classes from YOUR classpath
        |-- allocates instances, bypassing constructors
        `-- runs their readObject / readResolve hooks   <-- code executes HERE
        |
        v
   (Session) result     <-- your cast, your validation, your first look
                            ALREADY TOO LATE
```

The stream decides which classes get instantiated, and their hooks run before
your code sees anything. Writing `(Session) in.readObject()` does not protect
you, because the `ClassCastException` is thrown after the damage.

A **gadget chain** exploits this. The attacker does not supply malicious code;
they supply a carefully nested graph of ordinary classes that are already on
your classpath, chosen so that the side effects of their `readObject`,
`hashCode`, `equals`, or `toString` methods compose into something dangerous,
typically ending at reflection or `Runtime.exec`. The 2015 Apache Commons
Collections chain demonstrated this against WebLogic, JBoss, Jenkins, and
others, and it did not require a single line of vulnerable code in the
applications themselves. Any library with a suitable side effect is ammunition.

**Risk 2: denial of service from a tiny input.** A stream of a few dozen bytes
can describe a structure whose reconstruction is exponential. The classic is a
nest of `HashSet`s where each level contains the previous one twice: computing
hash codes on read takes time that doubles per level. Deep nesting similarly
overflows the stack. The receiver has no chance to check the size of the
resulting object graph before building it.

**Risk 3: invariants are bypassed.** As Chapter 4.4 showed and the mechanics
topic explained, no constructor runs, so a hand-crafted stream can produce an
object your constructors would never have allowed: a negative age, an empty
required list, a `Set` containing duplicates.

**Risk 4: the format becomes a permanent constraint.** Private field names and
types leak into the serialised form, so renaming a private field is a
compatibility break. Encapsulation is real at compile time and fictional at
serialisation time.

**Risk 5: practical limitations.** The format is Java-only, so no other language
can read it. It is verbose and slow compared with modern codecs. And it has no
schema, so you cannot inspect, validate, or evolve the data with tooling.

**If you must keep using it, three defences.**

The first is the simplest and the most effective: **never deserialise data that
crossed a trust boundary**. Serialisation is acceptable between two processes
you control, on an authenticated channel, ideally with the bytes signed or
encrypted.

The second is **filtering**, added in Java 9 and backported to 8. A filter is
consulted before any class is resolved, so an allowlist prevents the gadget
classes from ever being instantiated.

```java
ObjectInputFilter filter = ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter(
        "com.example.model.*;"     // allow our own model classes
      + "java.base/java.util.*;"   // allow the collections we actually use
      + "maxdepth=20;maxrefs=1000;maxbytes=100000;"   // and cap the work
      + "!*");                     // reject everything else

try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(source)) {
    in.setObjectInputFilter(filter);        // MUST be set before readObject
    Session s = (Session) in.readObject();
}
```

The same syntax works process-wide through the `jdk.serialFilter` system
property, and Java 17 added a filter *factory* for per-context policies. Note
that the pattern ends with `!*`: an allowlist that forgets to reject the
remainder allows everything.

The third is the **serialisation proxy pattern**, which is the most robust
structural fix. Instead of serialising the real class, you write a small private
nested class carrying the logical state, and reconstruct the real object through
its ordinary public constructor.

```java
public final class Period implements Serializable {
    private final Date start, end;

    public Period(Date start, Date end) {
        if (start.after(end)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("start after end");
        this.start = new Date(start.getTime());     // defensive copies
        this.end   = new Date(end.getTime());
    }

    private static class SerializationProxy implements Serializable {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        private final Date start, end;

        SerializationProxy(Period p) { this.start = p.start; this.end = p.end; }

        private Object readResolve() {
            return new Period(start, end);          // the CONSTRUCTOR runs: validation holds
        }
    }

    private Object writeReplace() {
        return new SerializationProxy(this);        // never write a real Period
    }

    private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) throws InvalidObjectException {
        throw new InvalidObjectException("proxy required");   // block forged streams
    }
}
```

This restores constructor validation, allows `final` fields, decouples the wire
format from the internal fields, and makes a forged stream useless. Its cost is
extra code and object allocation, and it cannot be used for classes that are
extendable or mutually referential.

**The alternatives, and how to choose.** Every serious system today uses an
explicit, schema-described format instead.

| Format               | Schema          | Human readable | Cross-language | Size and speed | Typical Java library |
| -------------------- | --------------- | -------------- | -------------- | -------------- | -------------------- |
| JSON                 | Optional (JSON Schema) | Yes     | Yes            | Verbose, adequate | Jackson, Gson     |
| Protocol Buffers     | Required `.proto` | No           | Yes            | Compact, fast     | `protobuf-java`   |
| Avro                 | Required, travels with data | No | Yes           | Compact, fast     | `avro`            |
| CBOR / MessagePack   | Optional        | No             | Yes            | Compact          | Jackson dataformats |
| XML                  | Optional (XSD)  | Yes            | Yes            | Very verbose     | JAXB              |
| Java serialisation   | Implicit, the class itself | No  | **No**         | Verbose, slow    | Built in          |

The decisive advantage is not performance. It is that these formats describe
**data**, not **objects**. Nothing in a JSON document names a class to
instantiate, so there is no gadget chain to build, and the mapping layer decides
what types may be produced.

```java
public record Session(String user, int requestCount) { }

ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(new Session("ada", 3));   // {"user":"ada",...}
Session back = mapper.readValue(json, Session.class);   // canonical constructor RUNS
```

One warning carries over: JSON libraries can be made unsafe by re-introducing
the same idea. Jackson's polymorphic default typing embeds Java class names in
the document and hands the attacker back the same power, so it must never be
enabled for untrusted input.

A short decision guide:

| Situation                                        | Use                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| Data crosses a trust boundary                     | JSON or Protobuf, never Java serialisation |
| A public API or anything another language reads   | JSON, or Protobuf for high volume     |
| High-volume internal service traffic              | Protobuf or Avro                      |
| Long-term storage needing schema evolution        | Avro or Protobuf                      |
| A quick deep copy of a graph you fully control    | Java serialisation is defensible      |
| Two JVMs you own, on a private authenticated link | Java serialisation with a strict filter |

**Where the platform is going.** The JDK team has stated the intent to remove
the current serialisation mechanism, and the direction of travel is visible
already: records deserialise through their canonical constructor, serialisation
filters are standard, and Project Amber is exploring a replacement built on
constructors and pattern matching rather than on reflective field injection.
Write new code as if the automatic mechanism is already gone, because for new
designs it should be.

> Key Takeaways
> - Deserialisation runs attacker-influenced code before your cast, so a cast
>   can never be a safety check.
> - A gadget chain composes ordinary classpath classes into an exploit without
>   any vulnerable code in your application.
> - A few bytes can describe a graph whose reconstruction is exponential, giving
>   cheap denial of service.
> - Constructors are bypassed, so a forged stream can produce objects your class
>   forbids.
> - Private field names and types become part of the compatibility contract,
>   which defeats encapsulation over time.
> - The first rule is simply never to deserialise data from outside a trust
>   boundary.
> - `ObjectInputFilter` allowlists classes and caps depth, references, and size,
>   and must end with a reject-everything-else pattern.
> - The serialisation proxy pattern routes reading through a real constructor
>   and rejects forged streams outright.
> - JSON, Protocol Buffers, and Avro describe data rather than objects, so they
>   carry no instruction to instantiate a class.
> - Jackson's polymorphic default typing reintroduces the gadget problem and
>   must stay off for untrusted input.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method that deserialises from a byte array, then add an
>    `ObjectInputFilter` that allows only your own package and the JDK base
>    module. Verify that a `java.util.ArrayList` and an arbitrary third-party
>    class are treated differently.
> 2. Build the nested-`HashSet` structure described above to six levels,
>    serialise it, and measure both the stream size and the time to read it
>    back. Extend it to twenty levels and predict the result before running it.
> 3. Convert a class with validating constructor and `final` fields to the
>    serialisation proxy pattern, then confirm that reading a stream containing
>    the real class throws.
> 4. Replace Java serialisation in a small program with Jackson and records.
>    Compare the output size and note which invariants are now enforced on read.
> 5. Given a service that accepts serialised objects over HTTP, list every
>    change you would make, ordered by how much risk each removes.
> 6. Interview: An endpoint calls `(Order) in.readObject()` on a request body
>    and the team argues the cast makes it safe. Explain precisely why it does
>    not. (Hint: describe the order of operations, and say when the
>    `ClassCastException` would be thrown relative to the hook methods.)

<a id="14-networking-in-java"></a>
## 14. Networking in Java

Chapter 13 moved bytes between a program and its own machine. Networking moves
them between machines that share no memory, no clock, and no guarantee of
staying reachable, which turns every method call into something that can be
slow, reordered, or silently lost. This chapter covers the addressing model
Java exposes, the TCP and UDP socket APIs, the modern HTTP client, and the
non-blocking machinery and protocol design decisions that serious network code
depends on.

<a id="141-networking-foundations"></a>
### 14.1 Networking Foundations

This subchapter covers the mental model underneath every later API: how Java
maps onto the TCP/IP stack, what an address and a port actually identify, and
how names become routable numbers.

#### The Java Networking Model

A program confined to one machine can treat its data as instantly available and
permanently correct. A networked program cannot. Between the caller and the
