**Coverage is a signal, never a target.** Line coverage tells you which lines
executed, not whether anything was verified. A test with no assertions gives
full coverage and zero confidence. Once coverage becomes a goal, people write
tests that inflate the number, and the metric stops measuring anything. Use it
to find code nobody tested at all, not to certify code that was.

Finally, the most reliable habit in practice: **when a bug is reported, write a
failing test that reproduces it before fixing it.** The test proves you
understood the bug, proves the fix works, and permanently prevents its return.

> Key Takeaways
> - Tests exist to make change safe, not to prove correctness.
> - Defect cost rises steeply with how late it is discovered.
> - A unit test exercises one behaviour with no I/O and runs in milliseconds.
> - The pyramid means many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few
>   end-to-end tests.
> - An inverted pyramid produces slow, flaky suites that everyone learns to
>   ignore.
> - FIRST names the five properties: fast, isolated, repeatable,
>   self-validating, timely.
> - Time, randomness, locale, and concurrency are the usual sources of
>   flakiness.
> - Assert observable behaviour, so that internal refactoring does not break
>   tests.
> - Coverage finds untested code but certifies nothing, and collapses when used
>   as a target.
> - Reproduce every reported bug with a failing test before fixing it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a class you have written and list its behaviours as sentences starting
>    with "it should". Count how many are currently verified anywhere.
> 2. Write two tests for a shopping cart total, one asserting the internal list
>    size and one asserting the total. Rename the internal field and observe
>    which test breaks.
> 3. Classify each as unit, integration, or end-to-end: verifying a discount
>    calculation, verifying a repository saves to PostgreSQL, verifying a
>    checkout flow through the web interface.
> 4. Find a test in any codebase that would still pass if the method body were
>    deleted, and explain what it is actually asserting.
> 5. Interview: A team reports 90% line coverage and frequent production
>    defects. What would you look at? (Hint: what does an executed line tell you
>    about whether anything was checked?)

#### JUnit Test Structure and Assertions

JUnit is the de facto testing framework for Java, and JUnit 5 is built from
three parts worth distinguishing, because the names appear in build files.

| Component        | Role                                                    |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| JUnit Platform   | Discovers and runs tests; what build tools and IDEs talk to |
| JUnit Jupiter    | The annotations and assertions you actually write against |
| JUnit Vintage    | Runs legacy JUnit 3 and 4 tests on the new platform      |

Tests live in `src/test/java`, mirroring the package structure of
`src/main/java`, a convention 15.2 explains. A test class is an ordinary class;
no inheritance or naming rule is required, though `ClassNameTest` is universal.

**Every test has the same three-part shape**, known as Arrange-Act-Assert or,
in behavioural phrasing, Given-When-Then.

```java
class BankAccountTest {

    @Test
    void withdrawalReducesBalance() {
        BankAccount account = new BankAccount(1000);   // ARRANGE: set up the world

        account.withdraw(300);                          // ACT: one action under test

        assertEquals(700, account.balance());           // ASSERT: verify the outcome
    }
}
```

Keeping those phases visually separate, with a blank line between them, makes a
test readable in seconds. A test with two "act" steps is usually two tests.

**Naming matters more than in production code**, because a test name is what you
read in a failure report, often months later and without context.

| Naming style                          | Example                                  |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `methodName_condition_expectedResult` | `withdraw_insufficientFunds_throws`      |
| Sentence form                          | `throwsWhenWithdrawingMoreThanBalance`   |
| `@DisplayName` for full prose          | `@DisplayName("rejects a withdrawal larger than the balance")` |

Avoid `test1`, `testWithdraw`, and anything that names only the method, because
they tell you nothing when they fail.

**The assertion catalogue** lives in `org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions`.

| Assertion                          | Verifies                                     |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `assertEquals(expected, actual)`   | Equality by `equals`; note the argument order |
| `assertSame(expected, actual)`     | Identity by `==`                              |
| `assertTrue` / `assertFalse`       | A boolean condition                           |
| `assertNull` / `assertNotNull`     | Nullness                                      |
| `assertArrayEquals`                | Element-wise array equality                   |
| `assertIterableEquals`             | Element-wise iterable equality                |
| `assertThrows`                     | That a call throws, and returns the exception |
| `assertDoesNotThrow`               | That a call completes normally                |
| `assertAll`                        | Several assertions, reporting every failure   |
| `assertTimeout`                    | That a call completes within a duration       |
| `fail("reason")`                   | Unconditional failure, for unreachable paths  |

Three of these deserve detail.

*`assertThrows` returns the exception*, so you can assert on its contents rather
than merely its type.

```java
@Test
void withdrawalBeyondBalanceIsRejected() {
    BankAccount account = new BankAccount(100);

    InsufficientFundsException e = assertThrows(          // returns the thrown exception
            InsufficientFundsException.class,
            () -> account.withdraw(500));                 // the code that must throw

    assertEquals(400, e.shortfall());                     // now assert its details
    assertEquals(100, account.balance());                 // and that nothing changed
}
```

*`assertAll` reports every failure*, where sequential assertions stop at the
first one and hide the rest.

```java
@Test
void createsAccountWithAllFields() {
    Account a = Account.open("ada", "EUR");

    assertAll("account",                                  // all four run regardless
            () -> assertEquals("ada", a.owner()),
            () -> assertEquals("EUR", a.currency()),
            () -> assertEquals(0, a.balance()),
            () -> assertTrue(a.isOpen()));
}
```

*Failure messages can be lazy.* Passing a `Supplier<String>` avoids building the
message on the passing path, which matters when the message is expensive.

```java
assertEquals(expected, actual, () -> "mismatch for " + buildExpensiveReport());
```

**Argument order is not cosmetic.** `assertEquals(expected, actual)` determines
which value the failure message calls expected. Reversing them produces reports
that send the next reader in the wrong direction.

**Floating point needs a delta**, because binary representation makes exact
equality unreliable.

```java
assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2, 1e-9);     // without the delta, this FAILS
```

**AssertJ is worth knowing**, because most professional codebases use it for its
fluent style and dramatically better failure output.

```java
// JUnit:   "expected: <3> but was: <2>"
assertEquals(3, cart.items().size());

// AssertJ: prints the full list contents on failure
assertThat(cart.items()).hasSize(3)
                        .extracting(Item::name)
                        .containsExactly("book", "pen", "lamp");
```

**Four mistakes recur in real test suites.**

| Mistake                              | Why it is a problem                          |
| ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| A test with no assertion              | Passes whatever happens; pure coverage theatre |
| Several unrelated behaviours per test | One failure hides the others; the name cannot describe it |
| `if` or loops inside a test           | The test itself now needs testing            |
| Duplicating the implementation's logic | Both change together, so the test proves nothing |

That last one is subtle and common: computing the expected value with the same
formula the code uses means a wrong formula passes its own test. Expected values
should be written as literals wherever possible.

> Key Takeaways
> - JUnit 5 splits into Platform, Jupiter, and Vintage, and Jupiter is the API
>   you write against.
> - Tests live in `src/test/java` mirroring the main package structure.
> - Every test reads as Arrange, Act, Assert, separated visually.
> - A test name is read at failure time, so it must state the behaviour.
> - `assertEquals` takes expected first, and reversing it misleads the reader.
> - `assertThrows` returns the exception so its contents can be asserted.
> - `assertAll` reports every grouped failure instead of stopping at the first.
> - Floating point comparisons need an explicit delta.
> - AssertJ gives fluent assertions and far more informative failure messages.
> - Never recompute the expected value with the implementation's own logic.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a test class for a `Stack` with tests for push, pop, and popping when
>    empty, using `assertThrows` for the last one.
> 2. Take four related assertions about one object and rewrite them with
>    `assertAll`. Break two deliberately and compare the reports.
> 3. Write `assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2)` and run it. Explain the failure, then
>    fix it two different ways.
> 4. Rewrite three JUnit assertions in AssertJ and compare the failure output
>    by breaking each one.
> 5. Interview: Why does `assertEquals` take the expected value first when the
>    result is the same either way? (Hint: what does the failure message say,
>    and who reads it?)

#### Test Lifecycle and Parameterized Tests

Tests need setup, and repeating that setup in every method is both noisy and a
source of accidental sharing. JUnit provides lifecycle hooks, and the rule
governing them follows from the isolation requirement of FIRST.

**JUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method.** This
is deliberate: a field assigned in one test cannot leak into another, so tests
cannot depend on execution order.

```text
   For a class with two @Test methods:

   new TestClass()  ->  @BeforeEach  ->  test1  ->  @AfterEach
   new TestClass()  ->  @BeforeEach  ->  test2  ->  @AfterEach
        ^ a FRESH instance, so fields start over

   @BeforeAll runs once before everything, @AfterAll once after.
   Both must be static, because no instance exists yet.
```

| Annotation     | Runs                          | Must be static | Typical use                     |
| -------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `@BeforeAll`   | Once, before all tests         | Yes            | Start a container, load a fixture file |
| `@BeforeEach`  | Before every test method       | No             | Build the object under test     |
| `@AfterEach`   | After every test method        | No             | Close resources opened per test |
| `@AfterAll`    | Once, after all tests          | Yes            | Stop the container              |

```java
class OrderServiceTest {

    private OrderService service;                 // fresh for every test

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        service = new OrderService(new InMemoryOrderRepository());
    }

    @Test
    void placesOrder() { /* uses a clean service */ }

    @Test
    void rejectsEmptyOrder() { /* also a clean service, unaffected by the above */ }
}
```

Annotating the class `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` reuses one instance
and allows non-static `@BeforeAll`, but it reintroduces the shared-state risk
the default was designed to prevent. Use it only when construction is genuinely
expensive.

**`@Nested` groups tests by context**, which keeps setup close to the tests that
need it and produces readable reports.

```java
class BankAccountTest {

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("when the account is overdrawn")
    class WhenOverdrawn {

        BankAccount account;

        @BeforeEach
        void overdraw() {                      // runs AFTER the outer @BeforeEach
            account = new BankAccount(-50);
        }

        @Test
        void rejectsWithdrawals() { /* ... */ }

        @Test
        void allowsDeposits() { /* ... */ }
    }
}
```

Nested classes must be inner classes, not `static`, so they can see the outer
instance.

**Parameterized tests remove copy-paste.** When the same behaviour must hold for
many inputs, writing one test per input buries the intent in duplication.

```java
// Before: three tests that differ only in data
@Test void rejectsEmpty()  { assertFalse(Validator.isValidEmail("")); }
@Test void rejectsNoAt()   { assertFalse(Validator.isValidEmail("ada.dev")); }
@Test void rejectsNoDomain(){ assertFalse(Validator.isValidEmail("ada@")); }

// After: one test, three cases, each reported separately
@ParameterizedTest(name = "rejects \"{0}\"")           // {0} is the argument
@ValueSource(strings = {"", "ada.dev", "ada@", "@example.com", "a b@x.com"})
void rejectsMalformedEmails(String candidate) {
    assertFalse(Validator.isValidEmail(candidate));
}
```

Each case is reported as a separate test, so a failure names the offending
input.

| Source annotation      | Supplies                                           |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `@ValueSource`         | One literal argument per run                        |
| `@NullSource`, `@EmptySource`, `@NullAndEmptySource` | The awkward edge cases     |
| `@CsvSource`           | Several arguments per run, written inline           |
| `@CsvFileSource`       | The same, from a resource file                      |
| `@EnumSource`          | Every constant of an enum, or a filtered subset     |
| `@MethodSource`        | Arbitrary objects from a static factory method      |
| `@ArgumentsSource`     | A custom provider, for full control                 |

`@CsvSource` covers the common multi-argument case.

```java
@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} + {1} = {2}")
@CsvSource({
        "1, 1, 2",
        "5, 3, 8",
        "-2, 2, 0",
        "0, 0, 0"
})
void addsCorrectly(int a, int b, int expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, Calculator.add(a, b));
}
```

`@MethodSource` handles arguments that are not literals.

```java
@ParameterizedTest
@MethodSource("discountCases")
void appliesDiscount(Order order, Money expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, pricing.total(order));
}

static Stream<Arguments> discountCases() {          // must be static, returns a Stream
    return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of(orderOf(1, "book"), Money.of(1250)),
            Arguments.of(orderOf(10, "book"), Money.of(11250)),   // bulk discount
            Arguments.of(orderOf(0), Money.ZERO));
}
```

**Other lifecycle-adjacent annotations** round out the toolkit.

| Annotation                 | Purpose                                              |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `@RepeatedTest(n)`         | Runs a test n times, useful for flakiness hunting     |
| `@Disabled("reason")`      | Skips a test; always give the reason                  |
| `@Timeout(5)`              | Fails a test that exceeds a duration                  |
| `@Tag("slow")`             | Labels tests so the build can include or exclude them |
| `@TempDir`                 | Injects a temporary directory, deleted afterwards     |

`@TempDir` pairs directly with Chapter 13's file work and removes a whole class
of test pollution.

```java
@Test
void writesReportToDisk(@TempDir Path dir) throws IOException {   // auto-cleaned
    Path out = dir.resolve("report.txt");

    reporter.writeTo(out);

    assertTrue(Files.exists(out));
    assertThat(Files.readString(out)).contains("TOTAL");
}
```

**Assumptions differ from disabling.** `@Disabled` always skips. An assumption
skips only when a runtime condition is unmet, which suits environment-specific
tests.

```java
@Test
void usesNativeLibrary() {
    assumeTrue(System.getProperty("os.name").startsWith("Linux"));   // skip elsewhere
    // ... the rest runs only on Linux
}
```

Finally, **do not make tests depend on execution order.** JUnit deliberately
does not guarantee it. `@TestMethodOrder` exists for the rare integration
scenario that genuinely models a sequence, and reaching for it in unit tests
signals shared state that should be removed instead.

> Key Takeaways
> - JUnit builds a new test instance per method, so fields cannot leak between
>   tests.
> - `@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` are static because no instance exists when they
>   run.
> - `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` reuses one instance and reintroduces shared-state
>   risk.
> - `@Nested` groups tests by context and keeps their setup local.
> - Parameterized tests turn duplicated methods into one test with named cases.
> - `@ValueSource` covers single arguments and `@CsvSource` covers several.
> - `@MethodSource` supplies arbitrary objects from a static factory returning a
>   stream.
> - `@TempDir` gives each test a private directory that is cleaned up
>   automatically.
> - Assumptions skip conditionally at runtime, unlike the unconditional
>   `@Disabled`.
> - Tests must never depend on execution order, and needing an order is a design
>   smell.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a test class with all four lifecycle annotations, each printing its
>    name, and run two tests. Write down the exact output order before running.
> 2. Convert five near-identical validation tests into one `@ParameterizedTest`
>    with `@ValueSource`, and give the cases a readable `name` pattern.
> 3. Use `@CsvSource` to test a function across at least six input combinations
>    including boundary values.
> 4. Write a test that creates files using `@TempDir`, then verify that the
>    directory no longer exists after the run.
> 5. Use `@MethodSource` to supply three `Order` objects with their expected
>    totals.
> 6. Interview: Why does JUnit create a new instance of the test class for every
>    test method rather than reusing one? (Hint: which of the FIRST properties
>    would a shared instance threaten?)

#### Designing Classes for Testability

When a class is hard to test, the instinct is to blame the testing tools. That
instinct is almost always wrong. **Difficulty testing a class in isolation is
evidence that the class cannot be used in isolation**, which is a design
problem that also makes it hard to reuse, reason about, and change.

Testability is therefore a proxy metric. A class that is easy to test tends to
have few dependencies, explicit inputs, and one responsibility, which are the
same properties Chapter 9 argued for on design grounds alone.

The enabling concept is a **seam**: a place where behaviour can be changed
without editing the code. A constructor parameter is the cheapest seam there is.
Code with no seams can only be tested exactly as it runs in production.

Here is a class with no seams at all.

```java
public class OrderService {
    // Created internally: a test cannot replace either of these
    private final EmailSender email = new SmtpEmailSender("smtp.corp.com");
    private final OrderRepository repo = OrderRepository.getInstance();   // global state

    public Receipt place(Order order) {
        repo.save(order);
        email.send(order.customerEmail(), "Order confirmed");   // sends REAL email in tests
        return new Receipt(order, LocalDateTime.now());         // hidden, changing input
    }
}
```

Testing this means running a real SMTP server, sharing a global repository with
every other test, and writing assertions that cannot pin down the timestamp. The
same class with its dependencies made explicit is trivially testable.

```java
public class OrderService {
    private final EmailSender email;
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final Clock clock;                       // time becomes an ordinary input

    public OrderService(EmailSender email, OrderRepository repo, Clock clock) {
        this.email = email;                          // constructor only assigns
        this.repo = repo;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public Receipt place(Order order) {
        repo.save(order);
        email.send(order.customerEmail(), "Order confirmed");
        return new Receipt(order, LocalDateTime.now(clock));    // reads the injected clock
    }
}
```

Nothing about the production behaviour changed. What changed is that a test can
now supply an in-memory repository, a recording email sender, and a clock frozen
at a known instant.

**The obstacles to testability are a short, recognisable list.**

| Smell in the code                     | Why it blocks testing                  | Fix                                  |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `new Collaborator()` inside the class  | No way to substitute it                | Inject through the constructor        |
| `Singleton.getInstance()`             | Global mutable state leaks across tests | Inject the instance                   |
| `LocalDateTime.now()`                 | A hidden, always-changing input          | Inject a `Clock`                      |
| `new Random()`                        | Non-deterministic results                | Inject a seeded `Random`              |
| `System.getenv(...)`                  | Behaviour depends on the machine         | Inject a configuration object         |
| Static methods that do real work       | Cannot be substituted or overridden      | Instance methods on an injected type  |
| I/O or registration in a constructor   | The object cannot be built in a test     | Constructors assign and validate only |
| A private method you want to test      | Signals a hidden responsibility          | Extract it into its own class         |
| `a.getB().getC().getD()`              | A test must construct the whole chain    | Ask the neighbour for what you need   |

**The `Clock` case is worth seeing in full**, because time is the dependency
people most often forget is a dependency.

```java
// Production wiring
var service = new SubscriptionService(Clock.systemDefaultZone());

// Test wiring: the test now controls "now"
Clock frozen = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-15T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
var service = new SubscriptionService(frozen);

assertTrue(service.isExpired(subscriptionEndingOn(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 14))));
assertFalse(service.isExpired(subscriptionEndingOn(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 16))));
```

Without this, the only way to test expiry is to create data relative to the real
current date, which produces tests that pass today and fail on the first of
some future month.

**Push side effects to the edges.** The most powerful structural move is to
separate calculation from communication. Pure logic that takes values and
returns values needs no doubles, no setup, and no cleanup. Everything that
touches the outside world lives in a thin layer around it.

```text
   IMPERATIVE SHELL                 FUNCTIONAL CORE
   (thin, few integration tests)    (thick, hundreds of fast unit tests)

   read rows from the database  -->  apply pricing rules       --> write result
   parse the HTTP request       -->  validate and decide       --> render response
   read the file                -->  transform the records     --> save the file

   ^ hard to test, so keep it small   ^ trivial to test, so put the logic here
```

A method like `Money total(List<Item> items, Discount d)` needs no mocks at all,
because it has no collaborators. Moving logic into that shape eliminates test
complexity rather than managing it.

**Do not test private methods.** The urge usually means a private method has
grown its own responsibility and wants to be a class. Extracting it gives you a
public API to test directly, and the original class gets simpler. Reaching for
reflection to invoke a private method is a workaround for a design signal.

**Interfaces at the boundaries, not everywhere.** Introduce an interface where
you genuinely need to substitute an implementation: persistence, messaging, the
clock, external services. Creating an interface for every class, each with one
implementation named `FooImpl`, adds indirection without adding a seam anyone
uses.

> Key Takeaways
> - Difficulty testing a class is evidence of a design problem, not a tooling
>   problem.
> - A seam is a place behaviour can change without editing the code, and
>   constructor parameters are the cheapest kind.
> - Creating collaborators internally or reaching for singletons removes every
>   seam.
> - Time and randomness are dependencies, and injecting a `Clock` makes expiry
>   logic deterministic.
> - Constructors should assign and validate, never perform I/O or registration.
> - Pure functions need no test doubles, so push logic into a functional core.
> - Keep the side-effecting shell thin, because that is the part requiring
>   integration tests.
> - Wanting to test a private method usually means a class is hiding inside
>   another.
> - Introduce interfaces at real substitution boundaries, not reflexively for
>   every class.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take the untestable `OrderService` above and refactor it to constructor
>    injection. Write one test asserting the receipt timestamp exactly.
> 2. Find a method in your own code calling `LocalDateTime.now()` or
>    `Math.random()`, inject the dependency, and write a deterministic test.
> 3. Identify a method that both calculates and writes to a file. Split it into
>    a pure function and a thin writer, then test the pure part with no setup.
> 4. Find a private method you once wanted to test, extract it into its own
>    class, and write tests for the new public API.
> 5. Interview: A colleague wants to use reflection to test a private method.
>    What would you suggest instead, and why? (Hint: what is the private method
>    telling you about the class's responsibilities?)

#### Test Doubles: Stubs, Fakes, and Mocks

A unit test must isolate the class under test, but real collaborators get in the
way. A repository needs a database, an email sender actually sends email, and a
payment gateway charges a real card. A **test double** is a stand-in that lets
the test run without them.

The name comes from a stunt double: something that resembles the real thing
closely enough for one specific scene, without being it.

The five kinds are worth distinguishing, because the words are used loosely and
the distinctions carry real consequences.

| Kind    | Behaviour                                              | Example                                    |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Dummy   | Passed to satisfy a parameter, never actually used      | `new Order(items, null)`                   |
| Stub    | Returns canned answers, verifies nothing                | A repository that always returns one order  |
| Spy     | A real or partial object that records how it was called | A sender that stores every message          |
| Mock    | Pre-programmed with expectations, and asserts on them   | Verifying that `send` was called once       |
| Fake    | A real, working, simplified implementation              | An in-memory repository backed by a map     |

**The deeper distinction is what you verify.**

*State verification* performs an action and asserts on the resulting state. It
is the default and the more robust choice, because it says nothing about how the
result was produced.

*Interaction verification* asserts that a collaborator was called. It couples
the test to the implementation, so it is justified only when the call **is** the
observable effect: sending an email, publishing an event, charging a card. There
is no state to inspect afterwards, so the interaction is the behaviour.

```java
// STATE verification: preferred where possible
@Test
void placedOrderIsRetrievable() {
    var repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();          // a FAKE
    var service = new OrderService(repo, noOpEmail(), fixedClock());

    service.place(order);

    assertEquals(Optional.of(order), repo.findById(order.id()));   // assert on outcome
}

// INTERACTION verification: justified, because sending IS the behaviour
@Test
void placingAnOrderNotifiesTheCustomer() {
    EmailSender email = mock(EmailSender.class);       // a MOCK
    var service = new OrderService(new InMemoryOrderRepository(), email, fixedClock());

    service.place(order);

    verify(email).send(eq("ada@example.com"), contains("confirmed"));
}
```

**Mockito is the standard library for this.** The essentials fit in a few lines.

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)                    // wires the annotations
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Mock  OrderRepository repo;                       // a double, created automatically
    @Mock  EmailSender email;
    @InjectMocks OrderService service;                 // constructed with the mocks above

    @Test
    void rejectsUnknownOrder() {
        when(repo.findById(42L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());      // STUBBING

        assertThrows(OrderNotFoundException.class, () -> service.confirm(42L));

        verify(email, never()).send(any(), any());     // assert something did NOT happen
    }

    @Test
    void storesTheOrderWithATimestamp() {
        var captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class);          // capture the argument

        service.place(order);

        verify(repo).save(captor.capture());
        assertNotNull(captor.getValue().placedAt());   // assert on what was passed
    }
}
```

`when(...).thenReturn(...)` stubs, `verify(...)` checks interactions,
`ArgumentCaptor` grabs an argument for detailed assertions, and
`thenThrow(...)` simulates failures that are otherwise hard to provoke.

**Four cautions save a great deal of pain.**

*Do not mock what you do not own.* A mock of a third-party client encodes your
belief about how that library behaves. If the belief is wrong, the test passes
and production fails. Wrap the library in a small interface of your own and mock
that instead, then cover the wrapper with a genuine integration test.

*Do not mock value objects.* Constructing a real `Money` or `Order` is simpler,
faster, and more honest than stubbing its getters.

*Prefer a fake for repositories.* An in-memory implementation is written once,
reused everywhere, and exhibits real behaviour such as a saved item being
findable afterwards. A stubbed repository can be programmed into states the real
one could never reach.

```java
public class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    private final Map<Long, Order> store = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    @Override public void save(Order o) { store.put(o.id(), o); }
    @Override public Optional<Order> findById(long id) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(id));     // genuinely behaves like a repository
    }
}
```

*Watch for over-mocking.* A test where every collaborator is a mock and every
assertion is a `verify` proves only that your code calls the methods you wrote
it to call. It restates the implementation, breaks on every refactor, and
catches almost no bugs. The signal is a test that must be rewritten whenever the
production code is reorganised without changing behaviour.

> Key Takeaways
> - A test double stands in for a collaborator that is slow, unreliable, or has
>   side effects.
> - Dummy, stub, spy, mock, and fake differ in how much behaviour they have and
>   what they verify.
> - State verification asserts on outcomes and survives refactoring.
> - Interaction verification is justified when the call itself is the observable
>   effect.
> - Mockito stubs with `when`, checks calls with `verify`, and inspects
>   arguments with `ArgumentCaptor`.
> - `verify(x, never())` asserts that something did not happen.
> - Never mock a third-party type; wrap it in your own interface and mock that.
> - Constructing real value objects beats stubbing them.
> - An in-memory fake repository is reusable and exhibits genuine behaviour.
> - A test made entirely of mocks and verifies restates the implementation and
>   catches little.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an in-memory fake for a repository interface and use it in three
>    tests without any mocking library.
> 2. Use Mockito to stub a repository that returns empty, and assert the service
>    throws. Then add a `verify` that no email was sent.
> 3. Use `ArgumentCaptor` to assert that the object passed to `save` had its
>    timestamp populated.
> 4. Take a test that verifies four interactions and rewrite it to assert on
>    resulting state instead. Compare which one survives renaming a private
>    helper.
> 5. Interview: When is `verify` the right assertion rather than checking state?
>    (Hint: what state does sending an email leave behind in your own system?)

#### Test-Driven Development Workflow

Test-driven development inverts the usual order: the test is written before the
code that satisfies it. The common objection is that this seems backwards, and
the common misunderstanding is that TDD is a testing technique. It is a
**design** technique whose tests are a by-product.

The reason it works is that writing the test first forces you to be the first
consumer of your own API. You experience the awkwardness of a bad signature
before you have built anything on top of it, and you cannot write untestable
code, because the test already exists.

The cycle has three steps and a strict order.

```text
        +---------------------------------------------+
        |                                             |
        v                                             |
    [ RED ]  write the smallest failing test          |
        |    it MUST fail, for the expected reason    |
        v                                             |
    [ GREEN ] write the simplest code that passes     |
        |     hardcoding is allowed here              |
        v                                             |
    [ REFACTOR ] improve the design, tests stay green |
        |                                             |
        +---------------------------------------------+
             each loop is minutes, not hours
```

Two rules make the cycle meaningful rather than ceremonial. **The test must
actually fail first**, because a test that passes before the code exists is
testing nothing. And **the refactor step is not optional**, because it is where
the design emerges; skipping it leaves a pile of code written to pass tests.

**A worked example.** Build a calculator that sums numbers in a string.

*Step one, red.* Start with the most trivial case.

```java
@Test
void emptyStringIsZero() {
    assertEquals(0, StringCalculator.add(""));   // does not compile yet: that counts as red
}
```

*Step one, green.* The simplest thing that passes. Hardcoding is legitimate.

```java
public static int add(String input) {
    return 0;                                     // yes, really
}
```

*Step two, red.* A second case forces generalisation. This is called
triangulation: one example can be faked, two cannot.

```java
@Test
void singleNumberIsItself() {
    assertEquals(5, StringCalculator.add("5"));   // fails against the hardcoded 0
}
```

*Step two, green.*

```java
public static int add(String input) {
    if (input.isEmpty()) return 0;
    return Integer.parseInt(input);
}
```

*Step three, red and green.* Now commas.

```java
@Test
void sumsCommaSeparatedNumbers() {
    assertEquals(6, StringCalculator.add("1,2,3"));
}
```

```java
public static int add(String input) {
    if (input.isEmpty()) return 0;
    int total = 0;
    for (String part : input.split(",")) {
        total += Integer.parseInt(part);
    }
    return total;
}
```

*Step four, refactor.* With three tests green, the implementation can be
rewritten freely using Chapter 8's streams, and the tests prove nothing broke.

```java
public static int add(String input) {
    if (input.isBlank()) return 0;
    return Arrays.stream(input.split(","))
                 .mapToInt(Integer::parseInt)     // refactored with tests as the safety net
                 .sum();
}
```

*Step five.* Add error behaviour the same way, starting from the failing test.

```java
@Test
void rejectsNegativeNumbers() {
    var e = assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
                         () -> StringCalculator.add("1,-2,3"));
    assertTrue(e.getMessage().contains("-2"));    // the message is part of the behaviour
}
```

Notice what happened across those steps: at no point was there a large block of
untested code, at no point was the design decided far in advance, and the final
refactor was safe because the tests already described the behaviour.

**What TDD actually buys you.**

| Benefit                          | Mechanism                                        |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Testable design by construction   | Untestable code cannot be written test-first      |
| No untested code paths            | Code exists only to satisfy a test                |
| Fast feedback                     | The loop is minutes, so mistakes are local        |
| Refactoring confidence            | Green tests before and after prove behaviour held |
| A specification that cannot rot   | Tests fail when they stop matching the code       |
| Smaller units                     | Large classes are painful to drive test-first     |

**When TDD is a poor fit**, and saying so is not heresy.

- Exploratory work where you do not yet know what you are building. Spike
  first, throw the spike away, then rebuild test-first.
- Learning an unfamiliar library, where you cannot predict the behaviour you
  would assert.
- Visual layout and rendering, where the assertion is "does it look right".
- Performance tuning, where the relevant feedback is a benchmark, not a test.

Two misconceptions are worth naming. TDD does not mean writing every test up
front; it means one small test at a time. And high test coverage is a
consequence of TDD, not its purpose. Practitioners keep doing it because the
code comes out better structured, not because the numbers look good.

> Key Takeaways
> - TDD is a design discipline, and the tests are a by-product.
> - The cycle is red, green, refactor, in that order, in loops of minutes.
> - The test must genuinely fail first, or it is verifying nothing.
> - The simplest passing code is correct at the green step, including hardcoded
>   values.
> - Triangulation adds a second example to force real generalisation.
> - The refactor step is where design emerges and must not be skipped.
> - Writing the test first makes you the first user of your own API.
> - Untestable designs cannot be produced test-first, which is the main
>   structural benefit.
> - Spike first for exploratory work, then rebuild test-driven.
> - Coverage is a side effect of TDD rather than its goal.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement the string calculator above from scratch, committing after each
>    green step. Do not write a line of production code before a failing test.
> 2. Extend it test-first to support newlines as separators alongside commas.
> 3. Write a failing test for a bug in existing code, confirm it fails for the
>    right reason, then fix it and watch it pass.
> 4. Implement a `RomanNumeral.toRoman(int)` converter test-first, adding one
>    numeral at a time and refactoring whenever duplication appears.
> 5. Interview: Why is it important that a new test fails before you write the
>    implementation? (Hint: what would a test that passes immediately have
>    proven about itself?)

<a id="152-build-tools-and-dependencies"></a>
### 15.2 Build Tools and Dependencies

This subchapter covers how a Java project is laid out, how Maven and Gradle turn
that layout into an artifact, and how to survive the dependency graph that any
real project accumulates.

#### Project Structure Conventions

Compiling a single file with `javac` is easy. A real project has hundreds of
source files, test files that must not ship, configuration that must, and
dependencies that must be on the classpath in the right order. Somebody has to
decide where all of it lives.

Before Maven, every project decided differently, so every newcomer and every
tool had to learn a bespoke layout. Maven's contribution was **convention over
configuration**: agree on one standard layout, and the build needs almost no
configuration at all. Gradle adopted the same layout, so it is now simply how
Java projects look.

```text
   my-app/
   |-- pom.xml                  build definition (or build.gradle.kts)
   |-- README.md
   |-- .gitignore
   |-- src/
   |   |-- main/
   |   |   |-- java/            production sources
   |   |   |   `-- com/example/app/OrderService.java
   |   |   `-- resources/       non-code files, PACKAGED INTO the artifact
   |   |       `-- application.properties
   |   `-- test/
   |       |-- java/            test sources, never packaged
   |       |   `-- com/example/app/OrderServiceTest.java
   |       `-- resources/       fixtures used only by tests
   |           `-- sample-orders.json
   `-- target/                  Maven output (Gradle uses build/)
       |-- classes/             compiled main classes
       |-- test-classes/        compiled test classes
       `-- my-app-1.0.0.jar     the packaged artifact
```

Four properties of this layout carry real consequences.

**Test packages mirror main packages.** A test for
`com.example.app.OrderService` lives at
`src/test/java/com/example/app/OrderServiceTest.java`. Because it is in the same
package, it can reach package-private members, which is the intended way to test
internals you do not want to make public.

**Resources are classpath entries, not files.** Anything under
`src/main/resources` is copied to the root of the artifact, so
`src/main/resources/config.properties` becomes `/config.properties` on the
classpath. This is where a very common bug lives.

```java
// WRONG: works when run from the IDE, fails once packaged.
// Inside a jar there is no such path on the filesystem.
try (InputStream in = new FileInputStream("src/main/resources/config.properties")) { }

// RIGHT: ask the classloader, which works from a directory or from inside a jar
try (InputStream in = App.class.getResourceAsStream("/config.properties")) {
    Properties props = new Properties();
    props.load(in);
}
```

The leading slash means "from the classpath root". Without it, the lookup is
relative to the class's own package.

**Build output is generated and disposable.** `target/` and `build/` are
recreated from source on every build and must never be committed. A `.gitignore`
that misses them is the most common first mistake in a new repository.

**Package names follow reverse domain order** and must match the directory
structure exactly: `com.example.app.billing` lives in
`com/example/app/billing`. Package names are lowercase by convention, and the
compiler enforces the directory correspondence.

For anything beyond a single deliverable, projects split into **modules**, each
with the same internal layout.

```text
   my-system/
   |-- pom.xml                  the parent: shared config, module list, versions
   |-- my-system-domain/        pure model and business rules, no frameworks
   |   |-- pom.xml
   |   `-- src/main/java/...
   |-- my-system-persistence/   depends on domain
   |   `-- ...
   `-- my-system-api/           depends on domain and persistence; the deployable
       `-- ...
```

The dependency arrows between modules are enforced by the build, which makes
architectural boundaries real rather than aspirational: the persistence module
simply cannot import from the API module if the build does not allow it.

The payoff for accepting the convention is that every IDE, continuous
integration system, static analysis tool, and code coverage agent already knows
where everything is. Deviating means configuring all of them.

> Key Takeaways
> - Convention over configuration means a standard layout needs almost no build
>   configuration.
> - Production code lives in `src/main/java` and tests in `src/test/java`.
> - Test packages mirror main packages, which grants access to package-private
>   members.
> - Files under `src/main/resources` are packaged into the artifact and read
>   from the classpath.
> - Reading a resource with `FileInputStream` works in an IDE and fails inside a
>   jar.
> - `getResourceAsStream("/name")` reads from the classpath root, with or
>   without a leading slash changing the meaning.
> - `target/` and `build/` are generated output and must be excluded from
>   version control.
> - Package names are reverse-domain, lowercase, and must match the directory
>   structure.
> - Multi-module projects make architectural boundaries enforceable by the
>   build.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create the standard layout by hand for a project with one class and one
>    test, and compile it without a build tool to see what the tool automates.
> 2. Put a properties file in `src/main/resources`, load it with
>    `getResourceAsStream`, package the project, and run it from the jar.
> 3. Change that code to `new FileInputStream(...)` and run it from the jar.
>    Record the exact exception.
> 4. Write a test that exercises a package-private method, and confirm it
>    compiles only when the test is in the matching package.
> 5. Interview: Why are `src/main/resources` files read through the classloader
>    rather than as file paths? (Hint: what does the deployed artifact actually
>    look like on disk?)

#### Maven Lifecycle and POM Basics

A build is a sequence of steps: resolve dependencies, compile, run tests,
package. Maven's model is that **the sequence is fixed and you plug behaviour
into it**. Learning Maven is mostly learning that sequence.

Three concepts hold the model together.

| Concept     | What it is                                                       |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Coordinates | `groupId:artifactId:version`, the global address of any artifact  |
| POM         | `pom.xml`, the Project Object Model: a declarative build description |
| Lifecycle   | An ordered list of phases; plugins bind goals to phases           |

**Coordinates are how the whole ecosystem names things.** The triple
`org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.10.2` identifies exactly one artifact in the
world, which is what makes automatic dependency resolution possible.

**The lifecycle is an ordered list of phases**, and the rule that explains most
Maven behaviour is that *running a phase runs every phase before it*.

```text
   validate -> compile -> test -> package -> verify -> install -> deploy

   mvn test      runs validate, compile, test
   mvn package   runs all of the above, then package
   mvn install   runs all of the above, then install
                 ^ you never need to chain them yourself
```

| Phase      | What happens                                                    |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `validate` | Checks the project is coherent and information is available      |
| `compile`  | Compiles `src/main/java` into `target/classes`                   |
| `test`     | Runs unit tests with Surefire; failures stop the build           |
| `package`  | Assembles `target/my-app-1.0.0.jar`                              |
| `verify`   | Runs integration tests with Failsafe, plus quality checks        |
| `install`  | Copies the artifact into the local repository at `~/.m2/repository` |
| `deploy`   | Uploads the artifact to a shared remote repository               |

`clean` belongs to a separate lifecycle, which is why the common incantation is
`mvn clean install`: two lifecycles, run in order.

**A POM, annotated.**

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- This project's own coordinates -->
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>my-app</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>   <!-- SNAPSHOT = under development, re-resolved -->
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <properties>
        <!-- Declared once, referenced below as ${junit.version} -->
        <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
        <junit.version>5.10.2</junit.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <version>${junit.version}</version>
            <scope>test</scope>          <!-- not on the production classpath -->
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>2.17.0</version>    <!-- default scope: compile -->
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.2.5</version>   <!-- always pin plugin versions -->
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

**Scopes decide which classpath a dependency joins**, and getting them right
keeps artifacts small and deployments correct.

| Scope      | Compile main | Compile tests | Packaged | Typical use                     |
| ---------- | ------------ | ------------- | -------- | ------------------------------- |
| `compile`  | Yes          | Yes           | Yes      | The default; ordinary libraries  |
| `provided` | Yes          | Yes           | **No**   | Servlet API, supplied by the container |
| `runtime`  | No           | Yes           | Yes      | JDBC drivers, logging backends   |
| `test`     | No           | Yes           | No       | JUnit, Mockito, AssertJ          |
| `import`   | n/a          | n/a           | n/a      | Pulls a BOM into dependency management |

A dependency in `runtime` scope is a useful discipline: a JDBC driver is needed
to run but must not be importable at compile time, which prevents accidental
coupling to a specific database.

**Repositories** are where artifacts come from and go to.

```text
   your build  --(1)-->  ~/.m2/repository        local cache; checked first
                --(2)-->  Maven Central           the public default
                --(3)-->  company Nexus/Artifactory  private or mirrored
```

`mvn install` places your artifact in the local cache so other projects on the
same machine can depend on it, which is the usual way to test a library change
before publishing.

**Parent POMs** hoist shared configuration. A parent declares versions in
`<dependencyManagement>`, and children inherit them without repeating a version
number, which is the main defence against the same library appearing at three
versions across a multi-module project.

Common commands worth memorising:

```bash
mvn clean install -DskipTests    # rebuild everything, skip tests (compile them though)
mvn test                          # just the unit tests
mvn verify                        # unit plus integration tests and checks
mvn dependency:tree               # what is actually on the classpath, and why
mvn help:effective-pom            # the POM after inheritance and interpolation
mvn versions:display-dependency-updates   # what is out of date
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Coordinates are `groupId:artifactId:version` and uniquely name any artifact.
> - The POM is declarative: it describes the project rather than scripting the
>   build.
> - Running a phase runs every preceding phase, so `mvn package` also compiles
>   and tests.
> - `clean` is a separate lifecycle, hence `mvn clean install`.
> - `SNAPSHOT` versions are re-resolved and belong only in development.
> - Scope decides which classpaths a dependency joins and whether it is
>   packaged.
> - `provided` dependencies compile but are not shipped, and `runtime` ones ship
>   but cannot be imported.
> - `install` publishes to the local repository so sibling projects can resolve
>   it.
> - Parent POMs centralise versions through `dependencyManagement`.
> - Pin plugin versions, or a build reproducible today breaks tomorrow.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a Maven project from scratch, add JUnit with `test` scope, and run
>    `mvn test`. Then inspect what appeared in `target/`.
> 2. Run `mvn compile`, then `mvn package`, and list which phases each executed.
> 3. Move a dependency from `compile` to `provided`, package the project, and
>    inspect the jar to see what changed.
> 4. Run `mvn help:effective-pom` on a project with a parent and identify three
>    settings that were inherited.
> 5. Interview: Why does `mvn package` run your tests when you only asked it to
>    package? (Hint: what is the relationship between a phase and the ones
>    before it?)

#### Gradle Build Scripts

Maven's declarative XML is predictable and verbose. The moment a build needs
genuine logic, such as generating sources or varying behaviour per environment,
XML fights back and you end up configuring a plugin to do something a single
line of code would express.

Gradle takes the opposite position: **the build script is a program**, written
in Kotlin or Groovy, and the build is a graph of tasks rather than a fixed
lifecycle. The cost is that a Gradle build can be as complicated as any other
program; the benefit is expressiveness and speed.

```kotlin
// build.gradle.kts, the Kotlin DSL (preferred: it gives IDE completion)

plugins {
    java                                    // adds compile, test, jar tasks
    application                             // adds a run task
}

group = "com.example"
version = "1.0.0"

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)   // downloads a JDK if needed
    }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()                          // where to resolve dependencies from
}

dependencies {
    implementation("com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:2.17.0")
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql:42.7.3")
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.10.2")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}

application {
    mainClass = "com.example.app.Main"
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()                      // required for JUnit 5
    testLogging { events("passed", "failed", "skipped") }
}
```

**Configurations are Gradle's version of scopes**, and one distinction is a
genuine design tool rather than a mere label.

| Configuration          | On your compile classpath | Exposed to consumers | Packaged |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------- | -------- |
| `implementation`       | Yes                       | **No**               | Yes      |
| `api`                  | Yes                       | **Yes**              | Yes      |
| `compileOnly`          | Yes                       | No                   | No       |
| `runtimeOnly`          | No                        | No                   | Yes      |
| `testImplementation`   | Test code only            | No                   | No       |

The `implementation` versus `api` distinction controls what leaks.

```text
   app  ---depends on--->  library  ---depends on--->  jackson

   library uses "implementation(jackson)":
       app CANNOT import jackson classes.
       library can upgrade or replace jackson without touching app.

   library uses "api(jackson)":
       app CAN import jackson classes.
       jackson is now part of library's public contract, forever.
```

Use `api` only when a dependency's types genuinely appear in your public
signatures. Defaulting to `implementation` keeps compile classpaths small, which
also makes builds faster.

**Tasks form a directed graph**, and Gradle runs only what is needed. Each task
declares its inputs and outputs, so a task whose inputs have not changed is
skipped as up to date.

```text
   compileJava --> processResources --> classes --> jar --> assemble
                                            |
                                            +--> compileTestJava --> test --> check --> build

   gradle build    runs the whole graph
   gradle test     runs only the path leading to test
   second run      most tasks report UP-TO-DATE and take zero time
```

```kotlin
tasks.register("printVersion") {
    doLast {                                   // the action runs at execution time
        println("Building version $version")
    }
}

tasks.named("jar") {
    dependsOn("printVersion")                  // wire it into the graph
}
```

**The Gradle Wrapper is not optional in practice.** Committing `gradlew`,
`gradlew.bat`, and `gradle/wrapper/` pins the exact Gradle version for everyone,
so the build does not depend on what each developer happens to have installed.
Always invoke `./gradlew build` rather than a globally installed `gradle`.

**Choosing between the two.**

| Aspect                | Maven                              | Gradle                             |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Build definition      | Declarative XML                    | Kotlin or Groovy code              |
| Learning curve        | Gentle; every project looks alike  | Steeper; builds can diverge widely |
| Custom logic          | Requires writing or finding a plugin | Inline in the script              |
| Incremental builds    | Limited                            | Strong, with input and output tracking |
| Build caching         | No                                 | Local and remote                   |
| Speed on large builds | Slower                             | Substantially faster               |
| Predictability        | High; hard to make strange         | Lower; a build can become a program to maintain |
| Common in             | Enterprise Java, Spring projects    | Android (mandatory), large polyglot builds |

Neither is wrong. Maven's rigidity is a feature on a team that wants every
project to behave identically; Gradle's flexibility pays off on large builds
where minutes of compile time matter.

> Key Takeaways
> - A Gradle build script is a Kotlin or Groovy program, not a declarative
>   document.
> - Gradle uses the same source layout as Maven but outputs to `build/`.
> - `implementation` hides a dependency from consumers, while `api` makes it
>   part of your public contract.
> - Defaulting to `implementation` keeps compile classpaths small and builds
>   fast.
> - Tasks form a graph, and Gradle skips any task whose inputs are unchanged.
> - `useJUnitPlatform()` is required for JUnit 5 to run at all.
> - Toolchains let the build declare and fetch the exact JDK version it needs.
> - Always run `./gradlew` so everyone uses the version pinned in the
>   repository.
> - Maven favours uniformity and predictability; Gradle favours flexibility and
>   speed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a Gradle project with the Kotlin DSL, add JUnit 5, and run
>    `./gradlew test`. Run it twice and compare the second run's output.
> 2. Register a custom task that prints the project version, and wire it to run
>    before `jar`.
> 3. Build a two-module project where the library declares a dependency with
>    `implementation`, then try to import that dependency from the consumer.
>    Switch it to `api` and try again.
> 4. Run `./gradlew build --scan` or `--profile` and identify the slowest task.
> 5. Interview: What does declaring a dependency as `api` rather than
>    `implementation` commit you to? (Hint: what happens to every consumer when
>    you later want to replace that library?)

#### Dependency Management and Transitive Conflicts

You declare five dependencies and your build downloads eighty. The extras are
**transitive dependencies**: the libraries your libraries need, and the ones
those need in turn. Build tools resolve them automatically, which is enormously
convenient right up until two of them disagree.

```text
   my-app
   |-- jackson-databind 2.17.0
   |   |-- jackson-core 2.17.0          <- transitive, you never asked for it
   |   `-- jackson-annotations 2.17.0
   `-- some-library 3.1.0
       `-- jackson-databind 2.12.0      <- and it wants a DIFFERENT version
           `-- jackson-core 2.12.0
```

**Only one version can win.** A classpath maps each fully qualified class name
to exactly one class file, so the build must choose a single version of
`jackson-core`. This is the **diamond dependency problem**, and its defining
characteristic is *when* it fails.

```text
   compile time   everything compiles: the chosen version has the classes
                  the compiler happened to need
        |
        v
   run time       NoSuchMethodError, NoClassDefFoundError, AbstractMethodError
                  a method that existed in 2.17 is missing from the 2.12 on the path
```

A `NoSuchMethodError` at runtime in code that compiled cleanly is almost always
a version conflict. The compiler saw one version and the JVM loaded another.

**The two tools resolve conflicts differently, and both rules surprise people.**

| Tool   | Rule                     | Consequence                                        |
| ------ | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Maven  | Nearest definition wins   | The shortest path from the root, with ties broken by declaration order. A *lower* version can win. |
| Gradle | Highest version wins      | Usually what you want, but silently upgrades libraries you never chose. |

Under Maven's rule, the diamond above resolves to `2.12.0` if `some-library` is
declared first and both paths are the same length, which is exactly the
counter-intuitive case that produces runtime failures.

**Diagnose before you fix.** Both tools will show you the resolved graph and the
reason for each choice.

```bash
mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath
./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency jackson-core     # why THIS version?
```

The output marks omitted versions and the conflict that caused each omission,
which turns guesswork into reading.

**Four ways to take control**, roughly in order of preference.

*Declare the version directly.* Under Maven's nearest-wins rule, a direct
dependency is always at distance one, so declaring it pins it.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-core</artifactId>
    <version>2.17.0</version>     <!-- direct: wins over any transitive version -->
</dependency>
```

*Use a bill of materials.* A BOM is a POM listing consistent versions for a
whole family of artifacts. Importing it means you never specify those versions
again and they can never disagree with each other.

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-bom</artifactId>
            <version>2.17.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>      <!-- imports the whole version set -->
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

Gradle expresses the same idea as `implementation(platform("..."))`. Spring Boot
distributes one of these, which is why Boot projects declare dependencies
without versions.

*Exclude an unwanted transitive dependency.* This is the tool for genuine
duplicates, such as two competing logging backends.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>some-library</artifactId>
    <version>3.1.0</version>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>commons-logging</groupId>
            <artifactId>commons-logging</artifactId>   <!-- replaced by a bridge -->
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
```

*Constrain versions in Gradle* without adding a dependency you do not otherwise
need.

```kotlin
dependencies {
    constraints {
        implementation("com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core:2.17.0") {
            because("2.12 lacks the streaming API we rely on")   // documents the reason
        }
    }
}
```

**Semantic versioning is the contract that makes any of this tractable.**

| Change     | Version part | Means                                          |
| ---------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `2.17.0` -> `3.0.0` | Major | Breaking changes; expect to edit code           |
| `2.17.0` -> `2.18.0` | Minor | New features, backward compatible               |
| `2.17.0` -> `2.17.1` | Patch | Bug fixes only                                  |

Treat it as a stated intention rather than a guarantee. Libraries break
compatibility in minor releases more often than anyone would like, which is why
upgrades still need a test suite behind them.

**Reproducibility requires pinned versions.** Version ranges and `SNAPSHOT`
dependencies mean the same source can produce different artifacts on different
days, which makes a failure impossible to reproduce and a release impossible to
audit. Pin exact versions for anything you ship.

**Every dependency is attack surface.** A 2021 vulnerability in Log4j affected
an enormous number of applications, most of which had never declared Log4j at
all: it arrived transitively, several levels deep, in something else. The
lessons are practical.

| Practice                        | Why                                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Scan dependencies continuously   | OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot, Snyk, `gradle dependencyCheckAnalyze` |
| Know your full graph             | A vulnerability in a library you never chose is still yours |
| Produce an SBOM                  | You cannot respond to an advisory without knowing what you ship |
| Prefer fewer dependencies        | Every one is code you did not review and must now patch  |
| Upgrade regularly, in small steps | Long gaps turn routine patches into risky migrations     |

The last row matters more than it sounds. A project that upgrades monthly
applies small, testable changes. A project that upgrades every three years faces
a wall of breaking changes at the worst possible moment, usually during a
security incident.

> Key Takeaways
> - Transitive dependencies arrive automatically, so a few declarations become a
>   large graph.
> - Only one version of a class can be on the classpath, which forces a choice.
> - Version conflicts compile cleanly and fail at runtime with
>   `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError`.
> - Maven picks the nearest definition, which can select a lower version.
> - Gradle picks the highest version, silently upgrading libraries you did not
>   choose.
> - `dependency:tree` and `dependencyInsight` show the resolved graph and the
>   reason for each choice.
> - Declaring a dependency directly pins it under Maven's nearest-wins rule.
> - A BOM keeps a family of artifacts at mutually consistent versions.
> - Version ranges and `SNAPSHOT` dependencies destroy build reproducibility.
> - Transitive dependencies are attack surface, so scan continuously and upgrade
>   in small steps.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run `mvn dependency:tree` or `./gradlew dependencies` on a real project and
>    count direct versus total dependencies.
> 2. Deliberately create a conflict by depending on two libraries needing
>    different versions of a third, then find the resolved version and the rule
>    that chose it.
> 3. Exclude a transitive dependency, rebuild, and confirm with the dependency
>    tree that it is gone.
> 4. Import a BOM and remove the explicit versions it now manages. Verify the
>    resolved versions are unchanged.
> 5. Run a vulnerability scan against a project with an older dependency set and
>    trace one finding back to the direct dependency that introduced it.
> 6. Interview: A method that compiles fine throws `NoSuchMethodError` in
>    production. What is your first hypothesis and how would you confirm it?
>    (Hint: what did the compiler see that the JVM did not?)

#### Packaging JARs and Executables

Compilation produces a directory of loose `.class` files. That is fine for the
build machine and useless for shipping. Packaging turns a build into a single
artifact that can be copied, versioned, and run.

**A JAR is a ZIP file with a manifest.** There is no magic beyond that.

```text
   my-app-1.0.0.jar
   |-- META-INF/
   |   |-- MANIFEST.MF              metadata: main class, version, classpath
   |   `-- services/                ServiceLoader registrations
   |-- com/example/app/
   |   |-- Main.class
   |   `-- OrderService.class
   `-- config.properties            whatever was in src/main/resources
```

```bash
unzip -l my-app.jar          # a jar really is just a zip
cat META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
```

**The manifest makes a jar executable.** Two entries matter.

```text
   Manifest-Version: 1.0
   Main-Class: com.example.app.Main        <- makes "java -jar" work
   Class-Path: lib/jackson-databind.jar lib/jackson-core.jar
   Implementation-Version: 1.0.0           <- readable at runtime for diagnostics
```

```bash
jar --create --file app.jar --main-class com.example.app.Main -C target/classes .
java -jar app.jar
```

**The trap that catches everyone**: `java -jar` **ignores `-cp` entirely**. When
you launch a jar, the classpath comes from the manifest's `Class-Path` and
nothing else.

```bash
java -cp "app.jar:lib/*" com.example.app.Main   # works: explicit classpath and class
java -jar app.jar -cp "lib/*"                   # the -cp is silently ignored
```

That is why a plain jar with dependencies almost never runs as-is, and why the
packaging strategies below exist.

| Strategy                  | How it works                                  | Trade-off                            |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Thin jar plus `lib/`      | `Class-Path` in the manifest points at a directory | Small artifact, but you must ship the directory intact |
| Fat (uber) jar            | Every dependency unpacked and merged into one jar  | One file to deploy; merge hazards below |
| Spring Boot executable jar | Dependencies kept as nested jars with a custom loader | No merge hazards; Boot-specific layout |
| WAR                       | Deployed into a servlet container              | Container-managed, largely legacy     |
| `jlink` image             | A trimmed JVM containing only required modules  | Small self-contained runtime; needs modular dependencies |
| `jpackage` installer      | Platform installer: `.msi`, `.deb`, `.dmg`      | Desktop distribution; one build per platform |

**Fat jars are the common default**, produced by the Maven Shade plugin or the
Gradle Shadow plugin.

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-shade-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.2</version>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <phase>package</phase>
            <goals><goal>shade</goal></goals>
            <configuration>
                <transformers>
                    <!-- merges META-INF/services entries instead of overwriting them -->
                    <transformer implementation=
                        "org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ServicesResourceTransformer"/>
                    <transformer implementation=
                        "org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer">
                        <mainClass>com.example.app.Main</mainClass>
                    </transformer>
                </transformers>
            </configuration>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

Those transformers are not optional decoration. Flattening many jars into one
creates three genuine hazards.

*Duplicate resource files silently overwrite.* If five dependencies each contain
`META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver`, a naive merge keeps one and the
`ServiceLoader` mechanism from Chapter 10 quietly stops finding the others. This
is why JDBC drivers and logging backends disappear from fat jars.

*Signed jars break.* A signature covers the original archive's contents, so
repackaging invalidates it and the JVM refuses to load the classes.

*Duplicate classes shadow each other.* Two versions of the same class in one
archive means whichever the packager wrote first wins, with no warning.

Spring Boot sidesteps all three by nesting dependency jars intact inside the
artifact and shipping a launcher that knows how to read them, which is why a
Boot jar's layout looks unusual.

```text
   my-app.jar
   |-- META-INF/MANIFEST.MF          Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher
   |-- org/springframework/boot/loader/...    the launcher
   `-- BOOT-INF/
       |-- classes/                  your code
       `-- lib/                      dependencies, as intact jars
```

**For self-contained distribution**, `jlink` builds a runtime image containing
only the modules your application uses, typically tens of megabytes rather than
a full JDK, and `jpackage` wraps an application into a native installer.

```bash
jlink --add-modules java.base,java.sql --output runtime --strip-debug --no-man-pages
jpackage --name MyApp --input target/ --main-jar app.jar --type deb
```

**Two finishing touches** separate a professional artifact from a working one.
Record the version and build metadata in the manifest so a running instance can
report exactly what it is, and enable reproducible builds so that the same
source produces byte-identical output, since jars otherwise embed timestamps.

```xml
<properties>
    <project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-01-15T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>
</properties>
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A jar is a ZIP archive plus a `META-INF/MANIFEST.MF`.
> - `Main-Class` in the manifest is what makes `java -jar` work.
> - `java -jar` ignores `-cp` completely, taking the classpath from the
>   manifest.
> - A fat jar merges every dependency into one archive for single-file
>   deployment.
> - Merging overwrites duplicate resources, which silently breaks
>   `ServiceLoader` registrations.
> - Shade and Shadow transformers exist to merge those service files correctly.
> - Repackaging invalidates signed jars, and duplicate classes shadow one
>   another without warning.
> - Spring Boot nests intact dependency jars with a custom loader, avoiding
>   merge hazards.
> - `jlink` produces a trimmed runtime and `jpackage` a native installer.
> - Embedding version metadata and fixing build timestamps make artifacts
>   diagnosable and reproducible.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a plain jar with a `Main-Class`, run it with `java -jar`, then unzip
>    it and read the manifest.
> 2. Add a dependency, rebuild the plain jar, and run it. Explain the
>    `NoClassDefFoundError`, then fix it two ways: with `Class-Path` and with a
>    fat jar.
> 3. Build a fat jar from a project using a JDBC driver, and check whether
>    `META-INF/services` survived the merge.
> 4. Compare the size of a plain jar, a fat jar, and a `jlink` image for the
>    same application.
> 5. Interview: Why does adding `-cp lib/*` to a `java -jar` command have no
>    effect? (Hint: where does the JVM look for the classpath in that mode?)

<a id="153-debugging-and-code-quality"></a>
### 15.3 Debugging and Code Quality

This subchapter covers the tools for understanding code that is misbehaving and
for preventing the next problem: debuggers, logging, automated analysis,
formatting, profiling, and documentation.

#### Interactive Debugging and Breakpoints

The universal first debugging technique is to add a print statement, rebuild,
and run again. It works, and it is slow: each cycle costs a rebuild, and you
only ever see the values you thought to print in advance.

A debugger removes both limits. It suspends the program mid-execution and lets
you inspect everything in scope. If printing is taking photographs at positions
you guessed beforehand, a debugger is pausing the film and walking around the
set.

**Breakpoints come in several kinds**, and knowing the less obvious ones is what
separates casual from effective debugging.

| Kind                      | Stops when                                 | Use it for                            |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| Line breakpoint           | Execution reaches a line                    | The default                           |
| **Conditional** breakpoint | A line is reached *and* an expression is true | The one bad iteration out of 10,000  |
| **Exception** breakpoint  | An exception is thrown, even if caught       | Finding silently swallowed exceptions |
| **Field watchpoint**      | A field is read or written                   | Answering "what changed this value?"  |
| Method breakpoint         | Entry or exit of a method                    | Interfaces with many implementations  |
| **Logging** breakpoint    | Never suspends; prints an expression and continues | Printing without editing or rebuilding |

The conditional breakpoint is the workhorse. Stepping through a loop a thousand
times to reach the failing case is wasted effort when the debugger can do it.

```java
for (Order order : orders) {          // set a breakpoint here with the condition:
    process(order);                   //   order.getId() == 4711
}                                     // it now stops only on the one that fails
```

The field watchpoint answers a question that is otherwise genuinely hard: some
field holds an unexpected value and nothing obvious assigned it. A watchpoint
stops at the assignment and shows you the stack that led there.

The logging breakpoint deserves more use than it gets. It gives you print-style
debugging with no source changes, no rebuild, and nothing to accidentally
commit.

**Stepping controls navigate once you are stopped.**

| Action           | Effect                                                       |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Step over        | Execute the current line fully, including any calls           |
| Step into        | Enter the method being called on this line                    |
| Step out         | Finish the current method and stop at the caller              |
| Run to cursor    | Continue until a chosen line, without setting a breakpoint    |
| Drop frame       | Discard the current frame and re-execute the call from its start |

Drop frame is the one people do not know exists. Stepping one line too far
normally means restarting the whole session; dropping the frame rewinds to the
method's entry instead. Side effects already performed are not undone, so it
suits pure computation better than I/O.

**The call stack is the most under-used panel.** Every frame has its own local
variables, and selecting a caller shows the state that produced the arguments
you are looking at.

