```text
   FRAMES                                VARIABLES (for the selected frame)
   > OrderService.validate(Order)  <--    order = Order{id=4711, total=null}
     OrderService.place(Order)            this  = OrderService@3f2a
     OrderController.submit(Request)      request = {"customer":"ada", ...}
     ... framework frames ...
       ^ click any frame to inspect the state at that level
```

The "evaluate expression" feature completes the picture: you can call methods,
construct objects, and test a fix hypothesis without changing code.

**Remote debugging** attaches to an already-running JVM through the Java Debug
Wire Protocol.

```bash
java -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:5005 -jar app.jar
#                          ^socket      ^JVM listens  ^do not wait  ^port
```

Setting `suspend=y` makes the JVM wait for a debugger before running a line,
which is how you debug something that fails during startup.

This is a serious security boundary. **A JDWP port is unauthenticated remote
code execution.** Never expose it publicly, never leave it enabled in
production, and bind it to localhost with an SSH tunnel if you must use it
against a remote host.

**Debugging concurrent code needs care**, because a breakpoint changes timing.
Suspending all threads at a breakpoint can hide the race you are hunting, and
suspending only one thread can let others race ahead into states that never
occur in production. Most IDEs let you choose the suspend policy per breakpoint,
and conditioning on a thread name is often the cleanest approach.

The general warning is the observer effect: a bug that disappears under a
debugger is usually a timing-dependent bug, and that disappearance is itself
diagnostic information.

**Hot swap** lets you edit a method body and continue without restarting. It
cannot add or remove methods or fields, since that would change the class shape,
but for tuning a condition or a calculation it removes the restart cycle
entirely.

**Finally, know when not to reach for the debugger.** If you can reproduce the
bug, writing a failing test is usually faster and leaves something permanent
behind. A debugger is for *understanding* unfamiliar behaviour; a test is for
*preventing* its return. The two are complements, and the best sequence is often
to debug until you understand, then write the test before fixing.

> Key Takeaways
> - A debugger inspects everything in scope, unlike prints that show only what
>   you anticipated.
> - Conditional breakpoints skip straight to the failing iteration.
> - Exception breakpoints catch exceptions that are being silently swallowed.
> - Field watchpoints reveal what assigned an unexpected value, and from where.
> - Logging breakpoints print without editing, rebuilding, or risking a commit.
> - Drop frame re-runs the current method, but does not undo side effects
>   already performed.
> - Every stack frame has its own variables, so selecting a caller shows how you
>   got here.
> - JDWP ports are unauthenticated remote code execution and must never be
>   exposed.
> - Breakpoints alter timing, so a bug that vanishes under a debugger is
>   probably a race.
> - Debug to understand, then write a failing test before fixing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Set a conditional breakpoint inside a loop over a thousand items so that it
>    triggers only on one specific element.
> 2. Add an exception breakpoint for `NumberFormatException` in code that
>    catches and ignores it, and find where it originates.
> 3. Use a field watchpoint to discover which method sets a field to `null`.
> 4. Attach a remote debugger to a locally running JVM started with JDWP, then
>    explain why `address=*:5005` would be dangerous on a public server.
> 5. Use "evaluate expression" to test a fix without editing code, then apply it
>    with hot swap and continue.
> 6. Interview: A bug reproduces reliably in production but never under the
>    debugger. What does that tell you? (Hint: what does suspending a thread do
>    to the interleaving of others?)

#### Logging Frameworks and Levels

A debugger requires that you be present while the code runs. Production code
runs at three in the morning, on a machine you cannot pause, for a user you
cannot ask. Logs are the only account of what happened, and they are written
before anyone knows which moment will matter.

**`System.out.println` is not logging.** It has no severity, no timestamp, no
source location, no thread name, no routing, and no way to turn off without
editing code. It cannot be sampled, filtered, or shipped anywhere, and it writes
synchronously to a stream that may be a slow pipe.

**Java's ecosystem separates the interface from the implementation**, which is
worth understanding because it explains the confusing number of logging
artifacts on a typical classpath.

```text
   your code and libraries
        |
        v
   SLF4J API          <- the FACADE you compile against
        |
        v
   a binding          <- chosen by the APPLICATION at deployment time
        |
   +----+----+-------------+
   v         v             v
   Logback   Log4j 2   java.util.logging
```

The reason for the split is that a library must not impose a logging backend on
the application embedding it. Libraries depend only on the facade; the
application picks the implementation. A project that pulls in three libraries
with three different loggers uses bridge artifacts to funnel them all into one.

**Levels express who should care**, and the most common mistake is choosing them
from the author's perspective rather than the reader's.

| Level   | Meaning                                                 | Volume in production |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `ERROR` | Something failed and needs human attention               | Rare; each one is a signal |
| `WARN`  | Unexpected but handled; may matter if it recurs          | Occasional            |
| `INFO`  | Significant lifecycle events: started, stopped, connected | Low and steady        |
| `DEBUG` | Diagnostic detail for investigating a problem            | Off by default        |
| `TRACE` | Very fine-grained flow, usually per-iteration            | Almost always off     |

The practical test for `ERROR` is whether a human should act on it. A handled,
expected condition such as a validation failure is not an error just because the
code took the unhappy path, and logging it as one trains people to ignore
errors.

**Parameterized logging is not a style preference.** String concatenation builds
the message whether or not the level is enabled.

```java
// BAD: the concatenation and every toString() run even when DEBUG is off
log.debug("Processing order " + order.getId() + " for " + customer.getName());

// GOOD: arguments are formatted only if DEBUG is actually enabled
log.debug("Processing order {} for {}", order.getId(), customer.getName());

// For a genuinely expensive argument, guard explicitly
if (log.isDebugEnabled()) {
    log.debug("state dump: {}", buildExpensiveDiagnosticReport());
}
```

In a hot loop, the first form costs allocations and string building on every
iteration for output nobody will ever see.

**Log exceptions by passing the throwable, never its message.**

```java
// BAD: discards the stack trace, which is the only useful part
log.error("Failed to place order " + id + ": " + e.getMessage());

// GOOD: the throwable goes LAST, with no placeholder, and the trace is printed
log.error("Failed to place order {}", id, e);
```

Equally, avoid log-and-throw. Logging an exception and then rethrowing it means
it gets logged again by whoever handles it, producing duplicate stack traces
that make an incident harder to read. Log where you handle, throw where you do
not.

**Context is what makes logs usable in a concurrent server.** With many requests
interleaving, as Chapter 12's servers do, individual lines are meaningless
without knowing which request they belong to. The Mapped Diagnostic Context
attaches key-value pairs to every log line from the current thread.

```java
try (MDC.MDCCloseable ignored = MDC.putCloseable("requestId", request.id())) {
    log.info("processing");        // every line inside now carries requestId
    service.handle(request);       // including lines from deep inside the call
}                                  // removed automatically, which matters on pooled threads
```

Forgetting to remove an MDC entry on a pooled thread leaks it into the next
request's logs, which is why the closeable form exists.

**Configuration lives outside the code**, so levels can change without a
rebuild.

```xml
<!-- logback.xml -->
<configuration>
    <appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
        <file>logs/app.log</file>
        <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.TimeBasedRollingPolicy">
            <fileNamePattern>logs/app.%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.log</fileNamePattern>
            <maxHistory>30</maxHistory>          <!-- bounded: disks fill up -->
        </rollingPolicy>
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{ISO8601} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} %X{requestId} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <logger name="com.example.app.pricing" level="DEBUG"/>   <!-- one package, verbose -->
    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="FILE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
```

For systems whose logs are collected centrally, emitting JSON rather than text
makes every field queryable instead of requiring fragile pattern matching.

**Two safety rules.** Never log secrets: passwords, tokens, keys, card numbers,
or personal data that regulation covers. Logs are copied, shipped, and retained
far more widely than the systems they describe. And treat logged values as
untrusted input, which is the lesson of the 2021 Log4Shell vulnerability, where
a logging library interpolated attacker-supplied text and executed a lookup
embedded in it, turning a log statement into remote code execution.

> Key Takeaways
> - Logs are the only account of a production system you cannot pause.
> - `System.out` has no levels, timestamps, context, routing, or off switch.
> - SLF4J is a facade so that libraries do not force a backend on applications.
> - Levels describe who should act, and `ERROR` should mean a human is needed.
> - Placeholder logging avoids building messages for disabled levels.
> - Pass the exception as the last argument, or you lose the stack trace.
> - Avoid log-and-throw, which duplicates traces during incidents.
> - MDC attaches request context to every line, and the closeable form prevents
>   leaks on pooled threads.
> - Configuration belongs outside the code so levels change without a rebuild.
> - Never log secrets, and treat logged values as attacker-controlled input.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace every `System.out.println` in a small project with SLF4J calls at
>    appropriate levels, then change the level in configuration without
>    recompiling.
> 2. Write a loop that logs at `DEBUG` with string concatenation and again with
>    placeholders, with `DEBUG` disabled, and measure the difference.
> 3. Log an exception both by concatenating `getMessage()` and by passing the
>    throwable. Compare the output.
> 4. Add an MDC request identifier in a multithreaded server and confirm that
>    interleaved lines can be grouped by request.
> 5. Configure a rolling file appender with a thirty-day history and verify the
>    rollover naming.
> 6. Interview: Why is `log.debug("x=" + x)` a problem when `DEBUG` is disabled?
>    (Hint: what has already happened before the logging method is even called?)

#### Static Analysis Tools

Tests tell you whether the code does what you checked. **Static analysis** tells
you whether the code contains patterns that are known to be wrong, without
running it at all. The two are complementary: tests find the bugs you thought
of, static analysis finds entire categories of defect across every line you
wrote, including the ones nobody tests.

The idea is that many bugs have a *shape*. An `equals` without a `hashCode`, a
result that is computed and discarded, a string compared with `==`: none of
these require understanding intent to flag, only pattern recognition.

```java
public class Money {
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { ... }
    // SpotBugs: HE_EQUALS_NO_HASHCODE - equals without hashCode breaks HashMap
}

String trimmed = name.trim();
name.trim();                       // RV_RETURN_VALUE_IGNORED: String is immutable,
                                   // this line does literally nothing

if (config.get("mode") == "fast")  // ES_COMPARING_STRINGS_WITH_EQ: reference comparison

Integer a = 1000, b = 1000;
if (a == b) { ... }                // compares references outside the cache range
```

Every one of those compiles cleanly and may pass tests that never exercise the
path.

**The tool landscape divides by what each looks for.**

| Tool                     | Analyses            | Finds                                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| SpotBugs                 | Compiled bytecode    | Bug patterns: null dereference, ignored results, bad `equals` |
| Error Prone              | During compilation   | Bug patterns, as compiler errors; Google's  |
| NullAway                 | During compilation   | Nullness contract violations                 |
| PMD                      | Source              | Dead code, complexity, questionable constructs |
| Checkstyle               | Source              | Naming, imports, formatting, required Javadoc |
| OWASP Dependency-Check   | The dependency graph | Dependencies with published vulnerabilities  |
| SonarQube                | Aggregates the above | Trends, quality gates, duplication, coverage |

Error Prone is distinctive because it runs as part of `javac` and can fail the
compilation, which means a whole class of mistakes never reaches a commit.

**Wire it into the build so it is not optional.**

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
    <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>4.8.3.1</version>
    <configuration>
        <effort>Max</effort>
        <threshold>Medium</threshold>          <!-- below this, do not report -->
        <failOnError>true</failOnError>        <!-- break the build on findings -->
    </configuration>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <phase>verify</phase>              <!-- runs during mvn verify -->
            <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

**Adoption strategy matters more than tool choice.** Enabling every rule on an
existing codebase produces thousands of findings, which everyone learns to
ignore, and the build gets a permanent exemption. The approach that works is a
**ratchet**: record the current findings as a baseline, fail the build only on
*new* ones, and reduce the baseline opportunistically.

```text
   Day 1:   4,312 existing findings recorded as the baseline
            build fails only if the count RISES
   Ongoing: every new commit must be clean
            the baseline shrinks as people touch old code
```

This gets you the benefit immediately without a months-long cleanup nobody has
budget for.

**False positives are real and must be handled honestly.** A finding that is
genuinely wrong should be suppressed narrowly, at the smallest scope, with a
comment saying why.

```java
@SuppressWarnings("PMD.AvoidCatchingGenericException")   // narrow, named rule
// The handler boundary must not let any exception reach the accept loop (14.2).
catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("handler failed", e);
}
```

A blanket `@SuppressWarnings("all")` on a class is how a tool stops being
useful.

**Know the limits.** Static analysis cannot determine intent, cannot find logic
errors where the code correctly does the wrong thing, and cannot tell you that a
requirement was misunderstood. It catches mechanical mistakes cheaply and
reliably, which is valuable precisely because it frees human review to focus on
design and correctness.

> Key Takeaways
> - Static analysis finds defects by pattern, without executing the code.
> - It complements tests by covering paths no test exercises.
> - SpotBugs analyses bytecode, Error Prone runs inside the compiler, PMD and
>   Checkstyle read source.
> - Error Prone can fail compilation, stopping known mistakes before commit.
> - Dependency scanners find published vulnerabilities in code you never wrote.
> - Wire analysis into the build so findings are not optional.
> - Enabling everything on a legacy codebase produces noise that gets ignored.
> - A baseline ratchet fails only on new findings and shrinks over time.
> - Suppress false positives narrowly, by rule name, with a written reason.
> - No tool infers intent, so logic errors and misunderstood requirements remain
>   human work.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add SpotBugs to a project, run it, and categorise the first ten findings as
>    genuine, stylistic, or false.
> 2. Write a class with `equals` but no `hashCode`, confirm the tool flags it,
>    and demonstrate the actual bug with a `HashSet`.
> 3. Configure the build to fail on findings above a threshold, then commit a
>    deliberate violation and observe the failure.
> 4. Suppress one finding narrowly with a justification comment, and explain why
>    a class-level suppression would be worse.
> 5. Interview: You inherit a codebase with four thousand static analysis
>    findings. How do you make the tool useful without a cleanup project?
>    (Hint: what has to be true of tomorrow's commits, rather than yesterday's?)

#### Code Style and Formatting Standards

Formatting does not change what a program does, which is exactly why teams argue
about it. The argument is worth ending quickly, and the reason is not
aesthetics.

**Consistent formatting reduces the effort of reading.** Code is read far more
often than written, and every deviation from an expected shape costs the reader
a fraction of a second of reorientation. More concretely, inconsistent
formatting destroys version control history: a commit that reformats a file
while changing one line shows as a hundred changed lines, so `git blame` stops
telling you who changed what and why.

```text
   WITHOUT a shared format          WITH a shared format
   diff shows 120 changed lines     diff shows 2 changed lines
   review focuses on whitespace     review focuses on the change
   blame points at the reformatter  blame points at the author
```

**The established conventions** are a starting point rather than something to
invent.

| Convention                | Origin                | Notable choices                       |
| ------------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Oracle Code Conventions    | The original, 1997    | 4-space indent, 80 columns             |
| Google Java Style          | Widely adopted today  | 2-space indent, 100 columns, explicit rules for everything |
| Spring / project-specific  | Framework ecosystems  | Tabs, 120 columns, varies              |

Chapter 1.2 already covered the naming rules these share, and they are worth
restating because they are the part a formatter cannot fix for you.

| Element              | Convention          | Example                  |
| -------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Class, interface, enum | `UpperCamelCase`  | `OrderService`           |
| Method, variable      | `lowerCamelCase`   | `placeOrder`, `totalDue` |
| Constant              | `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` | `MAX_RETRIES`            |
| Package               | `lowercase.dotted` | `com.example.billing`    |
| Type parameter        | Single capital     | `T`, `K`, `V`, `R`       |

**The decisive move is to automate it entirely.** A formatter that runs as part
of the build turns style from an opinion into a fact, and nobody reviews
whitespace again.

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>com.diffplug.spotless</groupId>
    <artifactId>spotless-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>2.43.0</version>
    <configuration>
        <java>
            <googleJavaFormat/>          <!-- one canonical format, no options to argue about -->
            <removeUnusedImports/>
            <importOrder/>
            <trimTrailingWhitespace/>
            <endWithNewline/>
        </java>
    </configuration>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>   <!-- fails the build if unformatted -->
            <phase>verify</phase>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

```bash
mvn spotless:apply     # reformat everything
mvn spotless:check     # verify, used in CI
```

`google-java-format` deliberately offers almost no configuration, which is its
main virtue: a format with no options has nothing to debate.

**Three supporting pieces** make this stick across a team.

*An `.editorconfig` file* gives every editor the basics, including for
non-Java files, without anyone configuring their IDE.

```ini
root = true

[*]
charset = utf-8
end_of_line = lf
insert_final_newline = true
trim_trailing_whitespace = true

[*.java]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
max_line_length = 100
```

*A pre-commit hook* formats before code ever leaves a machine, so CI never has
to reject a commit for whitespace.

*A one-off formatting commit*, recorded in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`, lets you
reformat an entire legacy codebase once while keeping `git blame` useful.

```bash
git blame --ignore-revs-file .git-blame-ignore-revs OrderService.java
```

**Line length deserves one honest note.** The 80-column limit originates in
physical terminals, and modern arguments for it are about side-by-side diffs and
the readability of long lines rather than hardware. Between 100 and 120 is the
common modern compromise. The specific number matters far less than everyone
using the same one.

**What automation cannot do** is the part that actually affects readability:
choosing names that say what something is, keeping methods short enough to hold
in mind, and ordering members so a reader meets them in a sensible sequence. A
perfectly formatted method named `doStuff` is still unreadable.

> Key Takeaways
> - Consistent formatting reduces reading effort and keeps diffs and blame
>   meaningful.
> - Reformatting while editing hides a real change inside noise.
> - Google Java Style and the Oracle conventions are the two common baselines.
> - Naming conventions are the part of style a formatter cannot fix for you.
> - Automating the format with Spotless turns style from opinion into build
>   output.
> - A formatter with no options, such as google-java-format, removes the debate
>   entirely.
> - `.editorconfig` gives every editor the basics with no per-developer setup.
> - Record a bulk reformat in `.git-blame-ignore-revs` to preserve history.
> - Line length choice matters much less than consistency.
> - Naming, method length, and member order remain human judgement.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add Spotless to a project, run `apply`, and inspect the resulting diff.
> 2. Configure the build to fail on unformatted code, commit a badly formatted
>    file, and observe the failure.
> 3. Write an `.editorconfig` and verify your editor respects it by typing in a
>    file with different settings.
> 4. Reformat a file, commit it, and compare `git blame` output with and without
>    an ignore-revs file.
> 5. Interview: Beyond preference, what concrete engineering problem does
>    inconsistent formatting cause? (Hint: what does a reviewer see when one
>    logical change touches a reformatted file?)

#### Profiling and Performance Measurement

The single most reliable fact about performance work is that **developers guess
wrong about where time goes**. Optimising the wrong thing is worse than doing
nothing, because it costs effort, adds complexity, and leaves the real
bottleneck untouched. The discipline is simple to state: measure, change,
measure again.

Chapter 12's discussion of Amdahl's law explains why this matters
mathematically. Making a function twice as fast yields nothing measurable if it
accounts for two percent of the runtime.

**Two kinds of profiler exist**, and the difference determines what you can
trust.

| Type            | How it works                                | Overhead | Accuracy                      |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------- | ----------------------------- |
| Sampling        | Periodically records every thread's stack    | Low, a few percent | Statistical; misses very short calls |
| Instrumenting   | Injects counters into every method entry and exit | High, can be 10x | Exact counts; distorts what it measures |

The distortion of an instrumenting profiler is not a minor caveat. Adding
overhead to every method call penalises code with many small calls, so the
profiler can report a bottleneck that only exists because it is measuring. For
finding where wall-clock time goes, sampling is almost always the right choice.

**The JDK ships the tool you should start with.** Java Flight Recorder is a
sampling profiler built into the JVM with roughly one percent overhead, designed
to be safe to leave enabled in production.

```bash
# Record 60 seconds from a running application
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar

# Or attach to an already-running process
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=app.jfr
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump filename=snapshot.jfr
```

The recording opens in JDK Mission Control, which shows processor time by
method, allocation by type, garbage collection pauses, lock contention, and I/O
waits in one place.

**Flame graphs** are the most useful visualisation of a sampled profile, and
`async-profiler` is the common way to produce them.

```text
   width = share of samples, so wider means more time spent

   |---------------------------- main ----------------------------|
   |------- handleRequest -------|-------- writeResponse ---------|
   |-- parse --|---- price ------|                                |
               |-- lookupTax ----|          <- 40% of total time, and it is
               |                 |             a database call in a loop
```

Reading one is mechanical: find the widest block that is not simply a caller of
one child, and that is where the time is.

**Memory problems need different tools.** A steadily growing heap that
eventually throws `OutOfMemoryError` is a leak in the Java sense: objects still
reachable that should not be, as Chapter 11 described.

```bash
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heap.hprof -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info          # quick summary
jmap -histo:live <pid> | head    # what is on the heap right now, by count
```

A heap dump opened in Eclipse MAT gives the decisive answer through its
dominator tree and "path to GC root", which shows exactly what is still holding
a reference to the objects you expected to be collected.

**Microbenchmarks in plain Java are almost always wrong.** This is worth
demonstrating, because the naive approach is so tempting.

```java
// WRONG in at least four distinct ways
long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
    result = compute(i);
}
System.out.println(System.currentTimeMillis() - start);
```

The problems: the JIT compiler has not warmed up, so the first iterations run
interpreted; the JIT may eliminate the loop entirely once it proves the result
is unused; `currentTimeMillis` has coarse resolution; and a garbage collection
during the measurement window silently inflates the result.

The Java Microbenchmark Harness exists because getting this right requires
defeating the compiler deliberately.

```java
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5)                       // let the JIT compile and stabilise
@Measurement(iterations = 10)
@Fork(2)                                      // fresh JVMs, to expose run-to-run variance
public class StringConcatBenchmark {

    @Param({"10", "1000"})                    // run the whole benchmark per value
    private int size;

    @Benchmark
    public String stringBuilder() {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) sb.append(i);
        return sb.toString();                 // RETURNED, so it cannot be optimised away
    }

    @Benchmark
    public void concatenation(Blackhole hole) {
        String s = "";
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) s += i;
        hole.consume(s);                      // Blackhole defeats dead-code elimination
    }
}
```

**Measure the right statistic.** Averages hide exactly the behaviour users
notice.

```text
   Endpoint latency over 10,000 requests
   mean      42 ms      <- looks fine
   p50       28 ms
   p95      110 ms
   p99      850 ms      <- one request in a hundred is terrible
   max    4,200 ms      <- and someone waited four seconds
```

If a page makes twenty such calls, nearly every page load hits the p99 at least
once. Tail latency is the user experience; report percentiles, not averages.

**A workable order of operations**, before reaching for any micro-optimisation.

| Step | Question                                            |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Is there a measured problem, with a target number?   |
| 2    | Where does the time actually go, per a profile?      |
| 3    | Is it algorithmic? An O(n²) loop beats any constant-factor tuning |
| 4    | Is it I/O? Queries in a loop, missing indexes, no batching, no caching |
| 5    | Is it allocation or garbage collection pressure?     |
| 6    | Only now, consider low-level tuning                  |

In practice, most real Java performance problems are found at steps 3 and 4, and
the fix is a better query or one fewer round trip rather than anything about the
language.

> Key Takeaways
> - Developers reliably guess wrong about bottlenecks, so always measure first.
> - Sampling profilers have low overhead and reflect reality; instrumenting ones
>   distort what they measure.
> - Java Flight Recorder ships with the JDK and is safe to run in production.
> - Flame graph width is share of time, so the widest non-pass-through block is
>   the target.
> - Heap dumps plus a dominator tree identify what is still referencing leaked
>   objects.
> - Naive timing loops are invalidated by JIT warmup, dead-code elimination,
>   clock resolution, and garbage collection.
> - JMH handles warmup, forking, and `Blackhole` consumption so results mean
>   something.
> - Report percentiles rather than averages, because tail latency is what users
>   experience.
> - Algorithmic and I/O problems dominate real Java performance work.
> - Optimise only against a measured target, then measure again afterwards.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Record a Flight Recorder session of a program doing real work and identify
>    the three methods consuming the most processor time.
> 2. Write the naive timing loop above for string concatenation, then rewrite it
>    with JMH. Explain the difference in the results.
> 3. Write a program that leaks by adding to a static collection, capture a heap
>    dump on `OutOfMemoryError`, and find the retaining reference.
> 4. Compute p50, p95, and p99 for a set of recorded latencies and explain what
>    the mean alone would have hidden.
> 5. Find a method calling a repository inside a loop, fix it with a batch
>    query, and measure before and after.
> 6. Interview: Why can a microbenchmark report that an empty method takes zero
>    nanoseconds? (Hint: what is the JIT allowed to do with code whose result
>    nobody uses?)

#### Effective Javadoc Documentation

Chapter 1.2 covered Javadoc's syntax: the comment form, the block tags, and how
the tool generates HTML. This topic is about the harder question of **what to
write**, because a correctly formatted comment that restates the method
signature is worse than no comment, since it must still be maintained.

The guiding principle is that **Javadoc documents a contract, not an
implementation**. A caller reads it to learn what they may rely on and what is
required of them. Anything that describes how the method currently works is a
promise you did not mean to make and will break on the next refactor.

```java
// USELESS: restates the signature, and the reader learns nothing
/**
 * Gets the balance.
 * @return the balance
 */
public long getBalance() { ... }

// USEFUL: states units, guarantees, and what the caller must know
/**
 * Returns the currently available balance in minor units of the account's
 * currency, excluding funds reserved by pending authorisations.
 *
 * @return the available balance; may be negative for overdraft accounts
 */
public long getBalance() { ... }
```

**A contract has four parts**, and a good comment covers whichever apply.

| Part            | Question it answers                        | Where it goes            |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------ |
| Purpose         | What does this accomplish, in the caller's terms | The summary sentence |
| Preconditions   | What must be true before calling            | `@param`, and `@throws` for violations |
| Postconditions  | What is guaranteed afterwards               | `@return` and the body   |
| Failure modes   | What can go wrong and how it is signalled   | `@throws`                |

**Four properties are invisible in a signature and belong in the
documentation**, because a caller has no other way to learn them.

*Nullability.* Whether a parameter may be null, and whether the return value
ever is. This is the most common source of production `NullPointerException`
between two correct components.

*Thread safety.* Whether an instance may be shared across threads, as Chapter 12
discussed. The absence of a statement is generally read as "not safe", so say so
explicitly when it is.

*Mutability and ownership.* Whether a returned collection is a live view or a
copy, and whether the callee retains a reference to a passed array.

*Units and ranges.* Milliseconds or seconds, minor units or major, inclusive or
exclusive bounds.

```java
/**
 * Transfers funds between two accounts atomically.
 *
 * <p>Either both balances change or neither does. The accounts are locked in a
 * fixed global order, so concurrent transfers between the same pair cannot
 * deadlock.
 *
 * <p>This method is thread-safe and may be called concurrently.
 *
 * @param from   the account to debit; must not be {@code null} and must be open
 * @param to     the account to credit; must not be {@code null}, must be open,
 *               and must use the same currency as {@code from}
 * @param amount the amount to move in minor units; must be positive
 * @return an immutable record of the completed transfer, never {@code null}
 * @throws InsufficientFundsException if {@code from} cannot cover {@code amount}
 * @throws CurrencyMismatchException  if the accounts use different currencies
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException   if {@code amount} is zero or negative
 * @since 2.1
 */
public Transfer transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) { ... }
```

Everything there is a commitment to the caller. None of it describes how the
transfer is implemented, so the body can be rewritten freely.

**What not to document.** Trivial accessors whose name says everything, private
implementation details that no caller can reach, and anything the code already
states unambiguously. Comments have a maintenance cost and rot silently, and a
comment contradicting the code is actively harmful because readers believe it.

**Writing documentation is a design tool.** If the contract is hard to state
without conditionals, that is evidence the method does too much.

```text
   "Returns the user, or null if not found, unless includeDeleted is true,
    in which case it returns the deleted user, except when the caller lacks
    permission, when it returns null anyway."

   The comment is not the problem. That is three methods.
```

Documentation difficulty is a design smell in the same way testing difficulty
is, and for the same underlying reason.

**Mechanics worth remembering.** The first sentence becomes the summary in the
generated index, so write it as a complete standalone statement ending in a
period. Use `{@code}` for anything that is literal code, since it escapes angle
brackets that would otherwise be interpreted as HTML. Use `{@link}` for
references a reader will want to follow. `@inheritDoc` pulls an overridden
method's documentation in rather than duplicating it. And `@deprecated` must
always say what to use instead, paired with the `@Deprecated` annotation so that
both the compiler and the reader are informed.

```java
/**
 * @deprecated Use {@link #transfer(Account, Account, Money)} instead, which
 *             makes the currency explicit. This method will be removed in 3.0.
 */
@Deprecated(since = "2.4", forRemoval = true)     // the annotation warns the compiler
public Transfer transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) { ... }
```

Generating and checking the output should be part of the build, since malformed
Javadoc fails the `javadoc` tool and broken links silently degrade the published
documentation.

```bash
mvn javadoc:javadoc              # generate into target/site/apidocs
javadoc -Xdoclint:all -d docs src/main/java/com/example/**/*.java
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Javadoc documents a contract for callers, not the current implementation.
> - A comment restating the signature adds maintenance cost and no information.
> - Cover purpose, preconditions, postconditions, and failure modes.
> - Nullability, thread safety, mutability, and units are invisible in a
>   signature and must be stated.
> - A returned collection should say whether it is a live view or a copy.
> - Skip documentation for trivial accessors and unreachable internals.
> - A contract that needs many conditionals to state is a method doing too much.
> - The first sentence is the generated summary and must stand alone.
> - `{@code}` escapes literal code and `{@inheritDoc}` avoids duplicating
>   overridden documentation.
> - `@deprecated` must name the replacement, alongside the `@Deprecated`
>   annotation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take three public methods you have written and document each contract,
>    stating nullability and thread safety explicitly.
> 2. Find a Javadoc comment that describes implementation rather than contract,
>    and rewrite it so an internal refactor would not invalidate it.
> 3. Document a method returning a collection, stating clearly whether callers
>    may modify it, then verify the code matches the claim.
> 4. Run `javadoc` with `-Xdoclint:all` on a package and fix every warning.
> 5. Deprecate a method properly with both the annotation and the tag, then
>    confirm the compiler warns at a call site.
> 6. Interview: A method's documentation needs four "unless" clauses to describe
>    what it returns. What does that suggest? (Hint: what is the comment
>    struggling to describe, and how many behaviours does the method have?)

<a id="16-database-connectivity-with-jdbc"></a>
## 16. Database Connectivity with JDBC

Almost every non-trivial application outlives the process that created its data,
which means the data lives in a database rather than in the heap. This chapter
covers JDBC, the standard Java API for talking to relational databases, from
opening a connection and reading a result set through to transactions, and ends
with the object-relational mapping tools built on top of it. The material here
is where correctness bugs become expensive, because a mistake in a transaction
boundary or a string-concatenated query corrupts or leaks real data.

<a id="161-jdbc-fundamentals"></a>
### 16.1 JDBC Fundamentals

This subchapter covers the shape of the JDBC API: how a driver is found and
loaded, how a connection is opened, how statements produce result sets, how SQL
types map onto Java types, and how the resources involved are reliably released.

#### JDBC Architecture and Driver Types

Relational databases are separate processes, usually on separate machines. They
speak their own wire protocols: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server each
have a different one, and none of them is Java. Without a standard, every
application would be written against one vendor's client library, and switching
databases would mean rewriting every line of data access code.

JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) solves this the same way the `List` interface
solves the problem of having many list implementations. It defines a set of
**interfaces** in `java.sql`, and each vendor ships a **driver**: a JAR
containing classes that implement those interfaces by speaking that vendor's
protocol. Your code is written against `Connection`, `Statement`, and
`ResultSet`; the objects you actually hold at runtime are
`org.postgresql.jdbc.PgConnection` or similar, and you never name that class.

The analogy is a power socket. Appliances are built against the socket's shape,
not against a particular power station. The plug adapter is the driver.

```text
  Your application code
  +-----------------------------------------------+
  |  Connection  Statement  ResultSet  (interfaces)|   java.sql
  +-----------------------------------------------+
                      |  implemented by
                      v
  +-----------------------------------------------+
  |  DriverManager / DataSource  (finds a driver)  |
  +-----------------------------------------------+
        |                 |                  |
        v                 v                  v
  +-----------+     +-----------+      +-----------+
  | Postgres  |     |  MySQL    |      |  Oracle   |     vendor drivers
  |  driver   |     |  driver   |      |  driver   |
  +-----------+     +-----------+      +-----------+
        |                 |                  |
        v                 v                  v
   wire protocol      wire protocol      wire protocol
        |                 |                  |
  +-----------+     +-----------+      +-----------+
  | Postgres  |     |  MySQL    |      |  Oracle   |     database servers
  +-----------+     +-----------+      +-----------+
```

Historically JDBC defined four driver types. Only one of them matters today, but
the numbering still appears in interview questions and old documentation.

| Type | Name                    | How it works                                              | Status                     |
| ---- | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| 1    | JDBC-ODBC bridge        | Translates JDBC calls into ODBC calls on the local machine | Removed in Java 8          |
| 2    | Native-API              | Java wrapper over a vendor's native C client library       | Obsolete; needs native code |
| 3    | Network protocol        | Talks to a middleware server that talks to the database    | Rare; adds a hop           |
| 4    | Thin / pure Java        | Implements the vendor wire protocol directly in Java       | The only one in use        |

A **type 4 driver** is a plain JAR with no native dependencies. It works on any
platform the JVM runs on, and it is what every current database ships. When you
add `org.postgresql:postgresql` to a build file, you are adding a type 4 driver.

One more distinction is worth fixing early, because the names are confusing.
JDBC is **the API**. A driver is **an implementation** of it. `DriverManager`
and `DataSource` are two different ways of **obtaining** a `Connection` from a
driver, and 16.2 explains why `DataSource` is the one you should use in real
applications.

> Key Takeaways
> - JDBC is a set of interfaces in `java.sql`; vendors supply implementations
>   called drivers.
> - Your code names only the interfaces, which is what makes database code
>   portable.
> - Four driver types were defined historically; only type 4, pure-Java thin
>   drivers, remain relevant.
> - A type 4 driver is an ordinary JAR dependency with no native components.
> - Portability is at the API level, not the SQL level: dialects still differ.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find the JDBC driver dependency for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite, and note
>    the group and artifact identifier of each.
> 2. Open a driver JAR with `jar tf` and locate a class that implements
>    `java.sql.Connection`. Confirm your own code never needs to name it.
> 3. Explain why a type 2 driver makes a build non-portable across operating
>    systems, while a type 4 driver does not.
> 4. Interview: If JDBC makes database code portable, why does switching from
>    MySQL to PostgreSQL still usually break an application? (Hint: the API is
>    standardised, but what travels through it as a string is not.)

#### Connection URLs and Driver Loading

Before a driver can be used, two things must happen: the driver class must be
loaded into the JVM, and the application must state which database it wants.
Both are handled through a single string, the **JDBC URL**.

A JDBC URL always has three parts.

```text
   jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/orders?ssl=true&connectTimeout=5
   ^--^ ^--------^   ^---------------------^ ^-------------------------^
    |       |                  |                        |
  scheme  subprotocol     database-specific        driver properties
          (which driver)   location and name       (vendor-defined)
```

The scheme is always `jdbc`. The subprotocol selects the driver. Everything
after that is defined by the vendor, which is why the URLs look so different.

| Database   | Example URL                                              |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| PostgreSQL | `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shopdb`                 |
| MySQL      | `jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shopdb?serverTimezone=UTC`   |
| Oracle     | `jdbc:oracle:thin:@//localhost:1521/ORCLPDB1`             |
| SQL Server | `jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=shopdb`     |
| H2, memory | `jdbc:h2:mem:testdb`                                      |
| SQLite     | `jdbc:sqlite:/var/data/app.db`                            |

**Driver loading used to be manual.** Code written before Java 6 begins with a
line whose purpose is easy to misread.

```java
// LEGACY: forces the class to load, which runs its static initialiser.
// That initialiser calls DriverManager.registerDriver(new Driver()).
// The returned Class object is deliberately discarded.
Class.forName("org.postgresql.Driver");
```

Since JDBC 4.0 this is unnecessary. `DriverManager` uses the **service loader**
mechanism: every driver JAR contains a file at
`META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver` naming its driver class, and `DriverManager`
reads those files from the classpath and registers what it finds. Writing
`Class.forName` today is harmless but marks the code as dated.

```java
// MODERN: no explicit loading. The driver on the classpath registers itself.
String url  = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shopdb";
String user = "app";
String pass = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD");   // never hard-code credentials

try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass)) {
    System.out.println(conn.getCatalog());
}
```

`DriverManager` chooses a driver by asking each registered driver whether it
accepts the URL, in registration order, and using the first that says yes. If
none accepts it, you get `No suitable driver found for ...`, which almost always
means the driver JAR is missing from the runtime classpath rather than that the
URL is malformed.

**Credentials do not belong in the URL or in source code.** Embedding a password
in a string literal puts it in version control, in build artifacts, and in any
stack trace that prints the URL. Read them from environment variables, a secrets
manager, or configuration outside the repository.

> Key Takeaways
> - A JDBC URL has the form `jdbc:<subprotocol>:<vendor-specific part>`.
> - The subprotocol is what selects the driver; the remainder is vendor-defined.
> - Since JDBC 4.0 drivers self-register through `META-INF/services`, so
>   `Class.forName` is obsolete.
> - `No suitable driver found` normally means a missing classpath entry, not a
>   bad URL.
> - Keep passwords out of URLs and source; read them from the environment or a
>   secret store.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the JDBC URL for a PostgreSQL database named `inventory` on host
>    `10.0.0.5`, port `6432`, with SSL required.
> 2. Extract `META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver` from a driver JAR and read its
>    contents. Explain how `DriverManager` uses it.
> 3. Run a program with the driver JAR removed from the classpath and record the
>    exact exception message, so you recognise it later.
> 4. Interview: A colleague insists `Class.forName` is still required or the
>    driver will not load. How would you check who is right? (Hint: what does
>    `DriverManager.drivers()` report before any connection is opened?)

#### Opening Connections with DriverManager

A `Connection` represents a single, stateful session with the database. It
carries the authenticated user, the current transaction, the auto-commit flag,
the isolation level, and the schema in use. Every other JDBC object, statements
and result sets alike, is created from a connection and dies with it.

The important thing to internalise is that **a connection is expensive**.
Opening one involves a TCP handshake, often a TLS handshake, authentication, and
server-side session setup. On a typical network that is tens of milliseconds,
which is longer than most of the queries you will run through it.

```text
  Opening a connection                  Running a simple query
  ------------------------------        -----------------------
  TCP handshake        ~1 ms            send SQL         ~0.2 ms
  TLS handshake       ~10 ms            server executes  ~0.5 ms
  authentication       ~5 ms            read rows        ~0.3 ms
  session setup        ~2 ms            ------------------------
  ------------------------------        total           ~1 ms
  total              ~18 ms
```

That ratio, roughly twenty to one, is the entire justification for connection
pooling, which 16.2 covers. Until then, treat `DriverManager.getConnection` as a
teaching tool and as the right choice for scripts and tests.

There are three overloads, and the two-argument form reads the credentials from
a `Properties` object, which is useful when the driver needs extra settings.

```java
// 1. URL only: credentials embedded in the URL or not required (e.g. H2 mem).
Connection a = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:h2:mem:testdb");

// 2. URL with user and password as separate arguments. The common form.
Connection b = DriverManager.getConnection(url, "app", password);

// 3. URL with a Properties bag: credentials plus driver-specific settings.
Properties props = new Properties();
props.setProperty("user", "app");
props.setProperty("password", password);
props.setProperty("ApplicationName", "order-service");  // shows up in pg_stat_activity
props.setProperty("connectTimeout", "5");               // seconds, driver-specific
Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(url, props);
```

**A connection must be closed.** An unclosed connection holds a socket and a
server-side session until a timeout fires, and databases enforce a hard limit on
concurrent connections. Leak them in a loop and the application stops being able
to reach the database at all, usually reported as
`FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`. The `try`-with-resources form covered
later in this subchapter is the only reliable way to avoid this.

Connections are also **not thread-safe**. A connection carries one transaction,
so sharing it across threads means two units of work committing each other's
changes. One thread, one connection, for the duration of one unit of work.

A useful sanity check after connecting is to interrogate the metadata, which
tells you what you are actually talking to.

```java
try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass)) {
    DatabaseMetaData meta = conn.getMetaData();
    System.out.printf("%s %s via driver %s%n",
            meta.getDatabaseProductName(),        // e.g. "PostgreSQL"
            meta.getDatabaseProductVersion(),     // e.g. "16.2"
            meta.getDriverVersion());
    System.out.println("valid: " + conn.isValid(2));   // round-trip, 2s timeout
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A `Connection` is one authenticated, stateful session and owns one
>   transaction at a time.
> - Opening one costs tens of milliseconds, far more than a typical query.
> - Every statement and result set is created from a connection and is invalid
>   once it closes.
> - Connections must always be closed, or the server's client limit is
>   exhausted.
> - Connections are not thread-safe; never share one between threads.
> - `DatabaseMetaData` and `isValid` are the quickest way to confirm what you
>   connected to.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Connect to an in-memory H2 database, print its product name and version,
>    and close the connection using `try`-with-resources.
> 2. Write a loop that opens 200 connections without closing them against a
>    local database and record the exact failure. Then fix it.
> 3. Measure the time to open a connection versus the time to run
>    `SELECT 1`, averaged over 50 iterations, and compare the two numbers.
> 4. Interview: Why is it wrong to store a `Connection` in a static field shared
>    by a web application's request threads? (Hint: name two pieces of state a
>    connection carries that belong to one unit of work.)

#### Statement Execution and ResultSet Traversal

With a connection in hand, work is done by creating a **statement**, executing
SQL through it, and reading whatever comes back. JDBC splits execution into
three methods because SQL statements come in two shapes: those that return rows
and those that return a count.

| Method            | Use for                              | Returns                          |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| `executeQuery`    | `SELECT`                             | a `ResultSet`                    |
| `executeUpdate`   | `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, DDL    | `int` rows affected (0 for DDL)  |
| `execute`         | Statements whose kind is not known   | `boolean`: true if rows follow   |

A `ResultSet` is **not** a collection. It is a **cursor**: a pointer that starts
just before the first row and is advanced by `next()`, which returns `false`
when there are no more rows. Rows are typically streamed from the server as you
read them, which is what makes it possible to process a million-row result
without a million-row list in memory.

```text
              +--------+--------+-----------+
   cursor --> |  (before first row)          |   next() -> true
              +--------+--------+-----------+
              |   1    | Ada    | 1815-12-10|   <-- cursor after first next()
              +--------+--------+-----------+
              |   2    | Alan   | 1912-06-23|
              +--------+--------+-----------+
              |   3    | Grace  | 1906-12-09|
              +--------+--------+-----------+
              |  (after last row)            |   next() -> false
              +------------------------------+
```

The canonical read loop is therefore a `while` over `next()`.

```java
String sql = "SELECT id, name, born FROM people ORDER BY name";

try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
     Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
     ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql)) {

    while (rs.next()) {                       // advance; false ends the loop
        long id      = rs.getLong("id");      // read by column label
        String name  = rs.getString("name");
        LocalDate born = rs.getObject("born", LocalDate.class);
        System.out.printf("%d %s %s%n", id, name, born);
    }
}   // rs, stmt and conn closed in reverse order
```

**Columns can be addressed by index or by label.** Indexes are **1-based**, not
0-based, which is the single most common beginner error in JDBC.

```java
String name = rs.getString(2);        // second column, 1-based
String same = rs.getString("name");   // clearer, survives column reordering
```

Prefer labels. Index access breaks silently the moment someone changes the
`SELECT` list, whereas a wrong label throws. The counter-argument is
performance, and it is negligible in almost every application.

**Read each column once, in order, if you care about the last drop of
performance**, because some drivers stream column data and do not buffer it.
This matters for large `CLOB` and `BLOB` columns and almost nowhere else.

For a single-row query, the loop collapses to an `if`, and it is worth being
explicit about the empty case rather than leaving a variable at its default.

```java
try (ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT count(*) FROM people")) {
    if (!rs.next()) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("count(*) returned no row");
    }
    long total = rs.getLong(1);
}
```

Result sets have a **type** and a **concurrency** setting that control whether
the cursor can move backwards and whether rows can be updated through it.

```java
Statement stmt = conn.createStatement(
        ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,   // allows previous(), absolute(), last()
        ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY);         // no updateXxx() through the cursor
```

Scrollable and updatable result sets exist, but they are rarely the right tool:
they force the driver to buffer, and an explicit `UPDATE` is clearer than
mutating a cursor. The default, `TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY` and `CONCUR_READ_ONLY`, is
the one to use unless you have a specific reason not to.

One practical control worth knowing is the **fetch size**, the number of rows
the driver pulls per round trip. The default is driver-specific and sometimes
means "all of them", which turns a large query into an out-of-memory error.

```java
stmt.setFetchSize(500);   // pull 500 rows per round trip instead of everything
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `executeQuery` returns rows, `executeUpdate` returns a count, `execute`
>   handles the unknown case.
> - A `ResultSet` is a forward-moving cursor, not an in-memory collection.
> - `next()` both advances the cursor and reports whether a row is present.
> - Column indexes start at 1; labels are safer and should be the default.
> - The default result set is forward-only and read-only, which is what you
>   normally want.
> - `setFetchSize` bounds how many rows are buffered per round trip on large
>   queries.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a `people` table, insert three rows with `executeUpdate`, and print
>    the returned counts.
> 2. Write a query loop that reads columns by label, then change the order of
>    the `SELECT` list and confirm the code still works. Repeat with indexes.
> 3. Write a method `long countRows(Connection, String table)` that returns the
>    row count, throwing if the query yields no row.
> 4. Load 100,000 rows with the default fetch size and with `setFetchSize(1000)`
>    while watching heap usage, and describe the difference.
> 5. Interview: Why does `rs.getString("name")` throw after the statement that
>    created the result set is closed? (Hint: what does the result set actually
>    hold, and where do the remaining rows live?)

#### Mapping SQL Types to Java Types

SQL and Java have separate type systems that were designed decades apart, and
they do not line up. SQL has `NUMERIC(12,2)`, `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`, and a
first-class `NULL` that applies to every column. Java has `int`, `BigDecimal`,
`OffsetDateTime`, and a `null` that only applies to references. JDBC's job is to
bridge the two, and most of the bugs in this area come from taking the bridge
for granted.

The mappings that matter in practice:

| SQL type                   | Best Java type          | Getter                              |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `INTEGER`, `INT`           | `int` / `Integer`       | `getInt`                            |
| `BIGINT`                   | `long` / `Long`         | `getLong`                           |
| `NUMERIC`, `DECIMAL`       | `BigDecimal`            | `getBigDecimal`                     |
| `REAL`, `DOUBLE PRECISION` | `double`                | `getDouble`                         |
| `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`          | `String`                | `getString`                         |
| `BOOLEAN`                  | `boolean` / `Boolean`   | `getBoolean`                        |
| `DATE`                     | `LocalDate`             | `getObject(col, LocalDate.class)`   |
| `TIME`                     | `LocalTime`             | `getObject(col, LocalTime.class)`   |
| `TIMESTAMP`                | `LocalDateTime`         | `getObject(col, LocalDateTime.class)` |
| `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | `OffsetDateTime`        | `getObject(col, OffsetDateTime.class)` |
| `UUID`                     | `java.util.UUID`        | `getObject(col, UUID.class)`        |
| `BLOB`, `BYTEA`            | `byte[]` or `InputStream` | `getBytes` / `getBinaryStream`    |
| `ARRAY`                    | `java.sql.Array`        | `getArray`                          |

**Money is never a `double`.** Binary floating point cannot represent `0.10`
exactly, so sums drift. Use `NUMERIC` in the database and `BigDecimal` in Java.

```java
// WRONG: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in binary floating point.
double total = rs.getDouble("amount");

// RIGHT: exact decimal arithmetic, matching the column's scale.
BigDecimal total = rs.getBigDecimal("amount");
```

**Use `java.time`, not `java.sql.Date`.** The legacy `java.sql.Date`,
`java.sql.Time`, and `java.sql.Timestamp` classes extend `java.util.Date`, are
mutable, and silently apply the JVM's default time zone. Since JDBC 4.2 the
generic `getObject(column, Class)` and `setObject` handle `java.time` types
directly, which removes a whole family of off-by-one-day bugs.

```java
// LEGACY: timezone-sensitive, mutable, and awkward to work with.
java.sql.Date old = rs.getDate("born");

// MODERN: unambiguous and immutable.
LocalDate born = rs.getObject("born", LocalDate.class);
```

**`NULL` is the trap that catches everyone.** The primitive getters cannot
return null, so they return `0` or `false` instead, and the only way to
distinguish "the value was zero" from "the value was NULL" is to ask afterwards.

```java
int discount = rs.getInt("discount_percent");   // NULL silently becomes 0
if (rs.wasNull()) {                             // must be called immediately after
    // the column really was NULL
}
```

`wasNull()` refers to **the most recently read column**, so it must be called
before reading anything else. The cleaner approach is to avoid primitives for
nullable columns entirely.

```java
// getObject returns a real null for a NULL column, so Optional works.
Integer discount = rs.getObject("discount_percent", Integer.class);
Optional<Integer> maybe = Optional.ofNullable(discount);
```

Writing a null has its own wrinkle: the driver often needs to know the column's
SQL type, because a bare `null` carries no type information.

```java
ps.setNull(3, Types.INTEGER);          // explicit and portable
ps.setObject(3, null, Types.INTEGER);  // equivalent
```

> Key Takeaways
> - SQL and Java type systems differ; JDBC bridges them but does not hide the
>   gaps.
> - Use `BigDecimal` with `NUMERIC` for money; `double` loses exactness.
> - Prefer `java.time` types through `getObject`/`setObject` over the legacy
>   `java.sql` date classes.
> - Primitive getters turn SQL `NULL` into `0` or `false` without warning.
> - `wasNull()` describes only the column read immediately before it.
> - Use wrapper types via `getObject` for nullable columns so `null` stays
>   `null`.
> - Writing a null usually requires `setNull` with an explicit `java.sql.Types`
>   constant.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a table with a nullable `INTEGER` column, insert a row with `NULL`
>    and a row with `0`, and show that `getInt` cannot tell them apart.
> 2. Rewrite that reading code using `getObject(col, Integer.class)` and
>    `Optional`, and confirm the two rows are now distinguishable.
> 3. Store `19.99` in a `DOUBLE PRECISION` column and in a `NUMERIC(10,2)`
>    column, sum each a thousand times, and compare the totals.
> 4. Read a `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` column into both `java.sql.Timestamp` and
>    `OffsetDateTime` while running the JVM with `-Duser.timezone=Asia/Tokyo`,
>    and explain the difference.
> 5. Interview: A report shows a total of `0` for customers who have never
>    ordered, and the team cannot tell those apart from customers whose total is
>    genuinely zero. Where would you look? (Hint: which getter was used, and
>    what does it do with `NULL`?)

#### Handling SQLException

Every JDBC method that touches the database declares `SQLException`, a
**checked** exception. That is deliberate: the database is a separate process
across a network, and failure is a normal outcome rather than a programming
error. A connection can be dropped mid-query, a constraint can be violated by
data the code could not have predicted, and a deadlock can be chosen for
rollback by the server.

The problem is that `SQLException` is one class covering everything from "your
SQL has a typo" to "the network cable was unplugged". Treating those the same
way is why so much JDBC code is written with a bare `catch (SQLException e)`
that logs and continues. To respond intelligently you need the three pieces of
information the exception carries.

| Accessor          | Meaning                                                         |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `getMessage()`    | Vendor's human-readable text; useful for logs, not for logic     |
| `getErrorCode()`  | Vendor-specific numeric code; precise but not portable           |
| `getSQLState()`   | Five-character SQL standard code; portable across vendors        |

`SQLState` is the one to branch on. Its first two characters are a class, and
the remaining three a subclass.

| SQLState | Meaning                            | Typical response                    |
| -------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `08xxx`  | Connection exception               | Retry, possibly against a replica   |
| `23000`  | Integrity constraint violation     | Report to the caller as invalid data |
| `23505`  | Unique violation                   | "That email is already registered"  |
| `40001`  | Serialization failure              | Retry the whole transaction         |
| `40P01`  | Deadlock detected (PostgreSQL)     | Retry the whole transaction         |
| `42xxx`  | Syntax error or access rule violation | Fix the code; never retry        |

Since Java 6 there is a friendlier alternative to parsing states by hand: a
hierarchy of subclasses that a good driver throws.

```text
  SQLException
  |
  +-- SQLTransientException            retrying may succeed
  |   +-- SQLTransientConnectionException
  |   +-- SQLTimeoutException
  |   +-- SQLTransactionRollbackException     deadlock, serialization failure
  |
  +-- SQLNonTransientException         retrying will fail the same way
  |   +-- SQLSyntaxErrorException
  |   +-- SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException
  |   +-- SQLDataException
  |   +-- SQLFeatureNotSupportedException
  |
  +-- SQLRecoverableException          may succeed after recovery steps
```

The single most useful distinction is **transient versus non-transient**, and it
maps directly onto "retry or do not retry".

```java
try {
    repository.save(order);
} catch (SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException e) {
    // The caller sent data that conflicts with a constraint. Not a bug, not
    // retryable: translate it into a domain error.
    throw new DuplicateOrderException(order.reference(), e);
} catch (SQLTransientException e) {
    // Network blip, timeout, or a deadlock victim. Safe to try again.
    throw new RetryableDataAccessException(e);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    // Everything else: a bug, a schema mismatch, or a permissions problem.
    log.error("SQLState={} code={}", e.getSQLState(), e.getErrorCode(), e);
    throw new DataAccessException(e);
}
```

**A single failure can carry several exceptions**, because a statement may
produce a chain of warnings and errors. `SQLException` implements `Iterable`,
and only iterating shows the whole picture.

```java
catch (SQLException e) {
    for (Throwable t : e) {              // walks the chain, not just the cause
        log.error("  {}", t.getMessage());
    }
}
```

Two habits are worth adopting. **Never swallow the exception**: an empty catch
block turns a data-loss incident into a mystery. And **never put SQL state
handling in the calling layer**: translate database exceptions into your own
domain exceptions at the boundary of the data access layer, so that business
code never imports `java.sql`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `SQLException` is checked because database failure is expected, not
>   exceptional.
> - Branch on `getSQLState()` for portable handling; `getErrorCode()` is
>   vendor-specific.
> - `SQLTransientException` means retry is reasonable;
>   `SQLNonTransientException` means it is not.
> - Constraint violations are user-input errors and should become domain
>   exceptions.
> - Iterate the exception, since one failure may chain several.
> - Translate at the data access boundary so upper layers never see
>   `java.sql` types.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Provoke a unique constraint violation and print the message, error code,
>    and SQL state. Compare them across two different databases.
> 2. Write a `catch` chain that turns a unique violation into a domain exception
>    and leaves everything else to propagate.
> 3. Implement a retry helper that re-runs a unit of work up to three times only
>    for `SQLTransientException`, with a short backoff between attempts.
> 4. Interview: Why is retrying a `SQLSyntaxErrorException` always wrong, while
>    retrying a `40001` is often right? (Hint: what would have to change between
>    the two attempts for the result to differ?)

#### Closing Resources with try-with-resources

Connections, statements, and result sets all hold resources that the garbage
collector does not manage: sockets, server-side cursors, and server-side
sessions. The JVM will happily collect a `Connection` object while the database
still believes the session is open. Releasing those resources is the
programmer's responsibility, and it must happen even when something throws.

Before Java 7 the correct code was notoriously verbose and almost always wrong
in at least one place.

```java
// LEGACY: this is what try-with-resources replaced. Note the nesting,
// the null checks, and that a failure in rs.close() hides the real exception.
Connection conn = null;
Statement stmt = null;
ResultSet rs = null;
try {
    conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
    stmt = conn.createStatement();
    rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT 1");
    ...
} finally {
    if (rs != null)   { try { rs.close(); }   catch (SQLException ignored) {} }
    if (stmt != null) { try { stmt.close(); } catch (SQLException ignored) {} }
    if (conn != null) { try { conn.close(); } catch (SQLException ignored) {} }
}
```

All three JDBC types implement `AutoCloseable`, so a single `try`-with-resources
header replaces the whole thing. Resources are closed in **reverse order of
declaration**, which is exactly the order JDBC needs.

```java
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(SQL);
     ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {

    while (rs.next()) { ... }

}   // closes rs, then ps, then conn, even if the body throws
```

```text
  declaration order        closing order
  -----------------        -------------
  conn   (1)               rs     (3)
  ps     (2)       ==>     ps     (2)
  rs     (3)               conn   (1)
```

**Suppressed exceptions** are the second thing this construct fixes. If the body
throws and a `close()` also throws, the close failure is attached to the
original exception rather than replacing it, and both appear in the stack trace
under a `Suppressed:` heading. The legacy code above simply lost one of them.

Two details are worth knowing. First, closing a `Statement` closes any
`ResultSet` it produced, and closing a `Connection` closes its statements, so
listing all three is belt and braces rather than strictly required. Listing them
is still the better habit, because it keeps the code correct when the connection
comes from a pool and outlives the statement.

Second, **`close()` on a pooled connection does not close the socket**. The
pool's wrapper intercepts it and returns the connection to the pool. This is
precisely why the same `try`-with-resources code is correct in both worlds, and
why "always close the connection" remains true even when pooling.

A common mistake is putting a resource creation expression inside the body,
where it is not managed.

```java
// WRONG: this ResultSet is never closed.
try (Connection conn = ds.getConnection();
     Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
    ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);   // not in the resource list
    while (rs.next()) { ... }
}
```

Here the result set survives only because closing `stmt` closes it, which is
true today and fragile tomorrow. Declare every resource in the header.

Finally, an existing variable can be used directly in the header since Java 9,
provided it is final or effectively final.

```java
Connection conn = pool.borrow();
try (conn) {              // Java 9+: manage an already-created resource
    ...
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - JDBC resources are operating-system and server resources, not garbage that
>   the collector reclaims.
> - `Connection`, `Statement`, and `ResultSet` all implement `AutoCloseable`.
> - `try`-with-resources closes in reverse declaration order, which matches
>   JDBC's required order.
> - A failure in `close()` is suppressed and attached to the original exception
>   rather than replacing it.
> - Declare every resource in the header; creating one in the body leaves it
>   unmanaged.
> - Closing a pooled connection returns it to the pool instead of closing the
>   socket.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite the legacy `finally` block above using `try`-with-resources and
>    count the lines removed.
> 2. Write code where both the body and `close()` throw, then print the stack
>    trace and locate the `Suppressed:` section.
> 3. Add logging to a custom `AutoCloseable` wrapper around a statement to prove
>    the closing order is the reverse of declaration.
> 4. Interview: A service using a connection pool exhausts it after a few hours
>    under load, with no errors in the logs. What single class of bug would you
>    look for first? (Hint: which object must return to the pool, and what
>    happens if an early `return` skips it?)

<a id="162-safe-and-efficient-data-access"></a>
### 16.2 Safe and Efficient Data Access

This subchapter covers the tools that turn working JDBC code into code fit for
production: parameterised statements that close the largest security hole in web
applications, batching that collapses thousands of round trips into a handful,
and pooling that removes the cost of opening connections.

#### PreparedStatement and Query Parameters

Almost every real query varies by some value: an identifier, a search term, a
date range. The obvious way to supply it is string concatenation, and the
obvious way is wrong for three separate reasons. `PreparedStatement` is the
right way, and it fixes all three at once.

A prepared statement is SQL with **placeholders**, written as `?`, sent to the
database **before** the values are known. The database parses it, checks it,
builds an execution plan, and hands back a handle. Values are then bound to the
placeholders and the statement is executed, possibly many times.

```text
  Statement (concatenated)              PreparedStatement
  ------------------------              -----------------
  build SQL string with value           send SQL with ? once
        |                                     |
  send whole string  ------> parse       parse, plan, cache
                             plan              |
                             execute     bind values -----> execute
                                               |
  (repeat: parse and plan again)         (repeat: bind and execute only)
```

The three problems it solves:

| Problem           | With concatenation                        | With parameters                      |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Security          | Values can change the statement's meaning | Values are never parsed as SQL       |
| Correctness       | Manual quoting, escaping, date formatting | Driver handles types and escaping    |
| Performance       | Every distinct string is parsed and planned | Parsed once, executed many times   |

```java
String sql = "SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE department = ? AND active = ?";

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {

    ps.setString(1, department);     // parameters are 1-based, like columns
    ps.setBoolean(2, true);

    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {   // note: no argument here
        while (rs.next()) { ... }
    }
}
```

Two details catch people out. Parameter indexes are **1-based**. And
`executeQuery()` on a `PreparedStatement` takes **no argument**, because the SQL
was supplied at creation time; calling the inherited `executeQuery(String)`
throws.

**Placeholders stand for values, not for identifiers.** This is the boundary
that surprises people: you cannot parameterise a table name, a column name, a
sort direction, or an operator, because those change the structure of the
statement rather than the data it acts on.

```java
// INVALID: the driver will not substitute a column name.
ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY ?");

// VALID approach: validate against a whitelist you control, then concatenate.
private static final Set<String> SORTABLE = Set.of("name", "email", "created_at");

String column = SORTABLE.contains(requested) ? requested : "name";
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY " + column;   // safe: closed set
```

**Binding a collection needs care**, because one `?` binds one value. The
portable solution is to generate the right number of placeholders.

```java
String placeholders = ids.stream()
        .map(id -> "?")
        .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));          // "?, ?, ?"
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (" + placeholders + ")";

try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    int i = 1;
    for (Long id : ids) {
        ps.setLong(i++, id);                          // bind each element
    }
    ...
}
```

Generating a different SQL string per list size defeats plan caching, so on
PostgreSQL the better form is a single array parameter.

```java
Array array = conn.createArrayOf("bigint", ids.toArray());
ps.setArray(1, array);      // one placeholder: WHERE id = ANY(?)
```

Finally, a practical note on when **not** to reach for `PreparedStatement`: for
DDL run once at startup, or a static query with no parameters, a plain
`Statement` is equally safe and marginally simpler. The rule is about values
