from outside the program, and every such value belongs in a parameter.

> Key Takeaways
> - `PreparedStatement` separates the statement's structure from its values.
> - Parameters prevent injection, handle escaping and type conversion, and allow
>   plan reuse.
> - Parameter indexes start at 1, and `executeQuery()` takes no argument.
> - Placeholders bind values only; identifiers must come from a whitelist you
>   control.
> - An `IN` clause needs one placeholder per element, or a single array
>   parameter.
> - Any value originating outside the program belongs in a parameter, without
>   exception.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert a concatenated `SELECT ... WHERE name = '" + name + "'` into a
>    parameterised query and verify it handles a name containing an apostrophe.
> 2. Write a method that takes a list of identifiers and builds the correct
>    number of placeholders, then binds them.
> 3. Attempt to parameterise a table name, record the error, and implement the
>    whitelist alternative.
> 4. Time 10,000 executions of the same query using a reused `PreparedStatement`
>    versus a new `Statement` each time.
> 5. Interview: A search endpoint allows sorting by any column name supplied in
>    the query string. How would you make it safe without losing the feature?
>    (Hint: placeholders are not available here, so what property must the set
>    of accepted values have?)

#### SQL Injection and Its Prevention

SQL injection has been at or near the top of every application security list for
twenty years, and the mechanism is simple enough to explain in a sentence: if
user input is concatenated into a SQL string, the user can write SQL.

Consider a login check built by concatenation.

```java
// VULNERABLE. Never write this.
String sql = "SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" + email
           + "' AND password_hash = '" + hash + "'";
```

With an ordinary email the statement is what the author intended. With the email
`' OR '1'='1' --` the database receives something else entirely.

```text
  Intended:
    SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = 'ada@example.com'
                           AND password_hash = 'abc123'

  Received:
    SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1' --' AND password_hash = '...'
                                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^
                                       always true   rest is now a comment
```

The `--` comments out the password check, `'1'='1'` is always true, and the
query returns every user. The first row is typically the administrator.

The damage is not limited to reading. Depending on the driver's settings and the
statement's position, an attacker may be able to terminate the statement and
append another, extract data through a `UNION`, or infer data one bit at a time
through timing or error differences ("blind" injection).

| Attack form       | Payload shape                    | Effect                          |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Authentication bypass | `' OR '1'='1' --`            | Condition always true           |
| Union-based       | `' UNION SELECT card_number ...` | Leaks other tables into results |
| Stacked queries   | `'; DROP TABLE users; --`        | Runs a second statement         |
| Blind boolean     | `' AND substr(pw,1,1)='a' --`    | Extracts data one character at a time |
| Time-based blind  | `' AND pg_sleep(5) --`           | Extracts data via response time |

**The fix is parameterisation, and it works because of where the split
happens.** With a prepared statement, the SQL text is parsed into a plan
*before* any value is supplied. The value is transmitted separately, in a typed
protocol field, and is placed into the already-built plan as data. There is no
parsing step left for it to influence. It is the difference between handing
someone a filled-in form and letting them rewrite the form.

```java
// SAFE. The input is data, never syntax, whatever it contains.
String sql = "SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ? AND password_hash = ?";
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setString(1, email);     // "' OR '1'='1' --" is just a strange email
    ps.setString(2, hash);
    ...
}
```

**Defences that do not work, or do not work alone:**

- *Escaping quotes by hand.* Easy to get wrong, and useless for numeric contexts
  where no quotes are involved at all.
- *Blacklisting words like `DROP` or `UNION`.* Bypassed with comments, case
  changes, and encoding. It also breaks legitimate input.
- *Client-side validation.* The attacker does not use your client.
- *Stored procedures.* Safe only if they parameterise internally; a procedure
  that concatenates is just as vulnerable.
- *An ORM.* Safe for generated queries, but native query strings in an ORM are
  concatenated like any other string.

**Defence in depth** still matters, because parameterisation protects the query
and nothing else. Give the application's database user only the privileges it
needs, so a successful injection cannot read tables it never uses or run DDL.
Validate input for shape and length because it is good practice anyway. Log
failures without echoing the offending SQL back to the user, since error
messages are an attacker's primary feedback channel.

A practical way to audit a codebase: search for string concatenation adjacent to
SQL keywords.

```bash
# Any '+' inside a string that also looks like SQL is worth a manual look.
grep -rEn '"(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE)[^"]*"\s*\+' --include='*.java' src/
```

> Key Takeaways
> - SQL injection happens when input is concatenated into a statement and is
>   then parsed as SQL.
> - It enables authentication bypass, data theft, data destruction, and
>   character-by-character extraction.
> - Parameterisation is the fix because parsing happens before values arrive.
> - Manual escaping, blacklists, and client-side validation are not defences.
> - Stored procedures and ORMs are safe only where they parameterise internally.
> - Restrict the application's database privileges so a breach has limited
>   reach.
> - Never return raw SQL error text to a caller.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a deliberately vulnerable login query in a local test database and
>    bypass it with `' OR '1'='1' --`. Then fix it with parameters and retry.
> 2. Show why escaping single quotes fails to protect a query whose parameter is
>    numeric and unquoted.
> 3. Write a grep or static-analysis rule that flags SQL string concatenation,
>    and run it over a project you have.
> 4. Create a database role with `SELECT` only on two tables, connect as it, and
>    confirm an injected `DROP TABLE` fails.
> 5. Interview: A team says their ORM makes injection impossible. What would you
>    ask to check that claim? (Hint: what escape hatch does every ORM provide
>    for queries it cannot express?)

#### CallableStatement and Stored Procedures

A **stored procedure** is code that lives in the database and runs there. It is
written in the database's own procedural language, `PL/pgSQL` for PostgreSQL or
`PL/SQL` for Oracle, and is invoked by name. JDBC calls them through
`CallableStatement`, a sub-interface of `PreparedStatement` that adds support
for **output parameters**: values the procedure writes back to the caller.

Why would logic live in the database at all? Two honest reasons. First, some
operations touch many rows and moving the logic to the data avoids shipping
those rows across the network. Second, when several applications in different
languages share one database, a procedure is the only place shared rules can
live. The counter-arguments are just as real: procedural SQL is hard to unit
test, hard to version alongside application code, and ties you to one vendor.

The call syntax is a JDBC escape sequence, in braces, which the driver
translates into whatever the vendor expects.

```text
  {call procedure_name(?, ?, ?)}          procedure, no return value
  {? = call function_name(?, ?)}          function, first ? is the return
       ^ registered as an OUT parameter
```

Each parameter is one of three kinds.

| Kind    | Direction                     | Setup required                          |
| ------- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `IN`    | Caller to procedure           | `setXxx(index, value)`                  |
| `OUT`   | Procedure to caller           | `registerOutParameter(index, sqlType)`  |
| `INOUT` | Both                          | Both of the above                       |

Here is a procedure that applies a discount and reports the new total.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
CREATE PROCEDURE apply_discount(
        IN  p_order_id   BIGINT,
        IN  p_percent    NUMERIC,
        OUT p_new_total  NUMERIC)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
    UPDATE orders
       SET total = total * (1 - p_percent / 100)
     WHERE id = p_order_id;

    SELECT total INTO p_new_total FROM orders WHERE id = p_order_id;
END;
$$;
```

```java
String call = "{call apply_discount(?, ?, ?)}";

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     CallableStatement cs = conn.prepareCall(call)) {

    cs.setLong(1, orderId);                              // IN
    cs.setBigDecimal(2, new BigDecimal("10"));           // IN
    cs.registerOutParameter(3, Types.NUMERIC);           // OUT: declare type first

    cs.execute();                                        // run the procedure

    BigDecimal newTotal = cs.getBigDecimal(3);           // read the OUT value
    System.out.println("new total " + newTotal);
}
```

Parameters can also be bound **by name**, which is far more readable when a
procedure has eight of them, though support varies by driver.

```java
cs.setLong("p_order_id", orderId);
cs.registerOutParameter("p_new_total", Types.NUMERIC);
```

A procedure may also return one or more result sets, in which case you read them
as usual and, if there are several, advance with `getMoreResults()`.

```java
boolean hasResultSet = cs.execute();     // true if the first result is rows
while (hasResultSet) {
    try (ResultSet rs = cs.getResultSet()) {
        while (rs.next()) { ... }
    }
    hasResultSet = cs.getMoreResults();  // move to the next result, if any
}
```

**Where stored procedures sit today.** Most new systems keep business logic in
the application, where it can be tested, reviewed, and deployed with the rest of
the code, and use procedures sparingly for genuinely set-based work. You will
still meet them constantly in established systems, so knowing
`CallableStatement` is not optional.

> Key Takeaways
> - A stored procedure is named, precompiled code executing inside the database.
> - `CallableStatement` extends `PreparedStatement` with `OUT` and `INOUT`
>   parameter support.
> - The call uses JDBC escape syntax, `{call name(?, ?)}`, translated by the
>   driver.
> - Every `OUT` parameter must be registered with its SQL type before execution.
> - Results are read by index or, where supported, by parameter name.
> - Procedures reduce network traffic and centralise rules but resist testing
>   and version control, and bind you to a vendor.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a procedure that takes a customer id and returns their order count as
>    an `OUT` parameter, then call it from Java.
> 2. Convert that procedure into a function and call it with the
>    `{? = call ...}` form.
> 3. Write a procedure returning two result sets and read both using
>    `getMoreResults()`.
> 4. Interview: Give one argument for and one against moving an order-validation
>    rule into a stored procedure. (Hint: think about who else writes to the
>    same table, and about what your test suite can execute.)

#### Batch Updates for Bulk Operations

Inserting ten thousand rows one statement at a time is slow, and the reason is
not the database. Each `executeUpdate` is a network round trip: send, wait,
receive. At a latency of one millisecond, ten thousand inserts spend ten seconds
waiting on the network no matter how fast the database is.

**Batching** collects statements on the client and sends them in one go.

```text
  Without batching                      With batching
  ----------------                      -------------
  app ---- insert 1 ----> db            app  ---- 1000 inserts ----> db
  app <--- result 1 ----- db            app  <--- 1000 results ----- db
  app ---- insert 2 ----> db
  app <--- result 2 ----- db            one round trip, not 1000
  ... 10,000 times
```

The API is three methods: `addBatch()` to queue, `executeBatch()` to send, and
`clearBatch()` to discard.

```java
String sql = "INSERT INTO readings (sensor_id, taken_at, value) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {

    conn.setAutoCommit(false);            // one transaction for the whole load

    int count = 0;
    for (Reading r : readings) {
        ps.setLong(1, r.sensorId());
        ps.setObject(2, r.takenAt());
        ps.setBigDecimal(3, r.value());
        ps.addBatch();                    // queue this row's parameters

        if (++count % 1000 == 0) {        // flush periodically: bound memory
            ps.executeBatch();
        }
    }
    ps.executeBatch();                    // send whatever remains
    conn.commit();
}
```

Three things in that example matter as much as `addBatch` itself.
**Auto-commit is off**, so the load is one transaction rather than ten thousand;
leaving it on forces a disk flush per statement and destroys the benefit.
**The batch is flushed every thousand rows**, because an unbounded batch buffers
every row's parameters in client memory. And **the final `executeBatch` outside
the loop** sends the remainder, which is the most commonly forgotten line.

`executeBatch()` returns an `int[]` with one entry per queued statement.

| Value                       | Meaning                                       |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `>= 0`                      | Rows affected by that statement               |
| `Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO` | Succeeded; the driver does not know the count |
| `Statement.EXECUTE_FAILED`  | That statement failed                         |

**Failure handling is the subtle part.** If one statement in a batch fails, the
driver may stop there or continue with the rest, and JDBC permits both. The
failure arrives as `BatchUpdateException`, which carries the counts for the
statements that were processed.

```java
try {
    ps.executeBatch();
} catch (BatchUpdateException e) {
    int[] counts = e.getUpdateCounts();       // may be shorter than the batch
    for (int i = 0; i < counts.length; i++) {
        if (counts[i] == Statement.EXECUTE_FAILED) {
            log.error("statement {} in the batch failed", i);
        }
    }
    conn.rollback();                          // the transaction saves you here
    throw e;
}
```

Because the behaviour varies, the reliable pattern is to run the batch inside a
transaction and roll the whole thing back on any failure, rather than trying to
reason about which statements survived.

One driver-specific detail worth knowing: **MySQL ignores batching unless you
ask for it.** Without `rewriteBatchedStatements=true` in the URL, its driver
sends the statements individually and the speedup never appears.

```text
  jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/app?rewriteBatchedStatements=true
```

Realistic gains for a bulk insert are large enough to change designs: it is
routine to go from a few hundred rows per second to tens of thousands.

> Key Takeaways
> - Batching exists to eliminate per-statement network round trips.
> - `addBatch()` queues, `executeBatch()` sends, and the return array reports
>   per-statement counts.
> - Always disable auto-commit around a batch, or each statement commits
>   separately.
> - Flush every few hundred or thousand statements so client memory stays
>   bounded.
> - The final `executeBatch()` after the loop is required and easy to forget.
> - `BatchUpdateException` carries partial counts; rolling back the transaction
>   is the dependable response.
> - MySQL needs `rewriteBatchedStatements=true` for batching to take effect.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Insert 50,000 rows one at a time and measure the elapsed time. Repeat with
>    batches of 1,000 and compare.
> 2. Repeat the batched load with auto-commit left on and explain the difference
>    you observe.
> 3. Deliberately violate a constraint on the 500th row of a batch, catch
>    `BatchUpdateException`, and report which statements succeeded.
> 4. Add a batch-size parameter and chart throughput for sizes 1, 10, 100, 1000,
>    and 10000. Identify where the gains flatten.
> 5. Interview: Why can a batch of 1,000,000 statements be slower than ten
>    batches of 100,000? (Hint: what is held on the client between `addBatch`
>    and `executeBatch`?)

#### Generated Keys and Metadata

Most tables have a surrogate primary key generated by the database: a sequence,
an identity column, or an auto-increment. After inserting a row you almost
always need that key, to insert child rows or to return the new resource's
identifier.

The tempting approach is to insert and then query for the maximum id, which is
wrong under concurrency: another transaction may have inserted between the two
statements, and you get its key instead of yours. JDBC provides the correct
mechanism, **generated keys**, which returns the key produced by *your* insert.

```java
String sql = "INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_at) VALUES (?, ?)";

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(
             sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)) {   // must ask at creation

    ps.setLong(1, customerId);
    ps.setObject(2, OffsetDateTime.now());
    ps.executeUpdate();

    try (ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()) {      // a normal ResultSet
        if (!keys.next()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("no generated key returned");
        }
        long orderId = keys.getLong(1);                 // first generated column
    }
}
```

The request must be made **when the statement is created**; you cannot ask for
keys afterwards. An alternative overload names the columns you want, which is
more portable than relying on column 1 and is required on some drivers.

```java
// Name the columns explicitly. Clearer and safer across vendors.
PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql, new String[] { "id" });
```

Behaviour varies more than you would like. Some drivers return only the primary
key, others every default-valued column; some return keys for a batch, others
only for the last row. PostgreSQL offers a native alternative that sidesteps the
whole question and returns anything you ask for.

```sql
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_at) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id, created_at
```

That is an ordinary query as far as JDBC is concerned, so you run it with
`executeQuery` and read the result set.

**Metadata** is the second topic here, and it answers questions about the shape
of data rather than its content. There are two kinds.

`ResultSetMetaData` describes the columns of a result you just obtained, which
is what lets generic code handle a query it did not write.

```java
ResultSetMetaData md = rs.getMetaData();
int columns = md.getColumnCount();
for (int i = 1; i <= columns; i++) {                     // 1-based again
    System.out.printf("%s : %s (%s), nullable=%d%n",
            md.getColumnLabel(i),      // the AS alias, or the column name
            md.getColumnTypeName(i),   // vendor type name, e.g. "varchar"
            md.getColumnClassName(i),  // Java class getObject will return
            md.isNullable(i));
}
```

This is exactly how a tool like a database browser or a generic CSV exporter
works: no knowledge of the schema, just the metadata of whatever came back.

`DatabaseMetaData` describes the database itself: its tables, columns, keys,
supported features, and version.

```java
DatabaseMetaData meta = conn.getMetaData();

// Catalog, schema, table-name pattern, table types. null means "any".
try (ResultSet tables = meta.getTables(null, "public", "%", new String[]{"TABLE"})) {
    while (tables.next()) {
        System.out.println(tables.getString("TABLE_NAME"));
    }
}

try (ResultSet cols = meta.getColumns(null, "public", "orders", "%")) {
    while (cols.next()) {
        System.out.println(cols.getString("COLUMN_NAME") + " "
                         + cols.getString("TYPE_NAME"));
    }
}
```

Metadata queries are how schema migration tools, code generators, and object
mappers discover what they are working with. They are also slow and should not
appear on a request path.

> Key Takeaways
> - `RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS` must be requested when the statement is prepared.
> - `getGeneratedKeys()` returns a result set holding the keys your insert
>   produced.
> - Selecting `max(id)` after an insert is a race condition, not an alternative.
> - Naming the key columns explicitly is more portable than relying on index 1.
> - PostgreSQL's `RETURNING` clause is a simpler, more capable option where
>   available.
> - `ResultSetMetaData` describes a result's columns and enables schema-agnostic
>   code.
> - `DatabaseMetaData` describes the database and underpins migration and code
>   generation tools.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Insert an order and its three line items in one transaction, using the
>    generated order id as the foreign key on each line.
> 2. Write a generic method that prints any `ResultSet` as aligned columns using
>    only `ResultSetMetaData`.
> 3. List every table and its columns in a schema using `DatabaseMetaData`, and
>    compare the output with the database's own catalogue view.
> 4. Implement the same insert using `RETURNING id` and compare the code with
>    the `getGeneratedKeys` version.
> 5. Interview: Two users register at the same moment and one receives the
>    other's account id. What implementation would produce that? (Hint: what
>    happens between an insert and a separate query for the newest row?)

#### Connection Pooling with DataSource

16.1 established that opening a connection costs tens of milliseconds while a
query costs one. A web application handling a hundred requests per second cannot
pay that cost per request, and databases cannot accept thousands of concurrent
connections anyway because each one consumes server memory and a process or
thread.

A **connection pool** solves both problems by opening a small number of
connections at startup and lending them out. A request borrows one, uses it, and
returns it. The expensive setup happens once per connection, not once per
request.

```text
   Without a pool                     With a pool
   --------------                     -----------
   request -> open  (18 ms)           request -> borrow (~0.05 ms)
              query ( 1 ms)                      query  ( 1 ms)
              close ( 1 ms)                      return (~0.05 ms)
   --------------------------          ---------------------------
   20 ms, and the DB sees one          1.1 ms, and the DB sees a
   new session per request             fixed set of long-lived sessions
```

The pool is exposed through `javax.sql.DataSource`, the interface that should
replace `DriverManager` in every application. It is a **factory for
connections**, and crucially it hides where they come from.

```java
// A DataSource is injected as an interface. Application code never knows
// whether it is pooled, nor which database it points at.
public class OrderRepository {
    private final DataSource dataSource;

    public OrderRepository(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
    }

    public Optional<Order> findById(long id) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE id = ?";
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();     // borrow
             PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setLong(1, id);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                return rs.next() ? Optional.of(map(rs)) : Optional.empty();
            }
        }   // close() returns the connection to the pool
    }
}
```

Note that the code is identical to the unpooled version. `close()` on a pooled
connection is intercepted by the pool's proxy and returns it rather than closing
the socket, which is why `try`-with-resources remains mandatory: **a connection
that is not closed is never returned**, and a few leaks under load exhaust the
pool and hang the application.

HikariCP is the de facto standard pool, chosen for being small and fast.

```java
HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shopdb");
config.setUsername("app");
config.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));

config.setMaximumPoolSize(10);            // the single most important setting
config.setMinimumIdle(10);                // keep the pool a fixed size
config.setConnectionTimeout(3_000);       // ms to wait for a free connection
config.setIdleTimeout(600_000);           // ms before an idle connection closes
config.setMaxLifetime(1_800_000);         // ms before a connection is retired
config.setLeakDetectionThreshold(20_000); // ms held before a warning is logged

DataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config);
```

| Setting                   | What it controls                     | Typical value        |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------- |
| `maximumPoolSize`         | Concurrent connections allowed       | 10 to 20 per instance |
| `minimumIdle`             | Connections kept ready               | Equal to the maximum |
| `connectionTimeout`       | Wait before giving up borrowing      | 2 to 5 seconds       |
| `maxLifetime`             | Retire connections before the server does | Under the DB's timeout |
| `leakDetectionThreshold`  | Warn about connections held too long | 20 to 60 seconds     |

**Pools should be small, which is counter-intuitive.** A database executes work
on a limited number of cores and disks; beyond that point more concurrent
connections mean more context switching and lock contention, not more
throughput. A pool of ten usually outperforms a pool of a hundred. Size it from
measurement, starting near `cores * 2` on the database, and remember that the
total across all application instances is what the server sees.

**When the pool is exhausted**, borrowing blocks until `connectionTimeout`
elapses and then throws. That is the correct behaviour, and the symptom to
recognise: requests suddenly taking exactly three seconds and then failing means
a leak or a query holding connections far too long, not a slow network.

> Key Takeaways
> - A pool reuses a small set of long-lived connections instead of opening one
>   per request.
> - `DataSource` is the interface to depend on; `DriverManager` belongs in
>   scripts and tests.
> - Closing a pooled connection returns it, so `try`-with-resources is still
>   required.
> - A leaked connection is never returned, and enough leaks hang the
>   application.
> - Small pools usually outperform large ones, since the database's real
>   parallelism is bounded.
> - Set `maxLifetime` below the database's own idle timeout to avoid handing out
>   dead connections.
> - Timeouts on borrowing are the visible symptom of leaks and long-running
>   queries.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace `DriverManager` with a HikariCP `DataSource` in an existing program
>    and measure the change in request latency.
> 2. Write a handler that deliberately fails to close its connection, run it
>    under load, and observe the pool exhausting.
> 3. Enable `leakDetectionThreshold` and confirm the warning identifies the
>    leaking code path.
> 4. Benchmark identical load against pool sizes of 5, 10, 50, and 200 and plot
>    throughput against size.
> 5. Interview: A service with `maximumPoolSize=100` is slower than the same
>    service with `maximumPoolSize=10`. Explain how that is possible. (Hint:
>    what does the database do with 100 simultaneous requests for the same disk
>    and the same locks?)

<a id="163-transactions-and-integrity"></a>
### 16.3 Transactions and Integrity

This subchapter covers the mechanism that keeps data consistent when operations
span several statements and several users at once: how transactions are
controlled from JDBC, what isolation levels actually buy you, and where
transaction boundaries belong in a layered application.

#### Auto-Commit Mode and Manual Control

A **transaction** is a group of statements that succeed or fail as one. The
standard example is a transfer: debit one account, credit another. If the
process crashes between the two statements, money has vanished. A transaction
makes that impossible, because until it commits, nothing it did is visible or
permanent, and if it never commits, everything it did is undone.

Transactions are conventionally described by four properties, **ACID**.

| Property     | Guarantee                                                       |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Atomicity    | All statements take effect, or none do                           |
| Consistency  | Constraints hold before and after; the database rejects violations |
| Isolation    | Concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work     |
| Durability   | Once committed, the change survives a crash                      |

**JDBC connections start in auto-commit mode**, meaning every statement is
wrapped in its own transaction and committed the moment it completes. That is
convenient for single-statement work and catastrophic for multi-statement work,
because it removes exactly the guarantee you need.

```java
// BROKEN: auto-commit is on, so these are two independent transactions.
// A failure or crash between them leaves money destroyed.
stmt.executeUpdate("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1");
// <-- committed already; a crash here loses 100 permanently
stmt.executeUpdate("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2");
```

Turning it off makes the connection wait for an explicit `commit()`.

```java
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
    conn.setAutoCommit(false);                 // begin a manual transaction

    try (PreparedStatement debit = conn.prepareStatement(
             "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?");
         PreparedStatement credit = conn.prepareStatement(
             "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?")) {

        debit.setBigDecimal(1, amount);
        debit.setLong(2, fromId);
        debit.executeUpdate();

        credit.setBigDecimal(1, amount);
        credit.setLong(2, toId);
        credit.executeUpdate();

        conn.commit();                         // both take effect, atomically
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        conn.rollback();                       // neither takes effect
        throw e;
    }
}
```

There is no `beginTransaction()` in JDBC. Setting auto-commit to `false` *is*
the begin, and a transaction implicitly starts again after each `commit()` or
`rollback()`.

```text
  setAutoCommit(false)
        |
        v
   [ transaction open ]  --- statements ---+
        |                                  |
        +--- commit()   --> durable -------+--> new transaction opens
        |                                  |
        +--- rollback() --> discarded -----+
```

**Two failure modes are worth naming.** Forgetting `commit()` means the work is
silently discarded when the connection closes or returns to the pool, which
presents as "the insert ran but the row is not there". And leaving auto-commit
off on a **pooled** connection leaks that state to the next borrower, which is
why every pool resets it on return. Restoring it yourself is good manners in
code that does not control the pool.

```java
boolean previous = conn.getAutoCommit();
conn.setAutoCommit(false);
try {
    ...
    conn.commit();
} finally {
    conn.setAutoCommit(previous);      // restore whatever the caller had
}
```

**Keep transactions short.** An open transaction holds locks and prevents the
database from cleaning up old row versions. Never make an HTTP call, wait on a
queue, or prompt a user inside one.

> Key Takeaways
> - A transaction makes several statements atomic: all of them apply, or none.
> - ACID names the four guarantees: atomicity, consistency, isolation,
>   durability.
> - JDBC connections default to auto-commit, one transaction per statement.
> - `setAutoCommit(false)` is how a transaction begins; there is no explicit
>   begin method.
> - A missing `commit()` silently discards the work.
> - Restore auto-commit before releasing a connection you did not create.
> - Hold transactions open for as little time as possible, and never across
>   network calls to other systems.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a transfer between two accounts with auto-commit on, kill the
>    process between the two updates, and inspect the balances.
> 2. Repeat with auto-commit off and a rollback on failure, and confirm the
>    balances are unchanged.
> 3. Write code that inserts a row and returns without committing, then query
>    for the row from another connection and explain the result.
> 4. Interview: A developer reports that their insert "works in the test but the
>    row disappears". What would you check first? (Hint: what happens to an
>    uncommitted transaction when the connection is returned to a pool?)

#### Commit, Rollback, and Savepoints

`commit()` and `rollback()` are all-or-nothing for the whole transaction, which
is usually what you want. Sometimes it is too coarse. Consider importing a
thousand records where a handful are malformed: rolling back the entire import
because of three bad rows wastes the other nine hundred and ninety-seven.

A **savepoint** is a named marker inside a transaction that you can roll back
to, undoing everything after it while keeping everything before it.

```text
  BEGIN
    insert A            <-- kept
    SAVEPOINT s1 -------+
    insert B            |   rollback(s1) undoes only this
    insert C  (fails)   |
    rollback(s1) -------+
    insert D            <-- kept
  COMMIT                    A and D are durable; B and C never happened
```

```java
conn.setAutoCommit(false);
int imported = 0, skipped = 0;

for (Record record : records) {
    Savepoint sp = conn.setSavepoint("row");      // marker before this row
    try {
        insert(conn, record);
        imported++;
        conn.releaseSavepoint(sp);                // discard the marker
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        conn.rollback(sp);                        // undo this row only
        skipped++;
        log.warn("skipped {}: {}", record.id(), e.getMessage());
    }
}
conn.commit();                                    // everything kept is durable
```

`releaseSavepoint` matters in long loops: each savepoint consumes server
resources, and thousands of unreleased ones are a real cost. Note also that on
PostgreSQL any error **aborts the transaction** until you roll back to a
savepoint, so the pattern above is not an optimisation there, it is the only way
to continue after a failed statement.

The three savepoint operations:

| Method                    | Effect                                              |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `setSavepoint()`          | Creates an unnamed marker and returns it             |
| `setSavepoint(String)`    | Creates a named marker, easier to read in logs       |
| `rollback(Savepoint)`     | Undoes work after the marker; transaction stays open |
| `releaseSavepoint(sp)`    | Discards the marker; work done since it is unaffected |

**Rollback is not free and it is not magic.** It undoes database changes only.
Anything else the code did inside the transaction persists: files written,
emails sent, messages published, in-memory caches updated. This is the single
most common source of inconsistency in systems that look transactional.

```java
conn.setAutoCommit(false);
try {
    orderRepository.insert(conn, order);
    emailService.sendConfirmation(order);     // WRONG: cannot be rolled back
    conn.commit();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    conn.rollback();     // the order is gone; the customer still got the email
    throw e;
}
```

The fix is to move side effects **after** the commit, or to record the intent in
the same transaction and let a separate process act on it afterwards.

```java
conn.setAutoCommit(false);
try {
    orderRepository.insert(conn, order);
    outbox.enqueue(conn, new ConfirmationEmail(order));  // same transaction
    conn.commit();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    conn.rollback();     // the intent to email is rolled back with the order
    throw e;
}
// a separate worker reads the outbox and sends, after the commit
```

One last rule: **always roll back on any exception, not just `SQLException`**. A
`NullPointerException` halfway through leaves a transaction open holding locks
until the connection is reclaimed.

> Key Takeaways
> - `commit()` makes the whole transaction durable; `rollback()` discards it.
> - A savepoint marks a point you can partially roll back to without ending the
>   transaction.
> - Partial rollback lets a bulk import skip bad records while keeping good
>   ones.
> - Release savepoints in long loops to avoid accumulating server-side state.
> - On PostgreSQL, a failed statement aborts the transaction unless a savepoint
>   is used.
> - Rollback undoes database work only; emails, files, and messages are not
>   reversed.
> - Defer side effects until after commit, or record them transactionally in an
>   outbox.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Import ten records where the fourth violates a constraint, using savepoints
>    so the other nine are committed.
> 2. Show that without savepoints on PostgreSQL, statements after the failure
>    raise "current transaction is aborted".
> 3. Write a transaction that inserts a row and then throws a
>    `RuntimeException`, and confirm the row is absent only if you roll back in
>    a `catch (Exception)` rather than `catch (SQLException)`.
> 4. Restructure a method that sends an email mid-transaction so that the email
>    cannot be sent for a rolled-back order.
> 5. Interview: An order-placement endpoint occasionally sends a confirmation
>    for an order that does not exist. What design would cause that, and how
>    would you fix it? (Hint: which of the two actions can be undone?)

#### Isolation Levels and Concurrency Anomalies

Isolation is the "I" in ACID, and it is the only one of the four that comes with
a dial. Perfect isolation, where concurrent transactions behave exactly as if
they ran one after another, is expensive: it requires locking that blocks other
work. So SQL defines four levels, each permitting more anomalies in exchange for
more concurrency.

To choose a level you need the vocabulary of what can go wrong.

**Dirty read**: reading a row another transaction has modified but not yet
committed. If that transaction rolls back, you acted on data that never existed.

```text
  T1: UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 WHERE id = 7
  T2:                     SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 7  --> 0
  T1: ROLLBACK                                                    (was never 0)
```

**Non-repeatable read**: reading the same row twice in one transaction and
getting different values, because another transaction committed in between.

```text
  T1: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 7   --> 500
  T2: UPDATE accounts SET balance = 100 WHERE id = 7 ; COMMIT
  T1: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 7   --> 100   (changed underneath)
```

**Phantom read**: re-running the same *query* and getting different *rows*,
because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching the condition.

```text
  T1: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE total > 100   --> 12
  T2: INSERT INTO orders (total) VALUES (250) ; COMMIT
  T1: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE total > 100   --> 13   (a new row appeared)
```

**Lost update**: two transactions read the same value, both compute a new one
from it, and the second write overwrites the first.

```text
  T1: read stock = 10
  T2: read stock = 10
  T1: write stock = 9   (sold one)
  T2: write stock = 9   (sold one)   --> two sales, one unit deducted
```

The four levels and what each permits:

| Level              | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom read | Cost      |
| ------------------ | ---------- | ------------------- | ------------ | --------- |
| `READ_UNCOMMITTED` | Possible   | Possible            | Possible     | Lowest    |
| `READ_COMMITTED`   | Prevented  | Possible            | Possible     | Low       |
| `REPEATABLE_READ`  | Prevented  | Prevented           | Possible*    | Moderate  |
| `SERIALIZABLE`     | Prevented  | Prevented           | Prevented    | Highest   |

*The standard permits phantoms at `REPEATABLE_READ`; PostgreSQL's snapshot-based
implementation prevents them anyway, which is a good illustration of how much
real behaviour differs from the standard.

Setting the level in JDBC is one call, made before the transaction's first
statement.

```java
conn.setAutoCommit(false);
conn.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ);
try {
    // every read in this transaction sees a consistent snapshot
    ...
    conn.commit();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    conn.rollback();
    throw e;
}
```

**Defaults differ by vendor**, which is a frequent source of behaviour that
changes when a system is migrated.

| Database   | Default level      |
| ---------- | ------------------ |
| PostgreSQL | `READ_COMMITTED`   |
| Oracle     | `READ_COMMITTED`   |
| SQL Server | `READ_COMMITTED`   |
| MySQL/InnoDB | `REPEATABLE_READ` |

**`SERIALIZABLE` does not mean "no errors".** On PostgreSQL it is implemented
optimistically: transactions run without extra blocking, and one is aborted with
SQL state `40001` if the engine detects that the outcome could not have arisen
from any serial order. Using it therefore requires a retry loop.

```java
for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) {
    try {
        runSerializableTransaction();
        return;
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        if (!"40001".equals(e.getSQLState()) || attempt == 3) throw e;
        Thread.sleep(50L * attempt);     // back off and try the whole thing again
    }
}
```

The practical guidance is unglamorous: **stay on the default, usually
`READ_COMMITTED`, and solve specific problems with specific tools.** Raise the
level only for a transaction that demonstrably needs it, and handle lost updates
with the locking strategies in the next topic rather than by turning the dial up
globally.

> Key Takeaways
> - Isolation trades concurrency against the anomalies a transaction may
>   observe.
> - Dirty reads see uncommitted data; non-repeatable reads see a row change;
>   phantoms see the row set change.
> - A lost update happens when two read-modify-write cycles overlap.
> - The four levels form a ladder from `READ_UNCOMMITTED` to `SERIALIZABLE`.
> - Defaults differ by vendor, so behaviour can change on migration.
> - PostgreSQL's `SERIALIZABLE` aborts conflicting transactions with state
>   `40001` and needs a retry loop.
> - Keep the default and address concrete problems with locking rather than
>   raising the level everywhere.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Open two connections and reproduce a non-repeatable read at
>    `READ_COMMITTED`, then show it disappears at `REPEATABLE_READ`.
> 2. Reproduce a lost update with two transactions that both read stock,
>    subtract one, and write it back.
> 3. Print the default isolation level for two different databases and explain
>    what would change for an application moved between them.
> 4. Implement a retry loop for `40001` and prove it works by forcing a
>    serialization conflict.
> 5. Interview: Why can raising every transaction to `SERIALIZABLE` reduce
>    throughput without removing all bugs? (Hint: what new failure does the
>    application now have to handle, and what happens if it does not?)

#### Optimistic and Pessimistic Locking

The lost update from the previous topic is the defining concurrency problem in
application code: two users load the same record, both edit it, and the second
save silently discards the first. Isolation levels do not solve it by
themselves, because the two transactions may not even overlap in time. Two
strategies do, and choosing between them is a design decision about how often
conflicts actually occur.

**Pessimistic locking assumes conflict is likely.** It takes a lock when reading
and holds it until the transaction ends, so nobody else can modify the row in
the meantime. In SQL this is `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

```java
conn.setAutoCommit(false);

// FOR UPDATE takes a row-level write lock. Any other transaction trying to
// read this row FOR UPDATE, or to update it, blocks until this one ends.
String sql = "SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = ? FOR UPDATE";
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setLong(1, productId);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        rs.next();
        int stock = rs.getInt("stock");
        if (stock < quantity) throw new OutOfStockException(productId);
    }
}

try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(
        "UPDATE products SET stock = stock - ? WHERE id = ?")) {
    ps.setInt(1, quantity);
    ps.setLong(2, productId);
    ps.executeUpdate();
}
conn.commit();      // lock released here
```

Add `NOWAIT` to fail immediately instead of blocking, or `SKIP LOCKED` to ignore
locked rows, which is the standard way to build a work queue in a database.

```sql
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
```

**Optimistic locking assumes conflict is rare.** It takes no lock. Instead each
row carries a version number, and an update only succeeds if the version is
still what the reader saw. If it is not, somebody else has written and the
update affects zero rows.

```text
  User A reads product 7, version 3        User B reads product 7, version 3
  A writes: WHERE id=7 AND version=3       B writes: WHERE id=7 AND version=3
     --> 1 row updated, version becomes 4      --> 0 rows updated: conflict
                                               B must reload and retry
```

```java
String sql = """
        UPDATE products
           SET stock = ?, version = version + 1
         WHERE id = ? AND version = ?
        """;                                  // version is the guard

try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setInt(1, newStock);
    ps.setLong(2, product.id());
    ps.setLong(3, product.version());         // the version we read earlier

    if (ps.executeUpdate() == 0) {            // zero rows means someone else won
        throw new OptimisticLockException(product.id());
    }
}
```

The zero-row result is the entire mechanism, and the caller's response is
normally to reload the record and either retry automatically or tell the user
the data changed.

| Aspect            | Pessimistic (`FOR UPDATE`)           | Optimistic (version column)        |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| Cost when no conflict | Lock overhead on every read      | None                               |
| Cost when conflict | Waiting                             | Wasted work, then a retry          |
| Failure mode      | Blocking, timeouts, deadlocks        | `0 rows updated`                   |
| Works across requests | No: locks die with the transaction | Yes: the version travels with the data |
| Best for          | Short transactions, contended rows   | Web forms, low contention          |

**The row about spanning requests is the decisive one for web applications.** A
user loading an edit form, making coffee, and saving ten minutes later cannot
hold a database lock for those ten minutes. Optimistic locking works because the
version is carried in the form and checked at save time.

**Deadlocks** are the hazard of pessimistic locking: two transactions each
holding a lock the other needs. The database detects the cycle and kills one
with a serialization or deadlock error.

```text
  T1: lock row A  ------------> wants row B
                                     ^
  T2: lock row B  ------------> wants row A
                (cycle: the database aborts one of them)
```

The usual mitigation is **consistent lock ordering**: if every transaction locks
accounts in ascending id order, no cycle can form. Combine that with short
transactions and a retry for the aborted victim.

> Key Takeaways
> - Lost updates occur when two read-modify-write cycles overlap, and need an
>   explicit strategy.
> - Pessimistic locking blocks others with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` for the life
>   of the transaction.
> - `NOWAIT` and `SKIP LOCKED` refine that behaviour, the latter underpinning
>   database work queues.
> - Optimistic locking adds a version column and guards updates with it,
>   detecting conflict by a zero-row result.
> - Only optimistic locking works across separate requests, which is why web
>   applications use it.
> - Pessimistic locking risks deadlocks; consistent lock ordering prevents the
>   cycles.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `version` column to a table and implement optimistic update checking,
>    then prove two concurrent updaters cannot both succeed.
> 2. Implement the same protection with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and compare the
>    two under a load test with high and low contention.
> 3. Build a job queue using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and run three workers
>    against it, confirming no job is processed twice.
> 4. Construct a deadlock with two transactions locking two rows in opposite
>    orders, capture the error, and fix it by ordering the locks.
> 5. Interview: A wiki loses edits when two people edit the same page. Which
>    strategy fits, and what does the user see when a conflict occurs? (Hint:
>    how long is the gap between reading the page and saving it?)

#### Transaction Boundaries in Layered Code

Knowing how to commit is easy. Knowing **where** to commit is the design
question, and getting it wrong produces systems that are correct in every unit
test and inconsistent in production.

The rule is: **a transaction boundary belongs at the boundary of a business
operation, not at the boundary of a database call.** "Place an order" is one
operation and therefore one transaction, even though it inserts an order, three
line items, and a stock adjustment.

The most common anti-pattern puts a transaction inside each repository method.

```java
// WRONG: each method opens its own connection and commits independently.
public class OrderService {
    public void placeOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.insert(order);        // transaction 1: commits
        for (Line line : order.lines()) {
            lineRepository.insert(line);      // transaction 2..n: commit
        }
        stockRepository.decrement(order);     // transaction n+1: may fail
    }                                         // leaves an order with no stock taken
}
```

Each call is atomic on its own, and the operation as a whole is not atomic at
all. A failure in `decrement` leaves a committed order whose stock was never
reduced.

The fix is to let the **service layer own the transaction** and have
repositories participate in one they are given.

```text
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  |  Controller / handler    no transaction knowledge  |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  |  Service    <-- transaction begins and ends HERE   |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  |  Repository   uses the connection it is given      |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  |  Database                                           |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
```

Passing the connection explicitly is the plainest way to express this.

```java
public class OrderService {
    private final DataSource dataSource;
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final StockRepository stock;

    public void placeOrder(Order order) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
            conn.setAutoCommit(false);
            try {
                long id = orders.insert(conn, order);      // same connection
                orders.insertLines(conn, id, order.lines());
                stock.decrement(conn, order.lines());       // same transaction
                conn.commit();                              // one boundary
            } catch (Exception e) {
                conn.rollback();
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The connection parameter on every repository method is explicit and noisy, which
is why frameworks hide it. Spring's `@Transactional` binds a connection to the
current thread so repositories can obtain "the current transaction's connection"
without it being passed, and 17.3 covers the mechanics. The **design** is
identical; only the plumbing differs.

Four rules make boundaries behave in practice.

**Do not nest transactions accidentally.** A service method that calls another
transactional service method must not start a second transaction; it should join
the existing one. This is exactly the problem propagation settings address in
Spring.

**Keep remote calls outside the boundary.** A payment gateway call inside a
transaction holds locks for the duration of someone else's network latency, and
cannot be rolled back anyway.

```java
// The external call happens first, outside the transaction.
PaymentResult payment = paymentGateway.charge(card, amount);   // slow, external
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
    conn.setAutoCommit(false);
    orders.insert(conn, order.withPayment(payment.reference()));
    conn.commit();                                             // fast, local
}
```

**Read-only work should say so.** Marking a transaction read-only lets the
database and pool skip bookkeeping, and documents intent.

```java
conn.setReadOnly(true);    // a hint: some drivers route to a replica
```

**Let exceptions cross the boundary.** The service decides to roll back; the
layer above decides what the user sees. A repository that catches and logs a
`SQLException` without rethrowing hides the very failure that should have
triggered the rollback.

> Key Takeaways
> - A transaction should span one business operation, not one database call.
> - Repositories must participate in a transaction, never start their own.
> - The service layer is the natural place to open, commit, and roll back.
> - Passing the connection explicitly makes the boundary visible; frameworks
>   hide it but keep the design.
> - Never call an external system inside a transaction; do it before or after.
> - Mark read-only work as read-only to save bookkeeping and express intent.
> - Swallowing exceptions in a repository defeats rollback entirely.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Refactor a service whose repository methods each commit so that one
>    transaction spans the whole operation.
> 2. Write a test that makes the last step of a multi-step operation fail and
>    asserts that nothing was persisted.
> 3. Move an external HTTP call out of a transaction and describe what improves,
>    naming the resource that is no longer held.
> 4. Sketch the method signatures a repository needs when the connection is
>    passed explicitly, and then when a framework binds it to the thread.
> 5. Interview: Where would you place the transaction boundary for "transfer
>    funds, then notify both account holders", and why? (Hint: which of those
>    three actions can be undone by a rollback?)

<a id="164-object-relational-mapping"></a>
### 16.4 Object-Relational Mapping

This subchapter covers why objects and tables fit together badly, the pattern
that isolates data access from the rest of an application, and the mapping tools
built on JDBC that automate most of the translation, along with the performance
traps they introduce.

#### The Object-Relational Impedance Mismatch

Object-oriented programs and relational databases are both excellent models, and
they disagree about almost everything. "Impedance mismatch" is borrowed from
electrical engineering, where connecting two circuits with different impedance
loses power at the junction. Connecting objects to tables loses something
similar, and every mapping tool is an attempt to minimise the loss.

Five specific disagreements account for most of the difficulty.

| Concern    | Object model                          | Relational model                      |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Identity   | Reference equality plus `equals`      | Primary key value                      |
| Structure  | Nested objects, arbitrary graphs       | Flat rows joined by foreign keys       |
| Inheritance | Built into the type system            | No concept of it at all                |
| Association | Directional references, collections    | Symmetric foreign keys and join tables |
| Navigation | Follow a reference, then another       | Join everything needed in one query    |

**Identity.** Java has three notions: the same reference, equal by `equals`, and
the same database row. A row loaded twice in one program can produce two objects
that are `equals` but not `==`, or two objects representing one row with
divergent state. Mapping tools solve this with an identity map, guaranteeing one
object per row per session.

**Structure and granularity.** An `Order` containing a list of `OrderLine`
objects and an embedded `Address` is one concept in Java and three or four
tables in SQL. Reassembling one object from several rows is the mapper's core
job.

```text
  Object graph                        Relational tables
  ------------                        -----------------
  Order                               orders
   +-- customer: Customer              id | customer_id | shipping_...
   +-- lines: List<OrderLine>         ------------------------------
   |     +-- product: Product          order_lines
   +-- shippingAddress: Address         id | order_id | product_id | qty
        (no table of its own)          ------------------------------
                                       customers, products
```

**Inheritance has no relational equivalent.** If `CreditCardPayment` and
`BankTransferPayment` both extend `Payment`, there are three ways to store them,
each with real costs.

| Strategy               | Layout                                   | Trade-off                         |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Single table           | One table, a discriminator column, nullable columns for every subtype | Fast, no joins; cannot enforce `NOT NULL` on subtype fields |
| Joined table           | A base table plus one table per subtype  | Properly normalised; every read is a join |
| Table per class        | One complete table per concrete subtype  | No joins; querying the base type needs a union, and keys must be shared |

**Navigation differs fundamentally.** In Java you write
`order.customer().address().city()`, following one reference at a time. Done
naively against a database that is three queries, and inside a loop over a
hundred orders it is hundreds of queries. SQL wants one join. This single
difference produces the N+1 problem covered at the end of this subchapter.

**The mismatch cannot be eliminated, only managed.** There are three honest
responses, and mature systems use more than one.

- *Write SQL by hand* with JDBC or a thin helper. Full control, no surprises,
  more code.
- *Use a mapper* such as Hibernate. Far less code for ordinary cases, at the
  price of understanding what it generates.
- *Stop mapping* and store documents or use a database whose model matches the
  data, when the data genuinely is not relational.

The mistake is believing a tool makes the mismatch disappear. It moves it: the
questions become "which fetch strategy" and "why did that generate 200 queries",
which are the same old questions in new clothes.

> Key Takeaways
> - Objects and relations model identity, structure, inheritance, association,
>   and navigation differently.
> - One object often spans several tables, so reassembly is the mapper's central
>   job.
> - Relational databases have no inheritance; the three mapping strategies each
>   trade normalisation against join cost.
> - Reference-by-reference navigation conflicts with set-based joins and is the
>   root of N+1 queries.
> - Mapping tools manage the mismatch rather than removing it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model an `Order` with lines, a customer, and an embedded address, then draw
>    the tables required and mark where one object spans several rows.
> 2. Write the DDL for a `Payment` hierarchy under all three inheritance
>    strategies and list one query each makes awkward.
> 3. Load the same row twice into two objects, modify one, and describe what the
>    program now believes about the row.
> 4. Interview: Name two things an object model expresses that a relational
>    schema cannot, and say how each is usually worked around. (Hint: consider
>    subtypes and the direction of a reference.)

#### The Data Access Object Pattern

Scattering JDBC across an application couples business logic to the database. A
service that opens connections, writes SQL, and reads result sets cannot be
tested without a database, cannot be reused against a different store, and mixes
two entirely different concerns in one method.

The **Data Access Object** (DAO) pattern, also called the Repository pattern in
domain-driven designs, puts all persistence for one type behind an interface
expressed in domain terms.

```text
  Service layer       "save this order"       knows nothing about SQL
        |
        v
  +-------------------+
  | OrderRepository   |   interface: findById, save, findByCustomer
  +-------------------+
        ^         ^
        |         |
  JdbcOrderRepo   InMemoryOrderRepo        one for production, one for tests
        |
        v
    database
```

The interface speaks about orders, not about rows.

```java
public interface OrderRepository {
    Optional<Order> findById(long id);
    List<Order> findByCustomer(long customerId);
    long save(Order order);
    void delete(long id);
}
```

Notice what is absent: no `Connection`, no `SQLException`, no SQL. The interface
is a contract the rest of the application can depend on, and the implementation
is free to satisfy it with JDBC, with an ORM, or with a hash map in a test.

```java
public class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {

    private static final String FIND_BY_ID =
            "SELECT id, customer_id, total, placed_at FROM orders WHERE id = ?";

    private final DataSource dataSource;

    public JdbcOrderRepository(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<Order> findById(long id) {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(FIND_BY_ID)) {
            ps.setLong(1, id);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                return rs.next() ? Optional.of(mapRow(rs)) : Optional.empty();
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            // Translate at the boundary: callers never import java.sql.
            throw new DataAccessException("finding order " + id, e);
        }
    }

    // One place that knows how a row becomes an Order.
    private Order mapRow(ResultSet rs) throws SQLException {
        return new Order(
                rs.getLong("id"),
                rs.getLong("customer_id"),
                rs.getBigDecimal("total"),
                rs.getObject("placed_at", OffsetDateTime.class));
    }
}
```

Four design points are doing the work here.

**The row mapper is extracted.** `mapRow` is the single place that knows the
column-to-field correspondence, so a schema change touches one method rather
than every query.

**Exceptions are translated.** `SQLException` is caught and rethrown as an
unchecked domain exception, so the service layer never handles SQL states and
never imports `java.sql`. This is the boundary discussed in 16.1.

**SQL is a constant, not an inline string.** Named constants make the statements
greppable and keep methods readable.

**Transactions are not started here.** As 16.3 established, boundaries belong in
the service layer, so methods that participate in a larger operation take a
`Connection` parameter.

```java
// Two overloads: one standalone, one participating in a caller's transaction.
public long save(Order order) {
    try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
        return save(conn, order);
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        throw new DataAccessException("saving order", e);
    }
}

public long save(Connection conn, Order order) throws SQLException { ... }
```

The payoff is testability. A service depending on `OrderRepository` can be
tested against an in-memory implementation in microseconds, while the JDBC
implementation is tested separately against a real database, typically in a
container.

```java
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Test
    void rejectsOrderBelowMinimum() {
        OrderRepository repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();   // no database
        OrderService service = new OrderService(repo);

        assertThrows(OrderTooSmallException.class,
                () -> service.place(anOrderTotalling("1.00")));
    }
}
```

A caution: do not let the interface leak the database back in. A method named
`findByCustomerIdJoinLinesOrderByPlacedAtDesc` is SQL spelled in Java. Keep the
vocabulary of the domain.

> Key Takeaways
> - A DAO hides all persistence for one type behind a domain-shaped interface.
> - The interface exposes no `Connection`, no SQL, and no `SQLException`.
> - A single row-mapping method localises knowledge of the schema.
> - Translate `SQLException` into an unchecked domain exception at this
>   boundary.
> - Offer an overload taking a `Connection` so the DAO can join a caller's
>   transaction.
> - The main payoff is testing services without a database.
> - Method names should describe domain questions, not the SQL that answers
>   them.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define a `CustomerRepository` interface and implement it with JDBC, keeping
>    all SQL inside the implementation.
> 2. Write an in-memory implementation of that interface and use it to test a
>    service class with no database running.
> 3. Extract a reusable `RowMapper<T>` functional interface and rewrite two
>    queries to use it.
> 4. Add a `save(Connection, Customer)` overload and use it from a service
>    method that saves a customer and an address in one transaction.
> 5. Interview: What signals that a repository interface has leaked persistence
>    concerns into the domain? (Hint: read the method names aloud and ask
>    whether a domain expert would recognise them.)

#### Introduction to JPA and Hibernate

The DAO pattern organises JDBC but does not reduce it. Every entity still needs
its mapping method, its insert, its update, and its select, and most of that
code is mechanical. Object-relational mapping tools automate it.

**Hibernate** is the ORM that popularised this in Java. **JPA**, the Jakarta
Persistence API, is the standard it inspired: a set of interfaces and
annotations, with Hibernate, EclipseLink, and others as implementations. The
relationship mirrors JDBC and its drivers.

```text
   Your code
      |  annotations and EntityManager      (jakarta.persistence)
      v
   +--------------------------------------------+
   |            JPA specification                |
   +--------------------------------------------+
      |                    |
      v                    v
   Hibernate          EclipseLink        implementations
      |                    |
      +---------+----------+
                v
              JDBC  ->  driver  ->  database
```

ORMs sit **on top of** JDBC. They do not replace it; they generate the SQL and
call the same `PreparedStatement` you would have written.

The central object is the `EntityManager`, obtained from an
`EntityManagerFactory` configured once at startup.

```java
EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("shop");
EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();

em.getTransaction().begin();

Order order = new Order(customer, OffsetDateTime.now());
order.addLine(new OrderLine(product, 2));

em.persist(order);                  // no INSERT is written by you

em.getTransaction().commit();       // Hibernate issues the INSERTs here
em.close();
```

The contrast with the JDBC version is the point:

| Operation        | JDBC                                            | JPA                               |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Insert           | Write SQL, bind parameters, read generated keys | `em.persist(entity)`              |
| Find by key      | Write SQL, execute, map the row                 | `em.find(Order.class, id)`        |
| Update           | Write SQL, bind changed columns                 | Modify the object; it is detected |
| Delete           | Write SQL, bind the key                         | `em.remove(entity)`               |
| Query            | SQL, mapped by hand                             | JPQL, mapped automatically        |

The update row is the one that surprises people. Inside a transaction, changing
a managed object's field is enough; the provider compares it against the state
it loaded and issues an `UPDATE` at flush time. This is **dirty checking**, and
the next topics explain the machinery behind it.

Queries are written in **JPQL**, which looks like SQL but names entities and
fields rather than tables and columns.

```java
// Entity name 'Order', field 'placedAt' -- not table and column names.
List<Order> recent = em.createQuery(
        "SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.customer.id = :cid AND o.placedAt > :since",
        Order.class)
    .setParameter("cid", customerId)      // named parameters, still bound safely
    .setParameter("since", cutoff)
    .getResultList();
```

**What you give up is worth stating plainly.** SQL is generated, so you must be
able to read the generated SQL to diagnose performance. Behaviour depends on
whether an object is managed, which is new state to reason about. And the
learning curve is real: lazy loading, flush timing, and cascade rules all bite
before they help.

A pragmatic position, common in production systems: use JPA for the routine
create-read-update-delete work that is most of an application, and drop to SQL,
through a native query or a JDBC template, for reporting and anything
performance-critical. The two coexist happily on the same connection and
transaction.

> Key Takeaways
> - JPA is the specification; Hibernate and EclipseLink are implementations.
> - ORMs generate SQL and run it through JDBC rather than replacing JDBC.
> - `EntityManager` is the entry point, obtained from a factory built at
>   startup.
> - `persist`, `find`, and `remove` replace hand-written statements, and updates
>   are detected automatically.
> - JPQL queries name entities and fields, not tables and columns.
> - The cost is indirection: you must read generated SQL and track entity state.
> - Mixing JPA for routine work with SQL for reporting is normal and healthy.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Configure a JPA persistence unit against an in-memory H2 database and
>    persist one entity.
> 2. Enable SQL logging and record how many statements a single `persist` of a
>    parent with three children produces.
> 3. Write the same "find orders for a customer since a date" query in JDBC and
>    in JPQL, and compare the amount of code.
> 4. Load an entity, change a field inside a transaction without calling any
>    save method, and confirm the change reaches the database.
> 5. Interview: If an ORM generates the SQL, why should a developer still be
>    able to read SQL? (Hint: what do you do when a page that should take 50
>    milliseconds takes 5 seconds?)

#### Entities, Identifiers, and Relationships

An **entity** is a class whose instances correspond to rows in a table. In JPA
it is an ordinary class with annotations describing that correspondence, and the
requirements are modest: the `@Entity` annotation, an identifier, and a
no-argument constructor the provider uses when building instances from rows.

```java
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")                       // needed: "order" is a SQL keyword
public class Order {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)   // the database assigns it
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "placed_at", nullable = false)
    private OffsetDateTime placedAt;

    @Column(precision = 12, scale = 2)        // maps to NUMERIC(12,2)
    private BigDecimal total;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)              // store the name, never the ordinal
    private OrderStatus status;

    protected Order() { }                     // required by JPA, not by callers

    public Order(OffsetDateTime placedAt) { this.placedAt = placedAt; }
}
```

`@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` deserves the comment it has. The default,
`ORDINAL`, stores the enum's position, so inserting a new constant in the middle
silently reinterprets every existing row.

**Identifier generation** has four strategies, and the choice affects batching
and performance more than it first appears.

| Strategy   | Mechanism                                  | Note                                        |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| `IDENTITY` | Auto-increment column; the key is known only after insert | Disables JDBC batching of inserts |
| `SEQUENCE` | Database sequence, read before insert      | Preferred where supported; allows batching  |
| `TABLE`    | A dedicated table simulating a sequence    | Portable, slow, contended                   |
| `AUTO`     | The provider chooses                        | Convenient, but hides the real behaviour    |

`SEQUENCE` is the default recommendation on PostgreSQL and Oracle precisely
because the provider can fetch keys in advance and batch the inserts, which
`IDENTITY` prevents.

**Relationships** are where entities stop being simple. Four annotations cover
the cardinalities.

```text
  @OneToOne     Order  ------- 1:1 -------  Invoice
  @ManyToOne    OrderLine  ---- N:1 ------  Order      (FK lives here)
  @OneToMany    Order  ------- 1:N -------  OrderLine
  @ManyToMany   Product  ----- N:M -------  Category   (join table)
```

The most important is `@ManyToOne`, because it is the side that owns the foreign
key and therefore the side that controls what is written.

```java
@Entity
public class OrderLine {

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)        // ALWAYS lazy: the default is EAGER
    @JoinColumn(name = "order_id", nullable = false)   // the FK column
    private Order order;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "product_id")
    private Product product;

    private int quantity;
}
```

```java
@Entity
public class Order {
    // mappedBy names the field on the OTHER side that owns the foreign key.
    // Without it, JPA assumes a join table and creates one.
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order",
               cascade = CascadeType.ALL,      // persist/remove lines with the order
               orphanRemoval = true)           // removing from the list deletes the row
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    // Keep both sides of the relationship consistent in one place.
    public void addLine(OrderLine line) {
        lines.add(line);
        line.setOrder(this);         // without this, order_id is written as NULL
    }
}
```

Three rules prevent most relationship bugs.

**Make every association lazy.** `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` default to
`EAGER`, meaning every load of an `OrderLine` also loads its `Order` and its
`Product`, whether or not you touch them. Override both.

**Set both sides.** Java references are directional; a foreign key is not. If
you add a line to the list but never set its `order` field, the owning side sees
null and the database gets null. A helper method like `addLine` is the standard
fix.

**Understand `cascade` and `orphanRemoval`.** Cascade propagates operations from
parent to children, which is right for lines that cannot exist without their
order and wrong for a `Product` shared by many lines. `CascadeType.ALL` on a
shared entity will eventually delete something it should not.

Finally, `equals` and `hashCode` on entities are genuinely tricky, because the
identifier is null before persisting and non-null afterwards. Basing them on the
id breaks any `HashSet` an entity was added to before saving. The safe options
are to use a business key, or to assign a UUID in the constructor.

> Key Takeaways
> - An entity needs `@Entity`, an `@Id`, and a no-argument constructor.
> - Store enums with `EnumType.STRING`; ordinals break when constants are
>   reordered.
> - `SEQUENCE` generation allows insert batching; `IDENTITY` disables it.
> - `@ManyToOne` owns the foreign key and controls what is written.
> - `mappedBy` marks the inverse side; omitting it produces an unwanted join
>   table.
> - Override the `EAGER` default on `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne`.
> - Keep both sides of a bidirectional association in sync with a helper method.
> - Cascade suits parent-child ownership and corrupts shared references.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Map `Order` and `OrderLine` with a bidirectional one-to-many, then save an
>    order with two lines and inspect the generated SQL.
> 2. Remove the `line.setOrder(this)` call and observe what is written to the
>    foreign key column.
> 3. Store an enum with the default `ORDINAL`, add a new constant at the start,
>    and show how existing rows change meaning.
> 4. Compare the SQL generated when inserting 100 entities with `IDENTITY`
>    against `SEQUENCE` generation.
> 5. Interview: Why is implementing `equals` on an entity using its generated id
>    dangerous? (Hint: what is the id's value between construction and commit,
>    and what happens to an object already inside a hash-based collection?)

#### Persistence Context and Entity Lifecycle

The `EntityManager` is not a thin wrapper over SQL. It maintains a
**persistence context**: an in-memory cache of the entities it is managing, plus
a record of what they looked like when loaded. Almost every behaviour that feels
like magic in JPA comes from this one structure.

The persistence context does three jobs.

**It is an identity map.** Within one context, one database row is represented
by exactly one object. Loading the same order twice returns the same instance,
so `==` holds, and there is no possibility of two divergent copies.

```java
Order a = em.find(Order.class, 1L);     // SELECT issued
Order b = em.find(Order.class, 1L);     // no SELECT: served from the context
assert a == b;                          // the same object, guaranteed
```

**It performs dirty checking.** At flush time the provider compares each managed
entity against its loaded snapshot and generates `UPDATE` statements for what
changed. This is why there is no `update` method.

```java
em.getTransaction().begin();
Order order = em.find(Order.class, 1L);
```
