```java
order.setStatus(OrderStatus.SHIPPED);   // just a setter on a plain object
em.getTransaction().commit();           // UPDATE orders SET status=? WHERE id=?
```

**It buffers writes.** `persist` does not necessarily issue an `INSERT`
immediately; statements are queued and flushed before a query that might be
affected, or at commit. This is what allows batching.

Entities move between four states, and knowing which state an object is in
explains most confusing behaviour.

```text
              new Order(...)
                    |
                    v
              [ TRANSIENT ]  not in the context, no database row
                    |
              persist()
                    v
              [ MANAGED ]  <----- find(), query results, merge()
                 |     ^          tracked; changes are written automatically
        detach() |     | merge()
        close()  |     |
                 v     |
              [ DETACHED ]  has a row, but no context is watching it
                    |
              remove()  (from MANAGED)
                    v
              [ REMOVED ]  scheduled for DELETE at flush
```

| State     | In the context | Has a row | Changes tracked |
| --------- | -------------- | --------- | --------------- |
| Transient | No             | No        | No              |
| Managed   | Yes            | Yes (or will have) | Yes    |
| Detached  | No             | Yes       | No              |
| Removed   | Yes            | Until flush | Deletion queued |

**The detached state causes the most confusion.** Once the `EntityManager`
closes, everything it managed becomes detached. Setters on a detached object
change nothing in the database, and accessing an unloaded lazy association
throws `LazyInitializationException`. This is exactly what happens when an
entity loaded in a service is modified in a web controller after the transaction
has ended.

```java
// The context is closed, so this object is detached.
order.setStatus(OrderStatus.CANCELLED);    // changes nothing in the database

// merge() copies the state onto a managed instance and returns THAT instance.
em.getTransaction().begin();
Order managed = em.merge(order);           // note: order itself stays detached
managed.setStatus(OrderStatus.CANCELLED);  // this one is tracked
em.getTransaction().commit();
```

The comment on `merge` is the detail people miss: it returns a different object,
and continuing to use the argument silently discards changes.

**Flushing** is the act of synchronising the context with the database, and it
happens automatically at commit and before queries whose results the pending
changes could affect. Calling `em.flush()` manually is occasionally necessary,
for example to surface a constraint violation at a specific point.

Two cache levels are worth distinguishing, because "the cache" means different
things to different people.

| Level | Scope                     | Enabled            |
| ----- | ------------------------- | ------------------ |
| First | One persistence context   | Always; cannot be turned off |
| Second | Shared across contexts   | Opt-in, configured per entity |

Finally, **the context should be short-lived**. It grows as entities are loaded,
so a context that loads a hundred thousand rows holds a hundred thousand objects
and their snapshots. In long loops, clear it periodically.

```java
for (int i = 0; i < records.size(); i++) {
    em.persist(toEntity(records.get(i)));
    if (i % 500 == 0) {
        em.flush();     // send the queued INSERTs
        em.clear();     // detach everything: release the memory
    }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The persistence context is an identity map plus a snapshot of loaded state.
> - One row maps to exactly one object per context, so repeated `find` calls
>   return the same instance.
> - Dirty checking makes explicit update calls unnecessary inside a transaction.
> - Entities are transient, managed, detached, or removed, and behaviour depends
>   on which.
> - Closing the context detaches everything, after which setters do nothing and
>   lazy access throws.
> - `merge` returns a managed copy; the object passed in stays detached.
> - The first-level cache is always on; the second level is opt-in and shared.
> - Flush and clear inside bulk loops to keep memory bounded.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Call `find` twice for the same id in one context and assert the two
>    references are identical. Repeat across two contexts.
> 2. Modify an entity inside a transaction with no save call and confirm from
>    the SQL log that an `UPDATE` was issued.
> 3. Load an entity, close the context, modify it, and show the change is lost.
>    Then fix it with `merge`, using the returned instance.
> 4. Persist 100,000 entities without `flush`/`clear`, observe heap growth, then
>    add them and compare.
> 5. Interview: A controller throws `LazyInitializationException` when rendering
>    a template, though the service loaded the entity successfully. What is
>    going on? (Hint: what state is the entity in by the time the template
>    runs?)

#### Lazy Loading and the N+1 Query Problem

Lazy loading is the mechanism that makes ORMs usable, and the N+1 problem is the
cost of using it without thinking. Both follow from the navigation mismatch
described at the start of this subchapter.

**Lazy loading** means an association is not fetched until it is used. Loading
an `Order` does not load its lines; the provider puts a **proxy** in the field,
and the first method call on that proxy triggers a query.

```text
  em.find(Order.class, 1)
        |
        v
   Order { id=1, lines = [ proxy, not yet loaded ] }      1 query
        |
  order.getLines().size()      <-- touching it
        |
        v
   SELECT * FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = 1           2nd query
```

That is efficient when you did not need the lines and disastrous in a loop.

```java
// N+1: one query for the orders, then one per order for its lines.
List<Order> orders = em.createQuery("SELECT o FROM Order o", Order.class)
                       .getResultList();          // 1 query -> 100 orders

for (Order order : orders) {
    total = total.add(order.getLines().stream()   // 1 query PER ORDER
                           .map(OrderLine::subtotal)
                           .reduce(ZERO, BigDecimal::add));
}
// 101 queries, ~1 ms each, for work a single join does in ~5 ms
```

The signature of this problem in production is a page that is fast with test
data and slow with real data, where the slowness scales linearly with row count
and the database shows thousands of near-identical small queries.

There are four fixes, and they suit different situations.

**A join fetch** loads the association in the same query. It is the usual answer
when you know you need the children.

```java
List<Order> orders = em.createQuery("""
        SELECT DISTINCT o FROM Order o
        LEFT JOIN FETCH o.lines
        """, Order.class).getResultList();   // 1 query, lines already populated
```

`DISTINCT` is needed because the join multiplies the parent row by the number of
children.

**An entity graph** expresses the same thing declaratively, which keeps the
query reusable with different fetch plans.

```java
EntityGraph<Order> graph = em.createEntityGraph(Order.class);
graph.addAttributeNodes("lines");

List<Order> orders = em.createQuery("SELECT o FROM Order o", Order.class)
        .setHint("jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph", graph)
        .getResultList();
```

**Batch fetching** does not eliminate the extra queries but collapses them,
turning N queries into N/size queries using an `IN` clause.

```java
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")
@BatchSize(size = 50)          // Hibernate: fetch lines for 50 orders at a time
private List<OrderLine> lines;
```

**A projection** avoids loading entities at all, which is often the best answer
for reports and list views that only display a few fields.

```java
// Select exactly what the screen needs, in one query, with no entities involved.
List<OrderSummary> summaries = em.createQuery("""
        SELECT new com.shop.OrderSummary(o.id, o.placedAt, sum(l.price * l.quantity))
        FROM Order o JOIN o.lines l
        GROUP BY o.id, o.placedAt
        """, OrderSummary.class).getResultList();
```

| Fix           | Queries      | Best for                                  |
| ------------- | ------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| Join fetch    | 1            | Known-needed associations on one query    |
| Entity graph  | 1            | The same query with different fetch plans |
| Batch size    | 1 + N/size   | Associations needed sometimes             |
| Projection    | 1            | Read-only lists and reports               |

**The eager trap.** The instinct on meeting N+1 is to mark everything `EAGER`.
That replaces one problem with a worse one: every load of an entity drags in its
whole object graph, so fetching a single order pulls its customer, the
customer's other orders, and their lines. Fetch strategy is a property of the
**use case**, not of the mapping, which is why the association stays lazy and
the query decides.

**How to detect it.** Turn on statement logging in development and count.

```text
  hibernate.show_sql=true
  hibernate.format_sql=true
  logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
```

Better still, assert on the count in tests, so a regression fails the build
rather than a user's page.

```java
// Using a query-counting datasource proxy such as datasource-proxy.
@Test
void listingOrdersUsesOneQuery() {
    SQLStatementCountValidator.reset();
    orderService.listRecent();
    SQLStatementCountValidator.assertSelectCount(1);   // fails if N+1 returns
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Lazy loading defers an association's query until the association is touched.
> - N+1 means one query for a list plus one per element, and it scales with data
>   volume.
> - `JOIN FETCH` with `DISTINCT` solves it for a known query.
> - Entity graphs express the fetch plan separately, so the query stays
>   reusable.
> - Batch fetching reduces N queries to N divided by the batch size.
> - Projections skip entities entirely and are usually right for lists and
>   reports.
> - Marking associations `EAGER` trades N+1 for uncontrolled graph loading.
> - Log and assert query counts so regressions fail tests, not users.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build 100 orders with 5 lines each, load them lazily in a loop, and count
>    the statements in the SQL log.
> 2. Rewrite the query with `LEFT JOIN FETCH`, confirm the count drops to one,
>    and explain why `DISTINCT` is required.
> 3. Apply a batch size of 25 to the association and record the resulting query
>    count.
> 4. Write a projection query returning only the fields a summary table
>    displays, and compare its timing with loading full entities.
> 5. Add an automated test asserting the query count for one endpoint, then
>    reintroduce the N+1 and confirm the test fails.
> 6. Interview: An endpoint takes 40 milliseconds in staging and 9 seconds in
>    production with the same code. What would you look at first? (Hint: what
>    differs between the two environments that would multiply a per-row cost?)

<a id="17-the-spring-framework"></a>
## 17. The Spring Framework

Spring is the framework most Java applications are built on, and it exists to
solve one problem: how objects find the other objects they depend on without
being welded to them. This chapter starts with that problem, builds up
dependency injection and the container that performs it, then covers the three
things Spring layers on top of it, aspect-oriented programming, data access, and
the web layer, finishing with the annotations that drive all of it.

<a id="171-inversion-of-control-and-dependency-injection"></a>
### 17.1 Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection

This subchapter builds the core idea from the ground up: why constructing your
own collaborators causes trouble, how inverting that responsibility fixes it,
and how Spring's container performs the inversion in practice.

#### Tight Coupling in Plain Java

Every object needs other objects to do its work. An order service needs a
repository, the repository needs a data source, the data source needs a
configuration. The question that determines an application's flexibility is a
narrow one: **who creates those collaborators?**

The obvious answer is that each class creates its own, with `new`.

```java
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final EmailSender emailSender;

    public OrderService() {
        // This class decides exactly which implementations it uses,
        // and how they are configured.
        this.repository = new JdbcOrderRepository(
                new HikariDataSource(loadConfig()));
        this.emailSender = new SmtpEmailSender("smtp.example.com", 587);
    }

    public void place(Order order) {
        repository.save(order);
        emailSender.sendConfirmation(order);
    }
}
```

This compiles, runs, and is a serious design problem. The class has taken on
three responsibilities that have nothing to do with orders.

| Responsibility            | Belongs to                                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Placing an order          | This class, correctly                       |
| Choosing implementations  | Whoever assembles the application           |
| Configuring them          | Configuration, loaded once at startup       |

Four concrete consequences follow, and each one costs real time.

**It cannot be tested.** Constructing an `OrderService` opens a connection pool
and requires a mail server. A test for "an order below the minimum is rejected"
now needs a database and SMTP running, which turns a one-millisecond unit test
into a fragile integration test.

```java
@Test
void rejectsOrderBelowMinimum() {
    OrderService service = new OrderService();   // opens a real connection pool
    ...                                          // and needs a real mail server
}
```

**Implementations cannot be swapped.** Sending mail through a different provider
means editing `OrderService`, a class that has nothing to do with mail. The same
applies to every other class that hard-codes `SmtpEmailSender`.

**Configuration is scattered.** The SMTP host lives inside a service class, so
finding every configuration value in the application means reading every class.

**Objects are duplicated.** Each service that constructs its own
`HikariDataSource` gets a separate connection pool. Ten services mean ten pools
and ten times the connections the database expects.

The dependency direction is what makes this rigid.

```text
  Tightly coupled                      Loosely coupled
  ---------------                      ---------------
  OrderService                         OrderService
       |  new                               |  depends on
       v                                    v
  JdbcOrderRepository  (concrete)      OrderRepository  (interface)
                                            ^
                                            |  implements
                                       JdbcOrderRepository

  The service is bound to a class.     The service is bound to a contract.
```

Programming against an interface is half the fix. The service should declare
*what* it needs, not *which* implementation, and something else should supply
it.

```java
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;   // an interface
    private final EmailSender emailSender;      // an interface

    // The caller supplies the collaborators. This class no longer
    // knows or cares which implementations they are.
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository, EmailSender emailSender) {
        this.repository = repository;
        this.emailSender = emailSender;
    }
}
```

The class is now testable with fakes, works with any implementation, and holds
no configuration. What has changed is that somebody else must do the assembling,
and that somebody is the subject of the rest of this subchapter.

> Key Takeaways
> - Every object needs collaborators; the design question is who creates them.
> - Using `new` inside a class binds it to specific implementations and their
>   configuration.
> - Hard-coded dependencies make unit tests require real infrastructure.
> - Swapping an implementation then means editing unrelated classes.
> - Self-constructed resources such as connection pools get duplicated per
>   class.
> - Depending on interfaces and accepting collaborators as parameters removes
>   all four problems.
> - The assembly work does not disappear; it moves somewhere that owns it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `ReportService` that constructs its own `JdbcTemplate` and a file
>    writer, then list everything a unit test of it would require.
> 2. Refactor that class to accept both collaborators as constructor parameters,
>    and write a test using in-memory fakes.
> 3. Count how many places in a small project call `new` on a class that
>    represents infrastructure rather than data.
> 4. Interview: A class is described as "hard to test". What is usually true
>    about its constructor? (Hint: what does the test have to provide before the
>    first assertion can run?)

#### Inversion of Control as a Design Principle

The previous topic ended by moving object creation out of the class that uses
the objects. That move has a name: **Inversion of Control**, usually shortened
to IoC. Something that the class used to control, namely obtaining its
collaborators, is now controlled by something else.

The name is broader than dependency management. Control is inverted whenever a
framework calls your code rather than your code calling a library.

```text
  Library style                        Framework style
  -------------                        ---------------
  your code -> calls -> library        framework -> calls -> your code

  You own the flow.                    The framework owns the flow.
  e.g. calling Collections.sort        e.g. Spring calling your controller
```

This is sometimes called the Hollywood Principle: "don't call us, we'll call
you". A servlet container calls your servlet; a test framework calls your test
method; Spring calls your controller. In all three cases you write the pieces
and something else decides when they run.

**Dependency Injection (DI) is the specific form of IoC that this subchapter is
about**: the inverted control is specifically the control over supplying
dependencies. The two terms are often used interchangeably, but the relationship
is that DI is one kind of IoC.

```text
  Inversion of Control  (broad principle)
      |
      +-- Dependency Injection      supplying collaborators from outside
      +-- Template Method           the base class controls the algorithm
      +-- Callbacks and listeners   the framework decides when to invoke
      +-- Service Locator           the object asks a registry for what it needs
```

The last entry is worth contrasting, because it is the alternative that looks
similar and behaves worse. With a **service locator**, the object still fetches
its own dependencies, just from a registry instead of with `new`.

```java
// SERVICE LOCATOR: the dependency is still hidden inside the class.
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository =
            ServiceRegistry.lookup(OrderRepository.class);   // hidden dependency
}

// DEPENDENCY INJECTION: the dependency is part of the public contract.
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {        // visible dependency
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
```

The difference is honesty. With injection, the constructor signature tells you
everything the class needs, and the compiler enforces it. With a locator, the
only way to discover the dependencies is to read the whole class body, and a
missing registration fails at runtime.

**The benefit that matters most in practice is testability**, and it is worth
seeing concretely.

```java
@Test
void sendsConfirmationAfterSaving() {
    var repository = new InMemoryOrderRepository();   // fast fake
    var emails = new RecordingEmailSender();          // records instead of sending
    var service = new OrderService(repository, emails);

    service.place(anOrder());

    assertEquals(1, emails.sent().size());            // no database, no SMTP
}
```

There is a cost, and it should be stated plainly. Indirection makes the flow
harder to follow: you can no longer see which implementation runs by reading the
calling class, and a wiring mistake surfaces at startup rather than at compile
time. For a small program this cost outweighs the benefit. For anything with a
test suite and more than a handful of services, it does not.

**A framework is not required.** You can practise dependency injection with
nothing but constructors, assembling everything in `main`. This is called *pure*
or *poor man's* DI, and it works well until the graph gets large.

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    DataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(config());        // one pool, shared
    OrderRepository repo = new JdbcOrderRepository(ds);
    EmailSender mail = new SmtpEmailSender(config());
    OrderService orders = new OrderService(repo, mail);    // assembled here
    new HttpServer(new OrderController(orders)).start();
}
```

That method is the **composition root**: the single place that knows every
concrete type. Spring's container is a mechanism for building this graph
automatically, from declarations, when writing it by hand stops scaling.

> Key Takeaways
> - Inversion of Control means something else owns a responsibility your code
>   used to own.
> - In framework style, the framework calls your code rather than the reverse.
> - Dependency injection is the specific inversion of who supplies
>   collaborators.
> - A service locator hides dependencies inside the class; injection puts them
>   in the signature.
> - The main practical payoff is that tests can supply fakes with no
>   infrastructure.
> - The cost is indirection and wiring errors that appear at startup, not at
>   compile time.
> - DI needs no framework; the composition root can be plain code in `main`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Assemble a three-class object graph by hand in `main` with no framework,
>    and identify the composition root.
> 2. Rewrite one class to use a static registry lookup instead, and list what
>    you lost.
> 3. Name three inversions of control in tooling you already use, outside of
>    dependency injection.
> 4. Interview: What can you tell about a class's dependencies by reading only
>    its constructor, and why does that matter? (Hint: compare it with having to
>    read every line of the class body.)

#### The Spring Container and ApplicationContext

Assembling an object graph by hand works until the graph has fifty nodes, at
which point `main` becomes a long, order-sensitive list of constructor calls
that must be edited every time a class gains a dependency. Spring's
**container** automates this. You declare what the objects are; it works out
the order and builds them.

An object managed by the container is called a **bean**. The container reads
bean definitions, resolves the dependencies between them, instantiates them in a
valid order, and holds them for the life of the application.

```text
   Configuration                Container                 Your objects
   -------------                ---------                 ------------
   @Configuration classes  -->  1. read definitions
   @Component classes           2. resolve dependencies   OrderController
   property files               3. instantiate in order  ->  OrderService
                                4. inject collaborators  ->  OrderRepository
                                5. run lifecycle hooks   ->  DataSource
                                6. hold until shutdown
```

The container is exposed through two interfaces. `BeanFactory` is the minimal
one and is rarely used directly. `ApplicationContext` extends it with everything
real applications need, and is what "the Spring container" normally means.

| Capability                 | `BeanFactory` | `ApplicationContext` |
| -------------------------- | ------------- | -------------------- |
| Bean instantiation and DI  | Yes           | Yes                   |
| Eager singleton creation   | No, lazy      | Yes, at startup       |
| Annotation processing      | No            | Yes                   |
| Property resolution        | No            | Yes                   |
| Internationalised messages | No            | Yes                   |
| Event publishing           | No            | Yes                   |
| Automatic `BeanPostProcessor` registration | No | Yes            |

Starting a container takes one line, given a configuration class.

```java
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.shop")          // find annotated classes under this package
public class AppConfig { }

public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Creating the context builds every singleton immediately.
        try (var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)) {

            // Ask for the top of the graph. Everything below it is already wired.
            OrderService orders = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
            orders.place(anOrder());

        }   // close() runs destruction callbacks on every singleton
    }
}
```

**Eager instantiation at startup is a deliberate design choice.** Every
singleton is created when the context starts, so a missing or ambiguous
dependency fails immediately with a clear error rather than at three in the
morning when a rarely used code path first runs. This is why a Spring
application that starts successfully is meaningfully more likely to be wired
correctly.

**`getBean` should appear roughly once per application.** Calling it from inside
a bean is a service locator, with all the drawbacks described in the previous
topic. The correct pattern is to retrieve the entry point once and let injection
supply everything else. In Spring Boot, even that call disappears.

The context is also a **resource for the beans inside it**, offering events,
property resolution, and a shutdown hook.

```java
@Component
public class OrderService {

    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;   // container facility

    public OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher events) {
        this.events = events;
    }

    public void place(Order order) {
        // Decouples the sender from the listeners entirely.
        events.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(order.id()));
    }
}

@Component
public class InventoryListener {
    @EventListener                                    // invoked by the container
    public void on(OrderPlacedEvent event) { ... }
}
```

There are several context implementations, chosen by how configuration is
supplied, and Spring Boot picks one for you.

| Implementation                          | Configuration source      |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`     | Java `@Configuration`     |
| `ClassPathXmlApplicationContext`         | XML on the classpath      |
| `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext` | Java, for web apps |

> Key Takeaways
> - The container builds and holds the object graph from declarations you write.
> - A container-managed object is a bean.
> - `ApplicationContext` is `BeanFactory` plus events, properties, and
>   annotation support.
> - Singletons are created eagerly at startup, so wiring errors fail fast.
> - Call `getBean` once at the entry point; calling it inside a bean is a
>   service locator.
> - Closing the context runs destruction callbacks, so use it as a resource.
> - Beans can depend on container facilities such as the event publisher.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Start an `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` with two components, retrieve
>    one, and confirm its collaborator was injected.
> 2. Print `context.getBeanDefinitionNames()` and identify which beans you
>    declared and which Spring added.
> 3. Remove a required bean and read the startup failure message, noting exactly
>    which part names the missing type.
> 4. Publish a custom event from one bean and consume it in two listeners.
> 5. Interview: Why does Spring create singletons eagerly rather than on first
>    use? (Hint: compare the cost of a slower startup with the cost of a wiring
>    error discovered in production.)

#### Constructor, Setter, and Field Injection

Spring can supply a dependency in three places: through the constructor, through
a setter, or directly into a field by reflection. They are not equivalent, and
the choice has real consequences for correctness.

**Constructor injection** passes dependencies as constructor arguments. This is
the recommended form for everything that is required.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;    // final: cannot be reassigned
    private final EmailSender emailSender;

    // Since Spring 4.3, @Autowired is unnecessary when there is exactly
    // one constructor. The container uses it automatically.
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository, EmailSender emailSender) {
        this.repository = repository;
        this.emailSender = emailSender;
    }
}
```

Four properties make this the default choice. The object is **fully
initialised** the moment it exists, so there is no window in which it is
half-built. The fields can be **final**, which makes them immutable and
thread-safe. The dependencies are **explicit** in the signature, so the class
is honest about what it needs. And the class is **usable without Spring**,
which means tests construct it with `new`.

**Setter injection** supplies the dependency after construction.

```java
@Service
public class ReportService {

    private ExportFormat format = ExportFormat.CSV;   // a working default

    @Autowired(required = false)          // optional: leave the default if absent
    public void setFormat(ExportFormat format) {
        this.format = format;
    }
}
```

This is the right tool for genuinely **optional** dependencies with a sensible
default, and for dependencies that can be reconfigured at runtime. It is the
wrong tool for required ones, because the object exists in an incomplete state
between construction and the setter call, and the field cannot be final.

**Field injection** writes straight into the field by reflection.

```java
@Service
public class InvoiceService {

    @Autowired
    private InvoiceRepository repository;   // concise, and a bad idea
}
```

It is the shortest to write and the one to avoid. The problems are not
stylistic.

| Problem                      | Consequence                                       |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Cannot be `final`            | The field is mutable for the object's whole life   |
| Invisible dependencies       | The public API says nothing about what is required |
| Not constructible with `new` | Tests need reflection or a full container          |
| Hides design smells          | Adding a tenth dependency costs one line, so nobody notices |

That last row matters more than it appears. A constructor with ten parameters is
visibly wrong and prompts a refactor. Ten annotated fields look tidy, so a class
quietly accumulates responsibilities.

```java
// The test tells the story: this is what field injection costs.
@Test
void withFieldInjection() {
    InvoiceService service = new InvoiceService();
    // repository is null. The only ways forward are reflection or
    // starting a Spring context for a test that needs neither.
}

@Test
void withConstructorInjection() {
    var service = new OrderService(new InMemoryOrderRepository(),
                                   new RecordingEmailSender());   // done
}
```

| Aspect                | Constructor      | Setter              | Field        |
| --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------- | ------------ |
| Required dependencies | Yes, enforced    | No                  | No           |
| Fields can be final   | Yes              | No                  | No           |
| Visible in the API    | Yes              | Yes                 | No           |
| Testable with `new`   | Yes              | Yes                 | No           |
| Circular dependencies | Fails at startup | Tolerated           | Tolerated    |
| Recommended for       | Everything required | Optional with defaults | Nothing  |

The last row of that table has a twist worth understanding. Constructor
injection **cannot** resolve a circular dependency, because neither object can
be built first, and Spring reports an error at startup. Setter and field
injection tolerate the cycle by building both objects and wiring them
afterwards. That sounds like an advantage and is not: a cycle between two
services is a design problem, and constructor injection surfaces it
immediately instead of letting it survive.

Spring also supports injecting collections of a type, which is how plugin-style
designs are built.

```java
@Service
public class ValidationService {

    private final List<Validator> validators;   // every Validator bean, injected

    public ValidationService(List<Validator> validators) {
        this.validators = validators;           // add a new @Component to extend
    }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Constructor injection is the default for every required dependency.
> - It guarantees a fully initialised object, allows final fields, and documents
>   requirements in the signature.
> - `@Autowired` is unnecessary on a class with a single constructor.
> - Setter injection suits optional dependencies that have working defaults.
> - Field injection hides dependencies, prevents final fields, and blocks
>   construction with `new`.
> - A constructor growing too long is useful feedback that field injection
>   suppresses.
> - Constructor injection rejects circular dependencies at startup, which is a
>   feature.
> - Injecting a `List<T>` supplies every bean of that type, enabling plugin
>   designs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same service three times, once per injection style, and try to
>    unit test each with plain `new`.
> 2. Create two services that depend on each other, first with constructor
>    injection and then with setter injection, and compare the startup
>    behaviour.
> 3. Define three implementations of a `Validator` interface and inject them all
>    as a list, then add a fourth without editing the consumer.
> 4. Take a class with eight field-injected dependencies and convert it to
>    constructor injection. Decide whether it should be split.
> 5. Interview: Why does the Spring team recommend constructor injection when
>    field injection works? (Hint: name one guarantee about object state and one
>    thing a test can do without a container.)

#### Bean Definitions and Component Scanning

The container needs to know which objects to manage. There are two ways to tell
it, and real applications use both because they suit different situations.

**Component scanning** is declaration by annotation. You mark a class, and
Spring finds it by searching packages at startup.

```java
@Service                       // "manage this class as a bean"
public class OrderService {
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) { ... }
}
```

```java
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.shop")     // search this package and everything below it
public class AppConfig { }
```

Scanning looks for classes carrying `@Component` or any annotation that is
itself annotated with `@Component`. That indirection is what makes the
stereotype annotations work: they are all specialisations of one idea.

```text
  @Component                      generic container-managed object
      |
      +-- @Service                business logic
      +-- @Repository             data access (adds exception translation)
      +-- @Controller             web request handling
      |      +-- @RestController  @Controller + @ResponseBody
      +-- @Configuration          declares other beans
```

Functionally, `@Service` and `@Component` are almost identical. They differ in
intent, which matters for readability, and `@Repository` and `@Controller` add
real behaviour covered in 17.3 and 17.4.

**Explicit `@Bean` methods** are declaration by code. A method inside a
`@Configuration` class returns an object, and the returned object becomes a
bean named after the method.

```java
@Configuration
public class DataConfig {

    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource(
            @Value("${db.url}") String url,           // injected from properties
            @Value("${db.user}") String user,
            @Value("${DB_PASSWORD}") String password) {

        var config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl(url);
        config.setUsername(user);
        config.setPassword(password);
        config.setMaximumPoolSize(10);
        return new HikariDataSource(config);          // this object becomes a bean
    }

    @Bean
    public OrderRepository orderRepository(DataSource dataSource) {
        // Parameters are resolved from the container, so this receives
        // the bean defined above.
        return new JdbcOrderRepository(dataSource);
    }
}
```

The decisive question when choosing between them: **do you own the class?**

| Situation                                  | Use               |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------- |
| Your own class, no construction logic      | `@Component` family |
| A third-party class such as `HikariDataSource` | `@Bean` method |
| Construction requires conditionals or configuration | `@Bean` method |
| Several beans of the same type with different settings | `@Bean` methods |

You cannot annotate a class from a library you did not write, which is why every
application has at least a few `@Bean` methods.

**Scanning can be narrowed** with filters, which matters for startup time in
large applications and for excluding classes that should not be beans.

```java
@ComponentScan(
    basePackages = "com.shop",
    excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(
            type = FilterType.REGEX,
            pattern = "com\\.shop\\.legacy\\..*"))     // skip the old package
public class AppConfig { }
```

**Bean names** default to the decapitalised class name, or to the method name
for a `@Bean`. Two beans cannot share a name; the later definition silently
overrides the earlier one in some configurations, which is a genuinely confusing
failure. Name them explicitly when there is any doubt.

```java
@Service("legacyOrderService")          // explicit name
public class OrderServiceV1 implements OrderService { }
```

A practical convention worth adopting: **put the configuration class in the root
package**. Spring Boot's `@SpringBootApplication` scans the package it lives in
and everything beneath, so a root-package placement means scanning just works.

```text
  com.shop                      <-- Application.class lives here
  com.shop.order                    scanned
  com.shop.order.web                scanned
  com.shop.billing                  scanned
  com.other                         NOT scanned
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Beans are declared either by annotation and scanning or by explicit `@Bean`
>   methods.
> - Scanning finds classes annotated with `@Component` or any annotation built
>   from it.
> - Stereotypes name intent; `@Repository` and `@Controller` also add behaviour.
> - `@Bean` methods are required for third-party classes and for construction
>   logic.
> - `@Bean` method parameters are resolved from the container like any other
>   injection point.
> - Default bean names come from the class or method name, and collisions cause
>   confusing overrides.
> - Place the configuration class in the root package so scanning covers the
>   application.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Declare one bean by annotation and one by a `@Bean` method, then list both
>    names from the context.
> 2. Move a component into a package outside the scan root and read the failure
>    it produces.
> 3. Define two `DataSource` beans with different settings using `@Bean`
>    methods, then observe the error when something injects `DataSource`.
> 4. Add an exclude filter that skips a package, and confirm its classes are no
>    longer registered.
> 5. Interview: You need a bean of a class from a third-party library. Which
>    declaration style is available, and why is the other one not? (Hint: what
>    would you have to modify to use annotations?)

#### Bean Scopes and Lifecycle Callbacks

A bean definition is a recipe. **Scope** answers a separate question: how many
objects does the container build from that recipe, and how long does each one
live?

The default is **singleton**, meaning one instance per container, shared by
every injection point. This is not the singleton design pattern, which is one
instance per classloader enforced by a private constructor; Spring's is one
instance per container, with an ordinary constructor.

```java
@Service          // singleton by default
public class OrderService { }
```

```text
  Singleton scope                    Prototype scope
  ---------------                    ---------------
  ControllerA ----+                  ControllerA ---> OrderService #1
                  |                                   (a new one, per injection)
                  +--> OrderService
                  |     (one shared)  ControllerB ---> OrderService #2
  ControllerB ----+
```

| Scope         | One instance per            | Available in |
| ------------- | --------------------------- | ------------ |
| `singleton`   | Container (the default)     | Everywhere   |
| `prototype`   | Injection or `getBean` call | Everywhere   |
| `request`     | HTTP request                | Web contexts |
| `session`     | HTTP session                | Web contexts |
| `application` | `ServletContext`            | Web contexts |
| `websocket`   | WebSocket session           | Web contexts |

**Singletons must be stateless**, and this is the single most important rule in
this topic. One instance serves every thread in the application, so a mutable
field is shared mutable state without synchronisation.

```java
@Service
public class BrokenOrderService {
    private Order current;                  // SHARED across all threads

    public void place(Order order) {
        this.current = order;               // thread A writes
        validate();                         // thread B may have overwritten it
        repository.save(this.current);      // the wrong order gets saved
    }
}
```

```java
@Service
public class CorrectOrderService {
    // Injected collaborators are fine: they are set once and never reassigned.
    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public void place(Order order) {
        validate(order);                    // state lives in parameters and locals,
        repository.save(order);             // which are per-thread by nature
    }
}
```

**Prototype scope** gives a fresh instance every time, which suits objects that
do carry state.

```java
@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class ImportJob {
    private int processed;      // safe: each user of this bean gets its own
}
```

There is a trap: a prototype injected into a singleton is resolved **once**, at
singleton construction, so the singleton keeps the same prototype instance
forever. The fix is to inject a provider and ask for a new one each time.

```java
@Service
public class ImportService {

    private final ObjectProvider<ImportJob> jobs;    // a factory, not an instance

    public ImportService(ObjectProvider<ImportJob> jobs) {
        this.jobs = jobs;
    }

    public void run(File file) {
        ImportJob job = jobs.getObject();            // a genuinely new instance
        job.process(file);
    }
}
```

**Lifecycle callbacks** let a bean run code after its dependencies are injected
and before it is destroyed.

```text
   instantiate  ->  inject dependencies  ->  @PostConstruct  ->  ready to use
                                                                      |
   destroy  <-  @PreDestroy  <-  context.close()  <--------------------+
```

```java
@Component
public class ConnectionWarmer {

    private final DataSource dataSource;

    public ConnectionWarmer(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
    }

    @PostConstruct                        // after injection, before first use
    public void warmUp() throws SQLException {
        try (var conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
            conn.isValid(2);              // pay the connection cost at startup
        }
    }

    @PreDestroy                           // on context shutdown
    public void reportShutdown() {
        log.info("shutting down");
    }
}
```

`@PostConstruct` exists because a constructor runs *before* injection completes
for setter and field injection, so initialisation depending on collaborators
cannot go there. With constructor injection, most initialisation can simply go
in the constructor, and `@PostConstruct` is reserved for work that should not
happen during construction, such as touching the network.

One important asymmetry: **`@PreDestroy` is never called on prototype beans**.
The container hands them out and forgets them, so anything holding a resource
must be closed by the code that requested it.

> Key Takeaways
> - Scope determines how many instances the container creates from one
>   definition.
> - The default, singleton, is one shared instance per container and is not the
>   singleton pattern.
> - Singleton beans must be stateless, because one instance serves all threads.
> - Injected final collaborators are safe state; mutable request data is not.
> - A prototype injected into a singleton is resolved once; use `ObjectProvider`
>   for a fresh instance.
> - `@PostConstruct` runs after injection, which a constructor cannot guarantee
>   for setter or field injection.
> - `@PreDestroy` runs at context shutdown, and never for prototype beans.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Inject the same singleton into two components and confirm the references
>    are identical, then repeat with prototype scope.
> 2. Add a mutable counter field to a singleton service, call it from twenty
>    threads, and observe the result.
> 3. Inject a prototype into a singleton, call it repeatedly, and show the same
>    instance is returned. Fix it with `ObjectProvider`.
> 4. Add `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` logging to a bean and run the
>    context inside a try-with-resources block.
> 5. Interview: A developer stores the current user in a field on an
>    `@Service` bean. What goes wrong and when? (Hint: how many instances exist,
>    and how many threads use them at once?)

#### Qualifiers, Primary Beans, and Ambiguity

Spring resolves an injection point by type. When exactly one bean matches, the
process is invisible. The interesting cases are when zero match or when more
than one does.

Zero matches produces `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at startup, and the fix is
to define the bean or widen the component scan. Multiple matches produces
`NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`, and there are four ways to resolve it.

```java
public interface NotificationSender { void send(Message message); }

@Component
public class EmailSender implements NotificationSender { }

@Component
public class SmsSender implements NotificationSender { }

@Service
public class AlertService {
    // AMBIGUOUS: two beans implement NotificationSender.
    public AlertService(NotificationSender sender) { ... }
}
```

**`@Primary` marks a default.** It is the right choice when one implementation
is what almost everything should get.

```java
@Component
@Primary                                   // chosen when nothing more specific asks
public class EmailSender implements NotificationSender { }
```

**`@Qualifier` names a specific bean.** It is the right choice at an injection
point that genuinely needs a particular implementation.

```java
@Service
public class AlertService {

    public AlertService(@Qualifier("smsSender") NotificationSender sender) {
        // "smsSender" is the default bean name of the SmsSender class
        this.sender = sender;
    }
}
```

The two combine well: mark the common case `@Primary`, and use `@Qualifier` at
the few places that need the exception.

**A custom qualifier annotation** is better than a string when the distinction
is meaningful, because it survives renames and is checked by the compiler.

```java
@Qualifier                                  // makes this a qualifier annotation
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Urgent { }

@Component
@Urgent
public class SmsSender implements NotificationSender { }

@Service
public class AlertService {
    public AlertService(@Urgent NotificationSender sender) { ... }
}
```

**Parameter names act as an implicit qualifier.** If no other rule applies,
Spring falls back to matching the parameter name against the bean name, which is
why this works without any annotation.

```java
// The parameter name "smsSender" matches the SmsSender bean's name.
public AlertService(NotificationSender smsSender) { ... }
```

This is convenient and fragile, since it breaks if the parameter is renamed or
if the build strips parameter names. Prefer an explicit qualifier.

Resolution proceeds in a fixed order, and knowing it explains most surprises.

```text
  1. Match by type              -> exactly one?  done
  2. Several matches?
       a. narrow by @Qualifier or a custom qualifier annotation
       b. otherwise take the @Primary bean
       c. otherwise match the bean name against the parameter name
       d. otherwise fail with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
```

| Mechanism            | Declared at        | Best for                             |
| -------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| `@Primary`           | The bean           | The sensible default for most callers |
| `@Qualifier("name")` | The injection point | A specific exception to the default  |
| Custom qualifier     | Both               | A meaningful distinction, type-safe  |
| Parameter name       | Implicit           | Nothing; too fragile to rely on      |

**Injecting all of them is often the real answer.** When several
implementations should all run, take a collection rather than picking one.

```java
@Service
public class AlertService {

    private final List<NotificationSender> senders;   // every implementation

    public AlertService(List<NotificationSender> senders) {
        this.senders = senders;
    }

    public void alert(Message message) {
        senders.forEach(s -> s.send(message));        // notify through all channels
    }
}
```

Order within that list is undefined unless you control it with `@Order` or by
implementing `Ordered`, which matters when the beans form a pipeline.

> Key Takeaways
> - Injection resolves by type first; ambiguity is an error, not a coin toss.
> - `@Primary` declares the default implementation on the bean itself.
> - `@Qualifier` selects a specific bean at the injection point.
> - Custom qualifier annotations are type-safe and survive renaming.
> - Parameter-name matching is a fallback that should not be relied upon.
> - Combining a `@Primary` default with targeted qualifiers is the usual design.
> - Injecting a `List` or `Map` of a type is correct when all implementations
>   should participate.
> - Use `@Order` when the collection's order matters.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create two implementations of one interface, inject the interface, and read
>    the resulting startup error.
> 2. Resolve it with `@Primary`, then override that choice at one injection
>    point with `@Qualifier`.
> 3. Write a custom qualifier annotation and use it in place of the string form.
> 4. Inject all implementations as a `List` and control their order with
>    `@Order`.
> 5. Interview: Two teams each add an implementation of the same interface and
>    the application stops starting. What are the two fixes, and which belongs
>    to which team? (Hint: one is declared on the bean, one at the injection
>    point.)

#### Java Configuration versus XML Configuration

Spring's configuration has been written three ways over its lifetime, and you
will meet all three. Knowing why the style changed explains a lot of code you
will read in older systems.

**XML came first.** Beans and their wiring were declared in files outside the
Java source.

```xml
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans" ...>

    <bean id="dataSource" class="com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource">
        <property name="jdbcUrl" value="${db.url}"/>
        <property name="username" value="${db.user}"/>
    </bean>

    <!-- The wiring is expressed by referring to another bean's id. -->
    <bean id="orderRepository" class="com.shop.JdbcOrderRepository">
        <constructor-arg ref="dataSource"/>
    </bean>

    <bean id="orderService" class="com.shop.OrderService">
        <constructor-arg ref="orderRepository"/>
    </bean>

</beans>
```

The appeal was that configuration lived entirely outside the code, so it could
be changed without recompiling. The cost was that **the compiler cannot check
any of it**: a typo in a class name, a renamed property, or a missing
constructor argument all fail at startup, and refactoring tools cannot follow a
class name inside a string.

**Annotations came next**, moving declarations onto the classes themselves.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) { ... }
}
```

This is concise and refactor-safe, but it only works for classes you own, and it
puts configuration inside the class it configures.

**Java configuration** is the current default and combines the strengths of
both: declarations are code, so the compiler checks them, but they live in a
dedicated configuration class rather than in the domain classes.

```java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource(@Value("${db.url}") String url) {
        var config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl(url);
        return new HikariDataSource(config);
    }

    @Bean
    public OrderRepository orderRepository(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new JdbcOrderRepository(dataSource);     // checked by the compiler
    }

    @Bean
    public OrderService orderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        return new OrderService(repository);
    }
}
```

| Aspect                  | XML                  | Annotations           | Java config          |
| ----------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------- |
| Compile-time checking   | None                 | Yes                   | Yes                  |
| Refactoring support     | Poor, names in strings | Full                | Full                 |
| Works for library classes | Yes                | No                    | Yes                  |
| Configuration separated from code | Yes       | No                    | Yes                  |
| Conditional logic       | Very limited         | Limited               | Full Java            |
| Verbosity               | High                 | Lowest                | Moderate             |

**One subtlety of `@Configuration` is worth understanding**, because it explains
behaviour that otherwise looks impossible. Spring subclasses configuration
classes with a proxy, so a direct call from one `@Bean` method to another
returns the existing singleton rather than a new object.

```java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(...); }

    @Bean
    public OrderRepository orderRepository() {
        // Looks like a second pool. Is not: the proxy returns the singleton.
        return new JdbcOrderRepository(dataSource());
    }

    @Bean
    public AuditRepository auditRepository() {
        return new JdbcAuditRepository(dataSource());   // the same instance again
    }
}
```

This is called **full mode**, and it depends on the class being annotated
`@Configuration`. Using `@Component` instead gives **lite mode**, where the
proxy is absent and each call really does create a new object, which is a subtle
and expensive bug when the object is a connection pool. Taking the dependency as
a method parameter avoids the question entirely and is the clearer style.

**Mixing is supported**, which matters when modernising an old application. A
Java configuration class can import legacy XML.

```java
@Configuration
@ImportResource("classpath:legacy-beans.xml")   // pull in existing XML
@ComponentScan("com.shop.modern")
public class AppConfig { }
```

The practical guidance: write Java configuration for third-party and
infrastructure beans, annotate your own classes, and treat XML as something you
read rather than write.

> Key Takeaways
> - XML, annotations, and Java configuration are three styles of the same
>   declarations.
> - XML has no compile-time checking and resists refactoring because names are
>   strings.
> - Annotations are concise but only apply to classes you own.
> - Java configuration is compiler-checked, works for library classes, and
>   supports real logic.
> - `@Configuration` classes are proxied, so inter-bean method calls return
>   singletons.
> - `@Component` gives lite mode with no proxy, where such calls create new
>   objects.
> - Taking dependencies as `@Bean` method parameters sidesteps the full versus
>   lite distinction.
> - XML can be imported into Java configuration, which is how legacy systems are
>   migrated.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Express the same three-bean graph in XML and in Java configuration, and
>    compare the failure you get from a misspelled class name in each.
> 2. Call one `@Bean` method from another inside a `@Configuration` class and
>    print the identity hash to confirm one instance.
> 3. Change `@Configuration` to `@Component` on that class and repeat the
>    previous exercise.
> 4. Import an XML file into a Java configuration class and inject a bean
>    declared in it.
> 5. Interview: Why can a `@Bean` method call another `@Bean` method and still
>    get a singleton? (Hint: what does Spring do to the configuration class
>    before instantiating it?)

<a id="172-aspect-oriented-programming"></a>
### 17.2 Aspect-Oriented Programming

This subchapter covers the second pillar of Spring: separating concerns that cut
across many classes, such as transactions, logging, and security, from the
business logic they surround, and understanding the proxy mechanism that makes
it work and the limits that mechanism imposes.

#### Cross-Cutting Concerns

Object-oriented decomposition organises code by **what it is about**. Orders go
in an order class, invoices in an invoice class. This works beautifully for
domain logic and fails for a specific category of requirement: the ones that
apply to everything.

Consider a service method that has been made production-ready.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    public Order place(Order order) {
        long start = System.nanoTime();                        // timing
        log.info("place() called with {}", order.id());        // logging

        if (!securityContext.hasRole("CUSTOMER")) {            // security
            throw new AccessDeniedException("not permitted");
        }

        Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();          // transaction
        conn.setAutoCommit(false);
        try {
            validate(order);                                   // the actual work
            repository.save(conn, order);                      // the actual work
            conn.commit();

            log.info("place() took {} ms",                     // timing
                     (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000);
            return order;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            conn.rollback();                                   // transaction
            log.error("place() failed", e);                    // logging
            throw e;
        } finally {
            conn.close();
        }
    }
}
```

Two lines do what the method is named for. Twenty do something else. And those
twenty lines will appear, near-identically, in every service method in the
application.

```text
              OrderService   InvoiceService   ShippingService
              ------------   --------------   ---------------
  logging          X               X                 X
  security         X               X                 X
  transactions     X               X                 X
  timing           X               X                 X
  business logic   A               B                 C
                   ^
                   the concerns cut ACROSS the class structure
```

A requirement that spans many otherwise-unrelated modules is a **cross-cutting
concern**. The common examples are transaction management, security checks,
logging and auditing, caching, performance monitoring, retry logic, and input
validation.

The cost of scattering them is concrete.

| Problem            | What it looks like in practice                         |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Duplication        | The same twelve lines in two hundred methods            |
| Inconsistency      | Some methods log the failure, some do not               |
| Tangling           | Business logic is unreadable under the surrounding code |
| Change amplification | Switching logging format means editing every method   |
| Forgetting         | A new method silently ships with no security check      |

Ordinary object-oriented tools help only partially. Inheritance forces every
service to extend one base class, which conflicts with modelling the domain.
A template method fixes the shape of every method. A decorator works but must be
hand-written and registered for each interface.

**Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP)** addresses this directly. The idea is to
write the cross-cutting code once, in one place, and declare *where* it applies
by a rule rather than by editing each site.

```java
// The business method, with the concerns removed.
@Service
public class OrderService {

    @Transactional                             // declared, not implemented here
    public Order place(Order order) {
        validate(order);
        return repository.save(order);
    }
}
```

```java
// The concern, written once, applied by a rule.
@Aspect
@Component
public class TimingAspect {

    @Around("execution(* com.shop..*Service.*(..))")   // where it applies
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();                      // run the real method
        } finally {
            log.info("{} took {} ms", pjp.getSignature(),
                     (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000);
        }
    }
}
```

The service is back to two lines of business logic. The timing code exists once
and covers every service method, including ones written next year.

**The trade-off is honest and should be stated.** Behaviour now happens that is
not visible in the method you are reading. A developer debugging `place()` sees
no transaction code, so understanding what actually runs requires knowing the
aspects exist. AOP therefore pays off for a small number of genuinely universal
concerns and becomes a maintenance problem when used for business rules.

> Key Takeaways
> - Cross-cutting concerns apply across many classes and resist object-oriented
>   decomposition.
> - Typical examples are transactions, security, logging, caching, and
>   monitoring.
> - Scattering them causes duplication, inconsistency, and unreadable business
>   logic.
> - Inheritance and decorators address the problem only partially.
> - AOP moves the concern into one module and declares where it applies by a
>   rule.
> - The cost is invisible behaviour, so AOP suits infrastructure rather than
>   business rules.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a service method and count the lines belonging to the domain versus
>    the lines belonging to infrastructure.
> 2. List five cross-cutting concerns in a project you know and note how each is
>    currently implemented.
> 3. Implement timing for two services with a hand-written decorator, then
>    describe what adding a third service costs.
> 4. Interview: Why is inheritance a poor tool for adding logging to every
>    service class? (Hint: how many base classes can a class have, and what else
>    might it need to extend?)

#### Join Points, Pointcuts, and Advice

AOP has its own vocabulary, and the terms are worth learning precisely because
they map onto the annotations you will write. There are five.

```text
   JOIN POINT   a point in execution where advice could apply
                (in Spring: always a method call on a bean)
        |
   POINTCUT     an expression selecting WHICH join points
                "every public method in com.shop.service"
        |
   ADVICE       the code to run, and WHEN relative to the join point
                "log before", "measure around", "rollback after throwing"
        |
   ASPECT       a class combining pointcuts and advice
        |
   WEAVING      the act of connecting them to the target
                (in Spring: creating a proxy at startup)
```

An analogy: the join points are every intersection on a road network, the
pointcut is the rule "all intersections downtown", the advice is "install a
traffic camera", and the aspect is the department that owns the policy.

**Advice types** determine when the code runs relative to the method.

| Annotation        | Runs                                  | Can it stop the method? |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `@Before`         | Before the method                     | Only by throwing        |
| `@AfterReturning` | After a normal return                 | No                      |
| `@AfterThrowing`  | After an exception escapes            | No                      |
| `@After`          | After either outcome, like `finally`  | No                      |
| `@Around`         | Surrounds the call                    | Yes, fully              |

```text
                +-------------------------------------------+
   @Around      |  before proceed()                          |
                |    +-----------------------------------+   |
   @Before      |    |                                   |   |
                |    |      the target method runs       |   |
   @AfterReturning -> on normal return                   |   |
   @AfterThrowing  -> on exception                       |   |
   @After          -> either way                         |   |
                |    +-----------------------------------+   |
                |  after proceed()                           |
                +-------------------------------------------+
```

```java
@Aspect
@Component
public class AuditAspect {

    @Before("execution(* com.shop.service.*.*(..))")
    public void logEntry(JoinPoint jp) {
        // JoinPoint exposes the signature and arguments, read-only.
        log.info("entering {} with {}", jp.getSignature().getName(),
                 Arrays.toString(jp.getArgs()));
    }

    @AfterThrowing(pointcut = "execution(* com.shop.service.*.*(..))",
                   throwing = "ex")            // binds the thrown exception
    public void logFailure(JoinPoint jp, Exception ex) {
        log.error("{} failed: {}", jp.getSignature().getName(), ex.getMessage());
    }

    @Around("execution(* com.shop.service.*.*(..))")
    public Object retry(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                return pjp.proceed();          // MUST be called, or the method
            } catch (TransientException e) {   // never runs at all
                if (attempt == 3) throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`@Around` is the most powerful because it receives a `ProceedingJoinPoint` and
decides whether, when, and how often to call `proceed()`. Forgetting to call it
silently skips the target method, which is the classic AOP bug.

**Pointcut expressions** use the AspectJ language. The `execution` designator
covers most needs, and its shape is worth memorising.

```text
  execution( modifiers? return-type  declaring-type.method(params) throws? )

  execution(  public   *       com.shop.service.*.*(..)  )
              ^        ^       ^                ^ ^  ^
              optional any     package          | |  any arguments
                       return                   | any method name
                       type                     any class
```

| Expression                                        | Matches                          |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `execution(* com.shop.service.*.*(..))`           | Any method in that package       |
| `execution(public * *(..))`                        | Any public method                |
| `execution(* save*(..))`                           | Methods whose name starts with `save` |
| `execution(* *(String, ..))`                       | First parameter is a `String`    |
| `within(com.shop.service..*)`                      | Any join point in that package tree |
| `@annotation(com.shop.Audited)`                    | Methods carrying that annotation |
| `bean(*Repository)`                                | Beans whose name ends in `Repository` |
| `this(com.shop.OrderService)`                      | The proxy is of that type        |
| `target(com.shop.OrderService)`                    | The target object is of that type |

**Named pointcuts avoid repeating the expression**, which matters because a
typo in a pointcut fails silently: the advice simply never runs.

```java
@Aspect
@Component
public class AuditAspect {

    @Pointcut("execution(* com.shop.service.*.*(..))")
    public void serviceMethods() { }            // an empty method: a name only

    @Pointcut("@annotation(com.shop.Audited)")
    public void audited() { }

    // Pointcuts compose with &&, || and !
    @Before("serviceMethods() && audited()")
    public void logAudited(JoinPoint jp) { ... }
}
```

**Annotation-driven pointcuts are usually the better design**, because they make
the behaviour visible at the point it applies instead of hiding it in a package
naming convention.

```java
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface Audited { }

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Audited                                   // the reader can see this applies
    public Order place(Order order) { ... }
}
```

This also survives refactoring: moving a class to a different package does not
silently switch the advice off.

> Key Takeaways
> - A join point is a candidate location; in Spring it is always a method call
>   on a bean.
> - A pointcut is an expression selecting join points; advice is the code that
>   runs.
> - An aspect packages pointcuts with advice, and weaving connects them to the
>   target.
> - The five advice types differ in timing and in whether they can prevent the
>   call.
> - `@Around` must call `proceed()`, or the target method never executes.
> - `execution` is the workhorse designator; `@annotation` and `within` cover
>   most of the rest.
> - Named `@Pointcut` methods let expressions be reused and composed.
> - A mistyped pointcut fails silently by matching nothing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `@Before` aspect that logs the name and arguments of every method
>    in one package.
> 2. Add an `@Around` aspect that measures execution time, then deliberately
>    omit `proceed()` and observe what happens.
> 3. Define an `@Audited` annotation and an aspect triggered by `@annotation`,
>    and apply it to two methods.
> 4. Write one pointcut matching any public method whose name starts with `find`
>    and which takes a `Long` first parameter.
> 5. Interview: An aspect appears correct but never runs. What are the first two
>    things you would check? (Hint: one concerns the expression, one concerns
>    whether the object is managed by the container.)

#### Proxy-Based Aspects in Spring

AOP needs a mechanism to intercept calls. AspectJ does it by rewriting bytecode
at compile time or class load time, which is powerful and requires extra build
tooling. **Spring takes a simpler route: it creates a proxy object at runtime**,
and understanding this explains both what works and what silently does not.

When a bean matches a pointcut, the container does not hand out the bean. It
hands out a wrapper that implements the same interface or extends the same
class, runs the advice, and delegates to the real object.

```text
  Without AOP                          With AOP
  -----------                          --------
  Controller                           Controller
      |                                    |
      v                                    v
  OrderService (the real object)       OrderService$$Proxy
                                           |  advice runs here
                                           v
                                       OrderService (the real object)
```

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    public Order place(Order order) { ... }
}

@Component
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService service;   // this is the PROXY, not the real bean

    public OrderController(OrderService service) {
        this.service = service;
        // Proof: the class name is not what you wrote.
        System.out.println(service.getClass());
        // e.g. class com.shop.OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
    }
}
```

Spring chooses between two proxying strategies.

| Strategy    | Requires                        | Proxies                  | Limitation                       |
| ----------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| JDK dynamic | The target implements an interface | Interface methods only | Cannot inject the concrete class |
| CGLIB       | A non-final class with a usable constructor | All public methods | Cannot proxy final classes or final methods |

Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB for everything, which avoids the common failure
where a class implements an interface, gets a JDK proxy, and then cannot be
injected by its concrete type.

```java
// With a JDK proxy, this fails: the proxy implements OrderService (the
// interface) but is NOT an instance of JdbcOrderService (the class).
public OrderController(JdbcOrderService service) { ... }   // no such bean
```

Enabling AOP is one annotation, and Spring Boot adds it automatically when
`spring-boot-starter-aop` is on the classpath.

```java
@Configuration
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy         // create proxies for beans matching any @Aspect
public class AopConfig { }
```

**Advice ordering** matters when several aspects match the same method. Without
direction the order is undefined; `@Order` fixes it, with lower values running
outermost.

```java
@Aspect
@Component
@Order(1)                       // outermost: runs first, returns last
public class SecurityAspect { }

@Aspect
@Component
@Order(2)                       // inside security, outside the method
public class TransactionAspect { }
```

```text
  call --> SecurityAspect (1) --> TransactionAspect (2) --> OrderService
       <--                    <--                       <--
```

That particular order is deliberate in real systems: an unauthorised call should
be rejected before a transaction is opened.

Three consequences of the proxy approach deserve naming now, with the last
covered in detail two topics further on.

**Only external calls are intercepted.** A call from one method of a bean to
another method of the same bean does not pass through the proxy, so no advice
runs.

**Only Spring-managed beans are proxied.** An object created with `new` has no
proxy and no advice, no matter what annotations its class carries.

**Only public methods are advised** under CGLIB, because private and final
methods cannot be overridden.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    @Transactional
    private void save(Order order) { ... }    // NEVER transactional: not overridable
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Spring implements AOP with runtime proxies rather than bytecode weaving.
> - Injected references to advised beans are proxies, not the objects you wrote.
> - JDK proxies require an interface; CGLIB subclasses the class and is Boot's
>   default.
> - Final classes, final methods, and private methods cannot be advised.
> - `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy` activates proxying, and Spring Boot adds it
>   automatically.
> - `@Order` controls the nesting of multiple aspects, lowest value outermost.
> - Advice runs only for external calls to container-managed beans.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print `getClass()` on an injected advised bean and on a non-advised one,
>    and compare the names.
> 2. Make a service class `final` and observe the startup failure when an aspect
>    targets it.
> 3. Apply two aspects to one method, then set `@Order` on each and confirm the
>    nesting changes.
> 4. Create a service instance with `new`, call an advised method, and show no
>    advice runs.
> 5. Interview: Why does Spring Boot proxy with CGLIB by default rather than JDK
>    proxies? (Hint: what type does the application usually inject, and what
>    does a JDK proxy actually implement?)

#### Declarative Transactions with @Transactional

16.3 established where transaction boundaries belong and showed the code that
implements them: get a connection, disable auto-commit, commit on success, roll
back on failure, restore state. That block is identical in every service method,
which makes it the textbook cross-cutting concern.

`@Transactional` replaces it with one annotation, and the aspect supplies the
rest.

```java
@Service
public class TransferService {

    private final AccountRepository accounts;

    @Transactional                      // the aspect opens, commits, rolls back
    public void transfer(long from, long to, BigDecimal amount) {
        accounts.debit(from, amount);
        accounts.credit(to, amount);    // if this throws, the debit is undone
    }
}
```

What the proxy actually does around that method:

```text
  proxy.transfer(...)
     |
     +-- get a connection, setAutoCommit(false)        [begin]
     |
     +-- target.transfer(...)  ------------------------ your code
     |        |
     |        +-- normal return  --> commit()
     |        |
     |        +-- RuntimeException --> rollback()
     |        |
     |        +-- checked Exception --> COMMIT (the default, and a trap)
     |
     +-- release the connection
```

**The rollback rule is the single most surprising default in Spring.** By
default, `@Transactional` rolls back for `RuntimeException` and `Error`, and
**commits** for checked exceptions. The reasoning is historical, following EJB
convention, and it catches nearly everyone once.

```java
// BUG: this commits. The checked exception does not trigger a rollback.
@Transactional
public void importFile(File f) throws IOException {
    repository.save(parse(f));
    throw new IOException("disk full");      // partial work is COMMITTED
}

// FIX: state which exceptions should roll back.
@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
```
