```java
public void importFile(File f) throws IOException { ... }
```

**Propagation** answers what happens when a transactional method calls another
one. The default, `REQUIRED`, joins the caller's transaction if there is one.

| Propagation      | With an existing transaction  | Without one            |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `REQUIRED`       | Join it (the default)         | Start a new one        |
| `REQUIRES_NEW`   | Suspend it, start a new one   | Start a new one        |
| `SUPPORTS`       | Join it                       | Run without one        |
| `NOT_SUPPORTED`  | Suspend it, run without       | Run without one        |
| `MANDATORY`      | Join it                       | Throw an exception     |
| `NEVER`          | Throw an exception            | Run without one        |
| `NESTED`         | Use a savepoint               | Start a new one        |

`REQUIRES_NEW` is the one with a genuine use case: writing an audit record that
must survive even when the business transaction rolls back.

```java
@Service
public class AuditService {

    // A separate transaction, committed independently of the caller's.
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void record(String event) {
        auditRepository.save(new AuditEntry(event));
    }
}
```

Be aware that this occupies a second connection while the first is suspended, so
a pool of ten can deadlock if every request does it.

The other settings mirror what 16.3 covered at the JDBC level.

```java
@Transactional(
    isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ,   // as in 16.3
    timeout = 10,                            // seconds before forced rollback
    readOnly = true,                         // hint: skips dirty checking in JPA
    rollbackFor = Exception.class,
    noRollbackFor = NotFoundException.class)
public Report generate(long id) { ... }
```

`readOnly = true` is worth applying to every query method. With JPA it tells
Hibernate to skip dirty-checking snapshots, which is a measurable saving on
large result sets.

**Where to put the annotation.** On the service layer, on public methods,
matching the business operation. Putting it on a repository method creates one
transaction per database call, which 16.3 identified as the anti-pattern that
makes multi-step operations non-atomic.

Two failure modes to recognise, both of which follow from the proxy mechanism
and are covered in the next topic: the annotation does nothing on a private
method, and it does nothing when the method is called from within the same
class.

> Key Takeaways
> - `@Transactional` replaces the manual begin, commit, and rollback block with
>   an aspect.
> - It rolls back on unchecked exceptions and commits on checked ones by
>   default.
> - Use `rollbackFor = Exception.class` whenever checked exceptions can escape.
> - `REQUIRED` joins an existing transaction and is the correct default.
> - `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the caller's transaction and needs a second
>   connection.
> - `readOnly = true` on query methods lets JPA skip dirty checking.
> - Annotate public service methods, not repository methods.
> - The annotation is silently ignored on private methods and on self-invoked
>   calls.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a transfer method that throws after the first update, and confirm
>    nothing is persisted.
> 2. Change the thrown exception to a checked one and observe that the work
>    commits. Fix it with `rollbackFor`.
> 3. Implement audit logging with `REQUIRES_NEW` and prove the audit row
>    survives a rolled-back caller.
> 4. Add `@Transactional` to a private method and demonstrate it has no effect.
> 5. Interview: A service method annotated `@Transactional` throws a checked
>    exception and the data is still saved. Is this a Spring bug? (Hint: what is
>    the documented default rollback rule, and why was it chosen?)

#### Logging, Security, and Caching Aspects

Transactions are the aspect Spring provides. The same machinery handles three
other concerns that appear in nearly every application, two of which Spring also
provides ready-made.

**Logging and auditing** is the concern most often written by hand, because the
requirements are application-specific.

```java
@Aspect
@Component
public class AuditAspect {

    private final AuditRepository audits;
    private final SecurityContext security;

    @AfterReturning(pointcut = "@annotation(audited)", returning = "result")
    public void record(JoinPoint jp, Audited audited, Object result) {
        // The annotation itself is bound as a parameter, so its
        // attributes configure the advice.
        audits.save(new AuditEntry(
                audited.action(),                       // from the annotation
                security.currentUser(),
                jp.getSignature().getName(),
                Instant.now()));
    }
}
```

```java
@Service
public class AccountService {

    @Audited(action = "CLOSE_ACCOUNT")      // visible, configurable, one line
    public void close(long accountId) { ... }
}
```

Binding the annotation as an advice parameter is the pattern that makes custom
aspects genuinely useful: one aspect, configured per site.

**Security** is provided by Spring Security, whose method-level checks are
aspects.

```java
@Service
public class DocumentService {

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")                    // evaluated before the call
    public void delete(long id) { ... }

    // SpEL can reference the arguments and the authenticated principal.
    @PreAuthorize("#ownerId == authentication.principal.id")
    public List<Document> listFor(long ownerId) { ... }

    @PostAuthorize("returnObject.owner == authentication.name")  // after the call
    public Document find(long id) { ... }
}
```

`@PreAuthorize` throws before the method runs, which is what you want for a
delete. `@PostAuthorize` runs the method first and then discards the result,
which is only appropriate when the decision depends on what was returned.

**Caching** is provided by Spring's cache abstraction, again as an aspect.

```java
@Service
public class ProductService {

    @Cacheable("products")                    // skip the method on a cache hit
    public Product findById(long id) {
        return repository.findById(id);       // runs only on a miss
    }

    @CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#product.id")   // invalidate on write
    public Product update(Product product) {
        return repository.save(product);
    }

    @CacheEvict(value = "products", allEntries = true)
    public void reindex() { ... }
}
```

```text
  caller --> proxy --> key in cache?  --yes--> return cached value
                            |                  (the method never runs)
                            no
                            |
                            v
                      target method --> store result --> return
```

| Annotation   | Effect                                                      |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@Cacheable` | Return the cached value if present; otherwise run and store  |
| `@CachePut`  | Always run the method, and update the cache with the result  |
| `@CacheEvict`| Remove one entry or all entries                              |
| `@Caching`   | Combine several of the above on one method                   |

Two cautions on caching. **Cache keys default to the method arguments**, so a
method whose result also depends on the current user or tenant will serve one
user's data to another unless the key includes it.

```java
@Cacheable(value = "documents", key = "#id + '-' + authentication.name")
public Document find(long id) { ... }
```

And **cache invalidation must cover every write path**. A row updated by a
different service, a scheduled job, or a database migration leaves the cache
stale, which is why time-based expiry is usually configured as a backstop.

The common thread across all four concerns is worth stating: **each is
configured declaratively at the point it applies and implemented once
centrally**, which is exactly what the first topic of this subchapter argued
for.

> Key Takeaways
> - Transactions, security, caching, and auditing are all implemented as aspects
>   over the same proxy mechanism.
> - Binding an annotation as an advice parameter lets one aspect be configured
>   per method.
> - `@PreAuthorize` blocks the call; `@PostAuthorize` discards the result
>   afterwards.
> - `@Cacheable` skips the method entirely on a hit, which is the whole point
>   and the whole risk.
> - Default cache keys are the arguments, so user-specific data needs an
>   explicit key.
> - Every write path must evict, and time-based expiry is a necessary backstop.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `@Audited` annotation and an aspect that records the method name
>    and the current user.
> 2. Add `@Cacheable` to a slow repository lookup and measure the second call.
> 3. Demonstrate a stale cache by updating a row through a method that does not
>    evict, then fix it.
> 4. Protect one method with `@PreAuthorize` using a SpEL expression that
>    references a method argument.
> 5. Interview: A caching bug leaks one customer's data to another. What is the
>    most likely cause? (Hint: what does the cache key consist of by default,
>    and what is missing from it?)

#### Proxy Limitations and Self-Invocation

Every limitation in Spring AOP follows from one fact established two topics ago:
**advice lives on the proxy, not on your object**. If a call does not go through
the proxy, no advice runs. This topic collects the consequences, because each
one produces a bug that looks like the framework is broken.

**Self-invocation is the big one.** When a method calls another method on the
same object, the call uses `this`, which is the target, not the proxy.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    public void processAll(List<Order> orders) {
        for (Order order : orders) {
            process(order);      // 'this.process(...)' -- bypasses the proxy
        }                        // @Transactional below does NOTHING here
    }

    @Transactional
    public void process(Order order) {
        repository.save(order);
    }
}
```

```text
  External call                        Self-invocation
  -------------                        ---------------
  caller --> PROXY --> target          caller --> PROXY --> target.processAll()
             ^                                                    |
             advice runs                                     this.process()
                                                                  |
                                                        target.process()
                                                        advice never runs
```

The same silence affects `@Cacheable`, `@PreAuthorize`, `@Async`, and every
custom aspect. Nothing fails; the behaviour simply does not happen, which makes
it hard to spot.

There are four fixes, in descending order of preference.

**Move the method to another bean.** This is almost always the right answer,
because the two methods have different responsibilities: one orchestrates, one
performs a unit of work.

```java
@Service
public class OrderProcessor {
    @Transactional
    public void process(Order order) { repository.save(order); }
}

@Service
public class OrderBatchService {
    private final OrderProcessor processor;      // a different bean: proxied

    public void processAll(List<Order> orders) {
        orders.forEach(processor::process);      // goes through the proxy
    }
}
```

**Inject yourself.** Ugly but occasionally pragmatic.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Lazy private final OrderService self;       // @Lazy breaks the cycle

    public OrderService(@Lazy OrderService self) { this.self = self; }

    public void processAll(List<Order> orders) {
        orders.forEach(self::process);           // explicitly via the proxy
    }
}
```

**Look the proxy up at runtime**, which requires `exposeProxy = true` on
`@EnableAspectJAutoProxy` and is the least readable option.

```java
((OrderService) AopContext.currentProxy()).process(order);
```

**Use AspectJ load-time weaving**, which modifies the bytecode so there is no
proxy and self-invocation works. It solves the problem completely at the cost of
a build-time or JVM-agent dependency, and is rare in practice.

**The other limitations** all share the same root cause.

| Limitation                       | Why                                              |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Private methods are not advised  | CGLIB cannot override them                        |
| Final methods are not advised    | Cannot be overridden                              |
| Final classes cannot be proxied  | Cannot be subclassed                              |
| `static` methods are not advised | Not dispatched on an instance                     |
| Objects created with `new` are not advised | The container never saw them           |
| Constructors are not advised     | The proxy's constructor runs, not an intercepted call |
| Fields are not intercepted       | Spring AOP only supports method join points       |

```java
@Service
public class ReportService {

    @Transactional
    private void save(Report r) { }          // silently non-transactional

    @Cacheable("reports")
    public final Report find(long id) { }    // final: silently uncached

    public ReportService() {
        loadDefaults();                      // no advice applies during construction
    }
}
```

**How to detect these problems**, since none of them produce an error:

- Print the injected bean's class; a name containing `$$SpringCGLIB$$` confirms
  it is proxied.
- Enable transaction logging and check whether a transaction is actually opened.

```text
  logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE
```

- Write a test that asserts the behaviour, such as a rollback, rather than
  assuming the annotation took effect.

```java
@Test
void processAllRollsBackEachOrder() {
    assertThrows(RuntimeException.class, () -> service.processAll(withOneBad()));
    assertEquals(0, repository.count());   // fails loudly if the proxy was bypassed
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Advice lives on the proxy, so any call that bypasses the proxy loses it.
> - Self-invocation through `this` is the most common way advice is silently
>   lost.
> - The preferred fix is moving the annotated method into a separate bean.
> - Self-injection with `@Lazy` and `AopContext.currentProxy()` are fallbacks.
> - Private, final, and static methods, and final classes, cannot be advised.
> - Objects created with `new` are never advised, regardless of annotations.
> - These failures are silent, so verify with proxy class names, transaction
>   logs, or behavioural tests.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build the self-invocation example, confirm no transaction is opened, then
>    fix it by extracting a second bean.
> 2. Enable transaction interceptor logging and compare the output for an
>    external call and a self-invoked one.
> 3. Annotate a private method with `@Cacheable` and prove the cache is never
>    consulted.
> 4. Write a test asserting rollback behaviour that would fail if the proxy were
>    bypassed.
> 5. Interview: A `@Transactional` method works when called from a controller
>    but not when called from another method in the same service. Explain the
>    mechanism. (Hint: which object does `this` refer to inside the target?)

<a id="173-spring-data-access"></a>
### 17.3 Spring Data Access

This subchapter applies the two previous ones to the database work of chapter
16: removing JDBC boilerplate with a template, managing transactions
declaratively, generating repository implementations, and keeping the schema in
step with the code.

#### JdbcTemplate and Boilerplate Reduction

Chapter 16 showed the correct shape of a JDBC query: obtain a connection,
prepare a statement, bind parameters, iterate the result set, map each row,
close everything, and translate the exception. Only two of those seven steps are
specific to the query being run. The other five are identical every time.

`JdbcTemplate` implements the five and asks you to supply the two. It is an
application of the **template method pattern**: the framework owns the
algorithm, your code fills in the variable parts.

```java
// Plain JDBC: 18 lines, of which 4 concern this particular query.
public Optional<Order> findById(long id) {
    String sql = "SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE id = ?";
    try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
         PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
        ps.setLong(1, id);
        try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
            if (!rs.next()) return Optional.empty();
            return Optional.of(new Order(rs.getLong("id"),
                                         rs.getLong("customer_id"),
                                         rs.getBigDecimal("total")));
        }
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        throw new DataAccessException("finding order " + id, e);
    }
}
```

```java
// JdbcTemplate: the same query, with the mechanics removed.
private static final String FIND_BY_ID =
        "SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE id = ?";

public Optional<Order> findById(long id) {
    // queryForObject throws if there is no row, so a list keeps it simple.
    return jdbcTemplate.query(FIND_BY_ID, ORDER_MAPPER, id).stream().findFirst();
}

// The row mapper is the one piece that is genuinely about this table.
private static final RowMapper<Order> ORDER_MAPPER = (rs, rowNum) ->
        new Order(rs.getLong("id"),
                  rs.getLong("customer_id"),
                  rs.getBigDecimal("total"));
```

The template handles connection acquisition and release, statement creation,
parameter binding, result set iteration, and exception translation. Notice that
`SQLException` never appears: `RowMapper` declares it, and the template
translates it into Spring's unchecked hierarchy, covered later in this
subchapter.

The core methods cover the operations chapter 16 introduced.

| Method                                    | Use for                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `query(sql, rowMapper, args...)`          | Many rows                            |
| `queryForObject(sql, rowMapper, args...)` | Exactly one row; throws otherwise    |
| `queryForObject(sql, Long.class, args...)`| A single scalar such as a count      |
| `queryForList(sql, args...)`              | Rows as `List<Map<String, Object>>`  |
| `update(sql, args...)`                    | Insert, update, delete; returns count |
| `batchUpdate(sql, batchArgsList)`         | Bulk operations                      |
| `execute(sql)`                            | DDL                                  |

```java
// A count, with no mapping at all.
long total = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
        "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", Long.class, customerId);

// An update: varargs become the bound parameters, in order.
int rows = jdbcTemplate.update(
        "UPDATE orders SET status = ? WHERE id = ?", status.name(), orderId);

// A batch, which is 16.2's batching with the loop written for you.
jdbcTemplate.batchUpdate(
        "INSERT INTO readings (sensor_id, value) VALUES (?, ?)",
        readings.stream()
                .map(r -> new Object[]{ r.sensorId(), r.value() })
                .toList());
```

**Generated keys** need a little more code, because the key must be captured.

```java
KeyHolder keyHolder = new GeneratedKeyHolder();

jdbcTemplate.update(connection -> {
    var ps = connection.prepareStatement(
            "INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (?, ?)",
            new String[]{ "id" });          // name the key column, as in 16.2
    ps.setLong(1, customerId);
    ps.setBigDecimal(2, total);
    return ps;
}, keyHolder);

long newId = keyHolder.getKey().longValue();
```

**`NamedParameterJdbcTemplate`** replaces positional `?` markers with names,
which is a real readability gain once a statement has more than three
parameters and removes an entire class of ordering bugs.

```java
String sql = """
        SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM orders
         WHERE customer_id = :customerId
           AND placed_at > :since
           AND status IN (:statuses)
        """;

var params = new MapSqlParameterSource()
        .addValue("customerId", customerId)
        .addValue("since", cutoff)
        .addValue("statuses", List.of("NEW", "PAID"));   // expands the IN list

List<Order> orders = namedTemplate.query(sql, params, ORDER_MAPPER);
```

That last line solves 16.2's `IN` clause problem outright: the template
generates the right number of placeholders from the collection's size.

**Where `JdbcTemplate` fits.** It does not map object graphs, manage entity
state, or generate SQL. That is the point: you write the SQL, so you know
exactly what runs. It remains the right tool for reporting queries, bulk
operations, and anywhere an ORM's generated SQL is not good enough, and it
coexists with JPA on the same transaction.

> Key Takeaways
> - `JdbcTemplate` implements the invariant parts of a JDBC operation and leaves
>   the SQL and mapping to you.
> - Connections, statements, iteration, and closing are handled, so resource
>   leaks are impossible.
> - `SQLException` is translated, so data access code throws unchecked
>   exceptions.
> - A `RowMapper` is the single place that knows how a row becomes an object.
> - `queryForObject` throws when there is not exactly one row; use `query` plus
>   a stream when zero is valid.
> - `NamedParameterJdbcTemplate` improves readability and expands collections in
>   `IN` clauses.
> - The template writes no SQL for you, which is precisely why it is
>   predictable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a plain JDBC finder with `JdbcTemplate` and count the lines
>    removed.
> 2. Write a `RowMapper` for a class with a nullable column, handling `NULL`
>    correctly as 16.1 described.
> 3. Call `queryForObject` for an identifier that does not exist and read the
>    exception, then rewrite it to return an `Optional`.
> 4. Use `NamedParameterJdbcTemplate` to run a query with an `IN` clause over a
>    list of varying size.
> 5. Interview: `JdbcTemplate` guarantees connections are closed. What property
>    of its design makes that possible? (Hint: who owns the `try`-with-resources
>    block, your code or the framework's?)

#### Spring Transaction Management

17.2 introduced `@Transactional` as an aspect. This topic covers the machinery
underneath it, because knowing what a `PlatformTransactionManager` is explains
how JDBC and JPA code can share one transaction and why the annotation works
identically across both.

The problem Spring solves here is that transaction APIs differ. Plain JDBC uses
`Connection.setAutoCommit` and `commit`. JPA uses
`EntityTransaction.begin` and `commit`. JTA spans several resources through a
transaction manager. Code written against any one of them is tied to it.

Spring defines a single abstraction and provides implementations.

```text
                    PlatformTransactionManager
                    (getTransaction, commit, rollback)
                              |
        +---------------------+---------------------+
        |                     |                     |
  DataSourceTransactionManager  JpaTransactionManager  JtaTransactionManager
        |                     |                     |
     JDBC Connection      EntityManager        several resources
```

| Implementation                 | Use with                        |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| `DataSourceTransactionManager` | `JdbcTemplate`, plain JDBC       |
| `JpaTransactionManager`        | JPA and Hibernate                |
| `JtaTransactionManager`        | Distributed, multi-resource      |
| `R2dbcTransactionManager`      | Reactive data access             |

```java
@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement          // activates the @Transactional aspect
public class TxConfig {

    @Bean
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new DataSourceTransactionManager(dataSource);
    }
}
```

Spring Boot configures all of this automatically, choosing the manager from
what is on the classpath.

**The key mechanism is thread binding.** When a transaction starts, the manager
binds the connection to the current thread in a `ThreadLocal`. Any
`JdbcTemplate` or `EntityManager` in that thread then obtains *that* connection
rather than borrowing a new one from the pool.

```text
   Thread handling request 42
   ---------------------------------------------------
   @Transactional method entered
        |
        +-- manager borrows connection C7, autoCommit=false
        +-- binds C7 to this thread  (TransactionSynchronizationManager)
        |
        +-- OrderRepository   --> JdbcTemplate --> asks for the thread's
        +-- PaymentRepository --> JdbcTemplate --> connection: gets C7
        |
        +-- commit C7, unbind, return to the pool
```

This is what makes 16.3's design work without passing a `Connection` through
every method signature. The repositories never mention a connection, yet they
all participate in the caller's transaction.

**The programmatic API** is available when a boundary does not align with a
method, such as when only part of a method should be transactional.

```java
@Service
public class ImportService {

    private final TransactionTemplate transactions;

    public ImportService(PlatformTransactionManager manager) {
        this.transactions = new TransactionTemplate(manager);
    }

    public void importAll(List<Record> records) {
        List<Record> valid = validate(records);     // outside the transaction

        transactions.execute(status -> {            // the boundary starts here
            valid.forEach(repository::save);
            if (shouldAbort()) {
                status.setRollbackOnly();           // roll back without throwing
            }
            return null;
        });

        notifyExternalSystem();                     // after commit, as 16.3 advised
    }
}
```

`setRollbackOnly()` is the programmatic equivalent of throwing: it marks the
transaction so that it cannot commit. It is also what happens internally when an
inner `REQUIRED` method fails, which produces a confusing error worth
recognising.

```text
  UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has
  been marked as rollback-only
```

That message means an inner transactional method threw, its exception was
caught by the caller, and the caller then tried to commit a transaction that had
already been doomed. The fix is either to let the exception propagate or to
give the inner method `REQUIRES_NEW` so it has a transaction of its own.

**Testing transactions** is where Spring's support pays off. A test annotated
`@Transactional` rolls back automatically at the end, so tests leave no trace in
the database.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@Transactional                        // each test method rolls back afterwards
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Test
    void savesAndFinds() {
        repository.save(anOrder());
        assertEquals(1, repository.count());
    }                                 // rolled back: the next test sees an empty table
}
```

One caveat: this means the test never verifies that a commit would succeed.
Constraint violations that fire at commit time, such as deferred constraints,
will not appear. Use `@Commit` or a separate integration test when that matters.

> Key Takeaways
> - `PlatformTransactionManager` abstracts JDBC, JPA, and JTA behind one
>   interface.
> - `@EnableTransactionManagement` activates the aspect; Spring Boot does it
>   automatically.
> - The manager binds the connection to the thread, so all repositories in that
>   thread share it.
> - Thread binding is why repositories need no `Connection` parameter.
> - `TransactionTemplate` handles boundaries that do not match a method.
> - `setRollbackOnly()` dooms a transaction without throwing.
> - `UnexpectedRollbackException` means an inner failure was swallowed by the
>   caller.
> - `@Transactional` on a test rolls it back, at the cost of never exercising a
>   real commit.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Configure a `DataSourceTransactionManager` explicitly and confirm two
>    repositories in one service method use the same connection.
> 2. Log the connection identity from two repositories inside one transactional
>    method and compare.
> 3. Reproduce `UnexpectedRollbackException` by catching an exception from an
>    inner `@Transactional` method, then fix it two different ways.
> 4. Write a repository test annotated `@Transactional` and prove the database
>    is unchanged afterwards.
> 5. Interview: How can a repository participate in a caller's transaction
>    without receiving a `Connection`? (Hint: where is the connection stored for
>    the duration of the call?)

#### Spring Data JPA Repositories

16.4 described the data access object pattern: an interface expressed in domain
terms, plus an implementation that talks to the database. In practice most of
those implementations are mechanical, since `findById`, `save`, `delete`, and
`findAll` look the same for every entity.

**Spring Data JPA writes the implementation for you.** You declare the
interface; the framework generates a proxy implementing it at startup.

```java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    // No implementation. None is needed.
}
```

That single line provides everything below.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;      // the generated proxy

    public void demo(Order order) {
        Optional<Order> found = repository.findById(1L);
        List<Order> all       = repository.findAll();
        Order saved           = repository.save(order);      // insert or update
        long count            = repository.count();
        repository.deleteById(1L);
        boolean exists        = repository.existsById(1L);
    }
}
```

The repository interfaces form a hierarchy, each adding capability.

```text
  Repository<T, ID>                 marker only
      |
  CrudRepository<T, ID>             save, findById, findAll, delete, count
      |
  PagingAndSortingRepository<T, ID> findAll(Pageable), findAll(Sort)
      |
  JpaRepository<T, ID>              flush, saveAllAndFlush, getReferenceById,
                                    List returns instead of Iterable
```

Choosing a narrower interface is a real design decision: extending
`CrudRepository` instead of `JpaRepository` keeps JPA-specific methods out of
the domain-facing contract.

**Paging and sorting** come free, which matters because unbounded `findAll` on a
large table is a production incident waiting to happen.

```java
// Page 2, 20 rows, newest first.
Pageable request = PageRequest.of(1, 20, Sort.by("placedAt").descending());

Page<Order> page = repository.findAll(request);

page.getContent();          // the 20 orders
page.getTotalElements();    // total rows, from a second COUNT query
page.getTotalPages();
page.hasNext();
```

`Page` runs an extra count query. When the total is not needed, `Slice` avoids
it and is meaningfully cheaper on large tables.

**Enabling it** requires one annotation, which Spring Boot supplies.

```java
@Configuration
@EnableJpaRepositories("com.shop.repository")   // where the interfaces live
@EntityScan("com.shop.domain")                  // where the entities live
public class JpaConfig { }
```

**What it does not do.** Spring Data does not remove the need to understand JPA.
Every warning from 16.4 still applies: `save` on a managed entity may issue no
SQL because dirty checking already did, lazy associations still throw after the
transaction ends, and `findAll` on a mapped entity still triggers N+1 queries if
associations are touched. The framework removes typing, not understanding.

One specific trap: **`save` is not an insert.** It calls `persist` for a new
entity and `merge` for one with an identifier, and `merge` issues a `SELECT`
first. In a bulk load that doubles the query count, so `saveAll` with batching
configured is the right tool.

> Key Takeaways
> - Spring Data JPA generates a repository implementation from an interface
>   declaration.
> - `JpaRepository` provides create, read, update, delete, counting, paging, and
>   sorting.
> - The interface hierarchy lets you expose only the capability you want.
> - `Page` includes a total and costs an extra count query; `Slice` does not.
> - Entity and repository locations must be visible to the configuration.
> - Every JPA behaviour from 16.4 still applies, including N+1 and lazy loading.
> - `save` performs a merge for entities with an identifier, which issues a
>   `SELECT`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Declare a repository interface for an entity and use all six inherited
>    methods without writing an implementation.
> 2. Print the runtime class of the injected repository and identify what
>    created it.
> 3. Page through a table of 1,000 rows with a page size of 50 and log the SQL,
>    noting the count query.
> 4. Replace `Page` with `Slice` and compare the statements issued.
> 5. Interview: You call `save` on an entity you loaded a moment ago inside the
>    same transaction, and no `UPDATE` appears in the log until commit. Why?
>    (Hint: which 16.4 mechanism has already noticed the change?)

#### Derived Query Methods and Custom Queries

The generated methods cover access by identifier. Real applications query by
everything else, and Spring Data offers three ways to express that, in
increasing order of control.

**Derived queries** are parsed from the method name. Spring Data reads the name
at startup, builds the query, and fails immediately if the name refers to a
field that does not exist.

```java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    // SELECT ... WHERE customer_id = ?
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(Long customerId);

    // SELECT ... WHERE status = ? AND total > ?
    List<Order> findByStatusAndTotalGreaterThan(OrderStatus status, BigDecimal min);

    // SELECT ... WHERE placed_at BETWEEN ? AND ? ORDER BY placed_at DESC
    List<Order> findByPlacedAtBetweenOrderByPlacedAtDesc(Instant from, Instant to);

    // Traverses the association: WHERE customer.email = ?
    List<Order> findByCustomerEmail(String email);

    // SELECT count(*) WHERE status = ?
    long countByStatus(OrderStatus status);

    // SELECT ... WHERE reference = ?  (returns at most one)
    Optional<Order> findByReference(String reference);

    // DELETE WHERE status = ?
    @Transactional
    long deleteByStatus(OrderStatus status);
}
```

The grammar has a fixed shape.

```text
  [find|read|get|count|exists|delete]  By  <Property><Operator>  [And|Or] ...
                                                                 [OrderBy<Property><Asc|Desc>]

  findByStatusAndTotalGreaterThanOrderByPlacedAtDesc
  ^^^^  ^^^^^^ ^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  verb  prop   and  prop + operator   sorting
```

| Keyword                  | Generated condition             |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| `Is`, `Equals`           | `= ?`                            |
| `GreaterThan`, `LessThan`| `> ?`, `< ?`                     |
| `Between`                | `BETWEEN ? AND ?`                |
| `Like`, `Containing`     | `LIKE ?`, `LIKE %?%`             |
| `StartingWith`           | `LIKE ?%`                        |
| `In`                     | `IN (?)`                         |
| `IsNull`, `IsNotNull`    | `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`         |
| `True`, `False`          | `= true`, `= false`              |
| `IgnoreCase`             | Wraps both sides in `lower()`    |

Derived queries are excellent up to about three conditions, after which the
method name becomes unreadable. A name like
`findByStatusAndCustomerIdAndTotalGreaterThanAndPlacedAtBetween` is a signal to
switch to the next option.

**`@Query` with JPQL** gives full control while keeping the query next to the
method it serves.

```java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    @Query("""
            SELECT o FROM Order o
             WHERE o.customer.id = :customerId
               AND o.placedAt > :since
             ORDER BY o.placedAt DESC
            """)
    List<Order> findRecentFor(@Param("customerId") Long customerId,
                              @Param("since") Instant since);

    // JOIN FETCH solves 16.4's N+1 problem in a declared query.
    @Query("SELECT DISTINCT o FROM Order o LEFT JOIN FETCH o.lines WHERE o.id = :id")
    Optional<Order> findWithLines(@Param("id") Long id);

    // A projection: no entities loaded, just the columns the caller needs.
    @Query("SELECT new com.shop.OrderSummary(o.id, o.total) FROM Order o")
    List<OrderSummary> summaries();

    // Native SQL when JPQL cannot express it.
    @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > ?1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED",
           nativeQuery = true)
    List<Order> lockNextBatch(BigDecimal minimum);

    // Modifying queries must say so, and need a transaction.
    @Modifying
    @Transactional
    @Query("UPDATE Order o SET o.status = :status WHERE o.placedAt < :cutoff")
    int expireOlderThan(@Param("status") OrderStatus status,
                        @Param("cutoff") Instant cutoff);
}
```

Two details in that block are easy to get wrong. `@Modifying` is required for
`UPDATE` and `DELETE`, and without it the query fails. And a modifying query
bypasses the persistence context, so entities already loaded hold stale values;
`@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true)` addresses that.

**Projections** avoid loading entities at all, which 16.4 identified as the
right answer for list views. An interface with getters is the lightest form.

```java
// Spring Data implements this at runtime from the matching entity properties.
public interface OrderSummary {
    Long getId();
    BigDecimal getTotal();
    String getCustomerName();      // traverses customer.name
}

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    List<OrderSummary> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);   // selects only 3 columns
}
```

**Custom implementations** handle anything the above cannot, such as a query
built dynamically from optional filters.

```java
public interface OrderRepositoryCustom {
    List<Order> search(OrderSearchCriteria criteria);
}

// The suffix "Impl" is the convention Spring Data looks for.
public class OrderRepositoryCustomImpl implements OrderRepositoryCustom {

    @PersistenceContext private EntityManager em;

    @Override
    public List<Order> search(OrderSearchCriteria c) {
        var cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
        var query = cb.createQuery(Order.class);
        var root = query.from(Order.class);

        var predicates = new ArrayList<Predicate>();
        if (c.status() != null) {
            predicates.add(cb.equal(root.get("status"), c.status()));
        }
        if (c.minimum() != null) {
            predicates.add(cb.greaterThan(root.get("total"), c.minimum()));
        }
        query.where(predicates.toArray(Predicate[]::new));   // only what was supplied

        return em.createQuery(query).getResultList();
    }
}

// The main interface extends both, and the generated proxy combines them.
public interface OrderRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>, OrderRepositoryCustom { }
```

| Approach            | Best for                                        |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Derived method      | One to three simple conditions                   |
| `@Query` JPQL       | Complex conditions, joins, fetch plans           |
| `@Query` native     | Vendor features JPQL cannot express              |
| Projection          | Read-only lists where full entities are wasteful |
| Custom implementation | Dynamic queries built from optional filters    |

> Key Takeaways
> - Derived queries are parsed from method names and validated at startup.
> - Keep derived names to about three conditions before switching to `@Query`.
> - `@Query` holds JPQL or native SQL beside the method it implements.
> - `JOIN FETCH` in a declared query is the direct fix for N+1.
> - `@Modifying` is mandatory for update and delete queries and needs a
>   transaction.
> - A modifying query leaves loaded entities stale unless the context is
>   cleared.
> - Interface projections select only the columns they declare.
> - Dynamic multi-filter searches belong in a custom `Impl` class.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write derived methods for three different conditions and log the generated
>    SQL for each.
> 2. Misspell a property in a method name and read the startup error, noting
>    that it is not a runtime failure.
> 3. Replace an unreadable five-condition derived method with a `@Query`.
> 4. Add a `JOIN FETCH` query and confirm with SQL logging that N+1 disappears.
> 5. Implement a search taking three optional filters using a custom
>    implementation and the criteria builder.
> 6. Interview: Why is a mistyped field name in a derived query method caught at
>    startup rather than when the method is called? (Hint: when does Spring Data
>    build the implementation?)

#### Data Access Exception Translation

Chapter 16 described `SQLException` and the SQL state codes that distinguish a
constraint violation from a connection failure. Two problems remain in practice.
It is a checked exception, so every layer must declare or handle it, and its
error codes are vendor-specific, so handling a unique violation means writing
code that only works on one database.

```java
// Without translation: the caller imports java.sql and hard-codes a vendor code.
try {
    repository.save(user);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    if ("23505".equals(e.getSQLState())) {         // PostgreSQL-specific
        throw new DuplicateEmailException(user.email());
    }
    throw new RuntimeException(e);
}
```

Spring translates instead. Every `SQLException` from a template or a Spring Data
repository is converted into a subclass of `DataAccessException`, which is
**unchecked** and **vendor-neutral**.

```text
  DataAccessException                              (unchecked root)
   |
   +-- NonTransientDataAccessException             retrying will not help
   |    +-- DataIntegrityViolationException
   |    |     +-- DuplicateKeyException
   |    +-- BadSqlGrammarException
   |    +-- InvalidDataAccessApiUsageException
   |    +-- EmptyResultDataAccessException
   |    +-- IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException
   |
   +-- TransientDataAccessException                retrying may succeed
   |    +-- QueryTimeoutException
   |    +-- ConcurrencyFailureException
   |         +-- DeadlockLoserDataAccessException
   |         +-- OptimisticLockingFailureException
   |
   +-- RecoverableDataAccessException
```

The hierarchy mirrors 16.1's transient versus non-transient split, so the
retry-or-not decision reads the same way.

```java
// With translation: no java.sql import, no vendor codes, no checked exception.
try {
    repository.save(user);
} catch (DuplicateKeyException e) {                 // same class on any database
    throw new DuplicateEmailException(user.email(), e);
} catch (TransientDataAccessException e) {
    throw new RetryableException(e);                // deadlock, timeout
}
```

**How the translation happens** depends on which tool raised the exception.

| Source                   | Mechanism                                             |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `JdbcTemplate`           | Built in; always translates                            |
| Spring Data repositories | Built in; always translates                            |
| Your own DAO class       | Only if annotated `@Repository`                        |

That last row is the practical reason `@Repository` exists rather than being a
synonym for `@Component`. It marks the class for a post-processor that adds a
translating aspect.

```java
@Repository                     // enables exception translation on this class
public class LegacyOrderDao {

    @PersistenceContext
    private EntityManager em;

    public Order find(long id) {
        // A PersistenceException here is translated into a DataAccessException.
        return em.find(Order.class, id);
    }
}
```

Translation works by consulting a mapping of SQL state and vendor error codes,
loaded from `sql-error-codes.xml` for the detected database. When a code is not
recognised the exception becomes a generic `UncategorizedSQLException` rather
than being guessed at, and custom codes can be registered.

**Being unchecked is a design decision worth understanding.** Spring's argument
is that almost no caller can meaningfully recover from a database failure, so
forcing every method to declare `throws SQLException` adds noise without
benefit. The layers that can handle it, a retry wrapper or a global error
handler, catch it deliberately; everything else lets it propagate.

```java
// Clean signature: the exception is still possible, just not in the way.
public Optional<Order> findById(long id) {
    return jdbcTemplate.query(FIND_BY_ID, ORDER_MAPPER, id).stream().findFirst();
}
```

Two specific exceptions to know by name, since they come up constantly:
`EmptyResultDataAccessException` from `queryForObject` when no row matched, and
`OptimisticLockingFailureException`, which is 16.3's version-column conflict
surfacing through the same hierarchy.

> Key Takeaways
> - Spring converts `SQLException` and JPA exceptions into unchecked
>   `DataAccessException` subclasses.
> - The hierarchy is vendor-neutral, so a duplicate key is one class on every
>   database.
> - It splits transient from non-transient, matching 16.1's retry decision.
> - Templates and Spring Data repositories translate automatically.
> - A hand-written DAO translates only when annotated `@Repository`.
> - Unrecognised vendor codes become `UncategorizedSQLException` rather than a
>   guess.
> - Unchecked exceptions keep signatures clean, on the argument that most
>   callers cannot recover.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Trigger a unique constraint violation through `JdbcTemplate` and print the
>    exception class.
> 2. Run the same failing insert on two different databases and confirm the
>    Spring exception type matches.
> 3. Write a DAO without `@Repository`, observe the untranslated exception, then
>    add the annotation.
> 4. Catch `EmptyResultDataAccessException` from `queryForObject` and convert it
>    into an `Optional`.
> 5. Interview: What does `@Repository` do that `@Component` does not? (Hint: it
>    marks the class for a post-processor that adds one specific aspect.)

#### Schema Migration with Flyway or Liquibase

Application code is versioned, reviewed, and deployed as a unit. The database
schema it depends on usually is not, and the gap causes a familiar class of
incident: code that expects a column deployed against a database that does not
have it yet.

The approaches that do not work are worth naming, because both are common.

**Hibernate's automatic schema generation** is the first. Setting
`hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto` to `update` makes Hibernate alter the schema to match
the entities at startup.

```text
  spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update     # convenient, and unsafe in production
```

It never drops or renames anything, so removed fields leave orphaned columns; it
cannot migrate data, so splitting a column is impossible; and the exact
statements it issues depend on the Hibernate version. It is fine for a local
development database and is not a migration tool.

**Hand-applied SQL scripts** are the second. Someone runs the script before the
deploy. This works until someone forgets, runs them out of order, or runs one
twice, and there is no way to tell what a given database has had applied.

**Migration tools** solve it by treating the schema as an ordered, versioned
sequence of scripts, and by recording in the database itself which have been
applied.

```text
  src/main/resources/db/migration/
      V1__create_orders.sql
      V2__add_status_to_orders.sql
      V3__create_order_lines.sql
      V4__backfill_order_totals.sql
      ^  ^                    ^
      |  version              description
      prefix

  On startup Flyway:
      1. reads the flyway_schema_history table
      2. finds V1..V3 applied, V4 not
      3. applies V4 inside a transaction
      4. records V4 with a checksum
```

```sql
-- V2__add_status_to_orders.sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20);

-- Backfill before adding the constraint, or existing rows violate it.
UPDATE orders SET status = 'COMPLETED' WHERE status IS NULL;

ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;
```

Adding Flyway to a Spring Boot application is a dependency and a directory; it
runs automatically before the application context finishes starting, so the
schema is always correct before any query runs.

| Aspect            | Flyway                          | Liquibase                          |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Migration format  | Plain SQL, or Java for logic    | XML, YAML, JSON, or SQL            |
| Database-agnostic | No, you write vendor SQL        | Yes, abstract change types         |
| Rollback          | Paid feature                    | Built in                           |
| Learning curve    | Minimal if you know SQL         | Steeper, a new vocabulary          |
| Best when         | One database, SQL-fluent team   | Several databases must be supported |

Most teams on a single database choose Flyway for the simplicity of writing the
SQL that will actually run.

**The rules that make migrations safe** are few and absolute.

**Never modify an applied migration.** The tool stores a checksum, so editing
`V2` after it has run fails the next startup with a validation error. That
failure is the feature: it means one version number always describes one schema.
Fix problems by adding `V5`.

**One logical change per migration**, so a failure leaves an understandable
state and a review covers one idea.

**Make migrations backward compatible when deploys are rolling.** During a
rolling deploy, old and new code run against one database at the same time, so a
dropped column breaks the instances that have not been replaced yet. The
standard technique is to expand, migrate, then contract across separate
releases.

```text
  Release 1   add the new column, write to both, read the old      (expand)
  Release 2   backfill, read the new column
  Release 3   stop writing the old column
  Release 4   drop the old column                                  (contract)
```

**Test migrations against a copy of production data**, because a statement that
takes ten milliseconds on an empty table can lock a large table for minutes.

> Key Takeaways
> - Schema changes need versioning and automation as much as code does.
> - Hibernate's automatic DDL cannot drop, rename, or migrate data, so it is a
>   development convenience only.
> - Migration tools apply ordered scripts once and record them in the database.
> - Flyway uses plain SQL; Liquibase abstracts change types across vendors.
> - Spring Boot runs migrations before the application is ready to serve
>   requests.
> - Never edit an applied migration; checksum validation will reject it.
> - Rolling deploys need backward-compatible changes, split into expand and
>   contract releases.
> - Test migrations on production-sized data, since locking is the real risk.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add Flyway to a Spring Boot project and create two migrations, then inspect
>    the history table.
> 2. Edit an already-applied migration and read the validation error at startup.
> 3. Write a migration that adds a non-null column to a populated table,
>    handling the existing rows.
> 4. Plan the four releases required to rename a column without breaking a
>    rolling deploy.
> 5. Interview: Why is editing an applied migration rejected rather than simply
>    re-run? (Hint: what would then be true of two databases that both claim to
>    be at version 2?)

<a id="174-spring-mvc-and-web-layer"></a>
### 17.4 Spring MVC and Web Layer

This subchapter covers how an HTTP request becomes a Java method call and a
Java object becomes an HTTP response: the dispatcher at the centre, the
controllers it routes to, the binding and validation of input, and the two
mechanisms for handling errors and cross-cutting request concerns.

#### Front Controller Pattern and DispatcherServlet

A web application receives HTTP requests and must decide which code handles
each one. The Servlet API's own answer is to map URL patterns to servlet
classes, which means every endpoint needs a servlet, and every servlet repeats
the same work: parse parameters, check authentication, choose a response
format, handle errors.

```text
  Servlet-per-endpoint                  Front controller
  --------------------                  ----------------
  /orders     -> OrderServlet           all requests -> DispatcherServlet
  /orders/*   -> OrderDetailServlet                          |
  /customers  -> CustomerServlet                 routing, binding, conversion,
  /invoices   -> InvoiceServlet                  error handling, all in one place
                                                             |
  each repeats parsing, error                                v
  handling, and formatting              OrderController.list(...)  plain method
```

The **front controller** pattern routes every request through one entry point
that performs the common work and then delegates. Spring MVC's implementation is
`DispatcherServlet`, and it is the only servlet a typical Spring application
has.

The request flow is worth knowing in order, because almost every "why is my
endpoint not working" question resolves to one of these steps.

```text
   HTTP request
        |
        v
   [1] DispatcherServlet receives it
        |
        v
   [2] HandlerMapping     which method handles this URL and verb?
        |
        v
   [3] HandlerAdapter     invoke it, resolving each parameter
        |                      |
        |                 [3a] HandlerInterceptor.preHandle
        |                 [3b] argument resolvers: @PathVariable, @RequestBody, ...
        |                 [3c] YOUR CONTROLLER METHOD RUNS
        |                 [3d] HandlerInterceptor.postHandle
        v
   [4] Return value handling
        |    +-- @ResponseBody? -> HttpMessageConverter writes JSON
        |    +-- a view name?   -> ViewResolver finds a template, renders it
        v
   [5] HTTP response
        |
        +-- on any exception: HandlerExceptionResolver (see @ControllerAdvice)
```

Each numbered step is a strategy interface with a default implementation you can
replace, which is what makes the framework configurable without being edited.

| Component                | Responsibility                                   |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `HandlerMapping`         | Map a request to a handler method                 |
| `HandlerAdapter`         | Invoke the handler, resolving its arguments       |
| `HandlerExceptionResolver` | Turn an exception into a response                |
| `HttpMessageConverter`   | Convert between Java objects and request bodies   |
| `ViewResolver`           | Resolve a view name to a template                 |
| `LocaleResolver`         | Determine the request's locale                    |

Registering the dispatcher was once a chore in `web.xml`, then a Java class, and
in Spring Boot it is automatic.

```java
// Pre-Boot: register the dispatcher and point it at the configuration.
public class WebInitializer extends
        AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer {

    @Override protected Class<?>[] getRootConfigClasses() {
        return new Class[]{ AppConfig.class };        // services, repositories
    }

    @Override protected Class<?>[] getServletConfigClasses() {
        return new Class[]{ WebConfig.class };        // controllers, view resolvers
    }

    @Override protected String[] getServletMappings() {
        return new String[]{ "/" };                   // everything
    }
}
```

That example shows a structure worth knowing even though Boot hides it: there
are **two contexts**. The root context holds services and repositories; the
servlet context holds web components and can see the root, but not the reverse.
This prevents a service from depending on a controller.

```text
   Root ApplicationContext          services, repositories, data sources
        ^
        |  visible to
        |
   Servlet WebApplicationContext    controllers, converters, view resolvers
```

**In Spring Boot none of this is written.** `spring-boot-starter-web` puts an
embedded Tomcat and the dispatcher on the classpath, auto-configuration
registers it at `/`, and a single context is used. The value of knowing the flow
is diagnostic: a 404 means step 2 found no mapping, a 400 means step 3b failed
to bind, and a 500 with no log line usually means step 4 could not serialise the
return value.

> Key Takeaways
> - The front controller pattern routes every request through one entry point.
> - `DispatcherServlet` is that entry point and is usually the only servlet
>   present.
> - Handler mapping, argument resolution, return value handling, and exception
>   resolution are separate strategies.
> - Each strategy is an interface with a replaceable default implementation.
> - Classic applications separate a root context from a servlet context, and the
>   servlet context can see the root.
> - Spring Boot configures and registers everything automatically.
> - Knowing the flow turns status codes into a diagnosis of which step failed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Draw the request flow from the socket to a controller method and mark where
>    JSON deserialisation happens.
> 2. Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG` and read the mapping
>    decisions for one request.
> 3. Request a URL with no mapping and one with a wrong method, and compare the
>    two status codes.
> 4. List every handler mapping at startup and find the one for your own
>    controller.
> 5. Interview: Why does the front controller pattern make a framework easier to
>    extend than one servlet per endpoint? (Hint: where does a new cross-cutting
>    behaviour have to be added in each design?)

#### Controllers and Request Mapping

A controller is an ordinary class whose methods handle requests. There is no
base class and no interface; annotations do the work, which is why controller
methods can be called directly in tests.

```java
@RestController                       // @Controller + @ResponseBody
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")        // a prefix for every method below
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService service;

    public OrderController(OrderService service) {    // constructor injection
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping                                        // GET /api/orders
    public List<OrderResponse> list() {
        return service.findAll().stream().map(OrderResponse::from).toList();
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")                               // GET /api/orders/42
    public OrderResponse get(@PathVariable long id) {  // 42 binds to id
        return OrderResponse.from(service.findById(id));
    }

    @PostMapping                                       // POST /api/orders
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)                // 201 instead of 200
    public OrderResponse create(@RequestBody @Valid CreateOrderRequest request) {
        return OrderResponse.from(service.place(request.toOrder()));
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)             // 204, empty body
    public void delete(@PathVariable long id) {
        service.delete(id);
    }
}
```

The HTTP-method-specific annotations are shorthand for `@RequestMapping` with a
method attribute, and they are clearer.

| Shorthand        | Equivalent                                          |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `@GetMapping`    | `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)`        |
| `@PostMapping`   | `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.POST)`       |
| `@PutMapping`    | `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.PUT)`        |
| `@PatchMapping`  | `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.PATCH)`      |
| `@DeleteMapping` | `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.DELETE)`     |

**Mappings can narrow on more than path and method**, which is how one URL
serves several representations or API versions.

```java
@PostMapping(
    value = "/import",
    consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,   // only if Content-Type matches
    produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,   // sets the response type
    headers = "X-Api-Version=2",                   // only for version 2 clients
    params = "mode=async")                         // only when ?mode=async present
public ImportResult importAsync(@RequestBody ImportRequest request) { ... }
```

A request that matches the path but not `consumes` produces 415, and one that
matches but not `produces` produces 406. Recognising those two codes saves time.

**Path variables** support patterns, which matters when a segment can contain
characters that would otherwise be treated as a delimiter.

```java
@GetMapping("/{id}")                      // one segment
@GetMapping("/{year}/{month}")            // several
@GetMapping("/files/{*path}")             // captures the remainder, including /
@GetMapping("/{id:[0-9]+}")               // regex: digits only, so /orders/new
                                          // can map to a different method
```

**Method parameters are resolved by type and annotation**, and the range of
supported types is wide.

```java
@GetMapping("/search")
public List<OrderResponse> search(
        @RequestParam String status,                         // ?status=NEW, required
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,          // optional with default
        @RequestParam(required = false) BigDecimal minimum,  // optional, may be null
        @RequestHeader("X-Tenant") String tenant,            // a header
        @CookieValue(value = "session", required = false) String session,
        Pageable pageable,                                   // Spring Data builds it
        Locale locale,                                       // from Accept-Language
        HttpServletRequest raw) { ... }                      // the escape hatch
```

**Return values are handled by type too.**

| Return type            | Result                                             |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| An object              | Serialised to the negotiated format, status 200     |
| `void`                 | Empty body, status 200 or the `@ResponseStatus`     |
| `ResponseEntity<T>`    | Full control over status, headers, and body         |
| `String` (`@Controller`) | A view name to resolve and render                 |
| `Optional<T>`          | 200 with the value, or 404 when empty               |
| `CompletableFuture<T>` | Asynchronous; the servlet thread is released        |

`ResponseEntity` is the right choice when the status depends on the outcome.

```java
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(@RequestBody @Valid CreateOrderRequest r) {
    Order order = service.place(r.toOrder());
    URI location = URI.create("/api/orders/" + order.id());

    return ResponseEntity.created(location)          // 201 plus a Location header
            .body(OrderResponse.from(order));
}
```

**Keep controllers thin.** A controller's job is to translate between HTTP and
the domain: bind input, call one service method, map the result to a response.
Business logic, transactions, and database access belong below it. A controller
that reads well is usually three to five lines per method.

**Use separate request and response types** rather than exposing entities
directly. An entity exposed as a response leaks the schema, serialises lazy
associations at the worst possible moment, and lets a client set fields it
should not.

```java
// A request type accepts only what a client may set.
public record CreateOrderRequest(@NotNull Long customerId,
                                 @NotEmpty List<LineRequest> lines) {
    public Order toOrder() { ... }
}

// A response type exposes only what a client should see.
public record OrderResponse(long id, String status, BigDecimal total) {
    public static OrderResponse from(Order order) { ... }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Controllers are plain classes; annotations define the mapping.
> - `@RestController` combines `@Controller` with `@ResponseBody`.
> - Method-specific shorthand annotations are clearer than `@RequestMapping`
>   with attributes.
> - Mappings can also narrow on content type, headers, and parameters, giving
>   415 and 406 respectively when they do not match.
> - Parameters are resolved by annotation and type, covering path, query,
>   header, cookie, and body.
> - `ResponseEntity` is for when status or headers depend on the outcome.
> - Controllers should translate and delegate, not contain logic.
> - Dedicated request and response types keep entities out of the API contract.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a controller with the five standard REST endpoints for one resource,
>    returning correct status codes.
> 2. Add a regex path variable so that a literal path segment and a numeric
>    identifier map to different methods.
> 3. Trigger 404, 405, 415, and 406 deliberately and note what each one tells
>    you about the mapping.
> 4. Return `ResponseEntity` with a `Location` header from a creation endpoint
>    and verify it.
> 5. Expose an entity with a lazy association directly and observe the
>    serialisation failure, then fix it with a response type.
> 6. Interview: Why should a controller return a dedicated response type rather
>    than a JPA entity? (Hint: name one security consequence and one from 16.4.)

#### Request Binding and Bean Validation

Everything arriving in an HTTP request is text. A path segment is a string, a
query parameter is a string, a JSON body is a byte stream. Turning that into
typed Java objects is **binding**, and confirming it makes sense is
**validation**. They are separate steps with separate failure modes.

**Binding** happens before the controller method runs.

```text
  GET /api/orders/42?status=NEW&since=2026-01-01

     "42"          -> @PathVariable long id          -> 42L
     "NEW"         -> @RequestParam OrderStatus      -> OrderStatus.NEW
     "2026-01-01"  -> @RequestParam LocalDate since  -> LocalDate
     JSON body     -> @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest -> object, via Jackson
```

Simple types are converted by Spring's conversion service; the request body is
deserialised by an `HttpMessageConverter`, which for JSON means Jackson. A
failure at this stage is a 400 before your code is reached, which is why a
malformed body never produces a `NullPointerException` in the controller.

**Complex parameters can bind without an annotation**, which is how HTML form
submissions and multi-parameter queries are handled.

```java
// Query parameters bind to the record's components by name.
public record OrderSearch(OrderStatus status, LocalDate from, LocalDate to) { }

@GetMapping("/search")
public List<OrderResponse> search(OrderSearch criteria) { ... }
// GET /api/orders/search?status=NEW&from=2026-01-01
```

**Custom converters** handle domain types, so a controller can take a value
object rather than a raw string.

```java
@Component
public class StringToOrderReferenceConverter
        implements Converter<String, OrderReference> {

    @Override
    public OrderReference convert(String source) {
        return OrderReference.parse(source);      // throws on invalid input -> 400
    }
}

@GetMapping("/{reference}")
public OrderResponse get(@PathVariable OrderReference reference) { ... }
```

**Validation** is a separate concern: the input parsed correctly, but is it
acceptable? Bean Validation, the Jakarta standard, expresses the rules as
annotations on the type rather than as `if` statements in the controller.

```java
public record CreateOrderRequest(

        @NotNull(message = "customerId is required")
        Long customerId,

        @NotEmpty(message = "an order needs at least one line")
        @Size(max = 100, message = "at most 100 lines per order")
        @Valid                                    // cascade into each element
        List<LineRequest> lines,

        @Email
        String notificationEmail,                 // null is valid; @Email allows it

        @Future(message = "delivery must be in the future")
        LocalDate requestedDelivery) { }

public record LineRequest(
        @NotNull Long productId,
        @Positive int quantity,
        @DecimalMin(value = "0.00", inclusive = false) BigDecimal unitPrice) { }
```

| Annotation                   | Checks                                  |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `@NotNull`                   | Not null; empty string passes            |
| `@NotEmpty`                  | Not null and not empty                   |
| `@NotBlank`                  | Not null and contains non-whitespace     |
| `@Size(min, max)`            | Length or collection size                |
| `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Positive`  | Numeric bounds                           |
| `@Email`, `@Pattern`         | String format                            |
| `@Past`, `@Future`           | Temporal bounds                          |
| `@Valid`                     | Cascade validation into a nested object  |

The distinction between `@NotNull`, `@NotEmpty`, and `@NotBlank` is a common
source of bugs: `@NotNull` accepts `""` and `"   "`, so a required text field
almost always wants `@NotBlank`.

**Triggering validation** requires `@Valid` on the parameter. Without it the
annotations are inert, which is the most common reason validation "does not
work".

```java
@PostMapping
public OrderResponse create(@RequestBody @Valid CreateOrderRequest request) {
    // Reaching this line guarantees every rule above passed.
    return OrderResponse.from(service.place(request.toOrder()));
}
```

A failure throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which by default produces a
400 with a body that exposes internal structure. Real APIs handle it explicitly,
which the next topic covers.

**Validating method parameters directly** needs `@Validated` on the class,
because those constraints are enforced by an aspect rather than by the binder.

```java
@RestController
@Validated                                   // enables parameter-level validation
public class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<OrderResponse> search(
            @RequestParam @Size(min = 3) String query,       // enforced by an aspect
            @RequestParam @Min(1) @Max(100) int limit) { ... }
}
```

**Custom constraints** keep domain rules declarative instead of scattering
checks.

```java
@Constraint(validatedBy = ValidReferenceValidator.class)
@Target(ElementType.FIELD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface ValidReference {
    String message() default "malformed order reference";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}

public class ValidReferenceValidator
        implements ConstraintValidator<ValidReference, String> {

    @Override
    public boolean isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext context) {
        return value == null || value.matches("ORD-\\d{8}");   // null is @NotNull's job
    }
}
```

Letting null pass is the convention: each annotation should check one thing, and
nullability is `@NotNull`'s responsibility.

**Validate at the boundary, and again where it matters.** Bean Validation on a
request type protects against malformed input. It does not replace domain
invariants, which belong in the domain objects themselves, because a service
called from a scheduled job never passes through a controller.

> Key Takeaways
> - Binding converts request text into typed objects before the controller runs.
> - Binding failures produce 400 responses without reaching your code.
> - Complex objects bind from query parameters by component name, with no
>   annotation.
> - Custom `Converter` beans let controllers accept domain types directly.
> - Bean Validation expresses rules as annotations on the type.
> - `@NotNull` permits empty and blank strings; text fields usually want
>   `@NotBlank`.
> - Rules are inert without `@Valid` on the parameter, and `@Valid` also
>   cascades into nested objects.
> - Method parameter constraints need `@Validated` on the class.
> - Request validation complements, but does not replace, domain invariants.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Bind a query string to a record with three components and confirm no
>    annotation is needed.
> 2. Write a custom `Converter` for a domain identifier type and use it as a
>    path variable.
> 3. Annotate a request type with five constraints, submit invalid input, and
>    inspect the default error response.
> 4. Demonstrate the difference between `@NotNull`, `@NotEmpty`, and `@NotBlank`
>    with three inputs.
> 5. Remove `@Valid` from a handler and show that the constraints stop being
>    enforced.
> 6. Interview: A team reports that their validation annotations are ignored on
>    one endpoint. What are the two most likely causes? (Hint: one concerns the
>    parameter, one concerns where the constraints are declared.)

#### REST Controllers and Content Negotiation

REST is an architectural style, not a framework feature, and applying it well is
mostly about using HTTP as it was designed rather than tunnelling everything
through `POST /doThing`.

Four principles do most of the work.

**Resources are nouns, identified by URLs.** The verb belongs to the HTTP
method.

| Operation          | RESTful                  | Not RESTful                 |
| ------------------ | ------------------------ | --------------------------- |
| List orders        | `GET /orders`            | `GET /getOrders`            |
| Fetch order 42     | `GET /orders/42`         | `GET /order?action=get&id=42` |
| Create an order    | `POST /orders`           | `POST /createOrder`         |
| Replace order 42   | `PUT /orders/42`         | `POST /updateOrder`         |
| Cancel order 42    | `POST /orders/42/cancel` | `POST /cancelOrder`         |

The last row shows the pragmatic exception: an operation that is genuinely an
action rather than a state replacement is modelled as a sub-resource.

**Methods have defined semantics**, and clients, proxies, and retry logic rely
on them.

| Method   | Safe | Idempotent | Meaning                             |
| -------- | ---- | ---------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `GET`    | Yes  | Yes        | Retrieve; must not change state      |
| `POST`   | No   | No         | Create, or a non-idempotent action   |
| `PUT`    | No   | Yes        | Replace the resource entirely        |
| `PATCH`  | No   | No         | Apply a partial change               |
| `DELETE` | No   | Yes        | Remove the resource                  |

Idempotence is what allows a client to retry a failed `PUT` safely. A `POST`
that creates a resource cannot be retried blindly, which is why creation
endpoints often accept an idempotency key.

**Status codes carry the outcome**, so clients do not have to parse the body.

| Code | Use for                                                   |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| 200  | Success with a body                                        |
| 201  | Created, with a `Location` header                          |
| 204  | Success with no body, typical for `DELETE`                 |
| 400  | Malformed or invalid request                               |
| 401  | Not authenticated                                          |
| 403  | Authenticated but not permitted                            |
| 404  | No such resource                                           |
| 409  | Conflict, such as an optimistic locking failure            |
| 422  | Well-formed but semantically invalid                       |
| 500  | A server fault the client cannot fix                       |

Returning 200 with `{"error": "not found"}` is the anti-pattern this table
exists to prevent: it forces every client to inspect the body to know whether
the call worked.

**Content negotiation** lets one endpoint serve several representations. The
client states what it wants with `Accept`; the server states what it sent with
`Content-Type`.

```text
  Request                                Response
  -------                                --------
  GET /api/orders/42                     200 OK
  Accept: application/json               Content-Type: application/json
                                         {"id":42,...}

  GET /api/orders/42                     200 OK
  Accept: application/xml                Content-Type: application/xml
                                         <order><id>42</id>...</order>

  GET /api/orders/42                     406 Not Acceptable
  Accept: application/pdf                (no converter produces PDF)
```

Spring performs this through `HttpMessageConverter` implementations, selected by
what is on the classpath and what the request asked for.

```java
@GetMapping(value = "/{id}",
            produces = { MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
                         MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE })
public OrderResponse get(@PathVariable long id) {
    return OrderResponse.from(service.findById(id));   // one method, two formats
}
```

**Jackson controls the JSON representation**, and a few annotations cover most
needs.

```java
public record OrderResponse(
        long id,

        @JsonProperty("order_status")                   // rename in JSON
        String status,

        @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING,
                    pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX")
        OffsetDateTime placedAt,

        @JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)      // omit when null
        String cancellationReason) { }
```

Global settings are usually better than per-field annotations for consistency.

```text
  spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE
  spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
  spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false
```

**Versioning** becomes necessary as soon as a client you do not control depends
on the API. Three approaches are common.

| Approach     | Example                                    | Trade-off                     |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| URL path     | `/api/v2/orders`                            | Obvious, but duplicates routes |
| Header       | `X-Api-Version: 2`                          | Clean URLs, harder to test by hand |
| Media type   | `Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json`      | Purest REST, least familiar   |

```java
@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", headers = "X-Api-Version=2")
```
