```java
public OrderResponseV2 getV2(@PathVariable long id) { ... }
```

Path versioning wins in practice because it is visible in logs and trivially
testable from a browser or a command line.

> Key Takeaways
> - REST models resources as nouns and uses HTTP methods as the verbs.
> - Safety and idempotence determine what a client may retry.
> - Status codes communicate the outcome, so a body should never be the only
>   signal.
> - Content negotiation uses `Accept` and `Content-Type` with message
>   converters.
> - An unsupported `Accept` yields 406; an unsupported `Content-Type` yields
>   415.
> - Jackson annotations shape JSON, but global configuration gives consistency.
> - Versioning by URL path is the most practical of the three common schemes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Design the URLs and methods for a resource with list, fetch, create,
>    replace, delete, and one action endpoint.
> 2. Return the correct status code from each endpoint and verify them with a
>    command-line client.
> 3. Add the XML converter dependency and serve the same endpoint as JSON and
>    XML by varying `Accept`.
> 4. Configure snake case globally and confirm the change without editing any
>    response type.
> 5. Add a second version of one endpoint behind a header and route between
>    them.
> 6. Interview: Why does it matter that `PUT` is idempotent but `POST` is not?
>    (Hint: think about a client whose connection drops before the response
>    arrives.)

#### Centralized Error Handling with @ControllerAdvice

Without deliberate error handling, every controller method grows a `try`/`catch`
block that maps exceptions onto status codes, duplicating logic and drifting out
of sync between endpoints.

```java
// The problem: this block, repeated in every method of every controller.
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<?> get(@PathVariable long id) {
    try {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(service.findById(id));
    } catch (OrderNotFoundException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(404).body(Map.of("error", e.getMessage()));
    } catch (AccessDeniedException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(403).body(Map.of("error", "forbidden"));
    } catch (Exception e) {
        log.error("unexpected", e);
        return ResponseEntity.status(500).body(Map.of("error", "internal"));
    }
}
```

`@ControllerAdvice` moves all of it into one class whose handlers apply across
every controller. It is the same idea as the aspects of 17.2: the concern is
cross-cutting, so it lives in one place.

```java
@RestControllerAdvice              // @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    public ErrorResponse handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException e) {
        return new ErrorResponse("ORDER_NOT_FOUND", e.getMessage());
    }

    // Validation failures: turn the framework exception into a useful body.
    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
    public ValidationErrorResponse handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        List<FieldError> errors = e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(fe -> new FieldError(fe.getField(), fe.getDefaultMessage()))
                .toList();
        return new ValidationErrorResponse("VALIDATION_FAILED", errors);
    }

    // 17.3's translated exceptions map cleanly onto status codes.
    @ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
    public ErrorResponse handleConflict(OptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
        return new ErrorResponse("CONFLICT", "the record changed, please retry");
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(DuplicateKeyException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
    public ErrorResponse handleDuplicate(DuplicateKeyException e) {
        return new ErrorResponse("DUPLICATE", "that value already exists");
    }

    // The catch-all. Log the detail; return none of it.
    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
    public ErrorResponse handleUnexpected(Exception e) {
        String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        log.error("unhandled error {}", id, e);        // full detail in the log
        return new ErrorResponse("INTERNAL_ERROR",
                "unexpected error, reference " + id);  // an id, not a stack trace
    }
}
```

That last handler contains the most important rule in this topic: **never return
exception details to a client**. A stack trace names your classes, framework
versions, and sometimes SQL, all of which help an attacker. Log the detail with
a correlation identifier and return the identifier.

**Handler selection is by exception type, most specific first**, so a handler
for `Exception` does not shadow one for `OrderNotFoundException`.

```text
  thrown: OrderNotFoundException
     |
     +-- handler for OrderNotFoundException ?  yes -> use it
     +-- handler for RuntimeException ?
     +-- handler for Exception ?
```

**Advice can be scoped** rather than global, which matters when an API and a
server-rendered UI need different error representations.

```java
@RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.shop.api")          // JSON errors
public class ApiExceptionHandler { }

@ControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.shop.web")              // rendered pages
public class WebExceptionHandler { }

@RestControllerAdvice(assignableTypes = OrderController.class) // one controller
public class OrderExceptionHandler { }
```

**A standard error format** is worth adopting, and RFC 7807 problem details is
the one Spring supports directly.

```java
@ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
public ProblemDetail handle(OrderNotFoundException e) {
    var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND,
                                                   e.getMessage());
    problem.setTitle("Order not found");
    problem.setType(URI.create("https://api.shop.com/errors/order-not-found"));
    problem.setProperty("orderId", e.orderId());       // domain-specific field
    return problem;
}
```

```json
{
  "type": "https://api.shop.com/errors/order-not-found",
  "title": "Order not found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "No order with id 42",
  "orderId": 42
}
```

**`@ControllerAdvice` also handles two other cross-cutting jobs**, which is
worth knowing because they appear in older code.

```java
@ControllerAdvice
public class GlobalModelAdvice {

    @ModelAttribute("supportedCurrencies")   // added to every model
    public List<String> currencies() { return List.of("EUR", "USD"); }

    @InitBinder
    public void configure(WebDataBinder binder) {
        binder.setDisallowedFields("id");    // never bind an id from input
    }
}
```

Finally, exceptions that map directly onto a status with no extra logic need no
handler at all.

```java
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)       // mapped wherever it is thrown
public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException { }
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `@ControllerAdvice` centralises exception handling across controllers.
> - `@RestControllerAdvice` adds `@ResponseBody` for JSON error responses.
> - Handlers are selected by exception type, most specific first.
> - Never expose stack traces or messages from unexpected exceptions; log with a
>   correlation id.
> - Handling `MethodArgumentNotValidException` turns validation failures into a
>   usable body.
> - Translated data access exceptions map naturally onto 409 and similar codes.
> - Advice can be scoped by package, annotation, or controller type.
> - `ProblemDetail` provides a standard error format without inventing one.
> - `@ResponseStatus` on an exception class covers the simplest cases.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a global handler covering not-found, validation, and unexpected
>    errors, returning a consistent body.
> 2. Convert `MethodArgumentNotValidException` into a response listing each
>    invalid field and its message.
> 3. Throw a runtime exception from a controller and confirm no stack trace
>    reaches the client while the log has one.
> 4. Return `ProblemDetail` from one handler and compare the body with your own
>    error type.
> 5. Create two advice classes scoped to different packages and verify each
>    handles only its own.
> 6. Interview: Why should an unexpected exception return a correlation
>    identifier rather than its message? (Hint: who reads the response, and what
>    might the message contain?)

#### Filters, Interceptors, and Request Lifecycle

Some concerns apply to every request regardless of which controller handles it:
authentication, request logging, correlation identifiers, CORS headers,
compression. Spring offers two places to put them, and choosing correctly
requires knowing where each sits in the request's journey.

```text
   HTTP request
       |
       v
   [ Servlet Filter chain ]          servlet-level, sees raw request/response
       |                             runs even when no handler matches
       v
   [ DispatcherServlet ]
       |
       v
   [ HandlerInterceptor.preHandle ]  Spring-level, knows the handler method
       |
       v
   [ argument resolution, controller method, return value handling ]
       |
       v
   [ HandlerInterceptor.postHandle ] before the view renders
       |
       v
   [ view rendering or body conversion ]
       |
       v
   [ HandlerInterceptor.afterCompletion ]
       |
       v
   [ Filter chain unwinds ]
       |
       v
   HTTP response
```

**A filter** is part of the Servlet API. It sees the raw request and response,
runs before Spring's dispatcher, and can wrap or replace either.

```java
@Component
@Order(1)                                      // filter chain order
public class CorrelationIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
                                    HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {

        String id = Optional.ofNullable(request.getHeader("X-Correlation-Id"))
                            .orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        MDC.put("correlationId", id);          // every log line in this request
        response.setHeader("X-Correlation-Id", id);
        try {
            chain.doFilter(request, response); // continue; omitting this blocks it
        } finally {
            MDC.clear();                       // the thread is reused: always clear
        }
    }
}
```

Extending `OncePerRequestFilter` rather than implementing `Filter` guarantees
the logic runs once even when the request is forwarded internally.

**An interceptor** is Spring's own, and its advantage is context: `preHandle`
receives the handler that is about to run, so it can read the controller
method's annotations.

```java
@Component
public class RateLimitInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {

    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request,
                             HttpServletResponse response,
                             Object handler) {

        if (handler instanceof HandlerMethod method) {
            // The interceptor can inspect the target method's annotations.
            RateLimited limit = method.getMethodAnnotation(RateLimited.class);
            if (limit != null && exceeded(request, limit.perMinute())) {
                response.setStatus(429);
                return false;               // false stops the request here
            }
        }
        return true;                        // true continues to the controller
    }

    @Override
    public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request,
                                HttpServletResponse response,
                                Object handler, Exception ex) {
        // Runs even when the handler threw; the right place for cleanup.
    }
}
```

```java
@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    private final RateLimitInterceptor rateLimit;

    @Override
    public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
        registry.addInterceptor(rateLimit)
                .addPathPatterns("/api/**")          // where it applies
                .excludePathPatterns("/api/health"); // and where it does not
    }
}
```

| Aspect                     | Filter                     | Interceptor                  |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Defined by                 | Servlet API                | Spring MVC                   |
| Runs for unmapped requests | Yes                        | No                           |
| Knows the handler method   | No                         | Yes                          |
| Can modify the body stream | Yes, by wrapping           | Not directly                 |
| Access to Spring beans     | Yes, if a bean itself      | Yes                          |
| Best for                   | Security, logging, CORS, compression | Business-aware checks, timing, model work |

The decision rule is short: **if it needs to know which controller method will
run, use an interceptor; otherwise use a filter.**

**`WebMvcConfigurer`** is the general customisation hook and covers more than
interceptors.

```java
@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                .allowedOrigins("https://shop.example.com")   // never "*" with credentials
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE")
                .allowCredentials(true)
                .maxAge(3600);
    }

    @Override
    public void addFormatters(FormatterRegistry registry) {
        registry.addConverter(new StringToOrderReferenceConverter());
    }

    @Override
    public void configureContentNegotiation(ContentNegotiationConfigurer c) {
        c.defaultContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON);
    }
}
```

Implementing the interface adds to Boot's auto-configuration. Annotating the
class `@EnableWebMvc` **replaces** it, which switches off content negotiation
defaults, static resource handling, and message converter setup. That is almost
never what you want in a Boot application, and it is a common way to break one.

**One caution about request bodies in filters:** the body is a stream and can be
read once. A filter that logs the body consumes it, and the controller then
receives nothing. Wrapping the request with `ContentCachingRequestWrapper` is
the supported way to read it twice, at the cost of buffering.

> Key Takeaways
> - Filters are servlet-level, run outside the dispatcher, and see every
>   request.
> - Interceptors are Spring-level and know which handler method will run.
> - `preHandle` returning false stops the request before the controller.
> - `afterCompletion` runs even when the handler threw, so cleanup belongs
>   there.
> - Thread-local state such as logging context must be cleared, since threads
>   are pooled.
> - `OncePerRequestFilter` prevents duplicate execution on internal forwards.
> - `WebMvcConfigurer` customises CORS, converters, and negotiation without
>   replacing defaults.
> - `@EnableWebMvc` disables Boot's web auto-configuration entirely.
> - A request body can be read only once unless the request is wrapped.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a filter that adds a correlation identifier to every response and to
>    the logging context.
> 2. Write an interceptor that rejects requests missing a header, and confirm it
>    does not run for an unmapped URL.
> 3. Implement timing in both a filter and an interceptor, and explain why the
>    two measurements differ.
> 4. Configure CORS for one path prefix and verify the preflight response.
> 5. Log a request body in a filter, observe the controller receiving an empty
>    body, then fix it with a caching wrapper.
> 6. Interview: You need to reject requests to methods annotated
>    `@AdminOnly`. Filter or interceptor, and why? (Hint: at which point does
>    the framework know which method will handle the request?)

<a id="175-core-spring-annotations"></a>
### 17.5 Core Spring Annotations

This subchapter consolidates the annotations the rest of the chapter introduced,
organised by what they do rather than by where they appeared, and finishes by
showing how Spring's own annotations are built so you can compose your own.

#### Stereotype Annotations

A **stereotype** marks a class as a container-managed bean and says what kind of
role it plays. Spring finds them during component scanning, described in 17.1.

The defining fact about them is that they are all `@Component` underneath.

```java
// This is Spring's actual definition, simplified.
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Component                          // <-- @Service IS a @Component
public @interface Service {
    @AliasFor(annotation = Component.class)
    String value() default "";
}
```

Spring treats an annotation carrying `@Component` anywhere in its own annotation
tree as a component. This is **meta-annotation** support, and it is the
mechanism behind the whole hierarchy.

```text
  @Component                     any Spring-managed bean
      |
      +-- @Service               business logic; no added behaviour
      |
      +-- @Repository            data access; ADDS exception translation
      |
      +-- @Controller            web handler; methods return view names
      |     |
      |     +-- @RestController  @Controller + @ResponseBody
      |
      +-- @Configuration         declares @Bean methods; ADDS proxying
```

| Annotation        | Layer              | Behaviour beyond registration                  |
| ----------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `@Component`      | Any                | None                                            |
| `@Service`        | Business logic     | None; communicates intent                       |
| `@Repository`     | Data access        | Exception translation, as 17.3 described        |
| `@Controller`     | Web                | Enables request mapping and view resolution     |
| `@RestController` | Web, REST          | As `@Controller`, plus `@ResponseBody` on every method |
| `@Configuration`  | Configuration      | Full-mode proxying, as 17.1 described           |

The two rows with real behaviour are the ones to remember. Using `@Component`
where `@Repository` belongs silently loses exception translation, and using
`@Component` instead of `@Configuration` silently loses inter-bean singleton
semantics.

```java
@Service                                        // intent: business logic
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;   // constructor injection, 17.1

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    @Transactional                              // the aspect from 17.2
    public Order place(Order order) {
        return repository.save(order);
    }
}

@Repository                                     // intent AND exception translation
public class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;    // the template from 17.3
    ...
}

@RestController                                 // intent AND @ResponseBody
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {
    private final OrderService service;
    ...
}
```

**Naming.** A stereotype's `value` sets the bean name, overriding the default
decapitalised class name.

```java
@Service("legacyPricing")                       // bean name: legacyPricing
public class PricingServiceV1 implements PricingService { }
```

**Why bother distinguishing them** when three of the five behave identically?
Three reasons hold up. The layer is visible at a glance, which helps navigation.
Pointcuts can target a stereotype, so `within(@org.springframework.stereotype.
Service *)` selects every service. And architecture tests can assert the
layering rules, such as no repository depending on a controller.

```java
// An ArchUnit rule that enforces the layering the stereotypes declare.
@ArchTest
static final ArchRule repositoriesDoNotDependOnControllers =
        noClasses().that().areAnnotatedWith(Repository.class)
                   .should().dependOnClassesThat()
                   .areAnnotatedWith(Controller.class);
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Every stereotype is a meta-annotated `@Component`, which is how scanning
>   finds them.
> - `@Service` and `@Component` are functionally identical and differ in intent.
> - `@Repository` adds exception translation and `@Configuration` adds proxying.
> - `@RestController` is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody` on every method.
> - The `value` attribute sets the bean name.
> - Correct stereotypes enable pointcuts and architecture rules that target a
>   layer.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace `@Repository` with `@Component` on a DAO and show that exception
>    translation stops.
> 2. Write a pointcut matching every class annotated `@Service` and log each
>    call.
> 3. Name two beans of the same type explicitly and inject each by name.
> 4. Interview: Which two stereotypes change behaviour rather than only
>    documenting intent, and what does each add? (Hint: one relates to chapter
>    16's exceptions, one to how `@Bean` methods call each other.)

#### Configuration and Bean Annotations

These annotations declare what beans exist and where their settings come from.
17.1 introduced the first two; this topic covers the full set as a reference.

**`@Configuration` and `@Bean`** declare beans in code.

```java
@Configuration
public class InfrastructureConfig {

    @Bean                                           // bean name: dataSource
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) {
        var config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl(props.url());
        config.setMaximumPoolSize(props.poolSize());
        return new HikariDataSource(config);
    }

    @Bean(initMethod = "start", destroyMethod = "stop")   // lifecycle for a
    public MetricsReporter metricsReporter() {            // third-party class
        return new MetricsReporter();
    }

    @Bean
    @Scope("prototype")                             // the scopes from 17.1
    public ImportJob importJob() {
        return new ImportJob();
    }
}
```

`initMethod` and `destroyMethod` are the `@Bean` equivalent of `@PostConstruct`
and `@PreDestroy`, and exist because you cannot annotate a class you do not own.

**Composition annotations** assemble configuration from several classes, which
is how a large application stays organised.

```java
@Configuration
@Import({ InfrastructureConfig.class, SecurityConfig.class })   // explicit
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.shop")                       // by scanning
@PropertySource("classpath:application.properties")             // external values
@EnableTransactionManagement                                    // 17.3's aspect
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy                                         // 17.2's proxies
@EnableJpaRepositories("com.shop.repository")                   // 17.3's repositories
@EnableCaching                                                  // 17.2's cache aspect
@EnableScheduling                                               // @Scheduled support
public class ApplicationConfig { }
```

The `@Enable*` family follows one pattern: each imports the configuration that
registers the beans for a feature. Spring Boot's auto-configuration applies most
of them for you based on the classpath.

| Annotation                    | Registers                                |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `@EnableTransactionManagement`| The `@Transactional` aspect               |
| `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy`     | The proxy creator for `@Aspect` beans     |
| `@EnableCaching`              | The caching aspect                        |
| `@EnableScheduling`           | The `@Scheduled` task scheduler           |
| `@EnableAsync`                | The `@Async` executor                     |
| `@EnableWebMvc`               | Full MVC configuration, replacing Boot's  |
| `@EnableJpaRepositories`      | Repository proxy generation               |

**Property injection** brings external configuration into beans.

```java
@Component
public class PaymentGateway {

    private final String endpoint;
    private final Duration timeout;

    public PaymentGateway(
            @Value("${payment.endpoint}") String endpoint,              // required
            @Value("${payment.timeout:5s}") Duration timeout) {         // default
        this.endpoint = endpoint;
        this.timeout = timeout;      // "5s" is converted to a Duration
    }
}
```

`@Value` supports defaults after a colon, Spring Expression Language, and type
conversion. It becomes unwieldy past a few properties, at which point
`@ConfigurationProperties` binds a whole group to a typed object.

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment")   // binds payment.* to these fields
@Validated                                     // 17.4's Bean Validation, at startup
public record PaymentProperties(
        @NotBlank String endpoint,
        @NotNull Duration timeout,
        @Min(1) @Max(10) int retries) { }
```

```text
  payment.endpoint=https://pay.example.com
  payment.timeout=5s
  payment.retries=3
```

This is the better choice for any group of related settings: it is typed,
validated at startup rather than at first use, and discoverable in one place.

**`@DependsOn`** forces an initialisation order when one bean has a side effect
another relies on and there is no injection between them.

```java
@Bean
@DependsOn("flywayMigration")          // ensure the schema exists first
public CacheWarmer cacheWarmer(OrderRepository repository) { ... }
```

Needing it is usually a sign that a dependency should be explicit instead.

**`@Lazy`** defers creation until first use, which contradicts the fail-fast
startup that 17.1 described as a feature. Use it for expensive beans that are
rarely needed, not as a way to silence a circular dependency.

```java
@Bean
@Lazy                                  // created on first injection or getBean
public ExpensiveReportEngine reportEngine() { ... }
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `@Configuration` with `@Bean` methods declares beans in code, with full
>   logic available.
> - `initMethod` and `destroyMethod` provide lifecycle hooks for third-party
>   classes.
> - `@Import`, `@ComponentScan`, and `@PropertySource` assemble configuration
>   from parts.
> - The `@Enable*` family each imports the configuration for one feature.
> - `@Value` injects single properties with defaults and type conversion.
> - `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a group to a typed, validated object and
>   scales better.
> - `@DependsOn` forces ordering and usually signals a missing explicit
>   dependency.
> - `@Lazy` defers creation and trades away fail-fast startup.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Declare a third-party class as a bean with an init and a destroy method,
>    and log both.
> 2. Inject the same setting with `@Value` and with `@ConfigurationProperties`,
>    then compare what happens when it is missing.
> 3. Add `@Validated` to a properties record and start the application with an
>    invalid value.
> 4. Split one configuration class into three and compose them with `@Import`.
> 5. Interview: When would you prefer `@ConfigurationProperties` over several
>    `@Value` annotations? (Hint: think about when an invalid value is
>    discovered.)

#### Injection and Wiring Annotations

These annotations control how the container satisfies a dependency. 17.1 covered
the mechanics; this topic is the reference, including the standard Java
alternatives you will meet in mixed codebases.

**`@Autowired`** requests injection by type. Modern code uses it rarely, because
a single constructor is injected automatically.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    // No @Autowired needed: one constructor means Spring uses it.
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) { ... }
}

@Service
public class ReportService {

    // With several constructors, one must be marked.
    @Autowired
    public ReportService(OrderRepository repository) { ... }

    public ReportService() { }        // for tests, not for the container
}
```

```java
// Optional dependencies: three ways to express the same thing.
@Autowired(required = false)
private MetricsCollector metrics;                       // null when absent

public OrderService(Optional<MetricsCollector> metrics) { ... }   // preferred

public OrderService(ObjectProvider<MetricsCollector> metrics) {
    this.metrics = metrics.getIfAvailable(NoOpCollector::new);    // with a fallback
}
```

**`@Qualifier` and `@Primary`** resolve ambiguity, as 17.1 detailed.

```java
@Component @Primary  public class EmailSender implements NotificationSender { }
@Component           public class SmsSender   implements NotificationSender { }

@Service
public class AlertService {
    public AlertService(@Qualifier("smsSender") NotificationSender sender) { ... }
}
```

**`@Value`** injects a value rather than a bean, and supports expressions.

```java
@Value("${app.name}")                              // a property
@Value("${app.retries:3}")                         // with a default
@Value("#{systemProperties['user.region']}")       // SpEL against system properties
@Value("#{orderProperties.maxLines * 2}")          // SpEL referencing another bean
@Value("${app.allowed.origins}")                   // comma-separated to List<String>
private List<String> origins;
```

**The Jakarta standard annotations** are supported and behave almost
identically, which matters in code that avoids Spring-specific imports.

| Spring        | Jakarta standard      | Difference                           |
| ------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `@Autowired`  | `@Inject`             | `@Inject` has no `required` attribute |
| `@Qualifier`  | `@Named("beanName")`  | `@Named` matches by name only         |
| `@Component`  | `@Named`              | `@Named` on a class also registers it |
| `@Scope("singleton")` | `@Singleton`  | Equivalent for the default scope      |

```java
@Named                                  // equivalent to @Component
public class OrderService {

    @Inject                             // equivalent to @Autowired
    public OrderService(@Named("smsSender") NotificationSender sender) { ... }
}
```

**Collection injection** gathers every bean of a type, which 17.1 showed as the
basis for plugin designs. The `Map` form is useful when the bean name carries
meaning.

```java
@Service
public class NotificationDispatcher {

    private final Map<String, NotificationSender> sendersByName;

    // Keys are bean names: "emailSender", "smsSender", ...
    public NotificationDispatcher(Map<String, NotificationSender> senders) {
        this.sendersByName = senders;
    }

    public void send(String channel, Message message) {
        sendersByName.get(channel + "Sender").send(message);   // dispatch by name
    }
}
```

**`@Lookup`** solves the prototype-in-singleton problem that 17.1 raised, as an
alternative to `ObjectProvider`.

```java
@Service
public abstract class ImportService {

    // Spring overrides this method to return a fresh prototype each call.
    @Lookup
    protected abstract ImportJob newJob();

    public void run(File file) {
        newJob().process(file);        // a new instance every time
    }
}
```

**Self-injection with `@Lazy`** is 17.2's workaround for self-invocation, and
`@Lazy` is what prevents the circular dependency error.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderService self;
    public OrderService(@Lazy OrderService self) { this.self = self; }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A class with one constructor needs no `@Autowired`.
> - `Optional<T>` and `ObjectProvider<T>` express optional dependencies better
>   than `required = false`.
> - `@Qualifier` and `@Primary` are the two halves of ambiguity resolution.
> - `@Value` injects properties and Spring Expression Language results, with
>   defaults and conversion.
> - `@Inject` and `@Named` are the Jakarta equivalents and interoperate with
>   Spring's.
> - Injecting a `List` gives every implementation; a `Map` keys them by bean
>   name.
> - `@Lookup` returns a fresh prototype from a singleton without
>   `ObjectProvider`.
> - `@Lazy` on a self-injected reference breaks the construction cycle.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with two constructors and observe the failure, then fix it
>    with `@Autowired`.
> 2. Express one optional dependency three ways and compare the code at the use
>    site.
> 3. Inject a `Map<String, Handler>` and dispatch to one implementation by key.
> 4. Replace Spring's annotations with `@Inject` and `@Named` in one class and
>    confirm it still wires.
> 5. Use `@Lookup` to obtain a prototype from a singleton and prove each call
>    returns a new instance.
> 6. Interview: Why is `Optional<T>` preferred over `@Autowired(required =
>    false)` for an optional dependency? (Hint: what does each communicate to
>    someone reading the constructor?)

#### Conditional and Profile Annotations

Applications run in several environments, and each needs different beans. A
local run wants an in-memory database and a mail sender that logs; production
wants a real pool and a real SMTP server. Hard-coding the choice means editing
code to deploy, which is exactly what configuration exists to avoid.

**Profiles** are named sets of beans, activated at runtime.

```java
@Configuration
@Profile("dev")                                 // only when "dev" is active
public class DevConfig {

    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return new EmbeddedDatabaseBuilder()
                .setType(EmbeddedDatabaseType.H2)
                .addScript("classpath:test-data.sql")
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    public EmailSender emailSender() {
        return message -> log.info("would send: {}", message);   // no real mail
    }
}

@Configuration
@Profile("prod")
public class ProdConfig {

    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) {
        return new HikariDataSource(toHikariConfig(props));
    }

    @Bean
    public EmailSender emailSender(MailProperties props) {
        return new SmtpEmailSender(props);
    }
}
```

Profiles are activated by property, environment variable, or command line, so
the same artifact runs everywhere.

```text
  spring.profiles.active=prod                    # in a properties file
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod                    # as an environment variable
  java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod,metrics
```

Expressions cover the cases a single name cannot.

```java
@Profile("!prod")                     // any profile except prod
@Profile({"dev", "test"})             // dev OR test
@Profile("prod & metrics")            // both active
```

**Profiles should describe the environment, not the feature.** A profile named
`postgres` that is only ever active alongside `prod` is better expressed as a
conditional on the property that actually decides.

**`@Conditional`** is the general mechanism, and profiles are one special case
of it. It registers a bean only when a condition evaluates true at startup.

| Annotation                       | Registers the bean when                    |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `@ConditionalOnProperty`         | A property has a given value                |
| `@ConditionalOnClass`            | A class is on the classpath                 |
| `@ConditionalOnMissingClass`     | A class is absent                           |
| `@ConditionalOnBean`             | Another bean is already defined             |
| `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`      | No such bean exists yet                     |
| `@ConditionalOnResource`         | A resource is present                       |
| `@ConditionalOnExpression`       | A SpEL expression is true                   |
| `@ConditionalOnWebApplication`   | The context is a web application            |

```java
@Configuration
public class FeatureConfig {

    // A feature toggle: on when the property is "true", and on by default.
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "features.audit.enabled",
                           havingValue = "true",
                           matchIfMissing = true)
    public AuditAspect auditAspect(AuditRepository repository) {
        return new AuditAspect(repository);
    }

    // Only register a Redis cache if the driver is actually present.
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnClass(name = "redis.clients.jedis.Jedis")
    public CacheManager redisCacheManager() { ... }

    // The fallback: used only when nothing else supplied a CacheManager.
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(CacheManager.class)
    public CacheManager simpleCacheManager() {
        return new ConcurrentMapCacheManager();
    }
}
```

`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is the annotation that makes Spring Boot's
auto-configuration overridable: every auto-configured bean is declared with it,
so defining your own simply wins. Chapter 18 covers the ordering that makes this
reliable.

**Custom conditions** cover anything the built-in set does not.

```java
public class OnLinuxCondition implements Condition {

    @Override
    public boolean matches(ConditionContext context, AnnotatedTypeMetadata md) {
        return System.getProperty("os.name").toLowerCase().contains("linux");
    }
}

@Bean
@Conditional(OnLinuxCondition.class)
public NativeFileWatcher fileWatcher() { ... }
```

**`@Profile` is itself implemented as a condition**, which is a good
illustration of the composition this subchapter closes with.

```java
// Spring's actual definition, simplified.
@Conditional(ProfileCondition.class)
public @interface Profile {
    String[] value();
}
```

**A caution about conditions and tests.** Because conditions are evaluated at
startup, a bean present in production may be absent in a test context, producing
a failure that looks unrelated. Spring Boot's condition evaluation report makes
this diagnosable.

```text
  java -jar app.jar --debug          # prints matched and unmatched conditions
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Profiles activate named groups of beans so one artifact runs in every
>   environment.
> - Activate them by property, environment variable, or command line argument.
> - Profile expressions support negation, alternatives, and conjunction.
> - Name profiles after environments, not features; features belong on
>   properties.
> - `@Conditional` is the general mechanism, and `@Profile` is built from it.
> - `@ConditionalOnProperty` implements feature toggles, with a default via
>   `matchIfMissing`.
> - `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is what lets applications override
>   auto-configuration.
> - The condition evaluation report explains why a bean is missing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define a `dev` profile with an embedded database and a `prod` profile with
>    a pooled one, and switch between them from the command line.
> 2. Add a feature toggle with `@ConditionalOnProperty` and verify both states.
> 3. Write a bean annotated `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` and override it with
>    your own definition.
> 4. Implement a custom `Condition` and apply it to one bean.
> 5. Run with `--debug` and locate one bean that was not registered, with the
>    reason.
> 6. Interview: How does `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` let you override a
>    framework default without editing the framework? (Hint: what must be true
>    about the order in which the two definitions are considered?)

#### Building Custom Annotations in Spring

Every annotation in this subchapter is built from smaller ones. Spring's
**meta-annotation** support, which makes `@Service` work as a `@Component`,
is available to your code too, and using it removes repetition and encodes
conventions your team otherwise has to remember.

**Composed annotations** combine several into one name.

```java
// Four annotations that always appear together on every API controller.
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@RestController                                     // meta-annotated
@RequestMapping(produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
@Validated
public @interface ApiController {

    @AliasFor(annotation = RequestMapping.class, attribute = "path")
    String[] value() default {};                    // forwards to @RequestMapping
}
```

```java
// Before
@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/api/orders", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
@Validated
public class OrderController { }

// After
@ApiController("/api/orders")
public class OrderController { }
```

`@AliasFor` is the mechanism that forwards an attribute from your annotation to
the one it is built on, and it is what makes composed annotations configurable
rather than fixed.

**A custom stereotype** gives a layer its own marker, which pointcuts and
architecture rules can then target.

```java
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Service
@Transactional                       // every use case is transactional
public @interface UseCase {
    @AliasFor(annotation = Service.class)
    String value() default "";
}

@UseCase                             // a bean, a service, and transactional
public class PlaceOrderUseCase {
    public Order execute(PlaceOrderCommand command) { ... }
}
```

**An annotation plus an aspect** is the pattern 17.2 introduced, and it is the
most useful of the three. The annotation declares intent at the call site; the
aspect implements it once.

```java
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Retryable {
    int attempts() default 3;
    long backoffMillis() default 100;
    Class<? extends Throwable> on() default TransientDataAccessException.class;
}
```

```java
@Aspect
@Component
public class RetryAspect {

    // Binding the annotation as a parameter gives the aspect its settings.
    @Around("@annotation(retryable)")
    public Object retry(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Retryable retryable)
            throws Throwable {

        Throwable last = null;
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= retryable.attempts(); attempt++) {
            try {
                return pjp.proceed();                       // 17.2: must be called
            } catch (Throwable t) {
                if (!retryable.on().isInstance(t)) throw t;  // not retryable: rethrow
                last = t;
                Thread.sleep(retryable.backoffMillis() * attempt);   // linear backoff
            }
        }
        throw last;
    }
}
```

```java
@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Retryable(attempts = 5, backoffMillis = 200)   // intent, visible in place
    public Receipt charge(Card card, BigDecimal amount) { ... }
}
```

**A custom validation constraint** is the same idea applied to 17.4's Bean
Validation, and was shown there. The pattern is identical: an annotation plus a
class that implements the behaviour.

**A custom conditional** composes with the previous topic's mechanism.

```java
@Target({ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "features.beta.enabled", havingValue = "true")
public @interface BetaFeature { }

@Bean
@BetaFeature                          // reads better than repeating the property
public NewPricingEngine pricingEngine() { ... }
```

**Three rules keep custom annotations useful rather than mystifying.**

`@Retention(RUNTIME)` is mandatory. The default, `CLASS`, means the annotation
is discarded before the JVM can see it, so Spring finds nothing and the
annotation silently does nothing.

`@Target` should be as narrow as the intent. A method-level concern annotated
onto a class is a bug waiting to happen.

**Do not hide too much.** An annotation that bundles seven behaviours saves
typing and costs comprehension. The test is whether a new team member can
predict what it does from its name.

Finally, remember that custom annotations backed by aspects inherit every
limitation from 17.2: they apply only to Spring-managed beans, only to public
methods, and not to self-invoked calls.

> Key Takeaways
> - Spring resolves meta-annotations, so your annotation can be built from its
>   own.
> - Composed annotations replace a repeated stack with one meaningful name.
> - `@AliasFor` forwards attributes to the meta-annotation, keeping them
>   configurable.
> - A custom stereotype gives a layer a marker that pointcuts and architecture
>   tests can target.
> - Annotation plus aspect is the general pattern for declarative behaviour.
> - Binding the annotation as an advice parameter lets each use site configure
>   the aspect.
> - `@Retention(RUNTIME)` is required, or the annotation is invisible at
>   runtime.
> - Custom annotations backed by aspects inherit every proxy limitation from
>   17.2.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create an `@ApiController` composed annotation and apply it to two
>    controllers.
> 2. Use `@AliasFor` so that your annotation's value sets the request mapping
>    path.
> 3. Build a `@Retryable` annotation and aspect, then prove the retry count is
>    read from the annotation.
> 4. Set retention to the default and demonstrate that the aspect stops
>    matching.
> 5. Write a `@UseCase` stereotype that is also transactional, and confirm both
>    behaviours apply.
> 6. Interview: Your custom annotation and its aspect work on one method but not
>    on another in the same class. What would you check first? (Hint: 17.2
>    listed several ways a call avoids the proxy.)

<a id="18-spring-boot-and-production-applications"></a>
## 18. Spring Boot and Production Applications

Chapter 17 covered what Spring does; this chapter covers what Spring Boot adds
on top, which is almost entirely about removing the setup work between an idea
and a running, deployable service. It walks from auto-configuration and starter
dependencies through configuration management, REST APIs, security, and the
testing and operational concerns that separate a demo from something you can put
in front of users.

<a id="181-spring-boot-fundamentals"></a>
### 18.1 Spring Boot Fundamentals

This subchapter explains what Boot actually automates, how it does it, and where
the automation stops, so that the framework stays a tool you direct rather than
a black box you hope behaves.

#### Convention Over Configuration

Setting up a Spring application before Boot was a project in itself. A basic web
service with a database needed a dispatcher servlet registration, a view
resolver, a component scan declaration, a data source, a transaction manager, an
entity manager factory, a Jackson converter, and a servlet container to deploy
into. None of it was hard. All of it was necessary, repetitive, and easy to get
subtly wrong.

The observation behind Spring Boot is that **the overwhelming majority of those
decisions are the same in every project**. Almost everyone wants JSON, a
connection pool, a transaction manager matching their persistence technology,
and an HTTP server on port 8080.

**Convention over configuration** means the framework assumes the common answer
and asks you only about the parts that differ. The convention is not a
restriction: every default can be overridden, and the framework's job is to be
right often enough that you rarely bother.

```text
  Configuration-first                  Convention-first
  -------------------                  ----------------
  declare everything                   declare the differences

  200 lines of XML or Java             application.properties:
  before the first endpoint              server.port=8081

  every project repeats it             the rest is assumed
```

The difference is visible in the smallest possible application.

```java
// A complete, runnable web service. There is no other file.
@SpringBootApplication
@RestController
public class Application {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }

    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() {
        return "hello";
    }
}
```

Running that starts an embedded Tomcat on port 8080, configures Jackson for
JSON, registers the dispatcher servlet, enables component scanning from this
package down, and sets up sensible logging. None of it was requested.

**Conventions Boot applies by default:**

| Area              | Convention                                          |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Server port       | 8080                                                 |
| Component scan    | The package containing the main class, and below     |
| Configuration file| `application.properties` or `application.yml`         |
| Static content    | `src/main/resources/static`                           |
| Templates         | `src/main/resources/templates`                        |
| Database          | An in-memory one if a driver is present and no URL set |
| JSON              | Jackson, if it is on the classpath                    |
| Logging           | Logback, with a readable console pattern              |

**Overriding is always a property away**, which is the property that makes the
convention acceptable rather than constraining.

```text
  server.port=8081
  spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE
  spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
```

**The risk is real and worth naming.** A developer who has only used Boot may
not know that a connection pool exists, what the transaction manager is, or why
the server returns JSON. When something breaks, the convention becomes invisible
machinery rather than a decision someone made. This is precisely why chapter 17
came first: Boot configures Spring, and diagnosing Boot means understanding what
it configured.

The healthy stance is to treat conventions as **defaults you have accepted**
rather than magic. Knowing that `server.port` exists, and that a
`DataSourceAutoConfiguration` class made the decision about your pool, turns the
framework back into something you can reason about.

> Key Takeaways
> - Most Spring configuration decisions are identical across projects.
> - Convention over configuration means the framework assumes the common answer.
> - A single annotated class is a complete, runnable web service.
> - Defaults cover the port, scanning, JSON, logging, static content, and the
>   database.
> - Every convention can be overridden with a property.
> - The cost is invisible machinery, which is why understanding plain Spring
>   matters.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a Boot application with one controller and run it with no
>    configuration file at all.
> 2. Change the port, the context path, and the JSON naming strategy using only
>    properties.
> 3. List five things the framework configured that you never declared.
> 4. Interview: What is the difference between a framework with good defaults
>    and a framework that is inflexible? (Hint: what must be true about every
>    default for the first description to apply?)

#### Starter Dependencies and Version Management

Before Boot, adding web support to a Spring project meant selecting perhaps a
dozen dependencies by hand, each with its own version, and then resolving the
conflicts between them. Spring Web needed a compatible Spring Core, which needed
a compatible Jackson, which had to agree with whatever the JSON test library
pulled in.

That failure mode has a name.

```text
  Dependency hell
  ---------------
  spring-webmvc 5.3.20  --needs--> spring-core 5.3.20
  spring-data-jpa 2.7.0 --needs--> spring-core 5.3.21
  some-library 1.4      --needs--> jackson 2.12
  spring-webmvc         --needs--> jackson 2.13

  Result: NoSuchMethodError at runtime, discovered in production.
```

**Starters** solve the first half. A starter is a dependency that contains no
code, only a curated list of other dependencies that are known to work together
for one purpose.

```xml
<!-- One dependency brings the entire web stack, already consistent. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

That single line pulls in Spring MVC, an embedded Tomcat, Jackson, validation,
and logging, at versions chosen to agree with each other.

| Starter                          | Provides                                     |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `spring-boot-starter-web`        | Spring MVC, embedded Tomcat, Jackson          |
| `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`   | Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, a connection pool |
| `spring-boot-starter-jdbc`       | `JdbcTemplate` and HikariCP                   |
| `spring-boot-starter-security`   | Spring Security and its filter chain          |
| `spring-boot-starter-validation` | Jakarta Bean Validation and Hibernate Validator |
| `spring-boot-starter-test`       | JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Spring Test        |
| `spring-boot-starter-actuator`   | Production endpoints, covered in 18.5         |
| `spring-boot-starter-webflux`    | The reactive web stack instead of MVC         |

**The parent POM solves the second half**: it declares a managed version for
every dependency Boot knows about, so your own declarations omit versions
entirely.

```xml
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.3.0</version>            <!-- the only version you choose -->
</parent>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <!-- no version: inherited from the parent -->
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
        <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
        <!-- no version: Boot manages this one too -->
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Upgrading Boot's version therefore upgrades a hundred coordinated libraries in
one edit, which is the main reason this arrangement matters.

**Overriding a managed version** is supported, for when you need a fix Boot has
not picked up yet.

```xml
<properties>
    <!-- Overrides the version the parent would otherwise choose. -->
    <jackson-bom.version>2.17.1</jackson-bom.version>
</properties>
```

Do this deliberately and sparingly: the whole guarantee is that the managed set
was tested together.

**When you cannot use the parent POM**, because your organisation has its own,
import the dependency management instead.

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>3.3.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>        <!-- versions only, no parent -->
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

**Inspecting what a starter pulled in** is a skill worth having, because
"where did this class come from" is a routine question.

```bash
# Print the full dependency tree, or filter it to one library.
mvn dependency:tree
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind

# Gradle equivalent
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath
```

**Excluding a transitive dependency** is how you swap one component for another,
most commonly replacing Tomcat with Jetty or Undertow.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

That exclusion also matters for auto-configuration, which the next topic covers:
Boot decides what to configure largely by looking at what is on the classpath,
so removing Tomcat and adding Jetty changes the decision automatically.

> Key Takeaways
> - A starter is a dependency containing no code, only a curated set of others.
> - Starters solve which libraries you need; the parent POM solves which
>   versions.
> - Declaring dependencies without versions is the normal, intended style.
> - Upgrading the Boot version coordinates an upgrade of everything it manages.
> - Versions can be overridden with a property, at the cost of the tested
>   guarantee.
> - `spring-boot-dependencies` imports version management without the parent.
> - Excluding a transitive dependency is how components such as the server are
>   swapped.
> - The dependency tree is the tool for answering where a class came from.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a project with only the web starter and list its transitive
>    dependencies.
> 2. Add the JPA starter and identify which connection pool and ORM arrived.
> 3. Replace Tomcat with Jetty via exclusion and confirm the change at startup.
> 4. Override one managed version with a property and verify it in the
>    dependency tree.
> 5. Interview: Why does declaring dependencies without version numbers make
>    upgrades safer rather than riskier? (Hint: who decides the versions, and
>    what have they done with that combination?)

#### Auto-Configuration Mechanics

Auto-configuration is the part of Boot that feels like magic, and it is worth
dismantling precisely because it is not. It is 17.5's conditional annotations
applied systematically, and understanding the mechanism turns startup problems
into a five-minute diagnosis.

**The principle:** Boot ships hundreds of configuration classes, each declaring
beans for one technology, and each guarded by conditions. At startup every one
is evaluated, and the ones whose conditions match contribute their beans.

```text
  Startup
     |
     +-- find every auto-configuration class on the classpath
     |
     +-- for each, evaluate its conditions:
     |        is the class present?
     |        is a property set?
     |        has the user already defined this bean?
     |
     +-- register the beans from those that matched
     |
     +-- user-defined beans always take precedence
```

Here is a simplified version of a real one, which shows every idea at once.

```java
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)          // only if JDBC is on the classpath
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "spring.datasource", name = "url")
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DataSourceProperties.class)
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)     // yield to a user's own bean
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties properties) {
        return properties.initializeDataSourceBuilder().build();
    }
}
```

`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is the line that makes the whole design work.
Defining your own `DataSource` bean means Boot's is never created, so overriding
a default requires no configuration flag and no framework edit.

**Ordering matters**, because "is this bean missing" depends on when you ask.
Boot guarantees that user configuration is processed first, and auto-
configuration classes declare their own relative order.

```java
@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
public class JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration { ... }   // needs the DataSource first
```

**How the classes are discovered.** Each library contributing auto-configuration
ships a file listing its classes, which Boot reads from every JAR on the
classpath.

```text
  META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports

  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcAutoConfiguration
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jackson.JacksonAutoConfiguration
  ...
```

This is the same service-loader idea as JDBC driver registration in 16.1: a JAR
announces what it provides, and the framework finds it without being told.

**The condition evaluation report** is the diagnostic tool, and knowing it
exists is the difference between guessing and reading the answer.

```bash
# Prints every auto-configuration, matched and unmatched, with the reason.
java -jar app.jar --debug
```

```text
  Positive matches:
  -----------------
     DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
        - @ConditionalOnClass found 'javax.sql.DataSource' (OnClassCondition)

  Negative matches:
  -----------------
     RedisAutoConfiguration:
        Did not match:
           - @ConditionalOnClass did not find 'redis.clients.jedis.Jedis'
```

When a bean you expected is missing, that report names the condition that
failed.

**Disabling an auto-configuration** is occasionally necessary, most often when
you want to configure something entirely yourself.

```java
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = { DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class })
public class Application { }
```

```text
  spring.autoconfigure.exclude=\
    org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
```

**Writing your own** is how shared libraries inside an organisation ship
ready-configured components.

```java
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(AuditClient.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "audit", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true")
@EnableConfigurationProperties(AuditProperties.class)
public class AuditAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean                    // always allow an override
    public AuditClient auditClient(AuditProperties properties) {
        return new AuditClient(properties.endpoint(), properties.apiKey());
    }
}
```

Listing that class in the imports file makes it apply automatically to any
project that adds the library.

> Key Takeaways
> - Auto-configuration is conditional bean registration applied systematically.
> - Conditions test the classpath, properties, and beans already defined.
> - `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is what lets your own bean silently win.
> - User configuration is processed before auto-configuration, so overriding
>   works.
> - Classes are discovered from an imports file in each JAR, like JDBC driver
>   registration.
> - The `--debug` condition report names exactly which condition failed.
> - Auto-configurations can be excluded by class or by property.
> - Custom auto-configuration is how internal libraries ship preconfigured
>   beans.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run an application with `--debug` and find three positive and three
>    negative matches.
> 2. Define your own `DataSource` bean and confirm from the report that Boot's
>    no longer applies.
> 3. Exclude one auto-configuration and identify what stops working.
> 4. Write an auto-configuration class for a small component, guarded by a
>    property and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`.
> 5. Interview: You add a library and a bean you did not declare appears in the
>    context. Explain the mechanism. (Hint: what file does the framework look
>    for inside every JAR?)

#### The Application Entry Point and @SpringBootApplication

A Boot application starts from an ordinary `main` method, which is a meaningful
departure from the deployment model that preceded it. There is no container to
install and no artifact to drop into a server directory; the application is a
program that happens to serve HTTP.

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class ShopApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ShopApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

**`@SpringBootApplication` is three annotations in one**, composed exactly as
17.5 described.

```java
// Spring's actual definition, simplified.
@SpringBootConfiguration        // a @Configuration, marked as the app's primary one
@EnableAutoConfiguration        // switch on the mechanism from the previous topic
@ComponentScan                  // scan this package and everything below it
public @interface SpringBootApplication { }
```

The `@ComponentScan` with no arguments is why **the main class's package
matters**. It scans its own package downward, so a class outside that tree is
invisible.

```text
  com.shop                    <-- ShopApplication lives here
  com.shop.order                  scanned
  com.shop.order.web              scanned
  com.shop.billing                scanned
  com.other.util                  NOT scanned: no beans found here
```

Placing the main class in the root package is the convention, and "my bean is
not being found" is nearly always a violation of it.

**What `SpringApplication.run` actually does**, in order:

```text
  1. decide the application type      servlet, reactive, or none
  2. load ApplicationContextInitializers and listeners from the classpath
  3. prepare the Environment          properties, profiles, command-line args
  4. print the banner
  5. create the ApplicationContext    the type chosen in step 1
  6. run auto-configuration and register all beans
  7. instantiate every singleton      eagerly, as 17.1 described
  8. start the embedded server
  9. call ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner beans
```

Step 1 is inferred from the classpath: the web starter yields a servlet
application, WebFlux yields a reactive one, and neither yields a plain
application that runs and exits.

**Customising the startup** is done with a builder when the defaults do not fit.

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    new SpringApplicationBuilder(ShopApplication.class)
            .bannerMode(Banner.Mode.OFF)                  // no banner in logs
            .web(WebApplicationType.SERVLET)              // force the type
            .profiles("prod")                             // 17.5's profiles
            .listeners(new StartupTimingListener())
            .run(args);
}
```

**Runners execute code after startup**, which is the correct place for work that
needs a fully built context.

```java
@Component
public class DataSeeder implements ApplicationRunner {

    private final ProductRepository repository;

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        // The context is fully started; the server is accepting requests.
        if (args.containsOption("seed")) {          // --seed on the command line
            repository.saveAll(sampleProducts());
        }
    }
}
```

`ApplicationRunner` receives parsed arguments; `CommandLineRunner` receives the
raw `String[]`. Use `@Order` when several must run in sequence.

**Command-line arguments become properties**, which is how the same jar is
configured per environment without a rebuild.

```bash
java -jar shop.jar --server.port=9090 --spring.profiles.active=prod --seed
```

**A non-web application** is written the same way, and is the right shape for a
batch job or a scheduled task.

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class ReportJob implements CommandLineRunner {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // exit() returns the code the runner produced, for the shell to read.
        System.exit(SpringApplication.exit(
                SpringApplication.run(ReportJob.class, args)));
    }

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {
        reportService.generateMonthly();
    }
}
```

**Graceful shutdown** matters in production, because a container that is stopped
mid-request drops it.

```text
  server.shutdown=graceful
  spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s
```

With this set, a shutdown signal stops accepting new requests, waits for
in-flight ones to finish, and then closes the context, running the
`@PreDestroy` callbacks from 17.1.

> Key Takeaways
> - A Boot application is an ordinary program with a `main` method.
> - `@SpringBootApplication` combines configuration, auto-configuration, and
>   component scanning.
> - Scanning starts at the main class's package, so it belongs in the root
>   package.
> - The application type is inferred from the classpath.
> - `SpringApplication.run` prepares the environment, builds the context, and
>   starts the server.
> - `SpringApplicationBuilder` customises startup when defaults do not fit.
> - `ApplicationRunner` and `CommandLineRunner` execute code once the context is
>   ready.
> - Command-line arguments override properties, so one artifact serves every
>   environment.
> - Graceful shutdown drains in-flight requests before the context closes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Move the main class into a sub-package and observe which beans stop being
>    found.
> 2. Write two runners with `@Order` and confirm the execution sequence.
> 3. Override the port with a command-line argument without editing any file.
> 4. Build a non-web Boot application that performs one task and exits with a
>    status code.
> 5. Enable graceful shutdown and verify an in-flight request completes after a
>    stop signal.
> 6. Interview: Why does the main class's package location affect which beans
>    exist? (Hint: one of the three composed annotations takes no arguments.)

#### Embedded Servers and Executable JARs

The traditional Java web deployment model was to build a WAR file and deploy it
into a servlet container that someone had installed and configured separately.
That split caused a specific class of problem: the application was tested
against one container version and deployed onto another, and the container's
configuration lived outside the project's version control.

**Boot inverts the relationship.** The server is a library the application
depends on, started by the application's own `main` method.

```text
  Deployed WAR                          Embedded server
  ------------                          ---------------
  install Tomcat on the server          the jar contains Tomcat
  configure server.xml separately       configuration is a property
  deploy app.war into webapps/          java -jar app.jar
  container version is environmental    container version is a dependency

  "works on my machine" is plausible    the artifact is the same everywhere
```

Configuration that used to live in the container's own files becomes ordinary
application properties.

```text
  server.port=8080
  server.servlet.context-path=/api
  server.tomcat.threads.max=200
  server.tomcat.accept-count=100
  server.compression.enabled=true
  server.shutdown=graceful
```

**Three servers are supported**, and switching is a dependency change.

| Server   | Model                     | Notes                                      |
| -------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Tomcat   | Thread per request        | The default; the most familiar and documented |
| Jetty    | Thread per request        | Lighter footprint, common in embedded uses  |
| Undertow | Non-blocking core         | Good throughput, smaller memory use         |

**The executable JAR** is the second half of the model. `java -jar app.jar` must
work, and that requires solving a problem the JVM does not solve by itself: the
standard class loader cannot load classes from a JAR nested inside another JAR.

Boot's solution is a custom layout and a custom loader.

```text
  app.jar
  |
  +-- META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
  |      Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher   <-- Boot's
  |      Start-Class: com.shop.ShopApplication                     <-- yours
  |
  +-- org/springframework/boot/loader/...     the launcher itself
  |
  +-- BOOT-INF/classes/                       your compiled code
  |      com/shop/ShopApplication.class
  |
  +-- BOOT-INF/lib/                           every dependency, as jars
         spring-core.jar
         tomcat-embed-core.jar
         ...
```

The JVM starts `JarLauncher`, which installs a class loader that can read the
nested JARs, and then invokes your `Start-Class`. This is why the manifest's
main class is not the one you wrote.

Building it requires the Boot plugin, which repackages the plain JAR.

```xml
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

```bash
mvn package                  # produces target/shop-1.0.jar, executable
java -jar target/shop-1.0.jar
```

**Layered JARs** exist for container builds and are covered again in 18.5. The
idea is that dependencies change far less often than application code, so
separating them into layers lets a container image reuse cached layers.

```bash
# List the layers the plugin defined, then extract them.
java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar list
# dependencies
# spring-boot-loader
# snapshot-dependencies
# application          <-- the only layer that changes on most builds
```

**WAR deployment is still possible**, and occasionally required by an
organisation's existing infrastructure.

```java
// Extending this class lets an external container find and start the app.
@SpringBootApplication
public class ShopApplication extends SpringBootServletInitializer {

    @Override
    protected SpringApplicationBuilder configure(SpringApplicationBuilder b) {
        return b.sources(ShopApplication.class);
    }
}
```

With the packaging set to `war` and the embedded server marked `provided`, the
same code builds a deployable WAR. Treat it as a compatibility path rather than
a target.

> Key Takeaways
> - Boot embeds the server as a dependency instead of deploying into an external
>   one.
> - Server configuration becomes application properties under version control.
> - Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow are interchangeable by dependency.
> - An executable JAR needs a custom loader because nested JARs are not
>   standard.
> - The manifest's main class is Boot's launcher; yours is the `Start-Class`.
> - The Maven or Gradle plugin repackages the artifact into that layout.
> - Layered JARs separate slow-changing dependencies from application code for
>   image caching.
> - WAR deployment remains available through `SpringBootServletInitializer`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Package an application and inspect the JAR's structure and manifest.
> 2. Replace Tomcat with Undertow and confirm the startup log names the new
>    server.
> 3. Configure the thread pool and context path through properties, then verify
>    both.
> 4. Extract the layers with layertools and identify which changes on a
>    code-only rebuild.
> 5. Interview: Why does `java -jar` on a Boot application not run your main
>    class directly? (Hint: what limitation of the standard class loader does
>    the packaging work around?)

#### Spring Boot versus Plain Spring

It is easy to treat Boot as a different framework. It is not: **Boot is Spring
plus opinions**. Every bean, every proxy, and every transaction in a Boot
application is the Spring machinery chapter 17 described. Boot contributes
defaults, dependency curation, packaging, and operational endpoints.

```text
   Spring Boot
   +------------------------------------------------+
   |  auto-configuration   starters   executable jar |
   |  actuator             externalised config        |
   +------------------------------------------------+
   |               Spring Framework                   |
   |  IoC container   AOP   MVC   transactions   data |
   +------------------------------------------------+
```

Setting the same application up both ways makes the boundary concrete.

```java
// PLAIN SPRING: everything declared, deployed as a WAR.
@Configuration
@EnableWebMvc
@ComponentScan("com.shop")
@EnableTransactionManagement
@EnableJpaRepositories("com.shop.repository")
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        var config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop");
        return new HikariDataSource(config);
    }

    @Bean
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean entityManagerFactory(
            DataSource ds) { ... }                  // roughly 15 more lines

    @Bean
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(
            EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return new JpaTransactionManager(emf);
    }
}
// plus a DispatcherServlet registration class, plus a deployment descriptor
```

```java
// SPRING BOOT: the same capabilities.
@SpringBootApplication
public class ShopApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ShopApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

```text
  spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
```

| Concern              | Plain Spring                     | Spring Boot                     |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Dependency versions  | Chosen and reconciled by you      | Managed by the parent POM        |
| Infrastructure beans | Declared explicitly               | Auto-configured, overridable     |
| Server               | External, installed separately    | Embedded, a dependency           |
| Artifact             | WAR deployed into a container     | Executable JAR                   |
| Configuration        | XML or Java configuration classes | Properties and YAML              |
| Operational endpoints| Written by you                    | Actuator, covered in 18.5        |
| Startup failures     | Often at first use                | At startup, with a report        |

**What Boot does not change:** the programming model. Constructor injection,
`@Transactional` and its proxy limitations, `@ControllerAdvice`, the persistence
context, and the N+1 problem all behave exactly as chapters 16 and 17 described.
A Boot-specific bug is almost always a configuration question; everything else
is a Spring question.

**When plain Spring is still the answer.** Organisations with a mandated
application server, or libraries that must embed into a host application, cannot
use the executable JAR model. Boot's starters can still be avoided while using
the framework underneath.

**The honest criticism** of Boot is that it lets people build systems they
cannot debug. A developer who has never declared a `DataSource` may not realise
a pool exists when `connectionTimeout` fires, and one who has never registered a
`DispatcherServlet` has no model for why a request returned 415. The defence is
not to avoid Boot; it is to know what it configured. The `--debug` report, the
actuator's bean and configuration endpoints, and the startup log are all
designed to make the invisible visible.

> Key Takeaways
> - Boot is not a separate framework; it configures Spring and packages it.
> - Auto-configuration, starters, embedded servers, and actuator are Boot's
>   additions.
> - The programming model, including proxies and transactions, is unchanged.
> - Boot moves infrastructure decisions from code into properties.
> - Failures surface at startup with a report instead of at first use.
> - Plain Spring remains appropriate for mandated servers and embedded
>   libraries.
> - The real risk is using defaults you cannot explain, which the diagnostic
>   tools address.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the explicit `@Configuration` that would replace one auto-configured
>    bean and compare the line counts.
> 2. Find three beans in a Boot application that you never declared and name the
>    auto-configuration responsible for each.
