> 3. Disable one auto-configuration, supply the bean yourself, and confirm the
>    application still works.
> 4. Take a Boot application and list which of its behaviours come from chapter
>    17 rather than from Boot.
> 5. Interview: A colleague says Spring Boot replaced Spring. Correct the
>    statement precisely. (Hint: what executes a `@Transactional` method in a
>    Boot application?)

<a id="182-configuration-and-profiles"></a>
### 18.2 Configuration and Profiles

This subchapter covers how settings reach a running application: the file
formats, binding them to typed objects, separating environments, keeping secrets
out of the repository, and the precedence rules that decide which value wins.

#### Properties and YAML Configuration Files

Any setting that differs between environments, or that you might reasonably want
to change without recompiling, belongs in configuration rather than in code. A
database URL, a thread pool size, a feature toggle, and a log level are all
configuration; a business rule is not.

Boot reads `application.properties` or `application.yml` from a set of standard
locations, and either format works identically.

```text
  spring.application.name=shop-service
  server.port=8080

  spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  spring.datasource.username=app
  spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10

  spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
  spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

  logging.level.com.shop=DEBUG
```

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: shop-service
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
    username: app
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10      # nesting removes the repeated prefix
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    open-in-view: false

server:
  port: 8080

logging:
  level:
    com.shop: DEBUG
```

| Aspect             | Properties                  | YAML                            |
| ------------------ | --------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Repetition         | Full key on every line      | Nested, each prefix written once |
| Lists              | Indexed keys                | Native list syntax               |
| Readability at size| Degrades                    | Better, if indentation is correct |
| Failure mode       | Rare; the format is trivial | Indentation errors, silent type surprises |
| Multiple documents | Not supported               | Supported with `---`             |

YAML wins for anything beyond a handful of settings, with one genuine caution:
it infers types, so unquoted values can surprise you.

```yaml
version: 1.10          # parsed as the number 1.1, not the string "1.10"
version: "1.10"        # correct
enabled: no            # older parsers read this as false; quote it
password: 0123456      # leading zero, may be read as an octal number
```

**Lists and maps** appear constantly in real configuration.

```yaml
app:
  allowed-origins:               # a list
    - https://shop.example.com
    - https://admin.example.com
  rate-limits:                   # a map
    default: 100
    premium: 1000
```

```text
  app.allowed-origins[0]=https://shop.example.com
  app.allowed-origins[1]=https://admin.example.com
  app.rate-limits.default=100
```

**Placeholders** let one value reference another, which avoids repeating a host
or a base path.

```text
  app.host=shop.example.com
  app.api-url=https://${app.host}/api        # composed from another property
  app.timeout=${APP_TIMEOUT:5000}            # environment variable with a default
```

**Multi-document YAML** keeps environment differences in one file, using the
profile activation covered two topics on.

```yaml
# Settings shared by every environment.
spring:
  application:
    name: shop-service
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: dev            # applies only when "dev" is active
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:shop
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/shop
```

**Where Boot looks for the files**, in increasing order of precedence:

```text
  1. classpath:/application.yml                 packaged in the jar
  2. classpath:/config/application.yml
  3. ./application.yml                          beside the jar
  4. ./config/application.yml                   the usual production location
```

A file next to the jar overrides the packaged one, which is how the same
artifact runs with different settings without being rebuilt.

```bash
# Point at a specific location, or add one to the search path.
java -jar app.jar --spring.config.location=file:/etc/shop/application.yml
java -jar app.jar --spring.config.additional-location=file:/etc/shop/
```

**Reading a value in code** uses 17.5's `@Value`, though the next topic argues
for a better alternative.

```java
@Component
public class RateLimiter {
    public RateLimiter(@Value("${app.rate-limits.default:100}") int limit) { ... }
}
```

**A practical habit:** add `spring-boot-configuration-processor` to the build.
It generates metadata from your own configuration classes, which gives
autocompletion and inline documentation for your properties in an IDE.

> Key Takeaways
> - Configuration holds anything that varies by environment or might change
>   without a rebuild.
> - `application.properties` and `application.yml` are equivalent in capability.
> - YAML removes prefix repetition and handles lists and maps natively.
> - YAML infers types, so version numbers and boolean-looking values need
>   quoting.
> - Placeholders compose values and supply defaults from environment variables.
> - Multi-document YAML keeps per-profile settings in one file.
> - Files beside the jar override packaged ones, so one artifact serves all
>   environments.
> - The configuration processor gives IDE support for your own properties.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert a properties file with twenty entries into YAML and compare the
>    readability.
> 2. Define a list and a map in YAML and inject both into a component.
> 3. Demonstrate the `1.10` type-inference surprise and fix it.
> 4. Override one setting by placing a file beside the jar without rebuilding.
> 5. Interview: Why does YAML's type inference cause bugs that properties files
>    do not have? (Hint: what is the type of every value in a properties file?)

#### Type-Safe Configuration Properties

Injecting individual values with `@Value` works and stops scaling quickly. A
component with eight settings has eight annotations, eight string keys that the
compiler cannot check, and no single place where the configuration for that
component is described.

```java
// The problem: keys as strings, no validation, no grouping.
@Component
public class PaymentGateway {
    public PaymentGateway(
            @Value("${payment.endpoint}") String endpoint,
            @Value("${payment.api-key}") String apiKey,
            @Value("${payment.timeout:5000}") int timeoutMillis,
            @Value("${payment.retries:3}") int retries,
            @Value("${payment.sandbox:false}") boolean sandbox) { ... }
}
```

A typo in any key fails at startup with a message about a missing placeholder,
and nothing checks that `retries` is positive.

**`@ConfigurationProperties` binds a whole group to a typed object.** The prefix
is declared once, and the fields are the keys.

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment")
@Validated                                       // 17.4's Bean Validation
public record PaymentProperties(

        @NotBlank
        String endpoint,

        @NotBlank
        String apiKey,                            // binds from payment.api-key

        @DefaultValue("5s")
        Duration timeout,                         // "5s" converts to a Duration

        @Min(0) @Max(10)
        @DefaultValue("3")
        int retries,

        @DefaultValue("false")
        boolean sandbox) { }
```

```yaml
payment:
  endpoint: https://pay.example.com
  api-key: ${PAYMENT_API_KEY}     # from the environment, see the secrets topic
  timeout: 5s
  retries: 3
```

**Relaxed binding** is what lets `api-key` in YAML reach `apiKey` in Java. Boot
accepts several spellings of the same property, which matters because
environment variables cannot contain dots or hyphens.

| Form                  | Example                | Typical source          |
| --------------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Kebab case            | `payment.api-key`      | YAML and properties files (preferred) |
| Camel case            | `payment.apiKey`       | Properties files         |
| Underscore            | `payment.api_key`      | Properties files         |
| Upper case underscore | `PAYMENT_API_KEY`      | Environment variables    |

That last row is the one that matters in containers: any property can be set as
an environment variable by upper-casing it and replacing punctuation with
underscores.

**Registering the class** is done one of two ways.

```java
// Either: list them where they are enabled.
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class)
public class ShopApplication { }

// Or: scan for them, which suits many properties classes.
@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan("com.shop.config")
public class ShopApplication { }
```

**Using them is ordinary injection**, and the component now has one dependency
instead of five.

```java
@Component
public class PaymentGateway {

    private final PaymentProperties properties;

    public PaymentGateway(PaymentProperties properties) {
        this.properties = properties;
    }

    public Receipt charge(Card card, BigDecimal amount) {
        return client.post(properties.endpoint())
                     .timeout(properties.timeout())
                     .send(...);
    }
}
```

**Nested and collection types bind naturally**, which is where the approach
really pays off.

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")
public record AppProperties(
        Security security,                      // a nested group
        List<String> allowedOrigins,            // a list
        Map<String, RateLimit> rateLimits) {    // a map of nested objects

    public record Security(Duration tokenTtl, String issuer) { }
    public record RateLimit(int perMinute, int burst) { }
}
```

```yaml
app:
  security:
    token-ttl: 15m
    issuer: shop-service
  allowed-origins:
    - https://shop.example.com
  rate-limits:
    default:
      per-minute: 100
      burst: 20
    premium:
      per-minute: 1000
      burst: 200
```

**Type conversion is richer than it looks.** Boot converts durations, data
sizes, enums, and resource paths from strings.

```java
Duration timeout;        // "5s", "500ms", "PT1M30S"
DataSize maxUpload;      // "10MB", "512KB"
OrderStatus status;      // enum name, case-insensitive
Resource template;       // "classpath:template.html"
```

**The decisive advantage is validation at startup.** With `@Validated`, an
invalid value stops the application immediately with a message naming the
property, rather than producing a failure at first use.

```text
  Binding to target failed:
      Property: payment.retries
      Value: 50
      Reason: must be less than or equal to 10
```

| Aspect              | `@Value`                  | `@ConfigurationProperties`     |
| ------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Keys                | A string per injection     | One prefix per group           |
| Grouping            | None                       | One class describes the group  |
| Validation          | None                       | Bean Validation at startup     |
| Nested and complex  | Awkward                    | Natural                        |
| Relaxed binding     | No                         | Yes                            |
| SpEL expressions    | Supported                  | Not supported                  |
| Best for            | One or two ad-hoc values   | Any real group of settings     |

> Key Takeaways
> - `@Value` does not scale past a couple of settings and offers no validation.
> - `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a prefixed group to a typed object.
> - Relaxed binding maps kebab case, camel case, and environment variable
>   spellings to one field.
> - Any property can be supplied as an upper-case underscore environment
>   variable.
> - Register with `@EnableConfigurationProperties` or
>   `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`.
> - Nested records, lists, and maps bind without extra code.
> - Durations, data sizes, enums, and resources convert from strings
>   automatically.
> - `@Validated` turns bad configuration into a startup failure naming the
>   property.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace five `@Value` annotations in one class with a properties record.
> 2. Add validation constraints and start the application with an invalid value.
> 3. Bind a map of nested objects and iterate it in a component.
> 4. Set one property through an environment variable using the upper-case form.
> 5. Bind a `Duration` and a `DataSize` from human-readable strings.
> 6. Interview: Why is a configuration error better discovered at startup than
>    at first use? (Hint: consider a deploy at 2am and a code path used once a
>    week.)

#### Profiles for Environment Separation

17.5 introduced profiles as conditional bean registration. In Boot they do more:
they also select which configuration files and which property blocks apply, and
they are the standard mechanism for running one artifact in several
environments.

**Profile-specific files** are found automatically by name.

```text
  application.yml              always loaded, the shared baseline
  application-dev.yml          loaded when "dev" is active
  application-test.yml         loaded when "test" is active
  application-prod.yml         loaded when "prod" is active
```

Profile-specific values override the baseline, so each file contains only what
differs.

```yaml
# application.yml -- shared by every environment
spring:
  application:
    name: shop-service
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
server:
  shutdown: graceful
```

```yaml
# application-dev.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:shop
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: create-drop     # acceptable locally, never in production
logging:
  level:
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG    # see the generated SQL while developing
```

```yaml
# application-prod.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/shop
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate        # 17.3: migrations own the schema
logging:
  level:
    root: WARN
    com.shop: INFO
```

**Activating a profile** is done from outside the artifact, which is the whole
point.

```bash
java -jar shop.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod java -jar shop.jar
```

```text
  spring.profiles.active=dev          # a default for local development only
```

**Profile-specific beans** work exactly as 17.5 described, and the two
mechanisms combine.

```java
@Configuration
@Profile("!prod")                        // everything except production
public class DevToolsConfig {

    @Bean
    public EmailSender emailSender() {
        return message -> log.info("would send: {}", message);   // never real mail
    }
}
```

**Profile groups** activate several profiles together, which keeps deployment
commands simple.

```yaml
spring:
  profiles:
    group:
      prod: prod-db, prod-cache, metrics    # one name activates three
```

**`@ActiveProfiles` sets them in tests**, which 18.5 returns to.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@ActiveProfiles("test")
class OrderServiceTest { }
```

**Three rules keep profiles from becoming a mess.**

**Name profiles after environments, not technologies.** A `postgres` profile
that is only ever active with `prod` should be a property, not a profile. The
exception is a genuine deployment variant such as `cloud` versus `on-premise`.

**Keep the number small.** Each additional profile multiplies the combinations
that are theoretically possible and never tested. Three or four is typical.

**Never let production depend on a profile being absent.** Configuration that
only works because nobody activated `dev` is fragile. Make production explicit.

```text
  Dangerous                              Safe
  ---------                              ----
  @Profile("!prod") on a security        @Profile("prod") on production beans
  bypass bean                            and an explicit prod activation

  forgetting to set the profile          forgetting to set the profile
  disables security                      fails to start
```

**Checking which profiles are active** at runtime is a one-line diagnostic and
is exposed by actuator, covered in 18.5.

```java
@Component
public class ProfileLogger implements ApplicationRunner {

    private final Environment environment;

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        log.info("active profiles: {}",
                 Arrays.toString(environment.getActiveProfiles()));
    }
}
```

When none are set, Boot activates `default`, which is why a missing activation
silently produces the baseline configuration rather than an error.

> Key Takeaways
> - `application-<profile>.yml` files are loaded automatically and override the
>   baseline.
> - Each profile file should contain only what differs from the shared
>   configuration.
> - Profiles are activated from outside the artifact, by argument, property, or
>   environment variable.
> - Profile-specific beans and profile-specific files work together.
> - Profile groups activate several names at once.
> - Name profiles after environments and keep their number small.
> - Never make a safe configuration depend on a profile being inactive.
> - With no activation, the `default` profile applies silently.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create dev and prod profile files differing in data source and log level,
>    and switch between them from the command line.
> 2. Define a bean that exists only outside production and prove it is absent
>    when `prod` is active.
> 3. Set up a profile group that activates three profiles from one name.
> 4. Log the active profiles at startup and run with none set.
> 5. Interview: Why is `@Profile("!prod")` on a security-relevant bean risky?
>    (Hint: what happens if someone forgets to set any profile at all?)

#### Externalized Configuration and Secrets

Configuration that lives inside the artifact cannot differ between environments
without rebuilding, and a secret that lives inside the artifact is not a secret.
Both problems are solved by **externalizing**: the running process obtains its
settings from its environment rather than from its own contents.

```text
  Internalised                          Externalised
  ------------                          ------------
  one jar per environment               one jar, many environments

  build for prod -> deploy              build once -> deploy anywhere
  credentials in the repository         credentials supplied at run time
  a config change needs a rebuild       a config change needs a restart
```

This is one of the twelve-factor principles, and the practical form is that
**environment variables and mounted files, not the packaged file, carry the
real values**.

**Environment variables** are the most portable mechanism and work everywhere.

```bash
export SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/shop
export SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=app
export SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD='...'
export SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
java -jar shop.jar
```

The upper-case underscore form is the relaxed binding from two topics back, so
`SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` sets `spring.datasource.url` with no configuration.

**Placeholders make the expectation explicit**, which is better than relying on
an invisible override.

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}                       # required: startup fails if absent
    username: ${DB_USER:app}             # optional, with a default
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}             # required
```

A missing required placeholder produces a startup failure naming the property,
which is exactly the fail-fast behaviour you want.

**What must never be committed:**

| Never in the repository        | Where it belongs                       |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| Database passwords              | Secret manager or environment          |
| API keys and tokens             | Secret manager or environment          |
| Private keys and certificates   | Mounted file with restricted permissions |
| Encryption keys                 | Secret manager or a key management service |
| Production hostnames (arguably) | Environment, to avoid disclosing topology |

Committing a secret is not fixed by deleting it in a later commit: git keeps
history, so the value must be **rotated**, not just removed.

**Secret managers** are the production answer, and the pattern is the same
regardless of which one an organisation uses.

```text
  Application startup
        |
        +-- authenticate to the secret store (instance identity, not a password)
        |
        +-- fetch secrets
        |
        +-- bind them as properties
        |
        +-- proceed with normal startup
```

| Mechanism                      | Typical context                         |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Environment variables          | Anywhere; the baseline                   |
| Docker or Kubernetes secrets   | Mounted as files or environment variables |
| HashiCorp Vault                | Self-managed, with dynamic credentials   |
| Cloud provider secret managers | Managed cloud deployments                |
| Spring Cloud Config            | Centralised configuration for many services |

**Kubernetes** is worth showing concretely, because it is the most common target
and it uses both forms.

```yaml
env:
  - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
    value: prod
  - name: SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:                     # injected from a Secret, not in the image
        name: shop-db
        key: password
volumeMounts:
  - name: config
    mountPath: /config                  # Boot reads ./config/application.yml
```

**A layered arrangement that works well** in practice:

```text
  application.yml            defaults, safe to commit, no secrets
  application-prod.yml       production structure, still no secrets
  environment variables      the actual credentials, injected at run time
  command-line arguments     one-off overrides during an incident
```

**Avoid printing secrets.** A logged configuration dump, an error message
containing a JDBC URL with credentials, or an actuator endpoint exposing the
environment are all common leaks. Boot sanitises known-sensitive keys in
actuator output, and 18.5 covers securing those endpoints.

```text
  # Extra keys to sanitise in actuator output.
  management.endpoint.env.show-values=never
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Externalized configuration lets one artifact run in every environment.
> - Environment variables map to properties through relaxed binding with no
>   setup.
> - Declaring placeholders makes required settings explicit and fails fast when
>   absent.
> - Secrets must never be committed; a committed secret must be rotated, not
>   deleted.
> - Secret managers authenticate the workload and supply values at startup.
> - Kubernetes supplies secrets as environment variables or mounted files.
> - Keep structure in committed files and values in the environment.
> - Guard against leaking secrets through logs, errors, and actuator endpoints.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Configure a data source entirely through environment variables with no
>    values in any file.
> 2. Use a required placeholder and confirm the startup failure when it is
>    unset.
> 3. Run the same jar twice with different environment variables and observe
>    both behaviours.
> 4. Mount a configuration file beside the jar and override one packaged value.
> 5. Find a project that logs its configuration at startup and check whether a
>    secret would appear.
> 6. Interview: A password was committed and removed in the next commit. Is the
>    problem solved? (Hint: what does a version control system keep by design?)

#### Configuration Property Precedence

With files, profiles, environment variables, and command-line arguments all able
to set the same property, one question decides behaviour: **which wins?** Boot
defines a strict order, and knowing it turns "the setting is being ignored" into
a solved problem.

The rule is simple to state: **later sources override earlier ones**, and the
ordering runs from packaged defaults up to explicit runtime overrides.

```text
  LOWEST precedence
  |
  |  1.  default properties (SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties)
  |  2.  @PropertySource on a @Configuration class
  |  3.  application.yml packaged in the jar
  |  4.  application-<profile>.yml packaged in the jar
  |  5.  application.yml outside the jar (./config/ or ./)
  |  6.  application-<profile>.yml outside the jar
  |  7.  OS environment variables
  |  8.  Java system properties (-D)
  |  9.  command-line arguments (--key=value)
  | 10.  SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON
  | 11.  @TestPropertySource and test properties
  |
  HIGHEST precedence
```

The shape of that list is deliberate. Anything you can change without rebuilding
beats anything baked into the artifact, and anything typed at the moment of
launch beats everything else.

```bash
# All four set the same property. The command-line argument wins.
# application.yml:        server.port: 8080
export SERVER_PORT=8081
java -Dserver.port=8082 -jar app.jar --server.port=8083
# The application listens on 8083.
```

**Profile-specific files beat the baseline** at the same level, which is why the
arrangement in the previous topic works.

```text
  application.yml            server.port: 8080
  application-prod.yml       server.port: 9090     <-- wins when prod is active
```

**`SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON`** sets many properties from one variable, which is
useful where a platform allows only a few environment variables.

```bash
SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON='{"server":{"port":9000},"logging":{"level":{"root":"WARN"}}}' \
  java -jar app.jar
```

**Diagnosing a property** is best done by asking the application rather than
reasoning about the list. The actuator environment endpoint, covered in 18.5,
reports every source and which one supplied the effective value.

```bash
curl localhost:8080/actuator/env/server.port
```

```json
{
  "property": { "source": "commandLineArgs", "value": "8083" },
  "activeProfiles": ["prod"],
  "propertySources": [
    { "name": "commandLineArgs",       "property": { "value": "8083" } },
    { "name": "systemProperties",      "property": { "value": "8082" } },
    { "name": "systemEnvironment",     "property": { "value": "8081" } },
    { "name": "applicationConfig: [classpath:/application.yml]",
      "property": { "value": "8080" } }
  ]
}
```

The `source` field answers the question directly. Reading this once is faster
than memorising the ordering.

**In code**, the `Environment` exposes the same information.

```java
@Component
public class ConfigDiagnostics implements ApplicationRunner {

    private final ConfigurableEnvironment environment;

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        // Sources are iterated highest precedence first.
        environment.getPropertySources()
                   .forEach(source -> log.info("source: {}", source.getName()));

        log.info("effective server.port = {}",
                 environment.getProperty("server.port"));
    }
}
```

**Three precedence mistakes** account for most confusion.

**Editing the packaged file and not rebuilding.** The jar contains a copy; the
source tree is not what runs.

**An environment variable left over from an earlier experiment.** It outranks
every file, so the file looks broken. Checking the effective source finds it
immediately.

**Assuming a profile file replaces the baseline.** It does not; it overrides key
by key. A key present only in `application.yml` still applies when a profile is
active, which is the intended design but surprises people who expect the files
to be alternatives.

> Key Takeaways
> - Later sources override earlier ones, from packaged defaults to command-line
>   arguments.
> - Anything external to the artifact beats anything packaged inside it.
> - Command-line arguments outrank system properties, which outrank environment
>   variables.
> - Profile-specific files override the baseline key by key, not wholesale.
> - `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON` sets many properties through one variable.
> - The actuator environment endpoint names the winning source for any property.
> - Stale environment variables are a common cause of apparently ignored
>   configuration.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Set the same property in a file, an environment variable, and a
>    command-line argument, and confirm which applies.
> 2. Query the actuator environment endpoint for one property and read its
>    source.
> 3. Set a property in both the baseline and a profile file, and verify the
>    override.
> 4. Leave a stale environment variable set and diagnose why a file change has
>    no effect.
> 5. Interview: A developer changes `application.yml`, rebuilds nothing, and the
>    running jar ignores it. Explain both reasons this could happen. (Hint: one
>    concerns the artifact, one concerns what else might set the same key.)

<a id="183-building-rest-services"></a>
### 18.3 Building REST Services

This subchapter assembles a complete, well-behaved HTTP API from the pieces
chapters 16 and 17 established: endpoint design, the types that cross the
boundary, serialization, validation and errors, persistence, documentation, and
keeping clients working as the API changes.

#### Designing Resource Endpoints

17.4 covered the mechanics of mapping a request to a method. Design is the
separate question of **which** endpoints should exist, and it is worth treating
deliberately because an API's shape is the hardest thing to change later.

The organising idea is that a REST API exposes **resources**, which are nouns
with identity, and that HTTP methods supply the verbs. Everything else follows.

**Start by naming the resources, not the operations.** A useful test: write the
list of things your system manages, then check that each has a URL.

```text
  Resources                URLs
  ---------                ----
  orders                   /orders          /orders/{id}
  customers                /customers       /customers/{id}
  products                 /products        /products/{id}
  an order's lines         /orders/{id}/lines
```

**Nest only to express ownership**, and only one level deep. Deep nesting
produces URLs that are long, rigid, and awkward when a sub-resource needs to be
addressed on its own.

```text
  Good     /orders/42/lines                   lines belong to an order
  Good     /lines/1001                        a line is also addressable directly
  Poor     /customers/7/orders/42/lines/1001  four levels; brittle and redundant
```

A practical rule: nest for **listing and creating** within a parent, and use a
flat URL for addressing an individual item.

**Filtering, sorting, and pagination belong in the query string**, not in the
path, because they select from a collection rather than identifying a resource.

```text
  GET /orders?status=NEW&customerId=7&placedAfter=2026-01-01
  GET /orders?sort=placedAt,desc&page=2&size=20
```

**Pagination should be the default on every collection**, because an unbounded
list endpoint is a production incident waiting for the table to grow.

```java
@GetMapping
public Page<OrderResponse> list(
        @RequestParam(required = false) OrderStatus status,
        @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "placedAt",
                         direction = Sort.Direction.DESC) Pageable pageable) {
    return service.find(status, pageable).map(OrderResponse::from);
}
```

`@PageableDefault` supplies the bound even when the client omits it, which is
the part that prevents the incident. Capping the maximum page size matters too.

```text
  spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size=100
```

**Actions that are not state replacements** are the case REST purism handles
badly. Cancelling an order is not a `PUT` of a new representation; it is a
transition with its own rules. Model it as a sub-resource.

```text
  POST /orders/42/cancel            an action with a clear meaning
  POST /orders/42/refunds           creates a refund; also a resource
  POST /users/7/password-reset      an action, not a field update
```

This is widely accepted and far clearer than contorting the model to avoid a
verb.

**Partial updates** need a decision, because `PUT` means replace.

| Method  | Semantics                        | Consequence for omitted fields   |
| ------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `PUT`   | Replace the whole representation | Cleared or reset to default       |
| `PATCH` | Apply a partial change           | Left untouched                    |

Accepting a `PUT` and treating absent fields as "leave alone" is the common bug:
a client that sends a subset silently wipes the rest.

**A worked endpoint set** for one resource, with the status codes 17.4 covered:

| Method and path         | Purpose               | Success | Notable failures      |
| ----------------------- | --------------------- | ------- | --------------------- |
| `GET /orders`           | List, paged           | 200     | 400 on bad filter     |
| `GET /orders/{id}`      | Fetch one             | 200     | 404                   |
| `POST /orders`          | Create                | 201     | 400, 409 on duplicate |
| `PUT /orders/{id}`      | Replace               | 200     | 404, 409 on conflict  |
| `PATCH /orders/{id}`    | Partial update        | 200     | 404, 400              |
| `DELETE /orders/{id}`   | Remove                | 204     | 404                   |
| `POST /orders/{id}/cancel` | Transition         | 200     | 404, 409 if not cancellable |

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService service;

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(
            @RequestBody @Valid CreateOrderRequest request) {

        Order order = service.place(request.toCommand());
        URI location = URI.create("/api/orders/" + order.id());

        return ResponseEntity.created(location)      // 201 with a Location header
                             .body(OrderResponse.from(order));
    }

    @PostMapping("/{id}/cancel")
    public OrderResponse cancel(@PathVariable long id,
                                @RequestBody @Valid CancelRequest request) {
        // Throws OrderNotCancellableException, mapped to 409 by the advice.
        return OrderResponse.from(service.cancel(id, request.reason()));
    }
}
```

**Consistency across the API matters more than any individual choice.** Pick one
convention for plurals, one for date formats, one for pagination, and one for
error bodies, and apply them everywhere. A client integrating with an API that
is uniformly imperfect has an easier time than one integrating with an API that
is inconsistently ideal.

> Key Takeaways
> - Model resources as nouns with identity; HTTP methods supply the verbs.
> - Nest one level to express ownership, and address individual items flatly.
> - Filtering, sorting, and pagination belong in the query string.
> - Every collection endpoint should be paged by default with a capped maximum.
> - Model genuine actions as sub-resources rather than distorting the model.
> - `PUT` replaces and `PATCH` amends; treating `PUT` as partial silently loses
>   data.
> - Return 201 with a `Location` header from creation endpoints.
> - Consistency across the API is worth more than perfection in any one
>   endpoint.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Design the full endpoint set for two related resources, including one
>    action endpoint.
> 2. Add default and maximum pagination to a list endpoint and verify both
>    bounds.
> 3. Implement `PUT` and `PATCH` for one resource and demonstrate the difference
>    with an omitted field.
> 4. Take an API that uses verbs in URLs and redesign it around resources.
> 5. Interview: Why is `POST /orders/42/cancel` acceptable in an otherwise
>    resource-oriented API? (Hint: what would the `PUT` equivalent require the
>    client to know and send?)

#### Data Transfer Objects and Mapping

17.4 stated the rule: do not expose entities through the API. This topic
explains why thoroughly and covers how to organise the alternative without
drowning in boilerplate.

A **data transfer object** (DTO) is a type whose only job is to cross a
boundary. Request DTOs describe what a client may send; response DTOs describe
what it receives. Neither is a persistence concern.

**Four reasons entities must not be exposed:**

**Coupling.** The API contract becomes the database schema. Renaming a column
breaks every client, so the schema can never be refactored.

**Over-exposure.** Every field is serialised, including ones a client should
never see. A `User` entity with a password hash, internal flags, and audit
columns leaks all of them by default.

**Mass assignment.** Deserialising a request directly into an entity lets a
client set any field it names, including `role`, `id`, or `accountBalance`.

```java
// DANGEROUS: the client controls every field of the entity.
@PostMapping("/users")
public User create(@RequestBody User user) {        // {"role":"ADMIN",...}
    return repository.save(user);                    // privilege escalation
}
```

**Lazy loading failures.** 16.4's `LazyInitializationException` fires during
serialisation, because Jackson touches an association after the transaction
ended. The stack trace points at the serialiser, not at the real cause.

```java
// The request DTO accepts only what a client may legitimately set.
public record CreateOrderRequest(
        @NotNull Long customerId,
        @NotEmpty @Valid List<LineRequest> lines,
        @Size(max = 500) String note) {

    public PlaceOrderCommand toCommand() {
        return new PlaceOrderCommand(customerId,
                lines.stream().map(LineRequest::toCommand).toList(), note);
    }
}

// The response DTO exposes only what a client should see.
public record OrderResponse(
        long id,
        String reference,
        String status,
        BigDecimal total,
        OffsetDateTime placedAt,
        List<LineResponse> lines) {

    public static OrderResponse from(Order order) {
        return new OrderResponse(
                order.id(),
                order.reference().value(),
                order.status().name(),
                order.total(),
                order.placedAt(),
                order.lines().stream().map(LineResponse::from).toList());
    }
}
```

Records are an excellent fit: immutable, concise, and with Jackson support
built in.

**Separate DTOs per operation** is usually right, because the fields differ.

```text
  CreateOrderRequest      customerId, lines, note        (no id, no status)
  UpdateOrderRequest      lines, note                    (customer is fixed)
  OrderResponse           id, reference, status, total   (never a note draft)
  OrderSummaryResponse    id, status, total              (for list endpoints)
```

The summary type matters: a list endpoint returning full representations of
fifty orders, each with its lines, is slow and usually wasteful.

**Where mapping code belongs.** Three options, in order of preference for most
codebases.

| Approach                         | Pros                                | Cons                          |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Static factory on the DTO        | Explicit, no dependency, greppable  | Manual, verbose for large types |
| A dedicated mapper class         | Testable, keeps DTOs passive        | An extra class per resource    |
| A generated mapper such as MapStruct | No boilerplate, compile-time checked | A build plugin and generated code to understand |

MapStruct generates the implementation at compile time, so there is no
reflection cost and mismatches are compile errors.

```java
@Mapper(componentModel = "spring")          // produces a Spring bean
public interface OrderMapper {

    // Fields with matching names map automatically.
    @Mapping(target = "reference", source = "reference.value")
    OrderResponse toResponse(Order order);

    List<OrderResponse> toResponses(List<Order> orders);
}
```

**A rule that prevents the most common leak:** map inside the transaction, or
ensure everything the DTO needs was fetched. This is 16.4's join fetch applied
at the API boundary.

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)              // 17.2: the mapping happens inside
public OrderResponse getOrder(long id) {
    Order order = repository.findWithLines(id)        // JOIN FETCH, no N+1
            .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
    return OrderResponse.from(order);        // lazy associations already loaded
}
```

**The objection to DTOs is boilerplate**, and it is fair for a small service
where the entity and the representation genuinely coincide. The counter is that
the coincidence rarely survives the first schema change, and the cost of
retrofitting DTOs to a public API is far higher than the cost of writing them
initially.

> Key Takeaways
> - DTOs decouple the API contract from the persistence model.
> - Exposing entities enables mass assignment, over-exposure, and schema
>   coupling.
> - Deserialising into an entity lets a client set fields it should not control.
> - Serialising an entity triggers lazy loading failures outside the
>   transaction.
> - Records are a natural fit for both request and response types.
> - Use different DTOs per operation, including a lighter summary for lists.
> - Static factories, dedicated mappers, and MapStruct are the three mapping
>   options.
> - Map inside the transaction or fetch eagerly, or lazy loading will fail.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Expose an entity with a sensitive field directly and confirm it appears in
>    the JSON.
> 2. Demonstrate mass assignment by posting a field the client should not
>    control, then fix it with a request DTO.
> 3. Serialise an entity with a lazy association outside a transaction and read
>    the failure.
> 4. Write a summary response type for a list endpoint and compare payload
>    sizes.
> 5. Replace manual mapping with MapStruct for one resource and inspect the
>    generated code.
> 6. Interview: Name two distinct risks of accepting a JPA entity as a
>    `@RequestBody`. (Hint: one is about what the client can set, one is about
>    what the database expects.)

#### Serialization with Jackson

Jackson turns Java objects into JSON and back. Boot configures it
automatically, and most of the time you never think about it. The exceptions,
dates, nulls, naming, and polymorphism, account for a large share of real API
defects, so they are worth knowing explicitly.

**The default behaviour:** public getters or record components become JSON
fields with matching names, and JSON fields bind back to constructor parameters
or setters.

```java
public record OrderResponse(long id, String status, BigDecimal total) { }
```

```json
{ "id": 42, "status": "NEW", "total": 199.99 }
```

**Global configuration is preferable to per-field annotations**, because
consistency across an API matters more than any individual choice.

```yaml
spring:
  jackson:
    property-naming-strategy: SNAKE_CASE       # orderId becomes order_id
    default-property-inclusion: non_null       # omit null fields entirely
    serialization:
      write-dates-as-timestamps: false         # ISO-8601 strings, not epoch numbers
      indent-output: false
    deserialization:
      fail-on-unknown-properties: false        # tolerate extra fields from clients
    time-zone: UTC
```

Two of those deserve explanation.

**`write-dates-as-timestamps: false` should always be set.** The default
serialises a `java.time` value as a number of seconds, which is unreadable and
loses the offset.

```json
{ "placedAt": 1758844800.000000000 }      // default: an epoch number
{ "placedAt": "2026-09-26T10:00:00Z" }    // with the setting: readable, unambiguous
```

**`fail-on-unknown-properties: false` is the tolerant reader principle.** A
client sending a field your version does not know should not get a 400; this is
what allows an API to add fields without breaking older clients, and it matters
again in the versioning topic.

**Per-field annotations** cover the cases global settings cannot.

```java
public record OrderResponse(

        long id,

        @JsonProperty("order_status")                   // an explicit name
        String status,

        @JsonFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd")             // date only, no time
        LocalDate deliveryDate,

        @JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_EMPTY)     // omit when empty
        List<String> tags,

        @JsonIgnore                                     // never serialised
        String internalNote) { }
```

| Annotation           | Effect                                            |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `@JsonProperty`      | Rename, or mark a field required for binding       |
| `@JsonIgnore`        | Exclude a field entirely                           |
| `@JsonInclude`       | Omit null or empty values                          |
| `@JsonFormat`        | Control date, time, and number formatting          |
| `@JsonAlias`         | Accept alternative incoming names                  |
| `@JsonAnySetter`     | Collect unmapped fields into a map                 |
| `@JsonView`          | Serialise different subsets for different contexts |

**`@JsonIgnore` is not a security control.** It prevents serialisation but, by
default, also blocks deserialisation of that field, and relying on it to protect
a sensitive attribute is fragile compared with simply not putting the field in
the DTO.

**Write-only fields** are the correct pattern for passwords and similar inputs.

```java
public record CreateUserRequest(
        String email,

        @JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.WRITE_ONLY)
        String password) { }          // accepted in requests, never in responses
```

**Polymorphic types** need explicit configuration, because JSON has no notion of
a Java subclass.

```java
@JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME,
              property = "type")                 // a discriminator field
@JsonSubTypes({
    @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = CardPayment.class, name = "card"),
    @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = TransferPayment.class, name = "transfer")
})
public sealed interface PaymentRequest permits CardPayment, TransferPayment { }
```

```json
{ "type": "card", "cardNumber": "...", "expiry": "2028-05" }
```

Never enable Jackson's default typing, which embeds arbitrary class names in the
JSON and has produced a long series of deserialisation vulnerabilities. Use an
explicit discriminator as above.

**Custom serializers** handle domain types that should not appear as nested
objects.

```java
public class MoneySerializer extends JsonSerializer<Money> {
    @Override
    public void serialize(Money value, JsonGenerator gen, SerializerProvider p)
            throws IOException {
        gen.writeString(value.amount() + " " + value.currency());   // "19.99 EUR"
    }
}

@Configuration
public class JacksonConfig {
    @Bean
    public Module moneyModule() {
        var module = new SimpleModule();
        module.addSerializer(Money.class, new MoneySerializer());
        return module;       // Boot picks up Module beans automatically
    }
}
```

**A debugging note:** when a response is unexpectedly empty or a field is
missing, the cause is almost always an absent accessor or a mismatched name.
Logging the serialised output during development finds it faster than reasoning
about it.

> Key Takeaways
> - Boot configures Jackson automatically; the defaults are mostly right.
> - Prefer global configuration over per-field annotations for consistency.
> - Always disable timestamp date serialisation so dates are readable ISO-8601.
> - Tolerating unknown properties lets clients and servers evolve
>   independently.
> - Use write-only access for inputs such as passwords rather than relying on
>   `@JsonIgnore`.
> - Polymorphic types need an explicit discriminator; never enable default
>   typing.
> - Custom serializers keep domain value types from leaking their structure.
> - A missing field is nearly always a missing accessor or a naming mismatch.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Serialise an `OffsetDateTime` with and without the timestamp setting and
>    compare.
> 2. Configure snake case globally and verify every endpoint changes without
>    editing DTOs.
> 3. Make a password field write-only and confirm it is accepted but never
>    returned.
> 4. Implement a polymorphic request with a discriminator and deserialise both
>    subtypes.
> 5. Write a custom serializer for a value type and register it as a module.
> 6. Interview: Why does tolerating unknown JSON properties make an API easier
>    to evolve? (Hint: consider a server that adds a field and a client that has
>    not been updated.)

#### Validation and Consistent Error Responses

17.4 covered Bean Validation and `@ControllerAdvice` separately. In a real
service they are one concern: every invalid input, every domain rule violation,
and every unexpected failure must produce a response a client can act on, in a
format that never varies.

**Design the error contract first.** A client integrating with your API writes
one piece of error-handling code, and it should work for every endpoint.

```json
{
  "type": "https://api.shop.com/errors/validation-failed",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "The request contains 2 invalid fields",
  "instance": "/api/orders",
  "traceId": "b4f2a1c8e9d34567",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "customerId", "message": "must not be null" },
    { "field": "lines[0].quantity", "message": "must be greater than 0" }
  ]
}
```

That shape is RFC 7807 problem details, extended with a field list and a trace
identifier. Spring's `ProblemDetail` supports it directly, which saves inventing
a format.

**Three layers produce errors**, and each needs mapping.

```text
  1. Binding and validation      malformed JSON, missing fields, constraint failures
        |                        -> 400, with field detail
  2. Domain rules                order not cancellable, insufficient stock
        |                        -> 409 or 422, with a domain error code
  3. Unexpected failures         bugs, database outages
                                 -> 500, with a trace id and no detail
```

**A complete handler** covering all three, building on 17.4's advice class:

```java
@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    // 1. Request body validation failures.
    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        problem.setTitle("Validation failed");
        problem.setType(URI.create("https://api.shop.com/errors/validation-failed"));
        problem.setProperty("errors", e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(fe -> Map.of("field", fe.getField(),
                                  "message", fe.getDefaultMessage()))
                .toList());
        return problem;
    }

    // Query and path parameter constraints, which throw a different exception.
    @ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleConstraint(ConstraintViolationException e) { ... }

    // Malformed JSON, a wrong type, or an unparseable body.
    @ExceptionHandler(HttpMessageNotReadableException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleUnreadable(HttpMessageNotReadableException e) {
        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        problem.setTitle("Malformed request body");
        return problem;      // deliberately no parser detail: it leaks structure
    }

    // 2. Domain rules, carrying a stable machine-readable code.
    @ExceptionHandler(DomainException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleDomain(DomainException e) {
        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(e.status(), e.getMessage());
        problem.setTitle(e.title());
        problem.setProperty("code", e.code());      // clients branch on this
        return problem;
    }

    // 16.3 and 17.3: an optimistic locking conflict is a 409.
    @ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleConflict(OptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.CONFLICT);
        problem.setTitle("The record was modified by someone else");
        return problem;
    }

    // 3. Everything else: log fully, disclose nothing.
    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleUnexpected(Exception e) {
        String traceId = MDC.get("traceId");        // 18.5's correlation id
        log.error("unhandled error, traceId={}", traceId, e);

        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
        problem.setTitle("Internal error");
        problem.setDetail("An unexpected error occurred");
        problem.setProperty("traceId", traceId);    // the client quotes this to support
        return problem;
    }
}
```

**A machine-readable code is what makes errors usable.** A client cannot branch
on an English sentence, and translating a message breaks it. A stable `code`
field lets clients handle specific cases and display their own text.

```java
public abstract class DomainException extends RuntimeException {
    public abstract String code();          // e.g. "ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE"
    public abstract HttpStatus status();
    public abstract String title();
}
```

**Choosing between 400, 409, and 422:**

| Status | Meaning                                        | Example                        |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| 400    | The request is malformed or fails a constraint   | Missing field, negative quantity |
| 422    | Well-formed and valid, but semantically rejected | Order total below the minimum  |
| 409    | Conflicts with the current state                 | Already cancelled, version stale |

Using 400 for everything is defensible and common; the distinction pays off when
clients need to retry differently.

**Validation groups** handle the case where rules differ by operation.

```java
public interface OnCreate { }
public interface OnUpdate { }

public record ProductRequest(
        @Null(groups = OnCreate.class)              // must be absent on create
        @NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class)           // required on update
        Long id,

        @NotBlank(groups = { OnCreate.class, OnUpdate.class })
        String name) { }

@PostMapping
public ProductResponse create(
        @RequestBody @Validated(OnCreate.class) ProductRequest request) { ... }
```

**Turn off the error detail Boot exposes by default** in production.

```yaml
server:
  error:
    include-message: never
    include-stacktrace: never
    include-binding-errors: never
```

Leaving these on leaks internal structure to anyone who sends a bad request.

> Key Takeaways
> - Define one error format and use it for every endpoint and every failure
>   type.
> - RFC 7807 problem details is a standard shape with framework support.
> - Binding failures, domain rule violations, and unexpected errors need
>   separate handling.
> - Include a stable machine-readable code so clients can branch without parsing
>   text.
> - Include a trace identifier on server errors and disclose nothing else.
> - 400 is malformed, 422 is semantically rejected, 409 conflicts with current
>   state.
> - Validation groups express different rules for create and update.
> - Disable Boot's default error detail in production.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a handler returning problem details for validation, domain, and
>    unexpected errors.
> 2. Return a field-level error list for a request with three invalid fields.
> 3. Add a stable error code to one domain exception and branch on it from a
>    test client.
> 4. Trigger malformed JSON and confirm the response leaks no parser detail.
> 5. Use validation groups so one DTO enforces different rules on create and
>    update.
> 6. Interview: Why should an error body carry a code as well as a message?
>    (Hint: what happens to client logic when someone improves the wording?)

#### Persistence Layer Integration

Chapters 16 and 17 covered persistence in depth. This topic is about the seam:
how the web layer and the data layer meet without each one's problems leaking
into the other.

**The layering, and what each layer may not do:**

```text
  Controller     HTTP only. No transactions, no repositories, no entities.
      |          Binds a request DTO, calls one service method, maps the result.
      v
  Service        The transaction boundary (16.3). Domain logic. Entities live here.
      |          Accepts and returns domain types or commands, never DTOs.
      v
  Repository     Data access only. No business rules.
      |
      v
  Database
```

Two rules do most of the work. **The transaction boundary is in the service**,
as 16.3 established, and **entities do not cross into the controller**, as the
DTO topic argued.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final ProductRepository products;

    @Transactional                                    // one business operation
    public Order place(PlaceOrderCommand command) {
        Customer customer = customers.findById(command.customerId())
                .orElseThrow(() -> new CustomerNotFoundException(command.customerId()));

        Order order = Order.forCustomer(customer);
        for (var line : command.lines()) {
            Product product = products.findById(line.productId())
                    .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(line.productId()));
            product.reserve(line.quantity());         // domain rule, may throw
            order.addLine(product, line.quantity());  // 16.4's both-sides helper
        }
        return orders.save(order);
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)                   // 17.2: skips dirty checking
    public Page<Order> find(OrderStatus status, Pageable pageable) {
        return status == null ? orders.findAll(pageable)
                              : orders.findByStatus(status, pageable);
    }
}
```

**`open-in-view` must be disabled**, and this is the single most important
setting in this topic.

```yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false        # Boot defaults to true, which is wrong for APIs
```

With it enabled, Boot keeps the persistence context open for the whole request,
so lazy associations load during serialisation. That sounds helpful and is
harmful: queries fire from the view layer, outside any transaction, producing
unpredictable N+1 behaviour and holding a connection for the entire request
including the time spent writing bytes to a slow client.

```text
  open-in-view: true                      open-in-view: false
  ------------------                      -------------------
  connection held for the whole request   connection held only in the service
  lazy loads succeed anywhere             lazy loads fail outside the service
  N+1 hides in the serializer             N+1 surfaces immediately as an error
  pool exhausted by slow clients          pool sized by actual database work
```

Disabling it converts a silent performance problem into a loud
`LazyInitializationException` during development, which is exactly the trade you
want.

**Fetch what the response needs, explicitly.** With the view open no longer
rescuing you, each query must load what the DTO will read. This is 16.4's join
fetch, now load-bearing.

```java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    @Query("SELECT DISTINCT o FROM Order o LEFT JOIN FETCH o.lines WHERE o.id = :id")
    Optional<Order> findWithLines(@Param("id") Long id);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = { "lines", "customer" })   // declarative fetch plan
    Page<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, Pageable pageable);
}
```

**Projections keep list endpoints cheap**, which matters most at exactly the
endpoints called most often.

```java
public interface OrderSummaryView {          // 17.3's interface projection
    Long getId();
    String getStatus();
    BigDecimal getTotal();
}

Page<OrderSummaryView> findAllBy(Pageable pageable);   // selects three columns
```

**Batching and pool sizing** are the two settings worth applying from the start.

```yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc:
          batch_size: 50                 # 16.2's batching, via JPA
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10              # 16.2: small pools outperform large ones
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000
```

Batching requires sequence-based identifiers, as 16.4 noted: `IDENTITY`
generation defeats it.

**Verify the query count in tests**, so the N+1 problem cannot return quietly.

```java
@Test
void listingOrdersIssuesOneQuery() {
    SQLStatementCountValidator.reset();
    orderService.find(null, PageRequest.of(0, 20));
    SQLStatementCountValidator.assertSelectCount(2);   // rows plus the page count
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Controllers handle HTTP, services own transactions, repositories access
>   data.
> - Entities stay inside the service layer; DTOs cross the web boundary.
> - Disable `open-in-view`, whose default hides N+1 queries and holds
>   connections.
> - With it disabled, each query must explicitly fetch what the response reads.
> - Join fetches and entity graphs express those fetch plans.
> - Projections keep frequently called list endpoints cheap.
> - Configure JDBC batching and a small connection pool from the start.
> - Assert query counts in tests so N+1 regressions fail the build.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Disable `open-in-view` and find every endpoint that then throws a lazy
>    initialisation error.
> 2. Fix one of them with a join fetch and confirm the query count.
> 3. Replace a list endpoint's full entities with a projection and compare
>    timings.
> 4. Enable Hibernate batching and verify from the SQL log that inserts are
>    grouped.
> 5. Write a test asserting the query count for one endpoint and then
>    deliberately break it.
> 6. Interview: Why is `open-in-view` enabled by default yet recommended
>    against? (Hint: what does it make easy for a beginner, and what does it
>    hide from everyone else?)

#### API Documentation with OpenAPI

An API that is not documented is an API that people integrate with by reading
your source code or by trial and error. Hand-written documentation solves this
briefly and then drifts, because nothing forces it to change when the code does.

**OpenAPI** is a machine-readable specification format for HTTP APIs.
Generating it from the code means the documentation cannot describe an endpoint
that does not exist.

```text
  Hand-written docs                     Generated from code
  -----------------                     -------------------
  a wiki page, edited manually          derived from controllers and DTOs
  drifts silently from reality          changes when the code changes
  no client generation                  clients generated in any language
  no interactive testing                a browsable, executable UI
```

**Setup is one dependency.** Springdoc scans the controllers and DTOs and serves
both the specification and a browser UI.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
    <version>2.5.0</version>
</dependency>
```

```text
  /v3/api-docs          the OpenAPI document, as JSON
  /swagger-ui.html      an interactive UI for exploring and calling endpoints
```

Much of the document is inferred: paths and methods from the mappings, request
and response schemas from the DTOs, required fields and bounds from the
validation annotations of 17.4. Well-typed code is already most of a
specification.

**Annotations fill in what types cannot express**: prose, examples, and the
error responses that do not appear in a method signature.

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
@Tag(name = "Orders", description = "Placing and managing customer orders")
public class OrderController {

    @Operation(summary = "Place a new order",
               description = "Reserves stock and creates an order in NEW status.")
    @ApiResponses({
        @ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = "Order created"),
        @ApiResponse(responseCode = "400", description = "Validation failed",
                     content = @Content(schema = @Schema(
                             implementation = ProblemDetail.class))),
        @ApiResponse(responseCode = "409", description = "Insufficient stock",
                     content = @Content(schema = @Schema(
                             implementation = ProblemDetail.class)))
    })
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(
            @RequestBody @Valid CreateOrderRequest request) { ... }
}
```

```java
public record CreateOrderRequest(

        @Schema(description = "Identifier of the ordering customer",
                example = "42", requiredMode = Schema.RequiredMode.REQUIRED)
        @NotNull Long customerId,

        @Schema(description = "At least one line is required")
        @NotEmpty @Valid List<LineRequest> lines) { }
```

**Examples are the highest-value addition.** A realistic request body in the
documentation saves every integrator an hour of guessing.

**Global information** goes in a bean.

```java
@Configuration
public class OpenApiConfig {

    @Bean
    public OpenAPI api() {
        return new OpenAPI()
                .info(new Info()
                        .title("Shop API")
                        .version("v1")
                        .description("Order and catalogue management"))
                .servers(List.of(
                        new Server().url("https://api.shop.com").description("prod"),
                        new Server().url("http://localhost:8080").description("local")))
                // Declares the auth scheme used in 18.4.
                .components(new Components().addSecuritySchemes("bearer",
                        new SecurityScheme().type(SecurityScheme.Type.HTTP)
                                            .scheme("bearer")
                                            .bearerFormat("JWT")))
                .addSecurityItem(new SecurityRequirement().addList("bearer"));
    }
}
```

**Client generation** is the payoff that justifies keeping the specification
accurate.

```bash
# Generate a typed client from the running service's specification.
openapi-generator-cli generate \
    -i http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs \
    -g typescript-fetch \
    -o ./client
```

**Contract testing** goes one step further: commit the specification and fail
the build when it changes unexpectedly, which turns an accidental breaking
change into a failed pull request.

```java
@Test
void apiContractHasNotChangedUnexpectedly() throws Exception {
    String current = mockMvc.perform(get("/v3/api-docs"))
            .andReturn().getResponse().getContentAsString();
    assertThatJson(current).isEqualTo(readResource("openapi-baseline.json"));
}
```

**Do not expose the UI in production** unless the API is genuinely public.

```yaml
springdoc:
  swagger-ui:
    enabled: false          # in the prod profile
  api-docs:
    enabled: false
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Generated documentation cannot drift from the code the way a wiki page does.
> - Springdoc derives paths, schemas, and constraints from mappings, DTOs, and
>   validation annotations.
> - Annotations add descriptions, examples, and the error responses types cannot
>   express.
> - Realistic examples are the single most useful thing to add.
> - A configuration bean supplies titles, servers, and security schemes.
> - The specification generates typed clients in any language.
> - Committing the specification turns breaking changes into build failures.
> - Disable the UI and the document in production unless the API is public.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add springdoc to a service and explore the generated UI without writing any
>    annotations.
> 2. Document one endpoint's error responses and confirm they appear.
> 3. Add examples to a request DTO and verify them in the UI.
> 4. Generate a client in another language from the specification and call one
>    endpoint.
> 5. Commit the specification and write a test that fails when it changes.
> 6. Interview: Why is generated documentation more trustworthy than
>    hand-written documentation? (Hint: what has to happen for each one to
>    become wrong?)

#### Versioning and Backward Compatibility

The moment a client you do not control depends on your API, you lose the ability
to change it freely. Versioning is how you keep changing it anyway, and the
first thing to understand is that **most changes do not need a new version at
all**.

**Compatible changes** can be made in place, provided clients follow the
tolerant reader principle from the Jackson topic.

| Change                                      | Compatible? |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Adding a new optional request field          | Yes         |
| Adding a new response field                  | Yes         |
| Adding a new endpoint                        | Yes         |
| Adding a new enum value in a response        | Risky: clients may not handle it |
| Making a required request field optional     | Yes         |
| Making an optional request field required    | No          |
| Removing or renaming a response field        | No          |
| Changing a field's type                      | No          |
| Changing a status code for an existing case  | No          |
| Tightening validation                        | No          |

The asymmetry is the rule worth memorising: **adding to a response is safe,
removing from it is not; relaxing a request is safe, tightening it is not.**

**When a breaking change is unavoidable**, three versioning schemes are in
common use, as 17.4 introduced.

| Scheme      | Example                                   | Assessment                   |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| URL path    | `/api/v1/orders`, `/api/v2/orders`        | Most practical; visible in logs, testable in a browser |
| Header      | `X-Api-Version: 2`                         | Clean URLs; harder to test and to cache |
| Media type  | `Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json`     | Purest; least familiar to most teams |

URL versioning wins on operability. You can see the version in an access log,
route it at a load balancer, and test it with a browser.

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v2/orders")
public class OrderControllerV2 {

    // V2 splits the single 'name' field into given and family names.
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderResponseV2 get(@PathVariable long id) {
        return OrderResponseV2.from(service.findById(id));
    }
}
```

**Version the contract, not the implementation.** Two controllers and two
response types are fine; two services and two repositories are a maintenance
disaster.

```text
  OrderControllerV1  -->  OrderResponseV1  --+
                                             +--> OrderService --> repository
  OrderControllerV2  -->  OrderResponseV2  --+
                          (mapping differs)       (one implementation)
```

**Deprecate before removing**, and give the schedule in the response itself.

```java
@Deprecated
@GetMapping("/api/v1/orders/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponseV1> getV1(@PathVariable long id) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header("Deprecation", "true")                      // RFC 8594
            .header("Sunset", "Sat, 31 Oct 2026 23:59:59 GMT")  // removal date
            .header("Link", "</api/v2/orders>; rel=\"successor-version\"")
            .body(OrderResponseV1.from(service.findById(id)));
}
```

Logging usage of deprecated endpoints is what turns the removal from a guess
into a decision: when the count reaches zero, removal is safe.

```java
@Component
public class DeprecationInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {

    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                             Object handler) {
        if (handler instanceof HandlerMethod method
                && method.hasMethodAnnotation(Deprecated.class)) {
            // Who is still calling this, and how often?
            log.warn("deprecated endpoint {} called by {}",
                     req.getRequestURI(), req.getHeader("User-Agent"));
            meterRegistry.counter("api.deprecated",
                                  "path", req.getRequestURI()).increment();
        }
        return true;
    }
}
```

**The expand-and-contract pattern** applies to APIs exactly as 17.3 applied it
to database schemas.

```text
  Step 1   add the new field alongside the old one, populate both
  Step 2   document the old field as deprecated
  Step 3   wait, measuring usage
  Step 4   remove the old field in a new version
```

**Practical guidance.** Keep the number of live versions very small, ideally
two. Every version is code that must be tested and kept working, and three
versions means every change is made three times. Publish a sunset date when a
version is deprecated, and hold to it.

> Key Takeaways
> - Most changes are compatible and need no new version.
> - Adding to responses and relaxing requests is safe; the reverse is not.
> - New enum values in responses can break strict clients.
> - URL path versioning is the most operable of the three schemes.
> - Version the contract with separate controllers and DTOs, sharing one
>   service.
> - Announce deprecation with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers.
> - Measure usage of deprecated endpoints so removal is evidence-based.
> - Expand and contract applies to APIs as it does to schemas.
> - Keep live versions to two; each one multiplies the maintenance cost.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Classify ten hypothetical changes to an endpoint as compatible or breaking.
> 2. Add a second version of one endpoint sharing the same service layer.
> 3. Add deprecation and sunset headers to the old version and verify them.
> 4. Write an interceptor that counts calls to deprecated endpoints.
> 5. Plan the four steps to rename a response field without breaking clients.
> 6. Interview: Why can adding a field to a response break a client, even though
>    it is usually safe? (Hint: what does a strict deserialiser do with a field
>    it does not recognise?)

<a id="184-security-essentials"></a>
### 18.4 Security Essentials

This subchapter covers how Spring Security decides who a caller is and what they
may do: the filter chain that intercepts every request, the authentication and
authorization model, storing passwords safely, stateless tokens, and enforcing
rules below the web layer.

#### Spring Security Filter Chain

Security cannot be a concern that each controller handles, for the reason 17.2
gave about cross-cutting concerns: a check that must be written in two hundred
places will be missing from one of them, and that one is the vulnerability.

Spring Security therefore sits **in front of** the application, as a chain of
servlet filters that run before `DispatcherServlet` sees the request. This is
17.4's filter position, used deliberately: a filter runs even for URLs that map
to no controller, so there is no path around it.

```text
   HTTP request
        |
        v
   +--------------------------------------------------+
   |  FilterChainProxy  ("springSecurityFilterChain")  |
   |                                                    |
   |   SecurityContextPersistenceFilter                 |  restore any existing auth
   |   HeaderWriterFilter                               |  security response headers
   |   CsrfFilter                                       |  CSRF token check
   |   LogoutFilter                                     |
   |   UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter             |  form login
   |   BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter                  |  JWT, see later topic
   |   ExceptionTranslationFilter                       |  401 and 403 decisions
   |   AuthorizationFilter                              |  the actual access check
   +--------------------------------------------------+
        |
        v
   DispatcherServlet -> controller
```

Each filter has one job, and the order is fixed and meaningful: authentication
filters must run before the authorization filter, and the exception translator
must wrap both so it can convert their failures into responses.

**The `SecurityContext`** is where the result of authentication lives. It is
held in a `ThreadLocal`, which is why 17.4's warning about clearing thread state
matters here too.

```java
// Available anywhere in the request's thread, including services.
Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
String username = auth.getName();
Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> authorities = auth.getAuthorities();
```

**Configuration is a bean**, replacing the older `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter`
that appears in pre-2022 examples.

```java
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            // Rules are evaluated in order; the FIRST match wins.
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())      // the essential catch-all

            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())           // safe only for stateless APIs
            .sessionManagement(s -> s
                .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .build();
    }
}
```

**Rule order is the most common source of security bugs here.** The first
matching rule decides, so a broad rule placed early makes every later rule
unreachable.

```java
// BROKEN: everything matches the first rule, so the admin rule never applies.
.requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated()
.requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")      // unreachable

// CORRECT: most specific first.
.requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
.requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated()
```

**`anyRequest().authenticated()` must be present.** Without a catch-all, a path
nobody wrote a rule for is unprotected, and new endpoints are unprotected by
default. Deny by default, permit explicitly.
