**Several chains** can coexist, which is how an API and a browser-facing
application live in one service with different rules.

```java
@Bean
@Order(1)                                       // evaluated first
public SecurityFilterChain apiChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")             // this chain handles only /api
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())           // stateless, token-authenticated
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .build();
}

@Bean
@Order(2)
public SecurityFilterChain webChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http                                  // everything else: browser-facing
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/", "/login").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())    // sessions and CSRF stay ON
        .build();
}
```

**CSRF deserves a precise rule** rather than the habit of disabling it.
Cross-site request forgery exploits the browser automatically attaching cookies
to requests triggered by another site. If your API authenticates with a header
that a browser does not attach automatically, such as a bearer token, CSRF does
not apply and disabling it is correct. If it authenticates with a cookie or a
session, CSRF protection must stay on.

| Authentication style      | CSRF protection |
| ------------------------- | --------------- |
| Session cookie            | Required         |
| Cookie-stored token       | Required         |
| `Authorization` header    | Not applicable; may disable |

**Security response headers** are written by default and are worth knowing.

```java
.headers(headers -> headers
    .frameOptions(f -> f.deny())                        // clickjacking
    .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp
        .policyDirectives("default-src 'self'"))
    .httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts
        .maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)))                    // force HTTPS
```

**Debugging** is best done by reading the chain rather than guessing.

```text
  logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG
```

The log names each filter the request passed and the rule that decided the
outcome.

> Key Takeaways
> - Security runs as servlet filters before the dispatcher, so no request
>   bypasses it.
> - Each filter has one responsibility, and the order is significant.
> - The authenticated principal lives in a thread-local `SecurityContext`.
> - Configuration is a `SecurityFilterChain` bean; the adapter class is
>   obsolete.
> - Authorization rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins, so
>   specific rules come first.
> - Always end with `anyRequest().authenticated()` so new endpoints are
>   protected by default.
> - Multiple chains with `securityMatcher` let an API and a web UI coexist.
> - Disable CSRF only when authentication does not rely on cookies.
> - Enable debug logging to see which filter and which rule decided.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Configure a chain with public, authenticated, and admin-only paths, and
>    test all three.
> 2. Place a broad rule before a specific one and demonstrate that the specific
>    rule never applies.
> 3. Remove the catch-all rule, add a new endpoint, and confirm it is
>    unprotected.
> 4. Define two chains with different matchers and verify each handles its own
>    paths.
> 5. Enable security debug logging and trace one denied request through the
>    filters.
> 6. Interview: Why is security implemented as a filter rather than as an aspect
>    on controllers? (Hint: what happens to a request whose URL matches no
>    controller at all?)

#### Authentication and Authorization Basics

Two questions look similar and are answered by entirely different machinery.
**Authentication** asks who the caller is. **Authorization** asks what that
caller may do. Confusing them produces both security holes and misleading error
responses.

```text
  Authentication              Authorization
  --------------              -------------
  "Who are you?"              "May you do this?"
  credentials -> identity     identity -> permission
  fails with 401              fails with 403
  runs once per request       runs per resource or method
```

The status codes encode the difference: **401 means "I do not know who you
are"**, and **403 means "I know who you are and the answer is no"**. Returning
403 to an anonymous caller hides the fact that authenticating would help.

**The authentication flow** in Spring Security has four participants.

```text
   request with credentials
        |
        v
   AuthenticationFilter          extracts credentials into an Authentication
        |
        v
   AuthenticationManager         delegates to the providers
        |
        v
   AuthenticationProvider        verifies; e.g. DaoAuthenticationProvider
        |                             |
        |                        UserDetailsService  loads the user
        |                        PasswordEncoder     compares the password
        v
   SecurityContext               holds the authenticated principal
```

**`UserDetailsService` is the single method you implement** to connect Spring
Security to wherever your users live.

```java
@Service
public class DatabaseUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {

    private final UserRepository users;

    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) {
        User user = users.findByEmail(username)
                // Deliberately the same exception for "no such user" as the
                // framework produces for a bad password, so responses do not
                // reveal which accounts exist.
                .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("bad credentials"));

        return org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User
                .withUsername(user.email())
                .password(user.passwordHash())        // the stored hash, never plain
                .authorities(toAuthorities(user.roles()))
                .accountLocked(user.isLocked())
                .disabled(!user.isActive())
                .build();
    }

    private List<GrantedAuthority> toAuthorities(Set<Role> roles) {
        return roles.stream()
                // "ROLE_" is the prefix hasRole() expects; hasAuthority() does not.
                .map(role -> new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + role.name()))
                .toList();
    }
}
```

**Roles versus authorities** is a naming convention that trips people up
constantly. There is one concept, `GrantedAuthority`; a "role" is simply an
authority whose name starts with `ROLE_`.

| Expression                    | Matches the authority   |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `hasRole("ADMIN")`            | `ROLE_ADMIN`             |
| `hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")`  | `ROLE_ADMIN`             |
| `hasAuthority("order:write")` | `order:write`            |
| `hasRole("order:write")`      | `ROLE_order:write`, almost certainly a bug |

A useful distinction in practice: **roles describe who someone is**, and
**authorities describe what they may do**. Coarse roles with fine-grained
permissions derived from them scales better than proliferating roles.

```java
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
    .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET,  "/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("order:read")
    .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("order:write")
    .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
    .anyRequest().authenticated())
```

**Authorization expressions** support more than a single check.

```java
.requestMatchers("/api/reports/**").hasAnyRole("ADMIN", "ANALYST")
.requestMatchers("/api/internal/**").access(
        new WebExpressionAuthorizationManager("hasRole('ADMIN') and isFullyAuthenticated()"))
.requestMatchers("/api/**").access(AuthorizationManagers.allOf(
        AuthenticatedAuthorizationManager.authenticated(),
        AuthorityAuthorizationManager.hasAuthority("api:access")))
```

**Reading the current user** inside application code is usually done by
injecting it rather than reaching for the holder.

```java
@GetMapping("/me")
public UserResponse currentUser(@AuthenticationPrincipal UserDetails principal) {
    return UserResponse.from(userService.findByEmail(principal.getUsername()));
}
```

This is preferable to `SecurityContextHolder` in a controller because it is
explicit, testable, and does not depend on thread-local state.

**Customising the failure responses** matters for an API, because the defaults
are designed for browsers.

```java
.exceptionHandling(ex -> ex
    .authenticationEntryPoint((req, res, e) -> {      // no credentials: 401
        res.setStatus(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED.value());
        res.setContentType("application/problem+json");
        res.getWriter().write(problemJson(401, "Authentication required"));
    })
    .accessDeniedHandler((req, res, e) -> {           // known user, denied: 403
        res.setStatus(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN.value());
        res.setContentType("application/problem+json");
        res.getWriter().write(problemJson(403, "Access denied"));
    }))
```

Without this, an unauthenticated API call can receive a redirect to a login page
that does not exist, which is confusing for every client.

**Never leak which accounts exist.** Distinct messages for "unknown user" and
"wrong password" let an attacker enumerate valid accounts. Use one message, and
apply the same timing where practical.

> Key Takeaways
> - Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides permission.
> - 401 means unauthenticated; 403 means authenticated but not permitted.
> - `UserDetailsService` is the single integration point for your user store.
> - A role is an authority prefixed with `ROLE_`; `hasRole` adds the prefix and
>   `hasAuthority` does not.
> - Roles describe identity and authorities describe permissions; prefer
>   fine-grained authorities.
> - Inject `@AuthenticationPrincipal` rather than reading the thread-local
>   holder.
> - Customise the entry point and denied handler so APIs return JSON, not
>   redirects.
> - Use one failure message so responses cannot be used to enumerate accounts.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a `UserDetailsService` backed by a repository and authenticate
>    against it.
> 2. Demonstrate the difference between `hasRole("ADMIN")` and
>    `hasAuthority("ADMIN")`.
> 3. Return problem details for both 401 and 403 and verify each from a client.
> 4. Inject the authenticated principal into a controller and return the current
>    user.
> 5. Design an authority scheme for three user types and four operations.
> 6. Interview: Why should a login endpoint give the same response for an
>    unknown username and a wrong password? (Hint: what can an attacker learn
>    from the difference?)

#### Password Storage and Hashing

A password database is the highest-value target in most applications, because
people reuse passwords. The design goal is that **a stolen database is not a
stolen set of passwords**, and meeting it requires understanding why the obvious
approaches fail.

**Plain text** needs no explanation: a database breach is total.

**A general-purpose hash such as SHA-256** is the approach that feels right and
is not. The hash is one-way, but it is also extremely fast, which is exactly
wrong. Modern hardware computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so an
attacker with the hashes simply tries every plausible password.

```text
  Attacking fast hashes
  ---------------------
  SHA-256 on a GPU rig       ~10,000,000,000 guesses/second
  every 8-character password  exhausted in hours
  every common password       exhausted in seconds
```

**Unsalted hashes** add a second failure: identical passwords produce identical
hashes, so one cracked hash reveals every account using that password, and
precomputed rainbow tables work against the whole database at once.

```text
  Unsalted                              Salted
  --------                              ------
  alice: 5e884898da280471...            alice: $2a$10$N9qo8uLO...  (salt inside)
  bob:   5e884898da280471...            bob:   $2a$10$kJ3mZq1P...
         ^ identical: same password             ^ different, despite the same password
```

**The correct approach is a deliberately slow, salted, adaptive hash.** Three
properties matter.

| Property  | Purpose                                                    |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Salted    | A unique random salt per password defeats rainbow tables and identical-hash leaks |
| Slow      | A cost measured in hundreds of milliseconds makes bulk guessing impractical |
| Adaptive  | A tunable work factor is raised as hardware improves        |

| Algorithm | Resists GPU attack | Resists custom hardware | Notes                         |
| --------- | ------------------ | ----------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| BCrypt    | Good                | Moderate                | The safe default; widely supported |
| SCrypt    | Good                | Good                    | Memory-hard                    |
| Argon2id  | Good                | Good                    | Current recommendation; needs more tuning |
| PBKDF2    | Moderate            | Poor                    | Acceptable where required by compliance |
| SHA-256   | No                  | No                      | Never for passwords            |

**Spring Security's `PasswordEncoder`** is the abstraction, and BCrypt is the
sensible default.

```java
@Configuration
public class PasswordConfig {

    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        // The strength is a log2 cost factor: 12 means 2^12 rounds.
        // Aim for roughly 250ms on your production hardware.
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);
    }
}
```

```java
@Service
public class UserService {

    private final PasswordEncoder encoder;
    private final UserRepository users;

    public User register(String email, String rawPassword) {
        // encode() generates a fresh random salt and embeds it in the output.
        String hash = encoder.encode(rawPassword);
        return users.save(new User(email, hash));
    }

    public void changePassword(User user, String current, String replacement) {
        // matches() re-hashes the candidate with the stored salt and compares
        // in constant time. Never compare hashes with equals().
        if (!encoder.matches(current, user.passwordHash())) {
            throw new BadCredentialsException("bad credentials");
        }
        user.setPasswordHash(encoder.encode(replacement));
    }
}
```

The stored value carries everything needed to verify it.

```text
  $2a$12$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMye  IjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy
  ^^^ ^^ ^-------------------^  ^-------------------------------^
  alg cost      salt (22 chars)        hash
```

**`DelegatingPasswordEncoder` handles migration**, which matters because you
will eventually need to move off whatever you chose.

```java
@Bean
public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    // Stored values are prefixed with {bcrypt}, {argon2}, and so on, so old
    // and new formats coexist. New passwords use the default.
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}
```

Upgrading on successful login is the standard pattern: when a user authenticates
with an old format, re-hash the password they just supplied with the new one.

**Rules that surround the hashing:**

- **Never log a password**, including in debug statements and exception
  messages.
- **Never email a password**, and never offer to recover one. An account that
  can recover a password is storing it reversibly.
- **Reset by expiring token**, single-use and short-lived.
- **Rate limit login attempts**, per account and per source. Slow hashing
  protects the database; rate limiting protects the live endpoint.
- **Check against known-breached password lists** rather than imposing complex
  composition rules, which push people toward predictable substitutions.
- **Require length over complexity.** A long passphrase beats eight characters
  with a symbol.

**Choosing the work factor** should be measured, not guessed.

```java
@Test
void bcryptCostIsAppropriate() {
    var encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    encoder.encode("a-test-password");
    long millis = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;

    // Slow enough to deter bulk guessing, fast enough for a login endpoint.
    assertThat(millis).isBetween(200L, 500L);
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Passwords must be stored so that a database breach does not reveal them.
> - Fast general-purpose hashes such as SHA-256 are unsuitable; speed is the
>   attacker's advantage.
> - Unsalted hashes expose identical passwords and enable rainbow tables.
> - Use a salted, slow, adaptive algorithm: BCrypt, SCrypt, or Argon2id.
> - `PasswordEncoder.encode` generates the salt; `matches` compares safely.
> - The stored string contains the algorithm, cost, and salt.
> - `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` lets formats coexist and supports migration.
> - Never log, email, or recover a password; reset with a short-lived token.
> - Rate limit logins, and prefer length and breach checks over composition
>   rules.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Hash the same password twice with BCrypt and explain why the outputs
>    differ.
> 2. Measure encoding time at cost factors 10, 12, and 14 and choose one.
> 3. Implement registration and password change using `PasswordEncoder`
>    correctly.
> 4. Configure a delegating encoder and verify a value in an older format still
>    authenticates.
> 5. Add rate limiting to a login endpoint and test it.
> 6. Interview: Why is BCrypt's slowness a feature rather than a performance
>    defect? (Hint: compare the cost of one login with the cost of ten billion
>    guesses.)

#### Token-Based Authentication with JWT

Session-based authentication stores state on the server: a cookie holds an
identifier, and the server keeps the session data. This works well for a single
application and causes friction for APIs serving mobile clients, single-page
applications, and other services, where sticky sessions or a shared session
store become the constraint.

**Token-based authentication moves the state into the token itself.** The client
presents a signed token on each request, and the server verifies the signature
rather than looking anything up.

```text
  Session-based                         Token-based
  -------------                         -----------
  client holds a session id             client holds a signed token
  server holds the session data         server holds only a key
  requires sticky sessions or a store   any instance can verify
  revocation is immediate               revocation needs extra machinery
```

**A JSON Web Token** has three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots.

```text
  eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsInJvbGVzIjpbIlVTRVIiXX0.dBjftJeZ4CVP...
  \_________________/ \_______________________________________/ \___________/
        header                        payload                     signature

  header    {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
  payload   {"sub":"42","roles":["USER"],"iat":1758844800,"exp":1758845700}
  signature HMAC-SHA256(base64(header) + "." + base64(payload), secret)
```

**The payload is encoded, not encrypted.** Anyone holding the token can read
it. The signature proves it has not been altered; it does not hide anything.
Never put a password, a card number, or personal data in a token.

| Claim | Meaning                                  |
| ----- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `sub` | Subject: who the token is about           |
| `iss` | Issuer: who created it                    |
| `aud` | Audience: who it is intended for           |
| `exp` | Expiry timestamp; verification must check it |
| `iat` | Issued-at timestamp                        |
| `jti` | A unique token id, useful for revocation lists |

**Spring Security's resource server support** handles validation, so writing a
filter by hand is unnecessary and error-prone.

```java
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class JwtSecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .securityMatcher("/api/**")
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())           // header auth: CSRF not applicable
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(jwt ->
                jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(authoritiesConverter())))
            .build();
    }

    // Maps a claim in the token onto Spring Security authorities.
    private JwtAuthenticationConverter authoritiesConverter() {
        var authorities = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
        authorities.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
        authorities.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");      // matches hasRole()
        var converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
        converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(authorities);
        return converter;
    }

    @Bean
    public JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${jwt.secret}") String secret) {
        var key = new SecretKeySpec(secret.getBytes(), "HmacSHA256");
        return NimbusJwtDecoder.withSecretKey(key).build();   // verifies signature and exp
    }
}
```

**Issuing a token** after a successful authentication:

```java
@Service
public class TokenService {

    private final JwtEncoder encoder;

    public String issue(UserDetails user) {
        Instant now = Instant.now();

        var claims = JwtClaimsSet.builder()
                .issuer("shop-service")
                .issuedAt(now)
                .expiresAt(now.plus(15, ChronoUnit.MINUTES))   // SHORT lifetime
                .subject(user.getUsername())
                .claim("roles", user.getAuthorities().stream()
                        .map(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority)
                        .map(a -> a.replaceFirst("^ROLE_", ""))
                        .toList())
                .build();

        return encoder.encode(JwtEncoderParameters.from(claims)).getTokenValue();
    }
}
```

**Revocation is the hard problem**, and it is the reason token lifetimes must be
short. A signed token is valid until it expires; there is no server-side record
to delete. Logging a user out, or disabling a compromised account, does not
invalidate tokens already issued.

The standard answer is a **two-token scheme**.

```text
  Access token     15 minutes    sent with every request; not checked against storage
  Refresh token    7 days        stored server-side; exchanged for a new access token
                                 revocable by deleting the stored record
```

```text
   login  --> access token (15m) + refresh token (7d)
                     |
      request -------+--> verify signature and exp, no lookup
                     |
      access expires --> POST /auth/refresh with the refresh token
                                 |
                          look it up, check it is not revoked
                                 |
                          issue a new access token
```

The window of exposure is therefore bounded by the access token's lifetime,
which is why fifteen minutes is typical and hours are not.

**Where to store tokens in a browser** is a genuine trade-off.

| Storage            | Vulnerable to | Notes                                 |
| ------------------ | ------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `localStorage`     | Cross-site scripting | Any injected script can read it   |
| In-memory variable | Lost on reload | Safest against theft; needs a refresh flow |
| `HttpOnly` cookie  | CSRF           | Script cannot read it; requires CSRF protection |

An `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie with CSRF protection is the
strongest common arrangement, at the cost of reintroducing the CSRF concern the
earlier topic set aside.

**Rules that prevent the known failure modes:**

- **Reject `alg: none` and never let the token choose the algorithm.** Pin it in
  the decoder configuration; this class of bug has broken many
  implementations.
- **Use a long, random secret** for HMAC, at least 256 bits, supplied from the
  environment as 18.2 described. For multiple services, prefer asymmetric RS256
  so verifiers hold only the public key.
- **Always validate expiry, issuer, and audience.** The library does this only
  if configured to.
- **Keep tokens out of URLs**, where they land in access logs and browser
  history.
- **Use HTTPS without exception.** A bearer token on a plain connection is a
  password in plain text.

> Key Takeaways
> - Tokens move session state to the client, so any instance can verify a
>   request.
> - A JWT is header, payload, and signature; the payload is readable by anyone.
> - Never place secrets or personal data in a token.
> - Spring Security's resource server support validates tokens; do not write the
>   filter yourself.
> - A signed token cannot be revoked, which forces short access token
>   lifetimes.
> - Pair a short access token with a stored, revocable refresh token.
> - Browser storage is a trade-off between cross-site scripting and CSRF
>   exposure.
> - Pin the algorithm, use a strong secret, validate expiry and issuer, and
>   require HTTPS.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Decode a JWT by hand and read its payload, confirming it is not encrypted.
> 2. Configure a resource server chain and authenticate a request with a bearer
>    token.
> 3. Map a custom claim onto Spring Security authorities and enforce a rule with
>    it.
> 4. Implement access and refresh tokens and demonstrate revoking the refresh
>    token.
> 5. Set a token to expire in ten seconds and observe the failure after it
>    lapses.
> 6. Interview: A user is disabled but keeps accessing the API for several
>    minutes. Explain why, and what limits the window. (Hint: what does the
>    server check on each request, and what does it not check?)

#### Method-Level Security

URL-based rules protect the web layer, and that is not the whole application. A
service method called by a scheduled job, a message consumer, or another service
never passes through the filter chain, so a rule expressed as a path pattern
does not apply to it.

**Method-level security** places the check on the method, where the operation
actually happens. It is implemented as an aspect, which means every limitation
from 17.2 applies: proxied beans only, public methods only, and no self-invoked
calls.

```java
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity            // prePostEnabled is true by default
public class MethodSecurityConfig { }
```

**`@PreAuthorize` evaluates before the method runs**, which is what you want for
anything with an effect.

```java
@Service
public class DocumentService {

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public void deleteAll() { ... }

    // SpEL can reference method arguments by name.
    @PreAuthorize("#ownerId == authentication.principal.id or hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public List<Document> listFor(long ownerId) { ... }

    // And can call a bean to express a domain rule.
    @PreAuthorize("@documentPermissions.canEdit(#id, authentication)")
    public Document update(long id, DocumentUpdate update) { ... }
}
```

```java
@Component("documentPermissions")
public class DocumentPermissions {

    public boolean canEdit(long documentId, Authentication authentication) {
        // Arbitrary logic, unit-testable in isolation from the web layer.
        return repository.findById(documentId)
                .map(doc -> doc.ownerEmail().equals(authentication.getName()))
                .orElse(false);
    }
}
```

Delegating to a bean is the pattern that keeps expressions readable. A SpEL
string longer than about eighty characters is hard to review and impossible to
unit test.

**`@PostAuthorize` runs the method and then decides**, which is appropriate only
when the decision depends on the result.

```java
@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerEmail == authentication.name")
public Document findById(long id) { ... }      // loaded, then possibly discarded
```

Be aware of what this means: the method's work is done and any side effects have
happened. Never use it on a method that writes.

**Filtering collections** applies a rule per element.

```java
// Removes elements the caller may not see, after the method returns.
@PostFilter("filterObject.ownerEmail == authentication.name")
public List<Document> findAll() { ... }

// Removes elements the caller may not submit, before the method runs.
@PreFilter("filterObject.ownerEmail == authentication.name")
public void saveAll(List<Document> documents) { ... }
```

`@PostFilter` is convenient and can be a performance trap: loading ten thousand
rows to discard nine thousand is worse than filtering in the query. Prefer a
repository method that filters in SQL, and reserve `@PostFilter` for small
collections.

| Annotation       | Runs         | Use for                                |
| ---------------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| `@PreAuthorize`  | Before       | Nearly everything, especially writes    |
| `@PostAuthorize` | After        | Decisions depending on the return value |
| `@PreFilter`     | Before       | Filtering an incoming collection        |
| `@PostFilter`    | After        | Filtering a small returned collection   |
| `@Secured`       | Before       | Simple role checks; no SpEL             |
| `@RolesAllowed`  | Before       | The Jakarta standard equivalent         |

**A custom annotation** applies 17.5's composition and makes intent clearer than
a repeated expression.

```java
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public @interface AdminOnly { }

@Service
public class ReportService {
    @AdminOnly                             // reads better, and is greppable
    public Report generateFinancials() { ... }
}
```

**Layering matters.** URL rules and method rules are complementary, not
redundant.

```text
  Filter chain        coarse, fast, covers every path including unmapped ones
       |              /api/admin/** requires ROLE_ADMIN
       v
  Method security     fine, contextual, covers non-web callers too
                      "this document belongs to you"
```

**The proxy limitations are the trap**, exactly as with `@Transactional`.

```java
@Service
public class ReportService {

    public void generateAll() {
        for (var id : ids) {
            generate(id);          // self-invocation: @PreAuthorize DOES NOT RUN
        }
    }

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public void generate(long id) { ... }
}
```

A security check that silently does not run is worse than one that is absent,
because the code reads as protected. Test the rules rather than assuming them.

```java
@Test
@WithMockUser(roles = "USER")                // not an admin
void nonAdminCannotDeleteAll() {
    assertThrows(AccessDeniedException.class, () -> documentService.deleteAll());
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - URL rules do not cover service methods invoked outside the web layer.
> - Method security places the check where the operation happens.
> - `@PreAuthorize` is the default choice and runs before any effect occurs.
> - `@PostAuthorize` runs the method first, so never use it on writes.
> - Delegate complex expressions to a bean so they are readable and testable.
> - `@PostFilter` discards rows after loading them; filter in the query instead.
> - Custom annotations make repeated rules clearer.
> - Method security is an aspect, so self-invoked and non-public calls are
>   unprotected.
> - Test authorization rules; a silently skipped check reads as protection.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Protect a service method with `@PreAuthorize` and call it as two different
>    users.
> 2. Write an expression referencing a method argument and enforce ownership.
> 3. Delegate a rule to a permission bean and unit test that bean directly.
> 4. Demonstrate that a self-invoked call bypasses `@PreAuthorize`, then fix it.
> 5. Create an `@AdminOnly` composed annotation and apply it.
> 6. Interview: Why is URL-based security insufficient on its own? (Hint: name
>    two callers of a service method that never send an HTTP request.)

<a id="185-testing-and-operating-spring-boot-applications"></a>
### 18.5 Testing and Operating Spring Boot Applications

This subchapter covers what happens after the code works: proving it keeps
working with tests at the right granularity, and running it somewhere real with
enough visibility to diagnose problems without a debugger.

#### Slice Tests and Full Context Tests

Chapter 15 established the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration
tests, few end-to-end tests. Spring Boot adds a specific hazard to that picture,
because starting an application context is slow, and `@SpringBootTest` makes it
trivially easy to start one for every test.

```text
  A suite that ignores the pyramid
  --------------------------------
  400 tests, each with @SpringBootTest
  context starts in ~4 seconds
  contexts differ, so caching does not help
  -> 20+ minutes, and nobody runs it before pushing
```

**Most tests need no Spring at all.** A service with constructor-injected
collaborators, as 17.1 argued for, is testable with plain `new`.

```java
// No context, no annotations, milliseconds.
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Test
    void rejectsOrderBelowMinimum() {
        var repository = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
        var service = new OrderService(repository, new RecordingEmailSender());

        assertThrows(OrderTooSmallException.class,
                () -> service.place(orderTotalling("1.00")));
    }
}
```

**Slice tests** load only the part of the context a layer needs. They are the
middle of the pyramid and the most under-used tool in Boot testing.

| Annotation          | Loads                                    | Excludes                    |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `@WebMvcTest`       | Controllers, advice, converters, filters  | Services, repositories       |
| `@DataJpaTest`      | Repositories, entities, a test database   | Controllers, services        |
| `@JdbcTest`         | `JdbcTemplate` and a data source           | Everything else              |
| `@JsonTest`         | Jackson configuration and mappers          | Everything else              |
| `@RestClientTest`   | REST client infrastructure                 | Everything else              |
| `@SpringBootTest`   | The whole application context              | Nothing                      |

**A controller slice** tests binding, validation, status codes, and JSON
without a database.

```java
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @MockitoBean                              // replaces the real bean in the slice
    private OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    void returnsNotFoundForUnknownOrder() throws Exception {
        when(orderService.findById(99L))
                .thenThrow(new OrderNotFoundException(99L));

        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders/99"))
               .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Order not found"));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsOrderWithNoLines() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/orders")
                       .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                       .content("""
                               { "customerId": 7, "lines": [] }
                               """))
               .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
               // Confirms 18.3's error contract, not just the status code.
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[0].field").value("lines"));
    }
}
```

This is the right place to test the web contract: status codes, the error
format, validation rules, and serialisation. The service is mocked because its
behaviour is tested elsewhere.

**A repository slice** tests queries against a real database engine.

```java
@DataJpaTest
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired private OrderRepository repository;
    @Autowired private TestEntityManager entityManager;

    @Test
    void findWithLinesFetchesLinesInOneQuery() {
        Order order = entityManager.persistFlushFind(orderWithThreeLines());
        entityManager.clear();               // force a genuine load, not the cache

        Order found = repository.findWithLines(order.getId()).orElseThrow();

        // 16.4: this must not trigger a second query.
        assertThat(found.getLines()).hasSize(3);
    }
}
```

`@DataJpaTest` is transactional and rolls back per test, as 17.3 described, and
by default replaces the configured data source with an embedded one. That
default is worth overriding, because an in-memory database does not enforce what
your production database enforces.

```java
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
class OrderRepositoryTest { }     // runs against the real engine, see Testcontainers
```

**Full context tests** are for the paths that must be verified end to end.

```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class OrderApiIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired private TestRestTemplate restTemplate;   // a real HTTP client

    @Test
    void placesAnOrderAndReadsItBack() {
        var created = restTemplate.postForEntity(
                "/api/orders", new CreateOrderRequest(7L, List.of(line())),
                OrderResponse.class);

        assertThat(created.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
        assertThat(created.getHeaders().getLocation()).isNotNull();

        var fetched = restTemplate.getForEntity(
                created.getHeaders().getLocation(), OrderResponse.class);
        assertThat(fetched.getBody().status()).isEqualTo("NEW");
    }
}
```

**Context caching is what keeps a Boot suite fast.** Spring caches a context and
reuses it across test classes with identical configuration. Anything that makes
a configuration unique, a different property, a different mocked bean, a
different active profile, creates a new context and another startup.

```text
  Five test classes, identical configuration   -> 1 context,  4s total
  Five test classes, each with one @TestPropertySource difference
                                               -> 5 contexts, 20s total
```

The practical advice is to standardise: use one test profile and one set of
mocked beans wherever possible, and resist per-class property tweaks.

> Key Takeaways
> - Starting a context is slow, so reach for it only when the test needs one.
> - Constructor injection makes most service tests plain JUnit with no Spring.
> - Slice tests load one layer and are the most under-used option.
> - `@WebMvcTest` is the right place to test status codes, validation, and the
>   error contract.
> - `@DataJpaTest` is transactional and rolls back, but defaults to an embedded
>   database.
> - Override that default so queries run against the real engine.
> - `@SpringBootTest` with a random port exercises the full stack over real
>   HTTP.
> - Contexts are cached by configuration; per-class differences multiply startup
>   time.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same test three ways: plain JUnit, a slice, and a full context,
>    and compare run times.
> 2. Test a controller's validation and error format with `@WebMvcTest` and no
>    database.
> 3. Write a repository test asserting that a join fetch avoids a second query.
> 4. Add a unique `@TestPropertySource` to three test classes and measure the
>    suite's slowdown.
> 5. Interview: Why does mocking a different bean in two test classes make a
>    suite slower? (Hint: what does Spring use as the cache key for a context?)

#### Mocking Beans and Test Configuration

A test needs collaborators it can control. In a slice or full-context test, the
container supplies the beans, so replacing one requires telling the container
rather than calling a constructor.

**`@MockitoBean` replaces a bean in the context** with a Mockito mock. It is the
current name; `@MockBean` is the deprecated predecessor that appears in most
existing code and examples.

```java
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @MockitoBean                       // replaces or adds this bean in the context
    private OrderService orderService;

    @MockitoSpyBean                    // wraps the REAL bean, recording calls
    private AuditService auditService;

    @Test
    void createReturnsLocationHeader() throws Exception {
        when(orderService.place(any())).thenReturn(anOrder(42L));

        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/orders").contentType(APPLICATION_JSON)
                       .content(validOrderJson()))
               .andExpect(status().isCreated())
               .andExpect(header().string("Location", "/api/orders/42"));

        verify(auditService).record(argThat(e -> e.type().equals("ORDER_PLACED")));
    }
}
```

The distinction matters: a **mock** has no behaviour until stubbed, so an
unstubbed method returns null or zero. A **spy** delegates to the real object
unless stubbed, which suits a collaborator whose real behaviour is wanted but
whose calls must be observed.

**Be aware of the caching cost.** Each distinct set of mocked beans produces a
distinct context, so scattering different mocks across many classes is the
slowdown the previous topic described. Grouping tests that share a configuration
is worth doing deliberately.

**Test configuration classes** supply replacements that are real objects rather
than mocks, which is often better: a fake repository backed by a map behaves
consistently without stubbing every call.

```java
@TestConfiguration            // NOT @Configuration: not picked up by scanning
public class TestClockConfig {

    @Bean
    public Clock clock() {
        // A fixed clock makes every time-dependent assertion deterministic.
        return Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-09-26T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    }
}

@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestClockConfig.class)          // opt in explicitly
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest { }
```

`@TestConfiguration` is deliberately not found by component scanning, so it
affects only the tests that import it.

**Overriding a bean** from the main configuration needs the class to be
considered first, or the property that permits overriding.

```java
@TestConfiguration
public class StubPaymentConfig {

    @Bean
    @Primary                            // 17.1: wins over the real bean
    public PaymentGateway paymentGateway() {
        return (card, amount) -> new Receipt("TEST-RECEIPT");
    }
}
```

**Properties can be set per test**, though each distinct set costs a context.

```java
@SpringBootTest(properties = {
        "app.feature.newPricing=true",
        "spring.jpa.show-sql=true"
})
class NewPricingTest { }

@SpringBootTest
@TestPropertySource(locations = "classpath:test-overrides.properties")
class OverriddenTest { }
```

**`@ActiveProfiles` selects the profile**, which is the cleanest way to swap a
whole set of beans as 18.2 described.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@ActiveProfiles("test")            // loads application-test.yml and @Profile("test") beans
class OrderServiceIntegrationTest { }
```

**Security in tests** needs its own handling, since 18.4's filter chain will
otherwise reject every request in a `@WebMvcTest`.

```java
@Test
@WithMockUser(username = "alice", roles = { "USER" })
void userCanReadOwnOrders() throws Exception {
    mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders")).andExpect(status().isOk());
}

@Test
@WithAnonymousUser
void anonymousIsRejected() throws Exception {
    mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
}

@Test
void postRequiresCsrfTokenWhenEnabled() throws Exception {
    mockMvc.perform(post("/api/orders").with(csrf())     // supplies a valid token
                   .contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content(json()))
           .andExpect(status().isCreated());
}
```

**Injecting a `Clock` rather than calling `Instant.now()`** deserves emphasis,
because time is the most common source of flaky tests, as chapter 15 noted.
Making it a dependency turns an untestable method into a deterministic one.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final Clock clock;                       // injected, not static

    public Order place(PlaceOrderCommand command) {
        return new Order(command, OffsetDateTime.now(clock));   // controllable
    }
}
```

The same reasoning applies to randomness, the default locale, and the default
time zone: each is a hidden input that a test cannot control unless it is
injected.

> Key Takeaways
> - `@MockitoBean` replaces a bean in the context; `@MockBean` is its deprecated
>   predecessor.
> - A mock returns defaults until stubbed; a spy delegates to the real object.
> - Each distinct set of mocks creates a new cached context, so group tests that
>   share one.
> - `@TestConfiguration` supplies test beans and is not picked up by scanning.
> - `@Primary` on a test bean overrides the production one.
> - `@ActiveProfiles` swaps whole sets of beans and configuration files.
> - `@WithMockUser` and the CSRF request post-processor make secured endpoints
>   testable.
> - Inject a `Clock` rather than calling `now()`, and do the same for
>   randomness.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Test a controller slice with a mocked service and assert on the response
>    body.
> 2. Replace a mock with a hand-written fake and compare the readability of the
>    test.
> 3. Write a `@TestConfiguration` providing a fixed clock and assert a timestamp
>    exactly.
> 4. Test a secured endpoint as an anonymous user, a regular user, and an admin.
> 5. Convert a service that calls `Instant.now()` into one that takes a `Clock`
>    and test it deterministically.
> 6. Interview: Why is a hand-written fake sometimes better than a mock? (Hint:
>    what happens to a mock-based test when the collaborator gains a new method
>    the code under test calls?)

#### Integration Testing with Testcontainers

Repository tests commonly run against H2 in memory because it is fast and needs
no setup. The problem is that H2 is not the database you deploy against, and the
differences are exactly where bugs hide.

```text
  Tested on H2                          Deployed on PostgreSQL
  ------------                          ----------------------
  no JSONB, no arrays, no ENUM          the schema uses all three
  different function names               to_char, date_trunc behave differently
  different locking behaviour            16.3's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE differs
  looser constraint enforcement          a constraint fires only in production
  migrations pass in compatibility mode  the real migration fails
```

A test suite that passes on H2 and fails in production is worse than no test,
because it produced confidence that was not warranted.

**Testcontainers** starts a real database in a Docker container for the test
run, and stops it afterwards. The test runs against the same engine and version
as production.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-testcontainers</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

**`@ServiceConnection` wires it automatically**, which removes the property
plumbing that older examples show.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection                       // sets spring.datasource.* automatically
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
            new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");
            // 'static' matters: one container for the whole class, not per test

    @Autowired private OrderRepository repository;

    @Test
    void enforcesTheUniqueReferenceConstraint() {
        repository.save(orderWithReference("ORD-00000001"));

        // 17.3's translated exception, from the real engine's real constraint.
        assertThrows(DataIntegrityViolationException.class,
                () -> repository.saveAndFlush(orderWithReference("ORD-00000001")));
    }
}
```

**A shared container across the whole suite** avoids paying the startup cost per
class. The singleton pattern is the standard approach.

```java
public abstract class AbstractIntegrationTest {

    // Started once per JVM; Ryuk removes it when the JVM exits.
    static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> POSTGRES =
            new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    static { POSTGRES.start(); }

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void properties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url", POSTGRES::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", POSTGRES::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", POSTGRES::getPassword);
    }
}
```

Every integration test class extends this, so the configuration is identical and
the context cache from two topics back actually works.

**Other services containerise the same way**, which is what makes the approach
worth the setup.

```java
@Container @ServiceConnection
static RedisContainer redis = new RedisContainer("redis:7-alpine");

@Container @ServiceConnection
static KafkaContainer kafka =
        new KafkaContainer(DockerImageName.parse("confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0"));

// A stub HTTP server for an external API, so tests do not call the real one.
@Container
static GenericContainer<?> wiremock =
        new GenericContainer<>("wiremock/wiremock:3.5.4").withExposedPorts(8080);
```

**Testing migrations is a major benefit.** With Flyway from 17.3 and a real
engine, the test proves the migrations apply cleanly to an empty database.

```java
@Test
void migrationsApplyToACleanDatabase() {
    // The container starts empty and Flyway runs during context startup.
    // If any migration is invalid, the context fails and so does this test.
    assertThat(jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
            "SELECT count(*) FROM flyway_schema_history WHERE success = false",
            Integer.class)).isZero();
}
```

**Data isolation between tests** has two options.

| Approach                    | Speed | Caveat                                    |
| --------------------------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `@Transactional` rollback    | Fast  | Never exercises a real commit, as 17.3 noted |
| Truncate tables after each   | Slower | Exercises commits; needs careful ordering |

For tests that must verify commit behaviour, such as anything involving
`REQUIRES_NEW` or deferred constraints, truncation is the honest choice.

**Local development benefits too.** Boot's `@ServiceConnection` support works in
a development-mode launcher, so `./mvnw spring-boot:test-run` starts the
application with real dependencies and no local installation.

```java
@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class LocalDevContainers {

    @Bean @ServiceConnection
    public PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres() {
        return new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");
    }
}
```

**The costs are real:** Docker must be available, including in the continuous
integration environment, and startup adds seconds. Both are worth paying for
tests that mean something. The pyramid still applies; these belong in the
integration layer, not in place of unit tests.

> Key Takeaways
> - H2 is not the production database, and the differences are where bugs hide.
> - Testcontainers runs the real engine and version for the duration of a test
>   run.
> - `@ServiceConnection` configures the data source automatically.
> - A static or singleton container avoids restarting it per test class.
> - Sharing one base class keeps configuration identical so context caching
>   works.
> - Databases, caches, brokers, and stub HTTP servers all containerise the same
>   way.
> - Real engines let you test migrations and genuine constraint enforcement.
> - Rollback isolation is fast but never exercises a commit; truncation does.
> - Docker availability and startup time are the costs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert an H2-based repository test to PostgreSQL with Testcontainers.
> 2. Write a test that passes on H2 and fails on PostgreSQL, using a
>    vendor-specific feature.
> 3. Share one container across three test classes and measure the time saved.
> 4. Add a test that proves the Flyway migrations apply to an empty database.
> 5. Containerise a second dependency and use it in an integration test.
> 6. Interview: Why can a test suite passing against H2 be worse than having no
>    integration tests? (Hint: what decision does a green suite lead a team to
>    make?)

#### Actuator Endpoints and Health Checks

A running application is opaque. Something outside it, a load balancer, an
orchestrator, a monitoring system, needs to answer questions the process cannot
be asked directly: is it alive, is it ready for traffic, what version is it, why
is it slow.

**Actuator** exposes those answers over HTTP, and it is one dependency.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

| Endpoint              | Provides                                        |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `/actuator/health`    | Liveness and readiness status                    |
| `/actuator/info`      | Build and version information                    |
| `/actuator/metrics`   | Metric values, as covered in the next topic      |
| `/actuator/prometheus`| Metrics in Prometheus format                     |
| `/actuator/env`       | Every property and its source, as 18.2 described |
| `/actuator/beans`     | Every bean in the context                        |
| `/actuator/configprops`| Bound `@ConfigurationProperties` values          |
| `/actuator/mappings`  | Every request mapping, useful for 404 diagnosis  |
| `/actuator/loggers`   | Read and change log levels at runtime            |
| `/actuator/threaddump`| A thread dump, for diagnosing a hang             |
| `/actuator/heapdump`  | A heap dump, for diagnosing a leak               |

**Only `health` and `info` are exposed by default**, which is the right default.
Exposing everything publicly leaks configuration, bean names, and dependency
versions.

```yaml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus     # be explicit about what is public
      base-path: /internal                  # move off the predictable path
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized         # never 'always' on a public endpoint
  server:
    port: 9090                              # a separate port, not routed publicly
```

Running actuator on a **separate port** is the strongest arrangement: the
management port is reachable from the cluster and the monitoring system, never
from the internet.

**Health indicators compose.** Boot contributes one per detected dependency, and
the overall status is the worst of them.

```json
{
  "status": "UP",
  "components": {
    "db":        { "status": "UP", "details": { "database": "PostgreSQL" } },
    "diskSpace": { "status": "UP", "details": { "free": 21474836480 } },
    "redis":     { "status": "UP" }
  }
}
```

**A custom indicator** covers a dependency Boot does not know about.

```java
@Component
public class PaymentGatewayHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final PaymentGateway gateway;

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try {
            var response = gateway.ping();       // must be fast and cheap
            return Health.up()
                    .withDetail("latencyMs", response.latencyMillis())
                    .build();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            // Degraded, not down: the application still serves reads.
            return Health.status("DEGRADED")
                    .withDetail("error", e.getMessage())
                    .build();
        }
    }
}
```

Two cautions. A health check is called frequently, so it must be cheap; a check
that runs a real query every second becomes load. And a dependency being down
does not always mean the application is down, which is why the degraded
distinction matters.

**Liveness and readiness are different questions**, and conflating them causes
restart loops.

```text
  Liveness   "is this process broken beyond recovery?"
             false -> the orchestrator KILLS and restarts the container

  Readiness  "can this instance serve traffic right now?"
             false -> the orchestrator stops ROUTING to it, but leaves it running
```

A database outage should fail **readiness**, not liveness. Failing liveness
restarts every instance, which does not fix the database and removes the
application as well.

```yaml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true          # adds /health/liveness and /health/readiness
  health:
    livenessstate:
      enabled: true
    readinessstate:
      enabled: true
```

```yaml
# Kubernetes probes, pointed at the right endpoint each.
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }
  periodSeconds: 5
```

**`/actuator/loggers` is the operational endpoint worth knowing**, because it
changes log levels on a running instance without a restart.

```bash
# Turn on debug logging for one package during an incident, then turn it off.
curl -X POST localhost:9090/actuator/loggers/com.shop.payment \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'
```

**Build information** in `/actuator/info` answers "which version is deployed",
which is the first question in most incidents.

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution><goals><goal>build-info</goal></goals></execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

**Secure the endpoints** with 18.4's filter chain if they share the application
port.

```java
.requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
.requestMatchers("/actuator/**").hasRole("OPS")
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Actuator exposes operational state over HTTP from one dependency.
> - Only health and info are exposed by default; expose others deliberately.
> - Run the management endpoints on a separate port where possible.
> - Health is composed from indicators, and the worst status wins.
> - Custom indicators must be cheap, since they are polled frequently.
> - Liveness failure restarts the process; readiness failure stops routing to
>   it.
> - A dependency outage belongs in readiness, not liveness.
> - The loggers endpoint changes log levels without a restart.
> - Build info answers which version is deployed, the first incident question.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Enable actuator and list which endpoints are exposed by default.
> 2. Write a custom health indicator that reports degraded when a dependency is
>    slow.
> 3. Configure liveness and readiness probes separately and explain what each
>    failure causes.
> 4. Change a package's log level at runtime through the loggers endpoint.
> 5. Move actuator to a separate port and secure the remaining endpoints.
> 6. Interview: Why should a database outage fail readiness rather than
>    liveness? (Hint: what does the orchestrator do in each case, and does it
>    help?)

#### Logging, Metrics, and Tracing

When a request is slow or fails in production, you cannot attach a debugger.
Three kinds of signal answer three different questions, and a system needs all
three.

```text
  Metrics   "is something wrong, and how bad?"     aggregated numbers over time
  Logs      "what happened in this specific case?" discrete events with detail
  Traces    "where did the time go, across services?"  one request end to end
```

**Logging** is configured by Boot with Logback and a readable console pattern.
Two changes matter for production.

**Structured output**, because a log line that a machine can parse is queryable.

```xml
<!-- logback-spring.xml: JSON in production, human-readable locally -->
<configuration>
    <springProfile name="!prod">
        <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/base.xml"/>
    </springProfile>

    <springProfile name="prod">
        <appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
            <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
                <includeMdcKeyName>traceId</includeMdcKeyName>
            </encoder>
        </appender>
        <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="JSON"/></root>
    </springProfile>
</configuration>
```

**Correlation**, so every line from one request can be found together. This is
17.4's filter, and modern Boot adds the identifiers automatically when tracing
is present.

```json
{ "timestamp":"2026-09-26T10:00:00Z", "level":"ERROR",
  "logger":"com.shop.OrderService", "message":"payment declined",
  "traceId":"b4f2a1c8e9d34567", "spanId":"1a2b3c4d", "orderId":42 }
```

Three logging rules worth stating plainly:

- **Never log secrets or personal data.** Logs are copied, shipped, and retained
  far more widely than a database.
- **Log at the right level.** `ERROR` means someone should look; a validation
  failure is `DEBUG` at most, or the signal is drowned.
- **Include context, not prose.** `orderId=42 status=DECLINED` is greppable;
  "something went wrong with the order" is not.

**Metrics** are aggregated numbers, and Boot uses Micrometer, a facade over
monitoring systems in the same way SLF4J is a facade over logging backends.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final Counter placed;
    private final Timer placeTimer;

    public OrderService(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.placed = Counter.builder("orders.placed")
                .description("Orders successfully placed")
                .tag("service", "shop")           // tags become query dimensions
                .register(registry);
        this.placeTimer = registry.timer("orders.place.duration");
    }

    public Order place(PlaceOrderCommand command) {
        return placeTimer.record(() -> {          // records count and latency
            Order order = doPlace(command);
            placed.increment();
            return order;
        });
    }
}
```

| Meter type  | Measures                          | Example                     |
| ----------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Counter     | A monotonically increasing count   | Orders placed                |
| Gauge       | A value that goes up and down      | Queue depth, pool usage      |
| Timer       | Count and duration distribution    | Request latency              |
| Distribution summary | A distribution of values  | Payload sizes                |

Boot already publishes HTTP request timings, connection pool usage, JVM memory
and garbage collection, and thread counts, so a lot is available before you add
anything.

**Cardinality is the trap.** Every distinct combination of tag values creates a
separate time series, so tagging with a user id or an order id can generate
millions and overwhelm the monitoring system.

```java
// WRONG: unbounded cardinality.
registry.counter("orders.placed", "orderId", String.valueOf(order.id()));

// RIGHT: a bounded set of values.
registry.counter("orders.placed", "channel", order.channel().name());
```

**The four signals worth alerting on**, for any request-serving service:

| Signal      | Question                          |
| ----------- | --------------------------------- |
| Latency     | How long do requests take?         |
| Traffic     | How many requests are arriving?    |
| Errors      | What proportion fail?              |
| Saturation  | How close to a limit is it?        |

**Tracing** follows one request across service boundaries, which logs and
metrics cannot do.

```text
  trace b4f2a1c8
  |
  +-- api-gateway          [=========================] 340ms
       +-- order-service   [==================]        280ms
            +-- postgres   [===]                        40ms
            +-- payment    [============]              210ms   <-- the time is here
                 +-- bank  [==========]                190ms
```

Micrometer Tracing propagates the context automatically, and Boot instruments
web requests and clients.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1          # 10% of requests; 100% is expensive at volume
```

```java
@Observed(name = "order.place")          // one annotation produces a span,
public Order place(PlaceOrderCommand command) { ... }   // a timer, and a counter
```

**The three signals reinforce each other.** A metric alert says error rate rose
at 10:04. A trace shows the time is in the payment call. The logs for that trace
id show the gateway returned a specific error. Each alone is much less useful.

> Key Takeaways
> - Metrics detect problems, logs explain individual cases, traces locate time
>   across services.
> - Use structured JSON logging in production and human-readable output locally.
> - Correlate logs with a trace identifier so one request's lines are findable.
> - Never log secrets or personal data, and reserve `ERROR` for actionable
>   failures.
> - Micrometer is a facade over monitoring backends, as SLF4J is over logging.
> - Counters, gauges, timers, and summaries cover the measurement types.
> - Tag cardinality must be bounded; identifiers as tags overwhelm the backend.
> - Alert on latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
> - Sample traces rather than recording every request at high volume.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Switch to JSON logging under a production profile and confirm both formats
>    work.
> 2. Add a trace identifier to the logging context and correlate several lines
>    from one request.
> 3. Register a counter and a timer, then read both from the metrics endpoint.
> 4. Add a high-cardinality tag deliberately and count the series produced.
> 5. Enable tracing across two services and follow one request through both.
> 6. Interview: You have metrics showing a latency spike. What do traces and
>    logs each add that metrics cannot? (Hint: one tells you where, one tells
>    you what.)

#### Containerizing and Deploying the Application

An executable JAR still depends on a JVM of the right version, on operating
system libraries, and on whatever configuration the host happens to have. A
**container image** packages all of it, so the artifact that was tested is the
artifact that runs.

```text
  JAR deployment                        Container image
  --------------                        ---------------
  install the right JDK on the host     the JDK is in the image
  host libraries must match             libraries are in the image
  configuration lives on the host       configuration is injected at run time
  "works on my machine" is possible     the image is byte-identical everywhere
```

**A naive Dockerfile works and is wasteful.**

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
COPY target/shop.jar app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

The problem is layering. The JAR is one layer of perhaps sixty megabytes, and
changing one line of code replaces all of it, so every deployment pushes and
pulls the whole thing.

**A layered build** uses 18.1's layertools so that dependencies, which rarely
change, are cached separately from application code, which changes constantly.

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: build and split the jar into layers.
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/shop.jar extract

# Stage 2: assemble the runtime image, most stable layer first.
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app

# Never run as root: a container escape then starts from an unprivileged user.
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
USER app

COPY --from=builder /build/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/application/ ./        # the only layer that usually changes

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```

**Or skip the Dockerfile entirely.** Boot builds an optimised image with
buildpacks, already layered and running as a non-root user.

```bash
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=shop:1.0
```

**JVM settings inside a container** are the detail that catches people. Modern
JVMs are container-aware and read the cgroup limit, but the default heap
fraction is conservative.

```dockerfile
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="\
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
```

`MaxRAMPercentage` rather than a fixed `-Xmx` lets the same image run correctly
under different memory limits. `ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` matters because a JVM
thrashing after an out-of-memory error is worse than a restarted one: the
orchestrator can replace a dead container but cannot fix a sick one.

**Set the container memory limit above the heap**, because the JVM also uses
metaspace, thread stacks, and direct buffers. A container limited to exactly the
heap size is killed by the operating system.

**A deployment manifest** ties together the topics of this chapter.

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
    - name: shop
      image: registry.example.com/shop:1.4.2       # never 'latest' in production
      ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }, { containerPort: 9090 }]

      env:
        - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE             # 18.2
          value: prod
        - name: SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD         # 18.2: never in the image
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef: { name: shop-db, key: password }

      resources:
        requests: { memory: "512Mi", cpu: "250m" }
        limits:   { memory: "1Gi",   cpu: "1000m" }

      livenessProbe:                               # 18.5
        httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
        initialDelaySeconds: 30
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }
        periodSeconds: 5

      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

**Graceful shutdown must be configured for rolling deploys to be seamless**, as
18.1 introduced. Without it, terminating a pod drops its in-flight requests.

```yaml
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
```

The orchestrator's termination grace period must exceed that timeout, or it
kills the process mid-drain.

**Startup time** matters when scaling to meet load. Two options exist when it
becomes a constraint.

| Approach                  | Startup       | Trade-off                            |
| ------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Standard JVM              | 2 to 8 seconds | None; the default                    |
| Class data sharing (CDS)  | 30 to 50% faster | A build step, little downside      |
| GraalVM native image      | Under 100ms   | Long builds, reflection needs configuration, no JIT peak performance |

**A deployment checklist** drawn from this chapter:

```text
  [ ] profiles set explicitly, never relying on a default          18.2
  [ ] secrets injected at run time, absent from the image          18.2
  [ ] actuator on a separate port, endpoints restricted            18.5
  [ ] liveness and readiness probes distinguished                  18.5
  [ ] graceful shutdown enabled, grace period longer               18.1
  [ ] structured logging with correlation identifiers              18.5
  [ ] connection pool sized deliberately                           16.2
  [ ] database migrations run and tested                           17.3
  [ ] error responses disclose no internals                        18.3
  [ ] image runs as a non-root user with a pinned tag              18.5
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A container image packages the JVM, libraries, and application as one
>   artifact.
> - Layer the image so dependencies are cached separately from application code.
> - Buildpacks produce an optimised, non-root image with no Dockerfile.
> - Use `MaxRAMPercentage` rather than a fixed heap so one image fits several
>   limits.
> - Set the container limit above the heap, since the JVM uses memory outside
>   it.
> - Exit on out-of-memory so the orchestrator can replace the instance.
> - Inject profiles and secrets as environment variables, never bake them in.
> - Graceful shutdown plus a longer termination grace period gives seamless
>   rolling deploys.
> - Pin image tags, run as non-root, and keep the root filesystem read-only.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a layered Dockerfile and compare image push times against a
>    single-layer one after a code change.
> 2. Build the same application with buildpacks and inspect the resulting
>    layers.
> 3. Run the image with two different memory limits and confirm the heap adapts.
> 4. Configure graceful shutdown and verify an in-flight request completes
>    during a rolling restart.
> 5. Deploy with liveness and readiness probes and observe the behaviour when a
>    dependency is stopped.
> 6. Work through the checklist above against a project you have and note what
>    is missing.
> 7. Interview: Why should a container be limited to more memory than the JVM
>    heap? (Hint: name three things the JVM allocates that are not on the heap.)

<a id="19-capstone-and-interview-preparation"></a>
## 19. Capstone and Interview Preparation

This chapter turns eighteen chapters of individual techniques into the two
things that get judged: a complete application you designed on purpose, and the
ability to explain any part of it under questioning. The first subchapter is
about building; the rest are the questions interviewers actually ask, organised
by the chapter that answers them, followed by the practical skills of performing
well in the room.

<a id="191-capstone-application-design"></a>
### 19.1 Capstone Application Design

This subchapter covers taking a project from a vague description to a
structured, reviewable codebase: extracting a model from requirements, choosing
a layering, applying patterns where they earn their place, improving code that
already exists, and working in a team.

#### Requirements Analysis and Domain Modeling

Most projects fail at the beginning, not at the end. Code that solves the wrong
problem is worse than no code, because it takes longer to remove than to write.
The first skill is therefore turning an ambiguous description into a model
precise enough to build from.

**Start by extracting the vocabulary.** A useful technique is to take the
requirements as prose and mark the nouns and verbs.

```text
  "A customer places an order containing one or more products. Each order has
   a shipping address. Orders can be cancelled while they are still pending.
   When an order ships, the customer is notified."

   nouns:  customer, order, product, shipping address
   verbs:  places, contains, cancel, ship, notify
```

The nouns are candidate types; the verbs are candidate behaviours. This is a
starting point, not an algorithm: some nouns are attributes rather than types,
and some verbs belong to a service rather than to an object.

**Distinguish the three kinds of type**, because getting this wrong produces
either anaemic data holders or objects that cannot be compared.

| Kind         | Identity                        | Mutability      | Example             |
| ------------ | ------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------- |
| Entity       | Has an identifier; two instances with the same id are the same thing | Usually mutable | `Order`, `Customer` |
| Value object | Defined entirely by its values   | Immutable       | `Money`, `Address`  |
| Service      | No identity or state             | Stateless       | `PricingService`    |

```java
// A VALUE OBJECT: no id, immutable, equal when the values are equal.
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {

    public Money {                                   // compact constructor
        if (amount.scale() > currency.getDefaultFractionDigits()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("too many decimal places");
        }
    }

    public Money plus(Money other) {
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) {      // an invariant the type enforces
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        }
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency);
    }
}

// An ENTITY: has identity, and its state changes over its lifetime.
public class Order {

    private final OrderId id;                        // identity, never changes
    private OrderStatus status;
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        // Two Orders are the same order when the ids match, regardless of state.
        return o instanceof Order other && id.equals(other.id);
    }
}
```

Using `BigDecimal` rather than `double` here is 16.1's rule about money, and
wrapping it in a `Money` type is what makes "currency mismatch" impossible to
forget.

**Put behaviour on the objects that own the data.** The alternative, classes
with only getters and setters plus a service that manipulates them, is called an
anaemic domain model, and it scatters rules that belong together.

```java
// ANAEMIC: the rule lives outside the object it constrains, so every caller
// must remember to check it.
if (order.getStatus() == OrderStatus.PENDING) {
    order.setStatus(OrderStatus.CANCELLED);
}

// RICH: the object enforces its own rule, and no caller can skip it.
public void cancel(String reason) {
    if (status != OrderStatus.PENDING) {
        throw new OrderNotCancellableException(id, status);
    }
    this.status = OrderStatus.CANCELLED;
    this.cancellationReason = reason;
}
```

**Model the invariants explicitly.** An invariant is something that must always
be true, and the best place for it is a constructor or a factory method, so an
invalid object cannot exist at all.

```text
  Invariants for Order
  --------------------
  an order always has at least one line
  the total equals the sum of the lines
  only a PENDING order can be cancelled
  a shipped order cannot be modified
```

```java
public static Order place(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines) {
    if (lines.isEmpty()) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("an order needs at least one line");
    }
    return new Order(OrderId.generate(), customer, lines);   // valid from birth
}
```

**Identify the aggregates**, meaning the clusters that change together and are
