loaded and saved as a unit. `Order` and its lines are one aggregate: a line has
no meaning without its order. `Customer` is a separate aggregate, referenced by
identifier rather than embedded.

```text
  Order aggregate                   Customer aggregate
  ---------------                   ------------------
  Order  (the root)                 Customer  (the root)
    +-- OrderLine                     +-- ContactDetails
    +-- ShippingAddress

  Order holds a CustomerId, not a Customer object.
  Changes inside an aggregate are one transaction (16.3).
```

This boundary is what determines your transaction boundaries from 16.3 and your
fetch strategies from 16.4, which is why it is worth deciding deliberately.

**Use a glossary and stick to it.** If the business says "order" and the code
says "purchase", every conversation needs translating. Name types after the
words the people who asked for the system use.

> Key Takeaways
> - Extract candidate types from the nouns and behaviours from the verbs, then
>   refine.
> - Entities have identity and change; value objects are immutable and compared
>   by value.
> - Value objects are the natural home for invariants such as currency
>   matching.
> - Put rules on the object that owns the data, rather than in a service that
>   manipulates it.
> - Enforce invariants in constructors and factories so invalid objects cannot
>   exist.
> - Aggregates cluster objects that change together and define transaction
>   boundaries.
> - Reference other aggregates by identifier, not by object.
> - Use the business's own vocabulary as type names.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a one-paragraph description of a library lending system and list the
>    candidate entities, value objects, and services.
> 2. Write a `Money` value object that refuses to add different currencies and
>    test both cases.
> 3. Convert an anaemic class with five setters into one that enforces its own
>    rules, and list the rules you moved.
> 4. Draw the aggregate boundaries for an order, its lines, a customer, and a
>    product, and say which are loaded together.
> 5. Interview: What distinguishes an entity from a value object, and why does
>    it matter for `equals`? (Hint: consider two objects holding the same data
>    but representing different things.)

#### Layered Architecture in Java Applications

A codebase with no structure becomes one where any class may call any other,
which means any change may affect anything. Layering is the cheapest structure
that prevents this: it defines a small number of levels and one rule about which
direction calls may go.

**The rule is that dependencies point inward or downward, never back.**

```text
  +----------------------------------------------------+
  |  Presentation     controllers, request and response  |   17.4, 18.3
  |                   types, HTTP concerns only          |
  +----------------------------------------------------+
                        |  calls
                        v
  +----------------------------------------------------+
  |  Application      services, use cases, transaction   |   16.3, 17.2
  |                   boundaries, orchestration          |
  +----------------------------------------------------+
                        |  calls
                        v
  +----------------------------------------------------+
  |  Domain           entities, value objects, rules     |   19.1
  |                   no framework, no database          |
  +----------------------------------------------------+
                        ^  implements interfaces from
                        |
  +----------------------------------------------------+
  |  Infrastructure   repositories, clients, messaging   |   16.4, 17.3
  +----------------------------------------------------+
```

The arrow from infrastructure pointing **up** is the important one. Rather than
the domain depending on the database, the domain declares an interface and the
infrastructure implements it. This is the dependency inversion principle from
chapter 9, and it is what keeps the domain testable without any infrastructure
at all.

```java
// In the DOMAIN package: an interface expressed in domain terms.
public interface OrderRepository {
    Optional<Order> findById(OrderId id);
    void save(Order order);
}

// In the INFRASTRUCTURE package: the implementation depends on the domain.
@Repository
public class JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    // Imports jakarta.persistence. The domain package does not.
}
```

**What each layer must not do** is more useful than what it may do.

| Layer          | Must not                                                   |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Presentation   | Contain business rules, open transactions, touch repositories |
| Application    | Know about HTTP, return DTOs, contain domain rules          |
| Domain         | Import any framework, know about persistence or HTTP        |
| Infrastructure | Contain business rules                                      |

```java
// A correctly thin controller: bind, delegate, map.  17.4
@PostMapping("/{id}/cancel")
public OrderResponse cancel(@PathVariable long id,
                            @RequestBody @Valid CancelRequest request) {
    return OrderResponse.from(orderService.cancel(new OrderId(id), request.reason()));
}

// A correctly focused service: transaction boundary and orchestration.  16.3
@Transactional
public Order cancel(OrderId id, String reason) {
    Order order = orders.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFound(id));
    order.cancel(reason);                  // the RULE lives in the domain object
    orders.save(order);
    events.publish(new OrderCancelled(id));
    return order;
}
```

**Package by feature, not by layer.** The instinctive arrangement groups every
controller together, which means one feature is spread across four packages and
nothing can be made package-private.

```text
  By layer (avoid)                   By feature (prefer)
  ----------------                   -------------------
  com.shop.controller                com.shop.order
      OrderController                    OrderController
      ProductController                  OrderService
  com.shop.service                       Order
      OrderService                       OrderRepository
      ProductService                 com.shop.product
  com.shop.repository                    ProductController
      OrderRepository                    ProductService
      ProductRepository                  Product

  a change touches 4 packages        a change touches 1 package
  everything must be public          internals can be package-private
```

Feature packaging makes the module boundaries visible and lets you see when one
feature reaches into another's internals.

**Enforce the rules automatically**, because conventions that are not checked
decay.

```java
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.shop")
class ArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domainIsFrameworkFree =
            noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
                       .should().dependOnClassesThat()
                       .resideInAnyPackage("org.springframework..", "jakarta.persistence..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule layersAreRespected = layeredArchitecture()
            .consideringOnlyDependenciesInLayers()
            .layer("Web").definedBy("..web..")
            .layer("Service").definedBy("..service..")
            .layer("Persistence").definedBy("..persistence..")
            .whereLayer("Web").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
            .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Web")
            .whereLayer("Persistence").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service");
}
```

**Do not over-layer a small project.** Three layers with a rich domain is the
right default. Adding separate mapper layers, command buses, and hexagonal ports
to a service with four endpoints costs more than it returns. Structure should
grow with the problem.

> Key Takeaways
> - Layering restricts which parts may call which, so changes stay local.
> - Dependencies point one way; infrastructure implements interfaces the domain
>   declares.
> - The domain must import no framework, which is what makes it testable
>   without one.
> - Controllers bind and delegate; services own transactions; domain objects own
>   rules.
> - Package by feature so a change touches one package and internals can stay
>   hidden.
> - Enforce the rules with architecture tests, or they erode.
> - Match the amount of structure to the size of the problem.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take an existing project and draw its actual dependency arrows, then mark
>    the ones going the wrong way.
> 2. Move a repository interface into the domain package and its implementation
>    into infrastructure.
> 3. Restructure one feature from package-by-layer to package-by-feature and
>    make two classes package-private.
> 4. Write an architecture test asserting the domain package imports no Spring
>    classes.
> 5. Interview: Why should a repository interface live in the domain package
>    rather than beside its implementation? (Hint: which package should be able
>    to compile without the other?)

#### Applying Patterns to a Full Project

Chapter 9 covered design patterns individually. Applying them to a real project
raises a different question, which is not "which pattern is this" but **"does
this problem justify a pattern at all"**. Patterns are solutions to recurring
problems, and using one where the problem is absent adds indirection with no
benefit.

**The test is whether the pattern removes a real, present difficulty.**

```java
// UNNECESSARY: a factory for a class with one implementation and no choice.
public class OrderFactory {
    public Order create(Customer c, List<OrderLine> l) { return new Order(c, l); }
}

// JUSTIFIED: the choice is genuine and the rule is worth naming.
public class PricingStrategyFactory {
    public PricingStrategy forCustomer(Customer customer) {
        return switch (customer.tier()) {
            case PREMIUM -> new PremiumPricing();
            case PARTNER -> new PartnerPricing();
            default      -> new StandardPricing();
        };
    }
}
```

**Patterns that earn their place in most projects:**

| Pattern            | The problem it solves                          | Where it appears           |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Repository         | Hiding persistence behind a domain interface    | 16.4, every project        |
| Strategy           | A rule with several interchangeable variants    | Pricing, shipping, ranking |
| Factory            | Non-trivial construction or a runtime choice    | Creating from a discriminator |
| Builder            | Objects with many optional fields               | Test data, request objects |
| Adapter            | Making a third-party API fit your interface     | Payment gateways, clients  |
| Observer or events | Decoupling a trigger from its consequences      | 17.1's application events  |
| Decorator          | Adding behaviour without editing the class      | Caching, retry, metrics    |

**A worked example: three patterns in one flow**, each solving a distinct
problem.

```java
// STRATEGY: the shipping cost rule varies by method, and new ones get added.
public interface ShippingCalculator {
    Money costFor(Order order);
}

@Component
public class ExpressShipping implements ShippingCalculator { ... }

@Component
public class StandardShipping implements ShippingCalculator { ... }
```

```java
// ADAPTER: the payment provider's API is not ours, and we may change provider.
public interface PaymentGateway {                       // our interface
    PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request);
}

@Component
public class StripeGatewayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {

    private final StripeClient stripe;                  // their API

    @Override
    public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) {
        // Translate our types into theirs, and their errors into ours.
        var response = stripe.charges().create(toStripeParams(request));
        return toPaymentResult(response);
    }
}
```

```java
// EVENTS: placing an order should not know who cares that it happened.
@Transactional
public Order place(PlaceOrderCommand command) {
    Order order = Order.place(command.customer(), command.lines());
    orders.save(order);
    events.publish(new OrderPlaced(order.id()));        // 17.1
    return order;
}

@Component
public class InventoryListener {
    @EventListener
    public void on(OrderPlaced event) { ... }           // added without editing above
}
```

**Recognise the anti-patterns as clearly as the patterns.**

| Anti-pattern          | Symptom                                                  |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| God class             | One class of 2,000 lines that everything depends on       |
| Anaemic domain model   | Entities with only getters and setters; rules in services |
| Service locator        | Classes fetching dependencies from a registry (17.1)      |
| Singleton as global state | Static mutable state that makes tests order-dependent |
| Premature abstraction  | An interface with exactly one implementation, forever     |
| Pattern fever          | A factory producing a builder producing a strategy, for one case |

**The single-implementation interface deserves a fair hearing**, because it is
often criticised unfairly. An interface with one implementation is justified
when it marks a boundary you intend to cross, such as a repository the domain
declares, or when it exists so tests can substitute a fake. It is unjustified
when it exists only because someone said to program to interfaces.

**A practical sequence for a capstone:** write the simplest thing that works,
then introduce a pattern at the moment the second variant appears. The second
pricing rule justifies a strategy; the first does not.

> Key Takeaways
> - A pattern is justified when it removes a difficulty that exists now.
> - Repository, strategy, adapter, builder, and events cover most real needs.
> - Adapters keep a third-party API from spreading through the codebase.
> - Events decouple an action from an open-ended set of consequences.
> - Anaemic models, god classes, and service locators are the common
>   anti-patterns.
> - A single-implementation interface is fine at a boundary or for testing, not
>   as a reflex.
> - Introduce a pattern when the second variant appears, not in anticipation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find a `switch` on a type or status in your code and decide whether
>    strategy would improve it.
> 2. Wrap a third-party client in an adapter and make the rest of the code
>    depend only on your interface.
> 3. Replace a direct call to three consequences with one published event and
>    three listeners.
> 4. Identify a class in any codebase with more than fifteen methods and propose
>    a split.
> 5. Interview: When is an interface with exactly one implementation
>    justified? (Hint: name two situations where the second implementation is a
>    test or a future boundary.)

#### Refactoring an Existing Codebase

Most professional work is changing code that already exists, usually code
nobody currently understands. Refactoring is the discipline of improving its
structure **without changing its behaviour**, and the phrase "without changing
its behaviour" is the whole difficulty.

**The prerequisite is a safety net.** Refactoring without tests is editing and
hoping. If the code has no tests, the first step is characterisation tests:
tests that record what the code does now, correct or not.

```java
// A characterisation test does not assert what SHOULD happen. It pins down
// what DOES happen, so a refactor that changes it fails loudly.
@Test
void currentBehaviourForExpiredCoupon() {
    var result = legacyPricer.price(cart, expiredCoupon());
    // Discovered by running it, not by reading the requirements.
    assertEquals(new BigDecimal("42.50"), result);
}
```

If a characterisation test reveals a bug, record it as a bug and keep the test
asserting the current behaviour until the fix is a deliberate, separate change.

**Work in small, reversible steps.** The rhythm is: make one change, run the
tests, commit. A refactor that takes three days before it compiles is a rewrite
wearing a disguise.

```text
  Safe rhythm                          Unsafe
  -----------                          ------
  extract method -> test -> commit     restructure everything -> hope
  rename -> test -> commit             one commit, 4,000 lines changed
  move class -> test -> commit         cannot bisect, cannot review
```

**The refactorings that do most of the work** are few, and modern IDEs perform
them mechanically, which is safer than editing by hand.

| Refactoring             | Applies when                                    |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Extract method          | A block needs a comment to explain it            |
| Rename                  | A name misleads or abbreviates                   |
| Introduce parameter object | Three or more parameters always travel together |
| Replace conditional with polymorphism | A `switch` on type repeats in several places |
| Extract class           | A class has two groups of fields used separately |
| Replace magic value with constant | A literal appears more than once      |
| Inline                  | An abstraction adds no clarity                    |

```java
// BEFORE: one method doing four things, with a comment per section.
public Invoice generate(Order order) {
    // calculate subtotal
    BigDecimal subtotal = BigDecimal.ZERO;
    for (OrderLine line : order.lines()) {
        subtotal = subtotal.add(line.price().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(line.qty())));
    }
    // apply discount
    if (order.customer().tier() == Tier.PREMIUM) { subtotal = subtotal.multiply(...); }
    // add tax
    BigDecimal tax = subtotal.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.21"));
    ...
}

// AFTER: each comment became a method name. Nothing else changed.
public Invoice generate(Order order) {
    Money subtotal = subtotalOf(order);
    Money discounted = applyDiscount(subtotal, order.customer());
    Money tax = taxOn(discounted);
    return new Invoice(discounted.plus(tax), tax);
}
```

**Refactor toward a goal, not in general.** "Tidy this up" produces endless
churn. "Make it possible to add a second payment provider" produces an adapter
and then stops.

**The strangler pattern** handles the case where a component is too large to
change safely: rather than rewriting it, route new behaviour to a new
implementation and shrink the old one over time.

```text
  Step 1   new code calls an interface; the old implementation sits behind it
  Step 2   a second implementation handles one case; route that case to it
  Step 3   move cases across one at a time, each with tests
  Step 4   the old implementation handles nothing; delete it
```

**Know when not to refactor.** Code that works, is rarely touched, and nobody
needs to understand is not costing anything. The justification for changing it
is a change you need to make, and the boy scout rule, leaving code slightly
better than you found it, applies to the file you were already editing.

**Measure whether it helped.** Cyclomatic complexity, class length, and coupling
are crude but directional. The better signal is how long the next change takes.

> Key Takeaways
> - Refactoring improves structure while behaviour stays identical.
> - Without tests it is not refactoring; write characterisation tests first.
> - A characterisation test records current behaviour, including bugs.
> - Work in small steps with tests and a commit after each one.
> - Extract method, rename, and introduce parameter object do most of the work.
> - Use the IDE's mechanical refactorings rather than editing by hand.
> - Refactor toward a specific goal so the work has an end.
> - Strangle large components incrementally rather than rewriting them.
> - Leave untouched, working, rarely read code alone.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write characterisation tests for a method you do not fully understand,
>    discovering the expected values by running it.
> 2. Take a forty-line method and extract one method per comment, running tests
>    after each extraction.
> 3. Find three parameters that always appear together and introduce a parameter
>    object.
> 4. Replace a repeated `switch` on an enum with polymorphism and compare the
>    diff sizes.
> 5. Interview: You are asked to add a feature to a 900-line untested class.
>    Describe your first two steps. (Hint: what must exist before any structural
>    change is safe?)

#### Code Review Practices

A code review is the last point at which a defect is cheap to fix, and chapter
15's table on defect cost makes that concrete. It is also the main way knowledge
spreads through a team, and the main way standards are either upheld or quietly
abandoned.

**What review is for, in priority order:**

```text
  1. Correctness           does it do what it claims, including edge cases?
  2. Security              can it be abused?  (18.4)
  3. Design fit            does it belong here, at this layer?  (19.1)
  4. Maintainability       will the next person understand it?
  5. Tests                 do they test behaviour, and would they catch a
                           regression?  (15.1)
  6. Style                 should be automated, not discussed
```

The last line matters: **arguing about formatting in a review is a process
failure**. A formatter and a linter in the build settle it, and the review
covers what tools cannot.

**What a reviewer should actually look for**, beyond reading the diff:

| Question                                        | Chapter |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| Are transaction boundaries at the business operation? | 16.3 |
| Could this query be N+1?                         | 16.4    |
| Is the `@Transactional` method self-invoked?      | 17.2    |
| Are entities leaking into the API?               | 18.3    |
| Is input from outside parameterised?             | 16.2    |
| Are errors leaking internal detail?              | 18.3    |
| Is a singleton holding mutable state?            | 17.1    |
| Does the test assert behaviour or implementation? | 15.1   |

**Write comments that are specific, kind, and actionable.** The difference is
not politeness for its own sake; vague or hostile comments produce defensive
authors and worse outcomes.

```text
  Unhelpful                            Helpful
  ---------                            -------
  "This is wrong."                     "If `lines` is empty, `get(0)` throws.
                                        Should an empty order be rejected in
                                        the factory instead?"

  "Why did you do it this way?"        "I'd expect the transaction to start in
                                        the service rather than here, so the
                                        two saves are atomic. Is there a reason
                                        it's in the controller?"

  "Use a stream."                      "Optional: a stream would read more
                                        directly here. Happy either way."
```

**Label the severity**, so the author knows what blocks the merge.

```text
  blocking:     must change before merge      a bug, a security issue
  suggestion:   worth doing, author decides    a clearer name, a simpler loop
  nit:          trivial, never blocking        a typo in a comment
  question:     I do not understand yet        genuinely asking
  praise:       this is good                   worth saying, and rarely said
```

**For authors**, the reviewable pull request is a skill of its own.

- **Keep it small.** Review quality collapses above roughly 400 lines. A 2,000
  line pull request receives "looks good to me" because thorough review is
  impossible.
- **One concern per change.** A refactor mixed with a feature hides the feature.
- **Write the description the reviewer needs**: what changed, why, how it was
  tested, and anything you are unsure about.
- **Respond to every comment**, even if only to say you disagree and why.
- **Separate mechanical changes.** A rename touching 60 files should be its own
  commit so the real change is visible.

```text
  Pull request description that works
  -----------------------------------
  What: adds cancellation to the order API.
  Why:  support asked for it; see TICKET-482.
  How:  Order.cancel enforces the PENDING rule; the controller maps the
        exception to 409 via the existing advice.
  Tests: unit tests for the rule, a slice test for the 409 mapping.
  Unsure about: whether cancellation should publish an event. Opinions welcome.
```

**Review your own diff first.** Reading the change as a stranger catches a
surprising share of the comments a reviewer would otherwise write.

> Key Takeaways
> - Review catches defects while they are still cheap and spreads knowledge.
> - Prioritise correctness and security over style, and automate style
>   entirely.
> - Look for the specific hazards earlier chapters named, such as N+1 and
>   self-invocation.
> - Make comments specific and actionable rather than evaluative.
> - Label severity so the author knows what blocks a merge.
> - Keep pull requests small and limited to one concern.
> - Write a description covering what, why, how it was tested, and open
>   questions.
> - Separate mechanical changes from meaningful ones.
> - Read your own diff before requesting review.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Review a pull request and classify each of your comments as blocking,
>    suggestion, nit, or question.
> 2. Rewrite three harsh or vague review comments to be specific and
>    actionable.
> 3. Split a large change you have made into three smaller, independently
>    reviewable ones.
> 4. Build a review checklist for your project from the hazards table above.
> 5. Interview: Why does review quality drop sharply with change size? (Hint:
>    what does a reviewer do when a change is too large to hold in their head?)

#### Version Control Workflow for Java Projects

Version control is where a team's changes meet. The workflow decides how often
they meet, and therefore how painful the meeting is. The single most important
variable is **how long a branch lives before it merges**.

```text
  Long-lived branches                  Short-lived branches
  -------------------                  --------------------
  two weeks of divergence              hours to two days
  large, conflicted merges             small, usually clean merges
  integration risk discovered late     discovered continuously
  reviews are too big to be useful     reviews are small and thorough
```

**The two workflows worth knowing:**

| Workflow      | Shape                                           | Suits                       |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Trunk-based   | Short branches merged to `main` daily; releases from `main` | Continuous delivery, most teams |
| Git flow      | Long-lived `develop`, `release`, and `hotfix` branches | Versioned products with supported releases |

Git flow is widely cited and usually heavier than a web service needs.
Trunk-based development with feature flags is the default for anything deployed
continuously.

```text
  Trunk-based
  -----------
  main   ---o------o------o------o------o--->   always releasable
             \    /  \   /  \   /
              o--o    o-o    o-o                branches live hours, not weeks
```

**Feature flags decouple merging from releasing**, which is what makes short
branches possible for large features. 17.5's conditional properties are exactly
this mechanism.

```java
@Service
public class PricingService {

    private final boolean newEngineEnabled;     // from configuration, 18.2

    public Money price(Order order) {
        // Incomplete work can be merged safely because it is not reachable.
        return newEngineEnabled ? newEngine.price(order) : legacyEngine.price(order);
    }
}
```

**Commit messages are documentation that survives.** The conventional format
separates a summary line from the reasoning.

```text
  Add optimistic locking to order updates

  Two users editing the same order could silently overwrite each other's
  changes because the update did not check the version column.

  Adds a version field to Order and guards the update with it, returning 409
  when the update affects zero rows.

  Refs: TICKET-482
```

The summary line should say what the change does in the imperative, under about
fifty characters. The body explains **why**, which is the part that cannot be
recovered from the diff.

**Rebase versus merge** is a question with a practical answer rather than a
correct one.

| Operation          | Effect                                   | Use for                      |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `git merge`        | Preserves history, adds a merge commit    | Merging a branch into `main` |
| `git rebase`       | Replays commits, producing a linear history | Updating your own unmerged branch |
| Squash merge       | Collapses a branch into one commit        | Keeping `main` readable      |

The one rule that matters: **never rebase a branch someone else has based work
on**, because it rewrites commits they already have.

**Java-specific practicalities:**

```text
  .gitignore
  ----------
  target/                  Maven output
  build/                   Gradle output
  *.class
  .idea/  *.iml            IntelliJ
  .settings/  .classpath   Eclipse
  *.log
  application-local.yml    local overrides with real credentials
```

Never commit build output, and never commit a local configuration file holding
credentials, as 18.2 established.

**Commit the wrapper**, `mvnw` or `gradlew`, so every developer and the CI
server use the same build tool version. This is the same reproducibility
argument as pinning dependency versions in 18.1.

**Protect `main`.** Require a passing build and at least one approval, and
disallow force pushes. A branch that anyone can overwrite is not a source of
truth.

**Tag releases** so a deployed version maps to an exact commit, which is the
first thing you need during an incident and connects directly to 18.5's build
info endpoint.

```bash
git tag -a v1.4.2 -m "Release 1.4.2"
git push origin v1.4.2
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Branch lifetime is the variable that determines merge pain.
> - Trunk-based development with short branches suits continuously deployed
>   services.
> - Feature flags let incomplete work merge safely without being released.
> - A commit message's body should explain why, since the diff already shows
>   what.
> - Rebase your own unmerged branch; never rebase one others have built on.
> - Ignore build output, IDE files, and local configuration holding
>   credentials.
> - Commit the build wrapper so everyone builds with the same tool version.
> - Protect `main` with required checks and reviews, and tag every release.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a feature you would branch for a week and describe how to deliver it
>    in three merges behind a flag.
> 2. Rewrite three commit messages from a project to explain why rather than
>    what.
> 3. Create a conflict deliberately, resolve it with merge, then repeat with
>    rebase and compare the histories.
> 4. Audit a repository's `.gitignore` for anything build-generated or secret
>    that is being tracked.
> 5. Interview: How do feature flags allow a large feature to be merged daily?
>    (Hint: what is the difference between code being present and code being
>    reachable?)

<a id="192-core-language-and-oop-questions"></a>
### 19.2 Core Language and OOP Questions

This subchapter revisits the material of chapters 2 to 5 as interviewers pose
it: what the question is really testing, what a weak answer sounds like, and the
detail that distinguishes someone who has used the feature from someone who has
read about it.

#### Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction

This is the most common opening question in a Java interview, and it is a trap
disguised as a gift. Almost every candidate can recite four definitions, so
reciting them distinguishes nobody. What the interviewer is listening for is
whether you can say **what each one buys you** and give an example from your own
code.

```text
  Weak answer                          Strong answer
  -----------                          -------------
  "Encapsulation is hiding data        "Encapsulation means the object owns its
   using private fields and             invariants. Our Order can only be
   getters and setters."                cancelled while PENDING, and because the
                                        status field is private, no caller can
                                        skip that check."
```

**Encapsulation** is about controlling change, not about hiding data. Getters
and setters for every field is not encapsulation; it is a public field with
extra typing.

```java
// NOT encapsulated: the invariant is unprotected despite the private field.
public class Order {
    private OrderStatus status;
    public void setStatus(OrderStatus s) { this.status = s; }   // any value, any time
}

// Encapsulated: the class controls its own transitions.
public class Order {
    private OrderStatus status;

    public void cancel(String reason) {
        if (status != OrderStatus.PENDING) {
            throw new OrderNotCancellableException(id, status);
        }
        this.status = OrderStatus.CANCELLED;
    }
}
```

**Inheritance** expresses that one type **is a** specialisation of another and
can be used wherever the parent is expected. The strong answer mentions that it
is the most overused mechanism in object-oriented programming, and that
composition is usually better.

```java
// WRONG: Stack is not a kind of ArrayList. Inheriting exposes add(index, e),
// remove(index), and set(index, e), all of which break stack semantics.
public class Stack<E> extends ArrayList<E> { }

// RIGHT: composition exposes exactly the stack operations.
public class Stack<E> {
    private final List<E> items = new ArrayList<>();      // HAS a list
    public void push(E item) { items.add(item); }
    public E pop() { ... }
}
```

The test is the **Liskov substitution principle**: if code written against the
parent breaks when given the child, the inheritance is wrong.

**Polymorphism** means one call site invoking different implementations
depending on the runtime type. The detail that separates a strong answer is
knowing there are two kinds, and that Java resolves them at different times.

| Kind                          | Also called          | Resolved at  |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------ |
| Overriding                    | Runtime polymorphism | Runtime, by the object's actual type |
| Overloading                   | Compile-time polymorphism | Compile time, by the declared types |

```java
List<Shape> shapes = List.of(new Circle(2), new Square(3));

for (Shape shape : shapes) {
    // The compiler knows only Shape. The JVM dispatches on the real class.
    System.out.println(shape.area());
}
```

The practical value is the open-closed principle: adding a `Triangle` requires
no change to the loop.

**Abstraction** means exposing what something does while hiding how. The strong
answer distinguishes it from encapsulation, because the two are routinely
conflated.

```text
  Abstraction      hides COMPLEXITY     "what can I do with this?"
                   an interface, an abstract class, a well-named method

  Encapsulation    hides STATE          "who is allowed to change this?"
                   private fields, controlled mutation
```

```java
// Abstraction: callers know the capability, not the mechanism.
public interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request);
}
// Whether it calls Stripe over HTTPS or writes to a file is not their concern.
```

**Prepare one example from your own work for each**, because "give me an example
from a project you worked on" is the standard follow-up and generic examples
land poorly.

> Key Takeaways
> - Reciting definitions distinguishes nobody; explain what each principle buys.
> - Encapsulation protects invariants, and a setter for every field defeats it.
> - Inheritance means "is a" and must satisfy Liskov substitution.
> - Composition is usually the better default; be ready to say why.
> - Polymorphism lets one call site serve many types, which is what makes code
>   open to extension.
> - Overriding resolves at runtime; overloading resolves at compile time.
> - Abstraction hides complexity, encapsulation hides state; keep them
>   distinct.
> - Have a concrete example from your own code ready for each.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with getters and setters for every field, then rewrite it so
>    it enforces one invariant, and list what the caller can no longer do.
> 2. Find an inheritance relationship in any codebase that violates Liskov
>    substitution and convert it to composition.
> 3. Explain each of the four principles in two sentences using one example from
>    your own project.
> 4. Interview: Is encapsulation the same as making fields private? (Hint:
>    consider a private field with a public setter that accepts any value.)

#### Abstract Classes versus Interfaces

This question tests whether you understand that since Java 8 the two have
converged considerably, and that the remaining differences are about **state and
constructors**, not about method bodies.

The answer that dates a candidate is "interfaces cannot have implementations",
which has been false since Java 8.

| Feature                    | Abstract class      | Interface                    |
| -------------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Instance fields             | Yes                 | No, only `public static final` |
| Constructors                | Yes                 | No                            |
| Method implementations      | Yes                 | Yes, `default` and `static`   |
| `private` methods           | Yes                 | Yes, since Java 9             |
| Access modifiers on methods | Any                 | `public` unless `private`     |
| How many can a class have   | One                 | Many                          |
| Purpose                     | Shared implementation and state | A capability contract |

**The decisive differences are the first two rows and the second to last.** An
abstract class can hold state and run constructor logic; an interface cannot. A
class can implement many interfaces but extend one class.

```java
// ABSTRACT CLASS: shared state and construction, plus a template method.
public abstract class HttpClient {

    private final Duration timeout;             // state: interfaces cannot do this
    private int requestCount;

    protected HttpClient(Duration timeout) {    // a constructor: nor this
        this.timeout = timeout;
    }

    // Template method: the algorithm is fixed, one step varies.
    public final Response send(Request request) {
        requestCount++;
        log(request);
        Response response = doSend(request, timeout);   // subclass supplies this
        log(response);
        return response;
    }

    protected abstract Response doSend(Request request, Duration timeout);
}
```

```java
// INTERFACE: a capability, implementable alongside others.
public interface Retryable {
    int maxAttempts();

    default boolean shouldRetry(Exception e) {   // a shared default, no state
        return e instanceof TransientException;
    }
}

public interface Cacheable {
    Duration cacheDuration();
}

// A class can declare several capabilities; it could extend only one class.
public class ProductClient extends HttpClient implements Retryable, Cacheable { }
```

**The rule of thumb:** use an interface to describe **what something can do**,
and an abstract class to share **how a family of things does it**. When in
doubt, start with an interface, because it leaves the single inheritance slot
free.

**`default` methods exist for a specific reason**, and knowing it is a good
signal. They were added in Java 8 so that `Collection` could gain `stream()` and
`forEach()` without breaking every existing implementation in the world.

```java
// Adding this to an interface does not break existing implementors.
public interface Collection<E> {
    default Stream<E> stream() {
        return StreamSupport.stream(spliterator(), false);
    }
}
```

They are a mechanism for **interface evolution**, not a way to build a base
class in disguise.

**The diamond problem** is a likely follow-up. Java permits multiple interface
inheritance, so two interfaces can supply the same default method, and the
compiler forces you to resolve it.

```java
interface A { default String greet() { return "A"; } }
interface B { default String greet() { return "B"; } }

class C implements A, B {
    @Override
    public String greet() {
        return A.super.greet();     // the explicit syntax for choosing one
    }                               // without this, the class does not compile
}
```

A class's implementation always wins over an interface default, and a more
specific interface wins over a less specific one.

> Key Takeaways
> - Since Java 8 interfaces can have implementations, so that is not the
>   difference.
> - Abstract classes hold instance state and have constructors; interfaces do
>   not.
> - A class extends one class but implements many interfaces.
> - Use interfaces for capability and abstract classes for shared
>   implementation.
> - Prefer an interface when unsure, to leave the inheritance slot available.
> - `default` methods exist to evolve interfaces without breaking implementors.
> - Conflicting defaults must be resolved explicitly with `A.super.method()`.
> - A class implementation beats an interface default.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an abstract class with a template method and two subclasses that vary
>    one step.
> 2. Define two interfaces with the same default method, implement both, and
>    resolve the conflict.
> 3. Take an abstract class with no state and convert it to an interface, noting
>    what changes.
> 4. Interview: Why were default methods added to Java 8, given that abstract
>    classes already existed? (Hint: what would adding `stream()` to
>    `Collection` have done to every existing implementation?)

#### Overloading versus Overriding

These two words sound similar and describe unrelated mechanisms. The question
tests precision, and the best way to demonstrate it is to name **when each is
resolved**, because that single fact explains every behaviour that follows.

| Aspect            | Overloading                      | Overriding                     |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Where             | Same class or a subclass          | Subclass, for an inherited method |
| Signature         | Must differ in parameters         | Must be identical               |
| Return type       | May differ                        | Same, or a covariant subtype    |
| Access            | May differ                        | Cannot be more restrictive      |
| Exceptions        | May differ freely                 | No new or broader checked exceptions |
| Resolved          | Compile time, by declared types   | Runtime, by the actual object   |
| Also called       | Static or compile-time binding    | Dynamic or runtime binding      |

**The classic demonstration** shows both in one snippet.

```java
class Parent {
    void greet() { System.out.println("Parent"); }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void greet() { System.out.println("Child"); }      // OVERRIDING

    void greet(String name) { System.out.println("Hi " + name); }   // OVERLOADING
}

Parent p = new Child();
p.greet();          // "Child": dispatched on the RUNTIME type
// p.greet("Ada");  // does not compile: Parent has no such method
```

The declared type decides **which methods exist**; the runtime type decides
**which implementation runs**.

**The trap question** almost always involves overload resolution with `null` or
with an inheritance hierarchy.

```java
class Printer {
    void print(Object o)  { System.out.println("Object"); }
    void print(String s)  { System.out.println("String"); }
    void print(Integer i) { System.out.println("Integer"); }
}

new Printer().print(null);        // prints "String"
```

The compiler picks the **most specific applicable** overload. `String` and
`Integer` are both more specific than `Object`, and since neither is a subtype
of the other the call would be ambiguous, except that here it compiles only
because... in fact with both `String` and `Integer` present this is a compile
error, and with only `Object` and `String` it selects `String`. The lesson to
state in an interview is that **overloading with null arguments is ambiguous by
design and should be avoided**, with an explicit cast when it cannot be.

```java
printer.print((Object) null);     // unambiguous, and honest about the intent
```

**Overriding has four rules**, and `@Override` enforces all of them.

```java
class Parent {
    protected Number compute() throws IOException { return 1; }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    public Integer compute() {        // wider access: allowed
        return 42;                     // covariant return: allowed
    }                                  // fewer exceptions: allowed
}
```

```java
class Broken extends Parent {
    @Override
    private Number compute() { ... }        // ERROR: narrower access
    @Override
    Number compute() throws Exception { }    // ERROR: broader checked exception
}
```

**Always write `@Override`.** It is not decoration: it turns a silent failure
into a compile error.

```java
class Order {
    // Intended to override Object.equals, but the parameter type is wrong,
    // so this OVERLOADS instead. Collections will never call it.
    public boolean equals(Order other) { ... }      // silent bug

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Order other) { ... }      // now a compile error
}
```

**Static methods are hidden, not overridden**, which is a favourite follow-up.

```java
class Parent { static String name() { return "Parent"; } }
class Child extends Parent { static String name() { return "Child"; } }

Parent p = new Child();
System.out.println(p.name());          // "Parent": resolved by the DECLARED type
```

Static methods belong to the class, so there is no dynamic dispatch. Private and
final methods likewise cannot be overridden, which is exactly the mechanism
behind 17.2's proxy limitations.

> Key Takeaways
> - Overloading differs in parameters and resolves at compile time.
> - Overriding replaces an inherited implementation and resolves at runtime.
> - The declared type determines which methods exist; the runtime type
>   determines which runs.
> - An override may widen access, return a covariant type, and throw fewer
>   checked exceptions.
> - Always write `@Override`, which turns a mistyped signature into a compile
>   error.
> - Overload resolution with `null` is ambiguous; cast explicitly or avoid it.
> - Static methods are hidden by the declared type, not overridden.
> - Private and final methods cannot be overridden, which is why proxies cannot
>   advise them.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with three overloads and predict which one a `null` argument
>    selects, then check.
> 2. Create an `equals` method taking the concrete type and show that a
>    `HashSet` ignores it.
> 3. Demonstrate that a static method is resolved by the declared type, not the
>    object.
> 4. Attempt an override that narrows access and read the compiler error.
> 5. Interview: Why does `@Override` matter if the code compiles without it?
>    (Hint: what happens when you misspell the method name or get a parameter
>    type wrong?)

#### The equals and hashCode Contract

This question is asked constantly because it has a right answer, it is easy to
get wrong, and getting it wrong produces bugs that look like the collections
library is broken.

**The contract** is three rules for `equals` and one linking it to `hashCode`.

```text
  equals must be:
    reflexive     x.equals(x) is true
    symmetric     x.equals(y) == y.equals(x)
    transitive    x.equals(y) and y.equals(z) implies x.equals(z)
    consistent    repeated calls return the same result if nothing changed
    null-safe     x.equals(null) is false

  hashCode must be:
    consistent with equals    equal objects MUST have equal hash codes
                              unequal objects MAY share a hash code
```

**Why the link matters** is the part worth explaining rather than reciting.
Hash-based collections find a bucket from the hash code and only then compare
with `equals`. If two equal objects hash differently, they land in different
buckets and the comparison never happens.

```text
  Overriding equals but not hashCode
  ----------------------------------
  a = new Point(1,2)   hashCode 12345   ->  bucket 5
  b = new Point(1,2)   hashCode 98765   ->  bucket 9      a.equals(b) is true

  set.add(a); set.contains(b)  ->  looks in bucket 9, finds nothing  ->  FALSE
```

```java
// The broken version: equal objects, but a HashSet holds both.
Set<Point> points = new HashSet<>();
points.add(new Point(1, 2));
points.add(new Point(1, 2));
System.out.println(points.size());     // 2, with equals overridden but not hashCode
```

**The correct implementation** is mechanical.

```java
public final class Point {

    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                    // cheap identity shortcut
        if (!(o instanceof Point other)) return false; // also handles null
        return x == other.x && y == other.y;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(x, y);      // must use the SAME fields as equals
    }
}
```

**Records do this for you**, which is the modern answer and worth giving.

```java
// equals, hashCode, and toString are generated from the components.
public record Point(int x, int y) { }
```

**The mutability trap** is the strongest follow-up to prepare for. Mutating a
field used in `hashCode` after inserting into a hash collection makes the object
unfindable, including by itself.

```java
Set<MutablePoint> set = new HashSet<>();
MutablePoint p = new MutablePoint(1, 2);
set.add(p);                         // stored in the bucket for hash(1,2)

p.setX(99);                         // the hash changes; the bucket does not

set.contains(p);                    // false: looks in the bucket for hash(99,2)
set.remove(p);                      // fails; the element is now unreachable
```

The rule that follows: **hash-based keys should be immutable**, or at least the
fields used in `hashCode` should be.

**`instanceof` versus `getClass()`** is the subtle design question.

| Approach     | Behaviour                                             |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `getClass()` | A subclass is never equal to its parent; symmetry is guaranteed |
| `instanceof` | A subclass may equal its parent, which can break symmetry |

```java
// The symmetry break with instanceof and an extended subclass:
Point p = new Point(1, 2);
ColourPoint c = new ColourPoint(1, 2, RED);

p.equals(c);     // true:  Point's equals only compares x and y
c.equals(p);     // false: ColourPoint's equals also compares colour
```

There is no clean fix, which is why the practical advice is to **make value
classes final**, or use composition rather than extending them.

**A note on `hashCode` quality.** Returning a constant is technically legal and
correct, and turns every hash map into a linked list, degrading lookups from
constant to linear time.

> Key Takeaways
> - `equals` must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and
>   null-safe.
> - Equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal ones may collide.
> - Hash collections locate a bucket by hash first, so a wrong hash makes equal
>   objects unfindable.
> - Override both or neither, using exactly the same fields in each.
> - Records generate correct implementations from their components.
> - Mutating a field used in `hashCode` after insertion makes the element
>   unreachable.
> - Keys in hash-based collections should be immutable.
> - `instanceof` risks breaking symmetry with subclasses; making value classes
>   final avoids it.
> - A constant `hashCode` is correct and degrades lookups to linear time.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class overriding only `equals`, add two equal instances to a
>    `HashSet`, and explain the size.
> 2. Add a correct `hashCode` and confirm the behaviour changes.
> 3. Insert a mutable object into a `HashSet`, change a hashed field, and try to
>    remove it.
> 4. Implement `equals` with `instanceof` in a parent and a subclass, and
>    demonstrate the symmetry violation.
> 5. Replace a hand-written value class with a record and compare the generated
>    behaviour.
> 6. Interview: What happens if `hashCode` always returns 1? (Hint: it is
>    correct; what does it do to the performance of a map with a million
>    entries?)

#### String Immutability and the String Pool

Strings are the most-used type in Java, and the questions about them test
whether you understand object identity, memory, and why `==` fails in a way
that surprises beginners.

**Strings are immutable**, meaning every apparent modification creates a new
object.

```java
String s = "hello";
s.toUpperCase();                    // creates "HELLO" and DISCARDS it
System.out.println(s);              // "hello": s never changed

s = s.toUpperCase();                // reassigning the reference is the only way
```

**Why immutability was chosen** is the interesting part, and there are four
reasons worth naming.

| Reason           | Explanation                                                |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Caching the hash | `hashCode` is computed once and stored, making strings fast map keys |
| Thread safety    | No synchronisation needed; an immutable object cannot race  |
| Security         | A file path or a connection string cannot be altered after a check |
| Pooling          | Identical literals can safely share one object              |

The security point is concrete: if strings were mutable, code could pass a
validated path to a method and another thread could change it between the check
and the use.

**The string pool** is a region where the JVM keeps one copy of each distinct
literal.

```text
  String a = "hello";          ---+
  String b = "hello";          ---+--> the SAME object in the pool
  String c = new String("hello");  --> a NEW object on the heap

     pool                 heap
     +---------+          +---------+
     | "hello" | <--a,b   | "hello" | <--c
     +---------+          +---------+

  a == b   true    (same pooled object)
  a == c   false   (different objects)
  a.equals(c)  true  (same contents)
```

```java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");
String d = c.intern();              // returns the pooled instance

System.out.println(a == b);         // true
System.out.println(a == c);         // false
System.out.println(a == d);         // true
System.out.println(a.equals(c));    // true
```

**This is why `==` must never be used to compare strings**, and it is the
practical point the question is really about. It sometimes works, for pooled
literals, which makes the bug intermittent and therefore worse.

**Compile-time constants are folded**, which produces another surprising
comparison.

```java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hel" + "lo";            // folded by the compiler into "hello"
System.out.println(a == b);         // true

String part = "hel";
String c = part + "lo";             // computed at runtime: a new object
System.out.println(a == c);         // false

final String constPart = "hel";     // a compile-time constant
String d = constPart + "lo";        // folded again
System.out.println(a == d);         // true
```

**Concatenation in a loop** is the performance question that follows.

```java
// BAD: each += creates a new String and copies everything. O(n^2).
String result = "";
for (String word : words) {
    result += word;                 // 10,000 words: ~50,000,000 character copies
}

// GOOD: one resizable buffer, appended in place. O(n).
StringBuilder builder = new StringBuilder();
for (String word : words) {
    builder.append(word);
}
String result = builder.toString();
```

The compiler optimises a single concatenation expression into a `StringBuilder`,
but it cannot do so across loop iterations, which is why the loop is the case
that matters.

| Class           | Mutable | Thread-safe | Use when                        |
| --------------- | ------- | ----------- | ------------------------------- |
| `String`        | No      | Yes         | Values, keys, anything shared    |
| `StringBuilder` | Yes     | No          | Building a string in one thread  |
| `StringBuffer`  | Yes     | Yes         | Legacy; almost never needed      |

**A security note worth mentioning** if passwords come up: because strings are
immutable and pooled, a password in a `String` stays in memory until garbage
collection and can appear in a heap dump. `char[]` can be overwritten
explicitly, which is why `Console.readPassword` returns one.

> Key Takeaways
> - Strings are immutable; every apparent change creates a new object.
> - Immutability enables hash caching, thread safety, security, and pooling.
> - The pool holds one instance per distinct literal, so literals share
>   identity.
> - `new String(...)` always creates a distinct object; `intern()` returns the
>   pooled one.
> - Never compare strings with `==`, because it works often enough to hide the
>   bug.
> - The compiler folds constant concatenations, which affects identity
>   comparisons.
> - Concatenating in a loop is quadratic; use `StringBuilder`.
> - Passwords belong in `char[]`, which can be cleared, not in `String`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Predict the result of five `==` comparisons among literals, `new String`,
>    and `intern`, then verify each.
> 2. Time string concatenation against `StringBuilder` for 50,000 appends.
> 3. Show that a compile-time constant concatenation is pooled and a runtime one
>    is not.
> 4. Explain why a `String` used as a `HashMap` key is efficient, referring to
>    hash caching.
> 5. Interview: Why does comparing strings with `==` sometimes work? (Hint: what
>    does the compiler do with two identical literals in the same class?)

#### Checked versus Unchecked Exception Scenarios

Java is nearly alone in having checked exceptions, and interviewers use the
topic to see whether you have an opinion informed by experience rather than a
memorised rule.

```text
  Throwable
  |
  +-- Error                     unchecked   JVM-level, do not catch
  |     OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError
  |
  +-- Exception                 CHECKED     must be declared or handled
        |   IOException, SQLException
        |
        +-- RuntimeException    unchecked   need not be declared
              NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException,
              IllegalStateException
```

**The intended distinction**: checked exceptions represent conditions a
reasonable caller might recover from, and unchecked ones represent programming
errors.

| Situation                          | Kind       | Why                             |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------- |
| A file does not exist               | Checked    | The caller can prompt or retry   |
| A network connection drops          | Checked    | The caller can retry             |
| A method argument is null           | Unchecked  | A bug in the calling code        |
| An index is out of bounds           | Unchecked  | A bug                            |
| An object is in the wrong state     | Unchecked  | A bug                            |
| The heap is exhausted               | Error      | Nothing useful can be done       |

**The criticism is real and you should be able to articulate it.** Checked
exceptions produce two common failures.

```java
// 1. The empty catch: the exception is silenced and the program continues
//    in an unknown state. This is the worst thing in the language.
try {
    process(file);
} catch (IOException e) {
    // ignore
}

// 2. Signature pollution: the exception propagates up through five layers,
//    each of which must declare it, coupling them all to an implementation
//    detail of the bottom one.
public void handleRequest() throws IOException, SQLException, ParseException { }
```

This is why Spring wraps `SQLException` into unchecked `DataAccessException`, as
17.3 described, and why most modern Java frameworks and libraries prefer
unchecked exceptions.

**The defence is also real**: a checked exception is a documented part of the
contract that the compiler will not let you ignore silently. The balanced answer
is that checked exceptions are appropriate at the boundary of a library where
recovery is genuinely expected, and a burden everywhere else.

**Wrapping, done correctly**, preserves the cause.

```java
// GOOD: translate to a domain exception, keeping the original for diagnosis.
public Config load(Path path) {
    try {
        return parse(Files.readString(path));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new ConfigLoadException("cannot read " + path, e);  // cause preserved
    }
}

// BAD: the stack trace of the real failure is lost forever.
} catch (IOException e) {
    throw new ConfigLoadException("cannot read config");          // no cause
}
```

**Three rules that come up as follow-ups:**

**`finally` runs even when the `try` returns**, and a `return` inside `finally`
discards the exception entirely.

```java
try {
    return compute();           // the value is evaluated, then finally runs
} finally {
    cleanup();                  // runs before the method actually returns
}

// NEVER do this: it swallows any exception from the try block.
try {
    throw new IllegalStateException();
} finally {
    return 42;                  // the exception vanishes silently
}
```

**`try`-with-resources replaces `finally` for anything closeable**, and handles
suppressed exceptions correctly, as 16.1 covered in detail.

**Catch the specific type, and order from specific to general.**

```java
try {
    ...
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {      // most specific first
    ...
} catch (IOException e) {                // broader
    ...
}
// Reversing these does not compile: the second would be unreachable.
```

**Never catch `Throwable` or `Error`.** Catching `OutOfMemoryError` and
continuing leaves a JVM that cannot be trusted; 18.5's `ExitOnOutOfMemoryError`
is the correct response.

> Key Takeaways
> - Checked exceptions are declared and enforced; runtime exceptions and errors
>   are not.
> - The intent is recoverable conditions versus programming bugs.
> - Checked exceptions cause empty catch blocks and signature pollution in
>   practice.
> - Modern frameworks translate them to unchecked exceptions at a boundary.
> - Always preserve the cause when wrapping, or the diagnosis is lost.
> - `finally` runs even on return, and returning from it discards exceptions.
> - Use `try`-with-resources for anything closeable.
> - Catch specific types first; never catch `Throwable` or `Error`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method that wraps an `IOException` in a domain exception with and
>    without the cause, and compare the stack traces.
> 2. Demonstrate that a `return` inside `finally` swallows an exception.
> 3. Take a method declaring three checked exceptions and redesign its
>    signature.
> 4. List five exceptions from the standard library and classify each as checked
>    or unchecked, explaining why.
> 5. Interview: Argue both for and against checked exceptions in thirty seconds
>    each. (Hint: one side is about the compiler enforcing a contract, the other
>    about what developers actually write in the catch block.)

#### Static, final, and Initialization Order

These keywords appear in almost every class, and the questions about them are
usually puzzles: given this code, what prints, and in what order? Answering
requires a model of when the JVM does what.

**`static` means the member belongs to the class**, not to an instance. There is
one copy, shared by every instance and accessible without one.

```java
public class Counter {
    private static int totalCreated;      // one, shared
    private final int id;                 // one per instance

    public Counter() { this.id = ++totalCreated; }
}
```

**`final` means the binding cannot be reassigned**, which is different from the
object being immutable. This distinction is the most common misunderstanding.

```java
final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ada");                    // fine: the LIST is mutable
names = new ArrayList<>();           // compile error: the REFERENCE is final
```

| Applied to | Meaning                                          |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Variable   | Can be assigned once                              |
| Field      | Must be assigned in the declaration or constructor |
| Method     | Cannot be overridden (and so cannot be proxied, 17.2) |
| Class      | Cannot be extended                                |
| Parameter  | Cannot be reassigned inside the method            |

**Initialization order** is the mechanism the puzzle questions test. It runs in
two phases, and the static phase happens once, when the class is first used.

```text
  CLASS loading (once, on first use)
    1. static fields set to defaults (0, false, null)
    2. static field initialisers and static blocks, IN SOURCE ORDER

  INSTANCE creation (every new)
    3. instance fields set to defaults
    4. the constructor implicitly calls super(...)
       -> the PARENT's steps 3 to 6 complete first
    5. instance field initialisers and instance blocks, IN SOURCE ORDER
    6. the constructor body
```

```java
public class Parent {
    static { System.out.println("1 parent static"); }
    { System.out.println("3 parent instance"); }
    Parent() { System.out.println("4 parent constructor"); }
}

public class Child extends Parent {
    static { System.out.println("2 child static"); }
    { System.out.println("5 child instance"); }
    Child() {
        // super() is implicit here and runs FIRST
        System.out.println("6 child constructor");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Child();
    }
}
// 1 parent static
// 2 child static
// 3 parent instance
// 4 parent constructor
// 5 child instance
// 6 child constructor
```

**The dangerous consequence** is that a parent constructor runs before the
child's fields are initialised, so calling an overridable method from a
constructor sees uninitialised state.

```java
class Parent {
    Parent() { init(); }                      // calls the OVERRIDDEN method
    void init() { }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    void init() {
        items.add("first");                   // NullPointerException:
    }                                         // items is still null here
}
```

The rule: **never call an overridable method from a constructor.**

**`static final` constants are special.** A `static final` primitive or `String`
initialised with a compile-time constant is inlined at the call site, which
means a dependent class must be recompiled when it changes.

```java
public class Config {
    public static final int VERSION = 1;       // inlined into callers
    public static final int TIMEOUT = readTimeout();   // NOT inlined: runtime value
}
```

**Static initialisers can fail**, producing an error that confuses people the
first time they meet it.

```java
static {
    RESOURCE = loadOrThrow();     // if this throws, the class fails to initialise
}
// The first access throws ExceptionInInitializerError; every LATER access
// throws NoClassDefFoundError, which hides the original cause.
```

**Static mutable state is a design problem**, worth saying explicitly since it
connects to 17.1's scope discussion: it is shared across threads without
synchronisation, it makes tests order-dependent, and it cannot be substituted.

> Key Takeaways
> - `static` members belong to the class, with one copy shared by all
>   instances.
> - `final` prevents reassignment of the reference, not mutation of the object.
> - Static initialisation runs once, on first use, in source order.
> - Instance initialisation runs the parent's chain fully before the child's
>   fields.
> - Never call an overridable method from a constructor; subclass fields are not
>   yet set.
> - `static final` compile-time constants are inlined into callers.
> - A failed static initialiser throws `ExceptionInInitializerError` once, then
>   `NoClassDefFoundError`.
> - Static mutable state breaks thread safety, testability, and substitution.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the parent and child example above and predict the output before
>    running it.
> 2. Show that a `final` collection field can still be modified.
> 3. Reproduce the constructor calling an overridden method and explain the
>    null.
> 4. Make a static initialiser throw and observe both error types across two
>    accesses.
> 5. Interview: Why is calling an overridable method from a constructor
>    dangerous? (Hint: at that moment, have the subclass's field initialisers
>    run?)

<a id="193-collections-generics-and-streams-questions"></a>
### 19.3 Collections, Generics, and Streams Questions

This subchapter covers the questions drawn from chapters 6 to 8, where
interviewers probe whether you can reason about performance characteristics and
type safety rather than just call the methods.

#### Choosing the Right Collection

"Which collection would you use here?" is a design question wearing a trivia
costume. The interviewer wants to hear you reason from the **access pattern** to
the data structure, not recite that `ArrayList` is backed by an array.

**Start from the questions the data must answer.**

```text
  Do I need key-value lookup?          -> a Map
  Do duplicates matter?                -> Set removes them, List keeps them
  Does order matter, and which order?  -> insertion, sorted, or none
  What operation dominates?            -> random access, insertion, search
  Is it shared between threads?        -> a concurrent implementation
```

| Need                                   | Choice                 | Why                        |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Indexed access, mostly reads            | `ArrayList`            | Contiguous array, O(1) get  |
| Frequent insertion or removal at the ends | `ArrayDeque`         | O(1) at both ends; beats `LinkedList` |
| Unique elements, no order                | `HashSet`              | O(1) contains               |
| Unique elements, insertion order         | `LinkedHashSet`        | O(1) plus a linked list     |
| Unique elements, sorted                  | `TreeSet`              | O(log n), navigable         |
| Key-value, no order                      | `HashMap`              | O(1) average                |
| Key-value, insertion or access order     | `LinkedHashMap`        | Also the basis of an LRU cache |
| Key-value, sorted by key                 | `TreeMap`              | Range queries, `floorKey`   |
| Enum keys                                | `EnumMap`              | Array-backed, very fast     |
| Shared across threads                    | `ConcurrentHashMap`    | Lock-striped, no global lock |
| Priority ordering                        | `PriorityQueue`        | O(log n) insert and poll    |

**The complexity table is worth knowing cold**, because it is asked directly.

| Operation        | `ArrayList` | `LinkedList` | `HashMap` | `TreeMap` |
| ---------------- | ----------- | ------------ | --------- | --------- |
| Get by index      | O(1)        | O(n)          | n/a       | n/a       |
| Get by key        | n/a         | n/a           | O(1) avg  | O(log n)  |
| Add at end        | O(1) amortised | O(1)       | O(1) avg  | O(log n)  |
| Add at front      | O(n)        | O(1)          | n/a       | n/a       |
| Remove by value   | O(n)        | O(n)          | O(1) avg  | O(log n)  |
| Contains          | O(n)        | O(n)          | O(1) avg  | O(log n)  |

**`LinkedList` is almost always the wrong answer**, and saying so shows
experience. Its O(1) insertion requires already holding the node, and reaching
that node is O(n). Every element is a separate object with two pointers, so it
has poor cache locality and much higher memory overhead. `ArrayDeque` beats it
for queue and stack use; `ArrayList` beats it for nearly everything else.

**Sizing matters more than people expect.**

```java
// Each growth copies the entire backing array. Presizing avoids all of it.
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>(expectedCount);

// A HashMap resizes when it passes 75% load. Presize to avoid rehashing.
Map<String, Order> index = new HashMap<>(expectedCount * 4 / 3 + 1);
```

**A worked reasoning example**, which is the shape of answer to give:

```text
  "I need to keep the 100 most recent events per user and look one up by id."

  -> lookup by id           a Map
  -> bounded, evict oldest  access-ordered LinkedHashMap with removeEldestEntry
  -> shared across threads?  if yes, wrap or use a purpose-built cache
```

```java
// An LRU cache in six lines, which is a common follow-up exercise.
public class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {

    private final int capacity;

    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);          // true = ACCESS order, not insertion
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity;        // evict the least recently accessed
    }
}
```

**Immutable collections** should be the default for anything you return.

```java
List<String> fixed = List.of("a", "b");          // immutable, rejects nulls
List<String> copy = List.copyOf(mutableList);    // a snapshot, not a view

// Collections.unmodifiableList returns a VIEW: the backing list can still change.
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutableList);
```

Returning an internal mutable collection lets callers modify your object's
state, which defeats the encapsulation of 19.2.

> Key Takeaways
> - Reason from the access pattern to the structure, not from memorised
>   descriptions.
> - `ArrayList` for indexed access, `ArrayDeque` for ends, `HashMap` for
>   lookup.
> - `LinkedList` is rarely correct: reaching a node is O(n) and locality is
>   poor.
> - `LinkedHashMap` preserves order and, in access order, implements an LRU
>   cache.
> - `TreeMap` and `TreeSet` add ordering and range queries at O(log n).
> - Presize collections when the count is known to avoid repeated copying.
> - Return immutable collections; `List.copyOf` snapshots while
>   `unmodifiableList` is a view.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Choose a collection for five described scenarios and justify each in one
>    sentence.
> 2. Benchmark `ArrayList` against `LinkedList` for 100,000 random-index reads.
> 3. Implement an LRU cache with `LinkedHashMap` and test the eviction order.
> 4. Show that `Collections.unmodifiableList` is a view by mutating the backing
>    list.
> 5. Interview: When would you genuinely choose `LinkedList`? (Hint: think about
>    whether you already hold the node, and whether `ArrayDeque` covers the case
>    anyway.)

#### HashMap Internals and Collision Handling

This is the deepest question routinely asked about collections, and it is
popular because it connects `hashCode`, data structures, and performance in one
answer.

**The structure is an array of buckets.** A key's hash selects a bucket; the
bucket holds the entries whose keys landed there.

```text
  map.put("Ada", 1)
      |
      +-- h = key.hashCode()
      +-- h = h ^ (h >>> 16)          spread the high bits into the low ones
      +-- index = h & (capacity - 1)  cheap modulo, since capacity is a power of 2
      |
      v
   table
   [0] -> null
   [1] -> ("Ada",1)
   [2] -> null
   [3] -> ("Bob",2) -> ("Eve",5)      a collision: two keys, one bucket
   ...
```

**The hash spreading step matters.** Because the index uses only the low bits,
two hash codes differing only in their high bits would collide constantly.
Exclusive-oring the high sixteen bits down mixes them in, cheaply.

**Collision handling has two modes**, and knowing the threshold is the detail
interviewers look for.

| Entries in one bucket | Structure    | Lookup within the bucket |
| --------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------ |
| Up to 8               | Linked list   | O(n)                     |
| 9 or more, table >= 64 | Red-black tree | O(log n)                |
| Back down to 6        | Reverts to a list | O(n)                 |

```text
  Before treeification            After treeification
  --------------------            -------------------
  [3] -> A -> B -> C -> ...       [3] ->      D
         (9 entries, O(n))                  /   \
                                           B     F
                                          / \   / \
                                         A  C  E   G     O(log n)
```

Treeification was added in Java 8 specifically to bound the damage from hash
collision denial-of-service attacks, where an attacker sends keys chosen to
collide.

**Resizing** happens when the size exceeds capacity times the load factor,
default 0.75.

```text
  capacity 16, load factor 0.75 -> resize at 12 entries
  new capacity 32, every entry rehashed into the larger table

  Cost: O(n) at that moment. Presizing avoids repeated resizes.
```

The 0.75 default is a deliberate balance: lower wastes memory, higher increases
collisions.

**Why keys must be immutable** connects straight back to 19.2's equals contract.

```java
Map<Point, String> map = new HashMap<>();
Point key = new Point(1, 2);
map.put(key, "value");          // stored in bucket for hash(1,2)

key.setX(99);                    // the hash changes; the entry does not move

map.get(key);                    // null: searches the bucket for hash(99,2)
```

**`HashMap` is not thread-safe**, and the failure mode is worth naming: before
Java 8 concurrent resizing could create a cycle in a bucket's linked list,
causing an infinite loop at 100% CPU. Java 8 changed the resize to preserve
order and removed that specific bug, but concurrent use still loses updates and
corrupts state.

| Implementation          | Thread safety              | Cost                      |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `HashMap`               | None                       | Fastest single-threaded    |
