| `Hashtable`             | Every method synchronised   | Legacy; one global lock    |
| `Collections.synchronizedMap` | Wrapper with one lock | Serialises all access     |
| `ConcurrentHashMap`     | Per-bin locking, lock-free reads | The correct choice   |

**`ConcurrentHashMap` differences** worth mentioning: it rejects null keys and
values, because a null return would be ambiguous between "absent" and "mapped to
null" in a concurrent setting, and its `size()` is an estimate rather than an
exact snapshot.

**`HashMap` allows one null key**, stored in bucket 0 since null has no
`hashCode`. `TreeMap` rejects null keys because it must compare them.

> Key Takeaways
> - A `HashMap` is an array of buckets indexed by a spread hash code.
> - The spreading step mixes high bits down, since only low bits index the
>   table.
> - Collisions form a linked list, converting to a red-black tree at eight
>   entries.
> - Treeification bounds the damage from deliberately colliding keys.
> - Resizing at 75% load rehashes every entry, so presize when the count is
>   known.
> - Mutating a key after insertion makes the entry unreachable.
> - `HashMap` is unsafe under concurrency; `ConcurrentHashMap` is the answer.
> - `ConcurrentHashMap` forbids nulls and reports an approximate size.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class whose `hashCode` always returns 1, insert 10,000 entries, and
>    time lookups against a normal implementation.
> 2. Presize a map for a million entries and compare insertion time with the
>    default.
> 3. Insert a mutable key, modify it, and demonstrate the entry cannot be
>    retrieved.
> 4. Run concurrent puts against a `HashMap` from ten threads and observe lost
>    updates.
> 5. Interview: Why does `ConcurrentHashMap` forbid null values when `HashMap`
>    allows them? (Hint: what would a null from `get` mean when another thread
>    may have just removed the key?)

#### Fail-Fast versus Fail-Safe Iterators

This question tests whether you understand that
`ConcurrentModificationException` is a **diagnostic aid rather than a
guarantee**, and that "fail-safe" is a misleading name.

**Fail-fast iterators detect structural modification and throw.** Most
`java.util` collections behave this way.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ada", "Bob", "Eve"));

for (String name : names) {
    if (name.equals("Bob")) {
        names.remove(name);          // ConcurrentModificationException
    }
}
```

**The mechanism** is a modification counter compared on each step.

```text
  ArrayList holds modCount, incremented on every structural change.
  The iterator records expectedModCount when created.

  each next() and remove():
      if (modCount != expectedModCount) throw new ConcurrentModificationException();
```

"Structural" means changing the size. Replacing an element with `set` does not
trigger it.

**The name is a warning, not a description.** The exception can be thrown by a
single thread, as above, and it is explicitly **best effort**: it may not fire
when it should. Never write logic that depends on catching it.

```java
// The classic false negative: removing the second-to-last element.
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
for (String s : list) {
    if (s.equals("b")) list.remove(s);      // NO exception: the loop just ends early
}
System.out.println(list);                    // [a, c] -- "c" was never visited
```

The `hasNext()` check is `cursor != size`, and after the removal both equal 2,
so the loop terminates before the check that would have thrown.

**The correct ways to remove while iterating:**

```java
// 1. The iterator's own remove, which updates expectedModCount.
Iterator<String> it = names.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().startsWith("B")) {
        it.remove();                        // safe
    }
}

// 2. removeIf, which is clearer and usually faster.
names.removeIf(name -> name.startsWith("B"));

// 3. Collect into a new collection, leaving the original untouched.
List<String> kept = names.stream()
        .filter(name -> !name.startsWith("B"))
        .toList();
```

**Fail-safe iterators** work on a snapshot or tolerate concurrent change, so
they never throw. The trade-off is that they may not reflect recent
modifications.

| Collection                | Iterator behaviour                                   |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `ArrayList`, `HashMap`    | Fail-fast; throws on structural modification          |
| `CopyOnWriteArrayList`    | Iterates an immutable snapshot taken at creation      |
| `ConcurrentHashMap`       | Weakly consistent; reflects some changes, never throws |
| `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`   | Weakly consistent                                     |

```java
// CopyOnWriteArrayList: the iterator sees the list as it was.
var list = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
for (String s : list) {
    list.add("c");             // no exception, and "c" is never iterated
}                              // each add copies the whole array: writes are O(n)
```

`CopyOnWriteArrayList` suits collections that are read constantly and written
rarely, such as a listener registry. It is a poor choice for anything
write-heavy.

**"Weakly consistent"** is the precise term for `ConcurrentHashMap`: the
iterator will not throw, will traverse elements present when it started, and may
or may not reflect changes made after.

> Key Takeaways
> - Fail-fast iterators throw `ConcurrentModificationException` on structural
>   change.
> - The mechanism is a modification counter checked on each step.
> - It is best effort and can miss violations, so never rely on catching it.
> - Removing the second-to-last element skips the last one silently.
> - Remove safely with `Iterator.remove`, `removeIf`, or by collecting a new
>   list.
> - Fail-safe iterators use a snapshot or weak consistency and never throw.
> - `CopyOnWriteArrayList` copies on every write; use it for read-heavy
>   collections.
> - `ConcurrentHashMap` iterators are weakly consistent, not snapshots.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Reproduce `ConcurrentModificationException` with a for-each loop and fix it
>    three ways.
> 2. Demonstrate the silent false negative by removing the second-to-last
>    element.
> 3. Iterate a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` while adding to it and explain what the
>    iterator sees.
> 4. Compare write throughput of `CopyOnWriteArrayList` against a synchronised
>    list.
> 5. Interview: Is `ConcurrentModificationException` a concurrency error?
>    (Hint: how many threads were involved in the example above?)

#### Type Erasure and Wildcard Questions

Generics are compile-time only. The compiler checks types and then **erases**
them, replacing type parameters with their bounds. Every generics question
follows from this one fact.

```java
// What you write
public class Box<T> { private T value; }
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

// What the bytecode contains
public class Box { private Object value; }
List names = new ArrayList();
// with casts inserted by the compiler at every read
```

**The consequences** are the material for the questions.

```java
// 1. Two generic types are the same class at runtime.
new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass();  // true

// 2. instanceof with a type argument does not compile.
if (list instanceof List<String>) { }        // error: illegal generic type

// 3. You cannot create an array of a generic type.
T[] array = new T[10];                       // error

// 4. Overloads differing only by type argument clash.
void process(List<String> s) { }
void process(List<Integer> i) { }            // error: same erasure

// 5. Static members cannot use the class's type parameter.
class Box<T> { static T instance; }          // error
```

**Why erasure was chosen** is a good thing to be able to say: backward
compatibility. Generics arrived in Java 5, and erasure allowed generic and
pre-generic code to interoperate on the same collections.

**Wildcards** exist because generics are **invariant**: `List<String>` is not a
`List<Object>`, even though `String` is an `Object`.

```java
List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objects = strings;      // error, and for good reason:
// objects.add(42);                  // would put an Integer into a List<String>
```

**PECS is the rule to quote**: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

```text
  ? extends T     a PRODUCER: you READ T out of it, cannot add
  ? super T       a CONSUMER: you WRITE T into it, reads come back as Object
```

```java
// The signature from Collections, which uses both in one method.
public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest,      // consumer: written to
                            List<? extends T> src) {   // producer: read from
    for (int i = 0; i < src.size(); i++) {
        dest.set(i, src.get(i));
    }
}
```

```java
// extends: safe to read as Number, unsafe to add anything.
List<? extends Number> producer = List.of(1, 2, 3);
Number n = producer.get(0);          // fine
// producer.add(4);                  // error: the actual list might be List<Long>

// super: safe to add Integer, reads come back as Object.
List<? super Integer> consumer = new ArrayList<Number>();
consumer.add(42);                    // fine
Object o = consumer.get(0);          // only Object is guaranteed
```

The reasoning to give aloud: with `? extends Number`, the list could be
`List<Long>`, so adding an `Integer` would corrupt it. With `? super Integer`,
the list holds at least `Integer`, so adding one is safe, but the element type
could be `Object`, so that is all a read can promise.

**Unbounded wildcards versus raw types** is a frequent follow-up.

```java
List<?> unknown = strings;       // type-safe: cannot add anything but null
List raw = strings;              // unsafe: unchecked warnings, no checking at all
```

Raw types exist only for compatibility with pre-Java 5 code and should never
appear in new code.

**Bridge methods** explain a subtle behaviour if it comes up.

```java
class StringBox implements Comparable<String> {
    public int compareTo(String other) { return 0; }
}
// Erasure makes the interface method compareTo(Object). The compiler generates
// a synthetic bridge method compareTo(Object) that casts and delegates, so
// polymorphism still works.
```

**Heap pollution and varargs** is the last common question.

```java
@SafeVarargs        // asserts the method does not store anything unsafe in the array
public static <T> List<T> listOf(T... items) {
    return Arrays.asList(items);
}
```

The warning exists because a generic varargs parameter creates an array of a
non-reifiable type, which erasure cannot fully check.

> Key Takeaways
> - Generics are checked at compile time and erased, leaving `Object` and casts.
> - Erasure was chosen for backward compatibility with pre-generic code.
> - You cannot use `instanceof` with a type argument, create generic arrays, or
>   overload on erasure.
> - Generics are invariant: `List<String>` is not a `List<Object>`.
> - PECS: use `? extends T` to read from a producer, `? super T` to write to a
>   consumer.
> - `? extends` forbids adding; `? super` returns only `Object` on reads.
> - `List<?>` is type-safe; a raw `List` disables checking entirely.
> - `@SafeVarargs` asserts a generic varargs method does not pollute the heap.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Show that two differently parameterised lists have the same runtime class.
> 2. Write a method summing a `List<? extends Number>` and explain why you
>    cannot add to it.
> 3. Implement `copy(dest, src)` with correct PECS bounds and test it with
>    several type combinations.
> 4. Attempt each of the five erasure consequences above and record the exact
>    compiler errors.
> 5. Interview: Why can you not write `new T[10]` inside a generic class? (Hint:
>    what does the JVM need to know at runtime to create an array, and what has
>    erasure removed?)

#### Stream, Lambda, and Optional Scenarios

Streams questions test whether you understand laziness, statelessness, and the
distinction between a pipeline and a loop, rather than whether you can chain
methods.

**A stream is not a collection.** It holds no data, it can be consumed once, and
nothing happens until a terminal operation runs.

```java
Stream<String> stream = names.stream().filter(n -> n.startsWith("A"));
// Nothing has executed yet: filter is LAZY.

List<String> result = stream.toList();     // the terminal operation runs it
stream.count();                             // IllegalStateException: already consumed
```

**Laziness enables short-circuiting**, which is the practical payoff.

```java
// Only the elements needed are processed, not the whole list.
Optional<Order> first = orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> o.total().compareTo(THRESHOLD) > 0)   // evaluated lazily
        .findFirst();                                      // stops at the first match
```

```text
  Processing order for [1, 2, 3, 4] with filter then map then findFirst
  -------------------------------------------------------------------
  element 1: filter -> false
  element 2: filter -> true, map -> result, findFirst -> DONE
  elements 3 and 4 are never touched
```

**Intermediate versus terminal** is the categorisation to know.

| Intermediate (lazy, returns a stream) | Terminal (eager, consumes the stream) |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `filter`, `map`, `flatMap`, `peek`     | `collect`, `toList`, `forEach`         |
| `distinct`, `sorted`, `limit`, `skip`  | `reduce`, `count`, `min`, `max`        |
| `mapToInt`, `boxed`                    | `anyMatch`, `allMatch`, `findFirst`    |

**Lambdas must not mutate external state**, and this is the rule most often
broken.

```java
// WRONG: a side effect, and broken outright if the stream is parallel.
List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
names.stream().filter(...).forEach(results::add);

// RIGHT: let the pipeline produce the result.
List<String> results = names.stream().filter(...).toList();
```

**Effectively final** is the compile-time rule: a lambda may capture a local
variable only if it is never reassigned.

```java
int count = 0;
names.forEach(n -> count++);       // error: count is not effectively final
```

**`Collectors` questions** usually centre on grouping.

```java
// Group orders by status.
Map<OrderStatus, List<Order>> byStatus = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status));

// Group and count in one pass: a downstream collector.
Map<OrderStatus, Long> counts = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status, Collectors.counting()));

// Sum a field per group.
Map<Long, BigDecimal> totalPerCustomer = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customerId,
                 Collectors.reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Order::total, BigDecimal::add)));

// Partition: grouping into exactly two buckets, keyed by boolean.
Map<Boolean, List<Order>> split = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> o.total().compareTo(BIG) > 0));
```

**`Optional` is for return values**, and misusing it is a common review comment.

| Use                              | Appropriate |
| -------------------------------- | ----------- |
| A method return that may be empty | Yes         |
| A field                           | No: not serialisable, adds a wrapper |
| A method parameter                | No: use an overload instead |
| A collection element              | No: use an empty collection |

```java
// WRONG: this is a longer way to write get() with a null check.
if (optional.isPresent()) {
    return optional.get();
} else {
    return fallback;
}

// RIGHT: the API is designed to avoid that shape.
return optional.orElse(fallback);
return optional.orElseGet(this::expensiveFallback);   // lazy: only if empty
return optional.orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id));
return optional.map(Order::total).filter(t -> t.signum() > 0);
```

`orElse` evaluates its argument always; `orElseGet` only when empty. Using
`orElse(expensiveCall())` is a real and common performance bug.

**Parallel streams** are the trap question. `parallel()` is easy to add and
usually unhelpful.

```java
// Justified: a large dataset, CPU-bound work, no shared state, a splittable source.
long count = hugeArrayList.parallelStream().filter(this::expensiveTest).count();

// Unjustified and often slower: small data, or IO-bound work, or an ordered
// operation that forces merging.
list.parallelStream().forEach(this::writeToDatabase);   // also exhausts the pool
```

The reasons to state: the common ForkJoinPool is shared by the whole JVM, so
blocking IO inside a parallel stream starves everything else; splitting and
merging has a fixed cost that small datasets never recover; and any shared
mutable state becomes a race.

> Key Takeaways
> - A stream holds no data, is consumed once, and does nothing until a terminal
>   operation.
> - Laziness allows short-circuiting, so `findFirst` stops early.
> - Intermediate operations return streams; terminal operations produce a
>   result.
> - Lambdas must not mutate external state, and captured locals must be
>   effectively final.
> - Use collectors to produce results rather than `forEach` with a side effect.
> - `groupingBy` with a downstream collector handles counting, summing, and
>   mapping.
> - `Optional` belongs in return types, not in fields, parameters, or
>   collections.
> - `orElse` always evaluates its argument; `orElseGet` is lazy.
> - Parallel streams help only for large, CPU-bound, stateless work on a
>   splittable source.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `peek` that prints to a filtered, mapped pipeline with `findFirst`
>    and observe how few elements are processed.
> 2. Group a list of orders by status and count each group in one pass.
> 3. Replace an `isPresent`/`get` block with the appropriate `Optional` method.
> 4. Demonstrate that `orElse` evaluates its argument even when the `Optional`
>    is present.
> 5. Benchmark a parallel stream against a sequential one for 100 elements and
>    for 10 million.
> 6. Interview: Why is performing blocking IO inside a parallel stream
>    dangerous? (Hint: which thread pool does it use, and who else is using it?)

<a id="194-memory-concurrency-and-jvm-questions"></a>
### 19.4 Memory, Concurrency, and JVM Questions

This subchapter covers chapters 11 and 12 as interview material: how memory is
organised and reclaimed, how to diagnose a leak, and the concurrency questions
that separate people who have debugged a race from people who have read about
one.

#### Stack, Heap, and Garbage Collection

The first question is usually the simplest: what is the difference between the
stack and the heap? The answer is about **lifetime and ownership**, not about
speed.

```text
  Thread 1 stack        Thread 2 stack            Heap (shared)
  --------------        --------------            -------------
  +------------+        +------------+            +-------------------+
  | frame: run |        | frame: main|            |  Order object      |
  |  order ----+--------+------------+----------> |  lines ----------+ |
  |  i = 5     |        |  o --------+----------> |                  | |
  +------------+        +------------+            |  ArrayList <-----+ |
  | frame: calc|        +------------+            +-------------------+
  |  total     |
  +------------+        one stack PER THREAD      one heap, ALL threads
```

| Aspect      | Stack                          | Heap                          |
| ----------- | ------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| Holds       | Frames: locals, parameters, references | Objects and their fields |
| Scope       | One per thread, private         | Shared by all threads          |
| Lifetime    | Popped when the method returns  | Until unreachable, then collected |
| Management  | Automatic, by frame              | Garbage collector              |
| Size        | Small, `-Xss`, typically 512KB to 1MB | Large, `-Xmx`             |
| Exhausted   | `StackOverflowError`            | `OutOfMemoryError`             |
| Thread safe | Inherently                      | Requires synchronisation       |

**The key insight:** a local variable holding an object lives on the stack, but
the object it references lives on the heap. Only the reference is popped when
the method returns.

**Garbage collection** reclaims objects that are no longer **reachable** from a
GC root, which is a precise definition worth giving.

```text
  GC roots: active thread stacks, static fields, JNI references
        |
        v
   [root] --> A --> B --> C          reachable: kept
              |
   [root] --> D                      reachable: kept

              E <--> F               a CYCLE, but unreachable from any root
                                     -> COLLECTED
```

Reachability rather than reference counting is why Java has no problem with
reference cycles, which is a good contrast to draw if the interviewer mentions
other languages.

**The generational hypothesis** underpins the whole design: most objects die
young.

```text
  Young generation                          Old generation
  +-----------------------------------+     +-------------------+
  |  Eden      |  S0    |  S1         |     |   Tenured         |
  +-----------------------------------+     +-------------------+
   allocation    survivor spaces              promoted after
   happens here  copy between them            surviving N collections

  Minor GC   frequent, fast, only the young generation
  Major GC   infrequent, slower, includes the old generation
```

Because most objects die in Eden, a minor collection only copies the few
survivors, which is why allocation in Java is cheap.

**Collectors** differ in what they optimise for.

| Collector  | Optimises for        | Typical use                        |
| ---------- | -------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Serial     | Small footprint       | Tiny heaps, single core             |
| Parallel   | Throughput            | Batch jobs where pauses are fine    |
| G1         | Balanced, bounded pauses | The default since Java 9        |
| ZGC        | Very low pause times   | Large heaps, latency-sensitive     |
| Shenandoah | Very low pause times   | Similar goals to ZGC               |

**`finalize()` is dead and should be named as such.** It was deprecated because
it is not guaranteed to run, delays collection, and can resurrect objects. The
replacements are `try`-with-resources for deterministic cleanup, as 16.1
covered, and `Cleaner` when a safety net is genuinely needed.

**`System.gc()` is a suggestion**, not a command, and calling it in application
code is almost always wrong: it can force a full collection and a long pause.

**The three reference types** occasionally come up.

| Type    | Collected when                              | Used for            |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| Strong  | Never while reachable                        | Ordinary references  |
| Soft    | Before `OutOfMemoryError`                    | Memory-sensitive caches |
| Weak    | At the next collection                        | `WeakHashMap`, listener registries |
| Phantom | After finalisation, for cleanup notification  | Resource cleanup     |

> Key Takeaways
> - The stack holds frames per thread; the heap holds objects shared by all
>   threads.
> - A local variable is on the stack; the object it points to is on the heap.
> - Collection is based on reachability from GC roots, so cycles are collected.
> - The generational hypothesis, that most objects die young, shapes the whole
>   design.
> - Minor collections handle the young generation and are fast; major ones are
>   not.
> - G1 is the default, balancing throughput against bounded pause times.
> - `finalize` is deprecated; use `try`-with-resources or `Cleaner`.
> - `System.gc()` is only a hint and usually harmful to call.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a recursive method with no base case and identify which error it
>    produces and why.
> 2. Allocate objects in a loop and observe minor collections with GC logging
>    enabled.
> 3. Create an unreachable reference cycle and show that it is still collected.
> 4. Run the same program under two collectors and compare pause distributions.
> 5. Interview: Why does Java not leak memory on reference cycles when reference
>    counting would? (Hint: what question does the collector actually ask about
>    each object?)

#### Diagnosing Memory Leaks

Java has garbage collection, so "Java cannot leak memory" is a claim candidates
sometimes make and it is wrong. A leak in Java is **an object that is still
reachable but will never be used again**, which the collector cannot detect
because reachability is all it knows.

**The classic causes** are worth memorising, because interviewers ask for
examples.

```java
// 1. A static collection that only ever grows.
public class Cache {
    private static final Map<String, Object> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
    public static void put(String k, Object v) { CACHE.put(k, v); }
    // Nothing removes. The static field is a GC root, so everything is kept.
}
```

```java
// 2. An unremoved listener: the registry holds the object forever.
button.addListener(this);     // without a matching removeListener, 'this' lives on
```

```java
// 3. ThreadLocal in a pooled thread: the thread never dies, so the value stays.
private static final ThreadLocal<Context> CONTEXT = new ThreadLocal<>();

public void handle(Request r) {
    CONTEXT.set(new Context(r));
    try {
        process();
    } finally {
        CONTEXT.remove();      // MANDATORY with a thread pool, as 17.4 noted
    }
}
```

```java
// 4. An inner class holding an implicit reference to its enclosing instance.
public class Screen {
    private final byte[] bigBuffer = new byte[10_000_000];

    // A non-static inner class keeps Screen alive for the task's lifetime.
    class Task implements Runnable {
        public void run() { ... }
    }
    // Making Task static, or using a lambda that captures nothing, fixes it.
}
```

```java
// 5. An unbounded key in a map whose keys are never removed, especially
//    when the key's hashCode changed after insertion (19.2).
```

**The diagnostic sequence** is what a good answer walks through in order.

```text
  1. Confirm it IS a leak.
     Watch the heap AFTER a full GC over hours. A flat post-GC floor is fine;
     a steadily climbing floor is a leak.

  2. Enable GC logging.
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log
     Look for collections becoming more frequent and reclaiming less.

  3. Take two heap dumps, minutes apart, under load.
     jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap1.hprof

  4. Compare them.
     Which class grew? Eclipse MAT's dominator tree answers this directly.

  5. Find the retention path.
     "Path to GC Roots" shows WHAT is keeping the objects alive. That path
     names the bug.
```

```bash
# Quick triage without a dump: what is on the heap right now, by class.
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -20

# Capture a dump automatically when the heap is exhausted.
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps -jar app.jar
```

**The dominator tree is the concept to name.** It shows, for each object, how
much memory would be freed if that object were released, which points at the
one container holding everything rather than at the million small objects
inside it.

```text
  Histogram says:            Dominator tree says:
  -------------------        --------------------
  byte[]      400 MB          OrderCache  retains 380 MB   <-- the actual bug
  String      120 MB              +-- HashMap
  HashMap$Node 80 MB                  +-- 200,000 CachedOrder
```

**Not every `OutOfMemoryError` is a leak.** Distinguishing the causes is a
strong answer.

| Message                          | Usual cause                              |
| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `Java heap space`                 | A real leak, or a heap too small for the load |
| `GC overhead limit exceeded`      | Collecting constantly, reclaiming almost nothing |
| `Metaspace`                       | Class loader leak, common with repeated redeploys |
| `Unable to create native thread`  | Thread leak; an unbounded executor        |
| `Direct buffer memory`            | Unreleased `ByteBuffer.allocateDirect`    |

**Prevention is mostly discipline**: bound every cache, remove every listener
and `ThreadLocal`, close every resource with `try`-with-resources, and prefer a
purpose-built cache with eviction over a `HashMap` that grows.

> Key Takeaways
> - A Java leak is an object still reachable but never used again.
> - Static collections, unremoved listeners, `ThreadLocal` in pooled threads,
>   and inner classes are the classic causes.
> - Always call `ThreadLocal.remove` in a `finally` when threads are pooled.
> - Confirm a leak by watching the post-collection floor, not the peak.
> - Compare two heap dumps taken under load minutes apart.
> - The dominator tree names the container responsible, which the histogram does
>   not.
> - Enable heap dump on out-of-memory in production.
> - Metaspace, thread, and direct buffer exhaustion are distinct failures with
>   distinct causes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program that leaks through a static map, watch the post-GC floor
>    climb, and capture a dump.
> 2. Analyse that dump and find the retention path back to the static field.
> 3. Reproduce a `ThreadLocal` leak using a fixed thread pool, then fix it.
> 4. Trigger `Metaspace` exhaustion by generating classes in a loop.
> 5. Interview: If Java has garbage collection, how can it leak? (Hint: what
>    exactly does the collector consider garbage, and is "unused" the same
>    thing?)

#### Thread Safety and Synchronization

"Is this class thread-safe?" is the question, and a strong answer starts by
defining the term: a class is thread-safe when it behaves correctly when used
from multiple threads **with no external synchronisation**.

**The problem is that operations that look atomic are not.**

```java
public class Counter {
    private int count;
    public void increment() { count++; }     // THREE operations, not one
}
```

```text
  count++ compiles to:
      read count        thread A reads 5      thread B reads 5
      add 1             A computes 6          B computes 6
      write count       A writes 6            B writes 6

  Two increments, one result. This is a LOST UPDATE.
```

**`synchronized` provides two guarantees**, and naming both is what
distinguishes a good answer. Most candidates name only the first.

```text
  1. MUTUAL EXCLUSION   only one thread holds the monitor at a time
  2. VISIBILITY         changes made before releasing the lock are visible
                        to the next thread that acquires it
```

Without the second guarantee, a thread could hold the lock correctly and still
read a stale value from its CPU cache.

```java
public class Counter {
    private int count;

    // Locks on 'this'. Equivalent to synchronized(this) { ... }
    public synchronized void increment() { count++; }

    public synchronized int get() { return count; }   // the GETTER needs it too
}
```

The getter needing synchronisation surprises people: without it there is no
happens-before relationship, so the reader may see a stale value.

**Lock granularity matters.** Synchronising a whole method serialises everything
in it.

```java
// A private lock object: better than locking on 'this', because external code
// cannot acquire your lock and deadlock you.
private final Object lock = new Object();

public void update(Order order) {
    Order prepared = expensiveComputation(order);   // OUTSIDE the lock
    synchronized (lock) {
        cache.put(order.id(), prepared);            // only the shared state
    }
}
```

**`synchronized` versus `ReentrantLock`:**

| Feature                | `synchronized`     | `ReentrantLock`               |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| Release                | Automatic, on exit  | Manual, must be in `finally`  |
| Timed acquisition      | No                  | `tryLock(timeout)`            |
| Interruptible          | No                  | `lockInterruptibly()`         |
| Fairness option        | No                  | Yes                           |
| Multiple conditions    | One wait set        | Several `Condition` objects   |
| Simplicity             | Higher              | Lower                         |

```java
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public boolean tryUpdate(Order order) {
    if (!lock.tryLock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {   // give up rather than block forever
        return false;
    }
    try {
        cache.put(order.id(), order);
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();                          // MUST be in finally
    }
    return true;
}
```

Use `synchronized` by default and `ReentrantLock` when you need timeouts,
interruptibility, or multiple conditions.

**The best strategy is to avoid shared mutable state entirely.**

| Strategy        | How                                                |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Immutability    | Final fields, no setters; inherently safe            |
| Confinement     | Keep state in a local or a `ThreadLocal`              |
| Concurrent collections | `ConcurrentHashMap` instead of a synchronised one |
| Atomics         | `AtomicInteger` for counters, lock-free               |
| Higher-level    | `ExecutorService`, `CompletableFuture`, queues        |

This is why 17.1 insisted that singleton beans be stateless: no shared mutable
state means no synchronisation question.

**The compound action trap** is a favourite follow-up: individually safe
operations do not compose into a safe sequence.

```java
// Each call is thread-safe. The SEQUENCE is not.
if (!map.containsKey(key)) {        // thread A checks: absent
    map.put(key, compute(key));     // thread B has put in between; A overwrites
}

// Correct: one atomic operation.
map.computeIfAbsent(key, this::compute);
```

**Double-checked locking** is the classic puzzle, and the answer hinges on
`volatile`, covered next.

```java
private volatile Singleton instance;      // volatile is REQUIRED here

public Singleton getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {                    // fast path, no lock
        synchronized (this) {
            if (instance == null) {            // re-check under the lock
                instance = new Singleton();
            }
        }
    }
    return instance;
}
```

Without `volatile`, another thread can observe a non-null reference to a
partially constructed object, because the constructor's writes may be reordered
with the reference assignment.

> Key Takeaways
> - Thread-safe means correct under concurrent use with no external
>   synchronisation.
> - `count++` is three operations and loses updates without synchronisation.
> - `synchronized` provides both mutual exclusion and visibility.
> - Getters need synchronisation too, or readers may see stale values.
> - Lock a private object rather than `this`, and hold the lock as briefly as
>   possible.
> - `ReentrantLock` adds timeouts, interruptibility, fairness, and multiple
>   conditions.
> - Prefer immutability, confinement, and concurrent collections over locking.
> - Individually atomic operations do not compose; use `computeIfAbsent` and
>   friends.
> - Double-checked locking requires `volatile` on the field.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run an unsynchronised counter from ten threads a million times and record
>    the result.
> 2. Fix it three ways: `synchronized`, `AtomicInteger`, and a `LongAdder`, then
>    compare throughput.
> 3. Demonstrate the check-then-act race with a map and fix it with
>    `computeIfAbsent`.
> 4. Rewrite a `synchronized` method to lock a private object and hold it for
>    fewer lines.
> 5. Interview: Why does a getter need synchronisation if it only reads?
>    (Hint: name the second guarantee `synchronized` provides besides mutual
>    exclusion.)

#### volatile, Atomics, and the Java Memory Model

These questions go one level below locking, into what the JVM is permitted to
do with your code. The Java Memory Model (JMM) is the specification that answers
"when is a write by one thread guaranteed to be visible to another".

**The problem is that three parties reorder your code.**

```text
  You write           the compiler may reorder
                      the JVM may reorder
                      the CPU may reorder, and caches may delay writes

  All are legal as long as a SINGLE-THREADED program cannot tell.
  A multi-threaded program absolutely can.
```

```java
// The visibility bug that surprises everyone.
private boolean running = true;              // not volatile

public void run() {
    while (running) { doWork(); }            // may loop FOREVER
}

public void stop() { running = false; }      // written by another thread
```

The reader thread may cache `running` in a register, and the JIT compiler is
entitled to hoist the read out of the loop entirely, because nothing in that
thread modifies it.

**`volatile` fixes visibility and ordering**, and does not provide atomicity.

```java
private volatile boolean running = true;     // every read sees the latest write
```

```text
  volatile guarantees
  -------------------
  visibility   a write is immediately visible to subsequent reads
  ordering     reads and writes are not reordered across the volatile access
               (everything before the write is visible after the read)

  volatile does NOT guarantee
  ---------------------------
  atomicity    count++ on a volatile field still loses updates
```

```java
private volatile int count;
public void increment() { count++; }      // STILL BROKEN: read-modify-write
```

**When `volatile` is sufficient:** a flag written by one thread and read by
others, or a reference published once, as in double-checked locking.

**Atomic classes provide lock-free atomicity** using a compare-and-swap
instruction.

```java
private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();

public void increment() {
    count.incrementAndGet();        // atomic: one CPU instruction, no lock
}

// The general form: retry until the swap succeeds.
public void updateMax(int candidate) {
    count.accumulateAndGet(candidate, Math::max);
}
```

```text
  Compare-and-swap
  ----------------
  read current value        v = 5
  compute new value         n = 6
  atomically: if the value is still 5, set it to 6, else retry

  No lock, no blocking. Under high contention the retries can waste CPU,
  which is why LongAdder exists for hot counters.
```

| Tool              | Atomicity | Visibility | Blocking | Use for                     |
| ----------------- | --------- | ---------- | -------- | --------------------------- |
| `volatile`        | No        | Yes        | No       | Flags, single publication    |
| `AtomicInteger`   | Yes       | Yes        | No       | Counters, compare-and-swap   |
| `LongAdder`       | Yes       | Yes        | No       | Very hot counters; faster under contention |
| `synchronized`    | Yes       | Yes        | Yes      | Compound actions             |
| `ReentrantLock`   | Yes       | Yes        | Yes      | Compound actions with timeouts |

**The happens-before relationship** is the formal vocabulary, and using it
correctly signals depth.

```text
  Guaranteed happens-before edges
  -------------------------------
  program order within a single thread
  unlocking a monitor  ->  any later locking of the same monitor
  writing a volatile   ->  any later read of that volatile
  Thread.start()       ->  everything in the started thread
  everything in a thread  ->  another thread's successful join()
  a final field's initialisation  ->  reading it after construction completes
```

**Final fields have a special guarantee**: if an object's final fields are set
in the constructor and the object does not escape during construction, other
threads are guaranteed to see them fully initialised. This is why immutable
objects are safe to share without synchronisation, and it is a good answer to
"why is immutability thread-safe".

```java
// Safe to publish to any thread with no synchronisation.
public final class Money {
    private final BigDecimal amount;        // final: guaranteed visible
    private final Currency currency;

    public Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
        this.amount = amount;
        this.currency = currency;
    }                                        // 'this' never escapes the constructor
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The compiler, JVM, and CPU may reorder operations that a single thread
>   cannot detect.
> - A non-volatile flag can be cached or hoisted, producing an infinite loop.
> - `volatile` guarantees visibility and ordering, never atomicity.
> - `volatile` suits flags and single publication, not read-modify-write.
> - Atomic classes give lock-free atomicity through compare-and-swap.
> - `LongAdder` outperforms `AtomicLong` for heavily contended counters.
> - Happens-before edges come from locks, volatiles, thread start and join, and
>   final fields.
> - Final fields set in a constructor are safely visible, which is why immutable
>   objects need no synchronisation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a loop reading a non-volatile flag stopped by another thread and see
>    whether it terminates.
> 2. Show that `volatile int count; count++` still loses updates under
>    contention.
> 3. Replace it with `AtomicInteger` and confirm the count is exact.
> 4. Benchmark `AtomicLong` against `LongAdder` with sixteen threads
>    incrementing.
> 5. Interview: You have a boolean flag written by one thread and read by
>    another. Is `volatile` enough? (Hint: is setting a boolean a
>    read-modify-write operation?)

#### Deadlock, Livelock, and Race Conditions

These three failures are grouped because interviewers ask you to distinguish
them, and because the distinctions are genuinely useful when diagnosing a
production hang.

| Failure        | Symptom                                  | Threads are     |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Deadlock       | Permanent hang, zero CPU                  | Blocked forever  |
| Livelock       | Permanent hang, high CPU                  | Busy, making no progress |
| Starvation     | One thread never progresses               | Others monopolise |
| Race condition | Wrong or intermittent results              | Running normally |

**A deadlock needs four conditions simultaneously**, and naming them is the
textbook answer.

```text
  1. mutual exclusion    a resource is held exclusively
  2. hold and wait       a thread holds one while waiting for another
  3. no preemption       a resource cannot be forcibly taken back
  4. circular wait       a cycle exists in the wait-for graph

  Break ANY ONE and deadlock is impossible.
```

```java
// The classic: two locks acquired in opposite orders.
public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount) {
    synchronized (from) {              // thread A locks account 1
        synchronized (to) {            // thread B has locked account 2 and
            from.debit(amount);        // is waiting for account 1
            to.credit(amount);
        }
    }
}
// transfer(a1, a2) in thread A and transfer(a2, a1) in thread B: deadlock.
```

```text
  Thread A: holds a1 -----> wants a2
                              ^
                              |
  Thread B: holds a2 -----> wants a1        a cycle
```

**The standard fix is a consistent lock ordering**, which breaks the circular
wait condition. This is 16.3's advice about database deadlocks applied to
in-memory locks.

```java
public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount) {
    // Order by a stable, unique property so every thread locks in the same order.
    Account first  = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;
    Account second = from.id() < to.id() ? to : from;

    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.debit(amount);
            to.credit(amount);
        }
    }
}
```

The alternative is `tryLock` with a timeout and a retry, which breaks the hold
and wait condition instead.

**Detecting a deadlock in production** is a practical question.

```bash
# Dump all thread stacks. The JVM detects and prints Java-level deadlocks.
jstack <pid>
jcmd <pid> Thread.print
```

```text
  Found one Java-level deadlock:
  =============================
  "Thread-1": waiting to lock monitor 0x... which is held by "Thread-0"
  "Thread-0": waiting to lock monitor 0x... which is held by "Thread-1"
```

Zero CPU plus a stalled application is the signature. High CPU plus a stall
points at livelock or a garbage collection death spiral instead.

**Livelock** is deadlock's noisy cousin: threads respond to each other and keep
changing state without progressing.

```java
// Both threads politely release and retry, repeatedly colliding.
while (!acquired) {
    if (lock.tryLock()) { ... }
    else { releaseMyLock(); Thread.sleep(100); retry(); }   // in lockstep forever
}
```

The fix is randomised backoff, so the two do not stay synchronised. This is the
same idea as network collision backoff.

**Race conditions** come in two named shapes, and using the names is worthwhile.

```java
// CHECK-THEN-ACT
if (!file.exists()) {           // another thread creates it here
    file.createNewFile();       // fails, or overwrites
}

// READ-MODIFY-WRITE
int current = counter.get();
counter.set(current + 1);       // another thread incremented in between
```

Both are fixed by making the compound operation atomic, with a lock, an atomic
class, or a purpose-built method such as `computeIfAbsent` or
`createNewFile`'s own atomic guarantee.

**Prevention, in order of preference:**

```text
  1. no shared mutable state         immutability, confinement
  2. higher-level abstractions       concurrent collections, executors
  3. atomic operations               compare-and-swap
  4. a single lock                   simple and easy to reason about
  5. multiple locks in a fixed order the last resort
```

**Testing for these bugs is genuinely hard**, and saying so honestly is better
than claiming otherwise. Stress tests with many threads, tools such as jcstress,
and thread dumps under load are the practical approaches; a passing test proves
very little.

> Key Takeaways
> - Deadlock is a permanent block at zero CPU; livelock is a permanent stall at
>   high CPU.
> - Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular
>   wait.
> - Breaking any one condition prevents it; consistent lock ordering is the
>   usual choice.
> - `tryLock` with a timeout breaks hold and wait instead.
> - `jstack` detects and reports Java-level deadlocks directly.
> - Livelock is fixed with randomised backoff.
> - Check-then-act and read-modify-write are the two race shapes.
> - Prefer no shared state, then high-level abstractions, then atomics, then
>   locks.
> - Concurrency bugs are hard to test; a passing test proves little.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the two-account transfer deadlock, reproduce it, and capture a thread
>    dump showing it.
> 2. Fix it by ordering locks on the account identifier and verify under load.
> 3. Implement the same fix with `tryLock` and a timeout, and compare the
>    failure modes.
> 4. Reproduce a check-then-act race on a map and fix it atomically.
> 5. Interview: An application hangs with zero CPU usage. What do you suspect
>    and what is your first command? (Hint: what distinguishes this from a
>    high-CPU stall?)

#### Executors and Concurrent Collections

Creating threads by hand is the beginner approach, and interviewers ask about
executors to check that you know why it does not scale.

**The problems with `new Thread`:**

```java
// One thread per task: unbounded, expensive, and unmanageable.
for (Request request : requests) {
    new Thread(() -> handle(request)).start();   // 10,000 requests = 10,000 threads
}
```

Each platform thread costs roughly a megabyte of stack and an operating system
thread. Ten thousand exhausts memory, and the context switching alone destroys
throughput. There is also no way to wait for completion, get a result, handle an
exception, or limit concurrency.

**An `ExecutorService` separates task submission from execution policy.**

```java
// A bounded pool with a bounded queue and an explicit rejection policy.
ExecutorService executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        4, 8,                                  // core and maximum pool size
        60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                 // idle timeout for extra threads
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),         // BOUNDED queue: back-pressure
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());   // slow the producer down
```

| Factory method              | Pool                        | Caution                     |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `newFixedThreadPool(n)`     | n threads, unbounded queue   | The queue can exhaust memory |
| `newCachedThreadPool()`     | Unbounded threads            | Can create thousands         |
| `newSingleThreadExecutor()` | One thread, unbounded queue  | Serialises everything        |
| `newWorkStealingPool()`     | ForkJoinPool                 | For CPU-bound work           |
| `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` | A virtual thread per task | Java 21+; for blocking IO |

**The unbounded queue is the hidden hazard** in `newFixedThreadPool`: tasks
accumulate without limit until the heap is gone. A bounded queue plus a
rejection policy gives back-pressure instead.

**`submit` versus `execute`** is a common question with a sharp answer.

```java
executor.execute(() -> risky());     // Runnable; an exception reaches the
                                      // thread's uncaught handler and is logged

Future<?> future = executor.submit(() -> risky());   // the exception is CAPTURED
// If nobody calls future.get(), the exception is SILENTLY SWALLOWED.
future.get();                         // throws ExecutionException, wrapping it
```

Silently swallowed exceptions from unexamined futures are a real production
problem worth mentioning.

**Shutdown must be explicit**, or the JVM does not exit.

```java
executor.shutdown();                                  // stop accepting new tasks
if (!executor.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    executor.shutdownNow();                           // interrupt running tasks
}
```

**`CompletableFuture`** composes asynchronous work without blocking.

```java
CompletableFuture<Order> order = CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> loadOrder(id), executor)        // always pass an executor
        .thenApply(this::enrich)                            // transform
        .thenCompose(o -> lookupCustomer(o.customerId()))   // chain another future
        .exceptionally(e -> {                               // handle failures
            log.error("failed", e);
            return Order.empty();
        });

// Combine independent calls that can run in parallel.
CompletableFuture.allOf(orderFuture, inventoryFuture).join();
```

Always supply an executor: the no-argument overloads use the common
ForkJoinPool, which is shared by the whole JVM and must not be blocked, exactly
as 19.3 warned about parallel streams.

**Virtual threads** are the modern answer if the interview covers recent Java.

```java
// Java 21+: each task gets a virtual thread. Blocking is cheap because the
// carrier thread is released while the virtual thread waits.
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (Request r : requests) {
        executor.submit(() -> handleBlockingIo(r));     // millions are feasible
    }
}
```

The key point to make: virtual threads make **blocking IO** cheap. They do not
make CPU-bound work faster, since the number of cores is unchanged.

**Concurrent collections** replace synchronised wrappers.

| Collection                | Replaces                            | Characteristics              |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `ConcurrentHashMap`       | `synchronizedMap`                    | Lock-free reads, striped writes |
| `CopyOnWriteArrayList`    | `synchronizedList`                   | Read-heavy, expensive writes  |
| `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`   | A synchronised queue                  | Non-blocking, unbounded       |
| `LinkedBlockingQueue`     | Hand-rolled wait/notify               | Blocking, optionally bounded  |
| `ArrayBlockingQueue`      | Hand-rolled wait/notify               | Blocking, fixed capacity      |

**Blocking queues are the standard producer-consumer tool**, and they remove the
need for `wait` and `notify` entirely.

```java
BlockingQueue<Task> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000);

// Producer: blocks when full, which is back-pressure.
queue.put(task);

// Consumer: blocks when empty, no polling loop needed.
Task task = queue.take();
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Creating a thread per task is unbounded, expensive, and unmanageable.
> - An executor separates what to run from the policy for running it.
> - `newFixedThreadPool` has an unbounded queue that can exhaust the heap.
> - A bounded queue with a rejection policy provides back-pressure.
> - `submit` captures exceptions in the `Future`; they vanish if nobody calls
>   `get`.
> - Shut executors down explicitly and await termination.
> - `CompletableFuture` composes async work; always pass your own executor.
> - Virtual threads make blocking IO cheap, not CPU work faster.
> - Blocking queues implement producer-consumer without `wait` and `notify`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Submit 10,000 tasks to a fixed pool with an unbounded queue and watch heap
>    usage.
> 2. Replace it with a bounded queue and a caller-runs policy, and observe the
>    back-pressure.
> 3. Submit a task that throws, never call `get`, and confirm nothing is
>    reported.
> 4. Build a producer-consumer pipeline with a `BlockingQueue` and three
>    consumers.
> 5. Run 10,000 blocking IO tasks on a platform thread pool and on virtual
>    threads, and compare.
> 6. Interview: Why should you pass an explicit executor to
>    `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync`? (Hint: which pool does the default use,
>    and what else in the JVM depends on it?)

<a id="195-framework-and-ecosystem-questions"></a>
### 19.5 Framework and Ecosystem Questions

This subchapter covers the questions drawn from chapters 15 to 18, where the
interviewer is usually checking whether you understand what the framework does
on your behalf rather than only how to call it.

#### JDBC, Transactions, and ORM

Data access questions are where candidates most often reveal that they have used
a framework without understanding it. The questions are practical and the wrong
answers have real production consequences.

**"Why `PreparedStatement` over `Statement`?"** should get three reasons, not
one.

```text
  1. Security     values never become SQL, so injection is impossible   16.2
  2. Correctness  the driver handles escaping, quoting, and type conversion
  3. Performance  the database parses and plans once, then reuses it
```

Most candidates give the first. Giving all three, and explaining that
parameterisation works because parsing happens **before** the value arrives, is
the distinguishing answer.

**"What do the isolation levels mean?"** expects the anomaly each one prevents,
not just the names.

| Level              | Prevents                                    |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| `READ_UNCOMMITTED` | Nothing                                      |
| `READ_COMMITTED`   | Dirty reads                                  |
| `REPEATABLE_READ`  | Dirty and non-repeatable reads               |
| `SERIALIZABLE`     | All three, including phantoms                |

The strong addition: `SERIALIZABLE` on PostgreSQL is optimistic and aborts
conflicting transactions with SQL state `40001`, so using it requires a retry
loop. Saying that demonstrates you have actually run it.

**"Where do transaction boundaries belong?"** is the design question from 16.3.

```java
// WRONG: each repository call is its own transaction, so the operation
// as a whole is not atomic.
public void placeOrder(Order order) {
    orderRepository.save(order);        // commits
    stockRepository.decrement(order);   // separate transaction; may fail
}

// RIGHT: one business operation, one transaction.
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order order) {
    orderRepository.save(order);
    stockRepository.decrement(order);
}
```

**"What is the N+1 problem?"** is asked in almost every interview touching
Hibernate.

```java
// 1 query for the orders, then 1 per order for its lines: 101 queries.
List<Order> orders = repository.findAll();
orders.forEach(o -> total(o.getLines()));
```

Name the fixes, in order: a `JOIN FETCH` query, an entity graph, batch fetching,
or a projection that avoids entities altogether. Adding that marking everything
`EAGER` is not a fix, because it loads the whole graph on every read, shows
judgement.

**"What does `@Transactional` not do?"** is the trap, and the answer is 17.2's
proxy limitations.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    public void processAll(List<Order> orders) {
        orders.forEach(this::process);   // self-invocation: NO transaction
    }

    @Transactional
    public void process(Order order) { ... }
}
```

Also worth stating: it rolls back on unchecked exceptions and **commits** on
checked ones by default, and it does nothing on a private method.

**"Explain the entity lifecycle."** Transient, managed, detached, removed, with
the crucial detail that a managed entity's changes are written automatically by
dirty checking, and that a detached entity's changes are not written at all.

**"When would you use `JdbcTemplate` instead of JPA?"** A good answer names
reporting queries, bulk operations, and anything where the generated SQL is not
good enough, and notes that the two coexist on the same transaction.

**"What is `open-in-view` and why disable it?"** This is an increasingly common
question and 18.3 answered it: it keeps the persistence context open through
serialisation, which hides N+1 queries in the view layer and holds a connection
for the whole request including slow clients.

> Key Takeaways
> - Parameterised statements give security, correctness, and plan reuse.
> - Name the anomaly each isolation level prevents, and mention retry for
>   serializable.
> - Transaction boundaries belong at the business operation, in the service
>   layer.
> - N+1 is fixed by join fetch, entity graphs, batching, or projections, never
>   by eager loading.
> - `@Transactional` does nothing on self-invoked or private methods.
> - It commits on checked exceptions unless `rollbackFor` is set.
> - Dirty checking writes changes to managed entities; detached entities are not
>   tracked.
> - Disable `open-in-view` so lazy loading failures surface during development.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Explain in two minutes why a prepared statement prevents injection, without
>    using the word "escape".
> 2. Write a self-invoked `@Transactional` call, prove no transaction opens, and
>    fix it.
> 3. Demonstrate N+1 with SQL logging and fix it two different ways.
> 4. Describe the four entity states and what a setter does in each.
> 5. Interview: A service method annotated `@Transactional` throws an
>    `IOException` and the data is still saved. Bug or expected? (Hint: what is
>    the documented default rollback rule?)

#### Dependency Injection and Bean Lifecycle

These questions test whether you understand the container as a mechanism or
treat it as magic. The most revealing answers are about **why** the
recommendations exist.

**"Why constructor injection?"** Four reasons, from 17.1.

```text
  1. the object is fully initialised the moment it exists
  2. fields can be final: immutable and thread-safe
  3. dependencies are visible in the signature
  4. the class can be constructed with new in a test
```

Add the fifth, which is the one that shows experience: **a constructor growing
to ten parameters is visible feedback that a class does too much, and field
injection hides it.**

**"Why is field injection discouraged?"** Because tests cannot construct the
object, fields cannot be final, and the dependencies are invisible in the public
API. The answer that it "uses reflection" is true and beside the point.

**"What is the default bean scope, and what does it require of your code?"** One
instance per container, shared by every thread, therefore **the bean must be
stateless**. Injected final collaborators are fine; mutable request state is
not. This is the single most consequential thing to know about Spring beans.

```java
@Service
public class BrokenService {
    private Order current;              // SHARED across all request threads
    public void place(Order o) { this.current = o; ... }
}
```

**"How do you inject a prototype into a singleton?"** The trap is that a
prototype is resolved once at singleton construction. `ObjectProvider` or
`@Lookup` gives a fresh instance per call.

**"What happens when two beans implement the same interface?"**
`NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` at startup, resolved with `@Primary` for the
default and `@Qualifier` at the injection point that needs the exception. The
good addition: if all of them should run, inject a `List<T>` instead of
choosing.

**"Describe the bean lifecycle."**

```text
  instantiate -> inject dependencies -> BeanPostProcessor (before)
      -> @PostConstruct -> afterPropertiesSet -> BeanPostProcessor (after)
      -> READY -> @PreDestroy -> destroy
```

The detail worth adding: **proxies are created by a `BeanPostProcessor` in the
last step**, which is exactly why `@Transactional` and `@PreAuthorize` work only
on externally invoked calls.

**"Why does Spring create singletons eagerly at startup?"** So wiring errors
fail immediately with a clear message rather than at three in the morning when a
rarely used path first runs. Trading startup time for fail-fast behaviour is a
deliberate choice.

**"What is a circular dependency and what should you do?"** Constructor
injection rejects it at startup; setter and field injection tolerate it. The
correct response is to treat it as a design signal and extract the shared
concern, not to reach for `@Lazy`.

**"What is AOP and how does Spring implement it?"** Cross-cutting concerns
separated from business logic, implemented with **runtime proxies** rather than
bytecode weaving. The consequences to name: only Spring-managed beans, only
public methods, and never self-invoked calls.

> Key Takeaways
> - Constructor injection guarantees full initialisation, allows final fields,
>   and enables plain testing.
> - A long constructor is useful feedback that field injection suppresses.
> - The default singleton scope requires beans to be stateless.
> - A prototype injected into a singleton resolves once; use `ObjectProvider`.
> - Ambiguity is resolved with `@Primary` and `@Qualifier`, or avoided by
>   injecting a list.
> - Proxies are added by a post-processor after initialisation.
> - Eager singleton creation trades startup time for fail-fast wiring errors.
> - Circular dependencies are a design signal, not something to work around.
> - Spring AOP uses proxies, so self-invocation and private methods are never
>   advised.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Explain in one minute why field injection makes a class harder to test.
> 2. Add mutable state to a singleton bean, hit it from twenty threads, and
>    describe the failure.
> 3. Inject a prototype into a singleton, prove the instance never changes, and
>    fix it.
> 4. Create a circular dependency with constructors, read the error, then
>    redesign to remove it.
> 5. Interview: Why does `@Transactional` work when a controller calls a service
>    but not when the service calls itself? (Hint: which object does `this`
>    refer to inside the target?)

#### Spring Boot, REST, and Auto-Configuration

Boot questions usually probe whether the candidate can explain the automation or
merely benefits from it.

**"What does Spring Boot actually add to Spring?"** The clean answer:
auto-configuration, starter dependencies with managed versions, an embedded
server and executable jar, externalised configuration, and actuator. The
programming model is unchanged. Saying "Boot replaced Spring" is a wrong answer
that comes up often.

**"How does auto-configuration work?"** Conditional bean registration,
discovered from an imports file in every jar, evaluated against the classpath,
properties, and beans already defined.

```java
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean          // this is why your own bean wins
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) { ... }
}
```

The follow-up: **how do you override it?** Define the bean yourself, and
`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` steps aside. The diagnostic: run with `--debug` and
read the condition evaluation report.

**"What does `@SpringBootApplication` do?"** Three annotations:
`@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, and `@ComponentScan`
with no arguments, which is why the main class's package determines what is
scanned.

**"Which configuration source wins?"** Later sources override earlier ones, from
packaged files up to command-line arguments. The practical answer is better than
reciting the list: query `/actuator/env/<property>` and read the `source` field.

**"How do you design a REST endpoint?"** Resources as nouns, HTTP methods as
verbs, correct status codes, pagination by default, and a consistent error
format. The details that show experience: 201 with a `Location` header for
creation, 409 for a conflict, and never exposing entities directly.

**"Why not return entities from a controller?"** Four reasons from 18.3: schema
coupling, over-exposure of fields, mass assignment on the request side, and lazy
loading failures during serialisation.

**"How do you version an API?"** URL path versioning is the practical default.
More important is knowing that **most changes need no version**: adding response
fields and relaxing request validation are compatible; removing fields and
tightening validation are not.

**"What is `@ControllerAdvice` for?"** Centralised exception handling, so every
endpoint returns the same error shape. The point to add: never return exception
messages or stack traces to a client; log them with a correlation identifier and
return the identifier.

**"What is actuator and what would you expose?"** Operational endpoints. Expose
health and metrics; keep `env`, `beans`, and `heapdump` off a public port. Then
the distinction that matters: **liveness failure restarts the process, readiness
failure stops routing to it**, so a database outage belongs in readiness.

> Key Takeaways
> - Boot adds auto-configuration, starters, an embedded server, configuration,
>   and actuator, leaving Spring's model intact.
> - Auto-configuration is conditional registration discovered from jar metadata.
> - `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is what makes your own bean override a default.
> - `@SpringBootApplication` scans from its own package downward.
> - Configuration precedence runs from packaged files up to command-line
>   arguments.
> - Design endpoints around resources with correct status codes and default
>   pagination.
> - Never expose entities; use request and response types.
> - Most API changes are compatible; adding is safe, removing is not.
> - Liveness restarts, readiness deroutes; put dependency outages in readiness.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Explain auto-configuration in ninety seconds without using the word
>    "magic".
> 2. Override an auto-configured bean and prove from the debug report that
>    Boot's no longer applies.
> 3. Set one property in three sources and identify the winner from the actuator
>    environment endpoint.
> 4. List ten changes to an endpoint and classify each as compatible or
>    breaking.
> 5. Interview: You add a library and a bean you never declared appears. Explain
>    the mechanism. (Hint: what file does Boot look for inside every jar on the
>    classpath?)

#### Build, Test, and Tooling Questions

These questions check professional habits. They are easy to answer well and
candidates often neglect them.

**"Maven or Gradle?"** Both are legitimate; having a reasoned preference matters
more than the choice.

| Aspect          | Maven                          | Gradle                        |
| --------------- | ------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| Build file      | Declarative XML                 | Kotlin or Groovy script        |
| Flexibility     | Convention-bound                | Arbitrary logic, easily abused |
| Speed           | Slower; no build cache by default | Incremental builds and caching |
| Learning curve  | Gentle                          | Steeper                        |
| Predictability  | High: builds look alike         | Lower: each project differs    |

**"What is the dependency scope for a test library?"** `test` in Maven,
`testImplementation` in Gradle. The follow-up about `provided` and
`compileOnly`, used for a servlet API supplied by a container, checks whether
you have built a WAR.

**"How do you resolve a version conflict?"** Inspect the tree, then pin the
version explicitly.

```bash
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath
```

Maven resolves conflicts by **nearest definition wins**, which is worth knowing
because it surprises people expecting the highest version.

**"Why commit the wrapper?"** So every developer and the CI server build with
the same tool version. Same reasoning as pinning dependency versions.

**"What makes a good unit test?"** FIRST: fast, isolated, repeatable,
self-validating, timely. Plus the habit that matters most: **assert observable
behaviour, not implementation**, so that refactoring does not break tests.

```java
// BRITTLE: asserts how it works.
verify(repository).save(any());
assertEquals(1, cart.getItemsList().size());

// ROBUST: asserts what it promises.
assertEquals(Money.of(1250), cart.total());
```

**"What is your view on code coverage?"** A signal, never a target. A test with
no assertions gives full coverage and zero confidence. Use it to find untested
code, not to certify tested code. Quoting Goodhart's law here is appropriate:
once a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring.

**"Mock or not?"** Mock what you do not own and what is slow or
nondeterministic: external services, clocks, randomness. Do not mock value
objects or the class under test. Prefer a hand-written fake over a mock when
the collaborator has meaningful behaviour, because a fake does not break when
the interface gains a method.

**"How do you test a Spring Boot application?"** The pyramid: plain JUnit for
services with constructor injection, slice tests for one layer, and full context
tests for critical paths. Add the practical point about **context caching**:
each distinct configuration starts a new context, so per-class property tweaks
multiply suite time.

**"Why Testcontainers instead of H2?"** Because H2 is not the production
database. Different SQL dialect, different locking, looser constraints, and
migrations that pass in compatibility mode and fail for real.

**"What tools do you use for quality?"** Name a static analyser, a formatter, a
coverage tool, and a dependency vulnerability scanner, and say that they run in
CI rather than on request.

```text
  Formatter          Spotless, google-java-format    style is not a review topic
  Static analysis    SpotBugs, Error Prone, Sonar     finds real defect patterns
  Coverage           JaCoCo                           a signal, not a gate
  Vulnerabilities    OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk     known CVEs in dependencies
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Have a reasoned preference between Maven and Gradle rather than a default
>   one.
> - Know the dependency scopes and how conflicts are resolved.
> - Maven resolves version conflicts by nearest definition, not highest version.
> - Commit the build wrapper so everyone builds identically.
> - FIRST describes a good unit test; asserting behaviour is what keeps tests
>   useful.
> - Coverage finds untested code and certifies nothing.
> - Mock what you do not own; prefer fakes for collaborators with behaviour.
> - Use the test pyramid in Boot and watch context caching.
> - Testcontainers exists because H2 is not your production database.
> - Quality tooling belongs in CI, not in a review comment.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find a transitive dependency conflict in a real project and resolve it
>    explicitly.
> 2. Rewrite a test that verifies a mock interaction into one asserting
>    behaviour.
> 3. Add a coverage report and find one class with high coverage and weak
>    assertions.
> 4. Add a formatter and a static analyser to a build and fix everything they
>    report.
> 5. Interview: A team has 90% coverage and frequent production defects. What
>    would you look at? (Hint: what does an executed line tell you about whether
>    anything was verified?)

<a id="196-practical-interview-skills"></a>
### 19.6 Practical Interview Skills

This subchapter is about performance rather than knowledge: how to behave when
you are being watched, how to approach the exercise formats that actually get
used, and how to talk about work you have done.

#### Live Coding and Whiteboard Technique

The most common reason candidates fail a live coding round is not missing
knowledge. It is starting to type immediately, going silent, and producing
something the interviewer cannot follow.

**What is actually being assessed:**

```text
  30%   can you decompose a problem
  25%   do you communicate while working
  20%   do you handle edge cases without prompting
  15%   is the code readable
  10%   is it optimal
```

Optimality is the smallest component and candidates optimise for it first.

**A five-step structure** that works for nearly every exercise:

```text
  1. CLARIFY     restate the problem; ask about inputs, size, and edge cases
  2. EXAMPLE     work one small case by hand, including an edge case
  3. APPROACH    describe your plan and its complexity BEFORE typing
  4. IMPLEMENT   write it, narrating as you go
  5. VERIFY      trace your example through the code; discuss improvements
```

**Step one is the one candidates skip and the one interviewers weight most**,
because ambiguity is deliberate. Good questions to ask:

```text
  What is the expected input size?          10 or 10 million changes the answer
  Can the input be null or empty?
  Are duplicates possible?
  Is the input sorted?
  Should I optimise for time or memory?
  Can I modify the input?
  What should happen on invalid input: exception, or a sentinel?
```

**Narrate your reasoning, including the false starts.** Silence is unreadable,
and an interviewer cannot give credit for thinking they cannot see.

```text
  Weak                                  Strong
  ----                                  ------
  [silence for four minutes]            "My first thought is nested loops,
  [starts typing]                        which is O(n squared). Since we only
                                         need to know whether the complement
                                         exists, a set gives O(n) with O(n)
                                         extra space. I'll do that unless memory
                                         is the constraint."
```

**Write the brute force first if you are stuck.** A working slow solution plus a
stated plan to improve it beats forty minutes of silence toward an optimal one.

```java
// "Let me get something correct first, then improve it."
public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {              // O(n^2), correct
        for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) {
            if (nums[i] + nums[j] == target) return new int[]{ i, j };
        }
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("no solution");
}

// "Now, trading space for time:"
public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();        // value -> index
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        Integer j = seen.get(target - nums[i]);          // has the complement
        if (j != null) return new int[]{ j, i };         // appeared already?
        seen.put(nums[i], i);
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("no solution");
}
```

**Handle edge cases without being asked.** Mentioning them earns credit even if
you decide not to code them.

```text
  null or empty input
  a single element
  all elements identical
  negative numbers, or zero
  integer overflow on a sum
  the maximum stated input size
```

**Write code as if it were going to be reviewed**, because it is. Meaningful
names, small methods, no single-letter variables except loop indices.

**Trace your own code before saying you are done.** Pick your example, walk
through line by line, and say the values aloud. Finding your own bug is a
positive signal; having the interviewer find it is not.

**If you are completely stuck**, say so and say what you have tried. "I'm stuck
on how to handle overlapping intervals. I've considered sorting by start time,
which gets me this far." Interviewers give hints to candidates who are visibly
working, not to silent ones.

> Key Takeaways
> - Communication and decomposition are weighted far above optimality.
> - Clarify the problem before writing anything; ambiguity is deliberate.
> - Work one example by hand, including an edge case.
> - State your approach and its complexity before typing.
> - Narrate continuously, including approaches you reject.
> - A working brute force with a stated improvement beats silent optimisation.
> - Raise edge cases unprompted.
> - Trace your own code before declaring it finished.
> - Say what you are stuck on; hints go to visibly working candidates.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Solve a problem while narrating aloud to a recording, then listen for gaps
>    of silence.
> 2. Write down eight clarifying questions for "find duplicates in a list"
>    before writing any code.
> 3. Solve one exercise brute force first, then optimise, timing yourself on
>    each.
> 4. Take a solution you wrote and list every edge case you did not handle.
> 5. Interview: Practise explaining your approach for sixty seconds before
>    touching the keyboard. (Hint: state the data structure, the complexity, and
>    the trade-off.)

#### Object-Oriented Design Exercises

A design round gives a deliberately open prompt, such as "design a parking
garage" or "design a vending machine", and lasts forty minutes. It tests whether
you can impose structure on ambiguity, which is most of senior engineering.

**A structure that fits the time:**

```text
  5 min    clarify scope and constraints; agree what is OUT of scope
  10 min   identify entities, value objects, and their relationships
  10 min   define the key interfaces and operations
  10 min   walk one scenario through your design end to end
  5 min    discuss extensions and trade-offs the interviewer raises
```
